problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1).

### Problem
If $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=n$ is such that the subset sums $\sum_{a\in S}a$ are distinct for all $S\subseteq A$ then\[N \gg 2^{n}.\]

### Context
Erdős called this 'perhaps my first serious problem' (in [Er98] he dates it to 1931). The powers of $2$ show that $2^n$ would be best possible here. The trivial lower bound is $N \gg 2^{n}/n$, since all $2^n$ distinct subset sums must lie in $[0,Nn)$. Erdős and Moser [Er56] proved\[ N\geq (\tfrac{1}{4}-o(1))\frac{2^n}{\sqrt{n}}.\](In [Er85c] Erdős offered \$100 for any improvement of the constant $1/4$ here.)

A number of improvements of the constant have been given (see [St23] for a history), with the current record $\sqrt{2/\pi}$ first proved in unpublished work of Elkies and Gleason. Two proofs achieving this constant are provided by Dubroff, Fox, and Xu [DFX21], who in fact prove the exact bound $N\geq \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #3 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/3).

### Problem
If $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}=\infty$ then must $A$ contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions?

### Context
This is essentially asking for good bounds on $r_k(N)$, the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ without a non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progression. For example, a bound like\[r_k(N) \ll_k \frac{N}{(\log N)(\log\log N)^2}\]would be sufficient.

Even the case $k=3$ is non-trivial, but was proved by Bloom and Sisask [BlSi20]. Much better bounds for $r_3(N)$ were subsequently proved by Kelley and Meka [KeMe23]. Green and Tao [GrTa17] proved $r_4(N)\ll N/(\log N)^{c}$ for some small constant $c>0$. Gowers [Go01] proved\[r_k(N) \ll \frac{N}{(\log\log N)^{c_k}},\]where $c_k>0$ is a small constant depending on $k$. The current best bounds for general $k$ are due to Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [LSS24], who show that\[r_k(N) \ll \frac{N}{\exp((\log\log N)^{c_k})}\]for some constant $c_k>0$ depending on $k$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #5 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/5).

### Problem
Let $C\geq 0$. Is there an infinite sequence of $n_i$ such that\[\lim_{i\to \infty}\frac{p_{n_i+1}-p_{n_i}}{\log n_i}=C?\]

### Context
Let $S$ be the set of limit points of $(p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log n$. This problem asks whether $S=[0,\infty]$. Although this conjecture remains unproven, a lot is known about $S$. Some highlights:- $\infty\in S$ by Westzynthius' result [We31] on large prime gaps,
- $0\in S$ by the work of Goldston, Pintz, and Yildirim [GPY09] on small prime gaps,
- Erdős [Er55] and Ricci [Ri56] independently showed that $S$ has positive Lebesgue measure,
- Hildebrand and Maier [HiMa88] showed that $S$ contains arbitrarily large (finite) numbers,
- Pintz [Pi16] showed that there exists some small constant $c>0$ such that $[0,c]\subset S$,
- Banks, Freiberg, and Maynard [BFM16] showed that at least $12.5\%$ of $[0,\infty)$ belongs to $S$,
- Merikoski [Me20] showed that at least $1/3$ of $[0,\infty)$ belongs to $S$, and that $S$ has bounded gaps.

In [Er65b], [Er85c], and [Er97c] Erdős asks whether $S$ is everywhere dense (but Weisenberg notes that clearly $S$ is closed so this is equivalent to asking whether $S=[0,\infty]$).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.title: Erdos Problem #7: Is there a distinct covering system all of whose moduli are odd?
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #7 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/7).

### Problem
Is there a distinct covering system all of whose moduli are odd?

### Context
Asked by Erdős and Selfridge (sometimes also with Schinzel). They also asked whether there can be a covering system such that all the moduli are odd and squarefree. The answer to this stronger question is no, proved by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBMST22].

Hough and Nielsen [HoNi19] proved that at least one modulus must be divisible by either $2$ or $3$. A simpler proof of this fact was provided by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBMST22], who also prove that if an odd covering system exists then the least common multiple of its moduli must be divisible by $9$ or $15$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: Here are a couple of elementary observations I would like to write down. First, a finite covering system only needs to cover almost all integers in order to cover all of them. Second, If we allow infinite covering systems, then the answer is strongly positive, since for every positive integer $k$, almost all integers are multiple of one of $p_{k+1},p_{k+2},...$, and we may use a collection of homogeneous congruences using only odd moduli.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
I wrote a brief note recording a folklore necessary condition for Erdős Problem~\#7.
If $\{a_i \bmod m_i\}_{i=1}^k$ is a distinct covering system and $L=\mathrm{lcm}(m_1,\dots,m_k)$, then\[
\sum_{\substack{d\mid L\\ d>1}} \frac{1}{d} \ge 1
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\sigma(L)\ge 2L,
\]so $L$ must be abundant.
In particular, any \emph{odd} distinct covering would require odd abundant $L$, hence $L\ge 945$
(since $945$ is the smallest odd abundant number).
This observation appears in community discussions (e.g.\ MathOverflow); my note provides a self-contained proof
and a small reproducible script listing candidate overall moduli $L$ (together with $\sigma(L)/L$) in a given range.

replies.author: DanielLarsen
replies.contentMd:
Let me just start by saying that this is a very preliminary assessment, and I am very ignorant of the literature around this problem, so everything I say should be taken with a very large grain of salt.

With that being said, while the general strategy doesn't seem crazy, it seems like the appendix is hiding all the difficulty. The key claim is that the $R$ of Hough-Nielsen is related with collision events. I don't see the explanation for that, and if that claim is false, the analysis provided falls apart. Generally, I see no particular reason to expect the distinctness of active $m_i$.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
If I understand correctly, there is a “gap” in the current Lean work in progress on this problem. The provided document attempts to prove (informally) that this gap can be filled by some existing results in literature, specifically results due to Hough-Nielsen and Shearer.

I note that this informal proof is likely generated by LLM by stylistic considerations and so exercise caution in accepting its validity.

I also note that the language used in the writeup is actively attempting to persuade the reader in a way that is not neutral. For example, the introduction states that the formalization is “close to completion”, and one literature result is explicitly stated to be “accepted in the Annals of Mathematics”.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #9 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/9).

### Problem
Let $A$ be the set of all odd integers $\geq 1$ not of the form $p+2^{k}+2^l$ (where $k,l\geq 0$ and $p$ is prime). Is the upper density of $A$ positive?

### Context
In [Er77c] Erdős credits Schinzel with proving that there are infinitely many odd integers not of this form, but gives no reference. Crocker [Cr71] has proved there are $\gg\log\log N$ such integers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Pan [Pa11] improved this to $\gg_\epsilon N^{1-\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$. Erdős believed this cannot be proved by covering systems, i.e. integers of the form $p+2^k+2^l$ exist in every infinite arithmetic progression.

The sequence of such numbers is [A006286](https://oeis.org/A006286) in the OEIS.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: The conjecture that integers of the form $p+2^k+2^l$ appear in every arithmetic progression of odd numbers, can be stated somewhat differently, as Erdos did. Let $p_{1},...,p_{n}$ be the first $n$ odd primes. Then there is  a $N(n)$ such that for all $N>N(n)$, there exist $k,l$, with $2^k+2^l<N$ and $N-2^k-2^l$ is not divisible by any of the $p_{i}$, for $i =1,...n$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #10 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/10).

### Problem
Is there some $k$ such that every large integer is the sum of a prime and at most $k$ powers of 2?

### Context
Erdős described this as 'probably unattackable'. In [ErGr80] Erdős and Graham suggest that no such $k$ exists. Gallagher [Ga75] has shown that for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $k(\epsilon)$ such that the set of integers which are the sum of a prime and at most $k(\epsilon)$ many powers of 2 has lower density at least $1-\epsilon$.

Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo98] have conjectured that at most $3$ powers of 2 suffice for all odd integers, and hence at most $4$ powers of $2$ suffice for all even integers. (The restriction to odd integers is important here - for example, Bogdan Grechuk has observed that $1117175146$ is not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$, and pointed out that parity considerations, coupled with the fact that there are many integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$ (see [[9]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/9)) suggest that there exist infinitely many even integers which are not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.title: Erdos Problem #11: Is every large odd integer $n$ the sum of a squarefree number and a power of 2?
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #11 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/11).

### Problem
Is every large odd integer $n$ the sum of a squarefree number and a power of 2?

### Context
Odlyzko has checked this up to $10^7$. Hercher [He24b] has verified this is true for all odd integers up to $2^{50}\approx 1.12\times 10^{15}$.

Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo98] have proved that this is very related to the problem of finding [Wieferich primes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wieferich_prime), which are $p$ for which $2^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod{p^2}$ - for example, if every odd integer is the sum of a squarefree number and a power of $2$ then a positive proportion of primes are non-Wieferich primes.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: soumya1729
sourceComments.contentMd:
Inspired by the recent advances, I + ChatGPT + Aristotle recently worked through this problem independently, and I wanted to leave a brief record of what came out of that exploration.

We did not obtain any new number-theoretic bounds, nor resolve the conjecture. What we did was to isolate and formalize a precise conditional reduction that seems to be implicit in earlier work (notably Granville-Soundararajan and related discussions), but not written down as a standalone statement.

Concretely, the obstruction to writing an odd integer $n$ as a squarefree number plus a power of two can be organized via the sets\[
A_p(n) := \{ k \in \mathbb{N} : 2^k \equiv n \pmod{p^2} \},
\]and one can show rigorously that, for odd $n$, each nonempty $A_p(n)$ is contained in a single residue class modulo $\operatorname{ord}_{p^2}(2)$, hence has upper asymptotic density at most $1/\operatorname{ord}_{p^2}(2)$. From this, one obtains the clean conditional implication that the conjecture holds provided\[
\sum_p \frac{1}{\operatorname{ord}_{p^2}(2)} < \infty.
\]This does not advance the arithmetic input-in particular, it does not address Wieferich primes or provide new lower bounds on multiplicative orders-but it makes explicit that no further analytic or combinatorial difficulty remains beyond this summability condition.

I am posting this simply to document the process and to clarify where the problem genuinely lies, rather than to claim novelty or priority. Very new to this field and this site, any word of advice would be greatly welcome.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
There are various links between the sum that you mention and this problem in the paper of Granville and Soundararajan.

The implication you state is not one of them, however, and I do not believe you have a proof - certainly Granville and Soundararajan could not find one. For example, even assuming that the sum is $<1$, Granville and Soundararajan are only able to prove that almost all integers $n\leq x$ can be written as the sum of a squarefree number and a power of $2$. (Assuming just the convergence of this sum, they could prove that almost all odd integers are the sum of a power of $2$ and the product of a squarefree number and a bounded powerful number.)

I assume that the implication you state was given to you by ChatGPT, which is wrongly paraphrasing the work of Granville and Soundararajan.

I suggest that you do not write this up and submit it to the arXiv, since there does not seem to be anything new or correct here. It is great that you are taking an interest in this problem, and I encourage you to continue to think about it, but until you are at the stage where you are able yourself to understand and independently verify any 'proof' that an LLM provides, it is unlikely that you have made progress on this problem.

Future comments which seem to be erroneous output from an LLM will not be shown here.

Of course, if you believe I am being unreasonably sceptical, the best way to proceed is to formalise a proof of such an implication in Lean!

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Given what Bloom said, you may want to share a draft here first. I can scrutinize whether there's some kind of misunderstanding. (Both have happened in the forum - that a result that looks good from AI turns out wrong, or turns out right.)

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
For soumya: I+[ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/697653b2-e5bc-8010-bc86-14799b69c058) mostly agrees with Bloom, in that there are links with G-S, but the conditional result seems unlikely to be easily obtainable.

In particular, your comment that there is no further combinatorial difficulty seems unlikely given G-S's identification of covering system in Theorem 5 as a key combinatorial consideration.

I've changed the wiki to "incorrect claim made". You're welcome to challenge this further e.g. if you believe it's correct and write up something I'll take a look.

But don't be discouraged! I'd still encourage any comment that you think have value, provided some checks are performed and you're reasonably confident.

replies.author: soumya1729
replies.contentMd: Thanks to both Nat and Professor Bloom for your invaluable feedback. I understand the shortcomings of the argument, will think about this further!

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #12 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/12).

### Problem
Let $A$ be an infinite set such that there are no distinct $a,b,c\in A$ such that $a\mid (b+c)$ and $b,c>a$. Is there such an $A$ with\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}>0?\]Does there exist some absolute constant $c>0$ such that there are always infinitely many $N$ with\[\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert<N^{1-c}?\]Is it true that\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}<\infty?\]

### Context
Asked by Erdős and Sárközy [ErSa70], who proved that $A$ must have density $0$. They also prove that this is essentially best possible, in that given any function $f(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$ there exists a set $A$ with this property and infinitely many $N$ such that\[\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert>\frac{N}{f(N)}.\](Their example is given by all integers in $(y_i,\frac{3}{2}y_i)$ congruent to $1$ modulo $(2y_{i-1})!$, where $y_i$ is some sufficiently quickly growing sequence.)

An example of an $A$ with this property where\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}\log N>0\]is given by the set of $p^2$, where $p\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ is prime.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #14 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/14).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$. Let $B\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be the set of integers which are representable in exactly one way as the sum of two elements from $A$.

Is it true that for all $\epsilon>0$ and large $N$\[\lvert \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash B\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}?\]Is it possible that\[\lvert \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash B\rvert =o(N^{1/2})?\]

### Context
Apparently originally considered by Erdős and Nathanson, although later Erdős attributes this to Erdős, Sárközy, and Szemerédi (but gives no reference), and claims a construction of an $A$ such that for all $\epsilon>0$ and all large $N$\[\lvert \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash B\rvert \ll_\epsilon N^{1/2+\epsilon},\]and yet there for all $\epsilon>0$ there exist infinitely many $N$ where\[\lvert \{1,\ldots,N\}\backslash B\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/3-\epsilon}.\]Erdös and Freud investigated the finite analogue in [ErFr91], proving that there exists $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that the number of integers not representable in exactly one way as the sum of two elements from $A$ is $<2^{3/2}N^{1/2}$, and suggest the constant $2^{3/2}$ is perhaps best possible.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.contentMd:
I believe the "recent Hungarian paper" is this reference: P. Erdős and R. Freud, A Sidon-problémakör (On Sidon-sequences and related problems, in Hungarian), Mat. Lapok 1991/2:1–44.  The entire volume is [available online](https://real-j.mtak.hu/9391/1/MTA_MatematikaiLapok_1991.pdf).

The claim appears at the top of page 34 (page 90 of 222 of the PDF):
"4.3.5. Utolsónak egy véges sorozatokról szóló kérdést említünk, amely az egyértel műen előálló számok arányára vonatkozik:
Maximálisan hány olyan szám lehet n-ig, amely egyértelműen áll elő a sorozat két tagjának összegeként?
Könnyű konstruálni olyan sorozatot, ahol a kivételek száma $2^{3/2}n^{1/2}$, és va lószínűleg ez (közel) optimális, azonban ilyen irányban szinte semmi sem ismeretes. Még a fentinél jóval nagyobb elemszámú sorozatokra sem tudjuk igazolni, hogy a kivételek száma legalább ekkora nagyságrendű kell hogy legyen."

"4.3.5. Finally, we mention a question about finite sequences, which concerns the proportion of numbers that occur uniquely:
What is the maximum number of numbers up to n that occur uniquely as the sum of two terms in the sequence?
It is easy to construct a sequence where the number of exceptions is $2^{3/2}n^{1/2}$, and this is probably (nearly) optimal, but almost nothing is known in this direction. Even for sequences with a much larger number of elements than the above, we cannot prove that the number of exceptions must be at least of this order of magnitude."

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #15 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/15).

### Problem
Is it true that\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^n\frac{n}{p_n}\]converges, where $p_n$ is the sequence of primes?

### Context
Erdős suggested that a computer could be used to explore this, and did not see any other method to attack this.

Tao [Ta23] has proved that this series does converge assuming a strong form of the Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture.

sourceMetadata.statusNote: This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
researchNotes: Erdős suggested that a computer could be used to explore this, and did not see any other method to attack this.
Tao [Ta23] has proved that this series does converge assuming a strong form of the Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture.

In [Er98] Erdős further conjectures that\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{1}{n(p_{n+1}-p_n)}converges and\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{1}{p_{n+1}-p_n}diverges. Weisenberg notes that the existence of infinitely many bounded gaps between primes (as proved by Zhang [Zh14]) implies the latter series does not converge. Weisenberg also has an argument which shows that, assuming the Hardy-Littlewood prime $k$-tuples conjecture, the series is unbounded in at least one direction (positive or negative).

Erdős further conjectured that\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{1}{n(p_{n+1}-p_n)(\log\log n)^c}converges for every $c>0$, and reports that he and Nathanson can prove that this series converges absolutely for $c>2$ (and can show, conditional on 'hopeless' conjectures about the primes, that this sum does not converge absolutely for $c=2$).

Sawhney has provided the following proof that this series converges absolutely for $c>2$: note that, whenever $c>1$, the contribution to the sum from gaps $p_{n+1}-p_n\geq \log n$ is convergent, so it suffices to consider only small gaps. The number of $n\leq X$ such that $p_{n+1}-p_n\in [\epsilon\log n,2\epsilon \log n)$ is bounded above by $\ll \epsilon X$ (this can be proved via the Selberg sieve). In particular, applying this bound for $\frac{1}{\log n}\leq \epsilon \leq 1$ of the shape $2^{-j}$ (of which there are at most $\log\log n$ possibilities) shows the desired convergence, since\sum \frac{1}{n(\log n)(\log\log n)^{c-1}}converges.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
Remarks and slight improvements on Tao's results [Ta23]. Let $f(n):=(-1)^{\pi(n)}$ and $F(x):=\sum_{n\le x}f(n)$.  Tao (following an observation of Said) records the equivalence\[
\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^n\frac{n}{p_n}\ \text{converges}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{(-1)^{\pi(n)}}{n\log n}
=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{f(n)}{n\log n}\ \text{converges}.
\]By partial summation with $g(x)=1/(x\log x)$,\[
\sum_{n\le X}\frac{f(n)}{n\log n}
=F(X)g(X)-F(2)g(2)+\int_2^X F(t)\,(-g'(t))\,dt,
\qquad -g'(t)\asymp \frac{1}{t^2\log t},
\]so a minimal analytic sufficient condition is the existence of $\varepsilon>0$ with\[
F(x)=O\!\left(\frac{x}{(\log x)^{\varepsilon}}\right),
\]since then $\int_2^\infty \frac{dt}{t(\log t)^{1+\varepsilon}}<\infty$ and the boundary term $F(X)/(X\log X)\to0$; hence Erdős' series converges.

A natural intermediate conjecture that targets exactly such a bound (and is weaker in spirit than full Hardy--Littlewood for all patterns) is parity mixing in short intervals: there exist functions $\lambda=\lambda(X)\to\infty$ and some $\delta>0$ such that, with $\Delta_\lambda(x):=\pi(x+\lambda\log x)-\pi(x)$,\[
\mathbb{E}_{x\in[X,2X]}\,(-1)^{\Delta_\lambda(x)}\ \ll\ (\log X)^{-\delta}.
\]This is a single Fourier-coefficient estimate for the distribution of prime counts in $(x,x+\lambda\log x]$; it asserts that the parity of $\Delta_\lambda(x)$ is asymptotically unbiased on average.  Combined with the same van der Corput/Weyl-differencing framework used by Tao, such a decay of $\mathbb{E}(-1)^{\Delta_\lambda(x)}$ at some slowly growing $\lambda(X)$ is designed to force cancellation in $f(n)=(-1)^{\pi(n)}$, plausibly yielding the needed logarithmic power saving $F(x)\ll x(\log x)^{-\varepsilon}$ and hence convergence.

A second, more distributional intermediate target is an anti-concentration / local limit statement for $\Delta_\lambda(x)$: for some $\lambda=\lambda(X)\to\infty$ and some $\eta>0$,\[
\sup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\ \textrm{Prob} _{x\in[X,2X]}\bigl(\Delta_\lambda(x)=k\bigr)\ \ll\ \lambda^{-\eta}
\quad\text{or even}\quad
\|L(\Delta_\lambda)-\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to 0.
\]Either form rules out concentration on one parity and typically implies parity mixing (for Poisson$(\lambda)$ one has $\mathbb{E}[(-1)^{\Delta}]=e^{-2\lambda}$).  Thus, proving any averaged local limit theorem (or even robust anti-concentration) for prime counts in length $\lambda\log x$ intervals would give a direct path to the analytic bound on $F(x)$ above, potentially avoiding the need for full high-order Hardy--Littlewood uniformity; Tao’s conditional proof obtains the requisite parity mixing via strong $k$-tuple input, so any alternative route to anti-concentration here would be genuinely new input toward the Erdős convergence problem.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #17 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/17).

### Problem
Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that every even number $n\leq p-3$ can be written as a difference of primes $n=q_1-q_2$ where $q_1,q_2\leq p$?

### Context
The first prime without this property is $97$. The sequence of such primes is [A038133](https://oeis.org/A038133) in the OEIS. These are called cluster primes.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #18 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/18).

### Problem
We call $m$ practical if every integer $1\leq n<m$ is the sum of distinct divisors of $m$. If $m$ is practical then let $h(m)$  be such that $h(m)$ many divisors always suffice.

Are there infinitely many practical $m$ such that\[h(m) < (\log\log m)^{O(1)}?\]Is it true that $h(n!)<n^{o(1)}$? Or perhaps even $h(n!)<(\log n)^{O(1)}$?

### Context
It is easy to see that almost all numbers are not practical. Erdős originally showed that $h(n!) <n$. Vose [Vo85] proved the existence of infinitely many practical $m$ such that $h(m)\ll (\log m)^{1/2}$.

The sequence of practical numbers is [A005153](https://oeis.org/A005153) in the OEIS.

sourceComments.contentMd: When formalizing, The Formal Conjectures Authors noticed an issue that needs to be documented: The original description is ambigous in that it doesn't clarify whether the same subset should be applied to all numbers < n! . However, it only makes sense if for every $m\lt n!$ a new subset is taken.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
You are indeed allowed to use all divisors of $n!$. So to fully spell out the second question: does there, for every $\epsilon > 0$, exist an $n_0$ such that for every $n \ge n_0$ and for every $m < n!$ there is a set $S_{m,n}$ such that

1) For all $i \in S_{m,n}$ we have that $i$ divides $n!$.
2) The sum $\sum_{i \in S_{m,n}} i$ is equal to $m$.
3) The size $|S_{m,n}|$ is smaller than $n^{\epsilon}$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: I think it's actually a little unclear - he just writes 'for a proof or disproof of'\[h(n) < (\log\log n)^{O(1)},\]which makes no sense as written without further quantifiers. Based on the context I think he meant this to be about $h(n!)$ (and then $\log\log n$ should become $\log n$) and this was just a typo.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
It's true that 'for a proof or disproof of $h(n) < (\log \log n)^C$' makes no sense without quantifiers, but the words before this inequality are 'for infinitely many $n$'. So I read this as 'for a proof or disproof of [the existence of infinitely many $n$ with] $h(n) < (\log \log n)^C$'. I therefore do not think it's about $h(n!)$ specifically.

Edit 3-2-2026: reading it again, I agree with Dogmachine and my past self, so I pressed the update button. Somewhat amusingly, as Erdős defined $h(n) = 0$ in [[Er81h]](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-33.pdf) if $n$ is not practical, the inequality $h(n) < (\log \log n)^C$ trivially holds for infinitely many $n$. But I'm afraid I don't get to claim \$250 quite this easily.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #20 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/20).

### Problem
Let $f(n,k)$ be minimal such that every family  $\mathcal{F}$  of $n$-uniform sets with $\lvert  \mathcal{F}\rvert \geq f(n,k)$ contains a $k$-sunflower. Is it true that\[f(n,k) < c_k^n\]for some constant $c_k>0$?

### Context
Erdős and Rado [ErRa60] originally proved $f(n,k)\leq (k-1)^nn!$. Kostochka [Ko97] improved this slightly (in particular establishing an upper bound of $o(n!)$, for which Erdős awarded him the consolation prize of \$100), but the bound stood at $n^{(1+o(1))n}$ for a long time until Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang [ALWZ20] proved\[f(n,k) < (Ck\log n\log\log n)^n\]for some constant $C>1$. This was refined slightly, independently by Rao [Ra20], Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan, and Park [FKNP19], and Bell, Chueluecha, and Warnke [BCW21], leading to the current record of\[f(n,k) < (Ck\log n)^n\]for some constant $C>1$. This proof was streamlined [by Hu](https://theorydish.blog/2021/05/19/entropy-estimation-via-two-chains-streamlining-the-proof-of-the-sunflower-lemma/). A constant of $C=64$ was achieved in the presentation [by Stoeckl](https://mstoeckl.com/notes/research/sunflower_notes.html).

In [Er81] Erdős offered \$1000 for a proof or disproof even just in the special case when $k=3$, which he expected 'contains the whole difficulty'. He also wrote 'I really do not see why this question is so difficult'.

Kostochka [Ko97] improved this slightly (in particular establishing an upper bound of $o(n!)$, for which Erdős awarded him the consolation prize of \$100), but the bound stood at $n^{(1+o(1))n}$ for a long time until Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang [ALWZ20] provedf(n,k) < (Ck\log n\log\log n)^nfor some constant $C>1$. This was refined slightly, independently by Rao [Ra20], Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan, and Park [FKNP19], and Bell, Chueluecha, and Warnke [BCW21], leading to the current record off(n,k) < (Ck\log n)^nfor some constant $C>1$. This proof was streamlined by Hu. A constant of $C=64$ was achieved in the presentation by Stoeckl.

In [Er81] Erdős offered \$1000 for a proof or disproof even just in the special case when $k=3$, which he expected 'contains the whole difficulty'. He also wrote 'I really do not see why this question is so difficult'.
The usual focus is on the regime where $k=O(1)$ is fixed (say $k=3$) and $n$ is large, although for the opposite regime Kostochka, Rödl, and Talysheva [KRT99] have shownf(n,k)=(1+O_n(k^{-1/2^n}))k^n.

sourceComments.contentMd:
While working on Problem #857 I found the infrastructure also covers the uniform setting. Base cases f(1,3)=2 through f(6,3)=19 are formally certified in Lean 4. The conjecture statement ErdosProblem20 is formally defined. The general bound remains open.

Repo: https://github.com/SproutSeeds/sunflower-lean

*EDIT*

@Terrance Tao

Thank you for asking, happy to disclose fully.

The development was built collaboratively using intelligence systems, primarily OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.2, extra-high reasoning effort) via the Codex CLI, and Anthropic Claude (Opus 4.5 and 4.6) via the Claude CLI. When Codex 5.3 and Claude Opus 4.6 released on the same day, I migrated to both gradually over the following 24-48 hours and continued the work on the newer models.

Regarding the Aristotle references you noticed: early in the project I made one call to Aristotle to understand generally how it would lay out a Lean formalization. After seeing the general format, I took that as a starting point for the example files and then built everything else using Codex and Claude instead of the Aristotle API. The Aristotle files in the repo are those initial examples and nothing more. All substantive development was done with Codex and Claude.

Codex and Claude are web services and the models themselves are opaque. What was not opaque was the process around them. I operated a structured orchestration process manually throughout, with explicit theorem targets, explicit acceptance criteria, and explicit rollback on failure. All building and verification was done locally, running 'lake build' on my own machine rather than relying on any cloud-based verification service. This kept the iteration loop tight: generate a proof attempt, build locally, accept or reject within seconds, move to the next target. That local feedback cycle was a significant part of what made the monotonic discipline practical to enforce in real time.

The discovery process itself was also collaborative. Rather than arriving at theorem targets in isolation, I worked with the intelligence systems in an exploratory research mode first: discussing the mathematical landscape, identifying which lemmas were likely load-bearing, and understanding what the proof tree needed structurally before any Lean was written. The intelligence system would surface candidate directions, and I would evaluate them by asking more questions, to other intelligence systems and to myself. I am not separate from this process. I think of myself as a question-asking machine that happens to have good intelligence systems around it, always absorbing, always narrowing. The evaluation was not me sitting apart from the system doing mathematics independently. It was me as part of the system, using questions as the mechanism for narrowing toward a target. This adaptive layer is what guided the sequencing of proof passes. It did not generate results blindly. It nudged the direction of exploration based on what was already proved, what gaps remained, and what the most tractable next step looked like given the current state of the development.

The core discipline was a monotonic sorry-free machine: every commit was only accepted if 'lake build' passed with zero sorries. If a proof attempt introduced a sorry, the commit was rejected and rolled back. This meant the proof tree could only grow and never regress. No sorry was ever allowed to persist across a commit boundary.

The process worked like this: I would give the intelligence system a specific theorem target, it would produce a proof attempt, I would run the Lean kernel to verify it, and only accept it if it compiled sorry-free. The Lean kernel itself is completely independent of any intelligence system. It is the ground truth. The intelligence system generated candidates; the kernel decided validity. This separation was intentional and is the reason I trust the results.

I chose Lean specifically as the backbone to keep my system honest.

Over time the manual orchestration process evolved into a full automated orchestration system, a multi-agent proof search engine with persistent sessions, a theorem ledger, and the same monotonic sorry-free discipline enforced automatically. That system is now built and could push this work significantly further. The current bottleneck is purely compute. Token costs through the Claude and Codex APIs limit how much I can afford to run it.

The SAT+LRAT certificates for M(5,3), M(6,3), and M(7,3) are fully reproducible independently. The LRAT files are in the repo and can be re-checked by any independent LRAT verifier without any involvement from an intelligence system.

I am glad to add a disclosure statement to the repo README.

sourceComments.author: Rynaldo Stoltz
sourceComments.contentMd:
ALWZ, Rao, and Stoeckl successfully proved the upper bound limitation of $f(n,k) < (C_k \log n)^n$. However, as observed by Stoeckl (2022), their entropic mathematics are fundamentally reliant on creating $R$-spread randomized subsets using iterative regularization loops.

The lingering open question has been whether the $\log n$ penalty is an inherent physical constant of maximal sunflower-free structures, or merely a byproduct of this spreadness-forcing regularization.

Our new computational data strongly points to the latter. Focusing strictly on the Erdős $k=3$ regime, we bypassed spreadness-regularization entirely. We designed a bitmask-accelerated Simulated Annealing solver to construct deterministic, maximally dense $k=3$ sunflower-free families for dimensions $n \in \{3,4,5,6\}$. Rather than theoretically forcing spreadness to satisfy entropy inequalities, we computationally extracted the true empirical $\kappa$-spreadness thresholds directly from these physically optimal constructions.

The data reveals a stark decoupling from the theoretical limits. As $n$ increases, the required normalized spreadness constant $C = \frac{\kappa}{\log_2 n}$ to avoid forming a 3-sunflower is strictly decaying ($2.44 \to 1.99 \to 1.23 \to 0.96$). The log n factor appears artificial.

Evidence suggests f(n,3) < Cⁿ with C ≈ 2-3, potentially eliminating the logarithmic factor entirely.

If the logarithmic penalty was physically required to build dense extremal families, the required $\kappa$ threshold would scale linearly alongside $\log n$. It decidedly does not. This topological structural decay isolates the $\log n$ parameter directly to the regularization loops used in current Sieve methodology, verifying that the current $(C \log n)^n$ bounds are mathematically artificial limits.

This exact computational data provides robust experimental validity to Erdős’s original instinct: the true maximal limit behaves squarely as $C^n$.

Mr. @TerenceTao We respectfully request your expert verification of:

1. Whether our f(4,3) ≥ 36 and f(5,3) ≥ 60 constructions represent legitimate improvements to known bounds.

2. If our spreadness decay evidence provides sufficient reason to reconsider the log n factor in theoretical descriptions.

3. Whether these computational results, if verified, warrant updating Erdős Problem #20

Our deterministic arrays, the combinatorial SA engine, and the exact mathematical spreadness metrics are open-sourced for peer evaluation here:[https://github.com/rynald0cst0ltziam/erdos-sunflower-decay](https://github.com/rynald0cst0ltziam/erdos-sunflower-decay) and our manuscript here [https://github.com/rynald0cst0ltziam/erdos-sunflower-decay/blob/main/MANUSCRIPT.md](https://github.com/rynald0cst0ltziam/erdos-sunflower-decay/blob/main/MANUSCRIPT.md)

sourceComments.author: Rene
sourceComments.contentMd: For context, existing lower bounds for fixed k, in particular k = 3, already grow like cⁿ for some c > 1, so a bound of the form f(n,k) ≤ (cₖ)ⁿ would not contradict known constructions. What still seems genuinely open is whether the current (log n)ⁿ overhead in the best upper bounds is inherent or just an artifact of the iterative regularization used to force spreadness. In the ALWZ framework and its refinements, the log n appears to come from repeatedly restricting the family until it becomes spread, rather than from the sunflower-extraction step itself. It would be very interesting to know whether the “popular witness” certifying non-spreadness can be exploited directly to build a sunflower, bypassing the regularization loop altogether. If there are post-ALWZ references, even in special classes of n-uniform families, that achieve a true (cₖ)ⁿ bound or that explain why such a bound cannot follow from spreadness-based methods alone, I would be grateful for pointers.

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
Lunjia Hu ([here](https://web.archive.org/web/20220502190641/https://theorydish.blog/2021/05/19/entropy-estimation-via-two-chains-streamlining-the-proof-of-the-sunflower-lemma/)) improved the position of $C$ given in the current best bound of [BCW21], though slightly.

Manuel Stoeckl ([here](https://mstoeckl.com/notes/research/sunflower_notes.html)) further refined the constant and gave this result:

There exists a universal constant $C≤64$, so that for any $r≥1$, $k≥2$, every set system containing $≥(Cr \log k)^k$ sets of size $≤k$ contains an r-petaled sunflower.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #23 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/23).

### Problem
Can every triangle-free graph on $5n$ vertices be made bipartite by deleting at most $n^2$ edges?

### Context
The blow-up of $C_5$ shows that this would be the best possible. The best known bound is due to Balogh, Clemen, and Lidicky [BCL21], who proved that deleting at most $1.064n^2$ edges suffices.

In [Er92b] Erdős asks, more generally, if a graph on $(2k+1)n$ vertices in which every odd cycle has size $\geq 2k+1$ can be made bipartite by deleting at most $n^2$ edges.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.contentMd: the version for general $k$ is false for small $n$ (i.e., if $n=1$, then one can consider a clique on $2k$ vertices plus an isolated vertex; and for $k\ge 2$ you must delete $>1$ edges).

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Zach, you will have to read the question again.
All odd cycles have to be large.
The clique has the opposite condition that all odd cycles are small.

So the statement is true for $n=1$, since a graph on $r=2k+1$ vertices whose odd cycles has size $r$ is either bipartite, or $C_r$ (adding a chord results in a smaller odd cycle).

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
I just want to check my understanding here: it seems to me that the hypothesis "all but finitely many" can be changed to "all"?

That's because if $A+A$ contains all but finitely many [non-negative] integers, it seems we can enlarge $A$ by finitely many terms so that $A+A$ now contains literally all [non-negative] integers and in doing so we don't change whether $\limsup 1_A * 1_A(n)$ is finite.  I was wondering whether someone could confirm this simple reasoning, because I feel that the modified conjecture sounds better.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
Partially, yes. If we allow $0 \in A$ (as otherwise $1$ is not representable), then the conjectures are indeed equivalent. But to me the modified conjecture does not sound better, to be honest. When considering additive bases (e.g. Waring's problem or Goldbach's conjecture) one generally only cares about being able to represent large enough integers. Perhaps because of that, the assumption $\mathbb{N} \subseteq A + A$ feels at first glance unusually strong to me, weakening the (perceived) strength of the conjecture. Even though, as you note, they are actually equivalent. But as so often in maths; there's many ways to prove or state a result, and it sometimes just comes down to personal preference :)

By the way, in this regard it is interesting to note that for the Erdős and Sárközy conjecture (Edit: which has since been moved to [#1145](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1145)) the equality $A + B = \mathbb{N}$ is written.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
Thanks.  In applications, and just as a mathematical statement, I definitely see the naturality of the sufficiently large assumption, but isolated by itself, I like the version without it.  Nonetheless, it's notable that Goldbach's original conjecture was "*Every* positive even integer can be written as the sum of two primes", by including $1$ as a prime.  And with Waring's problem, there are two versions: (following Wikipedia's notation) representing all integers is $g(k)$ while only sufficiently sufficiently large is $G(k)$.  And we literally know only 3 total values of $G(k)$, as compared with $g(k)$ where it's known for almost all $k$!

Re 0: maybe this page https://www.erdosproblems.com/definitions should specify whether $0\in\mathbb{N}$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
I'd rather leave it ambiguous whether $0\in \mathbb{N}$ - sometimes this makes sense, sometimes not. I think it's almost always obvious from the context whether $0$ is included or not (e.g. whether the statement is trivially true or false at $0$).

If anyone knows of any places on this site where it actually makes a non-trivial difference I'd be interested to know.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #30 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/30).

### Problem
Let $h(N)$ be the maximum size of a Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[h(N) = N^{1/2}+O_\epsilon(N^\epsilon)?\]

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Turán. It may even be true that $h(N)=N^{1/2}+O(1)$, but Erdős remarks this is perhaps too optimistic. Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] proved an upper bound of $N^{1/2}+O(N^{1/4})$, with an alternative proof by Lindström [Li69]. Both proofs in fact give\[h(N) \leq N^{1/2}+N^{1/4}+1.\]Balogh, Füredi, and Roy [BFR21] improved the bound in the error term to $0.998N^{1/4}$. This was further optimised by O'Bryant [OB22]. The current record is\[h(N)\leq N^{1/2}+0.98183N^{1/4}+O(1),\]due to Carter, Hunter, and O'Bryant [CHO25].

Singer [Si38] was the first to show that $h(N)\geq (1-o(1))N^{1/2}$ for all $N$. For a detailed survey of the literature we refer to [OB04].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] proved an upper bound of $N^{1/2}+O(N^{1/4})$, with an alternative proof by Lindström [Li69]. Both proofs in fact giveh(N) \leq N^{1/2}+N^{1/4}+1.Balogh, Füredi, and Roy [BFR21] improved the bound in the error term to $0.998N^{1/4}$. This was further optimised by O'Bryant [OB22]. The current record ish(N)\leq N^{1/2}+0.98183N^{1/4}+O(1),due to Carter, Hunter, and O'Bryant [CHO25].
Singer [Si38] was the first to show that $h(N)\geq (1-o(1))N^{1/2}$ for all $N$. For a detailed survey of the literature we refer to [OB04].
See also [[241]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/241) and [[840]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/840).
This problem is Problem 31 on Green's open problems list.
This is discussed in problem C9 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

sourceComments.author: Rynaldo Stoltz
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have been experimenting with computational approaches to Erdős Problem #30 (Sidon constant bounds) and recently attempted to improve the best known constant. Our current certified candidate gives:

h(N) ≤ N^{1/2} + 0.98173 N^{1/4} + O(1),

which slightly improves the previous record (C = 0.98183).

I put together an open search + certification pipeline, and all code, data, and certificate bundles are available here 👉 https://github.com/rynald0cst0ltziam/Erdos-Sidon-Records-30

Feedback, independent verification, and discussion are very welcome.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Just a heads up that I am working with a group (Carter, Georgiev, Gomez–Serrano, Hunter, O’Bryant, Wagner) to improve the constant further.  We were able to get 0.97633 in an [unpublished work](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2025/11/05/mathematical-exploration-and-discovery-at-scale/#comment-689052) by optimizing the [CHO25] argument using AlphaEvolve, but have since found a more efficient argument that gives better bounds (tentatively 0.947, subject to confirmation).  Details will hopefully appear soon.

sourceComments.contentMd: The optimal $N^{1/4}$ coefficient in the upper bound for $h(N)$ is [now recorded as $C_5$ in the optimization problems repository](https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/5a.html).

sourceComments.author: Sayan Dutta
sourceComments.contentMd:
The initial upper bound of $N^{1/2} + N^{1/4} + 1$ (which stood for about half a century) was not only proven by Erdős-Turán and Lindström. The exact same bound was also arrived at in three more ways by Ruzsa, Graham and Cilleruelo. I wrote about them in details in [this blog post](https://sayandutta314159.blogspot.com/2024/12/four-proofs-of-theorem.html).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #32 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/32).

### Problem
Is there a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ such that\[\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert = o((\log N)^2)\]and such that every large integer can be written as $p+a$ for some prime $p$ and $a\in A$?

Can the bound $O(\log N)$ be achieved? Must such an $A$ satisfy\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{\log N}> 1?\]

### Context
Such a set is called an additive complement to the primes.

Erdős [Er54] proved that such a set $A$ exists with $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\ll (\log N)^2$ (improving a previous result of Lorentz [Lo54] who achieved $\ll (\log N)^3$).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Such a set is called an additive complement to the primes.
Erdős [Er54] proved that such a set $A$ exists with $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\ll (\log N)^2$ (improving a previous result of Lorentz [Lo54] who achieved $\ll (\log N)^3$).

Wolke [Wo96] has shown that such a bound is almost true, in that we can achieve $\ll (\log N)^{1+o(1)}$ if we only ask for almost all integers to be representable. Kolountzakis [Ko96] improved this to $\ll (\log N)(\log\log N)$, and Ruzsa [Ru98c] further improved this to $\ll \omega(N)\log N$ for any $\omega\to \infty$.

The answer to the third question is yes: Ruzsa [Ru98c] has shown that we must have\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{\log N}\geq e^\gamma\approx 1.781.This is discussed in problem E1 of Guy's collection [Gu04], where it is stated that Erdős offered \$50 for determining whether $O(\log N)$ can be achieved.

sourceComments.author: msellke
sourceComments.contentMd:
For the "almost all integers" case of the problem, the mentioned result of [Wo96] has been improved. Kolountzakis (On the additive complements of the primes and sets of similar growth; Acta Arith. 77 (1996), 1–8) showed an upper bound $O(\log(x)\log\log(x))$. A further improvement is in the paper [Ru98c] of Ruzsa mentioned already: Theorem 1 shows that one can achieve $O(\omega(x)\log x)$ for any function $\omega$ that diverges as $x\to\infty$.

Additionally, although Ruzsa confirms the third question, he notes that it remains unclear in the "almost all integers" setting, and leaves a few versions of this as conjectures.

(The reference was located by GPT-5.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #33 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/33).

### Problem
Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be such that every large integer can be written as $n^2+a$ for some $a\in A$ and $n\geq 0$. What is the smallest possible value of\[\limsup \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}?\]Is\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}>1?\]

### Context
Such a set $A$ is called an additive complement of the set of squares. Erdős observed that there exist $A$ for which the $\limsup$ is finite and $>1$. Moser [Mo65] proved that, for any such $A$,\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}>1.06.\]The best-known lower bound is\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}\geq\frac{4}{\pi}\approx 1.273\]proved by Cilleruelo [Ci93], Habsieger [Ha95], and Balasubramanian and Ramana [BaRa01].

The problem of minimising the $\limsup$ appears to have been much less studied. van Doorn has [a construction](https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/The%20smallest%20set%20such%20that%20every%20positive%20integer%20is%20the%20sum%20of%20a%20square%20and%20an%20element%20from%20this%20set.pdf) of such an $A$ in which, for all $N$,\[\frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}< 2\phi^{5/2}\approx 6.66,\]where $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ is the golden ratio.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

The smallest possible value of $\limsup \frac{\left|A \cap \{1, 2, \ldots, N \} \right|}{N^{1/2}}$ is at most $2 \varphi^{5/2} \approx 6.66$, with $\varphi$ equal to the golden ratio. I have uploaded a proof [here](https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/The%20smallest%20set%20such%20that%20every%20positive%20integer%20is%20the%20sum%20of%20a%20square%20and%20an%20element%20from%20this%20set.pdf).

replies.contentMd:
Nice, thanks!

Looking into this problem again I discovered that there's a fair amount of literature into the $\liminf$ question (which I had unfairly overlooked initially, but have added here now). Surprisingly none of these papers appear to investigate the $\limsup$, but I haven't looked through them all in detail yet.

replies.author: Sayan Dutta
replies.contentMd:
This method generalises to additive complement of $k$-th powers in the following way (assuming my calculations were correct).

Define
$$C_k(r):=\frac{k\,r^{1-\frac 1k}(r-1)^{1-\frac 1k}}{r^{1-\frac 1k}-1}$$
for a given $k$, and a parameter $r$. Then, there exists an additive complement of $k$-th powers, $A_k$ for which
$$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A_k(x)}{x^{1-\frac 1k}} \,\le\, \inf_{r>1} C_k(r)$$
and it isn't hard to see that $C_k(r)$ minimises at $r=\rho_k^k$ where $\rho_k$ is the unique root of $x^{2k-1}-2x^k+1=0$ greater than $1$. For $k=3,4,5$, the RHS is approximately $7.93$, $9.02$ and $10.08$ respectively.

Needless to say, $C_2(\phi^2)=2\phi^{5/2}$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #36 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/36).

### Problem
Find the optimal constant $c>0$ such that the following holds.

For all sufficiently large $N$, if $A\sqcup B=\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ is a partition into two equal parts, so that $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert=N$, then there is some $x$ such that the number of solutions to $a-b=x$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ is at least $cN$.

### Context
The [minimum overlap problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_overlap_problem). The example (with $N$ even) $A=\{N/2+1,\ldots,3N/2\}$ shows that $c\leq 1/2$ (indeed, Erdős initially conjectured that $c=1/2$). The lower bound of $c\geq 1/4$ is trivial, and Scherk improved this to $1-1/\sqrt{2}=0.29\cdots$. The current records are\[0.379005 < c < 0.380876,\]the lower bound due to White [Wh22] and the upper bound due to the TTT-Discover LLM [YKLBMWKCZGS26], improving slightly on earlier bounds due to AlphaEvolve [GGTW25] and Haugland [Ha16].

This is discussed in problem C17 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #38 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/38).

### Problem
Does there exist $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ which is not an additive basis, but is such that for every set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ of Schnirelmann density $\alpha$ and every $N$ there exists $b\in B$ such that\[\lvert (A\cup (A+b))\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\geq (\alpha+f(\alpha))N\]where $f(\alpha)>0$ for $0<\alpha <1 $?

The Schnirelmann density is defined by\[d_s(A) = \inf_{N\geq 1}\frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N}.\]

### Context
Erdős [Er36c] proved that if $B$ is an additive basis of order $k$ then, for any set $A$ of Schnirelmann density $\alpha$, for every $N$ there exists some integer $b\in B$ such that\[\lvert (A\cup (A+b))\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\geq \left(\alpha+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2k}\right)N.\]It seems an interesting question (not one that Erdős appears to have asked directly, although see [[35]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/35)) to improve the lower bound here, even in the case $B=\mathbb{N}$. Erdős observed that a random set of density $\alpha$ shows that the factor of $\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2}$ in this case cannot be improved past $\alpha(1-\alpha)$.

This is a stronger property than $B$ being an essential component (see [[37]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/37)). Linnik [Li42] gave the first construction of an essential component which is not an additive basis.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Erdős [Er36c] proved that if $B$ is an additive basis of order $k$ then, for any set $A$ of Schnirelmann density $\alpha$, for every $N$ there exists some integer $b\in B$ such that\lvert (A\cup (A+b))\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\geq \left(\alpha+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2k}\right)N.It seems an interesting question (not one that Erdős appears to have asked directly, although see [[35]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/35)) to improve the lower bound here, even in the case $B=\mathbb{N}$. Erdős observed that a random set of density $\alpha$ shows that the factor of $\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{2}$ in this case cannot be improved past $\alpha(1-\alpha)$.

This is a stronger property than $B$ being an essential component (see [[37]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/37)). Linnik [Li42] gave the first construction of an essential component which is not an additive basis.

sourceComments.contentMd:
E. Landau has showed in [La37] that the order $k$ can be replaced by mean order $\lambda$.
A. Brauer in [[Br38]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01210651) has improved this inequality to:\[|(A∪(A+b))∩{1,…,N}|≥ α\{1+(1-α^{1/2})\lambda\}N\]S. Selberg in [Se44] has improved this to:\[|(A∪(A+b))∩{1,…,N}|≥ \alpha\{1+3(1-\alpha)/4\lambda\}\]Selberg's result is better for $\alpha > 1/9$ and Brauer's result for $\alpha < 1/9$.
For the case $1/9 \leq \alpha \leq 1/2$, the results have been improved by A. Brauer in [[Br55]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01187959).

[La37]: Über einige neuere Fortschritte der additiven Zahlentheorie, Cambridge, 19
[Se44]: S. Selberg, Note on a metrical problem in the additive theory of numbers. Arch. Math. Naturvidensk.47, 111–118 (1944).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #39 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/39).

### Problem
Is there an infinite Sidon set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that\[\lvert A\cap \{1\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}\]for all $\epsilon>0$?

### Context
The trivial greedy construction achieves $\gg N^{1/3}$. The first improvement on this was achieved by Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AKS81b], who found an infinite Sidon set with growth rate $\gg (N\log N)^{1/3}$. The current best bound of $\gg N^{\sqrt{2}-1+o(1)}$ is due to Ruzsa [Ru98].

Erdős [Er73] had offered \$25 for any construction which achieves $N^{c}$ for some $c>1/3$. Later he [Er77c] offered \$100 for a construction which achieves $\omega(N)N^{1/3}$ for some $\omega(N)\to \infty$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #41 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/41).

### Problem
Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set such that the triple sums $a+b+c$ are all distinct for $a,b,c\in A$ (aside from the trivial coincidences). Is it true that\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/3}}=0?\]

### Context
Erdős proved that if the pairwise sums $a+b$ are all distinct aside from the trivial coincidences then\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}=0.\]This is discussed in problem C11 of Guy's collection [Gu04], in which Guy says Erdős offered \$500 for the general problem of whether, for all $h\geq 2$,\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/h}}=0\]whenever the sum of $h$ terms in $A$ are distinct. This was proved for $h=4$ by Nash [Na89] and for all even $h$ by Chen [Ch96b].

I'm not sure if this is necessary, but I saw that some other problems have notes about trivial cases for clarity, so I'd like to comment here about $M = 1$ and $M = 2$. If it's not important, feel free to delete this comment!

For $M = 1$:
Take any $b \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ and set $B = \{b\}$. A singleton is Sidon, and\[
B - B = \{b - b\} = \{0\}.
\]For any nonempty $A$, we have $0 \in A - A$, so\[
(A - A) \cap (B - B) = (A - A) \cap \{0\} = \{0\}.
\]For $M = 2$:
This is also fairly intuitive, but the full proof is longer than I'd want for this comment, so I'll instead link a [ChatGPT thread](https://chatgpt.com/share/69720fff-7c18-8006-9ec2-663382e0e335).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: BrittB
sourceComments.contentMd:
Fascinating formalization for the M=3 case! This aligns perfectly with the empirical data I published on Zenodo last week (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18225902).

My computational verification focused on the harder general cases of n=4, 5, and 6, running simulations up to N=100,000. We found that while M=3 works, phase transitions and "Gap Geography" play a significant role in the asymptotes for n >= 4. Our data suggests the "Square Root Law" governs the gap distribution in these higher regimes.

It is excellent to see a formal proof for the base case that supports the general heuristic I proposed.

sourceComments.author: Daniil Sedov
sourceComments.contentMd:
$\textbf{Result}$

I published a Lean 4 formalization of a positive answer to the $M=3$ case of this problem: [github.com/Gusarich/erdos42](https://github.com/Gusarich/erdos42)

The proof is ~8,000 lines with a single external axiom: the "2/5 trichotomy" for strongly sum-free subsets of an interval (stated as Theorem 2.2 in Balogh–Liu–Sharifzadeh–Treglown, [arXiv:1409.5661](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.5661), and attributed there to Deshouillers–Freiman–Sós–Temkin, Astérisque 258, 1999).

A high-level explanation of the proof is in the README. The axiom could be formalized too, but it would require significant extra effort, and I wanted to share the results now.

I don't think the solution will generalize to other $M$ values, as the approach is fairly dependent on $M$ being exactly 3. But I hope it will be useful for future work on this problem, or maybe parts of the formalization could be reused!

$\textbf{Verification}$

I asked GPT-5.2 Pro to review the whole solution for correctness and soundness in separate sessions with memory turned off: some with web access, some without. All agreed that the solution is correct and complete, except for that single axiom.

I also used GPT-5.2 Pro with web access, Deep Research in ChatGPT, and Wide Research in Manus to find the relevant literature and any prior progress on the problem. Nothing directly relevant was found in multiple runs, only remotely related things. The approach itself also seems to be original.

$\textbf{How it was made}$

The whole proof was implemented by AI. There was absolutely no human input in the math or ideas. It was done by a pretty simple autonomous agent powered by GPT-5.2 in Codex CLI running 24/7 for 10 days on its own computer, using Aristotle for assistance with Lean and requesting help from GPT-5.2 Pro in ChatGPT for ideas and literature search.

The only human input during these 10 days was periodically pinging the agent asking "how's the progress" and sometimes acting as a bridge between the agent and GPT-5.2 Pro in ChatGPT, because the browser access was broken during the run.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Three trivial remarks:

1. A positive solution to this problem would imply a negative solution to (the first part of) #43, by choosing $A$ so that $|A|=f(N)$ (i.e., a maximal Sidon set).

2.  Without loss of generality one can take $A$ to be a maximal Sidon set (this was the original form of the problem).

3.  One can remove the requirement that $B$ be a Sidon set, because any sufficiently large set will also contain a large Sidon set by a greedy algorithm (of cardinality about square root of that of the original set).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #43 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/43).

### Problem
If $A,B\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ are two Sidon sets such that $(A-A)\cap(B-B)=\{0\}$ then is it true that\[ \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq\binom{f(N)}{2}+O(1),\]where $f(N)$ is the maximum possible size of a Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$? If $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$ then can this bound be improved to\[\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq (1-c+o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}\]for some constant $c>0$?

### Context
Since it is known that $f(N)\sim \sqrt{N}$ (see [[30]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/30)) the latter question is equivalent to asking whether, if $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$,\[\lvert A\rvert \leq \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-c+o(1)\right)\sqrt{N}\]for some constant $c>0$. In the comments Tao has given a proof of this upper bound without the $-c$.

In the comments Barreto has given a negative answer to the second question: for infinitely many $N$ there exist Sidon sets $A,B\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$ and $(A-A)\cap (B-B)=\{0\}$ and\[\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\geq (1-o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}.\]

sourceComments.author: BrittB
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have uploaded a summary of my computational verification for Problem #43. As discussed in the comments above, I confirm the negative resolution to the second part using the Bose-Chowla construction suggested by Kevin Barreto (e.g., finding a counterexample at N=35 where the binomial sum is 30 > 21). My simulations also provide data supporting the affirmative resolution of the first part, approaching Tao's asymptotic bound.

The full details and data can be found here: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18227962

sourceComments.author: Kevin Barreto
sourceComments.contentMd:
We give a negative answer to the second question. We make use of the following result:

$\textbf{Theorem}$ ([Bose–Chowla](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02566968)). Let $q$ be a prime power, then there exists a set $S\subseteq\{1,\,2,\dots,\,q^2-2\}$ of cardinality $|S|=q$ which is Sidon modulo $q^2-1$.

Note that a set that is Sidon modulo $m$ is trivially Sidon in $\mathbb{Z}$. We will use such an $S$ with $q$ odd, so that $q^2-1$ is divisible by $2$. We also need a trivial lemma:

$\textit{Lemma 1.}$ If $S$ is Sidon in an abelian group $G$, then for any $0\neq d\in G$, the equation $$s_1-s_2=d=s_3-s_4,\qquad s_i\in S,$$ implies $(s_1,s_2)=(s_3,s_4)$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ From $s_1-s_2=s_3-s_4$, we obtain $s_1+s_4=s_3+s_2$. By the Sidon property, $\{s_1,s_4\}=\{s_3,s_2\}$. If the matching were $s_1=s_2$, it would force $d=0$, which is excluded. Hence, $s_1=s_3$ and $s_4=s_2$, i.e. $(s_1,s_2)=(s_3,s_4)$. $\square$

When $S$ is Sidon modulo $m$, we may apply $\textit{Lemma 1}$ in $G=\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$. Now, fix an odd prime power $q$, and set $$M:=q^2-1,\qquad N:=\frac{M}{2}=\frac{q^2-1}{2},$$ and let $S\subseteq\{1,\,2,\,\dots,\,M-1\}$ be a Bose-Chowla Sidon set modulo $M$ with $|S|=q$. Furthermore, let $$S_{\mathrm{even}}:=S\cap 2\mathbb{Z},\qquad S_{\mathrm{odd}}:=S\cap(2\mathbb{Z}+1),$$ and write $a:=|S_{\mathrm{even}}|$, $b:=|S_{\mathrm{odd}}|$, so that $a+b=q$.

$\textit{Lemma 2.}$ One has $$a(a-1)+b(b-1)\leq N-1,$$ and consequently, $$(a-b)^2\leq 2q-3,$$ giving $\min\{a,b\}=\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q})$ as $q\to\infty$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ Work in the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$. Any difference of two even residues (or two odd residues) is an even residue. By $\textit{Lemma 1}$ applied to $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$, the directed differences within $S_{\mathrm{even}}$ give $a(a-1)$ distinct non-zero residues in $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$, all even. Likewise, the directed differences within $S_{\mathrm{odd}}$ give $b(b-1)$ distinct non-zero even residues. These two collections are disjoint, again by $\textit{Lemma 1}$, because they arise from disjoint collections of ordered pairs $(s,s')\in S\times S$ (one with both even, one with both odd). But, the set of non-zero even residues modulo $M=2N$ has size exactly $N-1$ (namely $\{2,\,4,\,\dots,\,2N-2\}$). Hence, $$a(a-1)+b(b-1)\leq N-1=\frac{q^2-3}{2}.$$ Now compute $$a(a-1)+b(b-1)=a^2+b^2-(a+b)=\frac{(a+b)^2+(a-b)^2}{2}-q=\frac{q^2+(a-b)^2}{2}-q.$$ Comparing with $(q^2-3)/2$ gives $(a-b)^2\leq 2q-3$. In particular, $$\min\{a,b\}=\frac{q-|a-b|}{2}\geq\frac{q-\sqrt{2q-3}}{2}=\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q}),$$ as claimed. $\square$

Now set $m:=\min\{a,b\}$, and choose subsets $E\subseteq S_{\mathrm{even}}$, $O\subseteq S_{\mathrm{odd}}$, with $|E|=|O|=m$, and define $$A_0:=\{e/2:e\in E\}\subset\{0,\,\dots,\,N-1\},\qquad B_0:=\{(o-1)/2:o\in O\}\subset\{0,\,\dots,\,N-1\}.$$ Write $A:=A_0+1$ and $B:=B_0+1$. Then, $A,B\subset[N]$ and $|A|=|B|=m$.

$\textit{Lemma 3.}$ The sets $A$ and $B$ are Sidon with $(A-A)\cap (B-B)=\{0\}$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ We prove $A$ is Sidon (the proof for $B$ is identical). It suffices to work with $A_0,B_0$ as shifts preserve the Sidon property. Suppose $$x_1+x_2=x_3+x_4,\qquad x_i\in A_0.$$ Write $x_i=e_i/2$ with $e_i\in E\subseteq S$. Then, $e_1+e_2=e_3+e_4$ in integers, hence also modulo $M$. Since $S$ is Sidon modulo $M$, we obtain $\{e_1,e_2\}=\{e_3,e_4\}$, and therefore $\{x_1,x_2\}=\{x_3,x_4\}$. Thus, $A_0$, and hence $A$, is Sidon. Moreover, suppose $d\in (A_0-A_0)\cap(B_0-B_0)$, then $\exists e_1,e_2\in E$ and $o_1,o_2\in O$ s.t. $$d=\frac{e_1-e_2}{2}=\frac{o_1-o_2}{2}.$$ Hence, $e_1-e_2=o_1-o_2$ as integers, and therefore also modulo $M$. By $\textit{Lemma 1}$ applied in $\mathbb{Z}/M\mathbb{Z}$, if this common residue is non-zero, then the ordered pairs must coincide, i.e. $(e_1,e_2)=(o_1,o_2)$, which is impossible because $e_i$ are even and $o_i$ are odd. Therefore, the common residue must be $0$, i.e. $e_1=e_2$ and $o_1=o_2$, so $d=0$. $\square$

$\textbf{Theorem 1.}$ For infinitely many $N$ (namely $N=(q^2-1)/2$ with $q$ an odd prime power), there exist Sidon sets $A,B\subset [N]$, with $|A|=|B|$ and $(A-A)\cap (B-B)=\{0\}$, such that $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\geq (1-o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}.$$ In particular, there is $\textbf{no}$ choice of absolute constant $c>0$ for which the given inequality in question holds for all such Sidon sets $A,B$ as $N\to\infty$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ We use our previously defined Sidon sets $A,B$. Since $|A|=|B|=m$, $$D(A,B):=\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}=2\binom{m}{2}=m(m-1).$$ By $\textit{Lemma 2}$ then, $$D(A,B)=\left(\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q})\right)\left(\frac{q}{2}-\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q})-1\right)=\frac{q^2}{4}+\mathcal{O}(q^{3/2}).$$ Recalling $q^2=2N+1$, this becomes $$D(A,B)=\frac{2N+1}{4}+\mathcal{O}((2N+1)^{3/4})=\frac{N}{2}+\mathcal{O}(N^{3/4}).$$ In particular, $D(A,B)=(1/2 + o(1))N$. On the other hand, $f(N)=(1+o(1))\sqrt{N}$, so $$\binom{f(N)}{2}=\frac{f(N)(f(N)-1)}{2}=\left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)N.$$ Combining these two results along the infinite sequence $N=(q^2-1)/2$ (with $q$ an odd prime power) yields $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\geq (1-o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}\text{ as }N\to\infty,$$ i.e. a failure to the inequality $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}\leq(1-c+o(1))\binom{f(N)}{2}$$ for any fixed $c>0$ for all sufficiently large $N$ in this sequence. $\square$

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Nice, surprisingly simple consequence of existing Sidon set constructions!  This looks within range of formalizability in Lean.

replies.author: Kevin Barreto
replies.contentMd: Now formalised in Lean 4 [here](https://live.lean-lang.org/#). The Erdős–Turán upper bound on the maximum size of a Sidon set and Bose–Chowla were formalised by Harmonic's Aristotle.

sourceComments.author: Kevin Barreto
sourceComments.contentMd: I believe $N=8, A=\{1,2,5\},\, B=\{1,3,8\}\subset \{1,\,\dots,\,8\}$ suffices for a counterexample to the second part. One can verify they are Sidon and $A-A=\{0,\,\pm 1,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4\}$, $B-B=\{0,\pm 2,\,\pm 5,\,\pm 7\}$, so $(A-A)\cap(B-B)=\{0\}$. Moreover, $\{1,4,6,8\}\subset\{1,\,\dots,\,8\}$ is Sidon, and a Sidon set of size $s\leq 8$ has $s(s-1)/2$ distinct positive differences, which must lie in $\{1,\,\dots,\,7\}$; hence $s(s-1)/2\leq 7$, so $s\leq 4$, i.e. $f(8)=4$. Now, $$\binom{|A|}{2}+\binom{|B|}{2}=2\binom{3}{2}=6=\binom{4}{2}=\binom{f(8)}{2},$$ i.e. we would have $c=0$, which is not strictly positive.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
This does technically refute Erdos's assertion (that he wrote that he was "sure" of), but it is possible that he intended this claim only for large $N$.

Asymptotically, it is known that $f(N) = (1+o(1)) \sqrt{N}$, so the claim here for large $N$ is equivalent to asking for $|A|= |B| \leq (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-c+o(1)) \sqrt{N}$ for some $c>0$.  Without the $c$, one can obtain this bound by the following standard argument.  By hypothesis one has the pointwise bound
$$ 1_A * 1_{-A}(n) + 1_B * 1_{-B}(n) \leq (|A|^2 + |B|^2) 1_{n=0} + 1$$
for any $n$; summing against $1_{[1,H]} * 1_{-[1,H]}(n)$ for some shift $H$ we conclude that
$$ \| 1_A * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell^2}^2 + \| 1_B * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell^2}^2 \leq (|A|^2+|B|^2) H + H^2.$$
From Cauchy-Schwarz one has
$$ \| 1_A * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell^2}^2  \geq \| 1_A * 1_{[1,H]} \|_{\ell_1^2}/(N+H) = |A|^2 H^2 / (N+H)$$
and similarly for $B$.  We conclude that
$$ (|A|^2+|B|^2) \frac{H^2}{N+H} \leq (|A|^2+|B|^2) H + H^2,$$
and on choosing say $H = \lfloor N^{1/2} \rfloor$ one can arrive at $|A|^2+|B|^2 = N + O(\sqrt{N})$ which gives $|A|=|B| \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{N} + O(1)$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Indeed - there are quite a few problems which Erdős only intended for 'all sufficiently large $N$' (in that there may well be counterexamples by the law of small numbers, and I doubt he checked many small counterexamples).

He often didn't bother to state this, taking it as read I think.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
KStar's comment here refers to the original version of the second part of the question, which was the following:

"If $\lvert A\rvert=\lvert B\rvert$ then can this bound be improved to\[\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}\leq (1-c)\binom{f(N)}{2}\]for some constant $c>0$?"

[As of right now, the question says $(1-c+o(1))$ instead of simply $(1-c)$.]

Pietro Monticone ran Aristotle in "informal mode" (the input is English text) and it found the counterexample $A=\{1, 2, 10, 22, 24\}$ and $B=\{3, 8, 14, 18, 21\}$ for $N=24$ (and verified it in Lean).  This is similar to the counterexample above, except even stronger: $\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2} = 20$, while $\binom{f(N)}{2}=15$.  In particular, all differences are uniquely represented either in $A$ or in $B$, except for $16$, $17$, and $19$.

For the original version of the question, KStar's example shows the optimal $c\le 0$, which is not strictly positive, while this would further show $c\le -1/3$, in particular ruling out $c=0$.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
I worked on the first question on September 2.  In my notes, I wrote "[Note: this second statement is almost certainly intended asymptotically.]" because I found the following counterexamples to the version of the question being discussed in this thread:

$n=8$, $A=\{1,2,8\}$, $B=\{1,3,6\}$, and $f(N)=4$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=6 \ge 6 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

$n=14$, $A=\{1,2,11,14\}$, $B=\{1,5,7,12\}$, and $f(N)=5$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=12 > 10 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

$n=23$, $A=\{1,2,14,21,23\}$, $B=\{1,4,9,15,19\}$, and $f(N)=6$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=20 > 15 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

$n=35$, $A=\{1,3,14,30,31,35\}$, $B=\{1,8,11,20,26,34\}$, and $f(N)=8$ so
$\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}+\binom{\lvert B\rvert}{2}=30 > 28 = \binom{f(N)}{2}$.

I apologize for not sharing these earlier.  For what it's worth, I believe that (the asymptotic versions of) both conjectures are false .. and doable?

### Problem
Let $N\geq 1$ and $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a Sidon set. Is it true that, for any $\epsilon>0$, there exist $M$ and $B\subset \{N+1,\ldots,M\}$ (which may depend on $N,A,\epsilon$) such that $A\cup B\subset \{1,\ldots,M\}$ is a Sidon set of size at least $(1-\epsilon)M^{1/2}$?

sourceComments.author: Daniil Sedov
sourceComments.contentMd:
GPT-5.2 Pro believes the statement is invalid in its current form. See its reasoning below:

---

As stated it has a quantifier bug: it says "for any $\epsilon>0$, there exist $M=M(\epsilon)$ and $B \subset \{N+1,\ldots,M\}$ …". But $N$ is arbitrary, so if I take $N > M(\epsilon)$ then $\{N+1,\ldots,M\} = \varnothing$ and you can't add anything. Then the conclusion $|A \cup B| \ge (1-\epsilon)M^{1/2}$ fails, e.g., for $A = \{1\}$ when $M$ is large.

So $M$ must depend on $N$ (or on $A$), i.e., "for all $N$ and all Sidon $A \subset [1,N]$ there exists some $M > M_0(A,\epsilon)$ and $B \subset (N,M]$ …". With the broken quantifiers, the statement is trivially false.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Yes, $M$ should depend on both $N$ and $A$ also. This is implicit (in general, by convention, existential variables introduced after universal variables are assumed to depend on them in an unspecified manner).

I added the $M(\epsilon)$ to especially highlight that it also depends on $\epsilon$, but do see that this might lead to confusion, so I'll edit it.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: I'd call this a "quantifier bug" in GPT-5.2 Pro!

replies.contentMd:
I believe GPT-5.2 Pro is providing value here and is not shown to be in possession of a "bug".

Also we don't know what question Gusarich asks. Maybe they asked if there is a trivial resolution to the problem or something like that.

replies.author: DanielLarsen
replies.contentMd: The proof of minimality seems incomplete to me. What if $a_k+1$ is prime (as apparently is the case for $k=15$ not to mention $k=1,2$)? It seems that $n_k$ is in fact maximal among $n$ with $\phi(n)=a_k$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: This proof is wrong - it says that the smallest $n$ such that\[\phi(n) = \prod_{i=1}^k (p_i-1)\]is $n=\prod_{i=1}^kp_i$. This fails already for $k=2$ - for example $\phi(3)=\phi(2\cdot 3)$. (There is an obvious problem in that one can just divide by $2$ without changing the value of $\phi(n)$. But even excluding this there are problems, such as\[\phi(3\cdot 5\cdot 7) = \phi(5\cdot 13)\]and $13<3\cdot 7$.)

replies.contentMd:
As a third voice, I'll simply confirm that the proof is wrong in step 1: minimality, like the other two comments. You can read [ChatGPT's reasoning](https://chatgpt.com/share/6963baf3-1258-8010-8757-ff8dd42d486f) here, which I haven't checked but aligns closely with the other comments.

I also note that this looks like it's generated by GPT 5.2 Instant from stylistic considerations, but I won't claim this as fact. So one advice is to explicitly at least use GPT-5.2 Thinking for mathematical problems. Another advice is to ask it to check the proof itself - GPT-5.2 Thinking can catch a nontrivial fraction of its own errors this way.
