sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: Most likely the answer is negative, i.e., if $n$ is minimal amongst all numbers with a given value of $\phi(n)$, then $n/\phi(n)$ must be bounded (or equivalently, $\sum_{p|n} 1/p = O(1)$).  Intuitively, if $n$ has too many prime factors, it should be possible to swap out some prime factors for others to reduce $n$ while maintaining exactly the same value of $\phi(n)$.  But it looks very difficult to prove this rigorously with our current analytic number theory technology!

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: This is a good heuristic. Just a minor refinement: such an argument should prevent n from having many *small* prime divisors. We cannot expect to prevent n from having many prime factors of any size. Namely, if there were infinitelly many Fermat primes, then their products (like $n=3*5*17*257$) would be good examples of such n. Luckily, such large primes do not contribute much to the sum of reciprocals, of course.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #52 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/52).

### Problem
Let $A$ be a finite set of integers. Is it true that for every $\epsilon>0$\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg_\epsilon \lvert A\rvert^{2-\epsilon}?\]

### Context
The sum-product problem. Erdős and Szemerédi [ErSz83] proved a lower bound of $\lvert A\rvert^{1+c}$ for some constant $c>0$, and an upper bound of\[\lvert A\rvert^2 \exp\left(-c\frac{\log\lvert A\rvert}{\log\log \lvert A\rvert}\right)\]for some constant $c>0$. The lower bound has been improved a number of times. The current record is\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg\lvert A\rvert^{\frac{1962}{1469}-o(1)}\]due to Cushman [Cu25] (note $1962/1469=1.3356\cdots$). A complete history of sum-product bounds can be found [at this webpage](http://thomasbloom.org/notes/sumproduct.html).

There is likely nothing special about the integers in this question, and indeed Erdős and Szemerédi also ask a similar question about finite sets of real or complex numbers. The current best bound for sets of reals is the same bound of Bloom above. The best bound for complex numbers is\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg\lvert A\rvert^{\frac{4}{3}+c}\]for some absolute constant $c>0$, due to Basit and Lund [BaLu19].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #61 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/61).

### Problem
For any graph $H$ is there some $c=c(H)>0$ such that every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices that does not contain $H$ as an induced subgraph contains either a complete graph or independent set on $\geq n^c$ vertices?

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa89], who proved that a complete graph or independent set must exist on\[\geq \exp(c_H\sqrt{\log n})\]many vertices, where $c_H>0$ is some constant. This was improved by Bucić, Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour [BNSS23] to\[\geq \exp(c_H\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}).\]This problem is [#80 in Extremal Graph Theory](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/RamseyTuranWithoutC5.html) in the graphs problem collection.

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
The [thesis](https://www.proquest.com/openview/e0419f0edce6b2c51c56f7b2ec1870d7/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&cbl=18750&diss=y) of H. T. Nguyen is a really nice account of this conjecture. Here's what it proves:

- A proof of the conjecture when $H$ is the five-vertex path.
- A proof of the conjecture in the setting of graphs of bounded VC-dimension.
- A proof of the conjecture for infinitely many prime graphs $H$
- A proof of the bound $2^{(\log n)^{1-(o)1}}$ when $H$ is an arbitrary path.
- A proof of the conjecture for excluding a hole and an antihole, and for excluding an arbitrary induced $(≥ 4)$-subdivision of $H$ and its complement.

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
This conjecture has been proven true for "nearly" all paths, i.e., for every path $H$, all $H$-free graphs with $n$ vertices have cliques or stable sets of size at least $2^{(\log n)^{1−o(1)}}$ by T. Nguyen, A. Scott and P. Seymour in ["Induced subgraph density. V. All paths approach Erdos-Hajnal(2024)"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15032)

In conclusion, the paper proves that $P_5$ satisfy this conjecture.

a variant of this question which is also open is to even show: there exists a $c=c(H)>0$ and a function $f=f_H$ with $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. so that every $H$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices either has a complete graph of size $n^c$ or an independent set of size $f(n)$.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #62 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/62).

### Problem
If $G_1,G_2$ are two graphs with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ then must there exist a graph $G$ whose chromatic number is $4$ (or even $\aleph_0$) which is a subgraph of both $G_1$ and $G_2$?

### Context
Erdős also asked [Er87] about finding a common subgraph $H$ (with chromatic number either $4$ or $\aleph_0$) in any finite collection of graphs with chromatic number $\aleph_1$.

Every graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contains all sufficiently large odd cycles (which have chromatic number $3$), see [[594]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/594). This was proved by Erdős, Hajnal, and Shelah [EHS74]. Erdős wrote [Er87] that 'probably' every graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contains as subgraphs all graphs with chromatic number $4$ with sufficiently large girth.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #64 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/64).

### Problem
Does every finite graph with minimum degree at least 3 contain a cycle of length $2^k$ for some $k\geq 2$?

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Gyárfás, who believed the answer must be negative, and in fact for every $r$ there must be a graph of minimum degree at least $r$ without a cycle of length $2^k$ for any $k\geq 2$.

This was solved in the affirmative if the minimum degree is larger than some absolute constant by Liu and Montgomery [LiMo20] (therefore disproving the above stronger conjecture of Erdős and Gyárfás). Liu and Montgomery prove a much stronger result: if the average degree of $G$ is sufficiently large then there is some large integer $\ell$ such that for every even integer $m\in [(\log \ell)^8,\ell]$, $G$ contains a cycle of length $m$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
The conjecture is confirmed for these cases:

(i) $K_{1,m}$-free graphs with minimum degree at least $m+1$ or maximum degree at least $2m-1$ by S. E. Shauger in [Sh98].
(ii) Planar claw-free graphs by D. Daniel and S. E. Shauger in [DaSh01].
(iii) 3-connected cubic planar graphs by C. C. Heckman and R. Krakovski in [HeKr13].
(iv) Cayley graphs on generalized quaternion groups, dihedral groups, semidihedral groups and groups of order $p^3$ in M. H. Ghaffari and Z. Mostaghim [[GhMo18]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/321195881_Erdos-Gyarfas_conjecture_for_some_families_of_Cayley_graphs).
(v) Cayley graphs of order $2p^2$ and $4p$ by M. Ghasemi and R. Varmazyar in [[GhVa21]](http://elib.mi.sanu.ac.rs/files/journals/mv/282/mvn282p37-42.pdf).
(vi) $P_8$-free graphs by Y. Gao and S. Shan in [[GaSh22]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01277).
(vii) $P_{10}$-free graphs by Z. Hu and C. Shen in [[HuSh24]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.05675).
(viii) Diameter-2 graphs by A. Carr in [[Ca26]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.19302).

Additionally:
K. Markstrom in [[Ma04]](http://abel.math.umu.se/~klasm/Uppsatser/cycex.pdf) has shown that any cubic counterexample to this conjecture must have at least 30 vertices.
P. S. Nowbandegani and H. Esfandiari in [[NoEs11]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312286036_An_Experimental_Result_on_the_Erdos-Gyarfas_Conjecture_in_Bipartite_Graphs) has shown that any bipartite counterexample must have at least 32 vertices.
P. S. Nowbandegani, H. Esfandiari, M. H. S. Haghighi and K. Bibak in [[NEHB14]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.5398) has shown that any cubic claw-free counterexample must have 114 vertices and every claw-free graph with minimum degree at least 3 has a cycle whose length is $2^k$ or $3\times2^k$, for some positive integer $k$.

[Sh98]: S. E. Shauger, Results on the Erd˝os-Gy´arf´as conjecture in K1,m-free graphs, Congr. Numer. 134 (1998) 61-65.
[DaSh01]: D. Daniel, S. E. Shauger, A result on the Erd˝os-Gy´arf´as conjecture in planar graphs, Congr. vol. 153 (2001) 129-139
[HeKr13]: C. C. Heckman, R. Krakovski, Erd˝os-Gy´arf´as conjecture for cubic planar graphs, Electron. J. Comb. 20(2) (2013) 7-43.

It seems like the second question has been claimed to be solved in the affirmative. From page 8:

"Indeed, in forthcoming work, Milojević, Pokrovskiy, Sudakov and [Montgomery] have been able to answer, for large $d$, a question of Erdős [[13]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02579174) by giving an exact extremal result corresponding to Theorem 2.3. That is, there is some $d_{0}$ such that for every $d\ge d_{0}$ among the $n$-vertex graphs $G$ with at least $d(n-d)$ edges, $\sum_{l\in C(G)}\frac{1}{l}$ is minimised exactly by the $n$-vertex graph with every possible edge between a set of $d$ vertices and a set of $n-d$ vertices, and no other edges."

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #66 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/66).

### Problem
Is there  $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{1_A\ast 1_A(n)}{\log n}\]exists and is $\neq 0$?

### Context
A suitably constructed random set has this property if we are allowed to ignore an exceptional set of density zero. The challenge is obtaining this with no exceptional set. Erdős believed the answer should be no. Erdős and Sárközy proved that\[\frac{\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert}{\sqrt{\log n}}\to 0\]is impossible. Erdős suggests it may even be true that the $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ of $1_A\ast 1_A(n)/\log n$ are always separated by some absolute constant.

Horváth [Ho07] proved that\[\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert \leq (1-\epsilon)\sqrt{\log n}\]cannot hold for all large $n$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #77 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/77).

### Problem
If $R(k)$ is the Ramsey number for $K_k$, the minimal $n$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $K_k$, then find the value of\[\lim_{k\to \infty}R(k)^{1/k}.\]

### Context
Erdős offered \$100 for just a proof of the existence of this constant, without determining its value. He also offered \$1000 for a proof that the limit does not exist, but says 'this is really a joke as [it] certainly exists'. (In [Er88] he raises this prize to \$10000). Erdős proved\[\sqrt{2}\leq \liminf_{k\to \infty}R(k)^{1/k}\leq \limsup_{k\to \infty}R(k)^{1/k}\leq 4.\]The upper bound has been improved to $4-\tfrac{1}{128}$ by Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe [CGMS23]. This was improved to $3.7992\cdots$ by Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin, and Wei [GNNW24].

A shorter and simpler proof of an upper bound of the strength $4-c$ for some constant $c>0$ (and a generalisation to the case of more than two colours) was given by Balister, Bollobás, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBCGHMST24].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

If he would ask for $R(6)$, the best strategy probably would be to destroy it before it can destroy us. If we would be so clever that we could give the answer by mathematics, we would just tell him: "if you try to do something you will see what will happent to you...". I think we are strong enugh now and the only evil spirit we have to feel is the one which is in ourselves (quoting somebody: I have seen the enemy and them are us). Now enough of the idle talk and back to Mathematics.'

Investigate open Erdos Problem #78 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/78).

### Problem
Let $R(k)$ be the Ramsey number for $K_k$, the minimal $n$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $K_k$.

Give a constructive proof that $R(k)>C^k$ for some constant $C>1$.

### Context
Erdős gave a simple probabilistic proof that $R(k) \gg k2^{k/2}$.

Equivalently, this question asks for an explicit construction of a graph on $n$ vertices which does not contain any clique or independent set of size $\geq c\log n$ for some constant $c>0$.

sourceComments.author: Neel Somani
sourceComments.contentMd:
Quick clarification question: my colleague has mentioned that Erdos's probabilistic bound $R(k)\gg 2^{k/2}$ can be derandomized via the method of conditional expectations, yielding a deterministic construction of a 2-coloring of $K_n$ with no monochromatic $K_k$ for $n\approx 2^{k/2}$.

Is such a derandomization considered "constructive" for the purposes of this problem, or would it make sense to clarify the question to ask for a substantially more explicit/efficient/algebraic construction (e.g. a fixed family of graphs)?

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Explicit.
The derandomization here only gives an existence proof. For $n$ large it would indeed not be efficient either.

An algebraic construction would be good, but other ways of constructing would be allowed as well.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: The term "constructive" is somewhat subjective in mathematics, but perhaps one concrete question would be to exhibit a deterministic algorithm that, for a given $k$, produces a graph on exponentially many vertices with Ramsey number at least $k$, in time that is guaranteed to be less than double exponential in $k$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #80 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/80).

### Problem
Let $c>0$ and let $f_c(n)$ be the maximal $m$ such that every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and at least $cn^2$ edges, where each edge is contained in at least one triangle, must contain a book of size $m$, that is, an edge shared by at least $m$ different triangles.

Estimate $f_c(n)$. In particular, is it true that $f_c(n)>n^{\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$? Or $f_c(n)\gg \log n$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Rothschild.  Alon and Trotter showed that, provided $c<1/4$, $f_c(n)\ll_c n^{1/2}$. Szemerédi observed that his regularity lemma implies that $f_c(n)\to \infty$.

Edwards (unpublished) and Khadziivanov and Nikiforov [KhNi79] proved independently that $f_c(n) \geq n/6$ when $c>1/4$ (see [[905]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/905)).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #81 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/81).

### Problem
Let $G$ be a chordal graph on $n$ vertices - that is, $G$ has no induced cycles of length greater than $3$. Can the edges of $G$ be partitioned into $n^2/6+O(n)$ many cliques?

### Context
Asked by Erdős, Ordman, and Zalcstein [EOZ93], who proved an upper bound of $(1/4-\epsilon)n^2$ many cliques (for some very small $\epsilon>0$). The example of all edges between a complete graph on $n/3$ vertices and an empty graph on $2n/3$ vertices show that $n^2/6+O(n)$ is sometimes necessary.

A split graph is one where the vertices can be split into a clique and an independent set. Every split graph is chordal. Chen, Erdős, and Ordman [CEO94] have shown that any split graph can be partitioned into $\frac{3}{16}n^2+O(n)$ many cliques.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #82 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/82).

### Problem
Let $F(n)$ be maximal such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $F(n)$ vertices. Prove that $F(n)/\log n\to \infty$.

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős, Fajtlowicz, and Stanton. It is known that $F(5)=3$ and $F(7)=4$.

Ramsey's theorem implies that $F(n)\gg \log n$. Bollobás observed that $F(n)\ll n^{1/2+o(1)}$. Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov [AKS07] have improved this to $n^{1/2}(\log n)^{O(1)}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Conjectured by Erdős, Fajtlowicz, and Stanton. It is known that $F(5)=3$ and $F(7)=4$.
Ramsey's theorem implies that $F(n)\gg \log n$. Bollobás observed that $F(n)\ll n^{1/2+o(1)}$. Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov [AKS07] have improved this to $n^{1/2}(\log n)^{O(1)}$.

In [Er93] Erdős asks whether, if $t(n)$ is the largest trivial (either empty or complete) subgraph which a graph on $n$ vertices must contain (so that $t(n) \gg \log n$ by Ramsey's theorem), then is it true thatF(n)-t(n)\to \infty?Equivalently, and in analogue with the definition of Ramsey numbers, one can define $G(n)$ to be the minimal $m$ such that every graph on $m$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $n$ vertices. This problem can be rephrased as asking whether $G(n) \leq 2^{o(n)}$.

Fajtlowicz, McColgan, Reid, and Staton [FMRS95] showed that $G(1)=1$, $G(2)=2$, $G(3)=5$, $G(4)=7$, and $G(5)\geq 12$. Boris Alexeev and Brendan McKay (see the comments and this site) have computed $G(5)=17$, $G(6)\geq 21$, and $G(7)\geq 29$.
See also [[1031]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1031) for another question regarding induced regular subgraphs.

sourceComments.author: bdmckay
sourceComments.contentMd: Working together with Paul Dyson, I now have graphs of order 29 with no regular subgraph of order 7.  Thus $G(7) \ge 30$.  More information will be provided when it is available.

sourceComments.author: bdmckay
sourceComments.contentMd:
At https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~bdm/data/ramsey.html I have put all the extremal graphs for regular induced subgraphs of order at least 4 (10 on 6 vertices), and order at least 5 (954 on 16 vertices).

I also provided the following:

* 2,808,915 graphs of order 20 with no regular subgraph of order 6. This is certainly not a complete collection but my computer got tired. I have verified that none of these extend to 21 vertices.

* 158,274 graphs of order 28 with no regular subgraph of order 7. This is also certainly not a complete collection. In this case I have NOT verified that none extend to 29 vertices as it would take my naive extender too long. If anyone has a clever idea on how to do this test quickly, I'd be very interested.

sourceComments.author: bdmckay

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: I assume you mean $G(6)$?

sourceComments.author: bdmckay
sourceComments.contentMd:
Define $G(k)=\min\{ n : F(n)\ge k \}$, that is $G(k)$ is the smallest order on which every graph has a regular induced subgraph of order $k$ or greater.  This is the same way Ramsey numbers are defined, and I find it easier on the brain.  $G$ determines $F$ due to monotonicity.

In 1997, I computed G(2)=2, G(3)=5, G(4)=7, G(5)=17 but didn't publish it. I just repeated that computation now with fresh code and got the same result.  The lexicographic product $P_4[P_4]$ is a short proof that $G(5)\ge 17$ but I don't know of a non-computational proof that $G(5)=17$.

Here are the counts, from 1 vertex to 16 vertices, of graphs which do not have a regular induced subgraph of order 5 or more:  1, 2, 4, 11, 31, 130, 728, 6027, 66308, 818276, 8336902, 45933753, 79888458, 23814804, 512906, 954.

I have examples to show that $G(6)\ge 19$ and $G(7)\ge 28$ and I'm still searching for larger examples.  I don't know why there should be a small leap from $G(5)$ to $G(6)$ then a large leap from $G(6)$ to $G(7)$, but the fact that there are 8 regular graphs of order 6 compared to only 6 of order 7 might have something to do with it

My simple code for $G(5)$ took about 25 hours to show $G(5)=17$ but it cannot find $G(6)$ in a reasonable amount of time.  I'm thinking about how to design a smarter algorithm.  (Brendan McKay).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Great, thanks Brendan, and welcome to the site!

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
There is some [discussion on GitHub](https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/issues/94) regarding computing this function: https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/issues/94

My computation of $G(5)=17$ is finishing up. The count for order 16 graphs agrees. I am using nauty.

Perhaps of most interest is this graph which demonstrates $G(6)\ge 20$: R?AAD@OiEg\O\A|c[Zew\eV^E~v~fw

Thank you for sharing your results, and for nauty.

replies.author: bdmckay
replies.contentMd: Now I also found a few graphs to show $G(6)\ge 20$, plus some for $G(7)\ge 29$.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: Out of curiosity, do you know how long the computation took in 1997?

replies.author: bdmckay
replies.contentMd: I think it was somewhere in the 700-hour range, but I didn't find the actual log files. It wasn't just a difference in cpu speed but also an inferior method. Incidentally, out of the 954 extremal graphs for $R(5)$, 24 are self-complementary.

sourceComments.author: zach hunter

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Interesting, thanks Zach. Do you know any non-trivial upper bounds for these?

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd:
$\alpha(n)$ (and the higher order modular analogues) should all be linear I believe.

meanwhile, $\beta(n)$ has a $O(n/\log(n))$ bound. the construction is take one clique of size $n/\log(n)$, two cliques of size $n/2\log(n)$, 4 cliques of size $n/4\log(n)$, and so on. this was observed in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.1213) by Caro, Shapira, and Yuster; the same construction also appears in this paper of Noga, Michael, and Benny (where they study $F(n)$ and related problems).

I'm inclined to believe this upper bound for $\beta$ is also tight (though I am a little less confident, compared to $\alpha$).

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: $F(n)$ and $t(n)$ [have now been computed up to $n \leq 10$](https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/issues/94 ), which seems long enough to merit submission to the OEIS.  If there are any Ramsey theory or SAT solver experts who might be able to extend the sequence a little further (or at least confirm the existing data), feel free to help out!

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: $t(n)$ is in fact known for $n\leq 42$, since $R(4)=18$ and $R(5)\geq 43$ (so that $t(n)=3$ for $6\leq n<18$ and $t(n)=4$ for $18\leq n\leq 42$).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Also [this paper](https://combinatorialpress.com/article/ars/Volume%20039/volume-39-paper-15.pdf) by Fajtlowicz, McColgan, Reid, and Staton computes $F(n)$ for $n\leq 11$ (so $F(n)=3$ for $5\leq n\leq 6$ and $F(n)=4$ for $7\leq n\leq 11$).

### Problem
The cycle set of a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is a set $A\subseteq \{3,\ldots,n\}$ such that there is a cycle in $G$ of length $\ell$ if and only if $\ell \in A$. Let $f(n)$ count the number of possible such $A$.

Prove that $f(n)=o(2^n)$.

Prove that $f(n)/2^{n/2}\to \infty$.

### Context

The first problem was solved by Verstraëte [Ve04], who proved\[f(n)\ll 2^{n-n^{1/10}}.\]This was improved by Nenadov [Ne25] to\[f(n) \ll 2^{n-n^{1/2-o(1)}}.\]One can also ask about the existence and value of $\lim f(n)^{1/n}$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #85 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/85).

### Problem
Let $n\geq 4$ and $f(n)$ be minimal such that every graph on $n$ vertices with minimal degree $\geq f(n)$ contains a $C_4$. Is it true that, for all large $n$, $f(n+1)\geq f(n)$?

### Context
The function $f(n)$ is a reformulation of the Ramsey number $R(C_4,K_{1,n})$, in that\[R(C_4,K_{1,n})=\min\{ m : f(m)\leq m-n\}\]and\[f(n)=\min\{ m : m\geq R(C_4, K_{1,n-m})\}.\]The behaviour of this Ramsey number more generally is [[552]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/552).

A weaker version of the conjecture asks for some constant $c$ such that $f(m)>f(n)-c$ for all $m>n$. This question can be asked for other graphs than $C_4$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
To see why $f(n) < \sqrt{n} + 1$ holds, let $\delta$ be the minimum degree of a graph with $n$ vertices that does not contain a $C_4$ and define, for every vertex $v$, the set $S_v$ of all unordered pairs of distinct neighbours of $v$.

Now, if $S_v \cap S_w \neq \emptyset$ for some distinct vertices $v$ and $w$, say $(x,y) \in S_v \cap S_w$, then $v, x, w, y$ would be a $C_4$. In order words, to prevent the graph from containing a $C_4$, we need to have that all sets $S_v$ are disjoint. Now we note that, in total, there are $\frac{1}{2}n(n-1)$ unordered pairs of vertices, while $S_v$ contains at least $\frac{1}{2} \delta (\delta-1)$ pairs for every vertex $v$. We therefore get, assuming the sets $S_v$ are pairwise disjoint,
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2}n(n-1) &\ge \sum_v |S_v| \\
&\ge \sum_v \frac{1}{2}\delta(\delta-1) \\
&= \frac{1}{2}n\delta(\delta-1).
\end{align*}In other words, $n-1 \ge \delta (\delta - 1)$, so that in particular $\delta < \sqrt{n} + \frac{1}{2}$. Note that this proof would have also worked for the average instead of minimum degree.

As for the lower bound $f(n) > \big(1 - o(1)\big)\sqrt{n}$, the polarity graph induced by the projective plane (see Theorem $1$ in [this](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1966-06.pdf) $1966$ paper by Erdős, Rényi and Sós for a construction) has $n = q^2 + q + 1$ vertices and minimum degree $q = \big(1 - o(1)\big)\sqrt{n}$, while it does not contain a $C_4$.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #86 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/86).

### Problem
Let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph (so that $Q_n$ has $2^n$ vertices and $n2^{n-1}$ edges). Is it true that every subgraph of $Q_n$ with\[\geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)n2^{n-1}\]many edges contains a $C_4$?

### Context
Let $f(n)$ be the maximum number of edges in a subgraph of $Q_n$ without a $C_4$, so that this conjecture is that $f(n)\leq (\frac{1}{2}+o(1))n2^{n-1}$.

Erdős [Er91] showed that\[f(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{c}{n}\right)n2^{n-1}\]for some constant $c>0$, and wrote it is 'perhaps not hopeless' to determine $f(n)$ exactly. Brass, Harborth, and Nienborg [BHN95] improved this to\[f(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{c}{\sqrt{n}}\right)n2^{n-1}\]for some constant $c>0$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #87 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/87).

### Problem
Let $\epsilon >0$. Is it true that, if $k$ is sufficiently large, then\[R(G)>(1-\epsilon)^kR(k)\]for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G)=k$?

Even stronger, is there some $c>0$ such that, for all large $k$, $R(G)>cR(k)$ for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G)=k$?

### Context
Erdős originally conjectured that $R(G)\geq R(k)$, which is trivial for $k=3$, but fails already for $k=4$, as Faudree and McKay [FaMc93] showed that $R(W)=17$ for the pentagonal wheel $W$.

Since $R(k)\leq 4^k$ this is trivial for $\epsilon\geq 3/4$. Yuval Wigderson points out that $R(G)\gg 2^{k/2}$ for any $G$ with chromatic number $k$ (via a random colouring), which asymptotically matches the best-known lower bounds for $R(k)$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #89 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/89).

### Problem
Does every set of $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determine $\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$ many distinct distances?

### Context
A $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ integer grid shows that this would be the best possible. Nearly solved by Guth and Katz [GuKa15] who proved that there are always $\gg n/\log n$ many distinct distances.

A stronger form (see [[604]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/604)) may be true: is there a single point which determines $\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances, or even $\gg n$ many such points, or even that this is true averaged over all points - for example, if $d(x)$ counts the number of distinct distances from $x$ then in [Er75f] Erdős conjectured\[\sum_{x\in A}d(x) \gg \frac{n^2}{\sqrt{\log n}},\]where $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is any set of $n$ points.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #90 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/90).

### Problem
Does every set of $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ contain at most $n^{1+O(1/\log\log n)}$ many pairs which are distance 1 apart?

### Context
The unit distance problem. In [Er94b] Erdős dates this conjecture to 1946. In [Er82e] he offers \$300 for the upper bound $n^{1+o(1)}$.

This would be the best possible, as is shown by a set of lattice points. It is easy to show that there are $O(n^{3/2})$ many such pairs. The best known upper bound is $O(n^{4/3})$, due to Spencer, Szemerédi, and Trotter [SST84]. In [Er83c] and [Er85] Erdős offers \$250 for an upper bound of the form $n^{1+o(1)}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #91 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/91).

### Problem
Let $n$ be a sufficently large integer. Suppose $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ has $\lvert A\rvert=n$ and minimises the number of distinct distances between points in $A$. Prove that there are at least two (and probably many) such $A$ which are non-similar.

### Context
For $n=3$ the equilateral triangle is the only such set. For $n=4$ the square or two equilateral triangles sharing an edge give two non-similar examples.

For $n=5$ the regular pentagon is the unique such set (which has two distinct distances). Erdős mysteriously remarks in [Er90] this was proved by 'a colleague'. (In [Er87b] this is described as 'a colleague from Zagreb (unfortunately I do not have his letter)'.) A published proof of this fact is provided by Kovács [Ko24c].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: For $n=3$ the equilateral triangle is the only such set. For $n=4$ the square or two equilateral triangles sharing an edge give two non-similar examples.

For $n=5$ the regular pentagon is the unique such set (which has two distinct distances). Erdős mysteriously remarks in [Er90] this was proved by 'a colleague'. (In [Er87b] this is described as 'a colleague from Zagreb (unfortunately I do not have his letter)'.) A published proof of this fact is provided by Kovács [Ko24c].
In [Er87b] Erdős says that there are at least two non-similar examples for $6\leq n\leq 9$.
The minimal possible number of distinct distances is the subject of [[89]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/89).

(But note that $A$ should be viewed as dependent on $n$, so the "for large $n$" in the problem statement above may be more accurately placed at the beginning of the problem rather than in the middle.)

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
Regarding "In [Er87b] Erdős says that there are at least two non-similar examples for $6\le n\le 9$":
Where does it say that in [Er87b]? I only see a general statement "for some $n \ge 6$ for large $n$; this probably will not be easy " on page 150. Might the claim about $6\le n \le9$ come from some other paper?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
This is given on p. 171 - he says for $n=6,7,8$ "it is easy to see that there is no uniqueness here", and mentions for $n=9$ the examples of a regular nonagon and the six vertices of a regular hexagon, its centre, and the mirror images of the centre with respect to the two neighbouring sides (the latter example given by Hegyi).

There is in fact no page 150 in [Er87b], so perhaps you're looking at the wrong paper?

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #92 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/92).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that there exists a set $A$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ in which every $x\in A$ has at least $f(n)$ points in $A$ equidistant from $x$.

Is it true that $f(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$? Or even $f(n) < n^{O(1/\log\log n)}$?

### Context
This is a stronger form of the unit distance conjecture (see [[90]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/90)).

The set of lattice points imply $f(n) > n^{c/\log\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$. Erdős offered \$500 for a proof that $f(n) \leq n^{o(1)}$ but only \$100 for a counterexample. This latter prize is downgraded to \$50 in [ErFi97].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #96 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/96).

### Problem
If $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ form a convex polygon then there are $O(n)$ many pairs which are distance $1$ apart.

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Moser. In [Er92e] Erdős credits the conjecture that the true upper bound is $2n$ to himself and Fishburn. Füredi [Fu90] proved an upper bound of $O(n\log n)$. A short proof of this bound was given by Brass and Pach [BrPa01]. The best known upper bound is\[\leq n\log_2n+4n,\]due to Aggarwal [Ag15].

Edelsbrunner and Hajnal [EdHa91] have constructed $n$ such points with $2n-7$ pairs distance $1$ apart. (This disproved an early stronger conjecture of Erdős and Moser, that the true answer was $\frac{5}{3}n+O(1)$.)

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Allan_Zhao
sourceComments.contentMd: I think the problem is already solved at https://arxiv.org/pdf/1605.08066.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I asked [Gemini Deepthink about this paper](https://gemini.google.com/share/45d4abcd99c7), and it pointed out that this 2016 paper has not appeared in any journal (it appears to be part of a PhD thesis), and that the proof was rather intricate, though it did not actually go through it.  (The author also appears to have ceased publication activity altogether around this time.)  So I would say that the status of this solution is "unconfirmed".  A separate [ChatGPT Deep research query](https://chatgpt.com/share/6965d9df-5f0c-800e-9490-4c1c14e60633) also declared the problem to remain open.

Perhaps the proof can be verified (or, if it has gaps, have the gaps repaired) with some attention from either a human or an AI, but this may require some non-trivial effort (the paper seems to contain some visual and/or algorithmic arguments, which AIs are still somewhat weak at currently).

EDIT: Page 38 of [this 2025 paper of Alon, Bucić and Sauermann](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00039-025-00698-x) declares the 2015 Aggarwal result to still be the best result on this problem, suggesting that the 2016 preprint has not gained community acceptance. (The Alon et al. paper, by the way, does solve the conjecture if the Euclidean norm is replaced by a "typical" norm on the plane.)

SECOND EDIT: [ChatGPT Pro is also skeptical](https://chatgpt.com/share/6965e658-9b88-800e-a178-732da36dc6dd), pointing out specific portions of the 2016 paper that deserve additional scrutiny, and noted that [these 2025 slides](https://oc.g-scop.grenoble-inp.fr/esperet/calamar/pascal2.pdf) label the main result of this 2016 paper as a "claim" rather than a theorem (see slide 35).

replies.author: uona
replies.contentMd:
Seeing that later papers still use a "weaker" bound instead of this one, some skepticism is warranted. One point of concern is that the author states Theorem 4, claiming that a unit distance graph on $n$ points in convex position has $\mathcal{O}(n)$ edges. However the proof is a bit elliptic, in Lemma 10 it chooses $u_2'$ via the constraint $u_2' > u_2$ and then claims, via a brief appeal to the left tree structure, that one may assume the relevant core path passes through $u_2'$, without explicitly choosing $u_2'$ to lie on that core path and then verifying that the ordering constraint $u_2' > u_2$ holds. The remainder of Lemma 10 is a nonlocal case analysis, with key cases handled by appeal to Lemma 7 and the final contradiction relying on geometric inequalities stated without a local derivation.

Possibly if the author expands to make it more explicit, it could be more easily refereed and plausibly accepted.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: I have been looking at the paper for a while but have trouble "parsing" it. The core definition is a "module", and the core mechanism revolves around decomposing graphs into modules. However, a "module" is not easy to visualize nor does it feel intuitive. ChatGPT argues that a "module" is defined to be easy to count, but the trouble may lie in showing the desired decomposition. I myself am not sure because I must admit I haven't fully parsed why you need this definition. Unfortunately that's all I have to say regarding the mathematical content.

I think this makes it kind of circular (and it seems ChatGPT/Gemini is relying too much on "authority" without explicit prompting steering otherwise).

problems.title: Erdos Problem #97: Does every convex polygon have a vertex with no other $4$ vertices equidistant from it?
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #97 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/97).

### Problem
Does every convex polygon have a vertex with no other $4$ vertices equidistant from it?

### Context
Erdős originally conjectured this (in [Er46b]) with no $3$ vertices equidistant, but Danzer found a [convex polygon](https://www.erdosproblems.com) on 9 points such that every vertex has three vertices equidistant from it (but this distance depends on the vertex). Danzer's construction is explained in [Er87b]. Fishburn and Reeds [FiRe92] have found a convex polygon on 20 points such that every vertex has three vertices equidistant from it (and this distance is the same for all vertices).

If this fails for $4$, perhaps there is some constant for which it holds? In [Er75f] Erdős claimed that Danzer proved that this false for every constant - in fact, for any $k$ there is a convex polygon such that every vertex has $k$ vertices equidistant from it. Since this claim was not repeated in later papers, presumably Erdős was mistaken here.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Erdős originally conjectured this (in [Er46b]) with no $3$ vertices equidistant, but Danzer found a convex polygon on 9 points such that every vertex has three vertices equidistant from it (but this distance depends on the vertex). Danzer's construction is explained in [Er87b]. If this fails for $4$, perhaps there is some constant for which it holds? In [Er75f] Erdős claimed that Danzer proved that this false for every constant - in fact, for any $k$ there is a convex polygon such that every vertex has $k$ vertices equidistant from it. Since this claim was not repeated in later papers, presumably Erdős was mistaken here.

Erdős suggested this as an approach to solve [[96]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/96). Indeed, if this problem holds for $k+1$ vertices then, by induction, this implies an upper bound of $kn$ for [[96]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/96).

The answer is no if we omit the requirement that the polygon is convex (I thank Boris Alexeev and Dustin Mixon for pointing this out), since for any $d$ there are graphs with minimum degree $d$ which can be embedded in the plane such that each edge has length one (for example one can take the $d$-dimensional hypercube graph on $2^d$ vertices). One can then connect the vertices in a cyclic order so that there are no self-intersections and no three consecutive vertices on a line, thus forming a (non-convex) polygon.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #98 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/98).

### Problem
Let $h(n)$ be such that any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line and no four on a circle, determine at least $h(n)$ distinct distances. Does $h(n)/n\to \infty$?

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #99 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/99).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with minimum distance equal to 1, chosen to minimise the diameter of $A$. If $n$ is sufficiently large then must there be three points in $A$ which form an equilateral triangle of size 1?

### Context
Thue proved that the minimal such diameter is achieved (asymptotically) by the points in a triangular lattice intersected with a circle. In general Erdős believed such a set must have very large intersection with the triangular lattice (perhaps as many as $(1-o(1))n$).

Erdős [Er94b] wrote 'I could not prove it but felt that it should not be hard. To my great surprise both B. H. Sendov and M. Simonovits doubted the truth of this conjecture.' In [Er94b] he offers \$100 for a counterexample but only \$50 for a proof.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #101 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/101).

### Problem
Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no five of which are on a line, the number of lines containing four points is $o(n^2)$.

### Context
There are examples of sets of $n$ points with $\sim n^2/6$ many collinear triples and no four points on a line. Such constructions are given by Burr, Grünbaum, and Sloane [BGS74] and Füredi and Palásti [FuPa84].

This is false: Solymosi and Stojaković [SoSt13] have constructed a set with no five on a line and at least\[n^{2-O(1/\sqrt{\log n})}\]many lines containing exactly four points.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #102 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/102).

### Problem
Let $c>0$ and $h_c(n)$ be such that for any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that there are $\geq cn^2$ lines each containing more than three points, there must be some line containing $h_c(n)$ many points. Estimate $h_c(n)$. Is it true that, for fixed $c>0$, we have $h_c(n)\to \infty$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Purdy. It is not even known if $h_c(n)\geq 5$ (see [[101]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/101)).

It is easy to see that $h_c(n) \ll_c n^{1/2}$, and Erdős at one point [Er95] suggested that perhaps a similar lower bound $h_c(n)\gg_c n^{1/2}$ holds. Zach Hunter has pointed out that this is false, even replacing $>3$ points on each line with $>k$ points: consider the set of points in $\{1,\ldots,m\}^d$ where $n\approx m^d$. These intersect any line in $\ll_d n^{1/d}$ points, and have $\gg_d n^2$ many pairs of points each of which determine a line with at least $k$ points. This is a construction in $\mathbb{R}^d$, but a random projection into $\mathbb{R}^2$ preserves the relevant properties.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #104 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/104).

### Problem
Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ the number of distinct unit circles containing at least three points is $o(n^2)$.

### Context
In [Er81d] Erdős proved that $\gg n$ many circles is possible, and that there cannot be more than $O(n^2)$ many circles. The argument is very simple: every pair of points determines at most $2$ unit circles, and the claimed bound follows from double counting. Erdős claims in a number of places this produces the upper bound $n(n-1)$, but Harborth and Mengerson [HaMe86] note that in fact this delivers an upper bound of $\frac{n(n-1)}{3}$.

Elekes [El84] has a simple construction of a set with $\gg n^{3/2}$ such circles. This may be the correct order of magnitude.

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #106 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/106).

### Problem
Draw $n$ squares inside the unit square with no common interior point. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum possible sum of the side-lengths of the squares. Is $f(k^2+1)=k$?

### Context
In [Er94b] Erdős dates this conjecture to 'more than 60 years ago'. Erdős proved that $f(2)=1$ in an early mathematical paper for high school students in Hungary. Newman proved (in personal communication to Erdős) that $f(5)=2$.

It is trivial from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that $f(k^2)=k$. Erdős also asks for which $n$ is it true that $f(n+1)=f(n)$.

sourceMetadata.statementMd: Draw $n$ squares inside the unit square with no common interior point. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum possible sum of the side-lengths of the squares. Is $f(k^2+1)=k$?

researchNotes: In [Er94b] Erdős dates this conjecture to 'more than 60 years ago'. Erdős proved that $f(2)=1$ in an early mathematical paper for high school students in Hungary. Newman proved (in personal communication to Erdős) that $f(5)=2$.
It is trivial from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that $f(k^2)=k$. Erdős also asks for which $n$ is it true that $f(n+1)=f(n)$.

It is easy to see that $f(k^2+1)\geq k$, by first dividing the unit square into $k^2$ smaller squares of side-length $1/k$, and then replacing one square by two smaller squares of side-length $1/2k$. Halász [Ha84] gives a construction that shows $f(k^2+2)\geq k+\frac{1}{k+1}$, and in general, for any $c\geq 1$,f(k^2+2c+1)\geq k+\frac{c}{k}andf(k^2+2c)\geq k+\frac{c}{k+1}.Halász also considers the variants where we replace a square by a parallelogram or triangle.

Erdős and Soifer [ErSo95] and Campbell and Staton [CaSt05] have conjectured that, in general, for any integer $-k<c<k$, $f(k^2+2c+1)=k+\frac{c}{k}$, and proved the corresponding lower bound. Praton [Pr08] has proved that this general conjecture is equivalent to $f(k^2+1)=k$.

Baek, Koizumi, and Ueoro [BKU24] have proved $g(k^2+1)=k$, where $g(\cdot)$ is defined identically to $f(\cdot)$ with the additional assumption that all squares have sides parallel to the sides of the unit square. More generally, they prove that $g(k^2+2c+1)=k+c/k$ for any $-k<c<k$, which determines all values of $g(\cdot)$.

Raj Singh [Ra26] has noted that $f(k^2+1)=k$ being true for all $k$ is equivalent to it being true for infinitely many $k$, which in turn is equivalent to the convergence of\sum_{k\geq 1}(f(k^2+1)-k).Both equivalences follow from the fact thatk(f(k^2+1)-k)is a non-decreasing function of $k$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #107 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/107).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be minimal such that any $f(n)$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line, contain $n$ points which form the vertices of a convex $n$-gon. Prove that $f(n)=2^{n-2}+1$.

### Context
The Erdős-Klein-Szekeres 'Happy Ending' problem. The problem originated in 1931 when Klein observed that $f(4)=5$. Turán and Makai showed $f(5)=9$. Erdős and Szekeres proved the bounds\[2^{n-2}+1\leq f(n)\leq \binom{2n-4}{n-2}+1.\]([ErSz60] and [ErSz35] respectively). There were several improvements of the upper bound, but all of the form $4^{(1+o(1))n}$, until Suk [Su17] proved\[f(n) \leq 2^{(1+o(1))n}.\]The current best bound is due to Holmsen, Mojarrad, Pach, and Tardos [HMPT20], who prove\[f(n) \leq 2^{n+O(\sqrt{n\log n})}.\]In [Er97e] Erdős clarifies that the \$500 is for a proof, and only offers \$100 for a disproof.

This problem is [#1 in Ramsey Theory](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/Convex.html) in the graphs problem collection.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

In ["Computer solution to the 17-point Erdos-Szekeres problem(2006)"](https://faculty.utrgv.edu/zhixiang.chen/cs6174/papers/Wylie_paper1.pdf) G. Szekeres and L. Peters made the following stronger conjecture (in simple words):

Every red-blue coloring of the edges of the ordered complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on $2^{k−2} + 1$ vertices contains an ordered subhypergraph with $k$ vertices and $k−2$ edges, which is a union of a red monotone path and a blue monotone path that are vertex disjoint except for their two common end-vertices.

This conjecture has been disproved by M. Balko and P. Valtr in ["A SAT attack on the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture(2017)"](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0195669817300847).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #108 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/108).

### Problem
For every $r\geq 4$ and $k\geq 2$ is there some finite $f(k,r)$ such that every graph of chromatic number $\geq f(k,r)$ contains a subgraph of girth $\geq r$ and chromatic number $\geq k$?

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Hajnal. Rödl [Ro77] has proved the $r=4$ case (see [[923]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/923)). The infinite version (whether every graph of infinite chromatic number contains a subgraph of infinite chromatic number whose girth is $>k$) is also open.

In [Er79b] Erdős also asks whether\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{f(k,r+1)}{f(k,r)}=\infty.\]See also [the entry in the graphs problem collection](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/SubgraphsOfLargeGirth.html) and [[740]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/740) for the infinitary version.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #111 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/111).

### Problem
If $G$ is a graph let $h_G(n)$ be defined such that any subgraph of $G$ on $n$ vertices can be made bipartite after deleting at most $h_G(n)$ edges.

What is the behaviour of $h_G(n)$? Is it true that $h_G(n)/n\to \infty$ for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi [EHS82]. Every $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ must have $h_G(n)\gg n$ since $G$ must contain, for some $r$, $\aleph_1$ many vertex disjoint odd cycles of length $2r+1$.

On the other hand, Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi proved that there is a $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that $h_G(n)\ll n^{3/2}$. In [Er81] Erdős conjectured that this can be improved to $\ll n^{1+\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #112 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/112).

### Problem
Let $k=k(n,m)$ be minimal such that any directed graph on $k$ vertices must contain either an independent set of size $n$ or a transitive tournament of size $m$. Determine $k(n,m)$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Rado [ErRa67], who showed $k(n,m) \ll_m n^{m-1}$, or more precisely,\[k(n,m) \leq \frac{2^{m-1}(n-1)^m+n-2}{2n-3}.\]Larson and Mitchell [LaMi97] improved the dependence on $m$, establishing in particular  that $k(n,3)\leq n^{2}$. Zach Hunter has observed that\[R(n,m) \leq k(n,m)\leq R(n,m,m),\]which in particular proves the upper bound $k(n,m)\leq 3^{n+2m}$.

See also [the entry in the graphs problem collection](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/DirectedPaths.html) - on this site the problem replaces transitive tournament with directed path, but Zach Hunter and Raphael Steiner have a simple argument that proves, for this alternative definition, that $k(n,m)=(n-1)(m-1)$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #114 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/114).

### Problem
If $p(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ is a monic polynomial of degree $n$ then is the length of the curve $\{ z\in \mathbb{C} : \lvert p(z)\rvert=1\}$ maximised when $p(z)=z^n-1$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58]. It is also listed as Problem 4.10 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.

In [Va99] it is just aked whether the length is at most $2n+O(1)$. This is true, as a consequence of result of Tao [Ta25] below.

### Deliverable

In [Va99] it is just aked whether the length is at most $2n+O(1)$. This is true, as a consequence of result of Tao [Ta25] below.

Let the maximal length of such a curve be denoted by $f(n)$.- The length of the curve when $p(z)=z^n-1$ is $2n+O(1)$, and hence the conjecture implies in particular that $f(n)=2n+O(1)$. - Dolzhenko [Do61] proved $f(n) \leq 4\pi n$, but few were aware of this work. - Pommerenke [Po61] proved $f(n)\ll n^2$. - Borwein [Bo95] proved $f(n)\ll n$ (Borwein was unaware of Dolzhenko's earlier work). The prize of \$250 is reported by Borwein [Bo95]. - Eremenko and Hayman [ErHa99] proved the full conjecture when $n=2$, and $f(n)\leq 9.173n$ for all $n$. - Danchenko [Da07] proved $f(n)\leq 2\pi n$. - Fryntov and Nazarov [FrNa09] proved that $z^n-1$ is a local maximiser, and solved this problem asymptotically, proving thatf(n)\leq 2n+O(n^{7/8}). - Tao [Ta25] has proved that $p(z)=z^n-1$ is the unique (up to rotation and translation) maximiser for all sufficiently large $n$.

Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58] also ask whether the length is at least $2\pi$ if $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert<1\}$ is connected (which $z^n$ shows is the best possible). This was proved by Pommerenke [Po59].

sourceComments.author: Kenneth Mendoza
sourceComments.contentMd:
We have computationally verified the EHP conjecture for all degrees $3 \leq n \leq 12$ using dual independent implementations (Python/mpmath and Rust/inari) with IEEE 1788 certified interval arithmetic and branch-and-bound optimization. Both implementations produce identical certified enclosures across x86_64 and arm64 architectures. The dominance margins increase monotonically from $17.1\%$ ($n=3$) to $71.4\%$ ($n=10$); all non-extremizer boxes are eliminated at level $0$ for $n \geq 5$. We also derive a new closed-form expression for $L(z^n - 1)$ valid for all $n$.

Combined with Tao's result [Ta25] for sufficiently large $n$, the conjecture is now verified for all $n \leq 12$ and all $n \geq N_0$. The remaining gap is $13 \leq n < N_0$.

Preprint and certified result JSON files with SHA-256 checksums: [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19229245](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19229245)

Code: [github.com/MendozaLab/erdos-experiments](https://github.com/MendozaLab/erdos-experiments/tree/main/papers/ehp-conjecture-114)

sourceComments.contentMd: Pommerenke [Po59] proves: if $\{z:|p(z)|<1\}$ is connected, then $|\{z:|p(z)|=1\}|\ge 2\pi$, with equality for $p(z)=z^n$. I wondered whether, when $\{z:|p(z)|<1\}$ has exactly $k\ge 2$ connected components, there must exist a uniform lower bound $c_k>0$ for $|\{z:|p(z)|=1\}|$. However, this is false: take $p(z)=z^k-R$ with $R>1$. Then $\{z: |z^k-R|<1\}$ has $k$ components, but as $R\to\infty$ the lemniscate $\{z:|z^k-R|=1\}$ shrinks and its total length tends to $0$.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
Terence Tao has resolved this problem (positively) for sufficiently large $n$. The paper "The maximal length of the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian lemniscate length in high degree" is available [on the arxiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12455), and there is an [accompanying blog post](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2025/12/15/the-maximal-length-of-the-erdos-herzog-piranian-lemniscate-in-high-degree/).

He notes that the problem almost has "decidable" status now, but there may be some issues with testing equality of real numbers.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #117 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/117).

### Problem
Let $h(n)$ be minimal such that any group $G$ with the property that any subset of $>n$ elements contains some $x\neq y$ such that $xy=yx$ can be covered by at most $h(n)$ many Abelian subgroups.

Estimate $h(n)$ as well as possible.

### Context
Pyber [Py87] has proved there exist constants $c_2>c_1>1$ such that $c_1^n<h(n)<c_2^n$. Erdős [Er97f] writes that the lower bound was already known to Isaacs.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #119 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/119).

### Problem
Let $z_i$ be an infinite sequence of complex numbers such that $\lvert z_i\rvert=1$ for all $i\geq 1$, and for $n\geq 1$ let\[p_n(z)=\prod_{i\leq n} (z-z_i).\]Let $M_n=\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert p_n(z)\rvert$.

Is it true that $\limsup M_n=\infty$?

Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ we have $M_n > n^c$?

Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$,\[\sum_{k\leq n}M_k > n^{1+c}?\]

### Context
This is Problem 4.1 in [Ha74] where it is attributed to Erdős.

The weaker conjecture that $\limsup M_n=\infty$ was proved by Wagner [Wa80], who show that there is some $c>0$ with $M_n>(\log n)^c$ infinitely often.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #120 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/120).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be an infinite set. Must there be a set $E\subset \mathbb{R}$ of positive measure which does not contain any set of the shape $aA+b$ for some $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ and $a\neq 0$?

### Context
The Erdős similarity problem.

This is true if $A$ is unbounded or dense in some interval. It therefore suffices to prove this when $A=\{a_1>a_2>\cdots\}$ is a countable strictly monotone sequence which converges to $0$.

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
We had formalised this statement and also Problem 94 from Green’s open problem set (and also Erdős problem 120) and accidentally forgot to require the set to be measurable, while still requiring a positive volume. A Google DeepMind prover agent found a Lean proof demonstrating that omitting the strict 'MeasurableSet' assumption (i.e. only asking for a set of positive outer Measure) in the specific problem that is also Green’s open problem 94, allows for an explicit counterexample. By treating $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$, the formalization verified that the $\mathbb{Z}$-span of a Hamel basis entirely avoids affine copies of the sequence $\{1, \frac12, \frac14, \dots\}$. Because coordinates over this basis are unique, repeatedly halving them forces any sequence $a \cdot 2^{-n} + b$ with $a \neq 0$ to eventually leave the set. This pathological set possesses strictly positive outer measure, but it is not a measurable set. Details can be found in the formal proof here:
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/153d79d6c82c76fe1bee860742af800840c974d9/FormalConjectures/GreensOpenProblems/94.lean#L174
See also https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3526
This variant is not explicitly mentioned here, but it might be interesting nonetheless. Perhaps this is a one of the special cases previously known, pointers to the literature would be welcome!

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: [De Reyna (1983)](https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1983-089-02/S0002-9939-1983-0712640-0/S0002-9939-1983-0712640-0.pdf) proved this positive outer measure variant with the stronger result, only requiring that $|A| \ge 3$ (!). However, de Reyna's proof is different, using transfinite induction. This is [found](https://chatgpt.com/share/69b57974-7e9c-8010-b08f-0ce85df1647f) by GPT-5.4 Thinking.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #122 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/122).

### Problem
For which number theoretic functions $f$ is it true that, for any $F(n)$ such that $f(n)/F(n)\to 0$ for almost all $n$, there are infinitely many $x$ such that\[\frac{\#\{ n\in \mathbb{N} : n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}\to \infty?\]

### Context
Asked by Erdős, Pomerance, and Sárközy [EPS97] who prove that this is true when $f$ is the divisor function or the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, but Erdős believed it is false when $f(n)=\phi(n)$ or $\sigma(n)$.

sourceComments.author: SkyYang
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think I made a counterexample to this.

A short counterexample to the current online formulation of Problem #122.

Let\[
R(x):=\frac{\#\{n\in \mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}.
\]I am only addressing the current online version of problem#122 as written above. I am not claiming to have resolved the historical original problem behind  Problem #122.

Assume throughout that\[
f:\mathbb{N}\to [0,\infty).
\]I claim that for every such nonnegative function \(f\), there exists an integer-valued function \(F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) such that\[
\frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\to 0 \qquad (n\to\infty),
\]but at the same time\[
R(x)<2 \qquad \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{N}.
\]This shows that the current online formulation is false under any natural interpretation in which the displayed ratio is supposed to become arbitrarily large as \(x\) varies.

Indeed, define\[
F(n):=1+\left\lceil n^2+f(n)^2\right\rceil \qquad (n\in\mathbb{N}).
\]Then \(F(n)\in\mathbb{N}\) and\[
F(n)\ge 1+n^2+f(n)^2.
\]Hence\[
0\le \frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\le \frac{f(n)}{n^2+f(n)^2}.
\]By the elementary inequality\[
n^2+f(n)^2\ge 2nf(n),
\]we get\[
\frac{f(n)}{n^2+f(n)^2}\le \frac{1}{2n}.
\]Therefore\[
0\le \frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\le \frac{1}{2n}\to 0.
\]Now fix \(x\in\mathbb{N}\), and let\[
A_x:=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}.
\]If \(n\in A_x\), then\[
n+f(n)<x+F(x).
\]Since \(f(n)\ge 0\), it follows that\[
n\le n+f(n)<x+F(x).
\]Thus every element of \(A_x\) is a natural number strictly smaller than \(x+F(x)\). Consequently,\[
\#A_x\le x+F(x).
\]Dividing by \(F(x)\), we obtain\[
R(x)=\frac{\#A_x}{F(x)}\le 1+\frac{x}{F(x)}.
\]But\[
F(x)\ge 1+x^2+f(x)^2\ge 1+x^2,
\]so\[
R(x)\le 1+\frac{x}{x^2+1}<2.
\]Hence\[
\frac{\#\{n\in \mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}<2
\qquad \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{N}.
\]

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd: I agree that the problem is incorrectly stated, as we could simply take $F(x)$ sufficiently fast growing, say $F(x) = x$. So my guess is that we should actually require $F(n)/f(n)$ to go to $0$ for almost all $n$, instead of the other way around. If that's not the fix, then surely we need at least some growth condition on $F$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Yes, I think this is the correct interpretation: in [Er97] and [Er97e] there was just a typo (reproduced here) writing $f/F$ where they meant $F/f$. (Although this is more than just a typo in [Er97], since he explicitly states that the width of the interval (here denoted $F(x)$) 'tends to infinity faster than does [the normal order of $f$]'.

Further evidence is looking at what [EPS97] actually prove - they don't state it as a main result, but their methods prove (implicitly) that there is an interval $I\subset [1,O(x)]$ of width\[\asymp \left(\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}\right)^{1/2}\]such that if $n\in I$ then $n+\omega(n)$ is in $J$, where $J$ is an interval of width $O((\log\log x)^{1/2})$ (and the normal order of $\omega$ is $\log\log x$).

The motivation for this sort of problem is to generalise results like 'there are infinitely many $m$ such that $n+\omega(n)=m$ has many solutions'. In this formulation we replace $m$ with a short interval instead, and want many values of $n+\omega(n)$ in this interval.

As is the case with many of the problems stated in [Er97] and [Er97e] there are definitely some errors here; also in the description of the results obtained (which don't really appear in [EPS97]). I'll email Pomerance to see if he can clarify and/or provide other references.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #123 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/123).

### Problem
Let $a,b,c\geq 1$ be three integers which are pairwise coprime. Is every large integer the sum of distinct integers of the form $a^kb^lc^m$ ($k,l,m\geq 0$), none of which divide any other?

### Context
A sequence is said to be $d$-complete if every large integer is the sum of distinct integers from the sequence, none of which divide any other. This particular case of $d$-completeness was conjectured by Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96], who (among other related results) prove this when $a=3$, $b=5$, and $c=7$.

As a partial record of progress so far, the sequence $\{a^kb^lc^m\}$ is known to be $d$-complete when:- $a=3$, $b=5$, $c=7$ (Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96]).
- $a=2$, $b=5$, $c\in \{7,11,13,17,19\}$ (Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96]).
- $a=2$, $b=5$, $c\in \{9,21,23,27,29,31\}$ - more generally, $a=2$, $b=5$, and any $c>6$ with $(c,10)=1$ such that there exists $N$ where every integer in $(N,25cN)$ is the sum of distinct elements of $\{2^k3^lc^m\}$, none of which divide any other (Ma and Chen [MaCh16]).
- $a=2$, $b=5$, $3\leq c\leq 87$ with $(c,10)=1$, or $a=2$, $b=7$, $3\leq c\leq 33$ with $(c,14)=1$, or $a=3$, $b=5$, $2\leq c\leq 14$ with $(c,15)=1$ (Chen and Yu [ChYu23b]).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
The following two papers contain the most recent results on this problem, as far as I know.

M. M. Ma, Y. G. Chen, *On d-complete sequences of integers*, Journal of Number Theory, Volume 164, 1–12, 2016.

Y. G. Chen, W. X. Yu, *On d-complete sequences of integers, II*, Acta Arithmetica, Volume 207, 861–181, 2023.

For example, with $a = 2$ and $b = 5$, this is now known for all $1 < c \le 87$ with $\gcd(c, 10) = 1$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #124 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/124).

### Problem
For any $d\geq 1$ and $k\geq 0$ let $P(d,k)$ be the set of integers which are the sum of distinct powers $d^i$ with $i\geq k$. Let $3\leq d_1<d_2<\cdots <d_r$ be integers such that\[\sum_{1\leq i\leq r}\frac{1}{d_r-1}\geq 1.\]Can all sufficiently large integers be written as a sum of the shape $\sum_i c_ia_i$ where $c_i\in \{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,0)$?

If we further have $\mathrm{gcd}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=1$ then, for any $k\geq 1$, can all sufficiently large integers be written as a sum of the shape $\sum_i c_ia_i$ where $c_i\in \{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,k)$?

### Context
The second question was conjectured by Burr, Erdős, Graham, and Li [BEGL96], who proved it for $\{3,4,7\}$.

The first question was asked separately by Erdős in [Er97] and [Er97e] (although there is some ambiguity over whether he intended $P(d,0)$ or $P(d,1)$ - certainly he mentions no gcd condition). A simple positive proof of the first question was provided (and formalised in Lean) by [Aristotle](https://aristotle.harmonic.fun/) thanks to Alexeev; see the comments for details.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
[Note: this comment was written before 2025/12/01, when the problem text was updated.]

[Aristotle](https://aristotle.harmonic.fun/) from Harmonic has [solved this problem all by itself](https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/ErdosProblems/Erdos124b.md), working only from the formal statement!  [Type-check it online!](https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.24.0&url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fplby%2Flean-proofs%2Frefs%2Fheads%2Fmain%2Fsrc%2Fv4.24.0%2FErdosProblems%2FErdos124b.lean)

A formal statement of the conjecture was available in the Formal Conjectures project.  Unfortunately, there is a [typo](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/issues/1306) in [that statement](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/f33f5ddb49f6077e34025917965bcd1bbd920d73/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/124.lean#L31-L46), wherein the comment says $\geq 1$ in the display-style equation while the corresponding Lean says "= 1".  (That makes the statement weaker.)  Accordingly, I have also corrected that issue and included a proof of the corrected statement.  Finally, I removed a lot of what I believed were unnecessary aspects of the statement, and Aristotle proved that too.  In the end, there are three different versions proven, of which this is my favorite:
theorem erdos_124 : ∀ k, ∀ d : Fin k → ℕ,
    (∀ i, 2 ≤ d i) → 1 ≤ ∑ i : Fin k, (1 : ℚ) / (d i - 1) →
    ∀ n, ∃ a : Fin k → ℕ,
    ∀ i, ((d i).digits (a i)).toFinset ⊆ {0, 1} ∧
    n = ∑ i, a i
I believe this is a faithful formalization of (a strengthening of) the conjecture stated on this page.

As mentioned by DesmondWeisenberg [above](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/124#post-234), there's an issue involving the power 1 (which corresponds to the units digit here) that means the conjecture in [BEGL96] differs from this.  I believe the version in [Er97] matches the statement here, in part because it lacks a gcd condition that is obviously necessary in [BEGL96].  I do not yet have access to [Er97e] to check the statement there.  The subtlety of this issue is unfortunate, given Aristotle's achievement!

Timing-wise, Aristotle took 6 hours and Lean took 1 minute.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
This is quite something, congratulations to Boris and Aristotle!

On one hand, as the nice sketch provided below by tsaf confirms, the final proof is quite simple and elementary - indeed, if one was given this problem in a maths competition (so therefore expected a short simple solution existed) I'd guess that something like the below would be produced. On the other hand, if something like this worked, then surely the combined talents of Burr, Erdős, Graham, and Li would have spotted it.

Normally, this would make me suspicious of this short proof, in that there is overlooked subtlety. But (a) I can't see any and (b) the proof has been formalised in Lean, so clearly it just works!

Perhaps this shows what the real issue in the [BEGL96] conjecture is - namely the removal of $1$ and the addition of the necessary gcd condition. (And perhaps at least some subset of the authors were aware of this argument for the easier version allowing $1$, but this was overlooked later by Erdős in [Er97] and [Er97e], although if they were aware then one would hope they'd have included this in the paper as a remark.)

At the moment I'm minded to keep this as open, and add the gcd condition in the main statement, and note in the remarks that the easier (?) version allowing $1$ and omitting the gcd condition, which was also asked independently by Erdős, has been solved.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)
