sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
G. Melfi in [this paper](https://www.rivmat.unipr.it/fulltext/2004-3s/pdf/16.pdf) has given the following related result:

A sequence $S = \{s_1, s_2,...\}$ of positive integers is a complete sequence, if $\Sigma (S) := \Sigma^\infty_{i=1} \epsilon_i s_i$, for $\epsilon_i \in \{0,1\}, \Sigma_{i=1}^\infty \epsilon_i < \infty$ contains all sufficiently large integers. Let $s \geq 1$ and $A$ be a (finite or infinite) set of integers greater than $1$. Let $Pow (A; s)$ be the nondecreasing sequence of positive integers of the form $a^k$ with $a \in A$ and $k \geq s$. for any $s \geq 1$, $Pow (A; s)$ is complete if and $\textbf{only if}$ $\Sigma_{a \in A} 1/(a-1) \geq 1$.

This $\textbf{only if}$ part of their conjecture has been disproved by Melfi in the above discussed paper.

P.S. [BEGL96] also asks the following:

What can we say about lower and upper asymptotic density of $Σ(Pow(A; s))$ when $A$ is finite and $\Sigma_{a \in A} \frac{1}{log a} > \frac{1}{log 2}$?
(According to page 13 of [this paper](https://d1wqtxts1xzle7.cloudfront.net/49421375/Su_alcune_successioni_di_interi20161007-18048-93q7b2-libre.pdf?1475831390=&response-content-disposition=inline%3B+filename%3DSu_alcune_successioni_di_interi.pdf&Expires=1764526230&Signature=SdSTgcb-5HsdlWk8ERoTbu7SUTCyK6F9fmxfoYAjU5RvFShTNcmUH4IeCUNWaQsu0zz-wHWOoCYrhhH0mpYZtplfZgBQOUlOW2P20hsQ0ovKcufJVVELUWs-CuSmolC1Q31lFe~u7GtW4BCciGHEaSPTQXIqBiIkGTKn-UbAnQy5PReMehSXhuShRYjVDTckey5II5yf1pO3yZ0oPXJNBCF3FjeL1Y8Ue4A3X0tMM2X1huG6kl08MG1Cllg1PWdgsiTL-F8mhv3F-cyzv4ru2uPT~zv4~d0JMF2PWCBbuCiN-7GFOUI5-aVZoMuu5wveoLrUZJpd71fK2o3F3HkgzA__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAJLOHF5GGSLRBV4ZA)).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Just to clarify, Pomerance's observation that Diophantine approximation shows the necessity of $\sum_{a \in A} 1/(a-1) \geq 1$ only applies in the case of finite $A$, whereas Melfi's example is for infinite $A$.  (In particular, the description of Pomerance's result in [p. 133, BEGL96] is not quite correct.)

Interestingly, (my reconstruction of) Pomerance's argument is almost identical to Gemini's failed heuristic argument: if $A$ is finite with $\sum_{a \in A} 1/(a-1) < 1$, then there will be infinitely many numbers $n$ that are larger than the sum of all the powers of $a$ preceding it (for this to hold, $n$ has to be slightly less than a power of $a$ for each $a$, which can be accomplished by the Kronecker approximation theorem). Hence $A$ cannot be complete.

This argument shows that the $\sum_{a \in A} 1/(a-1)=1$ case is quite delicate; at a bare minimum, it needs something like Baker's theorem to prevent powers of different $a$ from clustering too close together, which can create potential counterexamples. (And indeed, [p. 137, BEGL96] discusses this issue for specific sets such as {3,4,7}.)

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
For what it is worth, the Gemini and ChatGPT deep research tools did not turn up any significant new literature on this problem.

[Gemini offered the simple observation](https://gemini.google.com/share/2dce421b46ba") that if 1 is omitted then the gcd condition becomes necessary, explained the significance of the $\sum_i \frac{1}{d_i-1} \geq 1$ condition (linking it to some parallel work on Cantor sets, particularly the "Newhouse gap lemma"), but turned up no new direct references for this problem.

[ChatGPT used this very web page extensively as the main authoritative source](https://chatgpt.com/share/692c6e28-0cb4-800e-a5a4-4fa8ce792f30), for instance citing the Aristotle proof, as well as the other papers cited on this page, as well as the page for the related problem [125].  As such, no new information was gleaned, but readers may find the AI-generated summary of the situation to be amusing.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: As a further experiment, I gave this problem (in the weaker, solved formulation) to Gemini Deepthink with a hint to use Brown's criterion.  Interestingly, it declared that [it was unlikely that Brown's criterion was strong enough to solve this problem](https://gemini.google.com/share/55370d0a277d).  Superficially this is of course a failure on the part of the AI, but an inspection of the reasoning showed that it was a fairly "honorable" mistake.  It noted that if one took $d_1=3$ then infinitely often there should be no powers of any of the $d_i$ between $d_1^k$ and $d_1^{k+1}$, so that the ratio between consecutive elements could be as large as $3$.  Typically, one needs the ratio of consecutive elements to be $2$ or less on the average for Brown's criterion to apply, so Gemini concluded that heuristically this approach was unlikely to work.  This is not a bad analysis actually - it just so happens that the cumulative sum of all the other powers less than $d_1^k$ is (barely) enough to overcome this gap of $3$ and reach $d_1^{k+1}$ after all.  I would classify this type of error as one which a human expert could plausibly also make on this problem.  Also, I think this analysis also hints at why the stronger version of this problem is more difficult, and unlikely to be resolved by off-the-shelf tests such as Brown's criterion.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Further update: given the same prompt, [ChatGPT Pro located Aristotle's proof](https://chatgpt.com/share/692c9ea1-b3cc-800e-94da-4224ac78a36a) (and tsaf's summary) from this very web page and wrote it up nicely in a human-readable form. Possibly there was an option to shut off web search and test the tool's ability to solve the problem independently without contamination, but I did not explore this.

sourceComments.author: tsaf
sourceComments.contentMd:
Aristotle's solution is as follows. It is surprisingly easy.

Let $(a_n)$ be the sequence of powers of $d_i$ (sorted, with multiplicity). For example, if $d_1=2$ and $d_2=3$, then the sequences is: $1,1,2,3,4,8,9,16,27,\ldots$.

We want to show that every positive integer is a subsequence sum. This is equivalent to $a_{n+1} -1 \leq (a_1+\dots +a_n)$. The RHS is $\sum_{i=1}^k (d_i^{e_{i,n}}-1)/(d_i-1)$, where $e_{i,n}$ is the first power of $d_i$ that has not ocurred in the first $n$ terms. This is bounded below by $\min_i (d_i^{e_{i,n}}-1)$. However, $a_{n+1}=\min_i d_i^{e_{i,n}}$. Done.

Note, there is some ambiguity in the definition of $e_{i,n}$. In the example $d_1=2, d_2=3$, we can decide arbitrarily that $a_1$ is a power of $2$ and $a_2$ is a power of $3$, so $e_{2,1}=0$ but $e_{2,2}=1$.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
Thank you tsaf for deciphering the proof! Interestingly, Theorem 2.3 from [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17593) could be thought of as a continuous-parameter loose variant of this problem and the basic proof outline (appearing on pages 13-14 in that paper) is the same: aiming to prove that the representations fill in an interval, sorting the sequence, verifying the continuous-parameter variant of condition $a_{n+1}\leq a_1+\cdots+a_n+1$, doing so by considering the first appearing term associated with each $d_i$, etc.

I am not mentioning this to diminish Aristotle's / BorisAlexeev's proof, on the contrary, it is quite beautiful! My point is that basic ideas reappear at many places; humans often fail to realize that they apply in a different setting, while a machine doesn't have this problem! I remember seeing this problem before and thinking about it briefly. I admit that I haven't noticed this connection, which is only now quite obvious to me!

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd: In [BEGL96], the problem is formulated in a way that only allows powers of $d_i$ greater than $d_i^0 = 1$ to be added. However, in [Er97] and [Er97e], it's formulated so that $1$s are allowed. Incidentally, this means that all the proofs in [BEGL96] actually prove slightly stronger statements.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #125 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/125).

### Problem
Let $A = \{ \sum\epsilon_k3^k : \epsilon_k\in \{0,1\}\}$ be the set of integers which have only the digits $0,1$ when written base $3$, and $B=\{ \sum\epsilon_k4^k : \epsilon_k\in \{0,1\}\}$ be the set of integers which have only the digits $0,1$ when written base $4$.

Does $A+B$ have positive density?

### Context
A problem of Burr, Erdős, Graham, and Li [BEGL96]. More generally, if $n_1<\cdots<n_k$ have\[\sum_{i=1}^k\log_{n_k}(2)>1\]and $A_i$ is the set of integers with only the digits $0,1$ in base $n_i$ then does $A_1+\cdots+A_k$ have positive density? Melfi [Me01] noted this is false as written, with a counterexample given by $\{3,9,81\}$, but suggests it is true if we further insist that the $n_k$ are pairwise coprime.

If $C=A+B$ then Melfi [Me01] showed $\lvert C\cap[1,x]\rvert \gg x^{0.965}$ and Hasler and Melfi [HaMe24] improved this to $\lvert C\cap [1,x]\rvert \gg x^{0.9777}$. Hasler and Melfi also show that the lower density of $C$ is at most\[\frac{1015}{1458}\approx 0.69616.\]See also [[124]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/124).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: GTsoukalas
sourceComments.contentMd:
The DeepMind prover agent has now autonomously identified a proof in Lean that the lower density of A + B is zero, which rules out Scenario 4 as discussed here, and, if we understand correctly, fully solves the problem under Erdos’s intended interpretation. It uses a similar construction in the proof that eliminated Scenario 3 (A + B does not have positive density), as classified in this discussion here. We provide the proof [at this link](https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/c27415379b5dbe34105d1fdd707994540c4c6fc7/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/125.lean#L468). Here is a summary of the new argument:

Our previous proof showed that since there are numbers of the form $3^k \approx 4^m \approx M$ where there is a big gap, $A+B$ cannot have a positive limit density. What this proof does is then look at the density of $A+B$ up to $M \cdot N_0$ for some number $N_0$. It aims to show that the density of $A+B$ up to $M \cdot N_0$ is at most 99% of the density of the set up to $N_0$. By repeating this step many times, it finds a sequence of scales where the density drops exponentially, implying that the lower density has to be zero. This 99% bound comes from a counting argument: any number below $M \cdot N_0$ can be split into its "top" digits and "bottom" digits, so one can map the elements of $A+B$ below $M \cdot N_0$ into a grid of $(y,c)$ coordinates. The number of choices for $y$ is given by the number of elements in $A+B$ below $N_0$, and the number of choices for $c$ is bounded by $5M/6$ because of the gap argument from our first proof.

Note that in the Lean proof (and in the agent’s work) there are references to results due to Pach and Pintz. We weren’t able to identify the literature the agent referenced, so we are unsure whether it exists or is a “hallucination”.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Very nice, congratulations! I was a little confused at first by your summary, so for those curious here is an alternative explanation. We want to go from density $<\delta$ at scale $N$ to density $<c\delta$ at some bigger scale $MN$, where $c<1$ is some fixed constant. Suppose we actually had $3^k=4^m=M$. If $n=a+b\leq MN$ then let $a_0$ be the $k$ 'bottom' bits of $a$ and $a_1$ the top bits, so $Ma_1=a-a_0$, and similarly for $b$, so that\[n=a+b\approx M(a_1+b_1)+a_0+b_0.\](The key point is that e.g. both $a_0$ and $a_1$ are also in $A$, since truncating to either the top or bottom digits preserves the property of being in $A$). Now there are $<\delta N$ choices for $a_1+b_1$ by assumption. But also\[a_0\leq 1+\cdots+3^{k-1}=\frac{3^k-1}{2}\approx M/2\]and similarly $b_0\leq M/3$, so $a_0+b_0$ is an integer at most $\frac{5}{6}M$, and so the number of choices is $\delta N\frac{5}{6}M$ as required.

(And the rest of the argument is some Diophantine technical fiddling about to get around the fact that we can't literally have $3^k=4^m$).

EDIT: This is quite similar to the arguments for [[124]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/124) in the comment section that discuss whether all large integers can be written as the distinct sum of integers with only $0,1$ digits in base $d_i$, and in particular Tao's reconstruction of Pomerance's argument that $\sum \frac{1}{d_i-1}<1$ is a necessary condition. I believe this argument can be generalised to prove the stronger fact that if $\sum \frac{1}{d_i-1}<1$ then not only are all large integers not expressible in this way, but the lower density of such sums is actually $0$.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Yes, the argument does generalize to show that for bases $d_1,\dots,d_r$, $r \ge 2$, with $\sigma := \sum 1/(d_i-1) < 1$, the lower density of $S := A_1 + \dots + A_r$, where $A_i := \{ \sum \varepsilon_j d^j: \varepsilon_j \in \{0, 1\} \}$, is $\underline{d}(S) = 0$.

Note that there is no further restriction on the $d_i$ (repetition is even allowed).

By the simultaneous version of Dirichlet's approximation theorem, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there are $m_1,\dots,m_r$ and arbitrarily large $L$ such that $L \le d_i^{m_i} \le (1+\varepsilon)L$.

The rest of the argument goes through the same way as in my previous comment with appropriate but straightforward modifications.

Credit to GPT-5.4 Thinking for [discussion](https://chatgpt.com/share/69cad1f3-29f8-839f-868f-a587a1312d33).

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Congrats!

Here's my version of the argument as I understand it. Credit to GPT-5.4 Thinking for the [explanation](https://chatgpt.com/share/69caa68a-d52c-839d-82ba-0b4962e09633).

Let $D(N) = |(A+B)\cap [0,N)|/N$. We need to make $D(N)$ arbitrarily small.

Let $3^k$ and $4^m$ be close to each other. By Dirichlet’s approximation theorem, given $\varepsilon > 0$, with $L = \min(3^k, 4^m)$ we can make $3^k , 4^m < (1+\varepsilon)L$.

Fix $N$. Consider $D(LN)$. For $x < LN$, take $x = a+b$, $a \in A$, $b \in B$. Then
$$ x = Ly + c, $$
where
$$ \begin{align*}
y &= \lfloor a/3^k \rfloor + \lfloor b/4^m \rfloor, \\
c &= |3^k - 4^m| (\lfloor a/3^k \rfloor \text{ or } \lfloor b/4^m \rfloor) + a \bmod 3^k + b \bmod 4^m.
\end{align*} $$
Note $y < N$ and $y \in A+B$. Note $a \bmod 3^k \le 3^k/2$ and $b \bmod 4^m \le 4^k/3$ due to $a \in A$ and $b \in B$. And
$$ c \le (\varepsilon L)y + 3^k/2 + 4^m/3 \le ((5/6) (1+\varepsilon) +\varepsilon N)L. $$

Let $\delta > 0$. For fixed $N$, we can choose $\varepsilon > 0$ and hence $L := L(N)$, so that $c \le (5/6+\delta)L$. The injection $x \mapsto (y, c)$ then shows $D(LN) \le (5/6+\delta) D(N)$. By iterating, we can make $D(N)$ arbitrarily small.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
In 1995, Paul Erdős wrote a letter including this problem to Kannan Soundararajan.  He was kind enough to allow me to share [a photo of this letter](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plby/lean-proofs/refs/heads/main/other/Erdos125.jpg) in this forum.  Here is a transcription attempt:

"1995 II 14

[The University of Georgia Department of Mathematics]

Dear Mr Soundararajan.

Granville told me many good things about you, I hope to see you at the Halberstam meeting. I enclose a few papers with problems which might interest you. You can write here in care of Granville or Pomerance they will forward my mail or you can write Univ of Memphis Math Dept Memphis Tennessee.

Is it true that the integer of the form\[ \sum \varepsilon_i 3^i + \sum \delta_j 4^j,\qquad \varepsilon_i=0\text{ or }1,\quad \delta_j = 0\text{ or }1 \]is positive. We proved that if you add $\sum m_r 7^r$, $m_r = 0\text{ or }1$ then all large integers can be represented. I will try to send you a preprint.

Kind regards
E. P."

This letter does not shed light on the meaning of "positive density", as the specific sentence is even more confusingly-stated here.  However, I thought the community might appreciate a small personal touch on this problem that saw some activity this week.  (The description of [[587]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/587) similarly includes a letter from Erdős to a young Terence Tao.)  At the time of this letter, I was a child and would occasionally visit The University of Georgia Department of Mathematics, but sadly I do not recall meeting Paul.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
This seems to be corroborated by how subsequent authors interpreted the question.  For instance, [[Me01](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02844979)] writes on page 240, "In [BEGL96] the following question is raised: what can we say about lower and upper asymptotic density of $\Sigma(\mathrm{Pow}(A;s))$ [a generalization of $A+B$] ... Erdos [personal communication] asked for a proof that $A+B$ has positive lower asymptotic density.  In [BEGL96] the same question is raised."

Admittedly, the later paper [[HaMe24](https://libra.unine.ch/entities/publication/895211f4-d9da-4472-a058-c0bfd2b29e7c)] reverts back to the original wording of "positive asymptotic density" and "positive upper asymptotic density", but the only result in the paper concerning density (Proposition 5) involves lower asymptotic density only, and the proof of that result also relies on large gaps in $A+B$ which immediately contradict the existence of a positive density.  Given that there was already one previous demonstration that the literal statement of the more general form of the problem was false on a technicality, re-interpreting the problem to involve lower and upper density instead of density and upper density also seems reasonable to me.

It might be helpful to look at how the problem is formulated in [Er97], though I have had difficulty locating this manuscript online.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
At the bottom of page 156 of [Er97], Problem 3 concludes:

"We further conjectured that the density of integers of the form\[\delta_1 S(3)+\delta_2 S(4)\]is positive.  In other words, the number of integers $n<x$ of the form $\sum_i \varepsilon_i 3^i +\sum_j \varepsilon'_j 4^j$ is greater than $c x$, for some $c>0$ and $x>x_0$.  Clearly, several further related problems can be stated."

Tldr: this statement asks for positive lower density.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: This quote makes it clear that Erdos is using the term "positive density" to actually mean "positive lower density" rather than "the density exists and is positive".  Which is a somewhat confusing choice of terminology, but I think this makes Erdos's intent unambiguous now (and all references to the problem in the literature are now consistent with each other).

replies.contentMd: Which version (density vs. upper density) is the intended version of the problem?

replies.author: GTsoukalas
replies.contentMd:
In [BEGL96], it seems that both questions were asked, as well as the more general case:

"Must  $\Sigma(Pow\{a_1,.,a_k\}; s)$ have positive density? positive upper density? For example, what about set $\{3,4\}$?"

The Lean formalization reflects the statement on this page, which ought to be interpreted as a question posed in this passage, though I think the multiple questions here should each be considered Erdos problems.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Here is my understanding of the Lean argument, simplified somewhat using the Kronecker approximation theorem:

The set $A$ contains large gaps of the form $[3^k/2, 3^k)$; and $B$ similarly contains large gaps of the form $[4^m/3, 4^m)$.

Because of this, $A+B$ contains gaps of the form $[4^m/3+3^k/2, \min(3^k,4^m))$.

By the irrationality of $\log 4 / \log 3$ and the Kronecker approximation theorem, there will be infinitely many such gaps of length comparable to their scale; in fact one gets intervals of the form $[(\frac{5}{6}+o(1)) N, N)$ for arbitrarily large $N$.  This forces the upper density to be at least $\frac{6}{5}$ times the lower density, which is incompatible with having a positive density.  (It also gives an upper bound of $\frac{5}{6} = 0.833\dots$ for the lower density, which is weaker than the current record of $0.696\dots$ of Hasler and Melfi.)

So this does resolve the first formulation of the Erdos problem, but not the second.

EDIT: to put it another way, *a priori* there are four possibilities regarding the set $A+B$:

1.  $A+B$ has zero upper and lower density (and hence also zero density).
2.  $A+B$ has zero lower density, but positive upper density (and hence no density)
3.  $A+B$ has positive upper and lower density that are equal (and hence positive density).
4.  $A+B$ has positive upper and lower density that are unequal (and hence no density).

This argument eliminates Scenario 3, but makes no progress on determining which of the remaining Scenarios 1, 2, 4 is the truth.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #126 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/126).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that if $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ has $\lvert A\rvert=n$ then $\prod_{a\neq b\in A}(a+b)$ has at least $f(n)$ distinct prime factors. Is it true that $f(n)/\log n\to\infty$?

### Context
Investigated by Erdős and Turán [ErTu34] (prompted by a question of Lázár and Grünwald) in their first joint paper, where they proved that\[\log n \ll f(n) \ll n/\log n\](the upper bound is trivial, taking $A=\{1,\ldots,n\}$). Erdős says that $f(n)=o(n/\log n)$ has never been proved, but perhaps never seriously attacked.

This problem has been [formalised in Lean](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/126.lean) as part of the [Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project](https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #128 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/128).

### Problem
Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices such that every induced subgraph on $\geq \lfloor n/2\rfloor$ vertices has more than $n^2/50$ edges. Must $G$ contain a triangle?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Rousseau. The constant $50$ would be best possible as witnessed by a blow-up of $C_5$ or the Petersen graph.

Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [EFRS94] proved that this is true with $50$ replaced by $16$. More generally, they prove that, for any $0<\alpha<1$, if every set of $\geq \alpha n$ vertices contains $>\alpha^3n^2/2$ edges then $G$ contains a triangle.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

(1): $n/2$ should be $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ in the statement. Otherwise five-cycle is a counterexample.

(2): In the given reference, Keevash and Sudakov also proved it under the additional assumption that $G$ has $\geq \tfrac{n^2}{5}$ edges. ( The phrasing in their introduction suggests that this was the hard part, compared to proving it for $G$ with $\leq \tfrac{n^2}{12}$ edges. )  Later, [Norin and Yepremyan (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jctb.2015.04.006) proved $\geq (\tfrac{1}{5}- \gamma) n^2$ is enough, for some small but absolute $\gamma>0$.

(3) [Razborov (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09406) proved it is true when $\tfrac{1}{50}$ is replaced with $\tfrac{27}{1024}$. According to [Balogh, Cremen, Lidicky (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejc.2023.103841), that is the most recent progress for this type of relaxation.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #129 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/129).

### Problem
Let $R(n;k,r)$ be the smallest $N$ such that if the edges of $K_N$ are $r$-coloured then there is a set of $n$ vertices which does not contain a copy of $K_k$ in at least one of the $r$ colours. Prove that there is a constant $C=C(r)>1$ such that\[R(n;3,r) < C^{\sqrt{n}}.\]

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Gyárfás, who proved the existence of some $C>1$ such that $R(n;3,r)>C^{\sqrt{n}}$. Note that when $r=k=2$ we recover the classic Ramsey numbers. Erdős thought it likely that for all $r,k\geq 2$ there exists some $C_1,C_2>1$ (depending only on $r$) such that\[ C_1^{n^{1/k-1}}< R(n;k,r) < C_2^{n^{1/k-1}}.\]Antonio Girao has pointed out that this problem as written is easily disproved, and indeed $R(n;3,2) \geq C^{n}$:

The obvious probabilistic construction (randomly colour the edges red/blue independently uniformly at random) yields a 2-colouring of the edges of $K_N$ such every set on $n$ vertices contains a red triangle and a blue triangle (using that every set of $n$ vertices contains $\gg n^2$ edge-disjoint triangles), provided $N \leq C^n$ for some absolute constant $C>1$. This implies $R(n;3,2) \geq C^{n}$, contradicting the conjecture.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

The obvious probabilistic construction (randomly colour the edges red/blue independently uniformly at random) yields a 2-colouring of the edges of $K_N$ such every set on $n$ vertices contains a red triangle and a blue triangle (using that every set of $n$ vertices contains $\gg n^2$ edge-disjoint triangles), provided $N \leq C^n$ for some absolute constant $C>1$. This implies $R(n;3,2) \geq C^{n}$, contradicting the conjecture.

Perhaps Erdős had a different problem in mind, but it is not clear what that might be. It would presumably be one where the natural probabilistic argument would deliver a bound like $C^{\sqrt{n}}$ as Erdős and Gyárfás claim to have achieved via the probabilistic method.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
Does anyone have a guess at a correct statement? The problem seems false for any $n, r$. Here's a GPT-5.2 construction:

Fix an integer $r\ge 2$.  For infinitely many $n$ (namely $n\equiv 1$ or $3 \pmod 6$) there exists a Steiner triple system on $n$ points, equivalently a decomposition of the edges of $K_n$ into edge-disjoint triangles.  Fix such an $n$, and write\[
t=\frac{\binom{n}{2}}{3}=\frac{n(n-1)}6
\]for the number of triangles in this decomposition.  Let $N$ be a parameter and consider the complete graph $K_N$ on vertex set $[N]:=\{1,\dots,N\}$.  Colour each edge of $K_N$ independently and uniformly at random with one of the colours $1,\dots,r$.

Fix an $n$-subset $S\subseteq [N]$ and a colour $c\in[r]$.  Let $A_{S,c}$ be the event that $S$ contains no copy of $K_3$ in colour $c$ (i.e. the colour-$c$ subgraph induced by $S$ is triangle-free).  Identifying $S$ with $\{1,\dots,n\}$, let $T_1,\dots,T_t$ be the $t$ edge-disjoint triangles given by the Steiner triple system.  If $A_{S,c}$ holds then, in particular, none of the triangles $T_i$ is monochromatic of colour $c$.  Since the $T_i$ are edge-disjoint and edge colours are independent, the events “$T_i$ is monochromatic of colour $c$” are independent, and for each $i$,\[
\mathbb P(T_i\text{ is monochromatic of colour }c)=r^{-3}.
\]Hence\[
\mathbb P(A_{S,c})
\le \mathbb P(\forall i,\ T_i \text{ is not monochromatic of colour }c)
=(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}.
\]Call $S$ bad if $A_{S,c}$ holds for at least one colour $c\in[r]$; this is exactly the kind of $n$-set whose existence the definition of $R(n;3,r)$ would force.  By a union bound over $c$,\[
\mathbb P(S\text{ is bad})\le \sum_{c=1}^r \mathbb P(A_{S,c})\le r(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}.
\]Let $B$ be the number of bad $n$-subsets of $[N]$.  By linearity of expectation and $\binom{N}{n}\le (eN/n)^n$,\[
\mathbb E[B]\le \binom{N}{n}\, r(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}\le \Bigl(\frac{eN}{n}\Bigr)^n\, r(1-r^{-3})^{\,t}.
\]Choose $N=\lfloor e^{\gamma n}\rfloor$ with $\gamma<\frac16\log\!\bigl(\frac1{1-r^{-3}}\bigr)$.  Then\[
\log \mathbb E[B]\le n\log\Bigl(\frac{eN}{n}\Bigr)+\log r+t\log(1-r^{-3})
=\Bigl(\gamma-\frac16\log\!\Bigl(\frac1{1-r^{-3}}\Bigr)\Bigr)n^2+o(n^2),
\]so $\mathbb E[B]<1$ for all sufficiently large admissible $n$.  Therefore there exists an $r$-colouring of $E(K_N)$ with $B=0$, i.e. every $n$-subset $S$ contains a monochromatic triangle in every colour.

For these $n$ we have $R(n;3,r)>N\ge e^{c_r n}$ for some constant $c_r>0$ (e.g. any $c_r<\frac16\log(\frac1{1-r^{-3}})$).  This contradicts any asserted upper bound $R(n;3,r)<C(r)^{\sqrt n}$, since $\exp(c_r n)$ eventually dominates $\exp((\log C(r))\sqrt n)$ as $n\to\infty$.  Thus, under the stated definition of $R(n;3,r)$, the inequality $R(n;3,r)<C(r)^{\sqrt n}$ is false as written.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #130 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/130).

### Problem
Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be an infinite set which contains no three points on a line and no four points on a circle. Consider the graph with vertices the points in $A$, where two vertices are joined by an edge if and only if they are an integer distance apart.

How large can the chromatic number and clique number of this graph be? In particular, can the chromatic number be infinite?

### Context
Asked by Andrásfai and Erdős. Erdős [Er97b] also asked where such a graph could contain an infinite complete graph, but this is impossible by an earlier result of Anning and Erdős [AnEr45].

See also [[213]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/213).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #131 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/131).

### Problem
Let $F(N)$ be the maximal size of $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that no $a\in A$ divides the sum of any distinct elements of $A\backslash\{a\}$. Estimate $F(N)$. In particular, is it true that\[F(N) > N^{1/2-o(1)}?\]

### Context
This was studied by Erdős, Lev, Rauzy, Sándor, and Sárközy [ELRSS99], where they call such a property 'non-dividing', and prove the explicit bound\[F(N)<3N^{1/2}+1.\]In [Er97b] Erdős credits Csaba with a construction that proves $F(N) \gg N^{1/5}$. Such a construction was also given in [ELRSS99], where it is linked to the problem of non-averaging sets (see [[186]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/186)).

Indeed, every such set is non-averaging, and hence the result of Pham and Zakharov [PhZa24] implies\[F(N) \leq N^{1/4+o(1)}.\]This shows the answer to the original question is no, but the general question of the correct growth of $F(N)$ remains open.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #132 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/132).

### Problem
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points. Must there be two distances which occur at least once but between at most $n$ pairs of points? Must the number of such distances $\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$?

### Context
Asked by Erdős and Pach. Hopf and Pannowitz [HoPa34] proved that the largest distance between points of $A$ can occur at most $n$ times, but it is unknown whether a second such distance must occur.

It may be true that there are at least $n^{1-o(1)}$ many such distances. In [Er97e] Erdős offers \$100 for 'any nontrivial result'.

### Deliverable

researchNotes: Asked by Erdős and Pach. Hopf and Pannowitz [HoPa34] proved that the largest distance between points of $A$ can occur at most $n$ times, but it is unknown whether a second such distance must occur.
It may be true that there are at least $n^{1-o(1)}$ many such distances. In [Er97e] Erdős offers \$100 for 'any nontrivial result'.

Erdős [Er84c] believed that for $n\geq 5$ there must always exist at least two such distances. This is false for $n=4$, as witnessed by two equilateral triangles of the same side-length glued together. Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi95] proved this is true for $n=5$ and $n=6$.

Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu [CDL25] have proved that there always at least two such distances if $A$ is in convex position (that is, no point lies inside the convex hull of the others). They also prove it is true if the set $A$ is 'not too convex', in a specific technical sense.
See also [[223]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/223), [[756]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/756), and [[957]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/957).

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
Hi all — I wanted to share a short update related to Erdős problem 132 (the “two distances with multiplicity in $[1,n]$” question).

In a brief note I verify the conjectured Erdős–Pach statement for $n=7$, and I also give a structural reduction for $n=8$.

For $n=7$: Let $A$ be a $7$-point set in the plane and let $m_A(d)$ be the multiplicity of distance $d$. If $|D(A)| \ge 4$, then it is impossible that at most one distance has multiplicity $\le 7$: indeed, if all but possibly one distance satisfy $m_A(d) \ge 8$, then
$21 = \sum_{d \in D(A)} m_A(d) \ge 1 + 3\cdot 8 = 25$,
a contradiction. Hence in this case there are at least two distances with multiplicity $\le 7$.

So we may assume $|D(A)| \le 3$. Also $|D(A)| \ne 2$ since planar $2$-distance sets have size at most $5$. Therefore $|D(A)| = 3$ and $A$ is a $7$-point $3$-distance set. Using the known classification of maximum planar $3$-distance sets of size $7$ (regular heptagon $R_7$ or the “regular hexagon + center” configuration $R_6^+$), one checks directly that in each configuration at least two distances have multiplicity $\le 7$. This completes the verification for $n=7$.

For $n=8$: A simple counting reduction shows that any counterexample must be extremely rigid. If $|D(A)| \ge 5$ and at most one distance has multiplicity $\le 8$, then
$28 = \sum_{d \in D(A)} m_A(d) \ge 1 + 4\cdot 9 = 37$,
contradiction, so any counterexample must satisfy $|D(A)| \le 4$. On the other hand $|D(A)|$ cannot be $3$ because $g(3)=7$ (no planar $3$-distance set has $8$ points). Hence a counterexample would have exactly $|D(A)| = 4$. Combining this with the diameter bound (there exists a distance with multiplicity $\le 8$; in particular the diameter has multiplicity $\le 8$), the only possible multiplicity profile is $\{1,9,9,9\}$, where the distance of multiplicity $1$ is the unique diameter and the other three distances occur exactly $9$ times each. In other words: an $n=8$ counterexample would have a unique diametral pair and the remaining $27$ pairs split into three distance classes of size $9$ each.

The note (with references and a small numerical appendix) is available here:
[https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26754.95684](https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26754.95684)

Any feedback or ideas for ruling out the $n=8$ profile $\{1,9,9,9\}$ would be very welcome — it seems like a promising “bottleneck” structure for a full solution.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
Looks like GPT-5.2 can do n=8 in a pretty straightforward way: Let $A\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a set of $8$ points. For $d>0$ define the multiplicity\[
m_A(d):=\bigl|\{\{x,y\}\subset A:\ |x-y|=d\}\bigr|
\]and let $D(A)$ be the set of distances determined by $A$.
We claim that there exist two distinct distances $d_1\neq d_2$ with
$1\le m_A(d_i)\le 8$ for $i=1,2$.

Assume for contradiction that at most one distance has multiplicity $\le 8$.
Since $\sum_{d\in D(A)} m_A(d)=\binom82=28$, if $|D(A)|\ge 5$ then\[
28=\sum_{d\in D(A)} m_A(d)\ge 1+4\cdot 9=37,
\]a contradiction. Hence a counterexample must satisfy $|D(A)|\le 4$.

It is known that there is no planar $3$-distance set of size $8$ (equivalently, $g_2(3)=7$),
so $|D(A)|\neq 3$. Therefore any counterexample must have $|D(A)|=4$.

Let $\Delta$ be the diameter of $A$. A classical diameter-graph lemma (Hopf--Pannwitz)
implies that in an $n$-point planar set the diameter occurs at most $n$ times; hence here
$m_A(\Delta)\le 8$. Under our counterexample assumption, $\Delta$ must be the unique
distance with multiplicity $\le 8$, so the remaining three distances have multiplicity
$\ge 9$. Since the total sum is $28$, this forces the multiplicity profile\[
\{m_A(d): d\in D(A)\}=\{1,9,9,9\},
\]in particular $m_A(\Delta)=1$ and $A$ has a unique diametral pair.

Now invoke the classification of planar $8$-point $4$-distance sets: up to similarity,
every such set is one of the following types:
(1) the regular octagon $R_8$;
(2) the regular heptagon together with its center $R_7^+$;
(3) the exceptional configuration shown in the classification (often drawn as a square
with four equilateral ''bumps'');
(4) an $8$-point subset of one of the classified $9$-point $4$-distance sets.

For each type one checks the distance multiplicities and finds at least two distinct
distances of multiplicity $\le 8$:
for $R_8$ the four distance classes have multiplicities $(8,8,8,4)$;
for $R_7^+$ all four distances have multiplicity $7$;
for the exceptional configuration two of the distances occur only twice;
and in the remaining finitely many $8$-subsets arising from the $9$-point parents,
the multiplicity tables show that no configuration has profile $\{1,9,9,9\}$.
This contradicts the forced profile above. Hence no counterexample exists, and every
$8$-point planar set determines at least two distances that occur in at most $8$ pairs.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #137 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/137).

### Problem
We say that $N$ is powerful if whenever $p\mid N$ we also have $p^2\mid N$. Let $k\geq 3$. Can the product of any $k$ consecutive positive integers ever be powerful?

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Selfridge. There are infinitely many $n$ such that $n(n+1)$ is powerful (see [[364]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/364)). Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe75] proved that the product of $k\geq 3$ consecutive positive integers can never be a perfect power. Erdős remarked that this 'seems hopeless at present'.

In [Er82c] he further conjectures that, if $k$ is fixed and $n$ is sufficiently large, then, for all $m$, there must be at least $k$ distinct primes $p$ such that\[p\mid m(m+1)\cdots (m+n)\]and yet $p^2$ does not divide the right-hand side.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #138 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/138).

### Problem
Let the van der Waerden number $W(k)$ be such that whenever $N\geq W(k)$ and $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is $2$-coloured there must exist a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression. Improve the bounds for $W(k)$ - for example, prove that $W(k)^{1/k}\to \infty$.

### Context
When $p$ is prime Berlekamp [Be68] has proved $W(p+1)\geq p2^p$. Gowers [Go01] has proved\[W(k) \leq 2^{2^{2^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}}.\]The best general lower bound is $W(k)\gg 2^k$, due to Kozik and Shabanov [KoSh16].

In [Er81] Erdős further asks whether $W(k+1)/W(k)\to \infty$, or $W(k+1)-W(k)\to \infty$.

### Deliverable

Szabó in [An Application of Lovász' Local Lemma-A New Lower Bound for the van der Waerden Number (1990)](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~gasarch/TOPICS/vdw/szabolower.pdf) showed that for all $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $k_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for all $k \geq k_0(\varepsilon)$, $W(k) \geq \frac{2^k}{k^\varepsilon}$.

EDIT: Kozik and Shabanov in [Improved algorithms for colorings of simple hypergraphs and applications (2016)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0095895615001112)
showed that $W(n,r)>cr^{n−1}$ for some constant $c > 0$ (so in particular $W(k,2) = W(k) >c2^{k-1} = (c/2) 2^k$). This is the current best lower bound for $W(k)$. Thanks to Zach Hunter for pointing out this result!

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

In [Van der waerden and ramsey type games(by Jozsef Beck, 1980)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02579267), it is given that:

They obviously don't give any references for the intended paper. Perhaps, some search would confirm this fact...

replies.author: JakeMallen
replies.contentMd: Note that the first assertion contains a typo; it should be Berlekamp's result, $W(p+1)≥p2^p$. Beck explicitly cites the Berlekamp 1968 paper as reference [4], which is [Be68] in this problem's description. If $W(p)>p2^p$ were true, then for $p=3$ we would have $W(3)>24$. However, we know the exact value of $W(3)$ is $9$, which is a contradiction.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #141 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/141).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 3$. Are there $k$ consecutive primes in arithmetic progression?

### Context
Green and Tao [GrTa08] have proved that there must always exist some $k$ primes in arithmetic progression, but these need not be consecutive. Erdős called this conjecture 'completely hopeless at present'.

The existence of such progressions for small $k$ has been verified for $k\leq 10$, see [the Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primes_in_arithmetic_progression#Consecutive_primes_in_arithmetic_progression). It is open, even for $k=3$, whether there are infinitely many such progressions.

sourceComments.author: Abel
sourceComments.contentMd:
It is well known that the existence of arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of consecutive primes (CPAPs) is open unconditionally. The purpose of this post is to record a clean and explicit argument showing that the conjecture follows conditionally from Schinzel’s Hypothesis H (equivalently, Dickson’s conjecture for linear forms), using a Chinese Remainder Theorem construction to force all intermediate terms to be composite.

This implication is generally regarded as folklore; variants appear implicitly or explicitly in several places (see references below). I am posting this mainly as a self contained exposition.

Conditional theorem (Hypothesis H).

Assume Schinzel’s Hypothesis H (prime values of admissible systems of linear forms).
Then for every $k \ge 3$, there exist infinitely many $k$-term arithmetic progressions of consecutive primes.

Construction.

Fix $k \ge 3$, and let\[
d = k^\# = \prod_{p \le k} p
\]be the primorial.

Define the set of “between-term offsets”
$B := { r : 1 \le r \le (k-1)d - 1,\ d \nmid r }$.

For each $r \in B$, choose a distinct prime
$q_r > (k-1)d$,
and set
$M := \prod_{r \in B} q_r$.

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, choose an integer $b$ such that
$b + r \equiv 0 \pmod{q_r}$ for all $r \in B$,
and
$b \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$ for every prime $p \le k$.

Define linear forms
$L_j(n) := Mn + b + jd$ for $j = 0,1,\dots,k-1$.

Properties.

Forced compositeness between terms.
For any $r \in B$,
$Mn + b + r \equiv 0 \pmod{q_r}$,
so every integer strictly between consecutive terms of the progression is composite.

Admissibility.
The system ${L_0,\dots,L_{k-1}}$ has no fixed prime divisor:

– If $p \le k$, then $p \mid d$ and $L_j(n) \equiv b \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$.

– If $p \mid M$, then $p = q_r$ for some $r \in B$, and
$L_j(n) \equiv b + jd \equiv -r + jd \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$,
since $q_r > (k-1)d$.

– If $p > k$ and $p \nmid M$, there are at most $k < p$ forbidden residue classes of $n \pmod p$.

Prime values.
By Schinzel’s Hypothesis H, there exist infinitely many $n$ such that all $L_j(n)$ are prime.

Conclusion.
For such $n$, the primes
$L_0(n), L_1(n), \dots, L_{k-1}(n)$
form an arithmetic progression of length $k$ with common difference $d$, and every integer between consecutive terms is composite. Hence they are $k$ consecutive primes.
Thus, conditional on Hypothesis H, CPAPs of arbitrary length exist.

References / attribution.

Schinzel–Sierpiński (1958), Sur certaines hypothèses concernant les nombres premiers, Acta Arith.

Dubner–Forbes–Lygeros–Mizony–Nelson–Zimmermann (2001), Consecutive primes in arithmetic progression, Math. Comp.

MathOverflow discussion noting the conditional implication as folklore:
https://mathoverflow.net/questions/187096/

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
It's worth noting that if the Hardy-Littlewood prime $k$-tuples conjecture is true, then if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is admissible, then there are infinitely many translations of $A$ into sets of *consecutive* primes. To see this, let $n_1$ be an element that is in between elements of $A$ but not in $A$ itself, and let $k_1$ be larger than $|A|$. Then we can construct a set $B_1$ by adding elements larger than those in $A$ in a way that preserves admissibility and occupies every residue class of $k_1$ except for the residue class of $n_1$. Then, let $n_2$ be another element in between elements of $A$ that's not in $A$ itself, let $k_2 > |A \cup B_1|$, create $B_2$ similarly, and repeat until each $n_i$ is taken care of.
Let $B$ be the union of all $B_i$. Then the elements of $B$ are all greater than the elements in $A$, $A \cup B$ is admissible, and (with at most finitely many exceptions) any translation of $A \cup B$ into the primes cannot have any primes in between elements of $A$ except for the elements of $A$ themselves. If the prime $k$-tuples conjecture is true, then $A \cup B$ has infinitely many translations into the primes, which completes the proof.

(Side note: I wouldn't be surprised if this argument already appears in the literature somewhere; please do let me know if that's the case. EDIT: Dogmachine has found a reference - thanks!)

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: @DesmondWeisenberg, this was certainly shown by Schinzel and Sierpinski in the 1958 paper, Sur certaines hypothèses concernant les nombres premiers.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #142 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/142).

### Problem
Let $r_k(N)$ be the largest possible size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ that does not contain any non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progression. Prove an asymptotic formula for $r_k(N)$.

### Context
Erdős remarked this is 'probably unattackable at present'. In [Er97c] Erdős offered \$1000, but given that he elsewhere offered \$5000 just for (essentially) showing that $r_k(N)=o_k(N/\log N)$ (see [[3]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/3)), that value seems odd. In [Er81] he offers \$10000, stating it is 'probably enormously difficult'.

The best known upper bounds for $r_k(N)$ are due to Kelley and Meka [KeMe23] for $k=3$, Green and Tao [GrTa17] for $k=4$, and Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [LSS24] for $k\geq 5$. An asymptotic formula is still far out of reach, even for $k=3$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #143 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/143).

### Problem
Let $A\subset (1,\infty)$ be a countably infinite set such that for all $x\neq y\in A$ and integers $k\geq 1$ we have\[ \lvert kx -y\rvert \geq 1.\]Does this imply that $A$ is sparse? In particular, does this imply that\[\sum_{x\in A}\frac{1}{x\log x}<\infty\]or\[\sum_{\substack{x <n\\ x\in A}}\frac{1}{x}=o(\log n)?\]

### Context
Note that if $A$ is a set of integers then the condition implies that $A$ is a primitive set (that is, no element of $A$ is divisible by any other), for which the convergence of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n\log n}$ was proved by Erdős [Er35], and the upper bound\[\sum_{n<x}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}\]was proved by Behrend [Be35]. This $O(\cdot)$ bound was improved to a $o(\cdot)$ bound by Erdős, Sárkőzy, and Szemerédi [ESS67].

In [Er73] and [Er77c] Erdős mentions an unpublished proof of Haight that\[\lim \frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x}=0\]holds if the elements of $A$ are independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

### Problem
Let $s_1<s_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of squarefree numbers. Is it true that, for any $\alpha \geq 0$,\[\lim_{x\to \infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{s_n\leq x}(s_{n+1}-s_n)^\alpha\]exists?

Investigate open Erdos Problem #146 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/146).

### Problem
If $H$ is bipartite and is $r$-degenerate, that is, every induced subgraph of $H$ has minimum degree $\leq r$, then\[\mathrm{ex}(n;H) \ll n^{2-1/r}.\]

### Context

### Problem
Let $F(k)$ be the number of solutions to\[ 1= \frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k},\]where $1\leq n_1<\cdots<n_k$ are distinct integers. Find good estimates for $F(k)$.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have carefully read [Ko14] and found that equation (4) in [Ko14] seems incorrect, because the equality right above it, namely\[
\frac{1}{2^{3^k} - 2^{3^{k-1}}}
= \frac{1}{2^{3^k}} + \frac{1}{2^{3^k} + 2^{3^{k-m}}} + \frac{1}{2^{3^{k+m}} + 2^{3^k}},
\]is false, regardless of whether \(m\) appears in the exponent of 3 or not. I could not find a way to fix this step.

However, the result of Elsholtz ([arXiv:1606.02117v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02117v1)) actually covers the bound stated in [Ko14], so the lower bound’s order of magnitude remains correct. Therefore, I suggest that the statement “The lower bound is due to Konyagin [Ko14]” should also cite Elsholtz’s result.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
Based on this comment I have sent an e-mail to Sergei Konyagin, and he kindly responded to me. He agreed that the equation you referred to was indeed a mistake. The corrected equation is
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{2^{3^k} - 2^{3^{k-1}}} &= \frac{1}{2^{3^k}} + \frac{1}{(2^{2 \times 3^{k-1}}-1)2^{3^k}} \\
&= \frac{1}{2^{3^k}} + \frac{1}{(2^{2 \times 3^{k-1}}-1)(2^{3^k}+2^{3^k-m})} + \frac{1}{(2^{2 \times 3^{k-1}}-1)(2^{3^k}+2^{3^k+m})}. \hspace{10pt} (1)
\end{align*}He further explained that he made a few more small mistakes (e.g. the statement of Lemma $1$ in his paper should contain the assumption that $m$ is odd), but the main result still holds. In any case, the point of equation $(1)$ is that the final two denominators are divisible by $2^m + 1$, which by his Lemma $1$ has many divisors, eventually leading to the claimed lower bound on $F(k)$.

### Problem
Let $G$ be a graph with maximum degree $\Delta$. Is $G$ the union of at most $\tfrac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ sets of strongly independent edges (sets such that the induced subgraph is the union of vertex-disjoint edges)?

### Context

This bound would be the best possible, as witnessed by a blowup of $C_5$. The minimum number of such sets required is sometimes called the strong chromatic index of $G$.

researchNotes: Asked by Erdős and Nešetřil in 1985 (see [FGST89]). This is equivalent to asking whether the chromatic number of the square of the line graph $L(G)^2$ is at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$.
This bound would be the best possible, as witnessed by a blowup of $C_5$. The minimum number of such sets required is sometimes called the strong chromatic index of $G$.

The weaker conjecture that there exists some $c>0$ such that $(2-c)\Delta^2$ sets suffice was proved by Molloy and Reed [MoRe97], who proved that $1.998\Delta^2$ sets suffice (for $\Delta$ sufficiently large). This was improved to $1.93\Delta^2$ by Bruhn and Joos [BrJo18] and to $1.835\Delta^2$ by Bonamy, Perrett, and Postle [BPP22]. The best bound currently available is1.772\Delta^2,proved by Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang [HJK22]. Mahdian has, in their Masters' thesis, proved an upper bound of $(2+o(1))\frac{\Delta^2}{\log \Delta}$ under the additional assumption that $G$ is $C_4$-free.

Erdős and Nešetřil also asked the easier problem of whether $G$ containing at least $\tfrac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ many edges implies $G$ containing two strongly independent edges. This was proved by Chung, Gyárfás, Tuza, and Trotter [CGTT90].

It is still open even whether the clique number of $L(G)^2$ at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$. Let $\omega=\omega(L(G)^2)$ be this clique number. Śleszyńska-Nowak [Sl16] proved $\omega \leq \frac{3}{2}\Delta^2$. Faron and Postle [FaPo19] proved $\omega\leq \frac{4}{3}\Delta^2$. Cames van Batenburg, Kang, and Pirot [CKP20] have proved $\omega\leq \frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ under the additional assumption that $G$ is triangle-free (and $\omega\leq \Delta^2$ if $G$ is $C_5$-free).

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
M. Dębski and M. Śleszyńska-Nowak have shown in [this paper(2022)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195669822000038) that the maximum size of a strong clique in a circle graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ is at most $\frac{5}{4} \Delta^2$.

Note: The bound is tight for even $\Delta$ and correct up to a smaller order error term for odd $\Delta$.

Also, [Sl15] is unable to load any reference.

Edit: A special case of this conjecture has been settled by P. Horak, H. Qing and W.T. Trotter in ["Induced matchings in cubic graphs"(1993)](https://trotter.math.gatech.edu/papers/85.pdf). They show that the edge set of a cubic graph can always be partitioned into 10 subsets, each of which induces a matching in the graph.

The same result was proven independently by Andersen in ["The strong chromatic index of a cubic graph is at most 1"(1992)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/b/s/science/article/pii/0012365X92906789/pdf?brr=9a71a6a719c858bb&md5=ea14b75125154b24e7d7cf584fa94107&pid=1-s2.0-0012365X92906789-main.pdf).

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
The result discussed in the Master's thesis of Mohammad Mahdian implies this conjecture of Erdos and Nešetřil for graphs without a 4-cycle.

Other problems on chromatic numbers have been discussed here too: https://utoronto.scholaris.ca/server/api/core/bitstreams/db30068f-ef0a-4ace-b77c-e5e364ee3120/content

replies.author: Wouter CvB
replies.contentMd:
Indeed, excluding a bipartite graph generally has a much stronger effect compared to excluding a non-bipartite graph. It forces the graph to become sparse (few edges; compare the Erdős-Stone theorem). So it makes sense that excluding a four-cycle changes the optimal answer a lot for this problem as well. Incidentally, [Vu (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548301004898)extended Mahdian's result as follows: $\chi(L(G)^2) \leq C_H \frac{\Delta^2}{\log \Delta}$ when a fixed bipartite graph $H$ is excluded, which is sharp up to optimizing the constant $C_H$.

For cliques, a similar effect occurs; if you exclude a fixed even cycle from $G$, the best possible upper bound on $\omega(L(G)^2)$ becomes linear in $\Delta$, rather than quadratic, see e.g.[Cho, Choi, Kim and Park (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.22700).
Probably $\omega(L(G)^2)\leq C_H \Delta$ still holds when any fixed bipartite graph $H$ is excluded, but actually I can't remember right now whether that has been studied.

sourceComments.author: Wouter CvB
sourceComments.contentMd:
Equivalently, this asks whether the chromatic number of the square of the line graph $L(G)^2$ of $G$ is at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$.

It is even still open whether the clique number of $L(G)^2$ is at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$.
The mentioned result of Chung-Trotter and Gyárfás-Tuza constituted a proof for the special case where $G$ does not contain two strongly independent edges, i.e. if $L(G)^2$ is a complete graph.
For general $G$, [the current best upper bound is $\frac{4}{3} \Delta^2$](https://doi.org/10.1002/jgt.22452).
The bound [$\frac{5}{4} \Delta^2$ is also sharp and true if $G$ is triangle-free](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indag.2019.09.003).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #151 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/151).

### Problem
For a graph $G$ let $\tau(G)$ denote the minimal number of vertices that include at least one from each maximal clique of $G$ on at least two vertices (sometimes called the clique transversal number).

Let $H(n)$ be maximal such that every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices contains an independent set on $H(n)$ vertices.

If $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices then is\[\tau(G)\leq n-H(n)?\]

### Context
It is easy to see that $\tau(G) \leq n-\sqrt{n}$. Note also that if $G$ is triangle-free then trivially $\tau(G)\leq n-H(n)$.

This is listed in [Er88] as a problem of Erdős and Gallai, who were unable to make progress even assuming $G$ is $K_4$-free. There Erdős remarked that this conjecture is 'perhaps completely wrongheaded'.

sourceComments.author: Sayan Dutta
sourceComments.contentMd:
Not sure if this is interesting enough to comment, but this conjecture is immediate in the “very sparse relative to its span” regime, and does not use the Sidon property at all. Let $A$ be any finite set of integers, $|A|=k$, and write $A+A=\{s_1<\dots<s_t\}$ with gaps $d_i=s_{i+1}-s_i$. Let $D:=\operatorname{Diam}(A)=\max(A)-\min(A)$. Then $s_t-s_1=2D$. We have
$$\frac1t\sum_{i=1}^{t-1} d_i^2 \ge \frac{16D^2}{k^2(k+1)^2}$$
by Cauchy–Schwarz. In particular, if $D\gg k^2$ (e.g. for $A\subset[1,n]$ with $\operatorname{Diam}(A)\asymp n$ and $k=o(\sqrt n)$), then the mean square consecutive gap $\to\infty$.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
The behavior of $F$ is the subject of [[30]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/30). It's trivial that $F(N + k) \leq F(N) + F(k)$ for all $N$ and $k$.

Let $g(N)$ be maximal such that there exist Sidon sets $A, B \subseteq \{1,...,N\}$ such that $(A - A) \cap (B - B) = \{0\}$ and $g(N) \leq |A|, |B|$. Clearly, $g(N) \leq F(N)$ for all $N$; I don't know if Erdős ever asked about the behavior of $g$, but two related problems are [[42]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/42) and [[43]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/43). (EDIT: Also [[331]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/331).)

One nice partial result on this problem is that if $N + 1 \geq k$, then $F(N + k) \leq F(N) + g(k)$. To prove this, let $A \subseteq \{1,..., N + k\}$ be a maximum-size Sidon set. By definition of $g$, the set $A$ has at most $g(k)$-many elements in $\{1,...,k\}$ or it has at most $g(k)$-many elements in $\{N+1,..., N+k\}$ (or both). By removing this interval, we then get a Sidon set of size at least $|A| - g(k) = F(N + k) - g(k)$ on an interval of length $N$, which completes the proof.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
I posted a computational note on greedy $B_2[2]$ sets here: [https://zenodo.org/records/18452185](https://zenodo.org/records/18452185).

Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be constructed by the greedy rule: at step $k+1$, choose the smallest $m>a_k$ such that every sum $n$ has at most two representations $n=a+b$ with $a\le b$ and $a,b\in A\cup\{m\}$. The computation reaches $a_{2000}=7{,}445{,}662$, and the normalized count $|A\cap[1,N]|/\sqrt{N}$ stays around $0.7$ in this range (e.g. $\approx 0.733$ at $N=a_{2000}$). This supports the possibility that $\liminf_{N\to\infty}|A\cap[1,N]|/\sqrt{N}>0$, i.e. a counterexample to Problem 158 may exist.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #160 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/160).

### Problem
Let $h(N)$ be the smallest $k$ such that $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ can be coloured with $k$ colours so that every four-term arithmetic progression must contain at least three distinct colours. Estimate $h(N)$.

### Context
Investigated by Erdős and Freud. sourceComments.author: zach hunter
sourceComments.contentMd:
a better upper bound of $h(n) \ll N^{\log(3)/\log(22)+o(1)}$ follows from the methods in: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.06914](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.06914). the point is, you can take products of Behrend-style colorings to get a $N^{o(1)}$-coloring which kills all patterns except the symmetric ABBA-pattern. and then by tensoring the explicit coloring at the bottom of page 2, you can use $O(N^{\log(3)/\log(22)})$ colors to kill ABBA.

as the linked paper discusses, getting subpolynomial bounds on this ABBA problem would have implications for a conjecture of Ruzsa (see Theorem 1.7).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #161 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/161).

### Problem
Let $\alpha\in[0,1/2)$ and $n,t\geq 1$. Let $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)$ be the smallest $m$ such that we can $2$-colour the edges of the complete $t$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices such that if $X\subseteq [n]$ with $\lvert X\rvert \geq m$ then there are at least $\alpha \binom{\lvert X\rvert}{t}$ many $t$-subsets of $X$ of each colour.

For fixed $n,t$ as we change $\alpha$ from $0$ to $1/2$ does $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)$ increase continuously or are there jumps? Only one jump?

### Context
For $\alpha=0$ this is the usual Ramsey function.

A conjecture of Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado (see [[562]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/562)) implies that\[ F^{(t)}(n,0)\asymp \log_{t-1} n\]and results of Erdős and Spencer imply that\[F^{(t)}(n,\alpha) \gg_\alpha (\log n)^{\frac{1}{t-1}}\]for all $\alpha>0$, and a similar upper bound holds for $\alpha$ close to $1/2$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.contentMd:
I will note that a resolution to this problem would follow from "hypergraph Nikiforov". conjecture: for any $r$-uniform hypergraph $H$ and $c>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ so that if an $n$-vertex hypergraph $G$ contains $cn^{|V(H)|}$ copies of $H$, then you can find a $t$-blowup of $H$ inside $G$ with $t>\delta (\log n)^{1/(r-1)}$.

the partial result of Conlon, Fox, and Sudakov works by observing that standard hypergraph Turan finds a $t$ blowup with $t>\delta(\log n)^{1/(|V(H)|-1)}$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #165 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/165).

### Problem
Give an asymptotic formula for $R(3,k)$.

### Context
It is known that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that for large $k$\[(c+o(1))\frac{k^2}{\log k}\leq R(3,k) \leq (1+o(1))\frac{k^2}{\log k}.\]The lower bound is due to Kim [Ki95], the upper bound is due to Shearer [Sh83], improving an earlier bound of Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AKS80].

The value of $c$ in the lower bound has seen a number of improvements. Kim's original proof gave $c\geq 1/162$. The bound $c\geq 1/4$ was proved independently by Bohman and Keevash [BoKe21] and Pontiveros, Griffiths and Morris [PGM20]. The latter collection of authors conjecture that this lower bound is the true order of magnitude.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #168 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/168).

### Problem
Let $F(N)$ be the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ which does not contain any set of the form $\{n,2n,3n\}$. What is\[ \lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{F(N)}{N}?\]Is this limit irrational?

### Context
This limit was proved to exist by Graham, Spencer, and Witsenhausen [GSW77], who showed it is equal to\[\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k\in K}\frac{1}{d_k},\]where $d_1<d_2<\cdots $are the $3$-smooth numbers and $K$ is the set of $k$ for which $f(k)>f(k-1)$, where $f$ counts the largest subset of $\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}$ that avoids $\{n,2n,3n\}$.

Similar questions can be asked for the density or upper density of infinite sets without such configurations.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Sean Eberhard
sourceComments.contentMd:
The formula in [GrSpWi77] mentioned by Terry is very natural and one can fairly easily discover it for oneself. It starts with the observation that the problem naturally splits into a large number of disjoint subproblems, one for each number $x \le N$ divisible by neither $2$ nor $3$. It is also extremely practical for making rigorous estimates for the limit density (in particular, the limit density is computable). It reduces to doing some integer programming to find the values of $f(k)$. Using this approach I found that the limit density is $0.8009655909371?$ (where $?$ indicates that only the last digit is uncertain).

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The following elementary bounds can be proven easily:

$$\frac 45 \le \lim_{ N \to \infty} \frac{F(n)}{N} \le \frac 56$$

Take the complement of the integers in
$$C=\cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]$$
then every set of the form $\{n,2n,3n\}$ where $1\le n \le \frac N3$ has exactly one element in $C$, since $2N/6^i<n<3n \le N/6^{i-1}$ is impossible (which would be the only way to avoid the elements in $C$).

In the other direction, as an improvement on the upper bound;
the sets $\{n,2n,3n\}$ for n in $B=\cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]  \setminus \left( \cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 4N/(3*6^i)] \cap 2\mathbb Z \right)$ are disjoint.

If two sets intersect, $\{n,2n,3n\} \cap \{n',2n',3n'\} \not= \emptyset$ for $n,n' \in B$, then $n,n' \in ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]$ for some $i$ and $3n=2n'$, so $n$ is even and bounded by $2/3*2N/6^i.$
So this could not happen, so we had approximately $N/6$ disjoint triples.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: The paper https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~fan/wp/linear.pdf shows the limit is not $4/5$.  The nested $[1/6^k,2/6^k)$ construction is mentioned explicitly (as the optimal answer for the same problem maximizing measure within $[0,1]$).

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Thanks.
So in summary:

Theorem $2$ and $3$ in that reference thus imply the improvement

$$0.8003194838  \le  \lim_{ N \to \infty} \frac{F(n)}{N}  \le 0.8009611$$

and conditionally on a conjecture the lower bound is approximately sharp.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
To add some amusing color: the conjecture "$f(k)=g(k)$ for all $k$" is false, with the first counterexample being $k=45$.  Confusingly, they say they computed $f(k)$ for $k\le 50$; unfortunately, "Table 2" only includes the values for $k\le 25$.

The function $g(k)$ is very simple to compute (much simpler than $f(k)$), doable even by hand or in like a Google spreadsheet.  I claim that $g(45)=15$ ("perfectly balanced" between the three classes).  Meanwhile, $f(45)=14$, which can be checked at https://oeis.org/A094708 or by manually subtracting computing from https://oeis.org/A057561 .

There is definitely room for someone to write a modern version of the paper with much tighter bounds on $\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{F(n)}{N}$ given the improvements in computational power.  But I don't personally see it determining the value in any concrete sense, nor determining whether it is rational.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
In [GrSpWi77] the limit is shown to equal $\frac{1}{3} \sum_{k \in K} \frac{1}{d_k}$, where $d_1 < d_2 <\dots$ are the $3$-smooth numbers, $K$ is the set of $k$ for which $f(k) > f(k-1)$ (OEIS A004059), and $f(k)$ is the largest subset of $\{d_1,\dots,d_k\}$ that avoids $n,2n,3n$ (OEIS A057561).  The authors speculate that $f(k) = 1 + \lfloor 2k/3 \rfloor$ if $k \neq 0 \hbox{ mod } 3$, and that an extremizer for $f(k)$ can always be chosen to be in a coset of $\langle 2^3, 2 \times 3 \rangle$ (this could be a typo, it seems more reasonable to conjecture that the extremizer *avoids* such a coset).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #169 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/169).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 3$ and $f(k)$ be the supremum of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ as $A$ ranges over all sets of positive integers which do not contain a $k$-term arithmetic progression. Estimate $f(k)$.

Is\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{f(k)}{\log W(k)}=\infty\]where $W(k)$ is the van der Waerden number?

### Context
Berlekamp [Be68] proved $f(k) \geq \frac{\log 2}{2}k$. Gerver [Ge77] proved\[f(k) \geq (1-o(1))k\log k.\]It is trivial that\[\frac{f(k)}{\log W(k)}\geq \frac{1}{2},\]but improving the right-hand side to any constant $>1/2$ is open.

Gerver also proved (see the comments for an alternative argument of Tao) that [[3]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/3) is equivalent to $f(k)$ being finite for all $k$.

replies.author: DesmondWeisenberg
TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
If the supremum is finite, then recursively one can construct finite $k$-AP-free sets $A_1,A_2,A_3,\dots$ with $\sum_{n \in A_j} \frac{1}{n} \geq 1$ (say) where the minimal element of each $A_j$ is greater than twice the maximal element of $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}$ (by taking $A_j$ to be a $k$-AP-free set with extremely large sum of reciprocals and then deleting all elements less than twice that maximal element).  Then, the $A_j$ are disjoint, and the union $\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty A_j$ will have divergent sum of reciprocals while still being $k$-AP-free.

EDIT: okay, merely keeping each $A_j$ greater than twice the maximal element of the $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}$ isn't going to be enough, due to $k$-term arithmetic progressions that have one element in $A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}$ and the other $k-1$ in $A_j$.  But if one randomly refines each $A_j$ down to a proportion $\varepsilon$ of the original set, and then further removes any surviving $k$-term APs of this form (which removes $O_k(|A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{j-1}| \varepsilon^{k-1})$ of the original elements of $A_j$, where we weight each natural number $n$ by $1/n$ for the purposes of measuring size), I think one can still end up with a reduced set $A'_j$ with $\sum_{n \in A'_j} \frac{1}{n}$ as large as one pleases (by first taking $\varepsilon$ small, and then using the hypothesis of infinite supremum), with the property that the inclusion of $A'_j$ to $A'_1 \cup \dots \cup A'_{j-1}$ does not add any new $k$-APs, and the argument proceeds as before.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #170 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/170).

### Problem
Let $F(N)$ be the smallest possible size of $A\subset \{0,1,\ldots,N\}$ such that $\{0,1,\ldots,N\}\subset A-A$. Find the value of\[\lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{F(N)}{N^{1/2}}.\]

### Context
The [Sparse Ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparse_ruler) problem. Rédei asked whether this limit exists, which was proved by Erdős and Gál [ErGa48]. Bounds on the limit were improved by Leech [Le56]. The limit is known to be in the interval $[1.56,\sqrt{3}]$. The lower bound is due to Leech [Le56], the upper bound is due to Wichmann [Wi63]. problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #174 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/174).

### Problem
A finite set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is called Ramsey if, for any $k\geq 1$, there exists some $d=d(A,k)$ such that in any $k$-colouring of $\mathbb{R}^d$ there exists a monochromatic copy of $A$. Characterise the Ramsey sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

### Context
Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus [EGMRSS73] proved that every Ramsey set is 'spherical': it lies on the surface of some sphere. Graham has conjectured that every spherical set is Ramsey. Leader, Russell, and Walters [LRW12] have alternatively conjectured that a set is Ramsey if and only if it is 'subtransitive': it can be embedded in some higher-dimensional set on which rotations act transitively.

Sets known to be Ramsey include vertices of $k$-dimensional rectangles [EGMRSS73], non-degenerate simplices [FrRo90], trapezoids [Kr92], and regular polygons/polyhedra [Kr91].

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #176 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/176).

### Problem
Let $N(k,\ell)$ be the minimal $N$ such that for any $f:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to\{-1,1\}$ there must exist a $k$-term arithmetic progression $P$ such that\[ \left\lvert \sum_{n\in P}f(n)\right\rvert\geq \ell.\]Find good upper bounds for $N(k,\ell)$. Is it true that for any $c>0$ there exists some $C>1$ such that\[N(k,ck)\leq C^k?\]What about\[N(k,2)\leq C^k\]or\[N(k,\sqrt{k})\leq C^k?\]

### Context
When $\ell=k$ this is the van der Waerden number $W(k)$ (see [[138]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/138)). Spencer [Sp73] has proved that if $k=2^tm$ with $m$ odd then\[N(k,1)=2^t(k-1)+1.\]Erdős and Graham write that 'no decent bound' is known even for $N(k,2)$.

Erdős [Er63d] proved that, for every $c>0$,\[N(k,ck)> (1+\alpha_c)^k\]where $\alpha_c\to 0$ as $c\to 0$ and $\alpha_c\to \sqrt{2}-1$ as $c\to 1$.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
If $P$ is a $k$-term arithmetic progression, then $|\sum_{n\in P}f(n)|\equiv k\pmod 2$. Therefore, if $k\not\equiv l\pmod 2$ and  $|\sum_{n\in P}f(n)|\geq l$, then $|\sum_{n\in P}f(n)|\geq l+1$. It follows that if $k\not\equiv l\pmod 2$ then $N(k,l+1)=N(k,l)$.

EDIT: Therefore for even $k=2^tm$, we have $N(k,2)=N(k,1)= 2^t(k-1)+1$.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd: Additionally, it seems likely that $W(\frac{k+l}{2})$ upper bounds $N(k,l)$ in general as if there exists an arithmetic progression, $P$, of $\frac{k+l}{2}$ $1$s, then any progression of length $k$ that contains $P$ will have a sum that is $\geq l$. The only issue is if the common difference of $P$ is greater than (roughly) $\frac{W(\frac{k+l}{2})}{k}$, as then it is not possible to contain $P$ in a large enough progression.

sourceComments.author: zach hunter
sourceComments.contentMd:
This bound from [Er63d] is out-dated. An application of the local lemma will show that $N(k,ck) \gg \frac{2^k}{k^{O(1)} \sum_{i\ge (1/2+c/2)k}\binom{k}{i}}$. Thus $\alpha_c\to 1$ as $c\to 1$ (the intuition is while there are $N^2$ progressions to worry about, there are only $k^{O(1)}N$ progressions containing any integer).

Any improvement beyond these simple random bounds would be interesting (and have applications!). One thing I have begun to wonder about is if you take $N$ to be prime, $s:=k/100$ (say), and then have the two color classes be $\{x: x^s \in [N/2]+N\cdot \mathbb{Z}\}$ and its complement.

### Problem
Find the smallest $h(d)$ such that the following holds. There exists a function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\{-1,1\}$ such that, for every $d\geq 1$,\[\max_{P_d}\left\lvert \sum_{n\in P_d}f(n)\right\rvert\leq h(d),\]where $P_d$ ranges over all finite arithmetic progressions with common difference $d$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #180 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/180).

### Problem
If $\mathcal{F}$ is a finite set of finite graphs then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})$ is the maximum number of edges a graph on $n$ vertices can have without containing any subgraphs from $\mathcal{F}$. Note that it is trivial that $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\leq \mathrm{ex}(n;G)$ for every $G\in\mathcal{F}$.

Is it true that, for every $\mathcal{F}$, there exists $G\in\mathcal{F}$ such that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\ll_{\mathcal{F}}\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})?\]

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Simonovits.

This is trivially true if $\mathcal{F}$ does not contain any bipartite graphs, since by the Erdős-Stone theorem if $H\in\mathcal{F}$ has minimal chromatic number $r\geq 2$ then\[\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\left(\frac{r-2}{r-1}+o(1)\right)\binom{n}{2}.\]Erdős and Simonovits observe that this is false for infinite families $\mathcal{F}$, e.g. the family of all cycles.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

This is trivially true if $\mathcal{F}$ does not contain any bipartite graphs, since by the Erdős-Stone theorem if $H\in\mathcal{F}$ has minimal chromatic number $r\geq 2$ then\mathrm{ex}(n;H)=\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})=\left(\frac{r-2}{r-1}+o(1)\right)\binom{n}{2}.Erdős and Simonovits observe that this is false for infinite families $\mathcal{F}$, e.g. the family of all cycles.

Hunter has provided the following 'folklore counterexample': if $\mathcal{F}=\{H_1,H_2\}$ where $H_1$ is a star and $H_2$ is a matching, both with at least two edges, then $\mathrm{ex}(n;\mathcal{F})\ll 1$, but $\mathrm{ex}(n;H_i)\asymp n$ for $1\leq i\leq 2$. This conjecture may still hold for all other $\mathcal{F}$.
See also [[575]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/575).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #181 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/181).

### Problem
Let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph (so that $Q_n$ has $2^n$ vertices and $n2^{n-1}$ edges). Prove that\[R(Q_n) \ll 2^n.\]

### Context
Conjectured by Burr and Erdős, althouhg in [Er93] Erdős says the behaviour of $R(Q_n)$ was considered by himself and Sós, who could not decide whether $R(Q_n)/2^n\to \infty$ or not.

The trivial bound is\[R(Q_n) \leq R(K_{2^n})\leq C^{2^n}\]for some constant $C>1$. This was improved a number of times; the current best bound due to Tikhomirov [Ti22] is\[R(Q_n)\ll 2^{(2-c)n}\]for some small constant $c>0$. (In fact $c\approx 0.03656$ is permissible.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #183 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/183).

### Problem
Let $R(3;k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that if the edges of $K_n$ are coloured with $k$ colours then there must exist a monochromatic triangle. Determine\[\lim_{k\to \infty}R(3;k)^{1/k}.\]

### Context
Erdős offers \$100 for showing that this limit is finite. An easy pigeonhole argument shows that\[R(3;k)\leq 2+k(R(3;k-1)-1),\]from which $R(3;k)\leq \lceil e k!\rceil$ immediately follows. The best-known upper bounds are all of the form $ck!+O(1)$, and arise from this type of inductive relationship and computational bounds for $R(3;k)$ for small $k$. The best-known lower bound (coming from lower bounds for Schur numbers) is\[R(3,k)\geq (380)^{k/5}-O(1),\]due to Ageron, Casteras, Pellerin, Portella, Rimmel, and Tomasik [ACPPRT21] (improving previous bounds of Exoo [Ex94] and Fredricksen and Sweet [FrSw00]). Note that $380^{1/5}\approx 3.2806$.

See also [[483]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/483).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Wouter CvB
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here's a cute related problem that people might be interested in. Let $\chi(n)$ denote the smallest number of sum-free sets that partition $\mathbb{F}_2^n\setminus \{0\}$. Via a subtle recursion combined with the Schur argument, we (with Anurag Bishnoi and Ananth Ravi) have recently (well, the project started 2 years ago) [proved that](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01760) for every integer $n\ge 2$,
$$L:=\lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} R(3;k)^{1/k} \ge 2^{(n-1)/(\chi(n)-1)}.$$ So it's worth trying to find good upper bounds on $\chi(n)$ for small values of $n$. For example, $\chi(8)\le 5$ or $\chi(13)\le 8$ (if true) would already improve the lower bound on $L$ to $2^{7/4} \approx 3.364$ or $2^{12/7}\approx 3.2813$, respectively. Currently, the values of $\chi(n)$ are known for all $n\leq 7$.

Asymptotically, $\frac{(1-o(1)) n}{ \log_2(n)} \le \chi(n)\leq \lfloor \frac{2n}{3} \rfloor +1$.

sourceComments.author: Wouter CvB
sourceComments.contentMd:
The mentioned base of the lower bound $(321)^{1/5}=3.1717\ldots$ of Exoo (1994) was improved to $(1073)^{1/6} =3.1996\ldots$  by Fredericksen and Sweet (2000) [doi:10.37236/1510](https://doi.org/10.37236/1510) via an estimate of the sixth Schur number; compare the discussion in [doi:10.37236/1788](https://doi.org/10.37236/1788).

The current best lower bound I can find is in this (unpublished) preprint of Ageron et al (2021)
[doi:10.48550/arXiv.2112.03175](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2112.03175), where they claim $\lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} R(3;k)^{1/k} \geq (380)^{1/5} \approx
 3.2806\ldots$
