problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #184 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/184).

### Problem
Any graph on $n$ vertices can be decomposed into $O(n)$ many edge-disjoint cycles and edges.

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Gallai, who proved that $O(n\log n)$ many cycles and edges suffices. The graph $K_{3,n-3}$ shows that at least $(1+c)n$ many cycles and edges are required, for some constant $c>0$. In [Er71] Erdős suggests that only $n-1$ many cycles and edges are required if we do not require them to be edge-disjoint.

The best bound available is due to Bucić and Montgomery [BM22], who prove that $O(n\log^*n)$ many cycles and edges suffice, where $\log^*$ is the iterated logarithm function.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #187 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/187).

### Problem
Find the best function $f(d)$ such that, in any 2-colouring of the integers, at least one colour class contains an arithmetic progression with common difference $d$ of length $f(d)$ for infinitely many $d$.

### Context
Originally asked by Cohen. Erdős observed that colouring according to whether $\{ \sqrt{2}n\}<1/2$ or not implies $f(d) \ll d$ (using the fact that $\|\sqrt{2}q\| \gg 1/q$ for all $q$, where $\|x\|$ is the distance to the nearest integer). Beck [Be80] has improved this using the probabilistic method, constructing a colouring that shows $f(d)\leq (1+o(1))\log_2 d$. Van der Waerden's theorem implies $f(d)\to \infty$ is necessary.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #188 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/188).

### Problem
What is the smallest $k$ such that $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be red/blue coloured with no pair of red points unit distance apart, and no $k$-term arithmetic progression of blue points with distance $1$?

### Context
Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus [EGMRSS75] proved $k\geq 5$. Tsaturian [Ts17] improved this to $k\geq 6$. Erdős and Graham claim that $k\leq 10000000$ ('more or less'), but give no proof.

Erdős and Graham asked this with just any $k$-term arithmetic progression in blue (not necessarily with distance $1$), but Alon has pointed out that in fact no such $k$ exists: in any red/blue colouring of the integer points on a line either there are two red points distance $1$ apart, or else the set of blue points and the same set shifted by $1$ cover all integers, and hence by van der Waerden's theorem there are arbitrarily long blue arithmetic progressions.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Related reference: [Conlon, David, and Jacob Fox. "Lines in Euclidean Ramsey theory." Discrete & Computational Geometry 61.1 (2019): 218-225, https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.02166v4].

They study a generalization of this question in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and their Theorem 1.1, applied with $n=2$, yields the bound $k \le 2.15\cdot 10^9$, even though it is likely that one can optimize their proof to deduce a much better upper bound.

In the last paragraph of Section 3, they mention another related open problem of Erdos, which is currently not on this website.

sourceComments.author: msellke
sourceComments.contentMd:
The 2017 paper "A Euclidean Ramsey result in the plane" of Tsaturian shows $k\geq 6$. (Note that Lemma 2.2 should say side length $3$ instead of $\sqrt{3}$.)

Additionally, Theorem 1' in the 1973 paper "Euclidean Ramsey Theorems II" by Erdos-Graham-Montgomery-Rothschild-Spencer-Straus already showed that $k\geq 5$, i.e. any such two-coloring contains either a unit-distance pair of red points or a unit distance 4-AP of blue points. The work of [Ju79] showed that one can replace "unit distance 4-AP of blue points" by "congruent copy of any desired planar 4-point configuration.

Also relatedly, (G. Currier, K. Moore & C. H. Yip, "Any two-coloring of the plane contains monochromatic 3-term arithmetic progressions", Combinatorica 44 (2024), 1367–1380) shows that any two-coloring of the plane contains a monochromatic unit length 3-AP.

(These references were located by GPT-5.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #190 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/190).

### Problem
Let $H(k)$ be the smallest $N$ such that in any finite colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ (into any number of colours) there is always either a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression or a rainbow arithmetic progression (i.e. all elements are different colours). ### Context

sourceComments.contentMd:
Gerver and Ramsey proved that there exists an infinite $S$-walk in $\mathbb{Z}^3$ that has no $5^{11}+1$ collinear points. Recent work by Lidbetter in [Improved bound for the Gerver-Ramsey collinearity problem](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.disc.2023.113718) improved this bound to $189$.
It is not known if there exists an $n$ such that there exists an infinite $S$-walk in $\mathbb{Z}^n$ that avoids $3$ collinear points.

### Problem
Must every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ contain a monotone 4-term arithmetic progression? In other words, given a permutation $x$ of $\mathbb{N}$ must there be indices with either $i<j<k<l$ or $i>j>k>l$ such that $x_i,x_j,x_k,x_l$ are an arithmetic progression?

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
On a related question -

At the end of [DEGS77], there are a number of open questions asked. One is about the value of $$\alpha=\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}} \liminf_{n\to\infty} \frac{|A\cap[1,n]|}{n}$$ and $$\beta=\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}} \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{|A\cap[1,n]|}{n} $$ where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of all infinite subsets, $A$, of $\mathbb{Z}^+$ for which there exists a permutation of $A$ that does not contain a monotone $3$-term arithmetic progression.

In [On Permutations Avoiding Arithmetic Progressions](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X10003936), the authors show that $\alpha\geq 1/2$ and $\beta\geq 1/4$ by constructing sets $A$ that have these upper and lower densities. They conjecture that these bounds are tight.

Currently, there is no known method of finding non-trivial upper bounds for $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
The current statement
"Must every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ contain a monotone $4$-term arithmetic progression $x_1 < x_2 < x_3 < x_4$"
seems to cause some confusion, see
https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/524981-Formal-conjectures/topic/Erd.C5.91s.20196/near/537227537

https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/645#issuecomment-3247874428

Is it correct that the intention here is as follows?

"Must every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ contain a monotone $4$-term arithmetic progression, i.e. given a permutation $x$, there are indices $i, j, k, l$ such that either $i< j< k <l$ or $i > j > k > l$, and $a_i, a_j, a_k, a_l$ is an arithmetic progression (in that order)."

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: From p.337 of [ErGr79]: "Let us say that a sequence $(a_1,a_2,\dots)$ has a monotone AP of length $k$ if for some choice of indices $i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_k$, the subsequence $a_{i_1}, a_{i_2}, \dots, a_{i_k}$ is either an increasing or decreasing AP".  From this reading I believe your formulation is the intended one (especially given the ensuing discussion describing finite sets of integers with no monotone 3-APs, where a key point being that the first and last elements of a 3-AP have the same parity, suggesting that rearrangements of an AP that are not in increasing or decreasing order are not considered).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #202 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/202).

### Problem
Let $n_1<\cdots < n_r\leq N$ with associated $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ such that the congruence classes are disjoint (that is, every integer is $\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ for at most one $1\leq i\leq r$). How large can $r$ be in terms of $N$?

### Context
Let $f(N)$ be the maximum possible $r$. Erdős and Stein conjectured that $f(N)=o(N)$, which was proved by Erdős and Szemerédi [ErSz68], who showed that, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[\frac{N}{\exp((\log N)^{1/2+\epsilon})} \ll_\epsilon f(N) < \frac{N}{(\log N)^c}\]for some $c>0$. Erdős believed the lower bound is closer to the truth.

These bounds were improved by Croot [Cr03b] who proved\[\frac{N}{L(N)^{\sqrt{2}+o(1)}}< f(N)<\frac{N}{L(N)^{1/6-o(1)}},\]where $L(N)=\exp(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})$. These bounds were further improved by Chen [Ch05] and then by de la Bretéche, Ford, and Vandehey [BFV13] to\[\frac{N}{L(N)^{1+o(1)}}<f(N) < \frac{N}{L(N)^{\sqrt{3}/2+o(1)}}.\]The latter authors conjecture that the lower bound here is the truth.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #203 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/203).

### Problem
Is there an integer $m\geq 1$ with $(m,6)=1$ such that none of $2^k3^\ell m+1$ are prime, for any $k,\ell\geq 0$?

### Context
Positive odd integers $m$ such that none of $2^km+1$ are prime are called [Sierpinski numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number) - see [[1113]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1113) for more details.

Erdős and Graham also ask more generally about $p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r}m+1$ for distinct primes $p_i$, or $q_1\cdots q_rm+1$ where the $q_i$ are primes congruent to $1\pmod{4}$. (Dogmachine has noted in the comments this latter question has the trivial answer $m=1$ - perhaps some condition such as $m$ even is meant.)

sourceMetadata.statementMd: Is there an integer $m\geq 1$ with $(m,6)=1$ such that none of $2^k3^\ell m+1$ are prime, for any $k,\ell\geq 0$?
sourceMetadata.statusNote: This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
researchNotes: Positive odd integers $m$ such that none of $2^km+1$ are prime are called Sierpinski numbers - see [[1113]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1113) for more details.

Erdős and Graham also ask more generally about $p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r}m+1$ for distinct primes $p_i$, or $q_1\cdots q_rm+1$ where the $q_i$ are primes congruent to $1\pmod{4}$. (Dogmachine has noted in the comments this latter question has the trivial answer $m=1$ - perhaps some condition such as $m$ even is meant.)
researchNotesMd: Positive odd integers $m$ such that none of $2^km+1$ are prime are called [Sierpinski numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number) - see [[1113]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1113) for more details.

Erdős and Graham also ask more generally about $p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r}m+1$ for distinct primes $p_i$, or $q_1\cdots q_rm+1$ where the $q_i$ are primes congruent to $1\pmod{4}$. (Dogmachine has noted in the comments this latter question has the trivial answer $m=1$ - perhaps some condition such as $m$ even is meant.)

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: Any such number, If It exists, would have to be massive. It is all but confirmed that It has to be at least ten billion, a humble lower bound.

replies.author: uona
replies.contentMd: I agree with it having to be massive, but how do you know its confirmed to be at least ten billion? Anything helps, but if it was just heuristics/computation that's okay, too.

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: Heuristics. The smallest Sierpinski number has five digits, and any number sought here should satisfy at least double the ammount of constraints, meaning I expect a number with at least double the number of digits of 78557 would be required and in fact even more than that, so at least $10^{10}$, or ten billion. Does this makes some Sense?

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: Note that the question regarding the primes $q$ is equivalent to asking for an even positive integer $m$ such that the quadratic form $g(x,y)=mx^2+my^2+1$ is free of primes whenever $x,y$ are coprime positive integers and $x+y$ odd. If we remove such restrictions and simply allows any Integers as $x,y$, such $m$ does not exist by classical results of Iwaniec (see H. Iwaniec, Primes representes by quadratic polynomials in two variables, Acta Arith. 24 (1974), 435-459), since the form $g$ obeys some caveats, including being genuinely a function of two variables, that force It to contain primes. Perhaps someone well acquainted with the analytic theory can prove such $g$ will have primes even with the aforementioned restrictions on $x,y$?

sourceComments.author: uona
sourceComments.contentMd: I have been trying at this although most sieving methods aren't very helpful. My intuition tells me such an m shouldn't exist, as it would be crt frankenstein. How would I go about uploading progress/proof to the website that I am able to get - if any?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
This site isn't suitable for hosting full preprints, the comment section is intended for informal discussions. If you have a full proof I suggest writing it up as a paper in the traditional fashion, which can be uploaded to arxiv, and you can share a link here.

If you have some partial progress or relevant data you can share this here in a comment.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: If someone could explain what is meant in the problem with the primes $q$, that would be appreciated. As It stands, $m=1$ is a trivial solution.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: This seems to be how the question was literally posed in [[ErGr80, p. 27](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf)], but perhaps requiring $m$ to be even here would exclude the trivial examples?

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
The belief Dogmachine alludes to was made explicit in [this](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022314X08000462) paper by Filaseta, Finch and Kozek. They conjecture the following:

**Conjecture.** If $m$ is such that $2^km + 1$ is composite for all $k \ge 1$, then either $m$ is a perfect power, or the smallest prime factor of $2^km + 1$ remains bounded as $k$ tends to infinity.

They furthermore show the following result, which is somewhat related to the problem at hand:

**Theorem.** For every $l \in \mathbb{N}$ there is an $m$ such that $2^km^i+1$ is composite for all $1 \le i \le l$ and all $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: On further reflection, the separate problem about Sierpinski numbers and covering systems is worthy of a separate entry, now at [[1113]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1113), which includes these remarks.

sourceComments.author: emil467q
sourceComments.contentMd: Did a shallow search from 10 billion to 100 billion - No matches ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
For what it is worth, neither [Gemini](https://gemini.google.com/share/1d429581690d) nor [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/68f54d12-29cc-800e-bd12-6f0b94a557f7) found any new references on this problem, although ChatGPT provided some links to work on Sierpinski numbers and their relation to covering congruences, while also relying heavily on this very web page as an authoritative source.

Gemini hallucinated that they could solve this question with covering congruences, but then failed (twice) to construct such a system, admitting defeat halfway through in each instance when it found that the congruences it stated did not, in fact, cover all integers, but without amending the previous portion of the report (perhaps an artefact of the next token prediction architecture).  My understanding is that for various technical reasons, Gemini DeepResearch is not able to use powerful models such as Gemini DeepThink, and so seems to be tripped up by hallucinations a little more often than some other models.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd:
The remark about Sierpinski numbers became outdated in 1993. In a note on Sierpinski numbers, Anatoly Isotov gave examples that do not entirely use coverings. Nowadays, It is believed that all Sierpinski numbers either come from covering systems, or are perfect powers.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #208 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/208).

### Problem
Let $s_1<s_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of squarefree numbers. Is it true that, for any $\epsilon>0$ and large $n$,\[s_{n+1}-s_n \ll_\epsilon s_n^{\epsilon}?\]Is it true that\[s_{n+1}-s_n \leq (1+o(1))\frac{\pi^2}{6}\frac{\log s_n}{\log\log s_n}?\]

### Context
Erdős [Er51] showed that there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[s_{n+1}-s_n > (1+o(1))\frac{\pi^2}{6}\frac{\log s_n}{\log\log s_n},\]so this bound would be the best possible.

In [Er79] Erdős says perhaps $s_{n+1}-s_n \ll \log s_n$, but he is 'very doubtful'.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
For what it's worth, if $50 \le s_n \le 10^7$, then $s_{n+1} - s_n < \log s_n$. Furthermore, $s_{n+1} - s_n < \frac{1.74 \log s_n}{\log \log s_n}$ holds for all $s_n \le 10^7$ as well, and note that $\frac{\pi^2}{6} \approx 1.64$. I am not sure how much stock one should put in this data, but okay.

By the way, under the assumption of the ABC-conjecture, the upper bound $s_{n+1} - s_n \ll_{\epsilon} s_n^{\epsilon}$ was proven by Andrew Granville (*ABC allows us to count squarefrees*, Internat. Math. Res. Notices 19 (1998), 991-1009), which can be found [here](https://dms.umontreal.ca/~andrew/PDF/polysq3.pdf).

problems.title: Erdos Problem #212: Is there a dense subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that all pairwise distances are rational?
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #212 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/212).

### Problem
Is there a dense subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that all pairwise distances are rational?

### Context
Conjectured by Ulam. Erdős believed there cannot be such a set. This problem is discussed in [a blogpost](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2014/12/20/the-erdos-ulam-problem-varieties-of-general-type-and-the-bombieri-lang-conjecture/#more-7930) by Terence Tao, in which he shows that there cannot be such a set, assuming the Bombieri-Lang conjecture. The same conclusion was independently obtained by Shaffaf [Sh18].

Indeed, Shaffaf and Tao actually proved that such a rational distance set must be contained in a finite union of real algebraic curves. Solymosi and de Zeeuw [SdZ10] then proved (unconditionally) that a rational distance set contained in a real algebraic curve must be finite, unless the curve contains a line or a circle.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #213 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/213).

### Problem
Let $n\geq 4$. Are there $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, such that all pairwise distances are integers?

### Context
Anning and Erdős [AnEr45] proved there cannot exist an infinite such set. Harborth constructed such a set when $n=5$. The best construction to date, due to Kreisel and Kurz [KK08], has $n=7$.

Ascher, Braune, and Turchet [ABT20] have shown that there is a uniform upper bound on the size of such a set, conditional on the Bombieri-Lang conjecture. Greenfeld, Iliopoulou, and Peluse [GIP24] have shown (unconditionally) that any such set must be very sparse, in that if $S\subseteq [-N,N]^2$ has no three on a line and no four on a circle, and all pairwise distances integers, then\[\lvert S\rvert \ll (\log N)^{O(1)}.\]See also [[130]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/130).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #217 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/217).

### Problem
For which $n$ are there $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no three on a line and no four on a circle, which determine $n-1$ distinct distances and so that (in some ordering of the distances) the $i$th distance occurs $i$ times?

### Context
An example with $n=4$ is an isosceles triangle with the point in the centre. Erdős originally believed this was impossible for $n\geq 5$, but Pomerance constructed a set with $n=5$ (see [Er83c] for a description), and Palásti has proved such sets exist for all $n\leq 8$.

Erdős believed this is impossible for all sufficiently large $n$. This would follow from $h(n)\geq n$ for sufficiently large $n$, where $h(n)$ is as in [[98]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/98).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #218 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/218).

### Problem
Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$. The set of $n$ such that $d_{n+1}\geq d_n$ has density $1/2$, and similarly for $d_{n+1}\leq d_n$. Furthermore, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $d_{n+1}=d_n$.

### Context
In [Er85c] Erdős also conjectures that $d_n=d_{n+1}=\cdots=d_{n+k}$ is solvable for every $k$ (which is equivalent to $k$ consecutive primes in arithmetic progression, see [[141]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/141)).

Banks [Ba23] has given a heuristic argument, assuming a quantitative form of the prime tuples conjecture, that the first statement is true, and in fact for any $c\geq 0$ and $\epsilon>0$ the number of $n$ such that $p_n\leq x$ and $d_{n+1}\geq cd_n$ is\[\frac{\pi(x)}{c+1}+O\left(\frac{x}{(\log x)^{3/2+\epsilon}}\right).\]

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

So are there any rules to accepting conditional solutions for problems reduced to well-known conjectures?  I followed my (GPT assisted) work above with a uniform Hardy--Littlewood prime $k$-tuple conjecture obtain the solution.  Obviously no one is solving that any time soon, so where would this go?

Uniform Hardy--Littlewood correlations (conjectural).
Fix $k \ge 1$ and $\lambda > 0$. Uniformly for distinct integers\[
0 \le h_1 < h_2 < \cdots < h_k \le \lambda \log x,
\]one has\[
\sum_{n \le x} \prod_{j=1}^k \Lambda(n+h_j)
=
\bigl(\mathfrak{S}(\{h_1,\dots,h_k\}) + o_{k,\lambda}(1)\bigr)\,x,
\]where $\Lambda$ is the von Mangoldt function and
$\mathfrak{S}(\{h_1,\dots,h_k\})$ is the Hardy--Littlewood singular series.

Assume this conjecture holds for all $k \ge 1$.
Fix $\lambda > 0$. For $x$ large, form the scaled point set\[
\mathcal{P}_x
=
\left\{
\frac{p-x}{\log x} \in [0,\lambda]
:\ p \text{ prime},\ x < p \le x + \lambda \log x
\right\}.
\]Then $\mathcal{P}_x$ converges in finite-dimensional distributions
to a rate-$1$ Poisson point process on $[0,\lambda]$.

Let\[
0 \le a_1 < b_1 \le \cdots \le a_m < b_m \le \lambda,
\]and let $N_i(x)$ count primes in the interval\[
(x + a_i \log x,\ x + b_i \log x].
\]Joint convergence to independent Poisson random variables with means
$(b_i - a_i)$ follows by computing mixed factorial moments\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\prod_i (N_i)_{r_i}\right]
\]averaged over $x$.
Expanding these moments reduces to sums of the above type with
$k = \sum r_i$, where the shifts $h_j$ range over a set of size
$O(\log x)$.
The conjectural asymptotic supplies the main term, and the remaining
singular-series averages match those of a Poisson process.

Let $(T_0 < T_1 < T_2 < \cdots)$ be the points of a rate-$1$ Poisson point
process on $\mathbb{R}$, conditioned to have a point at $0$.
Then the successive gaps\[
G_i = T_{i+1} - T_i
\]are independent $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ random variables.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ random variables.
For each $c > 0$,\[
\mathbb{P}(Y \ge cX) = \frac{1}{1+c}.
\]In particular,\[
\mathbb{P}(Y > X) = \mathbb{P}(Y < X) = \tfrac12,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(Y = X) = 0.
\]Indeed,\[
\mathbb{P}(Y \ge cX)
=
\int_0^\infty \mathbb{P}(Y \ge cx)\,e^{-x}\,dx
=
\int_0^\infty e^{-cx}e^{-x}\,dx
=
\frac{1}{1+c}.
\]Assume the uniform Hardy--Littlewood conjecture above.
Choose a prime $p_n$ uniformly at random among primes $\le x$ and consider
the local prime configuration in the interval\[
[p_n,\ p_n + \lambda \log p_n].
\]After rescaling by $\log p_n$, the consecutive gaps\[
\left(
\frac{d_n}{\log p_n},
\frac{d_{n+1}}{\log p_n}
\right)
\]converge in distribution to independent $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ random variables
$(X,Y)$.
Therefore, for each fixed $c > 0$, the limiting density exists and equals\[
\delta(\{n : d_{n+1} \ge c\,d_n\})
=
\mathbb{P}(Y \ge cX)
=
\frac{1}{1+c}.
\]Taking $c = 1$ gives density $1/2$.
Since ties have density zero, the same limit holds with $\ge$ replaced by
$>$, and similarly for $<$.

replies.author: John N. Dvorak
replies.contentMd:
So to review the bidding of a conditional resolution:

1) We show that ($d_n = d_{n+1} \le y$) and ($d_n = d_{n+1} > y$) have density zero:

The argument partitions at $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$.
Small equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} \le y$) are bounded by uniform Brun sieve estimates for $3$-tuples.
Large equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} > y$) are bounded using the telescoping sum
$$\sum_{m \le \pi(x)} d_m = p_{\pi(x)+1} - 2 \ll x,$$
which implies that the number of gaps exceeding $y$ is $\ll x/y$.
With the choice $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$, both contributions are $o(\pi(x))$, so
$$T(x)/\pi(x) \to 0.$$

2) We follow Banks [Ba23] who gives a heuristic argument, assuming a quantitative form of the prime tuples conjecture, that the first statement is true, and in fact for any $c\geq 0$ and $\epsilon>0$ the number of $n$ such that $p_n\leq x$ and $d_{n+1}\geq cd_n$ is\[\frac{\pi(x)}{c+1}+O\left(\frac{x}{(\log x)^{3/2+\epsilon}}\right).\]

sourceComments.author: John N. Dvorak

Followed Terry Tao's suggestion above to use sieve theory methods.

After several iterations (and outstanding help from Kimi K2, Grok, and Gemini) on the optimal splitting threshold, the proof is now complete: equal consecutive prime gaps have asymptotic density zero, thereby reducing Erdős Problem #218 to showing that each strict inequality $d_{n+1} > d_n$ and $d_{n+1} < d_n$ has density $1/2$.

The argument partitions at $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$.
Small equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} \le y$) are bounded by uniform Brun sieve estimates for $3$-tuples.
Large equal gaps ($d_n = d_{n+1} > y$) are bounded using the telescoping sum
$$\sum_{m \le \pi(x)} d_m = p_{\pi(x)+1} - 2 \ll x,$$
which implies that the number of gaps exceeding $y$ is $\ll x/y$.
With the choice $y = (\log x)^{4/3}$, both contributions are $o(\pi(x))$, so
$$T(x)/\pi(x) \to 0.$$

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #222 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/222).

### Problem
Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of integers which are the sum of two squares. Explore the behaviour of (i.e. find good upper and lower bounds for) the consecutive differences $n_{k+1}-n_k$.

### Context
Erdős [Er51] proved that, for infinitely many $k$,\[ n_{k+1}-n_k \gg \frac{\log n_k}{\sqrt{\log\log n_k}}.\]Richards [Ri82] improved this to\[\limsup_{k\to \infty} \frac{n_{k+1}-n_k}{\log n_k} \geq 1/4.\]The constant $1/4$ here has been improved, most lately to $0.868\cdots$ by Dietmann, Elsholtz, Kalmynin, Konyagin, and Maynard [DEKKM22].

The best known upper bound is due to Bambah and Chowla [BaCh47], who proved that\[n_{k+1}-n_k \ll n_k^{1/4}.\]The differences are listed at [A256435](https://oeis.org/A256435) on the OEIS.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #233 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/233).

### Problem
Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$, where $p_n$ is the $n$th prime. Prove that\[\sum_{1\leq n\leq N}d_n^2 \ll N(\log N)^2.\]

### Context
Cramer [Cr36] proved an upper bound of $O(N(\log N)^4)$ conditional on the Riemann hypothesis. Selberg [Se43] improved this slightly (still assuming the Riemann hypothesis) to\[\sum_{1\leq n\leq N}\frac{d_n^2}{n}\ll (\log N)^4.\]The prime number theorem immediately implies a lower bound of\[\sum_{1\leq n\leq N}d_n^2\gg N(\log N)^2.\]This would imply in particular that $d_n\ll n^{1/2}\log n$ for all $n$, which is known only the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The values of the sum are listed at [A074741](https://oeis.org/A074741) on the OEIS.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Note that a positive solution to this problem would automatically imply the prime gap bound $d_n \ll n^{1/2} \log n$, which was established by Cramer under the Riemann hypothesis but is not known in general; even the strongest forms of the prime tuples conjecture are not known to imply this bound.  So it is extremely unlikely that one will be able to establish this result even assuming the prime tuples conjecture, if RH is not also assumed.  (*Possibly* one might be able to make some progress assuming *both* RH and the prime tuples conjecture, but it is not clear how these rather different inputs could be combined.)

EDIT: [this advice given on the wiki](https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/wiki/AI-contributions-to-Erd%C5%91s-problems#i-think-i-managed-to-get-my-favorite-ai-tool-to-solve-an-open-erd%C5%91s-problem--what-do-i-do-next) is relevant to this discussion.

Here is the solution verification using Gemini 3 Pro and ensuring it is satisfied with the proof: https://gemini.google.com/share/e4c5b5c457a1

Solution summary:
It converts $\sum d_n^2$ into a count of prime-free intervals and uses a standard sieve upper bound for prime-free intervals assuming a uniform Hardy–Littlewood k-tuple asymptotic. For rigor, I also prompted ChatGPT 5.2 Pro for a proof for the Selberg upper-bound sieve and corrected it with the feedback from Gemini 3 Pro.

Disclosure: I'm not a mathematician by profession. Do you see a gap that I may have missed here?

The reason is the conversation is phrased like this is an *exercise with known solution*, and GPT-5.2 Pro is operating on the mindset that, even if its solution has gaps, it should be fixable (since it’s an *exercise*). This is a dangerous mindset for LLMs to be in. I’ll find time to check it later, though.

replies.contentMd:
Hello, yes the part where it assumes the lemma was followed-up right after to be proven and it does it with some errors caught by Gemini. After feeding it the critique from Gemini, it improves the proof contingent on the Hardy-Littlewood k-tuple conjecture holding uniformly.

I even pasted the full chat from ChatGPT to Gemini again and the evaluation remains consistent: https://gemini.google.com/share/df2deded69d3

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
On page 87 (just above Theorem 3) of "[Gaps between primes, and the pair correlation of zeros of the zeta-function](http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/aa/aa41/aa4118.pdf#page=2)" by Heath-Brown, he conjectures this same result but with the exact asymptotic constant $2$.

Also, [Theorem 8 here](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.07609#page=16) (see equation (9) on page 3 for the definition of $\mathcal{C}(x)$) in "[Distribution of Large Gaps Between Primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.07609) by Funkhouser & Goldston & Ledoan almost derives that asymptotic conditional on some strong/uniform Hardy-Littlewood prime k-tuples conjectures.  (The missing ingredient is no very large gaps).

replies.author: Bhavya Patwa
replies.contentMd: You're right, thank you for coming with concrete data! My attempts were indeed futile and the LLM perfectly reconstructed past solutions probably learned from these papers. I will keep that in mind and the [AI disclaimer](https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/wiki/AI-contributions-to-Erd%C5%91s-problems) before I submit any solutions in the future.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: While I think one should be *rather careful* posting AI solutions here, I also think it is useful to know that this problem follows from Hardy-Littlewood tuple (and prime gap?) conjectures. Other problems have also had similar comments.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
After some back-and-forth with [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/696cc701-c5f0-8010-b9ef-6167745cea5b), it has come to believe that Hardy-Littlewood prime $k$-tuple conjecture was NOT shown to imply the problem either in Heath-Brown, Funkhouser-Goldston-Leodan, or Bhavya Patwa's GPT-5.2 Pro's shared chat. Feel free to scrutinize further, though!

Note: what Boris said regarding "HL + large gap tail" is still correct from Theorem 8 in FGL.

For Patwa: your shared chat does claim HL implies problem, which is still incorrect.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Cramer's bound was sharpened slightly to $\sum_{1 \leq n \leq N} d_n^2/n \ll \log^4 N$ (still assuming RH) in A. Selberg, On the normal density of primes in small intervals, and the difference between consecutive primes, Arch. Math. Naturvid. 47 (6), 87–105 (1943).  Only off from the expected truth by one power of log.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.contentMd:
Erdős also asks this question [here](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1940-10.pdf) (on page 440). Cramér's conditional proof of the bound $O(N (\log N)^4)$ is [here](https://www.impan.pl/pl/wydawnictwa/czasopisma-i-serie-wydawnicze/acta-arithmetica/all/2/1/93277/on-the-order-of-magnitude-of-the-difference-between-consecutive-prime-numbers) at the end of the paper.

Let $f(n)$ count the number of solutions to $n=p+2^k$ for prime $p$ and $k\geq 0$. Is it true that $f(n)=o(\log n)$?

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
Hooley in [this paper](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/zamm.19780580831) has proved under the assumption of the extended Riemann Hypothesis, that integers $n$ such that for all $1<2^k<n$ the number $n-2^k$ is prime < $O(x^{1-\lambda+\epsilon})$ for any sufficiently small positive number $\epsilon$, where $\lambda = \Pi_p (1- \frac{1}{p(p-1)})$.

This was further improved by Narkiewicz in [this paper](https://eudml.org/doc/263850) to $O(x^{1-\lambda/\log2 +\epsilon})$ under the same assumption.

P.S. Improving on the result of Mientka and Weitzenkamp, Uchiyama and Yorinaga have proved there are no other such $n\leq 2^{77}$ in a two paper series - [[1]](https://www.math.okayama-u.ac.jp/mjou/mjou1-46/mjou_pdf/mjou_19/mjou_19_129.pdf) and [[2]](https://www.math.okayama-u.ac.jp/mjou/mjou1-46/mjou_pdf/mjou_20/mjou_20_041.pdf).

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let $E_2(N)$ denote the number of natural numbers $n \leq N$ for which $n - 2^k$ is a prime number for all $k$ with $1 \leq k \leq \log_2 n$. Vaughan, [in this paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022314X73900590), has showed that for some suitable positive number $c$ and for every sufficiently large $N$,\[E_2(N) < N \exp (- \frac{c \log N \log \log \log N}{\log \log N})\]Furthermore, Mientka and Weitzenkamp in [this paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021980069800670) has verified that $7, 15, 21, 45, 75,$ and $105$ are the only values of $n$ for which $n - 2^k$ is a prime number for all $k$ with $1 \leq k \leq \log_2 n$ for $n \leq 2^{44}$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: Standard probabilistic heuristics suggest that the answer to this question is true, but only barely, and proving this rigorously seems well out of reach of current technology.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Why it suggests it barely?
If $2^k<n<2^{k+1}$, then except for $n-2^k$, all values to check are of the form $n-2^i>2^{k-1}$.
Hence the number of primes of the form $n-2^i$ is on average bounded by $3.$
Of course, there is some positive correlation on the chance, due to e.g. even vs odd, but so wondering which more detailed heuristical thoughts you had.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: For each $n$ in this range, there are $k$ values to check, each of which has about a $1/k$ chance of being prime, so the chance that they are all prime is about $1/k^k$... which dominates the total number of $n$ in this range, which is $2^k$ or so, but not by a huge margin... $\exp(-k \log k)$ versus $\exp(k)$.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Ok, the terms barely and huge margin are here maybe subjective.

This reasoning could apply to the "Erdos could not even prove..." part as well.
Since $\exp(k) \exp(-k \log k) = \exp(- \Theta(k \log k))$, the chance of having really large counterexamples is very small.
But starting from $n>10^4$, it is indeed still a chance, and a formal proof for excluding that is far from obvious.

One deduces similar formulas for the probability (e.g. using Poisson approximation) that it is above $c \log k$, and since we are speaking about the limit, that should be the case.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I guess for me "barely" is with regards to how optimal the bounds need to be in order to conclude the result.  For instance if the heuristic prediction for density was $\exp(-k \log k)$ and one managed somehow to get an argument that gave an upper bound of the shape $\exp(-k/\log k)$, this would usually be considered extremely close to the optimal bound, but in this case would be insufficient to conclude (even heuristically) that there are only finitely many counterexamples.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: It seems likely that one could deduce this from a sufficiently uniform version of the prime tuples conjecture.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
Indeed, looks like the following argument would work:

Let $c_1,c_2>0$ and put $c=\lfloor c_2\rfloor$. We seek a block of $>c_1\log x$ consecutive primes $\le x$ whose adjacent gaps all exceed $c$. A natural conditional route is to assume a short-interval, uniformly averaged Hardy--Littlewood $k$-tuple conjecture at the scale $T\asymp(\log x)^2$: for each fixed $m\ge1$, uniformly over intervals $I=[u,u+T]\subset[x/2,x]$ and distinct shifts $H=\{h_1,\dots,h_m\}\subset[0,T+c]$,\[
\#\{n\in I:\ n+h_i\ \text{prime for all }i\}
=
(1+o(1))\,\mathfrak S(H)\,\frac{T}{(\log x)^m},\]as $x\to \infty$, with $o(1)$ uniform in $I,H$. (One can weaken “uniform in $I$” to “for all but $o(1)$ of such intervals”, consistent with Maier-type irregularities.) This hypothesis implies both concentration of the prime count $N(I)$ around $T/\log x$ and Poisson-type statistics for rare local patterns such as prime pairs at separations $\le c$ inside a typical interval of length $T$.

Take $T=A(\log x)^2$ with fixed $A>c_1$ and partition $[x/2,x]$ into disjoint intervals $I_j$ of length $T$. By the $m=1,2$ cases, $N(I_j)$ has mean $\sim A\log x$ and variance $O(\log x)$, so $N(I_j)\ge c_1\log x$ for all but $o(1)$ of the $I_j$ (Chebyshev). Let $B(I_j)$ be the number of prime pairs $(p,q)\subset I_j$ with $0<q-p\le c$. Using the fixed-$m$ cases of the conjecture and inclusion--exclusion/moment methods (à la Gallagher), one gets that $B(I_j)$ converges in distribution to $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ with $\lambda=A\sum_{h=1}^c \mathfrak S(\{0,h\})$, hence $\mathbb P(B(I_j)=0)\to e^{-\lambda}>0$ for a positive proportion of intervals. Therefore some $I_j$ simultaneously satisfies $N(I_j)\ge c_1\log x$ and $B(I_j)=0$; the primes in that interval are automatically consecutive in the global sequence and, since there is no pair within distance $\le c$, every adjacent prime gap inside the block exceeds $c$, yielding $>c_1\log x$ consecutive primes $\le x$ with all pairwise differences $>c_2$.

sourceComments.author: Yongxi Lin
sourceComments.contentMd: "This is well-known if $c_1$ is sufficiently small." Does this mean that $\exists \epsilon, \forall 0 < c_1<\epsilon, \forall 0 < c_2, ...$ or $\forall 0 < c_2, \exists \epsilon, \forall 0 < c_1 <\epsilon...$? The first one is clearly stronger becauce $\epsilon$ does not depend on $c_2$.

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: I undertand It as the first option, or Else Erdos would likely had use Epsilon notation Instead of $c$'s.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I think only the weaker second formulation is easy to establish.  (There are $\sim x/\log x$ prime gaps in $[x/2,x]$, of which $O(c_2 x/\log^2 x)$ of them are of size $\leq c_2$ by standard sieve theory bounds; hence, by the pigeonhole principle, one can find a sequence of $\gg \frac{1}{c_2} \log x$ consecutive gaps in $[x,2x]$ of size $> c_2$, giving the second form (in fact one can take $c_1$ proportional to $1/c_2$.))  The stronger first version might still be true (it seems plausible from standard probabilistic heuristics, which in fact predict consecutive runs as large as $\gg_{c_2} \log x \log\log x$), but looks much harder to establish unconditionally.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #241 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/241).

### Problem
Let $f(N)$ be the maximum size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that the sums $a+b+c$ with $a,b,c\in A$ are all distinct (aside from the trivial coincidences). Is it true that\[ f(N)\sim N^{1/3}?\]

### Context
Originally asked to Erdős by Bose. Bose and Chowla [BoCh62] provided a construction proving one half of this, namely\[(1+o(1))N^{1/3}\leq f(N).\]The best upper bound known to date is due to Green [Gr01],\[f(N) \leq ((7/2)^{1/3}+o(1))N^{1/3}\](note that $(7/2)^{1/3}\approx 1.519$).

More generally, Bose and Chowla conjectured that the maximum size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with all $r$-fold sums distinct (aside from the trivial coincidences) then\[\lvert A\rvert \sim N^{1/r}.\]This is known only for $r=2$ (see [[30]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/30)).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #242 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/242).

### Problem
For every $n>2$ there exist distinct integers $1\leq x<y<z$ such that\[\frac{4}{n} = \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}.\]

### Context
The [Erdős-Straus conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Straus_conjecture). Perhaps the first place it appears in the literature is in a paper of Obláth [Ob50] (submitted in 1948), which describes it as a conjecture of Erdős.

The existence of a representation of $4/n$ as the sum of at most four distinct unit fractions follows trivially from a greedy algorithm.

researchNotes: The Erdős-Straus conjecture. Perhaps the first place it appears in the literature is in a paper of Obláth [Ob50] (submitted in 1948), which describes it as a conjecture of Erdős.
The existence of a representation of $4/n$ as the sum of at most four distinct unit fractions follows trivially from a greedy algorithm.

Schinzel conjectured (see [Si56]) the generalisation that, for any fixed $a$, if $n$ is sufficiently large in terms of $a$ then there exist distinct integers $1\leq x<y<z$ such that\frac{a}{n} = \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}.When $a=5$ this conjecture is due to Sierpiński [Si56]. For more background and results on this generalisation see Pomerance and Weingartner [PoWe25].
It suffices to prove this when $n$ is prime. This has been verified for all $n\leq 10^{18}$ [MiDu25].

There are many partial results, some of which are listed below.- Obláth [Ob50] noted it is true if $n+1$ is divisible by a prime $\equiv 3\pmod{4}$. This implies almost all $n$ have the required decomposition. - Arguing via parametric solutions, Mordell [Mo69] proved it is true for all $n$ except those congruent to one of $\{1,49,121,169,289,361\}$ modulo $840$. - Terzi [Te71] extended this to prove that it is true for all $n$ except those congruent to one of $198$ possible bad congruences modulo $120120$. - Vaughan [Va70] proved that the number of exceptions in $[1,x]$ is\leq x \exp(-c(\log x)^{2/3})for some constant $c>0$. - This conjecture is equivalent (see Theorem 1 of [BlEl22]) to the statement that, for any prime $p$, there exist integers $a,c,d\geq 1$ such that either $p\equiv -a/c\pmod{4acd-1}$ or $p\equiv -\frac{4c^2d+1}{k}\pmod{4cd}$ for some $k\mid 4c^2d+1$. - Bright and Loughran [BrLo20] have shown there is no Brauer-Manin obstruction to the existence of solutions. - If $f(n)$ counts the number of solutions then Elsholtz and Tao [ElTa13] have proved\sum_{p\leq N}f(p)=N(\log N)^{2+o(1)}and $f(p)\leq p^{3/5+o(1)}$ for all primes $p$. - Elsholtz and Planitzer [ElPl20] have proved that for almost all $n$f(n) \geq (\log n)^{\log 6+o(1)}.

sourceComments.author: leonchlon
sourceComments.contentMd:
I've been formalizing Erdős-Straus in Lean, 531 formalized items, 484 complete, hope it might be of use to one of you to finish this off: https://github.com/leochlon/erdstrau

Sorry-free lean4 proofs including: ES for $n = 420k + r$ with $k$ odd, $r \in \{121, 169, 289, 361\}$; all $n \equiv 529 \pmod{840}$ via CRT (174 declarations, witnesses like $(133, 23460, 71764140)$ for $n=529$); 348/420 coverage; 20 conditional certificates for $n \equiv 1 \pmod{840}$ (reducing to divisor conditions); and a formal refutation of one proposed ED2 covering scheme.

Showed the full conjecture reduces to one construction: given $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and $s^2 + p = qk$, find $\delta, b, c$ with $(4b-1)(4c-1) = 4p\delta + 1$ and $\delta \mid bc$. Setting $b = (q+1)/4$ works for small $q$; general case open.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
See the remarks for some well-known parametric solutions (which I assume your formalisation is using). In particular it's not too hard to prove via elementary methods that this conjecture follows from (and is in fact equivalent to) the statement that for any prime $p$, there exist integers $a,c,d\geq 1$ such that either $p\equiv -a/c\pmod{4acd-1}$ or $p\equiv -\frac{4c^2d+1}{k}\pmod{4cd}$ for some $k\mid 4c^2d+1$. This might be nice, and not too hard, to formalise, see Theorem 1 of [BlEl22] for a proof of the equivalence.

Using this you can prove the conjecture for many congruence classes, and can efficiently check it's true for all small primes $p$. One can certainly refine Mordell's modulo $840$ conditions for example - this was already done by Terzi in 1971 to a modulo $120120$ condition. I'm sure that by continuing computations one can forever narrow down the congruential conditions, but I don't think this is a viable path to the full conjecture.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: In case anyone is curious, [this file](https://github.com/leochlon/erdstrau/blob/5d0f0467ef8a0a87b708b54c40213697ce4d66b6/ESLean/Residues/R529.lean) contains the claimed proof of "Full CRT coverage for n ≡ 529 (mod 840)".  I think a quick look at this file is highly informative as to the source and veracity of the claimed results.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Aha, thanks for pointing that out Boris. So this isn't actually a proof of anything - it's just verifying the conjecture for a collection of small $n$, and appeals to 'periodicity' to extend this to an infinite congruence class. This does not work, since the statement is obviously not periodic, so I'm not sure what they have in mind here.

I do think, however, that a genuine formalisation of the known congruence classes cases (and/or the equivalence mentioned in my earlier comment) would be valuable, and presumably quite straightforward to do automatically, since this is just messing about with elementary identities.

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
Li Delang in [his paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022314X81900391) has proved that for any given positive integers $N$ and $k$ the number of integers $n<N$ for which the equation $4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z$ is unsolvable in positive integers x, y, z is not greater than $cN/(\log N)^k$, where $c$ is a constant depending only on $k$.

Also previously, Vaughan in [this paper](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematika/article/abs/on-a-problem-of-erdos-straus-and-schinzel/6622BF4A083315C30DF1114A6F600223) has given the upper bound on the count of possible exceptions as $N/\exp(c(\log N)^{2/3})$ for a positive constant $c$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
In the case $a = 4$, the conjecture has been verified for $n<5000$ by Straus, $n<8000$ by Bernstein [here](https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN243919689_0211?tify=%7B%22pages%22%3A%5B5%5D%2C%22pan%22%3A%7B%22x%22%3A0.495%2C%22y%22%3A0.757%7D%2C%22view%22%3A%22info%22%2C%22zoom%22%3A0.33%7D), $n<20000$ by Shapiro, $n<106128$ by Oblath in [Ob49], $n<171649$ by Rosati [here](http://www.bdim.eu/item?id=BUMI_1954_3_9_1_59_0&fmt=pdf), $n<400000$ by C. Ko, C. Sun and S. J. Chang in [KoSuCh64], $n<10^7$ by Yamamoto in [Ya65], $n<1.1 \times 10^7$ by Jollensten in [Jo??] and $n \leq 10^{17}$ by Salez [here](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.6307).

[Ob49]: R. Oblath, "Sur l'équation diophantienne $4/n = 1/x_1 + 1/x_2 + 1/x_3$" , Mathesis, 59 (1949), 308-316.
[KoSuCh64]: Chan Ko, Chi Sun, AND S. J. Chang, On equations $4/n = l/x + l/y + l/z$, Acta Sci. Natur. Szechuanensis 2 (1964), 21-35.
[Ya65]: K. Yamamoto, " On the diophantine equation $4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z$", Mem. Fac. Sci. Kyushu University Ser. A, 19 (1965), 37-47.
[Jo??]: R. M. Jollensten, A note on the Egyption problem, in “Proceedings of the Seventh Southeastern Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing” (F. Hoffman et al., Eds.), pp. 578-589, Winnipeg Utilitas Math. Publ. Inc., Winnipeg.

There is a lot of literature on this conjecture. Surprisingly, I came across a [paper](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/368513385_A_simple_direct_proof_of_the_Erdos--Straus_conjecture) which claims to solve the Erdos-Straus Conjecture. Another [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.07367v1) claims to be an "almost" complete proof of the Generalized Erdos Straus Conjecture.

I am highly skeptical of both these papers, but professionals can take a look at'em.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Thanks! Yes, this conjecture has attracted quite a few 'proofs' over the years. Of those that I have looked at, none have seemed credible.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #243 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/243).

### Problem
Let $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be a sequence of integers such that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}^2}=1\]and $\sum\frac{1}{a_n}\in \mathbb{Q}$. Then, for all sufficiently large $n\geq 1$,\[ a_n = a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1.\]

### Context
Erdős and Straus [ErSt64] proved that if $\lim a_n/a_{n-1}^2=1$ and $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is rational, and $a_n$ does not satisfy the recurrence, then\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} \frac{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]}{a_{n+1}}\left(\frac{a_n^2}{a_{n+1}}-1\right)>0.\]A sequence satisfying the reucrrence $a_n = a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1$ is known as [Sylvester's sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester%27s_sequence).

Duverney [Du01] proved a weaker version of this problem: if\[\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^2}-1\right)\]converges then $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is rational if and only if\[a_{n}=a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1\]for all large $n$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Such sequences can be described (after discarding a finite segment) via a deterministic recurrence applied to an initial pair $b,c$ of natural numbers; in particular, there are only countably many such sequences.

Indeed, if $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is rational, write $\frac{b_n}{c_n} = \sum_{n' \geq n} \frac{1}{a_n}$, then $\frac{b_n}{c_n} = \frac{1}{a_n} + \frac{b_{n+1}}{c_{n+1}}$.  Writing $b_n a_n = c_n + h_n$, we have $b_n | c_n + h_n$, $b_{n+1} = h_n$, and $c_{n+1} = c_n \frac{c_n+h_n}{b_n}$.  The condition $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}^2}=1$ means that $a_{n+1} = (1+o(1)) a_n^2$, that $\frac{b_n}{c_n} = (1+o(1)) \frac{1}{a_n}$, and thus $\frac{b_{n+1}}{c_{n+1}} = (1+o(1)) \frac{b_n^2}{c_n^2}$, which after some more algebra leads to $h_n = (1+o(1)) b_n$.  Because of this, for $n$ sufficiently large one can solve for $\frac{c_n+h_n}{b_n}$ exactly as the nearest integer $\lfloor \frac{c_n}{b_n}+1 \rceil$ to $\frac{c_n}{b_n}+1$, and so the pair $(b_n,c_n)$ iterates via the recurrence

$$ (b_{n+1}, c_{n+1}) = (b_n \lfloor \frac{c_n}{b_n}+1 \rceil - c_n, c_n \lfloor \frac{c_n}{b_n}+1 \rceil).$$
This iteration yields a sequence of the desired form if and only if $\mathrm{dist}(c_n/b_n, {\mathbf Z}) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ (or equivalently $b_{n+1} = (1+o(1)) b_n$).   If the $b_n$ stayed bounded, then this would force the $b_n$ to eventually become constant, at which point the $c_n$ must be multiples of $b_n$ and one can check that one becomes a Sylvester sequence at that point.  So the question comes down to whether there is a solution to the above recurrence in which the $b_{n+1}/b_n$ tend to $1$ but never actually equal $1$ (if $b_{n+1}=b_n$ one can check that $b_m = b_n$ for all $m > n$).

Heuristically, any such sequence should have a zero probability of $b_{n+1}/b_n$ converging to 1 (it requires $c_n/b_n$ to be inexplicably close to an integer for all sufficiently large $n$), which indicates that the answer to this question is "no" [EDIT: I meant "yes"]; but the recurrence looks quite difficult to analyze (especially as the $c_n$ grow doubly exponentially fast) and I see no plausible way to rigorously prove the claim.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
Very similar observations were made by Junnosuke Koizumi in [this recent preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05933). He formulated them as a conditional result: that the claim holds if and only if (what he calls) a "pseudo-greedy expansion" of a rational number (a variant of a greedy Egyptian fraction algorithm) always terminates. He gives some numerical evidence for the opposite heuristics than you, checking his Conjecture 6 for rationals $p/q$ such that $p,q\leq100000$ and also reasoning probabilistically "on average" (Remark 17). Thus, the question might in fact likely have positive answer, but it is hard to say what really is a good heuristics here.

Slightly off-topic: I suggested exploiting a bit more the connection between (ir)rationality questions and greedy algorithms for (restricted) Egyptian fractions, under somewhat open-ended [[282]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/282).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Thanks for the reference!  I misspoke in my previous reply, I was focused on the question on whether a counterexample (non-Sylvester sequence) existed, which of course is the negation of the original problem, so I agree with Koizumi's prediction that the answer here is positive.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: Now I see what you meant. I apologize for not reading the last paragraph carefully.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: After reading through Koizumi's manuscript I see that basically all the observations I made here are contained in that paper already.  Still, good to have it mentioned on this problem page.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: This type of problem is one step above other arithmetical problems, like, say, Erdos Straus conjecture, in terms of difficulty. Because  the latter at least can have at most countably many counterexampĺes, but here uncountably many exceptions could exist, making the prospect of eliminating every single one of them very ambitious.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: Progress here may be linked to progress on [Mahler's 3/2 problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_3/2_problem).  A key difficulty is that theoretically the integer parts $\lfloor C^k \rfloor$ could be almost all concentrated in a single residue class $b \hbox{ mod } W$, which would (morally at least) place an upper limit of $\phi(W)/W$ on the density.  If this type of concentration happened for a lot of $W$, then one could conceivably end up with zero density overall.  Excluding this type of scenario seems related to making more progress on the 3/2 problem.

researchNotes: Erdős [Er58b] proved that $\sum \frac{p_n^k}{n!}$ is irrational for every $k\geq 1$.

In [Er88c] he further conjectures that $\sum \frac{p_n^k}{2^n}$ is irrational for every $k$, and that if $g_n\geq 2$ and $g_n=o(p_n)$ then\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{p_n}{g_1\cdots g_n}is irrational. (The example $g_n=p_n+1$ shows that some condition on the growth of the $g_n$ is necessary here.)
The decimal expansion of this sum is A098990 on the OEIS.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: By summation by parts, this is equivalent to the irrationality of $\sum_n \frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{2^n}$.  It is possible that a sufficiently quantitative and uniform version of the prime tuples conjecture can resolve this problem, if it gives sufficient statistical control on the binary expansion of about $\log \log n$ consecutive prime gaps $p_{n+1}-p_n$ (which is usually of size $\asymp \log n$) to show that the binary expansion of $\sum_n \frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{2^n}$ cannot be periodic.  The theory of Shannon entropy may be helpful in this regard.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #252 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/252).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 1$ and $\sigma_k(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^k$. Is\[\sum \frac{\sigma_k(n)}{n!}\]irrational?

### Context
This is known now for $1\leq k\leq 4$. The cases $k=1,2$ are reasonably straightforward, as observed by Erdős [Er52]. The case $k=3$ was proved independently by Schlage-Puchta [ScPu06] and Friedlander, Luca, and Stoiciu [FLC07]. The case $k=4$ was proved by Pratt [Pr22].

It is known that this sum is irrational for all $k\geq 1$ conditional on either Schinzel's conjecture (Schlage-Puchta [ScPu06]) or Dickson's conjecture (Friedlander, Luca, and Stoiciu [FLC07]).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #256 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/256).

### Problem
Let $n\geq 1$ and $f(n)$ be maximal such that for any integers  $1\leq a_1\leq \cdots \leq a_n$ we have\[\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\left\lvert \prod_{i}(1-z^{a_i})\right\rvert\geq f(n).\]Estimate $f(n)$ - in particular, is it true that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that\[\log f(n) \gg n^c?\]

### Context
Erdős and Szekeres [ErSz59] proved that $\lim f(n)^{1/n}=1$ and $f(n)>\sqrt{2n}$. Erdős proved an upper bound of $\log f(n) \ll n^{1-c}$ for some constant $c>0$ with probabilistic methods. Atkinson [At61] showed that $\log f(n) \ll n^{1/2}\log n$.

This was improved to\[\log f(n) \ll n^{1/3}(\log n)^{4/3}\]by Odlyzko [Od82].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
I would like to add a follow-up to my earlier comment at 08:55 on 16 Sep 2025.
At that time I posed the following conjecture: For every choice of positive integers $s_1,\dots,s_n$, if $P_n(z) = \prod_{j=1}^n \bigl(1 - z^{s_j}\bigr) = \sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^k$, then $\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \ge 2n$. I have now proved this conjecture, details can be found in my next comment.

replies.author: bkbedert
replies.contentMd: Looking at the original paper of Erdös-Szekeres, it seems that this is essentially a more detailed write-up of their argument proving the lower bound $f(n)\geqslant\sqrt{2n}$. Though the observation from your previous post this bound $\sum_k|a_k|^2\geqslant 2n$ can be used to give $f(n)\geqslant 2\sqrt{n}$ by using the result of O’Hara--Rodriguez as a black box is new.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd: Thanks for your comment! Indeed the argument is close in spirit to Erdős–Szekeres, but the inequality $\sum_k |a_k|^2 \ge 2n$ is new, and combining it with O’Hara–Rodriguez gives $f(n)\ge 2\sqrt{n}$, which to my knowledge is the first general improvement since 1959.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
I have just written up my result proving that\[ f(n) \ge 2\sqrt{n}, \]and it is now available on arXiv: [arXiv:2509.14182](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14182). Although this is not a very major improvement (since Erdős even conjectured that for sufficiently large $n$, $f(n)$ grows faster than any power of $n$), I believe it is still worthwhile to record.

In fact, this can be viewed as a fix of the original 1959 proof of Erdős–Szekeres (See also Section 2 of my paper.) The original Erdős–Szekeres idea considered the identity\[\sum_{j=1}^r z^{a_j} - \sum_{j=1}^r z^{b_j} \;=\; \prod_{j=1}^n (1-z^{s_j}),\]where $\{a_j\}$ and $\{b_j\}$ are disjoint sets of integers. In this formulation all nonzero coefficients on the left-hand side are $\pm 1$. Since $z=1$ is a zero of multiplicity $n$, together with the classical Prouhet–Tarry–Escott problem, one would conclude that $P_n(z)$ has at least $2n$ nonzero coefficients $a_k$, hence\[\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \;\ge\; 2n.\]Applying Parseval’s identity gives\[\| P_n \|_{L^\infty(|z|=1)}^2 \geq \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |P_n(e^{it})|^2 dt = \sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \ge 2n,\]which in turn implies $f(n) \ge \sqrt{2n}$.

However, the gap is that the coefficients of $P_n(z)$ are not necessarily all $\pm 1$, so this argument fails.

In the paper of Billsborough–Freedman–Hart–Kowalsky–Lubinsky–Pomeranz–Sammel (Proc. AMS 149 (2021), 4233–4246, [link](https://math.gatech.edu/sites/default/files/images/erdosszekeresproductsnovember30.pdf)), the authors gave a corrected proof showing that $P_n(z)$ has at least $n$ nonzero coefficients, and by using a result of O’Hara and Rodriguez they again obtained $f(n) \ge \sqrt{2n}$. Moreover, they remarked:
"If the original Erdős--Szekeres proof could be fixed, the O’Hara--Rodriguez bound would give $f(n)\ge 2\sqrt{n}$."

My result may thus be regarded as precisely providing such a fix, thereby confirming their expectation.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
In my previous comment at 07:32 on 16 Sep 2025, I noted that the classical bound $f(n)\ge \sqrt{2n}$ can be slightly sharpened to $f(n)\ \ge\ \sqrt{2n+2}$.

Here I would like to suggest a stronger conjecture based on further experiments.

**Conjecture**. For every choice of positive integers $s_1,\dots,s_n$, if $P_n(z)=\prod_{j=1}^n(1-z^{s_j})=\sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^k$, then $$ \sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2\ \ge\ 2n.$$

If this conjecture is true, then by Corollary 1 of O’Hara--Rodriguez "Some properties of self-inversive polynomials", we have\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty(|z|=1)}^2 \ \ge\ 2\sum_k |a_k|^2 \ \ge\ 4 n,
\]and thus\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty(|z|=1)}\ \ge\ 2\sqrt{n},
\]which is stronger than the classical $\sqrt{2n}$ (and also the $\sqrt{2n+2}$ refinement).

Numerical evidence (global searches for small $n$).
For each $n$ I searched over many sequences $s=(s_1,\dots,s_n)$ (with repetitions allowed) and minimized $\sum_k|a_k|^2$; a representative minimizer is shown.
In all cases below the nonzero coefficients of $P_n$ are $\pm1$.\[
\begin{array}{c|c|l}
n & \min\sum |a_k|^2 & \text{one minimizing }(s_1,\dots,s_n)\\\hline
1 & 2  & (1)\\
2 & 4  & (1,2)\\
3 & 6  & (1,2,3)\\
4 & 8  & (1,2,3,5)\\
5 & 10 & (1,2,3,5,7)\\
6 & 12 & (1,2,3,4,5,7)\\
7 & 16 & (1,2,3,4,5,7,11)\\
8 & 16 & (1,2,3,5,7,8,11,13)\\
9 & 20 & (1,2,3,5,7,8,9,11,13)
\end{array}
\]Thus for $n=1,2,3,4,5,6,8$ we observe $\min\sum|a_k|^2=2n$, while for $n=7$ and $n=9$ the minimum is even larger ($16>2n$ and $20>2n$, respectively).

I would be very interested in proofs, counterexamples, or further data for larger $n$.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
According to Lubinsky’s "A Survey of Erdős–Szekeres Products" ([Springer link](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-87057-6_12), p.300), “Nor has there been an improvement on the lower bound $f(n) \ge \sqrt{2n}$ in general.”
I would like to point out a slight sharpening: in fact\[
f(n) \;\ge\; \sqrt{2n+2}.
\]Proof. Write\[
P_n(z) = \prod_{j=1}^n (1 - z^{s_j}) = \sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^k.
\]Since $z=1$ is a zero of multiplicity $n$, we have\[
\sum_{k=0}^N a_k (k)_j = 0, \qquad j=0,1,\dots,n-1,
\]where $(k)_j = k(k-1)\cdots(k-j+1)$.

Let $\operatorname{supp}(P_n)=\{t_1<\cdots<t_m\}$ be the exponents with $a_{t_i}\neq 0$. Restricting to $j=0,\dots,m-1$ gives a square system with coefficient matrix\[
F = \big[(t_i)_j\big]_{\;0\le j\le m-1}^{\;1\le i\le m}.
\]Using $(t)_j = j!\binom{t}{j}$, a standard change-of-basis argument gives\[
\det F = \prod_{1\le i<\ell\le m}(t_\ell - t_i) \;\neq\; 0.
\]Thus $m \ge n+1$, so $P_n$ has at least $n+1$ nonzero coefficients. (This bound is sharp, attained by $(1-z)^n$.)

Therefore\[
\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \;\ge\; n+1.
\]By Corollary 1 of O’Hara--Rodriguez "Some properties of self-inversive polynomials" ([JSTOR link](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2040432?seq=3)), if all zeros lie on the unit circle then\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty (|z|=1)}^2 \;\ge\; 2\sum_{k=0}^N |a_k|^2 \;\ge\; 2(n+1),
\]which yields\[
\|P_n\|_{L^\infty (|z|=1)} \;\ge\; \sqrt{2n+2}.
\]So the classical universal lower bound $\sqrt{2n}$ can be sharpened slightly to $\sqrt{2n+2}$.
This slight sharpening is clearly more useful than the original bound, and it is tight when $n=1$, since $f(1)=2>\sqrt{2}$.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
As a related remark, let $\{s_j\}_{j=1}^n$ be positive integers. In 1959, Erdős and Szekeres posed a number of problems about the size of polynomials of the form $$
\prod_{j=1}^n (1 - z^{s_j}),
$$ where $\{s_j\}_{j=1}^n$ are positive integers. A recent survey of these problems and related questions can be found in Lubinsky’s "A Survey of Erdős–Szekeres Products", available at [(link)](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-87057-6_12).

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
It seems that the second question in the problem statement has already been resolved in the negative. In fact, Belov and Konyagin proved in Corollary 0.3 of the paper "An estimate of the free term of a non-negative trigonometric polynomial with integer coefficients"([link](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=im&paperid=95&option_lang=eng)) that $$
\log f(n) = O\!\big((\log n)^4\big),
$$ so $f(n) \le \exp\!\big(C (\log n)^4\big)$. This shows in particular that no exponential lower bound of the form $\exp(n^c)$ can hold. Clearly, there is a lot of scope for work on both upper and lower bounds. The first question is still far from solved.

problems.title: Erdos Problem #257: Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set. Is\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}irrational?
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #257 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/257).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set. Is\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}\]irrational?

### Context
If $A=\mathbb{N}$ then this series is $\sum_{n}\frac{d(n)}{2^n}$, where $d(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$, which Erdős [Er48] proved is irrational. In general, if $f_A(n)$ counts the number of divisors of $n$ which are elements of $A$ then\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}=\sum_n \frac{f_A(n)}{2^n}.\]The case when $A$ is the set of primes is [[69]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/69). This case (and when $A$ is the set of prime powers) was settled in the affirmative by Tao and Teräväinen [TaTe25].

Erdős [Er68d] proved this sum is irrational whenever $(a,b)=1$ for all $a\neq b\in A$ and $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}<\infty$ (and thought that the condition $(a,b)=1$ could be dropped by complicating his proof).

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
The last claim in the comments, on $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-t_n}$ being irrational for integers $(t_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ such that $0<|t_n|<C$, is easily seen to be false, even when $A=\mathbb{N}$. This has already been disproved under [[264]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/264), in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17593) - see the more general Theorem 2.5, but a very short argument for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n+b_n}$ is also sketched in a paragraph on p.17.

However, the question was written quite ambiguously in [Er88c] (as Erdős forgot to say that $t_n\neq0$), so one might also interpret it by requiring $0<t_n<C$. In that case the negative answer also easily follows from the ideas of the same paper, but this is not explicitly written there. Thus, I sketch the same very simple argument here, without taking any extra credit. :-)

Consider the set of all sums $\sum_{n=100}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n-t_n}$, where each $t_n$ ranges over $1,2,3,4,5,6$. They form a non-degenerate interval (and thus can be equal to some rational numbers), which can be seen by choosing $t_n$ inductively, so that the series sums to a desired target value. Namely, in each step, choosing $t_n$ achieves an approximation precision dictated by the largest gap:\[ \frac{1}{2^n-t_n-1} -\frac{1}{2^n-t_n} = \frac{1}{(2^n-t_n-1)(2^n-t_n)} \leq \frac{1}{(2^n-6)^2}, \]while the values of the series' tail can fully cover an interval of length\[ \sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty} \Big( \frac{1}{2^k-6} -\frac{1}{2^k-1} \Big) > \frac{1}{2^{n+1}-6} -\frac{1}{2^{n+1}-1} = \frac{5}{(2^{n+1}-6)(2^{n+1}-1)} > \frac{1}{(2^n-6)^2} \]for $n\geq100$.

If one doesn't feel like working out the details, then rather just apply Lemma 4 (a) from [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18712) to the above collection of sums.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let \(q ≥ 2\) be an integer. We can use the following reference to settle some special cases:
Yohei Tachiya, “Irrationality of Certain Lambert Series,” Tokyo J. Math. 27 (2004), 73–85.
PDF: https://projecteuclid.org/journals/tokyo-journal-of-mathematics/volume-27/issue-1/Irrationality-of-Certain-Lambert-Series/10.3836/tjm/1244208475.pdf

Tachiya’s Theorem 1 states that for any period-2 sequence \({a_n}\) (not identically zero),\[
\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{1-q^n}\notin\mathbb{Q}.
\]Taking \(a_n=\mathbf{1}_{\{n\text{ is even}\}}\) (or \(a_n=\mathbf{1}_{\{n\text{ is odd}\}}\)), which are period-2 and not identically zero, we get\[
\sum_{n\in 2\mathbb{N}}\frac{1}{q^n-1}
= -\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{1-q^n}\notin\mathbb{Q},
\qquad
\sum_{n\in (2\mathbb{N}-1)}\frac{1}{q^n-1}
= -\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{1-q^n}\notin\mathbb{Q}.
\]Thus, for \(A = 2\mathbb{N}\) (positive even integers) or \(A = 2\mathbb{N} - 1\) (positive odd integers), the subseries\[
\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{q^n-1}
\]is irrational (in particular for \(q=2\) posed in the problem).

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: Well, ok, but the case of even positive integers is a consequence of a much older [paper by Erdős](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1948-04.pdf), by writing\[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{q^{2n}-1} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(q^{2})^{n}-1}. \]Similarly, the case of odd positive integers is a consequence of an older [paper by Borwein](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-314X(05)80041-1), by writing\[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{q^{2n-1}-1} = q \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(q^{2})^{n}-q}. \]

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
Thanks for pointing this out — you are right that the even- and odd-positive-integer cases follow from the much earlier results of Erdős and Borwein, respectively.
What Tachiya’s Theorem 1 offers here is a uniform way to handle any nontrivial period-2 coefficient sequence, not just the pure even or pure odd subsets.
Beyond these two special cases in this problem, I am not sure if it yields further consequences here, though.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd: The question about subseries of $\sum 1/(t^n-1)$ has been asked for every integer $t\geq2$, but I believe that the case $t=2$ is quite special. In the case $t=2$ the corresponding subsums form a fat (i.e., positive-measure) Cantor set, and it is very likely that it contains many rationals. If its gaps were even smaller (as for, say, $\sum 1/(2^n-2^{-2^n})$), then one could easily prove that it does not even miss many rationals within range. In the cases $t\geq3$ the subsums form a zero-measure Cantor set, which is quite possibly irrational.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
Erdős asked about variants of this problem even earlier, see for instance [this paper from 1965](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1969-09.pdf).
A simpler variant of this problem, where one has a bit more freedom and can choose, say, infinitely many terms of the form $\frac{1}{2^n-1}$ or $\frac{1}{11^m-1}$ has an easy negative answer, simply because the corresponding infinite subsums fill out a union of non-degenerate intervals (from which one simply picks a rational number); see Theorem 2.3 in [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17593).

The set\[ S = \Big\{ \sum_{n\in A} \frac{1}{2^n-1} : A\subseteq\mathbb{N} \Big\} \]appearing in [[257]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/257) now has empty interior, so the same trick no longer applies. However, the answer is very likely negative again. Namely, the above set $S$ still has positive Lebesgue measure, i.e., it is a fat Cantor set. Thus, $S$ "almost surely" contains, say, at least one of the dyadic rationals $1/2,1/4,1/8,\ldots$. However, this argument alone cannot be turned into a rigorous proof, since there exist fat Cantor sets containing no rational numbers; a nonconstructive proof was given by [Boes, Darst, and Erdős](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-05.pdf).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #258 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/258).

### Problem
Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots$ be a sequence of positive integers with $a_n\to \infty$. Is\[\sum_{n} \frac{\tau(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]irrational, where $\tau(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$?

### Context
Erdős and Straus [ErSt71] proved this is true if $a_n$ is monotone, i.e. $a_{n-1}\leq a_n$ for all $n$. Erdős [Er48] proved that $\sum_n \frac{d(n)}{t^n}$ is irrational for any integer $t\geq 2$.

Erdős and Straus further conjectured that if $a_{n-1}\leq a_n$ for all $n$ then\[\sum_{n} \frac{\phi(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]and\[\sum_{n} \frac{\sigma(n)}{a_1\cdots a_n}\]are both irrational.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #261 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/261).

### Problem
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that there exists some $t\geq 2$ and distinct integers $a_1,\ldots,a_t\geq 1$ such that\[\frac{n}{2^n}=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}\frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}?\]Is this true for all $n$? Is there a rational $x$ such that\[x = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}\]has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ solutions?

### Context
Related to [[260]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/260).

In [Er88c] Erdős notes that Cusick had a simple proof that there do exist infinitely many such $n$. Erdős does not record what this was, but a later paper by Borwein and Loring [BoLo90] provides the following proof: for every positive integer $m$ and $n=2^{m+1}-m-2$ we have\[\frac{n}{2^n}=\sum_{n<k\leq n+m}\frac{k}{2^k}.\]Tengely, Ulas, and Zygadlo [TUZ20] have verified that all $n\leq 10000$ have the required property.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

1) One should add the requirement that $a_1,\ldots,a_t$ are all mutually distinct integers. This is understood in all papers and it is needed to make the problem nontrivial.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #263 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/263).

### Problem
Let $a_n$ be a sequence of positive integers such that for every sequence of positive integers $b_n$ with $b_n/a_n\to 1$ the sum\[\sum\frac{1}{b_n}\]is irrational. Is $a_n=2^{2^n}$ such a sequence? Must such a sequence satisfy $a_n^{1/n}\to \infty$?

### Context
One possible definition of an 'irrationality sequence' (see also [[262]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/262) and [[264]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/264)). A folklore result states that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is irrational whenever $\lim a_n^{1/2^n}=\infty$.

Kovač and Tao [KoTa24] have proved that any strictly increasing sequence such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and $\lim a_{n+1}/a_n^2=0$ is not such an irrationality sequence. On the other hand, if\[\liminf \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^{2+\epsilon}}>0\]for some $\epsilon>0$ then the above folklore result implies that $a_n$ is such an irrationality sequence.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: One possible definition of an 'irrationality sequence' (see also [[262]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/262) and [[264]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/264)). A folklore result states that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is irrational whenever $\lim a_n^{1/2^n}=\infty$.

Kovač and Tao [KoTa24] have proved that any strictly increasing sequence such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and $\lim a_{n+1}/a_n^2=0$ is not such an irrationality sequence. On the other hand, if\liminf \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^{2+\epsilon}}>0for some $\epsilon>0$ then the above folklore result implies that $a_n$ is such an irrationality sequence.
