sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
Using a result of Liu--Sawhney ([arXiv:2404.07113v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07113v1)), I obtained the following nontrivial upper bound for the quantity $\delta(N)$ in this problem: for some absolute $c_0>0$ and all large $N$,\[
\delta(N)\le \exp \left(-c_0\,\frac{N}{(\log N)^3(\log\log N)^4}\right).
\]Details are given in this [note](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-311-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_311.pdf).

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: Nice observation! It is interesting that your bound is not terribly far from the upper bounds in [[317]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/317) (the obvious one or Woett's improvement), where one seems to have so much more freedom with finding *two* sums close to each other.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
To obtain a stronger upper bound for $\delta(N)$, I have successfully strengthened Liu--Sawhney [[arXiv:2404.07113v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07113v1), Lemma 4.1]! As a consequence, I obtain the following slightly stronger bound: there exists an absolute constant $c_0>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$,\[
\delta(N) \le  \exp \left(-c_0\,\frac{N}{(\log N)^3(\log\log N)^3}\right).
\]Details are given in [note_version2](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-311-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_311_v2.pdf).

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
This formulation, which appeared in the Erdős-Graham problem book, is slightly awkward, because the asked minimal quantity, call it $\delta(N)$, is easily seen to be the same as\[ \delta’(N) := \min \Big( \Big\{ \Big|1-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\Big| : A\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,N\} \Big\} \cap (0,\infty) \Big). \]Namely, if $A$ contains a strict subset $S$ with reciprocals of its elements summing to $1$, then\[ \sum_{n\in A} \frac{1}{n} - 1 \geq \frac{1}{N} + \sum_{n\in S} \frac{1}{n} - 1 = \frac{1}{N},  \]which is “quite large”. It certainly does not make the asymptotics of $\delta(N)$ and $\delta’(N)$ different, but with a bit of brute force verification for small $N$, one can show that, in fact, $\delta(N)= \delta’(N)$ for every $N\geq1$.
The first $25$ values of $\delta(N)$ can be computed as:
\begin{align*}
& 1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{6},\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{30},\\
& \frac{1}{30},\frac{1}{105},\frac{1}{120},\frac{1}{252},\frac{1}{360},\\
& \frac{1}{2310},\frac{1}{2310},\frac{1}{2310},\frac{1}{2772},\frac{1}{2772},\\
& \frac{1}{6160},\frac{1}{30940},\frac{1}{30940},\frac{5}{298452},\frac{5}{298452},\\
& \frac{11}{1244880},\frac{23}{17907120},\frac{1}{1105104},\frac{1}{1105104},\frac{1}{1593900}.
\end{align*}
From this modest amount of data one can see\[ e^{-0.71N} \leq \delta(N) \leq e^{-0.52 N} \quad \text{for }3\leq N\leq 25, \]so the conjecture is somewhat plausible. Also note that\[  \frac{1}{[1,\ldots,N]} = e^{-(1+o(1))N}, \]so the conjecture claims that $\delta(N)$ is exponentially small, but still much larger than the trivial bound.
All this is quite trivial, but I wrote it down anyway, before I forget. :-)

sourceComments.contentMd:
I asked Gemini Deep Research and ChatGPT to find references on the problem.

In about 10 mins Gemini Deep Research [made the following report](https://gemini.google.com/share/e57153d35fe1) on the problem. It related the question to the general Subset Sum Problem and to the whole vast literature on the Egyptian fractions, but it did not find anything closely related. It also suggested a few possible approaches: Greedy Algorithm, The Probabilistic Method, and Fourier-Analytic Methods; but all this is easier said than done. :-)

I could only run ChatGPT for a short period of time. It mentioned quite a few papers on the Egyptian fractions (like the best underapproximations of 1), but it also admitted that none of them are on multisets with large reciprocal values or on exponentially small gaps around 1, so they are not closely related to the problem.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
Does anyone know if Erdős and Graham posed precisely the exponential "gap" for a good reason?
For a finite multiset of positive integers $A$ denote\[ R(A) := \sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n} \]and\[ \epsilon(A) := \min\Big\{ 1 – R(S) \,:\, S\subseteq A,\, R(S)\leq 1 \Big\}.  \]The problem asks if inequality\[ \epsilon(A) \leq e^{- c R(A)} \]holds with some constant $c>0$.
Here is a simple example which comes close to showing that this is the best possible. For a positive integer $N$ take\[ A = \bigcup_{p\text{ prime},\ p\leq N} \{\underbrace{p,p,\ldots,p}_{p-1\text{ times}} \}. \]Then\[ R(A) = \sum_{p\text{ prime},\ p\leq N} \frac{p-1}{p} \sim \pi(N) = (1+o(1)) \frac{N}{\log N}, \]while $R(S)\neq1$ for every sub-multiset $S$ of $A$, so\[ \epsilon(A) \geq \prod_{p\text{ prime},\ p\leq N} \frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{N\#} = e^{-(1+o(1))N}.  \]Since $N=(1+o(1))R(A)\log R(A)$, this shows\[ \epsilon(A) \geq e^{- (1+o(1)) R(A) \log R(A)}  \]for this particular sequence of examples of multisets $A$. It is not clear to me if a better (e.g., exponential) lower bound is possible, even for these particular multisets $A$.
The actual conjectured inequality (the upper bound on $\epsilon(A)$) is a completely different story (many people here would know better), but I first want to clarify to myself how "optimal" it is. :-)

### Problem
Are there infinitely many solutions to\[\frac{1}{p_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{p_k}=1-\frac{1}{m},\]where $m\geq 2$ is an integer and $p_1<\cdots<p_k$ are distinct primes?

### Context
For example,\[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=1-\frac{1}{6}\]and\[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}=1-\frac{1}{42}.\]It is clear that we must have $m=p_1\cdots p_k$, and hence in particular there is at most one solution for each $m$. The integers $m$ for which there is such a solution are known as [primary pseudoperfect numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_pseudoperfect_number), and there are $8$ known, listed in [A054377](https://oeis.org/A054377) at the OEIS.

researchNotes: For example,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=1-\frac{1}{6}and\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}=1-\frac{1}{42}.It is clear that we must have $m=p_1\cdots p_k$, and hence in particular there is at most one solution for each $m$. The integers $m$ for which there is such a solution are known as primary pseudoperfect numbers, and there are $8$ known, listed in A054377 at the OEIS.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #317 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/317).

### Problem
Is there some constant $c>0$ such that for every $n\geq 1$ there exists some $\delta_k\in \{-1,0,1\}$ for $1\leq k\leq n$ with\[0< \left\lvert \sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right\rvert < \frac{c}{2^n}?\]Is it true that for sufficiently large $n$, for any $\delta_k\in \{-1,0,1\}$,\[\left\lvert \sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right\rvert > \frac{1}{[1,\ldots,n]}\]whenever the left-hand side is not zero?

### Context
Inequality is obvious for the second claim, the problem is strict inequality. This fails for small $n$, for example\[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}=-\frac{1}{12}.\]Arguments of Kovac and van Doorn in the comment section prove a weak version of the first question, with an upper bound of\[2^{-n\frac{(\log\log\log n)^{1+o(1)}}{\log n}},\]and van Doorn gives a heuristic that suggests this may be the true order of magnitude.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Define $Q_n$ to be the set of rationals that can be written as $\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a}$ for some subset $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. The first question asks whether the inequality $$\min_{\substack{q, q' \in Q_n \\ q \neq q'}} |q - q'| < \frac{c}{2^n}\hspace{20pt}(1)$$holds for some absolute constant $c$.

By the results in [#320](https://www.erdosproblems.com/320) we have $|Q_n| = \exp[\frac{n f(n)}{\log n}]$ for some $f(n)$ that goes to infinity with $n$ at a rate of $(\log \log \log n)^{1 + o(1)}$. As we have $q \in [0, \log n + 1]$ for all $q \in Q_n$, by the pigeonhole principle we obtain $$\min_{\substack{q, q' \in Q_n \\ q \neq q'}} |q - q'| \le \frac{\log n + 1}{\exp[\frac{n f(n)}{\log n}]} = \frac{1}{2^{\frac{n (\log \log \log n)^{1 + o(1)}}{\log n}}},\hspace{20pt}(2)$$a slight improvement over the bound from Vjeko's comment. Perhaps known concentration inequalities on random harmonic sums can improve upon $(2)$ further.

On the other hand, if $Q_n$ would simply be a set of $|Q_n|$ uniformly random numbers in the interval $[0, \log n + 1]$, then one would expect their minimum difference to be on the order of $\frac{1}{|Q_n|^{2 + o(1)}}$. This would in fact give a lower bound of the same shape as the upper bound in inequality $(2)$, perhaps casting some doubt on the validity of $(1)$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
As an intermediate goal proving that the first question can be answered in the negative:

A different version would be to consider
$$\prod_{1 \le i \le n} \left\lvert \sum_{1 \le i \le n} \frac{\delta_i}{p_i} \right\rvert  (1)$$
and prove that this becomes very large for large $n$.
Heuristically and experimentally, this is the case.

E.g. $\frac 15 + \frac 17 - \frac 13 = \frac1{3*5*7}$, i.e.,
$$3*5*7\left(\frac 15 + \frac 17 - \frac 13 \right)=1.$$

But for $n=19$, the minimum nonzero expression (1) becomes $5246939312687345$ (here $p_1=2$).

For the heuristics:
If one takes $x$ random numbers in $[0,1]$, the minimum absolute difference between two is of the order $1/x^2$
(see e.g. [[stackexchange]](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/419130/expected-min-distance-between-n-uniform-rvs)).
Now consider all sums of some of the reciprocals of primes (the difference of two is of the desired form).
Now a most filled interval of length $1/p_n$ cannot have more than $2^n$ elements. (the sums are not random uniformly distributed of course, so we estimate this dense part)
Now the minimum difference could be estimated to be at least $\frac{1}{p_n^2 2^{2n}}$.
On the other hand, $\prod_{1 \le i \le n} p_i = n^{(1+o(1))n}=\omega( p_n^2 4^n),$
and also $2^{p_n}$ is much larger than $p_n^2 4^n.$
***

One could also take $p_i^{\lfloor \log_{p_i}(x) \rfloor}$ everywhere, since then the lcm's correspond).
[if this would be bounded, the above would also be bounded]

replies.contentMd: I think that both questions are very likely to have affirmative answers and checking for small n confirms that. In this light, disproving the first one is much harder than proving the second one. However, the related claim for primes that you suggest looks interesting as well.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
Also, since you were mentioning the primes, they can be used to obtain a slightly weaker estimate than desired (than $c/2^n$). Namely sums of reciprocal distinct primes $\leq n$ are all distinct and they are well-concentrated, so some two of them are at most $2^{-(1+o(1)))n/\log n}$ apart. This gives $1/2^{(1+o(1))n/\log n}$ on the right hand side, but I am sure that many people are well-aware of that argument. The point is in obtaining $c/2^n$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Hereby some thoughts for improving the first question to $C/[1,2,...,n]$.
In that case, $C>13340$ is necessary.

For this, define
$$F(n)=lcm(1,2,..,n)\min_{>0} \left\lvert \sum_{1 \le i \le n} \frac{\delta_i}{p_i} \right\rvert  $$
where the minimum is taken over the nonzero sums.

Then it has been computed that $$F(19)=F(21)=874, F(22)= 299, F(25)=1995, F(28)=460$$
$$ F(29)=F(30)=13340, F(31)= 2057, F(32)=4114$$

Since the next lcm's do not change, we also have $F(33),F(34),F(35),F(36) \le 4114.$

These values are nevertheless larger than the ones that could be guessed with the above heuristic (already taking into account that sums may be equal). So the fact that the numbers are not at random, seems to be important.

In particular, I do not even dare to conjecture the answer to this variant.

***
Thoughts about the heuristic:

The number of different sums is smaller than $2^n$. (e.g. $1/(2x)=1/(3x)+1/(6x)$ indicates multiple sums can be equal)

For $n=32$, there were just a bit less than $2^{26}$ terms (63545344 to be exact),
and $\sum_{i=1}^{32} 1/i$ is around $4.$
$LCM(1..32)=2,677,114,440<exp(32)<2^{48}$.
And as such $LCM(1..32)*16/(2^{26})^2<1$, while $F(32)=4114$. So the heuristic estimate was pretty far off (especially since we know there is a denser part)
But if the heuristic would go through and it is just some randomness with big jumps, the answer of the variant still may be yes.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #318 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/318).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite arithmetic progression and $f:A\to \{-1,1\}$ be a non-constant function. Must there exist a finite non-empty $S\subset A$ such that\[\sum_{n\in S}\frac{f(n)}{n}=0?\]What about if $A$ is an arbitrary set of positive density? What if $A$ is the set of squares excluding $1$?

### Context
Erdős and Straus [ErSt75] proved this when $A=\mathbb{N}$. Sattler [Sa75] proved this when $A$ is the set of odd numbers. For the squares $1$ must be excluded or the result is trivially false, since\[\sum_{k\geq 2}\frac{1}{k^2}<1.\]This is false for some sets $A$ of positive density - indeed, it fails for any set $A$ containing exactly one even number. (Sattler [Sa82] credits this observation to Erdős, who presumably found this after [ErGr80].)

Sattler [Sa82b] proved the answer to the original question is yes, in that any arithmetic progression has this property.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Agustín Meza
sourceComments.contentMd:
For the positive density case: if there exists some $n \in A$ such that (say) f(n) = -1, and the set B of multiples of n in A such that f(m) = 1 for all $m \in B$ has positive upper density, then the result follows from theorem 2 of Bloom in [1]: if we consider $C := \{ \frac{m}{n} \in \mathbb{N}/ m \in B\}$, there exists a finite $S' \subset C $ such that $\sum_{c \in S'} \frac{1}{c}  = 1$, so that $\frac{f(n)}{n} + \sum_{c \in S'}\frac{f(cn)}{cn} = \frac{-1}{n} + \sum_{c \in S'}\frac{1}{cn} = \frac{-1}{n} + \frac{1}{n} = 0$, since we assume that f(cn) always equals 1. Therefore, the finite set $\{n\} \cup \{nc \in A / c \in S'\} \subset A$ satisfies the condition.
I think this approach might give a proof of the arithmetic progressions case as well by taking any function f to this case.
[1]: Bloom, T. F. (2021). On a density conjecture about unit fractions. arXiv preprint arXiv:2112.03726, 1(3), 4.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: It is because of the simiral reasoning that I find the question for squares difficult. One has too few chances to make up for the opposite sign. But, on the other hand, there is still quite a lot of arithmetic identities involving sums of reciprocal squares, so nothing is finitely decideable.

replies.author: Agustín Meza
replies.contentMd:
A kind of set which satisfy the conditions of the statement is the following: let $A^{+} \subset A$ be the elements of A for which f(a) and $A^{-} \subset A$ the ones for which f(a) = -1. If the sets $P^{+},P^{-}$ consisting of the primes in both $A^{+}$ and $A^{-}$ satisfy $\sum_{p \in P^{+}}\frac{1}{p}, \sum_{p \in P^{-}}\frac{1}{p} \to \infty$, then A satisfies the hypothesis of the problem.
Assuming that both $A^{+},A^{-}$ have positive lower natural density (I think the method could apply as well in the general case), from the previous comment, if the proposition is false, then for any $p \in P^{-}$ the set of multiples of p in $A^{+}$ has zero natural density. Therefore, for any fixed $p \in P^{-}$  we would have $\mathbb{E}_{n \le x} 1_{pn \in A^{+}} \to_{x} 0$. Taking a finite subset $S \subset P^{-}$ for which $\sum_{p \in S}\frac{1}{p} \ge C\epsilon^{-2}$ for some arbitrarily small $\epsilon > 0$ and some constant $C > 0$, due to Elliott's inequality we can say that there exists at least some $p \in S$ for which $\mathbb{E}_{n \le \frac{x}{p}}1_{pn \in A^{+}} = \mathbb{E}_{n \le x}1_{n \in A^{+}} + O(\epsilon)$. But since $\mathbb{E}_{n \le \frac{x}{p}}1_{pn \in A^{+}} \to_{x} 0$, if we take some $\epsilon$ sufficiently smaller than the lower density of A, it would be a contradiction.

sourceComments.author: DanielLarsen
sourceComments.contentMd: I have uploaded a [note](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-318/blob/main/318.pdf) which shows how the technical result from [[825]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/825) can be applied to the case where $A$ is the set of squares, excluding $1$. The greedy method works quite well here as a prelude to applying the circle method. The same method should also work for $k$th powers, once the first few are excluded.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
The case of squares (the last remaining one) can probably be solved by brute-force using calculations on various square identities. [Here's a note on it for the potential computer attack](https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos318.pdf) and a short explanation below. I couldn't do it on a laptop, will try to run it on a more powerful machine - if anyone is willing to try it too, they are most welcome. Also currently trying to run it through Aristostle to formalize if possible.

To obtain a computer-verifiable proof one must produce a finite certificate of unsatisfiability for a finite universe. Concretely, fix a bound $N$ and consider the Boolean variables $X_n$ for $2\le n\le N$, interpreted as $X_n=\text{true}\iff g(n)=+1$ and $X_n=\text{false}\iff g(n)=-1$. For each exact reciprocal-square identity\[
\sum_{u\in U}\frac1{u^2}=\sum_{v\in V}\frac1{v^2}
\]in a chosen finite library $B$, and for each scale $m$ such that $mU\cup mV\subseteq\{2,\dots,N\}$, add two CNF clauses forbidding the two opposite-monochromatic sign patterns on the scaled sets:\[
\neg\bigl(\forall u\in U\, X_{mu}\ \wedge\ \forall v\in V\, \neg X_{mv}\bigr),\qquad
\neg\bigl(\forall u\in U\, \neg X_{mu}\ \wedge\ \forall v\in V\, X_{mv}\bigr),
\]equivalently the clauses\[
\Big(\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg X_{mu}\Big)\ \vee\ \Big(\bigvee_{v\in V}X_{mv}\Big),\qquad
\Big(\bigvee_{u\in U}X_{mu}\Big)\ \vee\ \Big(\bigvee_{v\in V}\neg X_{mv}\Big).
\]Finally, enforce that the coloring is non-constant by adding $\bigvee_{n=2}^N X_n$ and $\bigvee_{n=2}^N \neg X_n$. If a SAT solver returns UNSAT for the resulting CNF, then this constitutes a finite certificate that every non-constant $g:\{2,\dots,N\}\to\{\pm1\}$ realizes some scaled identity in $B$ with opposite constant signs on the two sides, hence yields a finite set $T\subset\{2,\dots,N\}$ with $\sum_{m\in T}g(m)/m^2=0$. A fully checkable proof is obtained by recording (i) the explicit identity library $B$ (each identity verified independently by exact rational arithmetic), (ii) the bound $N$, and (iii) the solver-produced unsatisfiability certificate (e.g. a DRAT/FRAT proof) together with a standard proof checker verifying the certificate against the CNF.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I think this approach shows that the problem is "verifiable" - checkable in finite time if true - but does not demonstrate that it is "decidable" - resolvable in finite time both if the statement is true and if it is false.  The compactness theorem shows that if the claim for squares is true, then there is a finite bound $N$ on the coloring statement one needs to check, but if the claim is false, one has to check satisfiability for all $N$, and this cannot be done in finite time without some additional input such as a bound on $N$.

One can speculate that Sattler had an approach like this but found out that his SAT problems were actually solvable for the $N$ that he tried, leaving him with no conclusion.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
I don't understand the reduction to finite $N$.

It seems to me that the "non-constant" condition messes with things. No finite subset of the squares suffices to witness "non-constant" behavior, or on the flip side, it's easy to avoid solutions below any finite bound by setting $f(n)=1$ for all $n\le N$.

I may be missing a trick with "rescaling", but I'm suspicious. One test case I'm considering is the function that is $1$ everywhere except $f(p^2)=-1$ for a single large prime $p$. I feel like finite searches can't account for that?

[Update: maybe a better test case is $f(n^2)=-1$ iff $p\mid n$.]

replies.contentMd: Oh, good point.  I withdraw my previous remark, and will revert the classification of the problem to "open".

sourceComments.author: None
sourceComments.contentMd:
No.

General counterexample (works for ANY infinite A⊆ℕ, hence for infinite arithmetic progressions, positive-density sets, and the squares ≥4):

Let m := min(A). Define f:A→{−1,1} by
f(m) = −1  and  f(n)=+1 for all n∈A\{m}.
Then f is non-constant.

Claim: there is no finite nonempty S⊂A with  Σ_{n∈S} f(n)n = 0.

Proof:
- If m∉S, then Σ_{n∈S} f(n)n = Σ_{n∈S} n > 0.
- If m∈S, write S = {m} ∪ T with T⊂A\{m}.
  Then Σ_{n∈S} f(n)n = −m + Σ_{n∈T} n.
  If T=∅, the sum is −m < 0.
  If T≠∅, every n∈T satisfies n ≥ m+1 (in fact >m), so Σ_{n∈T} n ≥ m+1, hence the total is ≥ −m + (m+1) = 1 > 0.
So the sum is never 0.

Consequences:
1) If A is an infinite arithmetic progression in ℕ (A={a+kd : k≥0}), take m=a and the same f. No such S exists.
2) If A is any set of positive density (or any infinite subset of ℕ), same construction kills it.
3) If A is the set of squares excluding 1, then m=4; set f(4)=−1 and f(n)=+1 for all other squares. Any S either sums to >0 (if 4∉S) or to −4 or at least −4+9>0 (if 4∈S). So again no such S exists.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
The most obvious counterexample that Adenwalla mentions (one even number and other numbers odd) is credited to Erdős in [this paper of Sattler](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/1385725882900257) at the very beginning (p. 341). In that light I do not understand the omission about arbitrary sets of positive density. It seems that Erdős corrected himself between 1980 (publication year of the Erdős-Graham problem book) and 1982 (publication year of the above Sattler's paper).

The first question on arithmetic progressions seems to have been solved by Sattler as well, in [this paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/1385725882900269).

Sattler also claims the solution to the last question (on the squares greater than $1$) in both of the papers linked above (see the references). However, I did not find the announced third paper where this proof was supposed to be published. Perhaps Sattler could still be trusted. :-)

All in all, I think it is safe to mark this problem as fully solved by R. Sattler.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
Ok, I don't mind treating the last question (on squares greater than $1$) as an open problem. I was swayed by the claim that the annonunced paper "On Erdös' property P1 for the sequence of squares" is "to appear", but no journal was mentioned and also, as you say, it is possible that a mistake was found afterwards.

I don't see an easy proof or disproof. In fact, I personally find the question on squares harder than the other (mentioned and solved) cases. Just as you say, Graham's theorem (+ easy tricks) can be used to obtain representations like
$$\frac {1} {2^2} = \frac {1} {3^2} + \frac {1} {4^2} + \frac {1} {5^2} \
+ \frac {1} {7^2} + \frac {1} {12^2} + \frac {1} {15^2} + \frac {1}
{20^2} + \frac {1} {28^2} + \frac {1} {35^2} $$
also for other fractions $1/n^2$, so a potential counterexample cannot be a function that is $-1$ on one number and $1$ on the remaining ones. On the one hand, the multitude of identities with several terms on both sides makes the positive answer somewhat likely. On the other hand, such identities get increasingly more complicated and harder to adjust, so I really don't know; I don't even dare to guess if the claim is true or false.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
If $A$ has one even number, $x$, and all other numbers in A are odd, then a function $f$ such that $f(x)=-1$ and $f=1$ on all $A\backslash \{x\}$ would be a counterexample. This is as a sum of fractions with odd denominator cannot be equal to a fraction with even denominator. This extends to any $A$ where there exists an $x\in A$ such that $A\backslash\{x\}$ is a subset of a multiplicatively closed set and no multiple of $x$ is in said MCS.

An example is any $A$ where there exists a prime $p$ such that there is exactly one multiple of $p$ in $A$. Another is where all numbers in $A\backslash\{x\}$ are equivalent to $g$ mod $d$ for some $g$ and $d$, and $x$ is not equivalent to $g^k$ mod $d$ for any $k$.

The result of Graham described in [[282]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/282) provides further examples. If $x$ and $d$ are both divisible by $p^k$ for some prime $p$ and $k\geq 1$, and $a$ is not divisible by $p^k$, then let $A$ be the infinite arithmetic progression $a\mod d$ union $x$. It follows that $\frac{1}{x}$ cannot be written as the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators equivalent to $a \mod d$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #319 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/319).

### Problem
What is the size of the largest $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that there is a function $\delta:A\to \{-1,1\}$ such that\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{\delta_n}{n}=0\]and\[\sum_{n\in A'}\frac{\delta_n}{n}\neq 0\]for all non-empty $A'\subsetneq A$?

### Context
Adenwalla has observed that a lower bound of\[\lvert A\rvert\geq (1-\tfrac{1}{e}+o(1))N\]follows from the main result of Croot [Cr01], which states that there exists some set of integers $B\subset [(\frac{1}{e}-o(1))N,N]$ such that $\sum_{b\in B}\frac{1}{b}=1$. Since the sum of $\frac{1}{m}$ for $m\in [c_1N,c_2N]$ is asymptotic to $\log(c_2/c_1)$ we must have $\lvert B\rvert \geq (1-\tfrac{1}{e}+o(1))N$.

We may then let $A=B\cup\{1\}$ and choose $\delta(n)=-1$ for all $n\in B$ and $\delta(1)=1$.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #320 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/320).

### Problem
Let $S(N)$ count the number of distinct sums of the form $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ for $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$. Estimate $S(N)$.

### Context
Bleicher and Erdős [BlEr75] proved the lower bound\[\log S(N)\geq \frac{N}{\log N}\left(\log 2\prod_{i=3}^k\log_iN\right),\]valid for $k\geq 4$ and $\log_kN\geq k$, and also [BlEr76b] proved the upper bound\[\log S(N)\leq \frac{N}{\log N}\left(\log_r N \prod_{i=3}^r \log_iN\right),\]valid for $r\geq 1$ and $\log_{2r}N\geq 1$. (In these bounds $\log_in$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.)

Bettin, Grenié, Molteni, and Sanna [BGMS25] improved the lower bound to\[\log S(N) \geq  \frac{N}{\log N}\left(2\log 2\left(1-\frac{3/2}{\log_kN}\right)\prod_{i=3}^k\log_iN\right),\]valid for $k\geq 4$ and $\log_kN\geq 3/2$. (In particular this goes to infinity faster than the lower bound of Bleicher and Erdős.)

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
It is a coincidence by the fact that $20$ was exactly small enough that the sum of reciprocals being equal implied that a short (length 1) sum of reciprocal needed to be involved.

If equality would have been true for $n=21$, then there should have been a subset of $[1..20]$ of size $15$ which could be extended by $21.$
Since equal sums of reciprocals do not involve primes between $n/2$ and $n$, these can be neglected in the computation.
Then a bruteforce verification (added on the github link) can do the job.

For this, note that e.g. $1+\frac 1{21} = \frac1 2 + \frac 13+ \frac 17 + \frac 1{14}$
and $\frac 16 + \frac 1{21} = \frac 17+ \frac{1}{14}$,
so there were multiple crucial equalities of (longer) sums of reciprocals involving $21$.
On the other hand, $\frac 1a=\frac 1b + \frac1{21}$ has no solution where $0<a<b<21$.

The first "most wanted" is caught as such. Here "dead" (false) is less interesting than "alive".

(with that idea, it only has been checked that $R(20+x)=14+x$ for $1 \le x \le 3$ without much effort)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Wow, that was fast!  That seems like a satisfactory explanation to me.  Hopefully we can at least get the sequence R(n) extended enough that it can be sent to the OEIS as a distinct sequence from A384927.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
It is extended/computed till $n=39$.
At OEIS one usually prefers to also have the code for general $n$, which is not the case here (it would need to be adjusted for larger n).

replies.author: Cong
replies.contentMd:
Followed up on your great work here: https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/issues/161#issuecomment-3697977745

I have code for computing all values of N, and extended the sequence up to N=54. All details on GitHub :)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Using linear programming, I also got the following values.

$R(21+x)=15+x$ for $0 \le x \le 2$
$R(24+x)=17+x$ for $0 \le x \le 3$
$R(28+x)=20+x$ for $x \in \{0,1\}$,
$R(30+x)=21+x$ for $0\le x \le 2$,
$R(33+x)=23+x$ for $0\le x \le 1$ and
$R(35+x)=24+x$ for $0 \le x \le 4.$

So the sequence starts with
$$1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 15,15,\\16,17,17,18,19,20,20,21,21,22,23,23,24,24,25,26,27,28.$$

So for small values, $R(n+1)=R(n)$ if $n+1$ is quite smooth, with some exceptions such as $36.$
(Also, one can have combinations with $p,2p, \ldots, kp$ that do not have $p$
 in the denominator for $k$ (polylog) quite small wrt to $p$, is another reason why drawing conclusions is hard)

$\textbf{Idea efficient programming}$
The idea was to first find all pairs $(A,B)$ of disjoint subsets of $[n]$ for which the sum of reciprocals is equal.
Then $A \cup B$ cannot belong to a maximal set with the desired property.
Since $\frac 1{p^k}$ cannot be equal to $\sum_B 1/b$ when $v_p(b)<k$ for every $b \in B$,
and $\frac 1p \pm \frac 2p$ also has a factor $p$ in the denominator,
we know that $p,2p$ for $p> \frac n3$ and $16,32,27,25$ never belong to such sets $A \cup B.$
This made the computation of forbidden sets $A \cup B$ more efficient.
(for $n=32,$ there were already $81949$ many of them, for $n=33$ there were $245435$, for $n=35$ around $700k$ and for $n=36$ there were $2302966$, indicating that it becomes hard to compute; 2 hours with a common pc for $n=36$)
The program has been added for $n=36$ in https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/issues/161.

sourceComments.author: epistemologist
sourceComments.contentMd: [Initial numerical computation](https://gist.github.com/epistemologist/8b3ca106d7b5188a02e05fdd01c656ff) suggests that $R(N)$ agrees with [OEIS A384927](https://oeis.org/A384927) which is the maximum size of a subset $S \subseteq \{1 \cdots N\}$ such that for distinct $a,b \in S$, $(a + b)$ does not divide $ab$ - however, it is not immediately clear to me how these conditions are related as they do not seem to be equivalent.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd: We have $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = \frac{a+b}{ab}$. So if $a+b$ does divide $ab$, then $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}$ is a unit fraction as well. That at least shows that these conditions are related.

replies.author: epistemologist
replies.contentMd: I should have specified - the relation for 2 fractions is clear to me, but the generalization from just 2 to more than 2 is what I am stuck on.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #322 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/322).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 3$ and $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ be the set of $k$th powers. What is the order of growth of $1_A^{(k)}(n)$, i.e. the number of representations of $n$ as the sum of $k$ many $k$th powers? Does there exist some $c>0$ and infinitely many $n$ such that\[1_A^{(k)}(n) >n^c?\]

### Context
Connected to Waring's problem. The famous Hypothesis $K$ of Hardy and Littlewood was that $1_A^{(k)}(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$, but this was disproved by Mahler [Ma36] for $k=3$, who constructed infinitely many $n$ such that\[1_A^{(3)}(n)\gg n^{1/12}\](where $A$ is the set of cubes). Erdős believed Hypothesis $K$ fails for all $k\geq 4$, but this is unknown. Hardy and Littlewood made the weaker Hypothesis $K^*$ that for all $N$ and $\epsilon>0$\[\sum_{n\leq N}1_A^{(k)}(n)^2 \ll_\epsilon N^{1+\epsilon}.\]Erdős and Graham remark: 'This is probably true but no doubt very deep. However, it would suffice for most applications.'

Independently Erdős [Er36] and Chowla proved that for all $k\geq 3$ and infinitely many $n$\[1_A^{(k)}(n) \gg n^{c/\log\log n}\]for some constant $c>0$ (depending on $k$). In [Er65b] Erdős claims an unpublished proof that, if $B$ is the set of $k$th powers of any set of positive density, then\[\limsup 1_B^{(k)}(n)=\infty.\]This is discussed in problem D4 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Small point: the theorem $1^{(k)}_A(n) \gg n^{c/\log\log n}$ was independently proven by Erdős and Chowla&Pillai (not just Chowla). A reference taken from the 1965 paper by Erdős:

S. Chowla and S. S. Pillai, *The number of representations of a number as a sum of non-negative nth powers*, Quart. J. Math. Oxford, 7 (1936) 56-59.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #323 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/323).

### Problem
Let $1\leq m\leq k$ and $f_{k,m}(x)$ denote the number of integers $\leq x$ which are the sum of $m$ many nonnegative $k$th powers. Is it true that\[f_{k,k}(x) \gg_\epsilon x^{1-\epsilon}\]for all $\epsilon>0$? Is it true that if $m<k$ then\[f_{k,m}(x) \gg x^{m/k}\]for sufficiently large $x$?

### Context
This would have significant applications to Waring's problem. Erdős and Graham describe this as 'unattackable by the methods at our disposal'. The case $k=2$ was resolved by Landau, who showed\[f_{2,2}(x) \sim \frac{cx}{\sqrt{\log x}}\]for some constant $c>0$.

For $k>2$ it is not known if $f_{k,k}(x)=o(x)$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
A trivial remark: if one can construct such an $f$ which is only asymptotically Sidon (no collisions for $a,b$ large enough), then one can remove all such collisions by replacing $f(x)$ with $f(qx+r)$ for a suitable arithmetic progression $\{qx+r: x \in {\bf Z} \}$ that avoids all the collisions.

It is conceivable that one may be able to solve this problem assuming the Bombieri-Lang conjecture, in this spirit of [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01090).  If the integer (or rational) solutions to the three-dimensional variety $\{ (a,b,c,d): f(a)+f(b)=f(c)+f(d)\}$ (which presumably will be of general type for typical $f$) are trapped inside two-dimensional subvarieties, then one may be able to escape the integer points on these subvarieties by replacing $f$ with $f \circ Q$ for various polynomials $Q$.

Siegel's theorem on integral points should be able to manage any one-dimensional family of solutions, so the main problems are with the two-dimensional families.  The key algebraic geometry question seems to be the following: let $S$ be an irreducible surface in $\{ (a,b,c,d): f(a)+f(b)=f(c)+f(d)\}$ such that the covers $S_Q = \{(a',b',c',d'): (Q(a'),Q(b'),Q(c'),Q(d')) \in S \}$ are not of general type for any polynomial $Q$.  What does this imply about $S$?

sourceComments.author: Sayan Dutta
sourceComments.contentMd:
This problem has often been discussed in the context of Sidon sets. For more information, see **F30**, **D1** and **C9** in [Unsolved Problems in Number Theory](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0) by Richard Guy.

The best result so far is due to [Ruzsa](https://akjournals.com/view/journals/012/38/1-4/article-p367.pdf) where he proved the existence of a real $\xi \in [0,1]$ for which the set
$$\left \{n^5 + \left\lfloor \xi n^4\right\rfloor : n\ge n_0 \right \}$$
is a Sidon set for a suitable $n_0$.

It is easy to show that a linear or a quadratic polynomial cannot generate a Sidon set. [Dubickas and Novikas](https://doi.org/10.1002/mana.202000334) recently proved that a cubic polynomial doesn't generate a Sidon set either. As far as I know, it is not known whether a quartic polynomial can generate a Sidon set.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #327 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/327).

### Problem
Suppose $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ is such that if $a,b\in A$ and $a\neq b$ then $a+b\nmid ab$. Can $A$ be 'substantially more' than the odd numbers?

What if $a,b\in A$ with $a\neq b$ implies $a+b\nmid 2ab$? Must $\lvert A\rvert=o(N)$?

### Context
The connection to unit fractions comes from the observation that $\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}$ is a unit fraction if and only if $a+b\mid ab$.

Wouter van Doorn has given an elementary argument that proves that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has $\lvert A\rvert \geq (25/28+o(1))N$ then $A$ must contain $a\neq b$ with $a+b\mid ab$ (see the discussion in [[301]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/301)).

### Deliverable

replies.author: Sharvil Kesarwani
replies.contentMd:
Using a SAT solver, for the first part you can easily get beyond 1700 terms with runtimes of less than a minute. I've extended the OEIS page (A384927) with these elements. Interestingly, the density of these elements is roughly decreasing, but  was still $> 0.71$ for all the values I computed. The minimum I've found occurred at $N = 1716$ with a subset of size $1222$. I tried computing for $N = 2000$, but this computation started taking a very long time so I stopped it early.

For the second part, I was able to compute up to $N = 580$ and a subset of size $406$, and the minimum density found was $0.6996\dots$ with $N = 506$ and a subset of size $354$.
------
UPDATE: By switching to Google ORTools and using a MILP, I was able to push this a lot further to $N = 5000$ for the first part, and $N = 1000$ for the second part, and further computation is still possible although it will likely take 10s of minutes to compute for each value. The ratio has still stayed above $0.7$, with the lowest occurring at $N = 4991$ yielding a subset of size $3521$. For the second part, the ratio still stayed above $0.69$ - the lowest I found was at $N = 980$ with a subset of size $679$.

I was hoping I would get something for the first part dropping below $0.7$, but it seems we need to compute much larger terms to get there.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
An observation, more general states for sets with no $a<b$ satisfying $a+b \mid k ab$, which seemed important at some point, but didn't do the job at the end:

Let $P(x)$ denote the largest prime divisor of $x$.

Let $A=\{1 \le x \le N \colon P(x) \ge (kN)^{1/2} \}$.
Now if $a<b$ both belong to $A$, where $P(a)=p$ and $P(b)=q$ are the largest prime divisors.
If $p \not =q$, then $a+b$ is relative prime with both $p$ and $q$ and thus $pq(a+b) \nmid kab$ since $pq(a+b)>kN (a+b)>kab.$
If $p=q$, the property repeats on $a/p,b/p$.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
If $A$ satisfies the condition such that for $a,b\in A$ and $a
eq b$ then $a+b 
mid ab$, we say $A$ satisfies (1). If $B$ satisfies the condition such that for $a,b\in B$ and $a
eq b$ then $a+b 
mid 2ab$, we say $B$ satisfies (2). Then there exists an $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ satisfying (1) and a constant $c>0$ such that $A$ contains $cN$ even numbers if and only if there exists a $B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfying (2) such that $|B|=cN$. So a positive answer to the first question implies a negative answer to the third question.

Let $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ satisfy (1) and let $B\subseteq A$ be the set of even numbers in $A$. Assume there exists $c>0$ such that $|B|=cN$. Then for any $2a,2b\in B$ where $2a
eq 2b$, we have $2a+2b
mid 4ab$. Equivalently, $a+b
mid 2ab$. Then letting $C=\{a\mid 2a\in B\}$, we see that $C$ satisfies (2), $C\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ and $|C|=cN$.

Let $B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfy (2) such that $|B|=cN$. Then for $a,b\in B$, $a
eq b$, we have $a+b
mid 2ab$. Equivalently, $2a+2b
mid 4ab$. Let $A=\{2a\mid a\in B\}$. Then we have $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots, 2N\}$, $A$ satisfies (1) and $A$ contains $cN$ even numbers.

### Problem
Suppose $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a Sidon set. How large can\[\limsup_{N\to \infty}\frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}\]be?

### Context
Erdős proved that $1/2$ is possible and Krückeberg [Kr61] proved $1/\sqrt{2}$ is possible. Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] have proved this $\limsup$ is always $\leq 1$.

The fact that $1$ is possible would follow if any finite Sidon set is a subset of a perfect difference set (see [[44]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/44) and [[707]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/707)).

This question can also be asked for $B_2[g]$ sequences (i.e. where the number of solutions to $n=a_1+a_2$ with $a_1\leq a_2$ is at most $g$ for all $n$, so that a $B_2[1]$ set is a Sidon set). Kolountzakis [Ko96] constructed a $B_2[2]$ sequence where the $\limsup$ is $1$, and for larger $g$ constructions were provided by Cilleruelo and Trujillo [CiTr01].

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd: ByteDance Seed AI4Math [claims](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ByteDance-Seed/Seed-Prover/refs/heads/main/SeedProver-1.5/SeedProver-1.5.pdf#page=9) (see the bottom of page 9) that Seed-Prover 1.5 solved problem 330.

replies.author: old-bielefelder
replies.contentMd:
On bottom of page 9 several Erdos problems are claimed to have been solved by Seed-Prover 1.5:
> Seed-Prover 1.5 solved problem numbers 124, 198, 303, 316, 330, 350, 370, 379,
> 418, 449, 493, 499, 645, 728 and 958. However, based on our observations, these
> problems are mathematically relatively simple, or we proved a trivial or simplified
> version of them due to mis-formalization (these mis-formalized problems are not
> listed here).

In that paper no proofs for any of them are shown.
Why do you mention just No. 330?

EDIT: From that list only 330 and 728 are marked as open
in this database. And in the description of 728 it reads
"This problem is ambiguous, and there are a number of trivial solutions to the problem as written."
So, we should now wait for a paper with the claimed 330-proof.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: The rest are marked as solved on this site, except 124 (which Aristotle solved before the statement was changed) and 728 (which has known counterexamples from AlphaProof).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: It seems that there was a misstatement and misformalization of the problem that has since been fixed both here (on Dec 8?) and at the formal conjectures repository, see [this PR by Wouter](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/1358) from about two weeks ago.  Most likely ByteDance (dis)proved the misformalized version.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
In the defense of ByteDance, the report says verbatim:

“Erdős Seed-Prover 1.5 solved problem numbers 124, 198, 303, 316, 330, 350, 370, 379, 418, 449, 493, 499, 645, 728 and 958. However, based on our observations, these problems are mathematically relatively simple, or we proved a trivial or simplified version of them due to mis-formalization (these mis-formalized problems are not listed here). Our systems, whether using natural language or formal language, are still some distance away from truly helping to advance research on frontier open mathematical problems, which motivates our
pursuit of further research.”

So I wouldn’t say they “claim” to solve it. More like they observed that it likely cannot solve. I don’t think we need to wait for any claim, since there is no claim.

There’s the common perception that AI companies like to overhype. Let’s give due credit for transparent reporting when such credit is due.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
[FYI: This comment was edited.]

I would love to see their Lean solutions to problems 303 and 379.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd: The misformalized ones are not listed, so then it seems to read "problem 330 is solved and mathematically relatively simple", isn't it?

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
To those who reply to me about transparency, I am not associated with ByteDance or any AI company. But I believe we should not assign ill will toward others prematurely.

I see SeedProver 1.5 being advertised on Twitter. While they make claims about solving IMO and Putnam problems, I haven’t seen they claiming about Erdos problems or other open problems (in contrast to e.g. Aristotle which says Erdos problems directly - but Aristotle has proven itself here).

Twitter is seen by many people; this paper is seen by few. Judging by circumstances, I’m not sure why this is considered a problematic situation and would like us all to get along.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
For what it is worth, here is [a Gemini DeepResearch report](https://gemini.google.com/share/91ae0175f1d7) on the problem, giving some historical references on minimal (and strongly minimal) bases.  The report also mentioned [this recent paper of Chen, Sandor and Yang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11148) which constructs some (density zero) minimal bases that have relatively large essential sets.  The Gemini report's description of this paper does not quite seem to match the actual theorems in the paper from my reading, so I am somewhat skeptical of the accuracy of the report, but nevertheless this does appear to be the most recent related work on this problem (which appears to be open as far as I can tell).

[Claude found](https://claude.ai/share/225e3871-b03b-42a7-bb74-2d7ddddff90d) some recent work on other minimal basis problems of Nathanson [by Chen-Tang](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00174) and [by Sun](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022314X20302225), but was unable to locate anything on #330 specifically.

[ChatGPT DeepResearch also located](https://chatgpt.com/share/6945d56b-c65c-800e-9731-8547202ce89d) the Chen-Tang and Sun papers and noted some other recent constructions of minimal asymptotic bases, such as [this one by Nathanson](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14562), but again did not locate any work addressing #330 directly.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Gemini’s report has keywords “thin”, “g-adic” which by (human) web search matches to the paper: https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/25DD450A44C1C16F4030B5F7F97DBA00/S0004972715000805a.pdf/on_minimal_asymptotic_gadic_bases.pdf

So this looks like a summary of a wrong paper rather than pure hallucinations, plausibly due to miscommunication between subagents.

This failure mode is becoming more common: rather than pure hallucinations, LLMs are being given more advanced tasks which are prone to “misunderstanding” in several ways if they’re not sufficiently robust. This is also more difficult to detect (since it describes a real finding and so doesn’t sound “fake”). As LLM approaches human capabilities, we should expect even harder-to-detect failure modes, converging to human-level (e.g. mathematicians make mistakes all the time but laymen cannot tell these mistakes).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Nice diagnosis!  And a good reminder not to take these AI-generated reports at face value, even while they continue to provide somewhat useful information. (I really wish these tools reported confidence levels with their outputs, it would greatly increase their usability in actual work.)

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $D(A)$ be the set of those numbers which occur infinitely often as $a_1-a_2$ with $a_1,a_2\in A$. What conditions on $A$ are sufficient to ensure $D(A)$ has bounded gaps?

Investigate open Erdos Problem #334 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/334).

### Problem
Find the best function $f(n)$ such that every $n$ can be written as $n=a+b$ where both $a,b$ are $f(n)$-smooth (that is, are not divisible by any prime $p>f(n)$.)

### Context
Erdős originally asked if even $f(n)\leq n^{1/3}$ is true. This is known, and the best bound is due to Balog [Ba89] who proved that\[f(n) \ll_\epsilon n^{\frac{4}{9\sqrt{e}}+\epsilon}\]for all $\epsilon>0$. (Note $\frac{4}{9\sqrt{e}}=0.2695\ldots$.)

It is likely that $f(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$, or even $f(n)\leq e^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
I asked the Deep Research tool of Gemini for the relevant literature on this problem twice, and both times it couldn't really find anything interesting beyond the already mentioned result by Balog. It did mention that a bound of $f(n) < \exp(c \sqrt{\log n \log \log n})$ is known for sums $a+b+c$ of three elements instead of two (see e.g. [this](https://akjournals.com/view/journals/10473/67/4/article-p333.xml) paper by Sárközy), similar to how ternary Goldbach is significantly more approachable than binary Goldbach.

To paraphrase from the comments on Green's list: even a bound of $f(n) \le n^{0.1}$ seems extremely difficult, as it implies small quadratic non-residues. To elaborate on that, if all large enough $n$ can be written as $a+b$ with both $a$ and $b$ $n^{0.1}$-smooth, then this in particular holds for all sufficiently large primes $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. For these primes this implies that one of $a, b$ is a quadratic non-residue, implying that a quadratic non-residue exists which is at most $p^{0.1}$. The best known upper bound for this problem has exponent $\frac{1}{4\sqrt{e}} + \epsilon \approx 0.15$ instead of $0.1$, however.

Finally, in the Sárközy paper linked above he states that Erdős conjectures that the bound $f(n) < \exp(c \sqrt{\log n \log \log n})$ also holds for the binary problem considered here. I did not find the slightly stronger $f(n) < \exp(c \sqrt{\log n})$ conjectured anywhere.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #336 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/336).

### Problem
For $r\geq 2$ let $h(r)$ be the maximal finite $k$ such that there exists a basis $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of order $r$ (so every large integer is the sum of at most $r$ integers from $A$) and exact order $k$ (so every large integer is the sum of exactly $k$ integers from $A$).

Find the value of\[\lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}.\]

### Context
A simple example of the order of a basis differing from the exact order is given by $A=\cup_{k\geq 0}(2^{2k},2^{2k+1}]$, which has order $2$ but exact order $3$.

Erdős and Graham [ErGr80b] have shown that a basis $A$ has an exact order if and only if $a_2-a_1,a_3-a_2,a_4-a_3,\ldots$ are coprime. They also proved that\[\frac{1}{4}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{5}{4}.\]The best bounds known for the limit are\[\frac{1}{3}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{1}{2},\]the lower bound originally due to Grekos [Gr88] and the upper bound to Nash [Na93]. Improved bounds in the lower order terms were given by Plagne [Pl04].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

They also proved that\[\frac{1}{4}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{5}{4}.\]The best bounds known for the limit are\[\frac{1}{3}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{1}{2},\]the lower bound originally due to Grekos [Gr88] and the upper bound to Nash [Na93]. Improved bounds in the lower order terms were given by Plagne [Pl04].
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80b] showed $h(2)=4$. Nash [Na93] showed $h(3)=7$. The value of $h(4)$ is unknown, but it is known [Pl04] that $10\leq h(4)\leq 11$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #338 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/338).

### Problem
The restricted order of a basis is the least integer $t$ (if it exists) such that every large integer is the sum of at most $t$ distinct summands from $A$. What are necessary and sufficient conditions that this exists? Can it be bounded (when it exists) in terms of the order of the basis? What are necessary and sufficient conditions that this is equal to the order of the basis?

### Context
Bateman has observed that for $h\geq 3$ there is a basis of order $h$ with no restricted order, taking\[A=\{1\}\cup \{x>0 : h\mid x\}.\]Kelly [Ke57] has shown that any basis of order $2$ has restricted order at most $4$ and conjectured it always has restricted order at most $3$ (which he proved under the additional assumption that the basis has positive lower density). Kelly's conjecture was disproved by Hennecart [He05], who constructed a basis of order $2$ with restricted order $4$.

The set of squares has order $4$ and restricted order $5$ (see [Pa33]) and the set of triangular numbers has order $3$ and restricted order $3$ (see [Sc54]).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #340 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/340).

### Problem
Let $A=\{1,2,4,8,13,21,31,45,66,81,97,\ldots\}$ be the greedy Sidon sequence: we begin with $1$ and iteratively include the next smallest integer that preserves the Sidon property (i.e. there are no non-trivial solutions to $a+b=c+d$). What is the order of growth of $A$? Is it true that\[\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg N^{1/2-\epsilon}\]for all $\epsilon>0$ and large $N$?

### Context
This sequence is sometimes called the Mian-Chowla sequence. It is trivial that this sequence grows at least like $\gg N^{1/3}$.

Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] also asked about the difference set $A-A$, whether this has positive density, and whether this contains $22$. It does contain $22$, since $a_{15}-a_{14}=204-182=22$. The smallest integer which is unknown to be in $A-A$ is $33$ (see [A080200](https://oeis.org/A080200)). It may be true that all or almost all integers are in $A-A$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #341 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/341).

### Problem
Let $A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_k\}$ be a finite set of positive integers and extend it to an infinite sequence $\overline{A}=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots \}$ by defining $a_{n+1}$ for $n\geq k$ to be the least integer exceeding $a_n$ which is not of the form $a_i+a_j$ with $i,j\leq n$. An old problem of Dickson. Even a starting set as small as $\{1,4,9,16,25\}$ requires thousands of terms before periodicity occurs.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
After a longer back and forth with GPT-5.4 I've got some new partial results in the direction I wanted, namely: L-packets as an explanation for "hidden signal". [Here's the note that proves the following](https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos342-new.pdf):

If the classical Ulam sequence \(U(1,2)\) really has positive upper density, then the strange Fourier spike people see numerically is not a fluke. After passing to a Furstenberg limit, that spike turns into an actual eigenfrequency of a shift system built from the sequence. So the “hidden signal” in the Ulam numbers gets upgraded from an experiment to a real structural feature of a limiting dynamical system.

The key finite combinatorial input is that the initial segments \(A_{N} = U(1,2)\cap [1,N]\) contain very few ordered Schur triples \(x+y=z\), in fact at most \(3|A_{N}|\). By Green’s theorem, that means \(A_{N}\) is very close to a genuinely sum-free set \(B_{N}\). Informally, the Ulam sequence is behaving a lot like an almost sum-free set, and that is what forces a big Fourier coefficient to appear.

The last part explains what this says about the preferred Fourier phases. Those maximizing phases cannot wander all over \(\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}\); any limit point has to come from a finite spectral atom set. In the irrational case, the paper even gets a circle-factor picture and a non-uniform limiting phase distribution for the Ulam numbers and for the nearby sum-free cores. So the overall message is: assuming positive density, the Ulam sequence has real hidden harmonic structure, not just mysterious numerics.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
Actually there's a lot of cool numerical computations in [A Hidden Signal in the Ulam sequence](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.00267) by Steinerberger, especially related to the title hidden signal which comes from Fourier series, and here's something worth computing. I had this idea coming from Langlands program:

Let $(a_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be the Ulam sequence with $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, and for $n\ge 2$ let $a_{n+1}$ be the least integer $>a_n$ that has a unique representation $a_i+a_j$ with $1\le i<j\le n$. For each $n$ write $A_n=\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ and view $A_n$ as a subset of the cyclic group $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ by choosing a prime $p>2a_n$ (so that there is no wraparound for sums in $[0,2a_n]$). Define the discrete Fourier transform of the indicator $1_{A_n}$ by $S_n(k)=\sum_{x\in A_n} e^{2\pi i kx/p}$ for $k\in\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$.

Numerically there is a striking ''hidden signal'': for large $n$ one finds a frequency $k_n^*\in\{1,\dots,(p-1)/2\}$ maximizing $|S_n(k)|$ such that the associated angle $\alpha_n=2\pi k_n^*/p$ stabilizes near an irrational constant $\alpha\approx 2.571447\ldots$, and the normalized peak height $|S_n(k_n^*)|/n$ remains macroscopic (around $0.7$-$0.8$ at the scales tested).

A convenient way to package this phenomenon is via an $L$-packet (harmonic packet) hypothesis: not only is the fundamental mode $k_n^*$ large, but several harmonics $mk_n^*$ are simultaneously large, i.e. $|S_n(mk_n^*)|/n$ is far above the random baseline $n^{-1/2}$ for $1\le m\le L$. In our computations, for many values of $n$ one observes that the harmonics $m=2,3,4,5,6$ are themselves among the top few Fourier peaks and can have normalized magnitudes comparable to $0.2$-$0.6$, suggesting a genuinely structured packet rather than a single isolated spike. This connects directly with the numerical claim in [arXiv1507.00267](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00267) that, at large scales, the spectrum appears to be dominated by (essentially) two peaks and their harmonic footprints; in practice one can test this by ranking the values of $|S_n(k)|$ for $1\le k\le (p-1)/2$ and tracking the ranks of the harmonic family $mk_n^*$.

A further experiment (useful for probing whether $\alpha$ admits any simple ''closed form'' approximation) is to fit the observed maximizers $\alpha_n$ by low-complexity models suggested by the $L$-packet picture, e.g. by approximating $\theta_n=\alpha_n/(2\pi)$ with short eventually periodic continued fractions (quadratic irrationals), or by rational multiples of $\pi$. Concretely, one may compare candidate angles $\widehat\alpha$ by computing the packet statistics $n^{-1}\big|\sum_{j\le n} e^{i m\widehat\alpha a_j}\big|$ for $1\le m\le L$ together with the sign-bias $\#\{j\le n:\cos(\widehat\alpha a_j)<0\}/n$, which is near $1$ for angles tightly aligned to the hidden signal. The main point is that these computations are straightforward to reproduce (generate $A_n$, choose $p>2a_n$, FFT the indicator of $A_n$), and they provide a concrete starting point for community exploration of packet structure, harmonic stability, and possible arithmetic constraints on the limiting frequency.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
First of all, it's worth to add 3 main references on the problem:
[1] D. Ross, The Ulam Sequence: Structure and Randomness, PhD thesis, University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign, 2016
[2] S. Steinerberger. A Hidden Signal in the Ulam sequence. arXiv:1507.00267, 2015.
[3] F. Clément and S. Steinerberger. Small Gaps in the Ulam sequence. arXiv:2501.16285, 2025

Steinerberger's results suggest the Ulam sequence exhibits a "hidden signal"—a strong Fourier peak at an irrational frequency $\alpha \approx 2.571$. Not much is known really and it seems the problem wasn't researched extensively.

I managed to get an explanation with GPT-5.2 of why a "hidden signal" might arise and show some other heurestics towards the final answers. Below is a mean-field analysis explaining the stability of this signal and deriving a theoretical growth rate that closely matches empirical data (this is new, there was no explanation of this phenomenon before as I can see so far). [You can see the full write up here.](https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos342.pdf)

1. The Fourier Setup
Let $A_n = \{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ be the Ulam sequence. Define the Fourier sum at frequency $\alpha$ as $S_n = \sum_{j=1}^n e^{i \alpha a_j}$. Empirically, $S_n$ grows linearly along the negative real axis: $S_n \approx -c n$ with $c \approx 0.79$.

The number of representations of an integer $m$ as a sum of two terms, $s_n(m)$, is given via Fourier inversion (dominated by the DC term and the frequency $\alpha$):\[
s_n(m) \approx \frac{n^2}{q} + \frac{2 |S_n|^2}{q} \cos(\alpha m + \text{phase}(S_n)).
\]For $S_n$ to be stable on the negative real axis, its phase is $\pi$. Thus:\[
s_n(m) \approx \frac{n^2}{q} \left( 1 + 2c^2 \cos(\alpha m) \right).
\]2. The Phase-Locking Mechanism
The Ulam rule selects the smallest $m > a_n$ such that $s_n(m) = 2$ (uniquely representable). Since the average representation count is large ($\sim n$), finding a value as low as $2$ requires "destructive interference" from the dominant mode to cancel the baseline.\[
1 + 2c^2 \cos(\alpha m) \le 0 \implies \cos(\alpha m) \le -\frac{1}{2c^2}.
\]This inequality creates a feedback loop:

    Existence Threshold: For a solution to exist, the cosine must be able to dip low enough. This requires $-1/(2c^2) \ge -1$, implying $c \ge 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$. The empirical $c \approx 0.79$ satisfies this stability criterion.
    Phase Trapping: The new term $a_{n+1}$ is forced to have a phase $\phi = \alpha a_{n+1}$ inside a specific "trough" arc centered at $\pi$.

3. The Self-Consistent Field Equation
We can solve for the theoretical growth rate $c$. Let the "allowed arc" of phases be $[\pi - \delta, \pi + \delta]$.
The boundary of this arc is defined by the threshold condition:\[
\cos(\delta) = \frac{1}{2c^2} \quad (*).
\]Assuming the sequence samples phases uniformly within this allowed window (due to noise from other frequencies), the growth rate of the peak $S_n$ is the average projection of these new unit vectors onto the negative real axis:\[
c = \frac{1}{2\delta} \int_{-\delta}^{\delta} \cos(x) \, dx = \frac{\sin(\delta)}{\delta} \quad (**).
\]4. Results and Comparison
Solving the system of equations (*) and (**) numerically:\[
2 \cos(\delta) \sin^2(\delta) = \delta^2
\]yields the solution:\[
\delta \approx 0.867 \text{ rad} \quad (49.7^\circ), \qquad c_{\text{theory}} \approx 0.879.
\]This theoretical upper bound ($c \approx 0.88$) is remarkably close to the empirical value ($c \approx 0.79$). The discrepancy is naturally explained by "noise" ($L^2$ error terms) which effectively broadens the trapping window $\delta$, lowering the average cosine.

5. Implications for Open Problems
Infinitely many pairs $  a, a+2  $: Likely. The non-uniform distribution on the circle (with positive density in the support arc) implies that phases recur infinitely often in regions where the next trough (gap) is exactly 2. Since $  \alpha  $ is irrational, ergodicity ensures infinite visits to such phase sets. This is conjectural but fits the quasi-periodic picture.

Eventually periodic differences: Unlikely. The irrational rotation on the circle (modulo the trapping arc) prevents strict periodicity in gaps.

Density zero?: No—the persistent Fourier bias and positive $  c  $ are inconsistent with zero density (which would imply more random-like behavior). Computations stabilize around $  \sim 0.076  $.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
Interesting, my ChatGPT agrees with this critique, even though writing everything one prior prompt before. I think this shows what's known for writing code with AI. Simplifying, often when you have a problem A in a bigger codebase and try to solve it with LLMs, you often introduce a problem B, and then when you try to solve problem B, you get problem A back. This seems what's happening here, when I have this longer conversations with LLMs and putting various pieces together that then become incosistent.

Anyway, I'll rework it/simplify it. My main point here was to see whether we can have even conjecturally an explanation what is expected to happen here with this sentence, and I think "5. Implications for Open Problems" above are pretty good for that. Finally thanks for checking this that quickly! Feedback is always welcome to make some progress.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Thanks! That means the simple of strategy of asking ChatGPT to check its own work should work in your case too. (In my use, this often catches some minor errors by itself.)

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
Sure, and of course I do that multiple times, but that process almost never ends. You can do a funny exercise and ask ChatGPT about some paper that was well validated and accepted for publication (but without giving context on this, otherwise it gets influenced). If you ask to find gaps and errors in a paper, you're often get that even in verified/published papers.

So at some point, if you're especially working on harder problems, you should stop relying on LLMs, and either use your own expertise or go with Aristotle to try to formalize it.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: I get why you feel like that. In reality, just asking it to check its own work help tremendously. The approach is that it must *convince* you that the argument works (think peer review). This means you have to check some things, but it doesn't mean you need to check 100%. Of course, if the material is too hard and you can't become convinced/confident, then that's it; it doesn't work for that case. But there cases where it can work and save a lot of time.

replies.author: old-bielefelder
replies.contentMd:
In other circles people speak of "AI incest" when the same question on the same document is asked again and again. Instead of applying the same LLM-1 over and over again, it might help to apply several LLMs in turn (or in random order).

An incest crisis occured with top computer chess programs around 2003 and 2004. A complete newcomer (Fruit by Fabien Letouzy) broke the "cycle" and become the symbolic father of new top programs like Rybka, Houdini and others.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Yep, in theory independent checks are better. But currently, GPT-5.2 is better with enough gap that self-check is sometimes better.

But I also want to stress the key point - it must convince you, the human. That guards against this "blind spot" phenomenon, roughly up to the human's expertise level.

replies.author: Masty13
replies.contentMd:
In my experience with LLMs, I found the best approach is to have 3 SOTA models check and evaluate each other, (e.g Gemini 3 + Opus 4.5 + gpt 5.2). Model 1 is the main discussion partner who exchange feedback with you and writes/takes notes.

Model 2 checks what model 1 wrote then model 1 is fed the feedback from model 2 to evaluate and the process goes iteratively until Models 1 & 2 finally converge/agree on the same optimized output.

Then you take that output and do the same process iteratively with model 3 optimizing further until you reach a state of convergence between the 3 peer-reviewers.

The most important part in this process is obviously the human supervising them and assessing which model is being overly pedantic, which one is being overly agreeable, and which ideas/methods are actually worth pursuing. So it's essential to have sharp hallucination filters.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #345 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/345).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a complete sequence, and define the threshold of completeness $T(A)$ to be the least integer $m$ such that all $n\geq m$ are in\[P(A) = \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A\textrm{ finite }\right\}\](the existence of $T(A)$ is guaranteed by completeness).

Is it true that there are infinitely many $k$ such that $T(n^k)>T(n^{k+1})$?

### Context
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] remark that very little is known about $T(A)$ in general. It is known that\[T(n)=1, T(n^2)=128, T(n^3)=12758,\]\[T(n^4)=5134240,\textrm{ and }T(n^5)=67898771.\]Erdős and Graham remark that a good candidate for the $n$ in the question are $k=2^t$ for large $t$, perhaps even $t=3$, because of the highly restricted values of $n^{2^t}$ modulo $2^{t+1}$.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
In the comment above, Stijn shows the lower bound $T(x^k) > 2^{c k \log k}$, which perhaps can be further improved if $k$ is a power of two. On the other hand, I wondered whether any upper bound was known and found [this](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL20/Kim/kim6.pdf) paper by Kim, where they make a proof by Graham explicit and find an upper bound of $T(x^k) < 2^{ck^4}$. Since this latter bound holds for all positive integers, plausibly it can be improved for specific values to see if $T(x^k) > T(x^{k+1})$ can be deduced for some $k$. Lower and upper bound are still quite far off from each other though.

Kim, D. *On the largest integer that is not a sum of distinct positive nth powers*, Journal of Integer Sequences, Volume 20, Issue 7 (2017).

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
It may well that the answer is negative, i.e., that there aren't infinitely many such $k$ (if there is already even one of them).

\textbf{background}
The value of $T(n^k)$ is known for $k\le 8$, see [[oeis A001661]](https://oeis.org/A001661/list).

In particular, we know that $T(n^8)<T(n^9)$ by the estimate by [[Wiener23]](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL26/Wiener/wiener3.pdf).

\textbf{Remark on the growth of $T(x^k)$ and the candidates by EG}
The restrictedness is slightly larger; $n^{2^t} \equiv 0,1 \pmod{2^{t+2}}$ for every $t \ge 2$.

This implies that indeed, when $r \equiv -1 \pmod{2^{t+2}}$, there are combinations with at least $2^{t+2}-1$ odd $2^t$th powers needed.
From this, one gets immediately a lowerbound for $T(n^{2^t})$ equal to
$$\sum_{i=1}^{2^{t+2}-1}(2i-1)^{2^t}=(c+o(1)) \int_1^{2^{t+3}} x^{2^{t}} dx=(c+o(1))*2^{(t+3)2^t+3}$$ for some $0.375<c<1/2$.

But one can actually do a better estimate.
Let $n$ be the solution to $n^k=2^n$, so $$n=\log_2(e) k (\ln(k)+\ln(\ln(k))+o(1))=k (\log_2(k)+\log_2(\log_2(k)+O(1)).$$ Now, since there are only $2^{n-1}$ combinations of $1^k$ up to $(n-1)^k$, there is definitely a number in the range $[2^{n-1},2^n]$ which cannot be represented as the sum of different $k^{th}$ powers.

Thus $T(x^k)>2^{n-1}=2^{ k (\log_2(k)+\log_2(\log_2(k))+O(1))}.$
When $k=2^t$, we notice that this is of the form $\Theta\left(2^{ 2^t(t+\log_2(t))} \right)$,
which is larger than $\Theta \left( 2^{(t+3)2^t}\right)$.

The presented lower bound is far off from the correct bound, but also grows by a factor which is at least $ek \log_2(k).$

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
I am confused by this - you are deleting the elements $a_{n-k+1},\ldots,a_{n}$ where $n$ is fixed? But then you have fixed $n$, so you cannot later take $n$ arbitrarily large. Note that the 'threshold of completeness', past which we can represent all integers, is allowed to depend on which finite set of elements we deleted - in particular there is nothing saying Brown's criterion has to be applicable around $s_{n-k}$, since $n$ is fixed, and perhaps the completeness  of the new modified sequence only bites much later on.

(Regarding the first point, I think it is assumed from context that we are just talking about natural numbers, as in most problems regarding completeness, so all $a_n\geq 1$. I'll add a remark for clarity.)

EDIT: Perhaps your confusion comes from the two definitions of 'complete' that are out there. On this site (following Erdős' own convention) complete just means all sufficiently large integers are representable, not all integers. I'll add a remark clarifying this.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
I'm not sure if I understand your argument correctly. The inequality $a_{n+1} - 1 \le s_{n-k}$ does not have to hold for all large enough $n$. You seem to be removing the $k$ largest elements below $a_{n+1}$ for all $n$. But you first have to remove $k$ elements, and only then do all integers larger than some $N$ need to admit a representation. But this $N$ is allowed to depend on which $k$ elements you removed. And the first and third hypothesis cannot be incompatible, by the fact that Graham gave an example which satisfies all hypotheses.

Edit: I see Thomas beat me by two minutes ;)
Edit2: To be clear, 'complete' here means: all *sufficiently large* integers can be written as a sum of distinct elements.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #348 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/348).

### Problem
For what values of $0\leq m<n$ is there a complete sequence $A=\{a_1\leq a_2\leq \cdots\}$ of integers such that- $A$ remains complete after removing any $m$ elements, but
- $A$ is not complete after removing any $n$ elements?

### Context
The Fibonacci sequence $1,1,2,3,5,\ldots$ shows that $m=1$ and $n=2$ is possible. The sequence of powers of $2$ shows that $m=0$ and $n=1$ is possible. The case $m=2$ and $n=3$ is not known.

van Doorn [has shown](https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/Any%20multiset%20which%20is%20complete%20after%20removing%20any%20two%20elements%20remains%20complete%20after%20removing%20a%20specific%20infinite%20set.pdf) that no such sequence exists for $2\leq m<n$ if we interpret complete in the strong sense that\[\left\{ \sum_{n\in B}n : \textrm{ for all finite }B\subset A\right\}=\mathbb{N}.\]Erdős and Graham most likely meant the weaker notion of completeness which allows finitely many exceptions, however.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
If I understand correctly, the way this is formalised in Lean requires the multiset $A$ to have the property that the set
$$P(A) = \left \{\sum_{n \in B} B \subseteq A \text{ finite} \right\}$$ contains *all* positive integers, and a lot of texts define completeness this way. In the book by Graham and Erdős however, it is only required that $P(A)$ contains all sufficiently large integers, which is also often taken as a definition of completeness. For what it is worth, with the former interpretation that is used in the Lean formalisation I can fully settle this problem, and show that no such multiset exists for any $m, n$ with $2 \le m < n$.

Assume $A = \{a_1, a_2 \ldots, \}$ is such that $P(A \setminus \{a_i, a_j \}) = \mathbb{N}$ holds for all indices $i, j$. Set $s_1 = a_1$ and, for any $j \ge 2$, $s_j = a_i$ where $i$ is such that $a_{i-1} > s_1 + \ldots + s_{j-1}$. With the infinite set $S$ equal to $\{s_1, s_2, \ldots \}$, one can then check that $P(A \setminus S) = \mathbb{N}$ holds as well.

For a complete write-up, see [here](https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/Any%20multiset%20which%20is%20complete%20after%20removing%20any%20two%20elements%20remains%20complete%20after%20removing%20a%20specific%20infinite%20set.pdf). Perhaps the argument can be adapted to settle the second (intended) interpretation as well.

EDIT: Come to think of it, I don't think this argument can be easily adapted to the intended interpreation, because the sequence $a_n = F_n + (-1)^n$ with $F_n$ the $n$-th Fibonacci number has the property that $P(A \setminus \{a_i, a_j\})$ contains all large enough integers for all $i, j$, but no infinite subset $S$ exists for which  $P(A \setminus S)$ contains all large enough integers. See [#346](https://www.erdosproblems.com/346) and references for more information.

EDIT 25-09-2025: I have left a comment on the Lean forum and the formalisation has now been updated to reflect the intended meaning.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #349 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349).

### Problem
For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete (that is, all sufficiently large integers are the sum of distinct integers of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$)?

### Context
Even in the range $t\in (0,1)$ and $\alpha\in (1,2)$ the behaviour is surprisingly complex. For example, Graham [Gr64e] has shown that for any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in (0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha$ such that the sequence is complete consists of at least $k$ disjoint line segments. It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all $t>0$ and all $1<\alpha < \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$. Proving this seems very difficult, since we do not even know whether $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ is odd or even infinitely often.

### Deliverable
