replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
A few comments:

1) The theorem that the sequence is complete for all $1 < \alpha \le 1 + \frac{1}{\lceil t \rceil + 2 \lceil \sqrt{t} \rceil}$ seems to be improved such that the denominator $\lceil t \rceil + 2 \lceil \sqrt{t} \rceil$ decreases to some $D$ with $D = \lceil t \rceil + 2 \lceil \sqrt{t} \rceil - f(t)$, with $0 \le f(t) < C$ for some absolute constant $C$. I suppose this counts as an improvement, but it seems rather marginal. Especially since the corresponding $\alpha$ regions for all the small $t$ values (say $t \le 100$) can be quickly checked by other means (e.g. a computer) anyway.

2) On the topic of computer verification, the certified regions for $\alpha \ge 1.4$ are not all new. Table $2$ states for example that the sequence is complete for all pairs $(\alpha, t)$ with $\alpha \in [1.55, 1.60]$ and $t \in [1, 1.15]$. These values are however already covered by Proposition $5$ of my paper.

3) More importantly, the expansion of the certified regions is very minimal. For example, again referring to Table $2$, the sequence is verified to be complete for all pairs $(\alpha, t)$ with $\alpha \in [1.10, 1.15]$ and $t \in [1, 16]$. Using the Python code I put on [GitHub](https://github.com/Woett/Complete-sequences-data), it only takes my laptop $27$ seconds to prove the completeness of the sequence for this entire region. Expanding the $t$-values further to e.g. $[1, 20]$ takes an additional $39$ seconds. This is to say, anyone with a computer can easily do a whole lot more. I'm interested to see what someone with a supercomputer or with the patience to leave their computer running for a few days would get.

4) I apologize for my dismissive tone. I'm at least happy to hear that my calculations seem to have been independently verified, so thanks!

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have just uploaded my paper on this problem to the [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.23394).

Combined with (and relying on) the results from [Graham's 1964 paper](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/64_02_erdos.pdf), the case $\alpha \ge \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ is completely settled. Moreover, even though my paper does not fully resolve the problem for the remaining interval $1 < \alpha < \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$, I can at least give the full range of values of $t$ for which the resulting sequence is entirely complete, i.e. covers *all* positive integers.

In the spirit of Graham, [here](https://imgur.com/a/fAOkgkC) you can find a plot for part of the 2D plane which shows where the sequence is and isn't (entirely) complete. To describe it in words, this is the current state of affairs:

If $\alpha > 2$, the sequence is not complete for any $t > 0$.
If $\alpha = 2$, the sequence is complete if, and only if, $t = \frac{1}{2^k}$ for some $k \ge 1$.
If $5^{1/3} < \alpha < 2$ and $t \ge 1$, the sequence is not complete.
If $5^{1/3} < \alpha < 2$ and $t < 1$, it's complicated (but essentially known). See Graham's paper or the above image for more details.
If $\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \le \alpha \le 5^{1/3}$, the sequence is complete if, and only if, $t < \min\left(\frac{3}{\alpha^2}, \frac{5}{\alpha^3} \right)$.
If $1 < \alpha < \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$, the sequence is entirely complete if, and only if $t < \min\left(\frac{2}{\alpha}, \frac{3}{\alpha^2} \right)$.
If $1 < \alpha < \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ and $t \ge \min\left(\frac{2}{\alpha}, \frac{3}{\alpha^2} \right)$, the sequence might be complete without being entirely complete, but only partial results are known (see below).
If $\alpha = 1$, the sequence is complete if, and only if, $1 \le t < 2$.
If $\alpha < 1$, the sequence is not complete for any $t > 0$.

As for those partial results for the region where it's not fully known yet, one can observe that for any compact set contained in that region, determining whether the sequence is complete for all pairs $(t, \alpha)$ in that set, in principle reduces to a finite search. I have therefore done some coding and can show the following computer-assisted result:

If $\alpha \le 1.4$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 3$.
If $\alpha \le 1.3$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 5$.
If $\alpha \le 1.2$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 10$.
If $\alpha \le 1.1$, the sequence is complete for all $t \le 50$.

These ranges are mostly a proof of concept, and for anyone interested it shouldn't be too hard to extend them further.

The final result I prove in my paper is that the sequence is complete whenever $1 < \alpha \le 1 + \frac{1}{\lceil t \rceil + 2 \lceil \sqrt{t} \rceil}$, which (when we plot the values of $t$ and $\alpha$) is the first result that implies the completeness of the sequence for a region of infinite area!

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
How is this going as of Dec 2025? I skimmed through Graham's and your paper. It seems like all cases (both complete and entirely complete) are settled except for this $1 < \alpha < \varphi$ and $t > \min(2/\alpha, 3/\alpha^2)$ region, where "entirely complete" is settled (in the negative), but "complete" is open.

I also understand that you have an algorithm that can prove completeness in this region by covering it with squares and going one square at a time. (Although when you wrote "For any compact set $C \subset U$  it is in principle possible to tile the entirety of $C$ with these kinds of squares", it seems like this is an empirical observation rather than you knowing for certain that these squares must exist? - Correct me if I'm wrong.) The key tool seems to be Lemma 5.

Regardless of whether this is known for certain or just an empirical observation, it seems like you feel that an automated proof to some moderately large $t$ appears possible to generate. Has this been done?

If not, I think it would be interesting to do this up to $t \leq \text{some number}$, gather the results we have and the algorithm for future people to run, as a partial resolution of the problem. Because it seems like there is a bit of progress being done here since Graham already, but maybe some further idea is still required to settle $t$ large? (So it would make sense to publish this as a progress checkpoint.)

sourceComments.author: memeister27
sourceComments.contentMd:
Suppose we take $b_k$ to be the deduplicated increasing tail of $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$, and look at its subset sums. If for some $K_0$ there is an interval $[A,A+L]\subseteq\Sigma_{K_0}$ with cardinality $L+1\ge b_{K_0+1}$, then once the eventual overlap $b_{m+1}\le 2b_m-1$ (which eventually holds for large $m$ when $1<\alpha<2$, up to sporadic floor effects, and even $b_{m+2}\le b_{m+1}+b_m-1$ for $1<\alpha<\varphi$) has started to hold, the translate–overlap mechanism forces that from some point onward all sufficiently large integers are covered. So for $\alpha<\varphi$ it seems the whole problem reduces to finding one finite seed interval beyond the eventual regime.

What I am not sure about is whether this reduction is completely sound, or whether there could be a gap before the overlap inequality takes effect. Do we know that some seed must appear for every $t>0$ and $1<\alpha<\varphi$, or could it in principle fail entirely in the finite pre-asymptotic window? The seed condition I think has to be expressed in cardinalities ($L+1\ge b_{K_0+1}$), otherwise there is an off-by-one issue. Deduplication is required too, since the problem is about distinct integers. Is there an argument that guarantees a seed in all cases, or is this the open difficulty? If the latter, what kinds of computational (python) directions or heuristics might probe at guaranteeing the seed interval (e.g. generate sequence -> compute sums -> detect first covering interval)? Thank you.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd: Proving that such a seed always exists is essentially the difficulty, yes. Furthermore, you are correct that -as stated- the problem requires distinct integers of the form $\left \lfloor t \alpha^n \right \rfloor$, but that is not what Erdős and Graham wrote (or what I believe they intended), and also not what is assumed in Graham's 1964 paper. Every element $s_n = \left \lfloor  t \alpha^n \right \rfloor$ is allowed to be used once, even if $s_n = s_m$ for some $m \neq n$. For example, Theorem 2 in Graham's paper implies in particular that the sequence with $t = \frac{2}{3}$ and $\alpha = 1.7$ (which has $s_1 = s_2 = 1$ and $s_3 = 3$) is entirely complete, which would not be true if we are not allowed to use both $s_1$ and $s_2$. For what it's worth, I am currently writing up some slight extensions of Graham's results that I will hopefully link to in the coming week.

sourceComments.author: memeister27
sourceComments.contentMd:
The script below shows that for $t=1,\alpha=1.5$ and $\alpha=\varphi$ all integers up to $200{,}000$ are representable, while for $t=2,\alpha=1.4$ a few small numbers ($1,4,6,\dots$) are missing even though the density is very high. It is only a computation, not a proof, but it hopefully illustrates the behaviour discussed in Problem 349.

import math

def seq(t, a, n=40):
    return [int(t * a**k) for k in range(1, n+1)]

def cover(s, L=200000):
    r = [0] * (L+1)
    r[0] = 1
    for a in s:
        for x in range(L, a-1, -1):
            r[x] |= r[x - a]
    return sum(r[1:]) / L, [i for i in range(1, L+1) if not r[i]]

for t, a in [(1, 1.5), (1, (1 + 5**0.5) / 2), (2, 1.4)]:
    s = seq(t, a)
    d, m = cover(s)
    print(f"\nt={t}, α≈{round(a, 3)}")
    print("First terms:", s[:12])
    print(f"Density up to 200k: {d:.6f}")
    print("First missing:", m[:10] if m else "None")

We get:
t=1, α≈1.5
First terms: [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 17, 25, 38, 57, 86, 129]
Density up to 200k: 1.000000
First missing: None

t=1, α≈1.618
First terms: [1, 2, 4, 6, 11, 17, 29, 46, 76, 122, 199, 321]
Density up to 200k: 1.000000
First missing: None

t=2, α≈1.4
First terms: [2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, 21, 29, 41, 57, 80, 113]
Density up to 200k: 0.999975
First missing: [1, 4, 6, 11, 16]

It seems from these checks that the behaviour of $\lfloor t \alpha^n \rfloor$ could hinge on how closely it shadows a Fibonacci-type recurrence, with small floor-errors making it look complete below the golden ratio.

### Problem
Let $p(x)\in \mathbb{Q}[x]$. Is it true that\[A=\{ p(n)+1/n : n\in \mathbb{N}\}\]is strongly complete, in the sense that, for any finite set $B$,\[\left\{\sum_{n\in X}n : X\subseteq A\backslash B\textrm{ finite }\right\}\]contains all sufficiently large integers?

Graham [Gr63] proved this is true when $p(n)=n$. Erdős and Graham also ask which rational functions $r(x)\in\mathbb{Z}(x)$ force $\{ r(n) : n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ to be complete?

Graham [Gr64f] gave a complete characterisation of which polynomials $r\in \mathbb{R}[x]$ are such that $\{ r(n) : n\in \mathbb{N}\}$ is complete.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd: On their question about rational functions, observe that any function of the form $r(x) = \frac{p(x)q(x) + 1}{q(x)}$ with $p(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, $q(x) = x^n$ and $n \ge 2$ is hopeless, as any sum $$r(a_1) + \ldots + r(a_k) = \big(p(a_1) + \ldots + p(a_k)\big) + \left(\frac{1}{a_1^n} + \ldots + \frac{1}{a_k^n} \right)$$with $k > 1$ lies strictly between two integers, due to the fact that $\frac{1}{2^n} + \frac{1}{3^n} + \ldots < 1$. And this idea can be generalized to rule out many more $r(x)$ for which the remainder (when we divide $p(x)$ by $q(x)$) has degree at most $deg(q(x)) - 2$.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
As I alluded to in my previous comment, one can indeed solve this problem for the polynomial $p(n) = n^2$, simply by combining the proof of Theorem $2$ in Graham's $1963$ paper with Alekseyev's proof referenced in [#283](https://www.erdosproblems.com/283). For a full write-up see [here](https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/The%20set%20(x%5E2%20%2B%20x%5E(-1))%20is%20strongly%20complete.pdf), but it's just essentially a copy-pasted version of Graham's proof. And speaking of Graham, precisely this question (on whether the set of values of $n^2 + \frac{1}{n}$ is strongly complete) was also asked by him in this paper:

Graham, R. L. *On Sums of Integers Taken from a Fixed Sequence*, Proc. Wash. State Univ. Conf. on Number Theory, (1971), 22-40

His question can be found [here](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/71_08_integer_sums.pdf) as question $7$ on page $35$. He then further asks the way more general question whether this is even true with $n^2$ replaced by $f(n)$ for any strongly complete sequence $f(n)$, but this seems quite unlikely to me. Maybe something like $f(n) = F_n - 1$ with $F_n$ the $n$-th Fibonacci number could provide a counterexample.

Moreover, as I also alluded to, for the solution of $p(n) = n^2$ I don't think it would be too difficult to instead use the proof of Theorem $3$ in my paper, as opposed to Graham's proof. The advantage of this (if it indeed works) is that it becomes possible to give a sharp upper bound for the largest integer which is not in $\{\sum_{x \in X} X \subset A \setminus B \text{ finite}\}$.

Finally, whether it's also possible to generalize this further to all polynomials mentioned in the comments of #283, I'll leave to someone else.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Vjeko is right that it should be all sufficiently large integers. Moreover, the reference should instead be:

[Gr63] Graham, R. L., A theorem on partitions. J. Austral. Math. Soc. (1963), 435-441

which can be found [here](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/63_02_partitions.pdf).

In it, Graham proved that every integer $n \ge 78$ can be written as a sum $a_1 + \ldots + a_r$ of distinct positive integers with $\frac{1}{a_1} + \ldots + \frac{1}{a_r} = 1$, so that every $n \ge 79$ can be written as $(a_1 + \frac{1}{a_1}) + \ldots + (a_r + \frac{1}{a_r})$. He moreover proves that for every $m$ a positive integer $n_m$ exists such that all $n \ge n_m$ can be written as sum $a_1 + \ldots + a_r$ of distinct positive integers with $\frac{1}{a_1} + \ldots + \frac{1}{a_r} = 1$ and where $a_i \ge m$ for all $i$. This gives the strongly complete claim. And one could propose an OEIS sequence $s_1, s_2, \ldots$ for this as well, where $s_m$ is the smallest $n_m$ for which the above holds. It'll be annoying to calculate any $s_m$ for even moderate values of $m$, say $m = 10$, but Theorem $3$ in [this](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.02200) recent paper of mine gives the asymptotic formula $(\frac{1}{2} + o(1))(e^2 - 1)m^2$.

Compare with [#283](https://www.erdosproblems.com/283), by the way; #283 is stronger in the sense that the sum of reciprocals must be equal to $1$, but this problem is stronger because it considers polynomials in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ and asks for strongly complete as opposed to merely complete (which, isn't completeness not hard enough already?). In any case, the other recent [paper](https://github.com/Woett/A-normal-paper-is-probably-fine/blob/main/The%20binomial%20case%20of%20Graham's%20conjecture%20on%20polynomial%20representations%20with%20prescribed%20sum%20of%20reciprocals.pdf) I mention there (still a work in progress) solves at least the completeness part of this problem for many linear and quadratic polynomials.

In fact, combining the latter with either the proof of Theorem $3$ I mentioned earlier or with the original proof of Graham, I should be able to generalize this to strongly complete, at least for $p(n) = n^2$. And maybe for all the other polynomials for which we can prove completeness as well. I will try to write up the details shortly.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
This problem's wording needs to be changed from "... contains all sufficiently large rational numbers?" to "... contains all sufficiently large integers?". The property of representing all sufficiently large rationals was rather called "$\mathbb{Q}$-completeness" by Erdős and Graham.
In fact, the surrounding remarks make no sense in the present formulation, even the claim about $p(n)=n$. Namely, for arbitrarily large $N\in\mathbb{N}$, rational numbers in the interval $(N,N+1)$ can be represented only using the first $N$ terms of the sequence $(n+1/n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$. That way, at most $2^N$ rationals from $(N,N+1)$ can be represented, but there is infinitely many of them.

### Problem
Is there some $c>0$ such that every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of measure $\geq c$ contains the vertices of a triangle of area 1?

### Context
Erdős (unpublished) proved that this is true if $A$ has infinite measure, or if $A$ is an unbounded set of positive measure (stating in [Er78d] and [Er83d] it 'follows easily from the Lebesgue density theorem').

In [Er78d] and [Er83d] he speculated that perhaps $C=4\pi/\sqrt{27}\approx 2.418$ works, which would be the best possible, as witnessed by a circle of radius $<2\cdot 3^{-3/4}$.

Further evidence for this is given by a result of Freiling and Mauldin [Ma02], who proved that if $A$ has outer measure $>4\pi/\sqrt{27}$ then $A$ contains the vertices of a triangle with area $>1$. This also proves the same threshold for the original problem under the assumption that $A$ is a compact convex set.

Mauldin also discusses this problem in [Ma13], in which he notes that it suffices to prove this under the assumption that $A$ is the union of the interiors of $n<\infty$ many compact convex sets. Freiling and Mauldin (see [Ma13]) have proved this conjecture if $1\leq n\leq 3$.
researchNotesMd: Erdős (unpublished) proved that this is true if $A$ has infinite measure, or if $A$ is an unbounded set of positive measure (stating in [Er78d] and [Er83d] it 'follows easily from the Lebesgue density theorem').
In [Er78d] and [Er83d] he speculated that perhaps $C=4\pi/\sqrt{27}\approx 2.418$ works, which would be the best possible, as witnessed by a circle of radius $<2\cdot 3^{-3/4}$.

Further evidence for this is given by a result of Freiling and Mauldin [Ma02], who proved that if $A$ has outer measure $>4\pi/\sqrt{27}$ then $A$ contains the vertices of a triangle with area $>1$. This also proves the same threshold for the original problem under the assumption that $A$ is a compact convex set.

Mauldin also discusses this problem in [Ma13], in which he notes that it suffices to prove this under the assumption that $A$ is the union of the interiors of $n<\infty$ many compact convex sets. Freiling and Mauldin (see [Ma13]) have proved this conjecture if $1\leq n\leq 3$.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
I thought I'd remark that Erdős asked this problem at least a couple more times before the stated reference [Er83d, p. 323]: [here](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1978-40.pdf) (p. 122-123) in 1978-79 and [here](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-22897-6_4) (p. 30) in 1981. Also, R. Daniel Mauldin wrote about the problem in [this paper](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/R-Mauldin-2/publication/2363356_Some_Problems_in_Set_Theory_Analysis_and_Geometry/links/0c96052951f2fa7f84000000/Some-Problems-in-Set-Theory-Analysis-and-Geometry.pdf) from 2001 (Section 1) and [this paper](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-3-642-39286-3_13.pdf) from 2013 (Section 5). However, the problem still seems to be open.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: J_Koizumi_144
replies.contentMd: One useful fact stated in Mauldin's paper is the following: this problem is equivalent to the one in which we restrict attention to sets $A$ that are unions of finitely many closed disks of equal radius. Indeed, by the inner regularity of the Lebesgue measure, it suffices to consider only compact sets $A$. After covering $A$ by $\varepsilon$-disks centered at points of $A$, one can apply Besicovitch's covering theorem to obtain the desired equivalence.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
Even slightly better, a further reduction is easy to see: one can assume that $A$ is a finite union of congruent dyadic squares, which are sets of the form\[ \big[2^{-n}k,2^{-n}(k+1)\big) \times\big[2^{-n}l,2^{-n}(l+1)\big) \]for $k,l,n\in\mathbb{Z}$. They are better because they are disjoint and correspond to the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
After scaling by $2^n$, one can essentially think about the corresponding discrete problem: can one find $\omega(4^n)$ points inside the grid $[4^n]\times[4^n]$ such that no three of them form a triangle of area $\approx \alpha$ for some fixed $\alpha$ of the order $4^n$.
I'm not being precise here, I'm just saying that constructions of such large discrete sets would lead to the counterexample to the main problem and vice versa. Some careless discrete reformulations can go wrong, of course, e.g., if one targets the precise area $\alpha$ which is an odd number, while $A$ consists of points with both even coordinates.

replies.author: J_Koizumi_144
replies.contentMd:
Nice reduction! Based on your idea, I formulated a precise translation into a discrete problem. For an integer $N>0$, we say that a set of lattice points $S\subset \mathbb{Z}^2$ is $N$-avoiding if for every $q_1,q_2,q_3\in S$ we have\[
\bigl\lvert \mu(\triangle q_1q_2q_3) - N \bigr\rvert > \mathrm{diam}(\triangle q_1q_2q_3).
\]Let $f(N)$ denote the largest possible size of an $N$-avoiding set. Then the original question is equivalent to asking whether $f(N)=O(N)$ holds. For a proof of the equivalence, please see [here](https://jkoizumi144.com/notes/erdos352.pdf).

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: This is very nice and worth writing down. However, your discrete reformulation is combinatorially complicated and I still find it beneficial to play with simplified discrete models to gain intuition about the problem.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
Related to the above discretization, I can perhaps suggest the following discrete toy-problem, which, I believe, captures the essence of the original question:
Let $f(N)$ be cardinality of the largest set $A\subseteq[N]\times[N]$ such that no three points from $A$ span the triangle of area $\in[0.99N,1.01N]$. Is $f(N)=O(N)$?
This, at least in theory, leaves room for computer experimentation, to perhaps try to find the "worst" arrangements, or to investigate all "types" of possible behaviors.

There is some superficial similarity with the [No-three-in-line problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-three-in-line_problem), which could be considered as the search for triangles of area 0. However, $f(N)\leq2N$ is obvious there, unlike in this problem.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
It's not much of an idea, but it might be useful to first play with triangles which have one side parallel to the $x$-axis. Namely, either in continuous or discrete setting, if $A$ does not contain such a triple of points spanning a triangle of area $1$ and if $B$ is its projection onto the $y$-axis, then each (one-dimensional) horizontal section $A_y := A \cap (\mathbb{R}\times\{y\})$ (viewed as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$) only has to avoid certain differences (determined by $B$ and $y$).

Inside the grid $[N]\times [N]$ this leads to a more effective algorithm for finding the largest allowed $A\subseteq[N]\times[N]$, of complexity $O(2^{2N})$, rather than $O(2^{N^2})$. Using this, I computed, for example, sizes of the largest $A\subseteq[N]\times[N]$ avoiding, say, areas $(N-1)/2$, $N/2$, $(N+1)/2$:

grid 2x2,  forbidden areas = {1/2,1,3/2},  maximum points = 2,
grid 3x3,  forbidden areas = {1,3/2,2},  maximum points = 4,
grid 4x4,  forbidden areas = {3/2,2,5/2},  maximum points = 7,
grid 5x5,  forbidden areas = {2,5/2,3},  maximum points = 8,
grid 6x6,  forbidden areas = {5/2,3,7/2},  maximum points = 12,
grid 7x7,  forbidden areas = {3,7/2,4},  maximum points = 16,
grid 8x8,  forbidden areas = {7/2,4,9/2},  maximum points = 22,
grid 9x9,  forbidden areas = {4,9/2,5},  maximum points = 25,
grid 10x10,  forbidden areas = {9/2,5,11/2},  maximum points = 38.

These experimental results still don't say much, since this discrete problem is too sensitive on divisibility issues. For instance, there is no way that a triangle with vertices in $[10]\times[10]$ can have area $11/2$, so this condition is not restricting anything.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
To ask an obvious question: can someone give a set that is larger than the appropriately-sized circle (open disk)?

I calculate the radius of that circle as $r=\frac{2}{3^{3/4}}$ and its area as $c=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{27}} \approx 2.418$.

(I was not able to access [Er83d].)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Indeed, Erdős himself in [Er83d] guessed that perhaps $C=4\pi/\sqrt{27}$ works for the same reason. (He also said that 'if true this conjecture should perhaps not be difficult to prove'.)

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
In the first comment above, I linked to two sources older than [Er83d]: they are both freely accessible. In the first one, from 1978, Erdős already mentions precisely that constant as potentially working. (Mauldin, see above, also played with this stronger version of the conjecture.) I don't remember seeing that even this value of $c$ has been disproved somewhere.

However, one must be aware that there are numerous "local extremizers" for the problem: there is a sequence of area-1-triangle-avoiding sets $(A_N)_{N=1}^{\infty}$ with areas $\gg1$ but arbitrarily large diameters. For instance, for each $(m,n)\in[N]\times[N]$ take a disk around $(2m,2n)$ of radius $\frac{1}{100N}$ and let $A_N$ be the union of all these disks.

replies.author: J_Koizumi_144
replies.contentMd: FWIW, [Sas’s theorem](https://eudml.org/doc/88724) implies that any convex set of area greater than $c = 4\pi/\sqrt{27}$ contains a triangle of area $1$. Moreover, Mauldin's 2013 article mentioned in Vjeko's comment shows that the same constant $c$ is optimal even for unions of at most three convex sets.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #354 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/354).

### Problem
Let $\alpha,\beta\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that $\alpha/\beta$ is irrational. Is the multiset\[\{ \lfloor \alpha\rfloor,\lfloor 2\alpha\rfloor,\lfloor 4\alpha\rfloor,\ldots\}\cup \{ \lfloor \beta\rfloor,\lfloor 2\beta\rfloor,\lfloor 4\beta\rfloor,\ldots\}\]complete? That is, can all sufficiently large natural numbers $n$ be written as\[n=\sum_{s\in S}\lfloor 2^s\alpha\rfloor+\sum_{t\in T}\lfloor 2^t\beta\rfloor\]for some finite $S,T\subset \mathbb{N}$?

What if $2$ is replaced by some $\gamma\in(1,2)$?

### Context
This question was first mentioned by Graham [Gr71].

Hegyvári [He89] proved that this holds if $\alpha=m/2^n$ is a dyadic rational and $\beta$ is not. He later [He91] proved that, for any fixed $\alpha>0$, the set of $\beta$ for which this holds either has measure $0$ or infinite measure. In [He94] he proved that the set of $(\alpha,\beta)$ for which the corresponding set of sums does not contain an infinite arithmetic progression has cardinality continuum.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Include a rigorous proof, counterexample, or a precise explanation of the remaining gap.

Hegyvári [He89] proved that this holds if $\alpha=m/2^n$ is a dyadic rational and $\beta$ is not. He later [He91] proved that, for any fixed $\alpha>0$, the set of $\beta$ for which this holds either has measure $0$ or infinite measure. In [He94] he proved that the set of $(\alpha,\beta)$ for which the corresponding set of sums does not contain an infinite arithmetic progression has cardinality continuum.

Hegyvári [He89] proved that the sequence is not complete if $\alpha\geq 2$ and $\beta =2^k\alpha$ for some $k\geq 0$. Jiang and Ma [JiMa24] and Fang and He [FaHe25] prove that the sequence is not complete if $1<\alpha<2$ and $\beta=2^k\alpha$ for some sufficiently large $k$.
It is likely (and Hegyvári conjectures) that the assumption $\alpha/\beta$ irrational can be weakened to $\alpha/\beta \neq 2^k$ and either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ not a dyadic rational.

In the comments van Doorn proves the sequence is complete if $\alpha < 2<\beta<3$, and also proves that if either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational then the corresponding sequence with ceiling functions replacing the floor functions is complete.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
Aristotle from Harmonic found a [disproof](https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/ErdosProblems/Erdos354x.md) of the [statement](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/f33f5ddb49f6077e34025917965bcd1bbd920d73/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/354.lean) at the Formal Conjectures project, due to a [misformalization](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/issues/1309).  [Type-check it online!](https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.24.0&url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fplby%2Flean-proofs%2Frefs%2Fheads%2Fmain%2Fsrc%2Fv4.24.0%2FErdosProblems%2FErdos354x.lean)

I don't know whether I will keep posting comments like this as more misformalizations are inevitably found, but I think I would like to draw some attention to (a) how frequent misformalization is and (b) the fact that tools like Aristotle can help find some such issues automatically, including in cases with nontrivial arguments.

replies.author: John N. Dvorak
replies.contentMd:
I say keep going--these are really valuable to document. Misformalisations are (regrettably) not an edge case here; they’re a persistent, inherent risk whenever we translate informal conjectures into Lean. Especially at scale.

Having concrete examples where Aristotle (or similar tools) disprove a misformalized statement is essential to building our trust in these pipelines; and especially to harden the formal conjectures repo over time.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: I will keep [submitting issues to the Formal Conjectures project](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/issues?q=Erd%C5%91s%20is%3Aissue%20label%3Amisformalization%20author%3Aplby), but probably commenting on a forum page here only for misformalizations of interest.  For example, today Aristotle found [that n=0 was mistakenly allowed](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/issues/1343) in parts of [[366]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366), and that's not very interesting at all.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Using the deep research tool of ChatGPT I managed to find a few references I was not aware of previously, and I think my first comment here is mostly obsolete. Oh well. Long comment incoming! And by the way, as far as I know, in everything that follows the original problem with constant $\gamma = 2$ is considered, unless otherwise stated.

Okay, to start off,

N. Hegyvári, *Some remarks on a problem of Erdős and Graham*, Acta Math. Hung., Volume 53 (1989), 149-154

proves exactly Proposition 1 in my comment above; if $\alpha$ is a dyadic rational and $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, then the sequence under consideration is complete. On the other hand, using $\alpha \ge 2$ and $\beta = 2^l \alpha$ with $l \in \mathbb{N}$, he also shows that the set of pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which the sequence is not complete has the cardinality of the continuum.

Even though I cannot access this paper by Hegyvári, I can find his follow-up paper where he mentions that he had obtained the dyadic rational result:

N. Hegyvári, *On complete sequences*, Annales Univ. Sci. Budapest, Volume 34 (1991), 7-10.

In this second paper (which you can find [here](https://annalesm.elte.hu/annales34-1991/Annales_1991_T-XXXIV.pdf), pages 7-10) he furthermore proves that, for any fixed $\alpha > 0$, the set of $\beta$ for which the corresponding sequence is complete either has Lebesgue measure $0$, or has infinite measure. In order to prove this he makes use of the observation in my first comment that $P(2\alpha, \beta)$ implies $P(\alpha, \beta)$. But he didn't stop there!

N. Hegyvári, *On sumset of certain sets*, Publ. Math. Debrecen, Volume 45 (1994), 115-122

which can be found [here](https://publi.math.unideb.hu/load_doc.php?p=174&t=pap), shows that the set of pairs $(\alpha, \beta)$ for which the sequence does not even contain an infinite arithmetic progression, also has the cardinality of the continuum. This strengthens the second result from the first paper I mentioned. Both cardinality continuum results make use of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with $\frac{\beta}{\alpha}$ a power of two (i.e. rational), however. So they don't disprove the conjecture at hand.

Then, much more recently, we finally have the following two papers

X. W. Jiang, W. X. Ma, *A conjecture of Hegyvári*, Int. J. Number Theory, Volume 20 (2024), 915–933.
J. H. Fang, J. Y. He, *On a problem of Erdős and Graham*, Acta Math. Hung., Volume 175 (2025), 532-542.

Thanks to Terence who kindly sent me a copy of the second paper (and see his comment below as well!), both papers seem to extend Hegyvári's non-completeness results in the case that $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ is a power of two, but for $\alpha < 2$ and $\beta$ sufficiently large.

Long story short, I believe the following four results for specific $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are known:

**Proposition 1.** If exactly one of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is a dyadic rational, then the sequence is complete.
**Proposition 2.** If $\min(\alpha, \beta) < 2$ and $\max(\alpha, \beta) < 3$, then the sequence is complete.
**Proposition 3.** If $\alpha \ge 2$ and $\beta = 2^l \alpha$ with $l \in \mathbb{N}$, then the sequence is not complete.
**Proposition 4.** If $\alpha < 2$ and  $\beta = 2^l \alpha$ with $l \in \mathbb{N}$ sufficiently large, then the sequence is not complete.

Here, Propositions 1 and 3 are due to Hegyvári, while Proposition 4 is due to Jiang-Ma and Fang-He.

Long story even shorter, as far as I can tell there is no solution to the main problem yet. On the other hand, I do suspect that the first paper by Hegyvári either settles the case $\gamma = \sqrt{2}$ or perhaps even $1 < \gamma \le \sqrt{2}$ (possibly implicitly). If anyone has access to this paper and could check, that would be appreciated. And in other news, the hypothesis that $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$ is irrational can most likely be slightly weakened (if that wasn't clear already); Hegyvári conjectures that the sequence is complete if either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, and $\beta \neq 2^l \alpha$. In other words, Propositions 3 and 4 are conjecturally close to optimal.

The result I mentioned in my second post in this comment section (namely, that if we change all floor functions to ceiling functions, then the sequence is complete, as long as either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational) does seem to be new however, so perhaps I actually will keep working on my own paper on this subject.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: If it makes you feel any better, I had a fairly similar experience with [#243](https://www.erdosproblems.com/243), though with Vjeko playing the role of an AI deep research tool in that case.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd: That does make me feel better Terence, thank you ;)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I was able to get a hold of the Fang-He paper, but not the Jiang-Ma paper.  From what I can tell:

* Jiang-Ma showed that completeness fails when $1 < \alpha < 2$ and $\beta = 2^l \alpha$ for a sufficiently large $l$. In fact they prove something stronger than non-completeness but it is more technical to state.
* Fang-He reprove this statement with a simpler proof and say even more about the set of subset sums.

However they don't seem to claim anything about the case when $\beta/\alpha$ is not a power of two.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
At a first glance, it seems like there should be no fundamental difference in this question if we change all floor functions to ceiling functions, right? A priori there seems to be no reason why proving the completeness for one should be any easier or harder than for the other. Well, as fate would have it, I can resolve this problem.. But only if we use the ceiling function! Isn't that remarkable?

To elaborate on this, let me define two notions. We say that a sequence $S = (s_1, s_2, \ldots)$ is a $\Sigma$-sequence if a constant $c$ exists such that $s_{n+1} - \sum_{i=1}^n s_i \le c$ for all $n$. And we call a sequence precomplete if, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, there are $k$ consecutive integers that can all be written as the sum of distinct elements of $S$.

In his $1964$ paper 'Complete Sequences of Polynomial Values' (see [here](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/#64)), Graham proved that if $A = (a_1, a_2, \ldots)$ is a $\Sigma$-sequence and $B = (b_1, b_2, \ldots)$ is precomplete, then the union $(a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, \ldots)$ is complete.

Now, if $a_{n+1} \le 2a_n$ for all large enough $n$, then one can show that $A$ is a $\Sigma$-sequence. And the equality $a_{n+1} \le 2a_n$ is satisfied for all large enough $n$ if $a_n = \lceil 2^{n-1} \alpha \rceil$, but not if $a_n = \lfloor 2^{n-1} \alpha \rfloor$!

Moreover, to prove that $B = (b_1, b_2, \ldots)$ is precomplete for $b_n = \lceil 2^{n-1} \beta \rceil$, it turns out that it is sufficient to show that there are just two consecutive integers that can both be written as the sum of distinct elements of $B$. And for $b_n = \lceil 2^{n-1} \beta \rceil$ one can check that, unless $\beta$ is a dyadic rational, there is some $n$ such that $b_1 + b_2 + \ldots + b_{n-1}$ is equal to $b_n - 1$, finishing the proof.

All in all I can prove the following theorem: as long as either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, then $(\lceil \alpha \rceil, \lceil \beta\rceil, \lceil 2\alpha \rceil, \lceil 2\beta\rceil, \lceil 4\alpha \rceil, \lceil 4\beta\rceil, \ldots)$ is complete.

For a (first version of a) full write-up, see [here](https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/Completeness%20of%20exponentially%20increasing%20sequences%20II.pdf).

I plan to combine this write-up with another project I'm working on, and will submit a proper paper to the arXiv in the coming months. I'll make sure to link it once it's finished. In the mean time, perhaps someone else can use some of these ideas to put the ball into the back of the net ;) As it does feel like we're very close to solving this problem.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
This change of ceilings and floors may lead to no difference in result, but proving it can be of substantial different difficulty.
(I know an analogue of an olympiad question where this was the case e.g.)

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ denote the statement that the above sequence is complete, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are assumed to be positive reals. Then I can prove the following two propositions:

**Proposition 1.** If $\alpha = \frac{m}{2^n}$ is a dyadic rational (so in particular if $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$) and $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, then $P(\alpha, \beta)$ holds.
**Proposition 2.** If $\min(\alpha, \beta) < 2$ and $\max(\alpha, \beta) < 3$, then $P(\alpha, \beta)$ holds.

In general we see that $P(2\alpha, \beta)$ implies $P(\alpha, \beta)$, as the corresponding sequence for the former is a subsequence of the latter. In particular, to prove the first proposition it is sufficient to assume $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$.

So assume $\alpha = m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let us first note that the sequence $(\lfloor \alpha \rfloor, \lfloor 2\alpha \rfloor, \lfloor 4\alpha \rfloor, \ldots)$ then generates $m\mathbb{N}$. We therefore need to show that sums of distinct elements from $B = (\lfloor \beta \rfloor, \lfloor 2\beta \rfloor, \lfloor 4\beta \rfloor, \ldots)$ attain all residue classes modulo $m$.

Now, for every prime divisor $p$ of $m$, I claim that $B$ contains infinitely many elements not divisible by $p$, if $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational. Indeed, if $p$ divides $\lfloor 2^l \beta \rfloor$ for some $l$, let $r \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ be such that $2^l \beta = pr + \epsilon$ and choose $l'$ such that $1 \le 2^{l'} \epsilon < 2$. We then get that $\left \lfloor 2^{l+l'} \beta \right \rfloor = 2^{l'}pr + 1$ is not divisible by $p$.

Let $b_1 \pmod{m}, b_2 \pmod{m}, \ldots, b_k \pmod{m}$ be those residue classes modulo $m$ that appear infinitely often in $B$. We remark that it is not necessarily the case that there exists an $i$ such that $\gcd(b_i, m) = 1$. However, we do have $\gcd(b_1, \ldots, b_k, m) = 1$ by the aforementioned claim on prime divisors $p$ of $m$. We therefore get by the existence of the Frobenius number that all residue classes modulo $m$ appear among sums of the $b_i$, which was what we needed to prove.

As for the second proposition, note we may assume $\beta \ge \alpha > 1$; the first inequality by symmetry, and the second inequality by the aforementioned fact that $P(2\alpha, \beta)$ implies $P(\alpha, \beta)$. Now define, for $n \ge 1$, $s_{2n-1} = \lfloor 2^{n-1} \alpha \rfloor$ and $s_{2n} = \lfloor 2^{n-1} \beta \rfloor$. We then claim that $(s_1, s_2, \ldots)$ generates the entirety of $\mathbb{N}$, for which it is necessary and sufficient to show $s_{n+1} \le 1 + \sum_{i=1}^n s_i$ for all $n \ge 0$. This follows for $n = 0$ by the fact that $s_1 = \lfloor \alpha \rfloor = 1$, and it follows for $n = 1$ as $s_2 = \lfloor \beta \rfloor \le 2$. For $n \ge 2$ we get by induction
\begin{align*}
s_{n+1} &\le 2s_{n-1} + 1 \\
&\le 2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} s_i \\
&\le 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} s_i.
\end{align*}
In fact, the proof of this second proposition immediately generalizes to $\gamma \in (1,2)$ instead of $2$, and it even works in some cases for $\gamma \le 3$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #357 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/357).

### Problem
Let $1\leq a_1<\cdots <a_k\leq n$ be integers such that all sums of the shape $\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$ are distinct. Let $f(n)$ be the maximal such $k$.

How does $f(n)$ grow? Is $f(n)=o(n)$?

### Context
Asked by Erdős and Harzheim. In [Er77c] Erdős asks about an infinite such set of integers, and whether such a set must have density $0$. He notes that a simple averaging process implies $a_k \gg k\log k$ for infinitely many $k$, and so the lower density is $0$. He also asks whether $\sum\frac{1}{a_k}$ must converge.

Weisenberg in the comments observes that any set which satisfies [[874]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/874) also has this property, which implies $f(n)\geq (2+o(1))n^{1/2}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Asked by Erdős and Harzheim. In [Er77c] Erdős asks about an infinite such set of integers, and whether such a set must have density $0$. He notes that a simple averaging process implies $a_k \gg k\log k$ for infinitely many $k$, and so the lower density is $0$. He also asks whether $\sum\frac{1}{a_k}$ must converge.
Weisenberg in the comments observes that any set which satisfies [[874]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/874) also has this property, which implies $f(n)\geq (2+o(1))n^{1/2}$.

If $g(n)$ is the maximal $k$ such that there are $1\leq a_1,\ldots,a_k\leq n$ with all consecutive sums distinct (i.e. we drop the monotonicity assumption in the definition of $f$) then Hegyvári [He86] has proved that\left(\frac{1}{3}+o(1)\right) n\leq g(n)\leq \left(\frac{2}{3}+o(1)\right)n.The upper bound of Coppersmith and Phillips in [[867]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/867) impliesg(n) \leq \left(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{512}+o(1)\right)n.A similar question can be asked if we replace strict monotonicity with weak monotonicity (i.e. we allow $a_i=a_j$).

Erdős and Harzheim also ask what is the least $m$ which is not a sum of the given form? Can it be much larger than $n$? Erdős and Harzheim can show that $\sum_{x<a_i<x^2}\frac{1}{a_i}\ll 1$. Is it true that $\sum_i \frac{1}{a_i}\ll 1$?

See also [[34]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/34), [[356]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/356), [[670]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/670), and [[867]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/867). The multiplicative analogue is [[421]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/421).

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
Regarding "A similar question can be asked if we replace strict monotonicity with weak monotonicity (i.e. we allow $a_i=a_j$)"
I'm not quite sure how to make sense of this: Is the idea here to then allow only sums over intervals of length larger than $1$? or is it then allowed to take sums over length-$1$ intervals, but they are only counted once? Would $a_1, a_2, a_3 = 1, 1, 2$ have all distinct sums?
Is there a reference where this question is asked?

Boris Alexeev pointed me to this question when asking about our formalisation in Formal Conjectures of this problem.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
In [OLD AND NEW PROBLEMS AND RESULTS IN COMBINATORIAL NUMBER THEORY](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf), at the bottom of page 58. However, it just says 'What if we remove the monotonicity constraint and/or the distinctness constraint?'

I am not sure what it mean to remove the distinctness constraint, and perhaps 'remove the monotonicity constraint' merely means the version tackled in [He86].

replies.author: Moritz Firsching
replies.contentMd: Thanks! I also don't understand what removing the "distinctness constraint" would exactly mean. In the same paragraph the word "distinct" is mentioned for the blocks, so perhaps this condition is relaxed instead?

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd: I think a good interpretation of weak monotonicity is one where we don't compare sums over two different length $1$ intervals (as you said) and the rest is the same. Your example would not have al distinct sums due to $a_1+a_2=a_3$.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
As a remark, Beker's work on [[356]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/356) gives a nontrivial upper bound for $f(n)$. Define\[
S(a) = \left\{ \sum_{i=u}^v a_i : 1 \le u \le v \le k \right\}.
\]By [Be23b, Proposition 1.5], for any strictly increasing sequence \(1 \le a_1 < \cdots < a_k \le n\) one has\[
|S(a)| \le (c_4 + o(1)) n^2,
\qquad
c_4 = \frac{e^2 - 1}{2(e^2 + 1)}.
\]Now take an extremal configuration for $f(n)$: there exists some $k = f(n)$ and a strictly increasing subset \(1 \le a_1 < \cdots < a_k \le n\) such that all consecutive sums are distinct. In this case\[
|S(a)| = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}.
\]Combining the two bounds, we obtain \(\frac{k(k+1)}{2} \le (c_4 + o(1)) n^2\), and hence\[
f(n) \le \left(\sqrt{2c_4} + o(1)\right) n
= \left( \sqrt{\frac{e^2 - 1}{e^2 + 1}} + o(1) \right) n
\approx (0.8727 + o(1))\,n.
\][Be23b] Beker, A., On a problem of Erdős and Graham about consecutive sums in strictly increasing sequences. arXiv:2311.10087 (2023).

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
The upper bound of $f(n)\leq g(n)\leq\frac{2n}{3}$ follows from Hegyvári's paper.
Though this is a way of specifically tackling the monotone version of the problem.

sourceComments.contentMd:
The page numbers are [Er77c,p.70][ErGr80,p.58].

Another related question we can ask is: if we have $n$ positive integers with distinct consecutive sums, with no restrictions on monotonicity *or* on the upper bound of each individual number, what is the smallest sum of these integers? This is essentially equivalent to the $d = 1$ case of [[670]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/670), by letting the integers of the sequence correspond to the lengths of the gaps between points. Perhaps a "see also" to [[867]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/867) would make sense too.

Feel free to delete this comment after reviewing.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #358 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358).

### Problem
Let $A=\{a_1<\cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of solutions to\[n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.\]Is there such an $A$ for which $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$? Or even where $f(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$?

### Context
When $a_n=n$ the function $f(n)$ counts the number of odd divisors of $n$.

In modern language, this asks for the existence of a convex set $A$ such that $1_A\circ 1_A(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$.

### Deliverable

researchNotes: When $a_n=n$ the function $f(n)$ counts the number of odd divisors of $n$.
In modern language, this asks for the existence of a convex set $A$ such that $1_A\circ 1_A(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$.

Erdős and Moser [Mo63] considered the case when $A$ is the set of primes, and conjectured that the $\limsup$ of the number of such representations in this case is infinite. They could not even prove that the upper density of the set of integers representable in this form is positive.

In [ErGr80] they further asked whether $f(n)\geq 1$ for all large $n$ is possible, but Egami observed the answer to this is trivially yes, taking $a_n=n$. Perhaps they intended to restrict $f(n)$ to only count those representatives as the sum of at least two consecutive terms. (It is a classical fact that $n$ can be expressed as a sum of at least two consecutive positive integers if and only if $n\neq 2^k$.)
In [Er77c] Erdős writes 'This problem can perhaps be rightly criticized as being artificial and in the backwater of Mathematics but it seems very strange and attractive to me'.

Weisenberg observes that the finite analogue of this problem, asking how many integers up to some $x$ can be written as the sum of consecutive elements, is very similar to [[356]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/356).
This is reported in problem C2 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: I was able to find a red/blue construction that avoided the various pitfalls involving unwanted dependencies between events or inability to allocate disjoint intervals to exceptional elements, recovering the bound claimed in Nat's AI-generated solution of $\gg \log n$ representations for each large $n$. [Here is the writeup](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358.pdf).  One new ingredient is to impose some primality and coprimality conditions on certain dilation factors in order to avoid unwanted collisions between intervals.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Congrats!

replies.author: Aron Bhalla
replies.contentMd:
GPT-5.2 Thinking suggests the following corrections / possible small gaps:

* Lemma 2.3(a): the scale $\gg 2^{k-2c_0k}-O(2^{c_0k})$ seems to want $c_1$ rather than $c_0$, since it cites (2.11) (where $p \sim 2^{c_1k}$).
* Lemma 2.3(b): you are comparing $I_{n,p}$ and $I_{n',p}$ (same $p$), so the line “$\le 2p+2p'$” should read “$\le 4p$”.
* Clustered bound: since $m=\lceil 1/c_2\rceil$, $m/q \asymp 1/(c_2 q)$; so the appearance of $1/c_2^2$ looks like an extra factor of $1/c_2$.
* Prop 3.1 (Gaussian integral at the end): the exponent should be quadratic in $a$. It looks like it should be $\exp(-3a^2/(4q^3))$ rather than $\exp(-3a/(4q^3))$.
* Prop 3.1 The phrase “within 0.1 of a non-zero integer” should at least be “within 0.1 of an integer” (since $0$ mod 1 is also problematic). Also, it wasn’t fully convinced by the quick claim that this holds for $\ge (q/4)$ values of $j$ without a brief spacing/counting justification; perhaps a short counting sentence is missing.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: I have GPT [check the writeup](https://chatgpt.com/share/699c84c9-b3a4-8010-9450-0a9be96185f5) and it claims some minor issues/typos along with suggested fixes. They can be found in the second-to-last message. Personally, these look reasonable to me, but I'm not able to be sure because the argument is rather detailed.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Thanks to both for the corrections!  GPT 5.2 seems to do rather well as a referee actually, it seems that it "understood" the argument quite well.  Here is a [new version](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-1-1.pdf) addressing the points.

Interestingly, the only flaw in the GPT reports was an OCR problem, as they were starting from a PDF rather than the LaTeX source: on the bottom of page 11 of the original manuscript there was an expression $c_2 2^{k-(1-c_1)k'}$ and both instances of GPT interpreted this as involving $c_2^2$.  (It took me a while to figure out why they were complaining about this.)

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Yes, the OCR problem can be quite common. In my case, luckily GPT decides to view the PDF visually(!) as part of its checking and discovers it's not a genuine issue. However, even if it doesn't do this, I (the human) will look over the final issue list to see whether there are unexpected things that I can see.

In general, to have a chance at solving hard problems, GPT must able to referee itself as part of the process. A by-product is that it can referee others' works as well.

replies.author: Aron Bhalla
replies.contentMd:
GPT-5.2 Thinking is happier with the argument now. For completeness, it also suggests the following (minor) corrections:

* p.6 (Lemma 2.3(d) proof): sign typo that the very next sentence relies on
Current: after dividing by $n\asymp 2^k$, the proof states $\frac{p'_2q'}{p'_1}-\frac{p''_2q''}{p''_1}\ll 2^{(1-c_0)k}$.
Suggested: this should be $\ll 2^{-(1-c_0)k}$ (or comparably small), otherwise the “denominator $\Rightarrow$ must vanish” step doesn’t follow. Also on the same page: “Inderting” → “Inserting”, and “byt (2.5)” → “by (2.5)”.

* p.10 (Proposition 3.1 proof, first bullet): wrong variable in the quantifier phrase
Current: “… will stay at least $0.1$ away from an integer for $\gg q$ choices of $q$.”
Suggested: “… for $\gg q$ choices of $j$.” (Since the arithmetic progression is $(q-j)\theta$ as $j$ varies.)

* p.14 (Lemma 4.2 proof): minor notation consistency
You define $\mathcal Q_{k',n_p}$ and $\mathbf F_{n_p,q}$, but then write the random variable using $q\in \mathcal Q_{k'}$ and $1_{\mathbf F_q}$.
Suggested: change to $q\in \mathcal Q_{k',n_p}$ and $1_{\mathbf F_{n_p,q}}$

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Thanks for the further corrections!  I also noted a slight inaccuracy in my concentration of measure reference: Hoeffding's inequality was not quite strong enough to get the required bounds, but the Chernoff type bounds in Alon-Spencer work just fine.  [Here is the new version](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf).

replies.author: Aron Bhalla
replies.contentMd:
I have, since the release of GPT 5.4, been comparing its output with GPT 5.2. In our earlier conversation, 5.2 Thinking found no further corrections; however, running the PDF through 5.4 Thinking yielded the following additional observations:

* page 5 (Lemma 2.4(a) statement): the conclusion currently says that $I_{n,p}$ and $I_{n,p'}$ are disjoint. But the hypotheses involve the two intervals $I_{n,p}$ and $I_{n',p'}$, so the second interval in the conclusion should carry $n'$, not $n$.
Suggested: change the conclusion of Lemma 2.4(a) to say that $I_{n,p}$ and $I_{n',p'}$ are disjoint.

* page 9 (Proposition 2.1 proof / immediately after Proposition 2.1): the sentence “In view of the above proposition, we see that to show (2.2) and therefore Theorem 1.1 ...” has the wrong cross-reference. Proposition 2.2 is being used to prove (2.6), not (2.2). Also, in the preceding line, “sum of consecutive sum of elements” contains an extra “sum”.
Suggested: replace “to show (2.2)” with “to show (2.6)”, and replace “sum of consecutive sum of elements” with “sum of consecutive elements”.

* page 10 (Proposition 3.1 proof): in the middle-range estimate, the paper states that if $q^{-1.4} \le |\theta| \le 10/q$, then the arithmetic progression $(q-j)\theta$ “will stay at least $\gg q^{-0.4}$ away from an integer for $q/40 \le j \le q/20$”. This is false as written. For example, take $q=100$, $\theta=1/97$, and $j=3$. Then $q^{-1.4} \le \theta \le 10/q$, and $j=3 \in [q/40,q/20]$, but $(q-j)\theta = 97/97 = 1$, which is exactly an integer. So the displayed bound $\ll \exp(-cq^{0.2})$ is not established by the current argument.
Suggested: replace this step with a correct counting argument showing that for $\gg q$ values of $j$ in a suitable range, $(q-j)\theta$ stays $\gg q^{-0.4}$ away from the integers; that would suffice to recover the exponential decay. In its current form, this part of the proof needs amendment.

* page 12 (Proposition 2.2(i) proof): the proof says that the event $F_q$ depends only on the portion of $A_0$ in $\bigcup_{j=1}^m I_{n'*j,q}$, “which lies in $\Delta*{k'}$”. That should be $R_{k'}$, not $\Delta_{k'}$, because these intervals are red-admissible and hence lie in the red block $R_{k'}$.
Suggested: replace “lies in $\Delta_{k'}$” with “lies in $R_{k'}$”.

* page 13 (definition of $G_{n_p}$, before Lemma 4.1): the text says that $G_{n_p}$ is the event that $n_p$ is red-exceptional, “that is to say, there are fewer than $\lfloor c_2k\rfloor$ red-admissible intervals $I_{n_p,q}$”. This does not match the earlier definition of red-exceptional, which requires fewer than $\lfloor c_2k\rfloor$ representing red-admissible intervals. As written, the crucial word “representing” has been dropped.
Suggested: replace “there are fewer than $\lfloor c_2k\rfloor$ red-admissible intervals $I_{n_p,q}$” with “there are fewer than $\lfloor c_2k\rfloor$ representing red-admissible intervals $I_{n_p,q}$”.

* page 14 (Lemma 4.2 proof): the lower bound $ES \gg c_0k$ implicitly uses a lower bound on the number of admissible $q$’s in each associated red block, i.e. on #$Q_{k',n_p}$, analogous to the earlier bound proved on page 12 for #$Q_{k'}$. That counting step is not written out or cited here, but it is needed to justify the displayed lower bound for the mean.
Suggested: add a sentence explicitly proving, or referring back to the proof of, the lower bound #$Q_{k',n_p} \gg 2^{,k-(1-c_1)k'}$ (or the appropriate analogue), and then deduce $ES \gg c_0k$ from Proposition 3.1.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
Heads up: GPT-5.2 Thinking under my supervision, using my latest long-range workflow, appears to have obtained a full solution. I'm needing a little more time to finalize; it's about 30 pages (!).

This is notable because we want to find some ways to make AI tackle (autonomously or at least with limited human supervision) problems at a larger scale. If current models can do it under favorable circumstances, it is likely future models will be able to do it under less favorable circumstances, and so on.

An immediate problem I see is how to confidently verify such things; currently I simply do not know for sure.

This solution is loosely based on Tao's, but perhaps with elements of Chojecki's. The result is that there is an $A$ for which there exists $c > 0$ with $f(n) \ge c \log n$ for all large $n$. Moreover, this is optimal up to constants: for any $A$, we have $\liminf_{n\to\infty} f(n)/\log n \le 1$.

Will post solution soon!

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Unfortunately for this sort of problem the details *are* very important.  It is potentially possible that just by knowing the construction used by the AI proof to generate $A$, that a human expert can independently verify whether that construction has a good chance of working, but without that high level analysis or a Lean formalization, there is a high chance of some sort of basic bookkeeping error in the estimates.

For this specific problem I think some sort of weak "expander graph" property has to be established at some point to prevent the possibility of some subset of the survivors of the red representations somehow colliding into each other when the time comes to create blue representations.  Some back of the envelope calculations suggest that this sort of expansion can be guaranteed by a combination of several standard tools (Menger's theorem, Plunnecke's inequality, Chernoff bounds, etc.) but it is non-trivial, and I would be somewhat surprised if a largely autonomous AI could piece all the steps together correctly.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
There is a gap in the proof of Lemma 17; I will let [ChatGPT Pro explain the issue](https://chatgpt.com/share/69960c12-d6d0-800e-b24a-4902b82247d5).  The task of allocating disjoint intervals to each exceptional element is, in my view, the most delicate part of the whole strategy (which is where I think expander graph type ideas will be needed); _morally_ with enough randomness this should be possible, but because one needs to allocate disjoint intervals to _all_ exceptional elements (and not just _almost all_) one needs a lot of care in the arguments.

On the plus side, the modification of the original construction to randomize the portion of the red blocks (which Przemek's AI solution also employed) does seem to be a genuine improvement, in that it significantly reduces the size of the exceptional set- the original construction fluctuated like the divisor function, which is essentially log-normally distributed, whereas the random construction enjoys Chernoff bounds, allowing for an exponential improvement in the exceptional set sparsity from logarithmic to polynomial.  But it still is not enough to close the argument immediately. As suggested in my original post, one may need to introduce further colors than red and blue, and go through a couple rounds of reducing the size of the exceptional set until one reaches a point where allocating available intervals to all remaining survivors genuinely becomes straightforward.

An additional minor technical note: I am beginning to lean towards using essentially dyadic blocks such as $[x, 1.01 x]$ rather than shorter blocks $[x,x+x^\alpha]$ for the red/blue coloring, in particular alternating the 1.01-dyadic blocks between red and blue should suffice (and allow one to skip a few standard but tedious Chernoff-type steps).  A single blue block $[y, 1.01y]$ with $y \asymp x^{1-c}$ should be able to mop up all the $O(x^{1-\gamma})$ survivors in $[x, 2x]$ from red-block representations, for suitable choices of constants $0 < c < \gamma$, provided that one can verify a certain technical expander graph type property.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: It seems plausible that a modified random construction might do the trick here.  Divide the natural numbers into disjoint blocks of the form $[x, x + x^{0.99})$ (not 100% sure this is the optimal width, but something like this), and randomly color these blocks red and blue.  Take $A$ to consist of all of the numbers in red blocks (chosen at random), plus some unspecified set of numbers in blue blocks.  It seems likely that all but a fairly small set of integers can be represented multiple times as the sum of consecutive numbers in a red block (or, occasionally, spanning two adjacent red blocks); the exceptional set should only be a little bit denser than the (almost) primes.  Now one just has to fix the construction by expressing the elements in the exceptional set a couple times as sums of nearby numbers in a blue block (or, occasionally, spanning two adjacent blue blocks), in such a way that there are no collisions between the numbers used.  There is a lot of bookkeeping to do (and lots of concentration of measure estimates) but I think there is enough "room" in the parameters that something like this might work.  (One may need more than two colors, because the exceptional set might itself spawn a smaller exceptional set, but again I think with enough juggling of parameters one can fix this issue.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #359 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/359).

### Problem
Let $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be an infinite sequence of integers such that $a_1=n$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the least integer which is not a sum of consecutive earlier $a_j$s. What can be said about the density of this sequence?

In particular, in the case $n=1$, can one prove that $a_k/k\to \infty$ and $a_k/k^{1+c}\to 0$ for any $c>0$?

### Context
A problem of MacMahon, studied by Andrews [An75]. When $n=1$ this sequence begins\[1,2,4,5,8,10,14,15,\ldots.\]This sequence is [A002048](https://oeis.org/A002048) in the OEIS. Andrews conjectures\[a_k\sim \frac{k\log k}{\log\log k}.\]Porubsky [Po77] proved that, for any $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $k$ such that\[a_k < (\log k)^\epsilon \frac{k\log k}{\log\log k},\]and also that if $A(x)$ counts the number of $a_i\leq x$ then\[\limsup \frac{A(x)}{\pi(x)}\geq \frac{1}{\log 2}\]where $\pi(x)$ counts the number of primes $\leq x$.

See also [[839]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/839).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Porubský (Š. Porubský, On MacMahon's segmented numbers and related sequences, Nieuw Arch. Wisk., (3) 25 (1977) 403-408) showed that $$\liminf \frac{a_k \log \log k}{k \log^{1 + \epsilon} k} = 0$$holds for all $\epsilon > 0$ and every strictly increasing sequence of $a_k$ such that every positive integer can be written as a sum of one or more consecutive elements. In particular this holds for the sequence at hand.

I don't have access to the Porubský paper, but I found the above claim in

Guy, R. K. Research Problems become Unsolved Problems. The American Mathematical Monthly, 88(10) (1981), 755–761.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
With a computer implementation, the following values have been checked for $c=3/4$:
For $100 \le n \le 104$, the maximum size of such a family is respectively $34,37,32,38$ and $35$.
So yes, it does depend on $n$ in an irregular way.

For $2|n, 3 \nmid n$ and $n$ sufficiently large, it might be that an (maybe the unique) extremal construction consists of all multiples of $3$ and
the large elements ($n/2 \le x  \le cn$) which are equivalent to $n/2 \mod 3$.

For $6 \mid n$ and $n$ not too large, it may well be that an extremal construction is $[\frac n2, \lfloor cn \rfloor ] \cup [1,k]$ for the largest $k$ satisfying $\binom{k+1}{2}+ \lfloor cn \rfloor <n.$
This has size $n/4+O( \sqrt n)$.

For $6 \mid n$, $n$ large and $5 \nmid n$ ($n \equiv 4r \pmod 5$),
the construction
$\{ 1 \le x \le \lfloor cn \rfloor  \colon 5 \mid x \vee (x \equiv r \pmod 5 \wedge x>n/4) \vee (x \equiv 2r \pmod 5 \wedge x>n/2) \}$ nevertheless is of size $0.3n + O(1)$ and thus larger.
The latter construction also works for any other smallest prime $q$ not dividing $n$, so the exact form seems to depend on both the prime factorization of $n$ and the size of $n$.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The maximum of the above still doesnt give the optimum.

E.g. $2\mid n, 3\mid n-2$ and $c=3/4$.

Take the multiples of $3$ (bounded by $cn$) and the numbers which are $\equiv 1 \mod 3$ and between $n/2$ and $cn$.

Then one has a construction with $n/3$ elements, while the above constructions gave only $n/4$.

This construction also generalises to larger smallest prime(power) not dividing $n$, giving some other candidates.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
If $c\ge 1$, then the maximum is trivially $(c-1/2)n.$
Take all $m$ for which either $n\le 2m<2n$ or $m>n$.
(Sharpness by considering pairs $\{x,n-x\}$)

For $1/2<c<1$, the maximum is bounded by $cn/2+2.$
For this consider pairs $\{x,n-x\}$, find 2 elements with sum $(1-c)n-1$ and then $2$ other ls with sum $cn+1.$

Possible constructions:

For $1/b\le c<1/(b-1)$,
One can take those $n/b \le n <n/(b-1)$ and a few more or $n/(b+1) \le m \le n/b$ + some (a max set such that the sum of b eleements too large and of b-1 is too small and similar).

One can also take the smallest prime power $q \nmid n$ and take the multiples of $q$ (and a few more without sumset equal to $n \mod q$).

If the maximum would be the maximum among the ones obtained from size-constrant and modulo-constraint, similar to Erdos matching conjecture, it indeed depends on $n$ in a (periodic) irregular way.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
If $p$ is the smallest prime that does not divide $n$, then you can take $A$ to be the multiples of $p$ so $|A|=\lfloor \frac{\lfloor cn\rfloor}{p}\rfloor $.

Let $c\leq 1$. For an integer $k\geq 1$, the set $A=[\frac{n}{k+1},\frac{n}{k}]\cap\mathbb{N}$ always satisfies the condition. So letting $t=\lceil \frac{1}{c}\rceil$, we have $|A|\geq \max\{(c-\frac{1}{t})n, \frac{n}{t(t+1)}\}$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #364 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/364).

### Problem
Are there any triples of consecutive positive integers all of which are powerful (i.e. if $p\mid n$ then $p^2\mid n$)?

### Context
Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=8y^2+1$.

This conjecture was also made by Mollin and Walsh [MoWa86]. Erdős [Er76d] believed the answer to this question is no, and in fact if $n_k$ is the $k$th powerful number then\[n_{k+2}-n_k > n_k^c\]for some constant $c>0$. The abc conjecture implies there are only finitely many such triples.

### Deliverable

Do all pairs of consecutive [powerful numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powerful_number) $n$ and $n+1$ come from solutions to [Pell equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%27s_equation)? In other words, must either $n$ or $n+1$ be a square?

### Context
Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=2^3y^2+1$.

The list of $n$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ are both powerful is [A060355](https://oeis.org/A060355) in the OEIS.

The American Mathematical Monthly, 88(4), 272–274. https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.1981.11995246", the author has proved that "there exists an infinite number of pairs of consecutive odd powerful numbers, for eg: (25,27), each pair being associated with a certain Pell equation".

Also, in "https://www.fq.math.ca/Scanned/20-1/mcdaniel.pdf", W. L. McDaniel disproves a conjecture made by Golomb in [Go70] who conjectured that conjectured that "there are infinitely many integers that cannot be written as the difference of two powerful numbers.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
The Sentance paper proves that, every pair of powerful $n-1,n+1$ is associated with the solution of a Pell equation.
The latter is trivial:
$n$ has to be even and $n^2-1$ is powerful itself, so by definition of the form $my^2$ where $m \mid y.$

Nevertheless, the difference 2 result is not related to the difference 1 question.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #366 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366).

### Problem
Are there any 2-full $n$ such that $n+1$ is 3-full? That is, if $p\mid n$ then $p^2\mid n$ and if $p\mid n+1$ then $p^3\mid n+1$.

### Context
Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=8y^2+1$.

Note that $8$ is 3-full and $9$ is 2-full. Erdős and Graham asked if this is the only pair of such consecutive integers. Stephan has observed that $12167=23^3$ and $12168=2^33^213^2$ (a pair already known to Golomb [Go70]) is another example, but (by [OEIS A060355](https://oeis.org/A060355)) there are no other examples for $n<10^{22}$.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #367 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367).

### Problem
Let $B_2(n)$ be the 2-full part of $n$ (that is, $B_2(n)=n/n'$ where $n'$ is the product of all primes that divide $n$ exactly once). Is it true that, for every fixed $k\geq 1$,\[\prod_{n\leq m<n+k}B_2(m) \ll n^{2+o(1)}?\]Or perhaps even $\ll_k n^2$?

### Context
It would also be interesting to find upper and lower bounds for the analogous product with $B_r$ for $r\geq 3$, where $B_r(n)$ is the $r$-full part of $n$ (that is, the product of prime powers $p^a \mid n$ such that $p^{a+1}\nmid n$ and $a\geq r$). Is it true that, for every fixed $r,k\geq 2$ and $\epsilon>0$,\[\limsup \frac{\prod_{n\leq m<n+k}B_r(m) }{n^{1+\epsilon}}\to\infty?\]van Doorn notes in the comments that for $k\leq 2$ we trivially have\[\prod_{n\leq m<n+k}B_2(m) \ll n^{2},\]but that this fails for all $k\geq 3$, and in fact\[\prod_{n\leq m<n+3}B_2(m) \gg n^{2}\log n\]infinitely often.

This question is equivalent (up to constants) to [[935]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/935).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
If $k \le 2$, then $$\prod_{n \le m < n+k} B_2(m) \le n(n+1) \le 2n^2, \hspace{50pt} (1)$$so the supposed upper bounds of $n^{2+o(1)}$ and $c_kn^2$ are non-trivial only for $k \ge 3$. But already for $k = 3$ I believe that for every $c$, the left-hand side of $(1)$ is larger than $cn^2$ infinitely often.

Let $(x_j, y_j)$ be the solutions to the Pell equation $x^2 - 8y^2 = 1$, with $(x_0, y_0) = (1, 0)$ and $(x_{j+1}, y_{j+1}) = (3x_j + 8y_j, x_j + 3y_j)$. Taking $n_j = 8y_j^2$, we note $B_2(n_j) = n_j$ and $B_2(n_j+1) = n_j+1$.

Now define the indices $j_1 = 1$ and, for $t \ge 1$, $j_{t+1} = 5j_t + 2$. Then I think that the congruence relation $$x_{j_t}^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{5^t} \hspace{116pt} (2)$$holds for all $t$, and I am sure someone here is able to verify that $(2)$ (or something very similar) does indeed hold.

Assuming $(2)$ for the moment, we have $x_j = e^{O(j)}$ and $j_t = O(5^t)$, so that $n_{j_t} < x_{j_t}^2 = e^{O(5^t)}$. We deduce that $B_2(n_{j_t}+2) \ge 5^t > c \log n_{j_t}$ for some positive $c$ and all $t \ge 2$. For all $k \ge 3$ we therefore obtain $$\prod_{n \le m < n+k} B_2(m) \ge \prod_{n \le m < n+3} B_2(m) > c n^2 \log n$$infinitely often. And I would guess that this lower bound is probably improvable.

On the final question concerning $B_r(m)$ for $r \ge 3$, am I correct in thinking that it asks for some $\epsilon = \epsilon(r, k) > 0$ for which the $\limsup$ is unbounded? If so, then the existence of a positive $\epsilon(r, k)$ trivially implies the existence of a positive $\epsilon(r', k')$ for all pairs $(r', k')$ with $r' \le r$ and $k' \ge k$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
[Gemini Deepthink confirms](https://gemini.google.com/share/81a65aecfd70) that your argument negatively answers the second version of the problem.  One can streamline the argument as follows:

1. Define $n_j = (\alpha^{2j} - 2 + \alpha^{-2j})/4$, where $\alpha = 3 + \sqrt{8}$ (so $\alpha^{-1} = 3 - \sqrt{8}$).  Then
\begin{align*}
n_j &= 8 \times \left[\frac{\alpha^j - \alpha^{-j}}{2\sqrt{8}}\right]^2 \\
n_j+1 &= \left[\frac{\alpha^j + \alpha^{-j}}{2}\right]^2 \\
n_j+2 &= \frac{\alpha^{2j} + 6 + \alpha^{-2j}}{4}
\end{align*}
and both expressions in brackets are integers (OEIS [A001109](https://oeis.org/A001109) and [A001541](https://oeis.org/A001541) respectively). In particular, $n_j$ is a natural number (OEIS [A132592](https://oeis.org/A132592)), with $n_j, n_j+1$ already $2$-full.
2.  Observe the identity $\alpha^{\pm 3} = 99 \pm 35 \sqrt{8} = - 1 + 5 \times (20 \pm 7 \sqrt{8})$.  By induction one can show that $\alpha^{\pm 3 \times 5^{t-1}} = -1 + 5^t (a_t \pm b_t \sqrt{8})$ for various integers $a_t,b_t$ and all $t \geq 1$.

Now we set $j_t :=(3 \times 5^{t-1}-1)/2$ (which is an integer) and compute
\begin{align*}
 4(n_{j_t}+2) &= \alpha^{-1} \alpha^{3 \times 5^{t-1}} + 6 + \alpha \alpha^{-3 \times 5^{t-1}} \\
&= (3-\sqrt{8}) (-1 + 5^t (a_t + b_t \sqrt{8})) + 6 + (3+\sqrt{8}) (-1 + 5^t (a_t - b_t \sqrt{8}))\\
&= 5^t (6 a_t - 16 b_t)
\end{align*}
giving the key claim $5^t | n_{j_t}+2$.  Thus for $t \geq 2$
$$ \prod_{n_{j_t} \leq m < n_{j_t}+3} B_2(m) \geq n_{j_t} (n_{j_t}+1) 5^t \gg n_{j_t}^2 \log n_{j_t}.$$

This looks within range of being "vibe formalizable" in Lean, if anyone wants to give it a shot.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #368 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/368).

### Problem
How large is the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$?

### Context
Let $F(n)$ be the prime in question. Pólya [Po18] proved that $F(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$. Mahler [Ma35] showed that $F(n)\gg \log\log n$. Schinzel [Sc67b] observed that for infinitely many $n$ we have $F(n)\leq n^{O(1/\log\log\log n)}$.

The truth is probably $F(n)\gg (\log n)^2$ for all $n$. Erdős [Er76d] conjectured that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $F(n) <(\log n)^{2+\epsilon}$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.contentMd: At first sight, the mentioned paper [Pa24b] is about the largest prime factor of $n^2+1$ instead. There is no explicit mention of the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$. Is it implied by the result/methods?

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
Corollary 1.5 of [the paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.03566#page=3) says that there is an absolute constant $\kappa>0$ such that as $x<y$ vary over coprime positive integers, we have the smallest prime factor of $xy(x+y)$ is $\ge\kappa\cdot\frac{(\log \log y)^2}{\log \log \log y}$.

If we set $x=1$ and $y=n$, then we obtain the result mentioned in the problem description.

sourceComments.author: TongLL
sourceComments.contentMd:
It seems that C.Størmer showed that $F(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to \infty$ in 1897, which was cited in Mahler's 1935 paper in the link and D.H.Lehmer's 1964 paper "On a Problem of Størmer".
It is difficult to access Størmer's paper. Størmer presumably proved that $v_n​$ has a primitive prime factor when $n$ is sufficiently large, where $(v_n)$ satisfies
$${u_n}^2=k{v_n}^2+1$$for an increasing integer sequence $(u_n)$ and a given squarefree number $k>1$. This is an analog of Carmichael's theorem on Lucas sequences. Therefore, there are only finitely many positive integers $u$ such that $P(u^2-1)$ is smaller than a given bound. If we set $u=2n+1$, then it follows that $F(n)=P\left(\frac{u^2-1}{4}\right)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
