problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #369 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/369).

### Problem
Let $\epsilon>0$ and $k\geq 2$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there is a sequence of $k$ consecutive integers in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ all of which are $n^\epsilon$-smooth?

### Context
Erdős and Graham state that this is open even for $k=2$ and 'the answer should be affirmative but the problem seems very hard'.

Unfortunately the problem is trivially true as written (simply taking $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ and $n>k^{1/\epsilon}$). There are (at least) two possible variants which are non-trivial, and it is not clear which Erdős and Graham meant. Let $P$ be the sequence of $k$ consecutive integers sought for. The potential strengthenings which make this non-trivial are:- Each $m\in P$ must be $m^\epsilon$-smooth. If this is the problem then the answer is yes, which follows from a result of Balog and Wooley [BaWo98]: for any $\epsilon>0$ and $k\geq 2$ there exist infinitely many $m$ such that $m+1,\ldots,m+k$ are all $m^\epsilon$-smooth.
- Each $m\in P$ must be in $[n/2,n]$ (say). In this case a positive answer also follows from the result of Balog and Wooley [BaWo98] for infinitely many $n$, but the case of all sufficiently large $n$ is open.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Here’s my idea. So far I found no problems and I hope that it solves this problem.  I’m not good at English, and have no experience in writing papers. So I gave my idea to gpt and let gpt help me translate my words and write it in rigorous form. GPT also helped me a lot on searching for papers!
My proof is here:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MxgrA2haXKv_NKSa7sqUI2hZYyZ5JmfP/view?usp=drivesdk

My core idea is to choose pairwise coprime squarefree integers $r_j$ with $\varphi(r_j)/r_j<\varepsilon/2$ and then construct $a=C\,2^{Lu}3^{Lv}$ via CRT so that $a/j=b_j^{r_j}$ for $1\le j\le k-1$, which by the cyclotomic factorization $b_j^{r_j}-1=\prod_{d\mid r_j}\Phi_d(b_j)$ forces every prime divisor of $a-j$ to be $\ll N^{\varepsilon/2}$, while the irrationality of $\log 2/\log 3$ lets me choose $u,v$ so that $a\in(3N/4,N)$ for every sufficiently large $N$.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Thanks! I ran a standard [check](https://chatgpt.com/share/69c589da-f3c4-839a-b2d1-0aa7bc8d8f33), a near-autonomous checking process currently by GPT-5.4 Thinking which has proven useful anecdotally but is not guaranteed to be correct or complete. It found no issues.

This argument proves the second potential strengthening above. According to GPT, this line of argument is close to Balog-Wooley.

replies.contentMd: Thank you! I’ve also let gpt 5.4 and Claude opus 4.6 checked it for five times and they found no problems!

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
I don't see any immediate problems; this is very close to the Balog-Wooley argument of [BaWo98], but with a slightly different choice of parameters. (In particular I recommend that you rewrite this adding appropriate citations to the literature and that the main construction originates with [BaWo98].)

This argument looks ripe for formalisation; I see that Woett is already working on formalising some of these results, so this should be relatively straightforward, which would then remove any remaining doubt.

replies.contentMd: Congrats on the result. I suppose the question is somewhat open-ended.  Do you think this method can also tackle smaller intervals that are still large enough to contain primes, such as $[n-n^{21/40},n]$?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: See my other reply for a proof (using Theorem 2.1 of Bober, Fretwell, Martin, and Wooley) that tackles intervals of the shape $[n-n^{1-c},n]$ for some $c>0$ depending on $\epsilon$ and $k$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
It looks like this does then settle the most natural interpretation of this problem in the affirmative - congratulations SkyYang!

For further context, I wrote to Trevor Wooley, who noted that the problem they were addressing in [BaWo98] was slightly different, in that they were concerned with an stronger type of uniformity (and so they could hence only obtain this for infinitely many $N$ rather than all large $N$).

He also points out that Theorem 2.1 in [this paper](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/20171004smoothpoly.pdf) of Bober, Fretwell, Martin, and Wooley (which itself is a generalisation of the [BaWo98] argument) is another way to settle this problem in the affirmative, and in fact proves something stronger.

Namely, that theorem states that if $f(t)$ is a product of $k$ linear factors then there are polynomials $g$ of arbitrarily large degree $d$ such that $f(g(t))$ factors as a product of polynomials of degree $\ll d/(\log\log d)^{1/k}$. In particular, for any $\epsilon>0$, there exists a polynomial $g$ of degree $d=O_{k,\epsilon}(1)$ such that all prime divisors of\[(g(n)+1)\cdots (g(n)+k)\]are at most $\lvert g(n)\rvert^{\epsilon}$. Taking $n$ large and close to $(N/a)^{1/d}$, where $a$ is the leading coefficient of $g$, one deduces that, for all large $N$, there is an interval of $k$ consecutive integers in\[[N-O(N^{1-1/d}),N]\]all of which are $N^\epsilon$-smooth.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #371 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/371).

### Problem
Let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime factor of $n$. Show that the set of $n$ with $P(n)<P(n+1)$ has density $1/2$.

### Context
Conjectured by Erdős and Pomerance [ErPo78], who proved that this set and its complement both have positive upper density. The best unconditional lower bound available is due to Lü and Wang [LuWa25], who prove that\[\#\{ n<x :P(n)<P(n+1)\} > (0.2017-o(1))x,\]and the same lower bound for the complement.

In [Er79e] Erdős also asks whether, for every $\alpha$, the density of the set of $n$ where\[P(n+1)>P(n)n^\alpha\]exists.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Conjectured by Erdős and Pomerance [ErPo78], who proved that this set and its complement both have positive upper density. The best unconditional lower bound available is due to Lü and Wang [LuWa25], who prove that\#\{ n<x :P(n)<P(n+1)\} > (0.2017-o(1))x,and the same lower bound for the complement.
In [Er79e] Erdős also asks whether, for every $\alpha$, the density of the set of $n$ whereP(n+1)>P(n)n^\alphaexists.

Teräväinen [Te18] has proved that the logarithmic density of the set of $n$ for which $P(n)<P(n+1)$ is $1/2$. Tao and Teräväinen [TaTe19] have proved that the asymptotic density is $1/2$ at 'almost all scales'.

More generally, for any $0\leq \alpha \leq1$, Teräväinen [Te18] proved that the logarithmic density of the set of $n$ for which $P(n+1)>P(n)n^\alpha$ exists and is equal to\int_{[0,1]^2}1_{y\geq x+\alpha}u(x)u(y)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}ywhere $u(x)=x^{-1}\rho(x^{-1}-1)$ and $\rho$ is the Dickman function. Wang [Wa21] has proved the same value holds for the asymptotic density (and in particular provided an affirmative answer to the original question) conditional on the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture for friable integers.
The sequence of such $n$ is A070089 in the OEIS.
See also [[372]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/372) and [[928]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/928).

sourceComments.contentMd:
In Theorem 1.14 of [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.01195), Teräväinen proves a weaker version of [[928]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/928) with logarithmic density instead of natural density. (Thanks to Agustín Meza for the reference.) As a consequence, in Theorem 1.17, Teräväinen obtains a formula for a logarithmic density for this problem. If [[928]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/928) is true for natural density, then the solution for this problem should be as well.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #373 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/373).

### Problem
Show that the equation\[n! = a_1!a_2!\cdots a_k!,\]with $n-1>a_1\geq a_2\geq \cdots \geq a_k\geq 2$, has only finitely many solutions.

### Context
This would follow if $P(n(n+1))/\log n\to \infty$, where $P(m)$ denotes the largest prime factor of $m$ (see Problem [[368]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/368)). Erdős [Er76d] proved that this problem would also follow from showing that $P(n(n-1))>4\log n$.

The condition $a_1<n-1$ is necessary to rule out the trivial solutions when $n=a_2!\cdots a_k!$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: This would follow if $P(n(n+1))/\log n\to \infty$, where $P(m)$ denotes the largest prime factor of $m$ (see Problem [[368]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/368)). Erdős [Er76d] proved that this problem would also follow from showing that $P(n(n-1))>4\log n$.
The condition $a_1<n-1$ is necessary to rule out the trivial solutions when $n=a_2!\cdots a_k!$.

Surányi was the first to conjecture that the only non-trivial solution to $a!b!=n!$ is $6!7!=10!$. More generally, Hickerson (as reported in [Er76d]) conjectured that the only non-trivial solutions to the equation in the problem statement are9!=2!3!3!7!,10!=6!7!,10!=3!5!7!,and16!=14!5!2!.Luca [Lu07b] has shown that there are only finitely many solutions, conditional on the ABC conjecture, and proved unconditionally that the number of $n\leq x$ which admit a non-trivial solution is\leq \exp \bigg(f(x)\frac{\log (x)}{\log\log (x)}\bigg)for any function $f(x)$ which tends to infinity.
This is discussed in problem B23 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

In the case when $k=2$, Erdős [Er93] proved that if $n!=a_1!a_2!$ with $n-1>a_1\geq a_2$ thena_1\geq n-5\log\log n,and says it 'would be nice' to prove $a_1\geq n-o(\log\log n)$. Bhat and Ramachandra [BhRa10] replace the $5$ with $(1+o(1))\frac{1}{\log 2}$, and also prove that the same bound holds for arbitrary $k\geq 2$.

Numerical investigations on solutions to $n!=a_1!a_2!$ have been carried out by Caldwell [Ca94] and Habsieger [Ha19], and it is known that there are no solutions aside from $10!=6!7!$ for $n\leq 10^{3000}$.

In the case $A!B! = C!$, there has been significant improvements:

The equation has been studied by Caldwell for $C \le 10^6$ in [Ca94].
Also, Erd¨os in [Er93] proved $C − B ≤ 5 \log \log C$ , which was improved further to $C−B ≤ (1/ \log 2+o(1)) \log \log C$ by Bhat and Ramachandra in [this paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S0001434610090038).

Laurent Habseiger in his [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.08370) has checked the conjecture for $B ≤ 10^{3000}$ and give better explicit bounds such as\[C −B ≤ \frac{\log \log(B+1)}{\log 2} − 0.8803.\][Ca94]: C. Caldwell, The diophantine equation A!B! = C!, J. Recreat. Math. 26 (1994), 128–133.
[Er93]: P. Erd¨os, A consequence of a factorial equation, Amer. Math. Monthly 100 (1993), 407–408.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: Extremely general question, which speaks to its difficulty. It is essentially equivalent to the question of whether there are any numbers other than 9 and 10, which are not Jordan-Pólya numbers, but such that their factorials are products of smaller factorials. There are probably not.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #374 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/374).

### Problem
For any $m\in \mathbb{N}$, let $F(m)$ be the minimal $k\geq 2$ (if it exists) such that there are $a_1<\cdots <a_k=m$ with $a_1!\cdots a_k!$ a square. Let $D_k=\{ m : F(m)=k\}$. What is the order of growth of $\lvert D_k\cap\{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert$ for $3\leq k\leq 6$? For example, is it true that $\lvert D_6\cap \{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert \gg n$?

### Context
Studied by Erdős and Graham [ErGr76] (see also [LSS14]). It is known, for example, that:- no $D_k$ contains a prime,
- $D_2=\{ n^2 : n>1\}$,
- $\lvert D_3\cap \{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert = o(\lvert D_4\cap \{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert)$,
- the least element of $D_6$ is $527$, and
- $D_k=\emptyset$ for $k>6$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #375 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375).

### Problem
Is it true that for any $n,k\geq 1$, if $n+1,\ldots,n+k$ are all composite then there are distinct primes $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ such that $p_i\mid n+i$ for $1\leq i\leq k$?

### Context
Note this is trivial when $k\leq 2$. Originally conjectured by Grimm [Gr69]. This is a very difficult problem, since it in particular implies $p_{n+1}-p_n <p_n^{1/2-c}$ for some constant $c>0$, in particular resolving [Legendre's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_conjecture).

Grimm proved that this is true if $k\ll \log n/\log\log n$. Erdős and Selfridge improved this to $k\leq (1+o(1))\log n$. Ramachandra, Shorey, and Tijdeman [RST75] have improved this to\[k\ll\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right)^3.\]Laishram and Shorey [LaSh06] have verified this is true, for all $k\geq 1$, for all $n\leq 1.9\times 10^{10}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotesMd: Note this is trivial when $k\leq 2$. Originally conjectured by Grimm [Gr69]. This is a very difficult problem, since it in particular implies $p_{n+1}-p_n <p_n^{1/2-c}$ for some constant $c>0$, in particular resolving [Legendre's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_conjecture).

Grimm proved that this is true if $k\ll \log n/\log\log n$. Erdős and Selfridge improved this to $k\leq (1+o(1))\log n$. Ramachandra, Shorey, and Tijdeman [RST75] have improved this to\[k\ll\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right)^3.\]Laishram and Shorey [LaSh06] have verified this is true, for all $k\geq 1$, for all $n\leq 1.9\times 10^{10}$.
This is problem B32 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
See also [[860]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/860).

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The provenance of the claim that this conjecture implies $p_{n+1} - p_n < p_n^{1/2-c}$ is a little murky.  Theorem 1 of the [1971 paper of Erdos and Selfridge](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1971-24.pdf) gets the weaker bound $p_{n+1} -p_n \ll p_n^{1/2} / \log^{1/2} p_n$ (which is already enough to get Legendre's conjecture asymptotically) and assert without proof that the [result of Ramachandra](https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1112/jlms/s2-1.1.303) concerning the existence of non-smooth numbers in short intervals gets the power saving, but on page 15 they write "we do not give the details here".

Theorem 1 is proven by noting that if Grimm's conjecture held, then $\binom{n+k}{k}$ would have to be divisible by at least $k-\pi(k)$ primes larger than $k$, and this and standard prime number theorem and Stirling approximation estimates is enough to conclude.  I guess Ramachandra's result would allow one to say that some of these primes are actually rather large, but the actual calculations seem to require some care (one needs a "positive density" version of Ramachandra's result, I think).

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: More generally, Langevin conjectured that any sequence of consecutive numbers, all of which are composite, must form a set of multiplicatively independent numbers.

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
In [Grimm's conjecture on consecutive integers(2006)](https://www.isid.ac.in/~shanta/PAPERS/Grimm-IJNT.pdf), S. Laishram and T. N. Shorey have proved this conjecture for $n \leq 1.9 \times 10^{10}$ and for all k.

P. S. I believe the bound by [RST75] can be pushed further (under stronger conjectures like Elliot Halberstam Conjecture).

Edit: Earlier, there was an embarrassing careless mistake here.

Note; the cubic boune of RST75 is stronger than the quadratic bound.

By Cramer s conjecture, the bound of RST75 and the verification for small n, the answer to this problem should surely be positive.

### Problem
Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $105$?

### Context

researchNotes: Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75] have shown that, for any two odd primes $p$ and $q$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $pq$.

The sequence of such $n$ is A030979 in the OEIS.

The best result in this direction is due to Bloom and Croot [BlCr25], who proved that, if $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are sufficiently large primes, then there are infinitely many $n$ such that almost all of the base $p_i$ digits are $<p_i/2$. In other words, for all $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $p_1p_2p_3$, except for a factor of size $\leq n^\epsilon$.
This is mentioned in problem B33 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. It is also discussed in an article of Pomerance [Po15c].
Graham offered \$1000 for a solution to this problem (as mentioned in [Gu04] and [BeHa98]).

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
There is recent work in the direction of this problem at

Croot, Ernie; Mousavi, Hamed; Schmidt, Maxie, [On a conjecture of Graham on the p-divisibility of central binomial coefficients](https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1112/mtk.12249)
Mathematika 70, No. 3, Article ID e12249, 29 p. (2024).

They construct $n$ for which $\binom{2n}{n}$ is divisible by an unusually small number of powers of $p$ for any fixed set of small primes $p$ (e.g., $p=3,5,7$), although they cannot get this number down to zero (which is what is needed for this problem).

EDIT: I see now that the already cited paper [BlCr2025] mentions this previous work and improves upon it.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Yes, apologies I should have also cited the Croot, Mousavi, and Schmidt paper (which my paper with Croot improves). For reference, here is what the two papers say in terms of this problem.

Given a finite set of primes $P=\{p_1<\cdots<p_k\}$ let $f_P(n)$ be the $P$-divisible component of $\binom{2n}{n}$ (that is, the product of all maximal powers of $p_i\in P$ which divide $\binom{2n}{n}$). It is trivial that $f_P(n) \leq n^{O(k)}$.

Croot, Mousavi, and Schmidt proved that, for any $\epsilon>0$, if $p_1$ is sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$ and $k$, then there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f_P(n)\leq n^\epsilon$.

Croot and I in [BlCr25] proved that, provided $p_1$ is sufficiently large depending only on $k$ (e.g. $\geq 10^{94}$ for $k=3$) then, for any $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f_P(n) \leq n^\epsilon$.

So essentially we swapped the quantifiers round so that $\epsilon$ is now independent of the set of primes. We believe that a more careful version of our proof should allow one to prove that, if $p_1$ is large enough in terms of $k$, then there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f_p(n) \leq \exp(O(\sqrt{\log n}))$.

(Of course the conjecture is that, generalising the problem of Graham mentioned here, that if $p_1$ is sufficiently large in terms of $k$ then $f_P(n)=1$ for infinitely many $n$.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #377 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377).

### Problem
Is there some absolute constant $C>0$ such that\[\sum_{p\leq n}1_{p\nmid \binom{2n}{n}}\frac{1}{p}\leq C\]for all $n$ (where the summation is restricted to primes $p\leq n$)?

### Context
A question of Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75], who proved that if $f(n)$ is the sum in question then\[\lim_{x\to \infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x}f(n) = \sum_{k=2}^\infty \frac{\log k}{2^k}=\gamma_0\]and\[\lim_{x\to \infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)^2 = \gamma_0^2,\]so that for almost all integers $f(m)=\gamma_0+o(1)$. They also prove that, for all large $n$,\[f(n) \leq c\log\log n\]for some constant $c<1$. (It is trivial from Mertens estimates that $f(n)\leq (1+o(1))\log\log n$.)

A positive answer would imply that\[\sum_{p\leq n}1_{p\mid \binom{2n}{n}}\frac{1}{p}=(1-o(1))\log\log n,\]and Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus say there is 'no doubt' this latter claim is true.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The latter claim looks doable with current technology.  It suffices to show that, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and any $1 \leq k \leq \log^{1-\varepsilon} n$, that $\sum_{n^{1/(k+1)} < p \leq n^{1/k}} 1_{p\not \mid \binom{2n}{n}} \frac{1}{p} \ll \frac{\varepsilon}{k}$.  A necessary condition for $p\not \mid \binom{2n}{n}$ is that $\{ \frac{n}{p^j} \} \leq \frac{1}{2}$ for all $j$.  I think just taking $j = k-1, k-2, \dots, k-J$ for some $J \sim \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$, combined with  known prime number theorems in short intervals, should be able to get the required bound after some lengthy but routine calculations.

The main problem looks hard though, because of the contribution of the very small primes, where the difficulties are similar to those in #376.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #380 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/380).

### Problem
We call an interval $[u,v]$ 'bad' if the greatest prime factor of $\prod_{u\leq m\leq v}m$ occurs with an exponent greater than $1$. Let $B(x)$ count the number of $n\leq x$ which are contained in at least one bad interval. Is it true that\[B(x)\sim \#\{ n\leq x: P(n)^2\mid n\},\]where $P(n)$ is the largest prime factor of $n$?

### Context
Erdős and Graham only knew that $B(x) > x^{1-o(1)}$. Similarly, we call an interval $[u,v]$ 'very bad' if $\prod_{u\leq m\leq v}m$ is powerful. The number of integers $n\leq x$ contained in at least one very bad interval should be $\ll x^{1/2}$. In fact, it should be asymptotic to the number of powerful numbers $\leq x$.

We have\[\#\{ n\leq x: P(n)^2\mid n\}=\frac{x}{\exp((c+o(1))\sqrt{\log x\log\log x})}\]for some constant $c>0$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
In fact, if an interval $[u,v]$ is bad, it cannot contain any prime, which makes it quite short; for instance, assuming Cramer's conjecture, it forces $v-u \ll \log^2 u$.  If a bad interval $[u,v]$ does not contain any bad element, then all the elements must be $(v-u)$-smooth, which suggests that such intervals are very rare, presumably to the point where they cover $o(B'(x))$ elements.  But one still has to count the number of $n$ that are close enough to a bad number that they are contained in a bad interval around that number, but are not themselves bad.  This seems to be connected to such problems as counting the number of consecutive smooth numbers, for which we have made some progress in recent years, but perhaps not at the level of precision needed to solve this problem.

EDIT: I am puzzled by the claim in [ErGr80] that "we only know $B(x) > x^{1-\varepsilon}$", since we trivially have $B(x) \geq B'(x)$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd: Yeah, I do not understand that last remark either, as it was stated right after the bound on $B'(x)$ you mentioned. In any case, consider the integers $n \le x$ with $n+1 \in B'(x)$ and $P(n) < P(n+1)$. Can we even prove that their cardinality is $o(B'(x))$? This counting function $B'(x)$ could also be added to OEIS by the way.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
After looking at Paul Erdős and Ron L. Graham, On products of factorials, Bull. Inst. Math. Acad. Sinica 4:2 (1976), pp. 337-35 (particularly Fact 4), I suspect that they meant to write here was that $B(x) = o(x)$, since that is what is proved there.

Incidentally the constant $c$ can be worked out to be $\sqrt{2}$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The quantity $\# \{n \leq x: p|n \to p \leq n^{1/2}\}$ (which is $\sim (1-\log 2) x$, by the way) is not what is stated in [ErGr80, p.73]; instead, it is $B'(x) = \# \{ n \leq x: P(n)^2|n\} = x / \exp((c+o(1))(\log x \log\log x)^{1/2})$ for some absolute constant $c>0$, where $P(n)$ denotes the largest prime factor of $n$.  In other words, the problem asserts that the dominant type of bad intervals are the singletons.

A small additional observation: by Bertrand's postulate, $[u,v]$ cannot be bad if $v \geq 2u$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #382 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/382).

### Problem
Let $u\leq v$ be such that the largest prime dividing $\prod_{u\leq m\leq v}m$ appears with exponent at least $2$. Is it true that $v-u=v^{o(1)}$? Can $v-u$ be arbitrarily large?

### Context
Erdős and Graham report it follows from results of Ramachandra that $v-u\leq v^{1/2+o(1)}$.

Cambie has observed that the first question boils down to some old conjectures on prime gaps.
By [Cramér's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cram%C3%A9r%27s_conjecture), for every $\epsilon>0,$ for every $u$ sufficiently large there is a prime between $u$ and $u+u^\epsilon$.
Thus for $u+u^\epsilon<v$, the largest prime divisor of \( \prod_{u \leq m \leq v} m \) appears with exponent $1$.
Since this is not the case in the question, \( v - u = v^{o(1)} \).

### Deliverable

For any fixed $k$, there is therefore a positive 'probability' that there are $k$ consecutive integers around $q^2$ (for a prime $q$) all of whose prime divisors are bounded above by $q$, when $v-u\geq k$. See [[383]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/383) for a conjecture along these lines. A similar argument applies if we replace multiplicity $2$ with multiplicity $r$, for any fixed $r\geq 2$.
See also [[380]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/380).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #385 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/385).

### Problem
Let\[F(n) = \max_{\substack{m<n\\ m\textrm{ composite}}} m+p(m),\]where $p(m)$ is the least prime divisor of $m$. Is it true that $F(n)>n$ for all sufficiently large $n$? Does $F(n)-n\to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$?

### Context
A question of Erdős, Eggleton, and Selfridge, who write that 'plausible conjectures on primes' imply that $F(n)\leq n$ for only finitely many $n$, and in fact it is possible that this quantity is always at least $n+(1-o(1))\sqrt{n}$ (note that it is trivially $\leq n+\sqrt{n}$).

Tao has discussed this problem in [a blog post](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2024/08/19/erdos-problem-385-the-parity-problem-and-siegel-zeroes/).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #386 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/386).

### Problem
Let $2\leq k\leq n-2$. Can $\binom{n}{k}$ be the product of consecutive primes infinitely often? For example\[\binom{21}{2}=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7.\]

### Context
Erdős and Graham write that 'a proof that this cannot happen infinitely often for $\binom{n}{2}$ seems hopeless; probably this can never happen for $\binom{n}{k}$ if $3\leq k\leq n-3$.'

Weisenberg has provided four easy examples that show Erdős and Graham were too optimistic here:\[\binom{7}{3}=5\cdot 7,\]\[\binom{10}{4}= 2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7,\]\[\binom{14}{4} = 7\cdot 11\cdot 13,\]and\[\binom{15}{6}=5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13.\]The known values of $n$ for which $\binom{n}{2}$ is the product of consecutive primes are $4,6,15,21,715$ (see [A280992](https://oeis.org/A280992)).

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
A back of the envelope calculation suggests that one can rule out $\binom{n}{k}$ being square-free (and a fortiori, rule out being a product of consecutive primes) for $\exp(\log^{2/3+\varepsilon} n) \leq k \leq n/2$ and $n$ sufficiently large as in the Singmaster conjecture paper.  A sketch is as follows. Select a scale $P$ with $P \lll k \ll n \lll \exp(\log^{3/2-\varepsilon} P)$.  By the Legendre formula, for any prime $p \sim P$, the number of times $p$ divides $\binom{n}{k}$ is

$$ \sum_{j=1}^\infty \left\{\frac{k}{p^j}\right\} + \left\{\frac{n-k}{p^j}\right\} - \left\{\frac{n}{p^j}\right\}.$$
Each summand is non-negative, so we can truncate at say $j=1,2,3$.  The equidistribution estimates in Proposition 1.12 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.03335 basically tell us that each of these summands has a mean of 1/2 as $p$ varies, so this quantity is at least $3/2$ on the average, contradicting square-freeness.  (One can also use just the $j=1,2$ terms for this analysis if one also calculates the variance in addition to the mean.)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Just some additional intuition that the answer is likely no.

For fixed $k$, if $\binom{n}{k}$ is the product of consecutive primes for large $n$,
then $n, n-1, \ldots, n-k+1$ are all the product of some of the primes and some divisors of $k!$.
Since $k!$ is not a perfect power, the divisors differ by at least some constant.
(For large $k$, by AM-GM and a prime near $k$ (see also [[#391]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/391)), there are some of the $k$ divisors of $k!$ which differ by at least $e-o(1)$.)

This implies that when $n$ is large, the range of consecutive primes needs to be quite large.
But then there are very few options compared to what is needed to expect many solutions.

***

For $k=2$, this can be explained more explicit (and so for larger $k$ this was analogous).
We have that $n(n-1)$ equals $2$ times the product of some consecutive primes.
So $2 \prod_I p_i $ and $\prod_J p_j$ (where $I \cup J$ is an interval of integers) need to differ by at most one.
So for fixed size $\lvert I \cup J \rvert$, there are finitely many solutions (large consecutive primes are of the same order, by the results on prime gaps).
So there are finitely many solutions where $\binom n2$ is the product of at most $10$ consecutive primes.

For every bound $x$, there are at most $\Theta( x^{1/11} / \log(x) )$ products of $11$ or more consecutive primes bounded by $x$.
There are $\Theta(x^{1/2})$ many values of the form $\binom{n}{2}$ (actually of the form $\binom nk$ with $2 \le k \le n-2$) bounded by $x$.
Hence if those two sequences behave slightly random, we do not expect many common elements.

**
An independent computer search from Desmond did not result in any additional example, and based on the above, it seems reasonable to think there are no other examples.
[e.g. a new solution for $k=2$ would need $n>10^{500}$ (if no machine errors happened and some estimates work out)]
**
Nevertheless, the statement of Erdos and Graham that it seems undoable (at the moment) proving for $k=2$ there are finitely many solutions, still holds?

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Extending the improvement by Desmond, we conclude that both $((n-k/2,n/2]$ and $(n-k,n]$ should not contain any primes once $n$ is sufficiently large.

For $n$ sufficiently large.
*If $k$ satisfies $n^{0.525}<k \le n/3$, then there are primes in $p \in (n-k,n]$, $q \in (n/2,n-k]$ and $r \in ((n-k)/2,n/2]$.
So $p$<$q$$n^{k-1}$ and thus it is not equal to the product of the primes in $(n-k,n]$ (at most $k-1$)
For $7\le k \le \sqrt n$,
$\binom{n}{k}$>$n^{k/2}$, while there are less than $k/2$ primes in $(n-k,n]$, so again $\binom{n}{k} $>$ \prod_{n-k+1 \le p\le n} p.$
If $\sqrt n $<$ k \le n^{0.6}$,
then $\binom{n}{k} \gg n^{0.4k}$, while less than $k/3$ values in $(n-k,n]$ are primes. So again $\binom{n}{k} \not= \prod_{n-k+1\le p\le n} p.$

Note that if $((n-k)/2,n/2]$ contains any primes, while $(n-k,n]$ contains no primes and thus $k$<$n^{0.525}$, one would need $\binom{n}{k}= \prod_{(n-k+1)/2 \le p\le n/2} p.$ Now the same estimates as above are even clearer and it is not possible.

Thus both $((n-k)/2,n/2]$ and $(n-k,n]$ should not contain any primes.
Cramer's conjecture predicts that $k=O(\log^2 n)$, or updated by others to $\log^{2+o(1)}(n)$, is rather small in that case.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
No doubt this can be improved significantly, but in the spirit of ruling out examples in the interior of Pascal's triangle, here's a nice result to start us off: let $n$ be large, and suppose $\frac{n}{3} < k \leq \frac{n}{2}$. Then $\binom{n}{k}$ is not a product of consecutive primes.

To prove this, we start with four facts that aren't too hard to verify under the given hypotheses:
Fact 1: $\binom{n}{k}$ is not a multiple of any primes in $(\frac{n}{3}, k]$.
Fact 2: $\binom{n}{k}$ is a multiple of every prime in $(k, \frac{n}{2}]$.
Fact 3: $\binom{n}{k}$ is not a multiple of any primes in $(\frac{n}{2}, n - k]$.
Fact 4: $\binom{n}{k}$ is a multiple of every prime in $(n - k, n]$.

Using facts 2, 3, and 4, we see that if there are primes in both $(k, \frac{n}{2}]$ and $(\frac{n}{2}, n - k]$, then $\binom{n}{k}$ is not a product of consecutive primes. So suppose at least one of those intervals does not have any primes. Then we must have $k \sim \frac{n}{2}$. If $k \sim \frac{n}{2}$, then by Stirling's approximation, we have $\binom{n}{k} = (2 + o(1))^n$.

For the sake of contradiction, suppose $\binom{n}{k}$ is the product of consecutive primes. It is well-known that the product of primes up to $x$ is $e^{(1 + o(1))x}$. Combined with facts 1 and 4, it follows that $\binom{n}{k} = e^{(\frac{1}{2} + o(1))n}$. However, $e^\frac{1}{2} \not= 2$, so we have a contradiction.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Very nice Desmond! This feels like it can be strengthened significantly also (e.g. Fact 1 was overkill, since just missing out a single prime $\sim k$ would suffice). Presumably a version of this argument (perhaps importing a little technology from the paper Tao mentions) would suffice to rule out $k\in [\epsilon n, n/2]$ for $n\gg_\epsilon 1$.

replies.author: DesmondWeisenberg
replies.contentMd:
After thinking about it more, yes, I actually can prove the following (which is the same as what you suggested): let $2 \leq k \leq \frac{n}{2}$, and suppose $\binom{n}{k}$ is a product of consecutive primes. Then $k = o(n)$. No advanced machinery is needed - again, this just follows from Stirling's approximation and the primorial estimate.
We only need two facts this time:

Fact 1: $\binom{n}{k}$ is not a multiple of any primes in $(\frac{n}{2}, n - k]$.
Fact 2: $\binom{n}{k}$ is a multiple of every prime in $(n - k, n]$.

Since I proved in my previous comment that $k \leq \frac{n}{3}$ for all large $n$, it follows that for all large $n$ there is a prime in $(\frac{n}{2}, n - k]$. So, assuming $k$ is large enough for there to be a prime in $(n - k, n]$, the value of $\binom{n}{k}$ is at most the product of all primes in $(n - k, n]$.

Now, for the sake of contradiction, suppose $k \not= o(n)$. Then by standard results in analysis, we can choose some constant $c \in \left(0, \frac{1}{3}\right]$ and assume that $k \sim cn$. The product of all primes in $(n - k, n]$ is then $(e^c + o(1))^n$, so $\binom{n}{k} \leq (e^c + o(1))^n$. However, Stirling's approximation tells us that $\binom{n}{k} = \left(\frac{1}{c^c(1-c)^{1-c}} + o(1)\right)^n$. For all $c \in \left(0, \frac{1}{3}\right]$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{c^c(1-c)^{1-c}} > e^c,
\end{equation*}
so we have reached a contradiction.

This completes the proof that $k = o(n)$, but I still feel like we're just starting out - I used compactness for simplicity, but I'm sure my argument could be made more explicit and probably significantly improved. One goal might be to prove (assuming $n$ is sufficiently large and $k \leq \frac{n}{2}$) that $k$ must be small enough so there are no primes in $(n - k, n]$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: It is possible that the arguments from [my paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03335) with Matomaki, Radziwill, Shao, and Teravainen can be adapted to prove a similar result here, namely that one can exclude the possibility of a counterexample in the "interior" region of Pascal's triangle.

replies.author: DesmondWeisenberg
replies.contentMd: A result of Sander discussed in [[175]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/175) shows that there are no squarefree numbers far enough in the interior of Pascal's triangle. So that should be a good start.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #387 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/387).

### Problem
Is there an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for all $1\leq k< n$, the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ has a divisor in $(cn,n]$?

### Context
Erdős once conjectured that $\binom{n}{k}$ must always have a divisor in $(n-k,n]$, but this was disproved by Schinzel and Erdős [Sc58]. A counterexample is given by $n=99215$ and $k=15$. Schinzel conjectured (see problem B34 of [Gu04]) that, for all sufficiently large $k$ which are not prime powers, there exists an $n$ such that $\binom{n}{k}$ is not divisible by any integer in $(n-k,n]$.

In [Er78g] Erdős thought that this question had a negative answer.

### Deliverable

In [Er78g] Erdős thought that this question had a negative answer.
It is easy to see that $\binom{n}{k}$ always has a divisor in $[n/k,n]$.
Faulkner [Fa66] proved that, if $p$ is the least prime $>2k$ and $n\geq p$, then $\binom{n}{k}$ has a prime divisor $\geq p$ (except $\binom{9}{2}$ and $\binom{10}{3}$).
This is discussed in problems B33 and B34 of Guy's collection [Gu04], who says that Erdős conjectured this is true for any $c<1$ (if $n$ is sufficiently large).

(180180m+49603)(72072m+19841)(4290m+1181)(27720m+7631)(180180m+49601)\\
(120120m+33067)$

Easily these $15$ linear forms are admissible, so if the prime tuples conjecture on linear forms is true, then for infinitely many $m$ integers $\binom{360360m+99215}{15}$ is the product of $15$ prime factors, the smallest is $\frac{n-11}{84}$, the largest is $\frac{n-1}{2}$, giving that these factors are smaller than $\frac{n}{2}$, and the product of at least two of them is way larger than $n$, hence it has no divisor in the $(\frac{n}{2},n]$ interval.

To see this in practice for one $m$ value, the smallest solution is $m=494660932170922548$, found by wheel sieve+prp test+true primality tests in some ten days of computation. That is $\binom{n}{k}$ has no divisor in the $(\frac{n}{2},n]$ interval for $n=178256013517113649496495,k=15$. Ofcourse we'd need this for infinitely many $m$ to refute $c=\frac{1}{2}$. Btw $k=15$ is the smallest $k$ value for that this type of construction works if we need $k$ prime factors for some fixed $c<1$.

If Dickson's conjecture is true, then there are $a(k)\geq 0,b(k)>0$ integers for that there is a divisor in the $[f(k),n]=[\frac{n-a(k)}{b(k)},n]$ interval for large $n$, and this is sharp, so it is possible that $(\frac{n-a(k)}{b(k)},n]$ interval already contains no divisor. (and ofcourse this $[f(k),n]$ interval also contains a divisor if some numbers is not prime).

Furthermore: there is a divisor in the $[\frac{n-k+1}{\sqrt[k]{k!}},n]$ interval, and in lots case this is slightly better than the above $[\frac{n}{k},n]$ interval, since for "large" fixed $k$ as $n$ goes to infinity we have $\frac{n-k+1}{\sqrt[k]{k!}}$ is roughly $\frac{en}{k}$.

To see this better bound, observe that:
$\binom{n}{k}=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{n-i}{d_{i}}$, where $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}d_{i}=k!$. From this $\min(d_{i})\leq \sqrt[k]{k!}$ (this is also an Erdos problem, and it is close to optimal), giving that for some $i$ index:
$n\geq \frac{n-i}{d_{i}}\geq \frac{n-k+1}{\sqrt[k]{k!}}$.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Using [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/690570eb-9fc8-800e-bf1a-10b8f13b1109), I found a second reference where this problem is mentioned: page 351 of  P. Erdős, R. L. Graham: [On the prime factors of ${n\choose k}$](https://www.mathstat.dal.ca/FQ/Scanned/14-4/erdos.pdf#:~:text=k,en%20for), Fibonacci Quart. 14 (1976) no. 4, 348--352.  There are various references establishing the conjecture for *almost all* $n$ for a fixed $k$, mentioned in the ChatGPT response.  However, I actually think the answer to this question is negative if one fixes $k$ and chooses $n$ carefully, and matters seem to reduce to a covering congruence problem (of a type similar to that seen in the "large gaps between primes"/"Jacobsthal function" literature).  Namely, it seems the problem morally reduces to:

**Conjecture 1**: For any $m$, there exists $k > m$ such that one can cover $\{1,\dots,k\}$ by congruences $a_p \pmod{p}$ for $m \leq p \leq k$, such that $0 \leq a_p < p - (k \% p)$ for all $m \leq p < k$, where $k\% p \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ denotes the remainder of $k$ when dividing by $p$.

Indeed, suppose that this conjecture held.  Pick any $m$, let $k$ be as in the conjecture, and then pick a large $n$ with $n = k- a_p \pmod{p^j}$ whenever $p^j \leq k$, with the convention that $a_p=0$ for $p < m$.  By Kummer's theorem, $\binom{n}{k}$ is not divisible by any prime $p$ less than or equal to $k$, so one can express
$$ \binom{n}{k} = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{n-j}{b_j}$$
where $b_j$ is the product of all the prime powers $p^i$, $p \leq k$ that divide $n-j$, which is some number that depends on $k$ and the $a_p$ but does not otherwise depend on $n$.  Because of the covering hypothesis, each of the $b_j$ is divisible by at least one prime $m \leq p \leq k$, and so in particular $b_j \geq m$ and $\frac{n-j}{b_j} < \frac{n}{m}$.

With further sieving, one can find $n$ in say $[x,2x]$ for a large $x$ such that the integers $(n-j)/b_j$ are in fact coprime to all primes less than say $x^{\varepsilon_k}$ for some $\varepsilon_k > 0$ depending only on $k$.  So now the $(n-j)/b_j$, in addition to being bounded by $n/m$, are all almost primes with only $O_k(1)$ prime factors. With luck, a suitable counting argument should show that for most such $x$, the products of the factors of these almost primes all avoid the interval $(n/m,n]$, and so none of the factors of $\binom{n}{k}$ will lie in this interval; as $m$ is arbitrary, this would contradict the claim.

So the task now splits into two subtasks: firstly, to prove the conjecture, and secondly, to work out the sieve theory step indicated above.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
[I had an interesting conversation with ChatGPT about Conjecture 1 and beyond - link shared](https://chatgpt.com/share/6972388d-ab4c-8008-bea2-35bc03def3c1). Basically it showed how to arrive at slightly weakened Conjecture 1 using prime-gap machinery, using Maynard + yours results. Then it sketched what remains to be proved. I share the full conversation and an interesting part below. The conversation is in 3 messages:

- first message is a summary and potential attack strategies
- second message is on Weak Conjecture 1
- third message is on attacking the full Conjecture 1.

From GPT-5.2:

The Maynard / Ford--et al.\ prime-gap machinery can be viewed as giving \textbf{existence of coverings with forbidden residue sets} provided you can still choose residue classes with decent "hitting power". In your setting, the forbidden set for prime $p$ has size $k \bmod p$, so the allowed set has size $p - (k \bmod p)$.

A natural weakened target that matches what large-gap constructions already tolerate is:

Weakened Conjecture 1$\star$ (allow $o(k)$ survivors):
For every $m$, there exists $k > m$ and choices $r_p \in [k \bmod p, \dots, p-1]$ for primes $m \le p \le k$ such that \textbf{all but $o(k)$} integers $1 \le j \le k$ satisfy $j \equiv r_p \pmod p$ for some such prime $p$.

Why this is the right weakening:
Maynard explicitly notes that in the prime-gap construction it is ''permissible'' to leave a controlled number of survivors and then eliminate them later.

In your binomial application, leaving $o(k)$ ''bad'' indices $j$ (where you don't force a prime $\ge m$ into $b_j$) might still be salvageable: you'd get a product of $(k - o(k))$ factors $\le n/m$ plus a small exceptional set of larger factors, and then you can try to keep divisors out of $(n/m, n]$ by controlling how many ''large'' factors exist.

What you would need to import from prime-gap land? You'd want a ''covering lemma with constraints'' of this kind:

Given a set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}$ of remaining uncovered points, and a prime $p$, among the \textbf{allowed} residue classes $r \in [k \bmod p, \dots, p-1]$, there exists one that hits at least $\approx |A| / (p - (k \bmod p))$ points of $A$.

Then a greedy sieve over primes $p \in [m, k]$ would shrink the uncovered set by a multiplicative factor roughly\[
    \prod_{m \le p \le k} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{p - (k \bmod p)} \right),
\]which heuristically behaves like a power of $\log m / \log k$. This is exactly the kind of multiplicative shrinkage analysis that underlies ''greedy sieve'' discussions in the prime-gap literature and expositions.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #388 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/388).

### Problem
Can one classify all solutions of\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)\]where $k_1,k_2>3$ and $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$? Are there only finitely many solutions?

### Context
More generally, if $k_1>2$ then for fixed $a$ and $b$\[a\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=b\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)\]should have only a finite number of solutions.

See also [[363]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/363) and [[931]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/931).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.contentMd:
**Theorem.** For fixed $k_1 \neq k_2$ with both $\geq 4$, the equation $f_{k_1}(x) = f_{k_2}(y)$ (where $f_k(x) = x(x+1)\cdots(x+k-1)$) has only finitely many integer solutions. Combined with the equal-length case (zero solutions by strict monotonicity of $f_k$), this gives: for each fixed $(k_1, k_2)$ with both $> 3$, Problem 388 has only finitely many solutions.

**Proof sketch:** Apply Kulkarni-Sury's Theorem C (from their 2003 *Indagationes* paper, restated in their 2005 exposition) with $g = f_{k_2}$. Their theorem says infinitely many bounded-denominator solutions force $g$ into one of three exceptional families. We eliminate all three:- **Case 1** ($g = f_m \circ g_1$): forces $k_1 = k_2$ by degree, or contradicts the decomposition structure — the roots of $f_m$ form an arithmetic progression while $R_{k/2}$ roots do not.
- **Case 2** ($g = \varphi \circ g_1$ with $m$ even): same root-shape argument, or forces $k_1 = k_2$ by indecomposability of $R_k$.
- **Case 3** ($m = 4$, quadratic): impossible since $\deg(f_{k_2}) \geq 4$.

**Novelty assessment:** After checking the Kulkarni-Sury papers (2003 *Indagationes*, 2005 *Mathematics Student*, and the ISI Bangalore lecture notes), this corollary does not appear to be explicitly stated. The machinery is all there, but the specific application $g = f_n$ for Problem 388 seems to be new.

**Computational verification:** Exhaustive search for $k_2 = 4$ (using the algebraic identity $(m_2+1)(m_2+2)(m_2+3)(m_2+4) = (m_2^2+5m_2+5)^2 - 1$):- $(k_1, k_2) = (5, 4)$: zero solutions through $m_1 \leq 10^6$
- $(k_1, k_2) = (6, 4)$: zero solutions
- $(k_1, k_2) = (7, 4)$: exactly one solution, $(m_1, m_2) = (7, 62)$, the known identity $8 \cdot 9 \cdot 10 \cdot 11 \cdot 12 \cdot 13 \cdot 14 = 63 \cdot 64 \cdot 65 \cdot 66 = 17{,}297{,}280$

**What remains for the full problem:** The fixed-pair result does not give global finiteness when $(k_1, k_2)$ varies. Deep research into Stirling constraints, prime gap bounds, smooth number theory, and Sylvester-type refinements (Laishram-Shorey) suggests that current unconditional tools are insufficient to prove uniform finiteness. The full problem likely requires a new mechanism beyond what Bilu-Tichy, Baker bounds, or Dickman estimates can provide.

Full proof note with complete case analysis and references available. This work was conducted with AI assistance (Claude for orchestration/analysis, GPT-5.4 for proof architecture/computation, Gemini for literature survey).

replies.author: MalekZ
replies.contentMd:
I am currently not at my main device so unfortunately I am unable to access my notes. Here is a rough copy. "# Problem 388 — Full Note

## Theorem

For fixed k₁ ≠ k₂ with both ≥ 4, the equation f_{k₁}(x) = f_{k₂}(y), where f_k(x) = x(x+1)···(x+k−1), has only finitely many integer solutions. Combined with the equal-length case (zero solutions by strict monotonicity of f_k for k ≥ 2), this gives: for each fixed pair (k₁, k₂) with both > 3, Problem 388 has only finitely many solutions.

## Proof

We apply Theorem C of Kulkarni and Sury (Indagationes Mathematicae 14(3–4), 2003, pp. 457–462; exposition in Mathematics Student 74, 2005) to g = f_{k₂}.

**Theorem C (Kulkarni-Sury).** Let f, g ∈ ℤ[x] with deg(f) = m ≥ 2 and deg(g) = n ≥ 2. If the Diophantine equation f(x) = g(y) has infinitely many integer solutions with bounded denominators, then g must belong to one of three exceptional families (up to linear changes of variable):

1. g = f_m ∘ g₁ for some polynomial g₁ (a functional decomposition through a power)
2. g = φ ∘ g₁ where φ is a Dickson polynomial of even degree m
3. m = 4 and g₁ is quadratic

We take f(x) = f_{k₁}(x) (degree k₁) and g(y) = f_{k₂}(y) (degree k₂), with m = k₁, n = k₂.

**Eliminating Case 3.** This requires m = 4, i.e., k₁ = 4, and deg(g₁) = 2, forcing deg(g) = deg(f_m ∘ g₁) = 4 · 2 = 8 or deg(g) = k₂ ≥ 4. But Case 3 specifically requires the composed polynomial to have a quadratic inner function and m = 4, giving total degree 8. Since k₂ can be any value ≥ 4, this would require k₂ = 8 and a specific decomposition. The polynomial f₈(y) = y(y+1)···(y+7) is indecomposable over ℤ as a composition with a quadratic inner factor (its roots {0,−1,...,−7} cannot be partitioned into fibers of a quadratic), so this case is eliminated.

**Eliminating Case 2.** This requires g = φ ∘ g₁ where φ is a Dickson polynomial D_m of even degree. Dickson polynomials have the property that their critical values come in matched pairs (symmetric about the origin). The polynomial f_{k₂}(y) = y(y+1)···(y+k₂−1) does not have this symmetry for any k₂ ≥ 4: its roots form an arithmetic progression {0,−1,...,−(k₂−1)}, which is symmetric about −(k₂−1)/2, but the resulting polynomial's value distribution does not match the Dickson pattern. More precisely: if f_{k₂} = D_m ∘ g₁, then by comparing degrees, deg(g₁) = k₂/m. The root structure of D_m ∘ g₁ imposes that the roots of f_{k₂} must partition into fibers of g₁ that are permuted by the Dickson symmetry x ↦ −x. For k₂ ≥ 4 with roots in arithmetic progression, this is impossible unless k₁ = k₂ (contradicting k₁ ≠ k₂).

**Eliminating Case 1.** This requires g = f_m ∘ g₁, i.e., f_{k₂} = f_{k₁} ∘ g₁. Comparing degrees: k₂ = k₁ · deg(g₁). If deg(g₁) = 1, then k₁ = k₂, contradicting our assumption. If deg(g₁) ≥ 2, then the roots of f_{k₂} must partition into deg(g₁) groups of k₁ consecutive values under g₁. The roots of f_{k₂} are {0,−1,...,−(k₂−1)}, an arithmetic progression with common difference 1. The roots of f_{k₁}(g₁(y)) are the solutions to g₁(y) ∈ {0,−1,...,−(k₁−1)}, which form k₁ disjoint fibers of g₁. For these fibers to together produce an arithmetic progression of length k₂ = k₁ · deg(g₁), the polynomial g₁ must map these fibers in a very rigid way. For deg(g₁) ≥ 2, the fibers of g₁ are roots of quadratics (or higher), which cannot all be singletons — but the roots of f_{k₂} ARE all singletons (distinct integers in arithmetic progression). This forces deg(g₁) = 1, hence k₁ = k₂. Contradiction.

Since all three cases are eliminated, Theorem C guarantees that f_{k₁}(x) = f_{k₂}(y) has only finitely many integer solutions. ∎

## Novelty Assessment

After checking the Kulkarni-Sury papers (2003 Indagationes, 2005 Mathematics Student, and the ISI Bangalore lecture notes), this specific corollary — applying Theorem C with g = f_n to resolve Problem 388 for fixed pairs with both k₁, k₂ ≥ 4 — does not appear to be explicitly stated. The machinery is all in place; the application appears to be new.

## Computational Verification

For k₂ = 4, using the algebraic identity (m² + 1)(m² + 2)(m² + 3)(m² + 4) = (m² + 5m + 5)² − 1:

| (k₁, k₂) | Solutions through m₁ ≤ 10⁶ |
|-----------|---------------------------|
| (5, 4) | Zero |
| (6, 4) | Zero |
| (7, 4) | Exactly one: (m₁, m₂) = (7, 62), giving 8·9·10·11·12·13·14 = 63·64·65·66 = 17,297,280 |

## What Remains

The fixed-pair result does not give global finiteness when (k₁, k₂) varies. Current unconditional tools (Bilu-Tichy, Baker bounds, Dickman estimates, Laishram-Shorey) appear insufficient to prove uniform finiteness across all pairs. The full problem likely requires a new mechanism.

## References

1. A. Kulkarni and B. Sury, "On the Diophantine equation 1 + x + x²/2! + ··· + xⁿ/n! = g(y)," Indagationes Mathematicae 14(3–4), pp. 457–462, 2003.
2. A. Kulkarni and B. Sury, "Diophantine equations with Bernoulli polynomials," Mathematics Student 74, 2005.
3. Y.F. Bilu and R.F. Tichy, "The Diophantine equation f(x) = g(y)," Acta Arithmetica 95, pp. 261–288, 2000.

## Disclosure

This work was conducted with AI assistance (Claude for orchestration/analysis, GPT-5.4 for proof architecture/computation, Gemini for literature survey). All mathematical content has been verified by the human author."

sourceComments.author: Nik Nigro
sourceComments.contentMd:
Define the rising factorial

$$(m)^{(k)} = (m+1)(m+2)\dots(m+k) = \frac{(m+k)!}{m!}$$

We seek integer solutions to

$$(m_1)^{(k_1)} = (m_2)^{(k_2)}$$

with $k_1, k_2 \geq 4$ and the disjointness condition

$$m_1 + k_1 \leq m_2$$

**Lemma 1.** Any solution with $m_1 + k_1 \leq m_2$ must satisfy $k_1 > k_2$.

**Proof.** From $m_1 + k_1 \leq m_2$ we have for all $i \in \{1, \dots, k_1\}$ and $j \in \{1, \dots, k_2\}$:

$$m_2 + j \geq m_2 + 1 \geq m_1 + k_1 + 1 > m_1 + i$$

So every RHS factor exceeds every LHS factor. If $k_2 \geq k_1$ then the product $(m_2+1)(m_2+2)\dots(m_2+k_1)$ already exceeds $(m_1+1)(m_1+2)\dots(m_1+k_1)$, hence $\text{RHS} > \text{LHS}$, contradiction.

**Lemma 2 (smoothness obstruction).** Let $A = m_1 + k_1$. In any solution, every integer in the block

$$[m_2+1, m_2+k_2]$$

has all prime factors $\leq A$.

**Proof.** If a prime $p > A$ divides the RHS product then the $p$-adic valuation $v_p(\text{RHS}) \geq 1$, while $v_p(\text{LHS}) = 0$ since all LHS factors are $\leq A$. This contradicts equality.

Thus any solution requires a short interval of length $k_2 \geq 4$ to consist entirely of $A$-smooth numbers, which seems to be the main obstruction mechanism toward finiteness.

**Example.** There is a non-overlapping solution

$$8 \cdot 9 \cdot 10 \cdot 11 \cdot 12 \cdot 13 \cdot 14 = 63 \cdot 64 \cdot 65 \cdot 66$$

corresponding to $(m_1, k_1, m_2, k_2) = (7, 7, 62, 4)$.

**Conjecture.** This is the only solution with $k_1, k_2 \geq 4$ and $m_1 + k_1 \leq m_2$. A bounded search (details available) found no other solutions within moderate ranges.

sourceComments.contentMd:
I realized that this problem has some similarities with #849 (Singmaster's conjecture).  In terms of falling factorials $(n)_m = n (n-1) \dots (n-m+1)$, it asks for collisions $(n_1)_{m_1} = (n_2)_{m_2}$ with $m_1,m_2 \geq 3$ and $n_2 \geq n_1 + m_1$. In Theorem 1.8 of [[MRSTT22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.03335)] we show that $(n)_m = t$ has at most two solutions in the interior region $\exp(\log^{2/3+\varepsilon} n) \leq m \leq n$ if $n$ is large enough depending on $\varepsilon$, although this unfortunately does not quite impact this problem.  We observed the "trivial" collision
$$ ((a)_b)_{(a)_b-a} = ((a)_b-1)_{(a)_b-a+b-1}$$
but this is ruled out in this problem by the $n_2 \geq n_1+m_1$ condition.

Is it true that for every $n\geq 1$ there is a $k$ such that\[n(n+1)\cdots(n+k-1)\mid (n+k)\cdots (n+2k-1)?\]

### Context

The similarity with #396 has already been noted.  If one makes the change of variables $(n',k') = (n+k-1, n)$, the similarity becomes more obvious: removing the primes, the question now asks whether, for every $k$, there exists $n$ such that
$$ \prod_{i=0}^k (2n-i) | (k-1)! \binom{2n}{n}.$$

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
Computational note for [[389]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/389). For $n=25$, I searched for a $k\ge 1$ such that\[
25\cdot 26\cdots (25+k-1)\ \mid\ (25+k)(25+k+1)\cdots (25+2k-1).
\]I checked all $1\le k\le 12{,}000{,}000$ and found no solution in this range, hence\[
k_{\min}(25) > 12{,}000{,}000.
\](Of course this does \emph{not} prove nonexistence of such a $k$ for $n=25$; it is only a lower bound.)

Method: track prime-adic valuation differences\[
d_p(k)=v_p\!\Big(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(n+k+j)\Big)-v_p\!\Big(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(n+j)\Big),
\]and update incrementally via\[
d_p(k+1)=d_p(k)+v_p(n+2k)+v_p(n+2k+1)-2v_p(n+k),
\]factoring each integer using a precomputed smallest-prime-factor table up to $n+2k_{\max}+1$.
As a sanity check, the implementation reproduces the sample solutions $n=2\Rightarrow k=5$ and
$n=3\Rightarrow k=4$, and agrees with the known value $n=4\Rightarrow k=207$ (consistent with
[OEIS A375071](https://oeis.org/A375071), noting the index shift).

The problem seems to be hard. How much easier does the task become if
$n(n+1)...(n+k-1)$ and $(n+k)(n+k+1)...(n+2k-1)(n+2k)$ are compared?
So, here the second product gets additional factor $(n+2k)$ "for free".
The sequence of minimal $k$ should grow slower. Much slower?!

And one more question: Has someone for small $n$ computed what
the second smallest $k$ with the property asked by Erdos and Straus ist?
How does that sequence develop?

sourceComments.author: old-bielefelder
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let us call a pair (n,k) ES-nice if the divisibility condition holds for it. Looking at A375071 and doing some numerical computations leads me to the conjecture:

(2m+1,k) is ES-nice, if (2m,k+1) is ES-nice.
If this is true, the restricted version of problem 389 to odd numbers n = 2m+1 might be somewhat simpler than 389 itself.

The converse direction holds often but not always.

ES-nice pairs (n,k) I checked:
(2,k) is ES-nice for k = 5, 14, 27, 41, 44, 65, 90, 109, 125, 139,
(3,k) is ES-nice for k = 4, 13, 18, 26, 40, 43, 64, 75, 86, 89, 102, 108, 124, 138,

(4,k) is ES-nice for k = 207, 457,
(5,k) is ES-nice for k = 206, 456,

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
I didnot see any reason why this conjecture should be true.
You have divisibilities with a lot of common terms, so it is not surprising that it often works.
Basically one wants that $2m+2k+1$ has a crucial prime factor of $\prod_{i=1}^k (2m+i)$,
where crucial means that it did not appear in $\prod_{i=1}^k (2m+k+i)$ with sufficiently high multiplicity. That happens rarely, but there are cases.
E.g. when $n=4$ and $k=987$ or $3993$,
or $n=6$ and $k=19500$.
So conjecture refuted.

sourceComments.contentMd: This is equivalent to asking whether for every $n$, there exists a $k$ such that $$\binom{n+k-1}{k}\big|\binom{n+2k-1}{k},$$ but perhaps this was where the problem came from.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
This problem shares many features with #391, and in particular many of the techniques in [this recent paper of Alexeev, Conway, Rosenfeld, Sutherland, Uhr, Ventullo, and myself](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20170) may be relevant here.

One can summarize the arguments in [EGS82] as follows.  In both the upper and lower bound one should think of the product $a_1 \dots a_k$ by starting from $(n+1) \dots 2n = n! \binom{2n}{n}$, removing some factors $b_1,\dots,b_r$ in $(n,2n]$, and then adding some factors $c_1,\dots,c_s$ in $(2n, f(n)]$.  Thus, one can rewrite the equation $n! = a_1 \dots a_k$ as
$$ b_1 \dots b_r = \binom{2n}{n} c_1 \dots c_s \quad (1)$$
for some $n < b_1 < \dots < b_r \leq 2n$ and $2n < c_1 < \dots < c_s \leq f(n)$.

For the lower bound: every prime $p$ in $(2n/4, 2n/3]$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ once (by Kummer's theorem), which means exactly one of $2p$ or $3p$ has to be in the $\{b_1,\dots,b_r\}$.  By the prime number theorem, this creates $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$ factors of $2$ or $3$ on the LHS of (1); since $\binom{2n}{n}$ only has $O(\log n)$ factors of each (by Kummer again), these factors have to be absorbed by the $c_1,\dots,c_s$; but $(2n,f(n)]$ only contains $O(f(n)-2n + \log n)$ copies of both $2$ and $3$, which easily leads to the lower bound $f(n)-2n \gg \frac{n}{\log n}$ (assuming $n$ large enough of course).

For the upper bound: factorize $\binom{2n}{n}$ into prime powers $p^a$; one can check (again from Kummer) that all such factors are at most $2n$.  For each such prime power, add $2^i p^a$ to the collection $b_1,\dots,b_r$, where $i$ is chosen so that $2^i p^a \in (n,2n]$.  This balances out all the factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$, but creates excess powers of 2 on the LHS; one can calculate this excess (using the prime number theorem) to be $O(\frac{n}{\log n})$.  To balance out this excess, add various $b_j$ to the LHS and $2b_j$ to the RHS for greedily chosen $n < b_j < n + O(n/\log n)$; this will establish $f(n)-2n \ll \frac{n}{\log n}$.

The lower bound analysis is wasteful because it does not take into account the primes $p \in (2n/6, 2n/5]$, $p \in (2n/8, 2n/7]$, etc. (though the first few intervals should provide the dominant contribution to the bound).  The upper bound analysis is wasteful because it only uses even numbers for the $c_j$ to balance powers of 2 on the LHS; one should also be able to balance powers of 3, 5, etc. with more effort.

One key idea in the paper linked above is that products of consecutive integers $\prod_{j=1}^H (N+j)$ have prime factorizations that do not depend very strongly on the starting point $N$: the number of times a prime $p$ divides $\prod_{j=1}^H (N+j)$ is almost the same as the number of times it divides $\prod_{j=1}^H (N'+j)$ if $p$ is small compared to $N,N',H$.  This should allow one to introduce blocks of consecutive integers on the left and right-hand sides of (1) to help balance the prime factorizations, though actually carrying out this strategy could be complicated.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #393 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/393).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ denote the minimal $m\geq 1$ such that\[n! = a_1\cdots a_t\]with $a_1<\cdots <a_t=a_1+m$. What is the behaviour of $f(n)$?

### Context
Erdős and Graham write that they do not even know whether $f(n)=1$ infinitely often (i.e. whether a factorial is the product of two consecutive integers infinitely often).

Let $F_m(N)$ count the number of $n\leq N$ such that $f(n)=m$. Berend and Osgood [BeOs92] proved that, for each fixed $m$, $F_m(N)=o(N)$. Bui, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BPZ23] have shown that\[F_m(N)\ll_m N^{33/34}.\]A result of Luca [Lu02] implies that $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, conditional on the [ABC conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture).

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: Some initial observations inspired by the numerical data.  The obvious factorization $n! = 2 \dots n$ gives $f(n) \leq n-2$ for all $n>2$.  It also seems that $f(n) = n-O(\log n)$ for all but a few exceptional $n$. Indeed, suppose that $m=f(n) < n - C \log n$ for a large $C$.  By Kummer's theorem, $2$ divides $n!$ $n-O(\log n)$ times, and if $2^k$ is the largest power of $2$ that divides one of the $a_i$, then the number of powers of $2$ dividing $a_1 \dots a_t$ is at most $\sum_{j=1}^k \min( \frac{m}{2^j}+1, t)$, which one can bound by $m+k$ by ignoring the $t$ factor; thus $k > 10 \log n$ (say) by hypothesis, which makes at least one of the $a_i$ of size at least $2^k \geq n^{10}$ hence all of them are at least this size since $m \leq n$.  By Stirling's formula this gives the bound $t k \ll n \log n$, so $t$ is less than a small multiple of $n$.  The inequality $n - O(\log n) \leq \sum_{j=1}^k \min( \frac{m}{2^j}+1, t) \ll k + t \log \frac{m}{t}$ then forces $k \gg n$, and hence $t = O(\log n)$. Thus $n!$ has somehow been factored into only $O(\log n)$ factors that are distance $O(n)$ apart and size at least $n^{10}$, which seems like quite a rare occurrence.  These factors would need to be divisible by a lot of small primes, and perhaps one could rule a lot of scenarios out using the abc conjecture or similar tools.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
To continue the previous analysis: suppose that one has $t = O(\log n)$ for some large $n$ as above.  For any prime $p \leq n^{0.99}$, $p$ divides $n! = a_1 \dots a_t$ about $n/p$ times, but if $l > 10 \log n$ (say) then at most one of the $a_1,\dots,a_t$ can be divisible by $p^l$.  From this and the assumption $t = O(\log n)$ one can conclude that one of the $a_i$ is divisible by $p$ at least $0.99 n/p$ times (say).    The product $\prod_{p \leq n^{0.99}} p^{0.99 n/p}$ is something like $(n!)^{0.98}$, so by the pigeonhole principle one should be able to find two $a_i,a_j$ each of which is divisible by a product of prime powers $p^{0.99 n/p}$ of size $\gg a_i^{0.95}, a_j^{0.95}$ say, which makes the radical of $a_i$ or $a_j$ of size $O(a_i^{0.1})$ or $O(a_j^{0.1})$.  But as $a_i = a_j + O(n)$ and $a_i, a_j \geq n^{10}$, this would violate the abc conjecture.  So I think one can get a bound of the form $f(n) = n - O(\log n)$ assuming the abc conjecture.

Another observation: if one can find some small $j,l$ such that $(j+1) \dots (j+l) | \binom{n+j}{j} = \frac{(j+1) \dots (j+n)}{n!}$, then this almost certainly leads to the bound $f(n) \leq n-l-1$, because $(j+l+1) \dots (j+n)$ is now a moderately large multiple of $n!$ and one should be able to remove some terms from this product to recover $n!$ exactly.  Thus for instance the trivial $1 | \binom{n+0}{0}$ gives the trivial bound $f(n) \leq n-2$, $2 \times 3 | \binom{n+1}{1}$ or $3 \times 4 | \binom{n+2}{2}$ should lead to $f(n) \leq n-3$, and so forth.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Perhaps this is similar to the argument of Luca [Lu02], which conditional on ABC shows that, for any fixed polynomial $P$, there are finitely many solutions to $P(x)=n!$ (which as noted in the problem description implies $f(n)\to \infty$).

I had a quick look at Luca's paper and it's not written in a quantitative way, but the argument should be easily adapted to give quantitative control in this specific case; I suspect it would then end up being the same as the argument you sketch.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Over at [the database](https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/issues/92), swrlly has made an initial computation of the first few values of $f(n)$, up to $n=11$, and some upper bounds for $n$ up to $19$, via a simple brute-force method.  If any computation-minded folks would like to try confirming and/or extending these values, perhaps using a more efficient approach, that would be great; then we can work on submitting this new sequence to the OEIS (it does not appear to already be there).

p.s. the OEIS display code should be modified so that only strings of the form "Axxxxxx" are linked; the "in progress" string does not link to anything useful.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #394 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/394).

### Problem
Let $t_k(n)$ denote the least $m$ such that\[n\mid m(m+1)(m+2)\cdots (m+k-1).\]Is it true that\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{x^2}{(\log x)^c}\]for some $c>0$?

Is it true that, for $k\geq 2$,\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_{k+1}(n) =o\left(\sum_{n\leq x}t_k(n)\right)?\]

### Context
In [ErGr80] they mention a conjecture of Erdős that the sum is $o(x^2)$. This was proved by Erdős and Hall [ErHa78], who proved that in fact\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}x^2.\]Erdős and Hall conjecture that the sum is $o(x^2/(\log x)^c)$ for any $c<\log 2$.

Since $t_2(p)=p-1$ for prime $p$ it is trivial that\[\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\gg \frac{x^2}{\log x}.\]Erdős and Hall [ErHa78] also note that $t_{n-1}(n!)=2$ and $t_{n-2}(n!)\ll n$, which $n=2^r$ shows is the best possible. They ask about the behaviour of $t_{n-3}(n!)$ and also ask ask whether, for infinitely many $n$,\[t_k(n!)< t_{k-1}(n!)-1\]for all $1\leq k<n$. They proved (with Selfridge) that this holds for $n=10$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

They ask about the behaviour of $t_{n-3}(n!)$ and also ask ask whether, for infinitely many $n$,\[t_k(n!)< t_{k-1}(n!)-1\]for all $1\leq k<n$. They proved (with Selfridge) that this holds for $n=10$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #396 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/396).

### Problem
Is it true that for every $k$ there exists $n$ such that\[\prod_{0\leq i\leq k}(n-i) \mid \binom{2n}{n}?\]

### Context
Erdős and Graham write that $n+1$ always divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ (indeed $\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ is the $n$th [Catalan number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_number)), but it is quite rare that $n$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$.

Pomerance [Po14] has shown that for any $k\geq 0$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $n-k\mid\binom{2n}{n}$, although the set of such $n$ has upper density $<1/3$. Pomerance also shows that the set of $n$ such that\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)\mid \binom{2n}{n}\]has density $1$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Include a rigorous proof, counterexample, or a precise explanation of the remaining gap.

sourceComments.author: JustinDehorty
sourceComments.contentMd:
$\large\textbf{Extending OEIS A375077 through } k=13$

$\textbf{Exhaustive search, validation, and a formally verified barrier theorem}$

Over the past several months I have been running an exhaustive computational search for [[396]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/396) witnesses, extending OEIS A375077 with 6 new terms at the initial time of discovery (2 new terms at the time of this post). The full codebase, validation certificates, and a machine-checked proof are publicly available at [github.com/jdehorty/erdos396](https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396).

New values:

$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
k & a(k) & \text{Search range} & \text{Date found*} \\ \hline
8 & 339{,}949{,}252 & 0\text{–}340\text{M} & \text{2025-01-17} \\
9 & 1{,}019{,}547{,}844 & 0\text{–}17.6\text{B} & \text{2026-03-16 (corrected)} \\
10 & 17{,}609{,}764{,}994 & 0\text{–}17.6\text{B} & \text{2025-01-20} \\
11 & 1{,}070{,}858{,}041{,}585 & 0\text{–}2\text{T} & \text{2026-02-09} \\
12 & 5{,}048{,}891{,}644{,}646 & 0\text{–}6.15\text{T} & \text{2026-02-11} \\
13 & 18{,}253{,}129{,}921{,}842 & 0\text{–}25\text{T} & \text{2026-02-16}
\end{array}$

*Note: Dates reflect my own personal records of when each value was first found, not when results were submitted or published. The jumps in pace (particularly from k=11 onward) correspond to successive sieve improvements: the v1 prefilter (7x), the fused sieve pass (15x), and finally Kummer-based valuation for all primes (31x single-threaded throughput).

Each value has a computational certificate of minimality: every integer below the claimed witness has been checked and ruled out.

Note on $k=9$: the original governor-run search found a witness at $17{,}609{,}764{,}993$. A subsequent full validation pass (checking every integer, not just governor-run candidates) found the true minimum at $1{,}019{,}547{,}844$.

$\textbf{Method.}$ The search is built around the Governor Set $G = \{n : n \mid \binom{2n}{n}\}$ (OEIS A014847, density $\approx 12.3\%$ by Ford-Konyagin). All known witnesses have every block term $n, n-1, \ldots, n-k$ in $G$. A fused segmented sieve strips small prime factors and checks the Kummer carry condition $\nu_p(n) \leq \nu_p\!\binom{2n}{n}$ inline, rejecting ${\sim}87\%$ of integers in a single pass. The $\sqrt{2n}$ large-prime-factor barrier provides additional fast rejection. Runs of $k+1$ consecutive governors are candidate witnesses, each verified by the full inequality $\sum_{i=0}^{k} \nu_p(n-i) \leq \nu_p\!\binom{2n}{n}$ at every prime $p$.

$\textbf{The Small Prime Barrier Theorem.}$ The governor-run search cannot detect witnesses where some block term fails to be a governor. I proved that any such non-governor failure must occur at a prime $p < 2k+1$. For $k=13$ this is just 9 primes: $\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\}$. The proof uses Kummer's theorem and a carry invariance lemma for base-$p$ self-addition; the bound $2k+1$ is tight (via Bertrand's postulate). The Small Prime Barrier Theorem and its tightness are formally verified in Lean 4 + Mathlib (no sorry/admit); the formal proof covers the carry invariance lemma, the barrier theorem itself, and the tightness result via Bertrand's postulate - not the computational search.

This yields a provably complete validation method: screen every integer at the barrier primes, then fully verify survivors. The validate binary implements this for $k=8$ through $k=13$, producing minimality certificates independent of the Governor Set Completeness Conjecture.

$\textbf{Verification.}$ The repository includes: (1) a Rust verifier and a stdlib-only Python verifier for witness validity; (2) the Lean 4 formal proof of the Small Prime Barrier Theorem (justifying the completeness of the validation algorithm); (3) published validation certificates with coverage invariants and build metadata tied to specific source revisions; (4) an independent report checker that recomputes invariants from the JSON reports. Full details at [github.com/jdehorty/erdos396](https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396).

Note: AI usage comprised GPT-5.4 Pro (extended thinking) and Google Gemini 3.1 DeepThink for proof exploration and adversarial review, and Claude Opus 4.6 for coding the Rust-based search pipeline and Lean 4 formalization. The Lean 4 formal proof is machine-checked (no sorry/admit), and all computational claims are backed by deterministic validation certificates; see docs/trust.md in the repository.

replies.author: JustinDehorty
replies.contentMd:
Thanks for the review! I've created GitHub issues for each finding and will address them there, but to provide a brief summary and clarify a few points:

1) ValidateBatch residual misclassification ([issue](https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396/issues/1))

This is an interesting point by GPT-5.4. The batch path is indeed missing a guard that the naive reference implementation has, which means a small barrier prime can technically be misclassified as a large-prime failure when the sieve limit falls below the barrier threshold. Technically speaking, this is a real soundness gap in the validator's general contract and I'll fix it.

That said, this does not affect the quality of any published results. The bug requires the batch's maximum $n$ to be below $2k^2$, which for $k=11$ means $n < 242$. With the default batch size of $10^6$, the very first batch is already six orders of magnitude above this threshold. No validation run I've produced has come anywhere near triggering this. The certified minima stand.

2) Search misses cross-worker runs ([issue](https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396/issues/2))

This is also an interesting point. The search binary is the fast discovery pass. In the original planning phase, it was very important to me to have a separate validation pass, since the possibility of a false negative could exist in theory. For example, in exceedingly rare circumstances, there could exist a valid Erdős 396 witness where some term $m=n-j$  in the falling factorial divides the ambient binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$, even though m itself does not divide $\binom{2m}{m}$. Part of the reason I held off so long in posting my results is that I don't consider the integers technically "discovered" unless both false positives AND false negatives are ruled out. And since the initial forward pass does not protect against these extremely rare scenarios where n = m+j creates an extra prime that m does not have on its own, it is necessary to have that backwards certifier as a backstop. So the architecture is intentional: the search discovers candidates quickly, and the "validate" pass provides the provably complete certificate.

However, I do appreciate the observation that varying the worker count can silently change search output. From a correctness standpoint, this is a good suggestion. I'm open to hardening this by overlapping worker ranges or stitching boundary state in the aggregation pass, and I'll think about the best way to do that. To be clear, this does not affect the certified minima, since the validate binary checks every integer independently and its results are not impacted by the search tool's parallelism.

3) Corollary 6 documentation ([issue](https://github.com/jdehorty/erdos396/issues/3))

Fair note. Technically, if you look at the source code, the inline comments at the call site clearly describe stage 1 as the contrapositive of the barrier theorem applied as a pre-filter. The detailed docs also describe the two-stage structure accurately. But I agree the top-of-file header comment compresses the story by branding the whole algorithm as "Corollary 6," and that could be more precise. I'll tighten the wording there. Of course, since this is purely a documentation issue, it does not affect any of the results.
