problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #424 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/424).

### Problem
Let $a_1=2$ and $a_2=3$ and continue the sequence by appending to $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ all possible values of $a_ia_j-1$ with $i\neq j$. Is it true that the set of integers which eventually appear has positive density?

### Context
Asked by Hofstadter. The sequence begins $2,3,5,9,14,17,26,\ldots$ and is [A005244](https://oeis.org/A005244) in the OEIS. This problem is also discussed in section E31 of Guy's book Unsolved Problems in Number Theory.

In [ErGr80] (and in Guy's book) this problem as written is asking for whether almost all integers appear in this sequence, but the answer to this is trivially no (as pointed out to me by Steinerberger): no integer $\equiv 1\pmod{3}$ is ever in the sequence, so the set of integers which appear has density at most $2/3$. This is easily seen by induction, and the fact that if $a,b\in \{0,2\}\pmod{3}$ then $ab-1\in \{0,2\}\pmod{3}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #425 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/425).

### Problem
Let $F(n)$ be the maximum possible size of a subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that the products $ab$ are distinct for all $a<b$. Is there a constant $c$ such that\[F(n)=\pi(n)+(c+o(1))n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}?\]If $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ is such that all products $a_1\cdots a_r$ are distinct for $a_1<\cdots <a_r$ then is it true that\[\lvert A\rvert \leq \pi(n)+O(n^{\frac{r+1}{2r}})?\]

### Context
Erdős [Er68] proved that there exist some constants $0<c_1\leq c_2$ such that\[\pi(n)+c_1 n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}\leq F(n)\leq \pi(n)+c_2 n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}.\]This problem can also be considered in the real numbers: that is, what is the size of the  the largest $A\subset [1,x]$ such that for any distinct $a,b,c,d\in A$ we have $\lvert ab-cd\rvert \geq 1$? Erdős had conjectured (see [Er73] and [Er77c]) that $\lvert A\rvert=o(x)$.

In [ErGr80] Erdős and Graham report that Alexander had given a construction disproving this conjecture, establishing that $\lvert A\rvert\gg x$ is possible. Alexander's construction is given in [Er80], and we sketch a simplified version. Let $B\subseteq [1,X^2]$ be a Sidon set of integers of size $\gg X$ and\[A=\{ X e^{b/X^2} : b\in B\}.\]It is easy to check that\[\lvert ab-cd\rvert \geq X^2\lvert 1-e^{1/X^2}\rvert \gg 1\]for distinct $a,b,c,d\in A$, and (after rescaling $A$ by some constant factor) this produces a set of size $\gg X$ with the desired property in the interval $[X,O(X)]$. Furthermore, a simple modification allows for $A$ to also be $1$-separated.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #430 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/430).

### Problem
Fix some integer $n$ and define a decreasing sequence in $[1,n)$ by $a_1=n-1$ and, for $k\geq 2$, letting $a_k$ be the greatest integer in $[1,a_{k-1})$ such that all of the prime factors of $a_k$ are $>n-a_k$.

Is it true that, for sufficiently large $n$, not all of this sequence can be prime?

### Context
Erdős and Graham write 'preliminary calculations made by Selfridge indicate that this is the case but no proof is in sight'. For example if $n=8$ we have $a_1=7$ and $a_2=5$ and then must stop.

Sarosh Adenwalla has observed that this problem is equivalent to (the first part of) [[385]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/385). Indeed, assuming a positive answer to that, for all large $n$, there exists a composite $m<n$ such that all primes dividing $m$ are $>n-m$. It follows that such an $m$ is equal to some $a_i$ in the sequence defined for $[1,n)$, and $m$ is composite by assumption.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #431 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/431).

### Problem
Are there two infinite sets $A$ and $B$ such that $A+B$ agrees with the set of prime numbers up to finitely many exceptions?

### Context
A problem of Ostmann, sometimes known as the 'inverse Goldbach problem'. The answer is surely no. The best result in this direction is due to Elsholtz and Harper [ElHa15], who showed that if $A,B$ are such sets then for all large $x$ we must have\[\frac{x^{1/2}}{\log x\log\log x} \ll \lvert A \cap [1,x]\rvert \ll x^{1/2}\log\log x\]and similarly for $B$.

Elsholtz [El01] has proved there are no sets $A,B,C$ (all of size at least $2$) such that $A+B+C$ agrees with the set of prime numbers up to finitely many exceptions.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #436 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/436).

### Problem
If $p$ is a prime and $k,m\geq 2$ then let $r(k,m,p)$ be the minimal $r$ such that $r,r+1,\ldots,r+m-1$ are all $k$th power residues modulo $p$. Let\[\Lambda(k,m)=\limsup_{p\to \infty} r(k,m,p).\]Is it true that $\Lambda(k,2)$ is finite for all $k$? Is $\Lambda(k,3)$ finite for all odd $k$? How large are they?

### Context
Asked by Lehmer and Lehmer [LeLe62], who note that for example $\Lambda(2,2)=9$ - indeed, $9$ is always a quadratic residue, and if $10$ isn't then either $2$ or $5$ is, and hence at least one of $1,2$ or $4,5$ or $9,10$ is a consecutive pair of quadratic residues (and similarly there are infinitely many $p$ for which there are no consecutive quadratic residues below $9,10$).

A similar argument of Dunton [Du65] proves $\Lambda(3,2)=77$, and Bierstedt and Mills [BiMi63] proved $\Lambda(4,2)=1224$. Lehmer and Lehmer proved that $\Lambda(k,3)=\infty$ for all even $k$ and $\Lambda(k,4)=\infty$ for all $k\leq 1048909$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Graham [Gr64g] proved that $\Lambda(k,l)=\infty$ for all $k\geq 2$ and $l\geq 4$.

The remaining questions are to examine whether $\Lambda(k,3)$ is finite for all odd $k\geq 5$, and the growth rate of $\Lambda(k,2)$ and $\Lambda(k,3)$ as functions of $k$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Thanks! It's interesting from a modern perspective to read this paper (from 1962) on a 'machine proof'.

In particular they write:

"The referee comments that the proof of Theorem 1, described below,
is "not a machine proof in the sense of the theorem-proving programs now being developed." This is true. The aim of most writers on this subject is to consider a very general program enabling a digital computer to prove a wide class of theorems at a very low level, beginning with the axioms, setting its own goals, and trying to achieve them without human intervention. This is, in a way, a simulation problem. Speculations about such programs involve (significantly) such notions as decidability. Meanwhile, no really new theorems seem to emerge. Perhaps too
much is expected of a single program."

The last sentence in particular strikes a chord...

Investigate open Erdos Problem #445 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/445).

### Problem
Is it true that, for any $c>1/2$, if $p$ is a sufficiently large prime then, for any $n\geq 0$, there exist $a,b\in(n,n+p^c)$ such that $ab\equiv 1\pmod{p}$?

### Context
Heilbronn (unpublished) proved this for $c$ sufficiently close to $1$. Heath-Brown [He00] used Kloosterman sums to prove this for all $c>3/4$.

This is discussed in [this MathOverflow question](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/69509/small-residue-classes-with-small-reciprocal).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #450 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/450).

### Problem
How large must $y=y(\epsilon,n)$ be such that the number of integers in $(x,x+y)$ with a divisor in $(n,2n)$ is at most $\epsilon y$?

### Context
It is not clear what the intended quantifier on $x$ is. Cambie has observed that if this is intended to hold for all $x$ then, provided\[\epsilon(\log n)^\delta (\log\log n)^{3/2}\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$, where $\delta=0.086\cdots$, there is no such $y$, which follows from an averaging argument and the work of Ford [Fo08].

On the other hand, Cambie has observed that if $\epsilon\ll 1/n$ then $y(\epsilon,n)\sim 2n$: indeed, if $y<2n$ then this is impossible taking $x+n$ to be a multiple of the lowest common multiple of $\{n+1,\ldots,2n-1\}$. On the other hand, for every fixed $\delta\in (0,1)$ and $n$ large every $2(1+\delta)n$ consecutive elements contains many elements which are a multiple of an element in $(n,2n)$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #451 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/451).

### Problem
Estimate $n_k$, the smallest integer $>2k$ such that $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n_k-i)$ has no prime factor in $(k,2k)$.

### Context
Erdős and Graham write 'we can prove $n_k>k^{1+c}$ but no doubt much more is true'.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here is a heuristic proof of this Problem.
Let\[
\mathcal P_k=\{p:\ p\ \text{prime},\ k<p<2k\},\qquad
M_k=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}p.
\]The condition that the whole block $[n-k,n-1]$ contains no multiple of any $p\in\mathcal P_k$ is equivalent to saying that the $k$ integers $n-1,\dots,n-k$ are all coprime to $M_k$. For a fixed $p\in\mathcal P_k$, the interval $[n-k,n-1]$ contains a multiple of $p$ iff\[
n\equiv 1,2,\dots,k\pmod p.
\]Thus the allowed residues mod $p$ are exactly the $p-k$ classes $\{0,k+1,\dots,p-1\}$. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the number of allowed residue classes mod $M_k$ is\[
A_k=\prod_{p\in\mathcal P_k}(p-k),
\]so the exact density of admissible $n$ is\[
D_k \ :=\ \frac{A_k}{M_k}
\ =\ \prod_{\substack{k<p<2k\\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}}
\left(1-\frac{k}{p}\right).
\]Using summation over primes and the prime number theorem one obtains the asymptotic\[
\log\frac{1}{D_k}=(\log 4+o(1))\,\frac{k}{\log k}.
\]Numerically (for $1\le k\le 50$), $\log n_k$ grows on the $\frac{k}{\log k}$ scale and closely tracks $(\log 4)\frac{k}{\log k}$; in this range we in fact observe\[
\log n_k \ \le\ (\log 4)\,\frac{k}{\log k},
\]while we cannot replace $\log 4$ by $\log 3$.
Heuristically one expects $n_k\asymp D_k^{-1}$; making this rigorous appears to be the remaining difficulty.
Details of the proofs and numerical evidence can be found on my GitHub page [here](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/Notes-on-Erdos-Problem-451/blob/main/Notes_on_Erdos_Problem_451_Density_and_Heuristics.pdf).

### Problem
Let $\omega(n)$ count the number of distinct prime factors of $n$. What is the size of the largest interval $I\subseteq [x,2x]$ such that $\omega(n)>\log\log n$ for all $n\in I$?

### Context
Erdős [Er37] proved that the density of integers $n$ with $\omega(n)>\log\log n$ is $1/2$. Investigate open Erdos Problem #456 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/456).

### Problem
Let $p_n$ be the smallest prime $\equiv 1\pmod{n}$ and let $m_n$ be the smallest integer such that $n\mid \phi(m_n)$.

Is it true that $m_n<p_n$ for almost all $n$? Does $p_n/m_n\to \infty$ for almost all $n$? Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p-1$ is the only $n$ for which $m_n=p$?

### Context
[Linnik's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linnik%27s_theorem) implies that $p_n\leq n^{O(1)}$. It is trivial that $m_n\leq p_n$ always.

If $n=q-1$ for some prime $q$ then $m_n=p_n$. Erdős [Er79e] writes it is 'easy to show' that for infinitely many $n$ we have $m_n <p_n$, and that $m_n/n\to \infty$ for almost all $n$.

Unless I'm missing something, we always have $\phi(p_n) = p_n - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$, so that $m_n \le p_n$ for all $n$. So I'm guessing that Erdős meant to say that $p_n > m_n$ holds infinitely often. In this case, take $n = 2^{2k+1}$. Since $\phi(2n) = n$, we have $m_n \le 2n$. On the other hand, $n+1$ is divisible by $3$, so that $p_n \ge 2n+1 > m_n$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #458 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/458).

### Problem
Let $[1,\ldots,n]$ denote the least common multiple of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Is it true that, for all $k\geq 1$,\[[1,\ldots,p_{k+1}-1]< p_k[1,\ldots,p_k]?\]

### Context
Erdős and Graham write this is 'almost certainly' true, but the proof is beyond our ability, for (at least) two reasons:- Firstly, one has to rule out the possibility of many primes $q$ such that $p_k<q^2<p_{k+1}$. There should be at most one such $q$, which would follow from $p_{k+1}-p_k<p_k^{1/2}$, which is essentially the notorious [Legendre's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_conjecture).
- The small primes also cause trouble.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #460 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/460).

### Problem
Let $a_0=0$ and $a_1=1$, and in general define $a_k$ to be the least integer $>a_{k-1}$ for which $(n-a_k,n-a_i)=1$ for all $0\leq i<k$. Does\[\sum_{0<a_i< n}\frac{1}{a_i}\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$? What about if we restrict the sum to those $i$ such that $n-a_j$ is divisible by some prime $\leq a_j$, or the complement of such $i$?

### Context
This question arose in work of Eggleton, Erdős, and Selfridge, who could prove that $a_k <k^{2+o(1)}$ for $k$ large enough depending on $n$, but conjectured that in fact $a_k\ll k\log k$ is true.

The problem above is from [Er77c]. This question is stated slightly differently in [ErGr80], which has $a_0=n$ instead of $a_0=0$ and $1\leq i<k$ instead of $0\leq i<k$. The material difference this makes is that the main formulation above has $(a_k,n)=1$ for all $k\geq 1$, which is not imposed in the second formulation. Furthermore, in both [Er77c] and [ErGr80] this is stated without the restriction to $a_k<n$ in the sum, although perhaps this was implicitly intended. Without this condition the sum is infinite since the sequence of $a_k$ contains $n+p$ for all primes $p>n$ (this observation was made by Svyable using ChatGPT).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Thomas Bloom
sourceComments.contentMd:
This problem is stated differently in [Er77c] and [ErGr80]. An easier way to phrase the difference is that in [Er77c] we have $(a_k,n)=1$ for all $k\geq 1$ but this is not guaranteed in the [ErGr80] formulation. For example with $n=6$ the [Er77c] sequence begins $0,1,5$ while the [ErGr80] sequence begins $6,1,2$.

As written, the sum trivially diverges, since it contains $a_k=n+p$ for all large primes $p$. This is the trivial solution posted on Reddit that natso26 mentions.

Perhaps a condition like $a_k\leq n$ was intended, but neither source mentions this, and without any further reference or motivation given for this problem I don't think we can resolve what was actually meant.

The proof posted by Przemek Chojecki would resolve this stronger version if $f(n)=\sum_{a<n} \frac{1}{a}1_{P^-(n-a)>a}\to \infty$. Averaging this over $n\leq N$ and using estimates on rough numbers show (I think) that it grows like $\log\log n$ on average. It's not clear to me whether this $\to \infty$ along all $n$ though.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
You're right, in either formulation, if one sums over all $k$ without any upper cut-off on $a_k$, then the series is automatically divergent: for every prime $p>n$ the term $a=n+p$ must occur in the greedy sequence, because before reaching $n+p$ all previously chosen translates satisfy $n-a_i\in[-p+1,n-1]$, so none is divisible by $p$ (the only multiple of $p$ in that interval is $0$, which never arises as $n-a_i$ in these constructions); hence $\gcd(n-(n+p),\,n-a_i)=\gcd(p,\,n-a_i)=1$ for all earlier $i$, making $n+p$ admissible at the moment it becomes available and therefore impossible for the greedy rule to skip.  Comparing $\sum_{p>n}1/(n+p)$ with $\sum_p 1/p$ gives divergence for every fixed $n\ge2$.

If instead one imposes the natural ''nontrivial'' restriction $a_k<n$ (or $a_k\le n$), then the above argument disappears and one can at least prove an averaged divergence statement from the forced ''rough'' contribution.  Writing $P^-(m)$ for the least prime factor of $|m|$ (with $P^-(\pm1)=\infty$), set\[
f(n):=\sum_{a=1}^{n-1}\frac1a\,\mathbf 1_{\{P^-(n-a)>a\}},
\]so that (by the forced-rough lemma) the truncated greedy sum $S_{<n}(n):=\sum_{a_k\le n-1}1/a_k$ satisfies $S_{<n}(n)\ge f(n)$ for every $n$ in both formulations.  Averaging over $n\le N$ and changing variables $m=n-a$ yields $\sum_{n\le N}f(n)=\sum_{a\le N-1}\frac1a\,\Phi(N-a,a)$, where $\Phi(x,y)$ counts $y$-rough integers $\le x$; Buchstab’s asymptotic for $\Phi(x,y)$ (uniform for $a\in[N^{1/3},N^{1/2}]$, where $u=\log(N-a)/\log a\in[2,3]$ and hence $\omega(u)\gg1$) gives $\Phi(N-a,a)\gg N/\log a$ on that range, and thus\[
\frac1N\sum_{n\le N}f(n)\ \gg\ \sum_{N^{1/3}\le a\le N^{1/2}}\frac1{a\log a}\ \asymp\ \log\log N.
\]In particular $\limsup_{n\to\infty}f(n)=\infty$ and hence $\limsup_{n\to\infty}S_{<n}(n)=\infty$; what remains open is whether $f(n)\to\infty$ (and thus $S_{<n}(n)\to\infty$) along all $n$.

I've re-written the note to discuss both cases and give the full proofs. I think this solves the problem. See here: https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos-460-v2.pdf

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Your note still does not solve the problem, since it does not establish $f(n)\to \infty$ for all $n$, which is what is required.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
You are right. Also I went deeper into trying to prove it, and it comes down to a conjecture which looks adjacent to recent results by Gafni-Tao, but is currently out of reach. I've updated https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos-460-v2.pdf with the discussion around this dyadic strategy and a plausible conjecture that would imply this pointwise divergence.

At least we have a clear picture what is interesting/hard about the problem.

Yes, I think I'll add $a_k\leq n$ (with an explanation in the remarks). It doesn't seem interesting/significant enough to warrant creating another problem as a minor variant.

I've tried without success to find anything hinting at this problem in the papers of Eggleton, Erdős, and Selfridge, but to no avail. sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
As Kevin Barreto mentioned, we might have $a_0=0$ with $i=0$ included in $gcd$ condition. The full proof of both versions is here: https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos-460.pdf - here's the sketch:

Fix $n\ge2$ and define a greedy increasing sequence $(a_k)$ by requiring the translates $n-a_k$ to be pairwise coprime: in Case A one enforces $\gcd(n-a_k,n-a_i)=1$ for all $1\le i<k$, while in Case B one includes $i=0$ with $a_0=0$, which is equivalent to adding the standing constraint $\gcd(a_k,n)=1$. To study Erdős' divergence question for $\sum_k 1/a_k$ (and its natural subsums), the note introduces a dichotomy for $1\le a\le n-1$: call $a$ rough if the least prime factor $P^{-}(n-a)$ exceeds $a$ (equivalently, $n-a$ has no prime divisor $\le a$), and proper otherwise. This yields a canonical subsum $S_{\mathrm{rough}}(n)=\sum_{k:\,a_k\le n-1,\ P^{-}(n-a_k)>a_k}1/a_k$, with complementary ''proper'' subsum capturing the genuinely interactive part of the greedy dynamics.

The main reduction is that the rough part is forced and admits an explicit description independent of the history: for any $a<n$ with $P^{-}(n-a)>a$, one has $\gcd(n-a,n-a')=1$ for every $a'<a$ (since any common prime divisor would divide $a-a'$ and hence be $\le a$), so such an $a$ is admissible at every stage once it becomes available (and in Case B this automatically includes coprimality with $n$). A greedy minimality argument then shows the process cannot skip any rough $a$: if $a$ were the least skipped rough integer, at the first step where $a_{k-1}<a<a_k$ it would be admissible, contradicting the definition of $a_k$ as the least admissible choice. Consequently the set of rough values appearing with $a_k<n$ is exactly $R(n)=\{1\le a\le n-1: P^{-}(n-a)>a\}$, and hence\[
S_{\mathrm{rough}}(n)=\sum_{a\in R(n)}\frac1a=\sum_{\substack{1\le a\le n-1\\ P^{-}(n-a)>a}}\frac1a,
\]giving an explicit, history-free lower bound for $\sum_k 1/a_k$ in both cases and reducing the divergence problem to estimating this rough sum plus the remaining proper contribution.

### Problem
Let $s_t(n)$ be the $t$-smooth component of $n$ - that is, the product of all primes $p$ (with multiplicity) dividing $n$ such that $p<t$. Let $f(n,t)$ count the number of distinct possible values for $s_t(m)$ for $m\in [n+1,n+t]$. Is it true that\[f(n,t)\gg t\](uniformly, for all $t$ and $n$)?

### Context
Erdős and Graham report they can show\[f(n,t) \gg \frac{t}{\log t}.\]

sourceComments.contentMd: It's ambiguous from the reference whether the authors intend to exclude the prime $n$ from the problem. If they do, then this is more or less a question about the distribution of semiprimes $pq$ with $p,q = x^{1/2} \log^{O(1)} x$ in intervals of length $O(x^{1/2} \log^2 x)$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think one can disprove that $f(N) = o(N)$ for all $N$ as follows.  Let $\sigma_k(n)$ denote the sum of the divisors of $n$ excluding the top $k$ factors (or $0$, if the number of divisors $\tau(n)$ is at most $k$).  It is a standard calculation (factoring $n=dm$) that
$$ \sum_{n \leq x} \sigma(n) = \sum_{d \leq x} d \sum_{m \leq x/d} 1 \ll \sum_{d \leq x} x \ll x^2,$$
so $\sigma(n) = O(x)$ on the average.  Suppose that we can more generally show
$$ \sum_{n \leq x} \sigma_k(n) \ll x^2 / k^{1.1} \quad (1)$$
for all $k \geq 1$.  By Markov's inequality and the union bound, and the summability of $\sum_k 1/k^{1.1}$, we conclude that for any $C_0$, the number of $n \leq x$ such that $\sigma_k(n) \geq C_0 x$ for at least one $k$ is at most $O( x / C_0 )$, hence we have $f(N) \leq x$ for at most $O(x/C_0)$ of the $N \in [C_0 x, 2C_0 x]$, which is enough to disprove $f(N) = o(N)$ by taking $C_0$ large enough.

It remains to prove (1). In order for a factor $d$ of $n=dm$ to contribute to $\sigma_k(n)$, there must be at least $k$ factors of $dm$ that are at most $m$, so either $\tau(m) \gg k^{0.1}$ or $d$ has $\gg k^{0.9}$ factors of size at most $m$.  The contribution of the first case is at most
$$ \sum_{m \leq x} (\tau(m)/k^{0.1})^{100} \sum_{d \leq x/m} d \ll \frac{x^2}{k^{10}} \sum_m \frac{\tau(m)^{100}}{m^2} \ll \frac{x^2}{k^{10}}$$
which is acceptable (one could also have used the divisor bound $\tau(m) = m^{o(1)}$ here).  The contribution of the second case is at most
$$ \sum_{m \leq x} \sum_{d \leq x/m} d (\sum_{r \leq m: r|d} 1 / k^{0.9})^2$$
$$ \ll \sum_{m } \sum_{r_1,r_2 \leq m} \frac{x^2}{m^2 [r_1,r_2] k^{1.8}}$$
$$ \ll \sum_{m } \sum_{r_1,r_2} \frac{x^2}{m^{1.8} [r_1,r_2]^{1.1} k^{1.8}}$$
$$ \ll \frac{x^2}{k^{1.8}}$$
which is also acceptable (there is a lot of room to spare here ultimately coming from the fact that divisor functions are typically logarithmic in size, so presumably one could clean up this argument somehow; in particular, standard anatomy of integers heuristics predicts that (1) should in fact exhibit exponential decay in $k$).

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
That was so simple!
The following is a trivial remark, but the claim that you prove:\[ \#\{N\in[C_0 x,\infty) : f(N)\leq x\} \ll \frac{x}{C_0}, \]also disproves any kind of statement $f(N)=o(N)$ for "almost all" $N$.
Moreover, an immediate consequence is\[ \frac{\#\{N\in[1,X] : f(N)/N\leq \delta\}}{X} \ll \delta^2, \]which is perfectly in line with the above experimental results, like less than $6\%$ of the ratios $f(N)/N$ being less than $1/2$. Nice!
Perhaps the only meaningful quantitative improvement would be to show that this quotient is $o(\delta^2)$, which seems to be achievable as well, but I need to think about it.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I think an estimation of second moments such as $\sum_{n \leq x} \sigma_k^2(n)$ might suffice to get the improved bound; the computations get messy, but on the other hand there is a lot of room and one can do rather crude estimations here.  My intuition here is that it is only the really powerful numbers $n$ that can cause unusually small values of $f(N)/N$, and such numbers are asymptotically quite rare.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
Makes sense.
Also, now when I think about your proof, I am slightly confused why you even need to consider $\sigma_k$ (and sum the bounds in $k$) and not just use the trivial bound $\sum_{n\leq x}\sigma(n)\ll x^2$ (on the largest quantity dominating all $\sigma_k$).
Edit: Nevermind this. For a moment I forgot what the problem was about. :-)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
We need to sum in $k$, which is in principle unbounded (in particular, it can be large compared to $C_0$), because the definition of $f(N)$ does not specify $k$ in advance.

More precisely, one has $f(N) = \inf_k f_k(N)$, where $f_k(N)$ is the least $n$ for which $\sigma_k(n)=N$ (or $\infty$ if no such $n$ exists).  The "trivial" bound controls each individual event $f_k(N) \leq x$, but the event $f(N) \leq x$ is the union of all such events and so one needs to sum in $k$ if one wishes to use the union bound.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
I thought I'd share some experimental data on this problem. I don't have any other ambitions with it. In fact, these sums of divisors behave so erratically that I'll be amazed if someone can prove anything nontrivial rigorously and unconditionally.

I entered the sizes of sets $D'_n:=D_n\setminus\cup_{m<n}D_m$ as OEIS sequence [A387502](https://oeis.org/A387502). It is unclear what Erdős and Graham wanted to know about these numbers. There are many zeros in the sequence, i.e., many empty sets $D'_n$ (also see below), which can be conditionally deduced from (certain special cases of Schinzel's hypothesis), say, having infinitely primes $r$ of the form $r=pq+p+q$, $p<q$ primes, since then $D'_r=\emptyset$. On the other hand, the sets $D'_n$ can likely become arbitrarily large: the largest one I could find is $D'_{75600}$ of cardinality $24$. The very likely candidates are the numbers $n$ with large $\sigma(n)$. In reality, the record values of the cardinalities of $D'_n$ are attained for $n=2, 12, 36, 144, 336, 1320, 1980, 5040, 8400, 25200, 75600$.

I also entered sizes of the unions $\cup_{m\leq n}D_m=\cup_{m\leq n}D'_m$ as OEIS sequence [A387503](https://oeis.org/A387503). From it one can see that the first $1000$ sets $D'_n$ have average size $0.924$, the first $10000$ have average size $0.8697$, and I also computed that the first $100000$ sets $D'_n$ have average size $0.8349$. This should also hint again that a positive share of the sets $D'_n$ are empty.

Regarding the behavior of the function $f$, the same problem is also mentioned in the [book by Guy](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0) and attributed to Erdős. There is a slight difference in the book: that the number $1$ is always counted in as the smallest divisor, but effectively this makes no difference, and the function $f$ only gets shifted by $1$. It seems that Guy's book was a better-known reference, since the values of $f$ already appear as OEIS sequence [A167485](https://oeis.org/A167485) (but again, note the indices shifted by $1$). Function $f$ is clearly undefined for $n=1,4$ (as the two smallest divisors $>1$ cannot add up to $1$ or $4$), and I'm not sure if it is known to be well-defined for all other $n$ (but experimentally it seems so). OEIS mentions this following from a certain stronger version of Goldbach's conjecture, but it would also follow from versions of Vingradov's theorem. For instance if sufficiently (but concretely) large odd $N$ are sums of distinct primes $p,q,r\in[x,x^2]$, then $N$ appears in the set $D_{pqr}$, which makes $f(N)$ finite (i.e., well-defined).

The claim $f(N)=o(N)$ seems experimentally unlikely. In fact, $31.279\%$ of the numbers $N\leq100000$ even have $f(N)>100000$. Similarly, only less than $36\%$ of the ratios $f(N)/N$, for $5\leq N\leq10000$, are $\leq1$, only less than $27\%$ of them are $\leq0.9$, and only less than $6\%$ of them are $\leq0.5$: quite unlikely if one had $f(N)/N\to0$. A very easy observation (mentioned in the OEIS comments) is that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sigma(n)/n=\infty$ by taking $N=\sigma(n)-1$ implies $\liminf_{N\to\infty}f(N)/N=0$, so at least this is an unconditional but rather trivial result.

### Problem
Let $A$ be the set of all $n$ such that $n=d_1+\cdots+d_k$ with $d_i$ distinct proper divisors of $n$, but this is not true for any $m\mid n$ with $m<n$. Does\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\]converge?

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #470 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/470).

### Problem
Call $n$ [weird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weird_number) if $\sigma(n)\geq 2n$ and $n$ is not pseudoperfect, that is, it is not the sum of any set of its divisors.

Are there any odd weird numbers? Are there infinitely many primitive weird numbers, i.e. those such that no proper divisor of $n$ is weird?

### Context
Weird numbers were investigated by Benkoski and Erdős [BeEr74], who proved that the set of weird numbers has positive density. The smallest weird number is $70$.

Melfi [Me15] has proved that there are infinitely many primitive weird numbers, conditional on the fact that $p_{n+1}-p_n<\frac{1}{10}p_n^{1/2}$ for all large $n$, which in turn would follow from well-known conjectures concerning prime gaps.

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #472 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/472).

### Problem
Given some initial finite sequence of primes $q_1<\cdots<q_m$ extend it so that $q_{n+1}$ is the smallest prime of the form $q_n+q_i-1$ for $n\geq m$. Is there an initial starting sequence so that the resulting sequence is infinite?

### Context
A problem due to Ulam. For example if we begin with $3,5$ then the sequence continues $3,5,7,11,13,17,\ldots$. It is possible that this sequence is infinite.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
That sequence should work indeed.
Heuristically reasons:
$q_n+q_i-1$ is odd, and residues are not fixed modulo an odd prime.
The probability that a number of the order $x$ is prime is roughly $1/ \log x$.
Thus on average $q_{n+1}=q_n+\log(q_n)^{2+o(1)}$ and the expectation of failing should be small (we estimate $q_n=n^{1+o(1)}$ and probability of failing $(1-1/\log q_n)^n=exp(-n^{1-o(1)})$.
An easy check shows that the list continues at least a million steps, and $\sum_{n=10^6}^{\infty} \exp(-n^{1-o(1)})$ will be very small.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #474 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/474).

### Problem
Under what set theoretic assumptions is it true that $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be $3$-coloured such that, for every uncountable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$, $A^2$ contains a pair of each colour?

### Context
A problem of Erdős from 1954. In other words, when is it the case that\[2^{\aleph_0}\not\to [\aleph_1]_3^2?\]Sierpinski and Kurepa independently proved that this is true for $2$-colours. Erdős proved that this is true under the [continuum hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuum_hypothesis) that $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1$, and offered \$100 for deciding what happens if the continuum hypothesis is not assumed.

Shelah [Sh88] proved, on the other hand, that it is consistent without the continuum hypothesis that\[2^{\aleph_0}\to [\aleph_1]_3^2,\]although with a very large value of $\mathfrak{c}$. It remains open whether it is consistent to have a negative answer assuming $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$. (This specific question is asked in [Va99].)

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #475 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/475).

### Problem
Let $p$ be a prime. Given any finite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p\backslash \{0\}$, is there always a rearrangement $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_t\}$ such that all partial sums $\sum_{1\leq k\leq m}a_{k}$ are distinct, for all $1\leq m\leq t$?

### Context
A problem of Graham, who proved it when $t=p-1$. A similar conjecture was made for arbitrary abelian groups by Alspach. Such an ordering is often called a valid ordering.

This has been proved for $t\leq 12$ (see Costa and Pellegrini [CoPe20] and the references therein) and for $p-3\leq t\leq p-1$ (see Hicks, Ollis, and Schmitt [HOS19] and the references therein).

### Deliverable

This has been proved for $t\leq 12$ (see Costa and Pellegrini [CoPe20] and the references therein) and for $p-3\leq t\leq p-1$ (see Hicks, Ollis, and Schmitt [HOS19] and the references therein).

replies.contentMd:
To clarify, the current solution of Graham's conjecture (for sufficiently large $p$) is divided across 4 papers, and all 4 are required to cover the full range of subsets $S\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$. The small $S$ case is covered in [BeKr24], the medium $S$ case (between $\omega(1)$ and $p^{1-o(1)}$) is covered [PhSa25], the dense case (up until $|S|\leq (1-o(1)p$)) is in [BBKMM25], and the remaining ultra-dense case is in [MuPo25] (but this was only made explicit in [BBKMM25]). The techniques in all 4 regimes are fairly different.

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
AlphaProof found a counterexample to the previous formulation of this problem.This was an formal version, which can be summarised as follows:

1. Pick $f = X^2 - X + 1$
2. Now $A$ can't be finite.
3. If $A$ is infinite there are two elements $a, b$ which differ by a positive multiple of $4$ (say $a = b + 4x$)
4. Now consider the pairs $(a, f(2x))$ and $(b, f(2x + 1))$. The point being that $f(2x + 1) - f(2x) = 4x$, so these give two representations of the same number.

This proof can be generalised to all polynomials of degree $2$ of the form $ax^2 + bx + c$ where $a | b$ and $b ≠ 0$.

Formalised statement and proof (cleaned up and generalised from the AlphaProof proof) see here:
https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/24a4308a38b97e3e5b7da6ccff57157de432a1c1/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/477.lean#L44

 So this gives an infinite family of degree $2$ polynomials for which no such $A$ exists.

[ErGr80] mentions

[Sek59](http://dml.cz/dmlcz/100376) Milan Sekanina, Замечания к фактoризации беcкoнечнoй цикличеcкoй группы, Czechoslovak Mathematical Journal, Vol. 9 (1959), No. 4, 485–495

and if I understand correctly the $X^2$ counterexample is also mentioned on page 490 there. And then the question is asked for other monomials $X^k$ for $k\ge3$.

We added those variants to formal-conjectures: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/1510/

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
This can be generalised even when $b=0$. It suffices to show that for any monic quadratic polynomial $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$, there exists an integer $n$ such that for all integers $k$, there is $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $f(x)-f(y)=kn$. That is, all multiples of $n$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$. This is because any set $A$ must be infinite, and so $A-A$ must contain some multiple of $n$.

Let $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ with $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$. Note that if all multiples of $n$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$, then for any $d\in\mathbb{Z}$, all multiples of $n$ are in the difference set of $f(x)+d$.

It has been shown that $x^2$ and $x^2-x+1$ each have difference sets that contain all multiples of $4$. The same then holds true for $(x+k)^2$ and $(x+k)^2-(x+k)+1$ for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. As $(x+k)^2=x^2+2kx+k^2$ and $(x+k)^2-(x+k)+1=x^2+(2k-1)x+k^2-k+1$, we have covered $x^2+bx+c$ for any $b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$ (that is, the difference set of any polynomial of this form contains all multiples of $4$).

Then, for any $a\in\mathbb{Q}$ and monic quadratic $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ such that $a\times f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$, all multiples of $4a$ are in the difference set of $a\times f(x)$. Therefore any polynomial of the form $ax^2+bx+c$ where $a|b$ contains all multiples of $4a$ in its difference set.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
This can actually be generalised for all quadratic polynomials $f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}$. Consider $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$. Then the difference set of $f(x)$ contains all terms of the form $$f(x+2l)-f(x)=(4ax+4al+2b)l.$$ As $x$ can be any integer, this is all terms of the form $$4al^2+2bl\mod 4al\equiv 2bl\mod 4al.$$ As we can vary $l$ to be any integer, the family of congruences $\{2bl\mod 4al\mid l\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ covers all multiples of $4a+2b$ (if $b\neq 0$, we can take multiples of $2b$).

EDIT: A simpler way to see this is to take $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ with $b\neq0$ and consider $f(k)-f(-k)=2bk$ for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. So all multiples of $2b$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$.

 If $b=0$ then $f(x+1)-f(x-1)=4ax$, so all multiples of $4a$ are in the difference set of $f(x)$.

Then for any infinite $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$, there must be some multiple of $2b$ and some multiple of $4a$ in $A-A$.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
Take $f(x) =x^2$. Then for any $a, b\in A$ and integers $m, n$, we want to avoid $a-b=m^2-n^2$ unless $a=b$. All odd numbers $>1$ and multiples of 4 can be expressed as a difference of two positive squares. So $A-A$ can only contain terms that are $2\mod 4$ or $0, 1$.

 Then letting $|A|\geq 5 $, there must be and $a, b, c, d, e\in A$ such that $a<b<c<d<e$. Then no two of $a, c, e$ have difference $1$ or $0$. So we must have $a-b\equiv b-c\equiv a-c \equiv 2\mod 4$. But $$a-c=(a-b) +(b-c) \equiv 2+2\equiv 0\mod 4. $$
So $|A|\leq 4$, but this is clearly not enough to represent all integers.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
The claim is also trivially false for any $f$ that is non-injective on the natural numbers, such as $f(x) = (x-1)^2$.  (EDIT: I see the formalized statement in Lean avoids this loophole by enumerating using $(a,f(n))$ rather than $(a,n)$.) In order to avoid such trivialities, I would imagine the question should be interpreted in the sense indicated in the remarks, that no $A$ exists for any $f$.

EDIT: On checking [[ErGr80, p 95-96](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf)] it appears that (a) one is indeed enumerating $(a,f(n))$ rather than $(a,n)$, and (b) the problem should be understood in the strong sense that no such $A$ exists for any polynomial $f$ of degree at least two.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd: I see. It seems likely that a similar argument would work for quadratics generally, as their difference set is the union of infinitely many arithmetic progressions, but would be harder for higher degree polynomials.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Yes, agreed - I'll rephrase the problem statement to make this clearer.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd: One could also ask this question about representations of the form $a + f(n)$ where $n$ is allowed to be any integer (as opposed to just a positive integer).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #478 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/478).

### Problem
Let $p$ be a prime and\[A_p = \{ k! \pmod{p} : 1\leq k<p\}.\]Is it true that\[\lvert A_p\rvert \sim (1-\tfrac{1}{e})p?\]

### Context
Since $A_p/A_p=\{1,\ldots,p-1\}$ it follows that $\lvert A_p\rvert \gg p^{1/2}$. The best known lower bound is due to Grebennikov, Sagdeev, Semchankau, and Vasilevskii [GSSV24],\[\lvert A_p\rvert \geq (\sqrt{2}-o(1))p^{1/2},\]which follows from proving that $\lvert A_pA_p\rvert=(1+o(1))p$.

Wilson's theorem implies $(p-2)!\equiv 1\pmod{p}$, and hence $\lvert A_p\rvert\leq p-2$. It is open whether even $\lvert A_p\rvert<p-2$. This has been verified for all primes $p<10^9$ (see [GSSV24]). Results on $\lvert A_p\rvert$ on average were obtained by Klurman and Munsch [KlMu17].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #479 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/479).

### Problem
Is it true that, for all $k\neq 1$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $2^n\equiv k\pmod{n}$?

### Context
A conjecture of Graham. It is easy to see that $2^n\not\equiv 1\mod{n}$ for all $n>1$, so the restriction $k\neq 1$ is necessary. Erdős and Graham report that Graham, Lehmer, and Lehmer have proved this for $k=2^i$ for $i\geq 1$, or if $k=-1$, but I cannot find such a paper. Tang has written a short [note](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/Erdos-Problem-479-Note/blob/main/A_note_on_Erdos_Problem_479.pdf) giving a proof for this case.

As an indication of the difficulty, when $k=3$ the smallest $n$ such that $2^n\equiv 3\pmod{n}$ is $n=4700063497$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

This website states that “Erdős and Graham report that Graham, Lehmer, and Lehmer have proved this for $k = 2^i$ for $i \ge 1$, or if $k = -1$, but I cannot find such a paper.” I have also tried to locate this manuscript, but without success.

Fortunately, I have just written a short [note](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/Erdos-Problem-479-Note/blob/main/A_note_on_Erdos_Problem_479.pdf) in which I give a complete proof of the case $k = 2^i$ for all $i \ge 1$, and survey the existing results for the set\[
A(k) := \{ n \ge 1 : 2^n \equiv k \pmod n \},
\]recording all integers $k$ for which $A(k)$ is currently known to be infinite. In short, this problem remains open for every fixed $k$ other than\[k \in \{0,-1,-2, 2^i : i \ge 1\}.\]This [note](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/Erdos-Problem-479-Note/blob/main/A_note_on_Erdos_Problem_479.pdf) is available on my GitHub page ([here](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/Erdos-Problem-479-Note/blob/main/A_note_on_Erdos_Problem_479.pdf)).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #483 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/483).

### Problem
Let $f(k)$ be the minimal $N$ such that if $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is $k$-coloured then there is a monochromatic solution to $a+b=c$. Estimate $f(k)$. In particular, is it true that $f(k) < c^k$ for some constant $c>0$?

### Context
The values of $f(k)$ are known as Schur numbers. The best-known bounds for large $k$ are\[(380)^{k/5}-O(1)\leq f(k) \leq \lfloor(e-\tfrac{1}{24}) k!\rfloor-1.\]The lower bound is due to Ageron, Casteras, Pellerin, Portella, Rimmel, and Tomasik [ACPPRT21] (improving previous bounds of Exoo [Ex94] and Fredricksen and Sweet [FrSw00]) and the upper bound is due to Whitehead [Wh73]. Note that $380^{1/5}\approx 3.2806$.

The known values of $f$ are $f(1)=2$, $f(2)=5$, $f(3)=14$, $f(4)=45$, and $f(5)=161$ (see [A030126](https://oeis.org/A030126)). (The equality $f(5)=161$ was established by Heule [He17]).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Wan (1997) proved [$R(3;k)\leq \tfrac{e−e^{-1}+3}{2}\cdot k!+1$, and](https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0118(199711)26:3<119::AID-JGT1>3.0.CO;2-U)[Xu Xiaodong, Xie Zheng and Chen Zhi (2002)](https://caod.oriprobe.com/articles/4335071/UPPER_BOUNDS_FOR_RAMSEY_NUMBERS_Rn__3__AND_SCHUR_N.htm) improved this to $R(3;k) \leq (e−\tfrac{1}{6})\cdot k!+1$. problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #486 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/486).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$, and for each $n\in A$ choose some $X_n\subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Let\[B = \{ m\in \mathbb{N} : m\not\in X_n\pmod{n}\textrm{ for all }n\in A\textrm{ with }m>n\}.\]Must $B$ have a logarithmic density, i.e. is it true that\[\lim_{x\to \infty} \frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{\substack{m\in B\\ m<x}}\frac{1}{m}\]exists?

### Context
Davenport and Erdős [DaEr36] proved that the answer is yes when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$. An alternative elementary proof was later given by Davenport and Erdős in [DaEr51].

The problem considers logarithmic density since Besicovitch [Be34] showed examples exist without a natural density, even when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
On inspection of [[Er61, p.236](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-22.pdf)] there is indeed an "activation threshold" condition ($b \geq a_i$ in (I.26.1) of that paper, or one should replace "$m \notin X_n \pmod{n}$" with "$m<n$ or $m \notin X_n \pmod{n}$" in the current formulation) that is currently absent, and as GPT-5.2 claims, without this condition one can easily create sparse congruence conditions that occasionally disrupt the logarithmic density and provide a cheap negative answer to the question as currently stated.

EDIT: As a side note, I am glad that the discussion of AI-generated solutions on this site is maturing from just focusing on whether an Erdos problem as literally stated on this web site was solved by the AI tool, to also addressing more holistic questions of whether the statement proven was actually in the spirit of what Erdos was intending, and what the natural variants of that statement are and how they connect with the rest of the literature. (In particular I hope we resist efforts to "benchmax" the number of solved problems on this site at the expense of understanding the broader context of these problems.)

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd: Some not so very deep thoughts: first, if this is true for a collection of sets $X_n$, then it is also true for the collection of their complements. Second, for finite sets $A = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}$, this reduces to the case $|A| = 1$ with the single element in $A$ taken to be the least common multiple of the $a_i$. In this case $B$ even has a natural density. Third, since it is known for $X_n = \{0\}$, it is also true for $X_n = \{c\}$ for any $c \in \mathbb{N}$. Finally, the logical next step would be to consider what happens if $|X_n| = 1$ for all $n$ and $X_n \subset X$ for some finite set $X$. Perhaps this isn't too difficult either.

### Problem

In [Er61] this problem is as stated above, but with $a\mid n$ in the definition of $B$ replaced by $a\nmid n$. This is most likely a typo (especially since the problem is also given as stated above in [Er66]). There have been several counterexamples given for this alternate problem. Cambie has observed that, if $A$ is the set of primes bounded above by $n$, and $m=2n$, then\frac{\lvert B\cap [1,m]\rvert }{m}=\frac{\pi(2n)-\pi(n)+1}{2n}\sim \frac{1}{2\log n}while\frac{\lvert B\cap [1,n]\rvert}{n}=\frac{1}{n}.Further concrete counterexamples, found by Alexeev and Aristotle, are given in the comments section.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The commentary gives an example where $A$ is a singleton of size around $n/2$, and the ratio is close to 2.  There is a somewhat different example where $A$ now consists of numbers much smaller than $n$, and the ratio is about 1.03; nowhere near a counterexample, but still uniformly bounded away from 1, and indicative of the complexity of the problem.

The counterexample comes from taking $A$ to be the primes between $n^{1/3}$ and $n^{1/2}$, and $m$ to be extremely large compared to $n$.  The density at $m$ is then about $1 - \prod_{n^{1/3} < p < n^{1/2}} (1-\frac{1}{p})$, which by Mertens' theorem is about $1/3 = 0.333\dots$.  The density at $n$ can be computed by inclusion-exclusion to be about $\sum_{n^{1/3} < p < n^{1/2}} 1/p - \sum_{n^{1/3} < p_1 < p_2 < n^{1/2}} 1/p_1 p_2$ which computes to $\log(3/2) - \frac{1}{2} \log^2(3/2) = 0.32326413$.  The ratio here is $1.03114853\dots$.

Some tweaking of this type of example seems to permit a slightly larger ratio than this, but it doesn't look like it gets close to 2.  Proving this concretely looks tricky though.   In the spirit of [this paper of Granville-Soundararajan](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0308009), the main task involves proving an inequality involving alternating sums of various integrals, which looks somewhat complicated.

replies.author: MalekZ
replies.contentMd:
Your example with primes between \(n^{1/3}\) and \(n^{1/2}\) lines up well with what I see in a systematic computational search. Across 6,207 primitive pairs \((a,b,T)\) with \(F(s) \geq 5\), the peak density ratio \(\sup_{m>s} \frac{F(m)/m}{\delta}\) falls in the range \([1.035, 1.373]\), with the highest values coming from systems where the tail \(T\) contains many small primes consistent with your construction. Over 1.15 million per-residue checks found zero violations of the split inequality.

On the structural side, I found an exact identity that may be relevant. Writing \(Q_\ell, Q_a, Q_b\) for the quotient-tail families, the Möbius subtraction \(F(n) = A_{Q_a}(\lfloor n/a\rfloor) + A_{Q_b}(\lfloor n/b\rfloor) - A_{Q_\ell}(\lfloor n/\ell\rfloor)\) rewrites as a sum of three non-negative counting functions:\[F(n) = A_{Q_\ell}(w) + A_{\min(Q_a \cup \{A\})}(u) + A_{\min(Q_b \cup \{B\})}(v)\]where \(A = \ell/a\), \(B = \ell/b\), and \(w, u, v\) are the respective quotients. (Verified across 1,805 systems with zero failures.) This eliminates the cancellation that makes the original three-term formula hard to bound.

Combined with a bridge lemma splitting active vs. inactive moduli, this reduces the full inequality to bounding the positive oscillation \(W^+_{Q_{\leq y}}/y\) of the active sieve at the ratio peak. Computationally this holds across 2,648 systems with 69%+ margins, but proving it is exactly where things get stuck, 13 natural approaches have been killed with explicit counterexamples.

The full reduction chain with verification code is written up; happy to share if useful. Would be very curious whether the alternating integral framework you mention could handle the non-multiplicative case that arises here.

replies.author: MalekZ
replies.contentMd:
Progress on Conjecture 4.8 (pair-tail split doubling) and a specific remaining gap

Hi Mr. Chojecki,

I've been working on the pair-tail split doubling conjecture (Conjecture 4.8 in your paper) using the quotient-tail framework from your Section 8, and I've made significant progress but hit a specific wall. I wanted to share what I have and ask whether you see a path through the remaining gap.

What I've proved

Starting from the quotient-tail decomposition
$$F_{a,b\mid T}(x) = A_{Q_a}\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{x}{a}\right\rfloor\right) + A_{Q_b}\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{x}{b}\right\rfloor\right) - A_{Q_\ell}\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{x}{\ell}\right\rfloor\right),$$
I built a reduction chain:

1. Exact periodicity. $F(n) = \delta n + c_{n \bmod P}$ with $\delta_{a,b\mid T} = \frac{\delta(Q_a)}{a} + \frac{\delta(Q_b)}{b} - \frac{\delta(Q_\ell)}{\ell} > 0$.

2. Visible-slab reduction. The finite-window split inequality reduces to checks (V1), (V2), (V3) on the base visible slab $S_{\mathrm{vis}} = [N_0, \min(N_1, P-1)] \cap \mathbb{Z}$.

3. Low-$F$ elimination. All visible-slab residues with $F(s) = 2$ or $F(s) = 3$ are automatically harmless (the threshold $2F(s)/s > 1/a + 1/b$ suffices). $F(s) = 4$ reduces to an explicit exceptional family, which I closed completely — including the sub-exceptional scaling family $(48k, 54k, \{64k, 72k, 81k\})$ via a scaling law: the quotient tails $\hat{Q}_{48k} = \hat{Q}_{54k} = \{3,4\}$ are $k$-independent, so $F_k(qk+t) = F_1(q)$, collapsing the infinite family to a finite base computation on 5103 residues.

4. Window-bound theorem. For any window length $L$, $F(n) - F(n-L) \leq c(L)$ with $c(L)/L \to \delta$. This gives an inductive propagation principle that eliminates envelope comparisons beyond the visible slab.

So the split inequality holds for all pair-tail systems where every visible-slab residue has $F(s) \leq 4$, plus the specific exceptional families at $F = 4$.

The remaining gap: $F(s) \geq 5$ on the visible slab

The endgame reduces to: for every visible-slab $s$ with $F(s) \geq 5$ and every $m > s$, prove
$$\frac{F(m)}{m} < \frac{2F(s)}{s}.$$

I've verified this computationally across tens of thousands of systems with zero counterexamples. The margins are consistently 30–50% of the slab ratio.

What I've tried and what fails:

- Universal bound $F(m)/m \leq \delta + W^+/m$ combined with $2F(s)/s \geq 10/s$: closes 98.6% of systems but fails when $3W^+ + |W^-| \geq 10$.

- Per-residue bound $W^+ < 2F(s) - \delta s$: false. Counterexample at $(11, 15 \mid \{28, 31\})$, $s = 43$.

- Combinatorial charging ($\Delta_a + \Delta_b \geq 2\Delta_\ell + 1$): the strong form is false.

- Two-route via Proposition 5.1: killed by $G = $ first 14 primes at $n = 198$.

The split inequality holds in every case, but every bound overshoots because the global $W^+$ is achieved at a different residue than the ratio peak $\sup_m F(m)/m$.

The structural picture

The inequality appears to be "soft" — it holds because the factor of 2 creates a multiplicative buffer that the periodic corrections cannot fully consume. At the ratio-maximizing $m^*$, the correction $c_{m^*}$ is always much less than $W^+$ (typically $c_{m^*}/W^+ \approx 0.3$–$0.5$). But I cannot prove this universally.

Questions

1. Do you see a way to prove $F(m)/m < 2F(s)/s$ for $F(s) \geq 5$ using the quotient-tail structure? Perhaps through the cluster expansion / Janson bound machinery from your Section 8?

2. Is there a known technique for bounding $c_m/m$ (the ratio peak of periodic corrections) rather than $W^+/m$?

3. Do you think Conjecture 4.8 is provable by this route, or does it require a fundamentally different approach for large tails?

Happy to share the full proof chain, computational code, and counterexamples to the failed bounds.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
[Note: this comment was written before 2025/12/01, when the problem text was updated.]

I agree that the problem in [Er61,p.236] is correctly transcribed here.  However, consider the full context:
"Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \le n$ be any sequence of integers, $b_1 < b_2 < \cdots$ the integers no one of which is a multiple of any $a$. $B(x) = \sum_{b_i\le x} 1$. Is it true that for every $m > n$
$\frac{B(m)}{m} < 2 \frac{B(n)}{n}?$
It is easy to see that in [that equation] $2$ can not be replaced by any smaller constant, to see this let the $a$'s consist of $a_1$, $n = 2 a_1 - 1$, $m = 2 a_1$."

The example at the end doesn't make sense for this problem.  However, it makes perfect sense for the problem where the $b_i$s actually consist of the *multiples* of elements in A, not the non-multiples.  Morever, that version has no small counterexamples.  Indeed, for small $n$ and $m$, the limiting extremal examples are precisely the ones Erdős describes with $n=2a_1-1 < 2a_1 = m$.

In summary, I think a new problem should be added (if it's not present already! -- I couldn't find it) where non-multiples is changed to multiples!

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
Assuming the following inequality holds, this version of the problem is straightforward.

For $A=\{a_1<\ldots<a_k\}\subset \mathbb{N}$ and an integer $n\geq a_k$, assume we have $$\sum_{\emptyset\neq I=\{a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r}\}\subseteq A} (-1)^{r+1}\big\lfloor\frac{n}{lcm(a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r})}\big\rfloor\geq -1+ \sum_{\emptyset\neq I=\{a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r}\}\subseteq A}(-1)^{r+1} \frac{n}{lcm(a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r})}.$$

Then by the IEP, $B(n):=|B\cap[1,n]|=\sum_{\emptyset\neq I=\{a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r}\}\subseteq A} (-1)^{r+1}\big\lfloor\frac{n}{lcm(a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r})}\big\rfloor$ so for $m>n\geq a_k$, $$\frac{B(n)}{n}= \sum_{\emptyset\neq I=\{a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r}\}\subseteq A} \frac{(-1)^{r+1}}{n}\big\lfloor\frac{n}{lcm(a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r})}\big\rfloor \geq \frac{-1}{n}+ \sum_{\emptyset\neq I=\{a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r}\}\subseteq A}(-1)^{r+1} \frac{1}{lcm(a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r})}$$

$$\geq \frac{-1}{n}+\sum_{\emptyset\neq I=\frac{-1}{n}+\{a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r}\}\subseteq A} \frac{(-1)^{r+1}}{m}\big\lfloor\frac{m}{lcm(a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_r})}\big\rfloor=\frac{-1}{n}+\frac{B(m)}{m}.$$

So $\frac{B(n)+1}{n}\geq \frac{B(m)}{m}$, and if $B(n)>1$, then $\frac{2B(n)}{n}>\frac{B(n)+1}{n}\geq \frac{B(m)}{m}$.

When  $B(n)=1$, we have $A=\{a\}$ and $a\leq n<2a$. It is clear that $\frac{2B(n)}{n}=\frac{2}{n}>\frac{1}{a}$ and that for any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $ka\leq m<(k+1)a$, we have $\frac{B(m)}{m}=\frac{k}{m}\leq \frac{1}{a}$. So $\frac{2B(n)}{n}>\frac{B(m)}{m}$.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Regarding "the following inequality", the difference is actually rather big.

Take $A=\{x+1,x+2, \ldots, x+k\}$ and $n=2x$.
Then for $x$ sufficiently large. We have $LHS=k$ and $RHS=-1+2k-o(1)$.

Also the cardinalities of $B \cap [1,n]$ and $B \cap [k+1,k+n]$ can differ by more than $\lvert A \rvert$. So it is not an easy problem in general (for $\lvert A \rvert$ small it indeed is)

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
"Also the cardinalities of $B\cap [1,n]$ and $B\cap [k+1,k+n]$ can differ by more than |A|."

Is that for the example of $A$ that you gave, with $k=|A|$? Then they would differ by about $|A|/2$.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
No, for another example (or $k,n$ are used multiple times).
The translation can be with a huge difference.

E.g. for a set $A=\{a,b,c\}$ of size $3$, one can translate such that the number of multiples of $a,b,c$ and $abc$ is one larger, while the number of multiples of $ab,ac,bc$ is the same (here $a,b,c$ are pairwise relative prime).

So that example was just to indicate that the problem is far from trivial.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
I agree that this was simply misstated and should be corrected. Some more evidence for this is that the question is also discussed in problem E5 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. And there it is correctly stated.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: Thomas Bloom
sourceComments.contentMd: I agree with everyone that this problem statement was just a typo, and it meant to ask for multiples rather than non-multiples. I will just correct the statement and note the non-multiple problem in the remarks; I don't think it warrants creating a separate problem, since it was likely never actually a question intended by Erdős.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
I agree that Erdős never intended the incorrect statement, and so one can imagine that as a collection of "ideal" Erdős problems (the volume on the shelf next to "The Book", which has all the solutions?), the incorrect statement doesn't belong here.  Nonetheless, I would like to (softly) present two alternate arguments.
First, we already have comments here and (importantly) material external to the site that address the problem as written.  For example, I posted a [Lean proof](https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos488.lean) on GitHub and of course there's the Formal Conjectures project as well as the community database.  (I also have existing personal communication and documents that reference the current problem.)
Second, Erdős did in fact write this problem down incorrectly in a paper.  This is not just a misformalization by someone else, but by Erdős himself -- in an immutable medium.
Perhaps both arguments are philosophically about what it means to be an "archival" resource.

(These arguments also apply to #124, but there's a difference of degree.  This problem was already labeled as solved a long time ago, and there's an accepted formal proof, etc.  I accept if your view differs and feel free to do what you think is right with both problems.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Both reasonable points. I never intended this site to be too strict an archival resource; rather something that begins with many inevitable errors and typos that slowly converges to be an accurate compilation of Erdős problems.

I do now avoid e.g. renumbering of problems, conscious that these have become a somewhat standardised way of referring to some problems, used by a number of other sites and papers.

In instances where there is an error in the problem statement that is then repeated in e.g. a formalised statement, but then pointed out here, I still think that the error should be corrected here (and then hopefully this correction can propagate through the ecosystem eventually), and a comment in this section can serve as an archival record of the changes made.

This is an interesting case though, since as you say technically Erdős did ask the question as written here - it's just he almost surely did not intend to! And I do want to be careful about speculating too much about what he was thinking, lest this site become more "my impression of Erdős" (inevitably very partial and flawed) rather than what Erdős himself said.

However, there are a number of precedents of multiple very similar questions forming a single problem on this site, which I think this falls under. So I think it might be most appropriate to list both versions in this problem, noting the likely typo - then external references to this problem still make sense.

Thoughts from others welcome!

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
For what it's worth, I agree with your proposed solution of correcting the problem statement (and changing it from disproved to open), and noting the other (presumed misstated) version as a comment below. By some coincidence I just found [this](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1966-20.pdf) 1966 paper in Hungarian, where Erdős (see page 150, or 16 of the pdf-file) also mentioned this problem! And lo and behold, here he does state the correct version.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
[Note: this comment was written before 2025/12/01, when the problem text was updated.]

The smallest counterexample appears to be
$A=\{2, 3, 5, 7\}$, $n=9$, and $m=13$,
which has $\lvert B\cap[1,n]\rvert=\lvert\{1\}\rvert=1$ and $\lvert B\cap[1,m]\rvert=\lvert\{1,11,13\}\rvert=3$,
but $\frac{3}{13} > 2\cdot\frac{1}{9}$.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
[Note: this comment was written before 2025/12/01, when the problem text was updated.]

This problem has a [formalized statement](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/488.lean) available at the Formal Conjectures project.

Aristotle from Harmonic found [its own counterexample](https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/ErdosProblems/Erdos488b.md) for this problem, provided only with that Lean statement! My understanding is that this was entirely by itself, without the information on this page.  [Type-check it online!](https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.24.0&url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fplby%2Flean-proofs%2Frefs%2Fheads%2Fmain%2Fsrc%2Fv4.24.0%2FErdosProblems%2FErdos488b.lean)

Its counterexample is $n=13$, $m=200$, and $A=\{2,3,5,7,11,13\}$.

Some comments:
1. I [still](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/488#post-1862) think Erdős mis-stated the conjecture accidentally, and the correct statement should be added as another problem.
2. Aristotle has shown that it can find mis-statements and counterexamples. (See also [here](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/56#post-1845).) It appears to be a useful tool to make sure you have stated your conjecture correctly, especially including necessary hypotheses and negations!
3. Of course, this would be more useful if it found a counterexample to a problem where a human hasn't already. Hopefully soon!

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.title: Erdos Problem #500: What is $\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)$? That is, the largest number of $3$-edges which can placed...
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #500 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/500).

### Problem
What is $\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)$? That is, the largest number of $3$-edges which can placed on $n$ vertices so that there exists no $K_4^3$, a set of 4 vertices which is covered by all 4 possible $3$-edges.

### Context
A problem of Turán. Turán observed that dividing the vertices into three equal parts $X_1,X_2,X_3$, and taking the edges to be those triples that either have exactly one vertex in each part or two vertices in $X_i$ and one vertex in $X_{i+1}$ (where $X_4=X_1$) shows that\[\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)\geq\left(\frac{5}{9}+o(1)\right)\binom{n}{3}.\]This is probably the truth. The current best upper bound is\[\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)\leq 0.5611666\binom{n}{3},\]due to Razborov [Ra10].

See also [[712]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/712) for the general case.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #501 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/501).

### Problem
For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ let $A_x\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded set with outer measure $<1$. Must there exist an infinite independent set, that is, some infinite $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $x\not\in A_y$ for all $x\neq y\in X$?

If the sets $A_x$ are closed and have measure $<1$, then must there exist an independent set of size $3$?

### Context
Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa60] proved the existence of arbitrarily large finite independent sets (under the assumptions in the first problem).

Gladysz [Gl62] proved the existence of an independent set of size $2$ under the assumptions of the second question.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: JakeMallen
sourceComments.contentMd:
According to the problem's description, I think the problem status should be updated.

1. [He72] showed that the answer to the first question is no, assuming CH. Therefore this question should get the NOT PROVABLE status.

2. [NPS87] proved that if the sets $A_x$ are closed, there exists an infinite independent set (Corollary 1). This strictly satisfies the requirement for a set of size 3, so this question should get the PROVED status.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: When the problem has multiple components, I am taking the status of the joint problem to be the intersection of the statuses of the components (i.e., the strongest status that applies to all components).  Unfortunately, the intersection of NOT PROVABLE and PROVED is still OPEN.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Thanks, I had misread the result of [NPS87], so didn't realise their result proved the second question.

The only remaining question is really whether the first question is provable/true without the continuum hypothesis. Whether or not  Hechler's result answers the spirit of the question is delicate I think, and best answered by an expert in the area.

The paper "The Erdős-Hajnal problem list" by Péter Komjáth ([available online](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/erdoshajnal-problem-list/9FBE6099BE9441516445D0B95F4B1208)) includes this as Problem 38.

The first problem here is part (C) and the theorem of (Newelski–Pawlikowski–Seredyński is stated there.

problems.title: Erdos Problem #503: What is the size of the largest $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ such that every three points from...
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #503 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/503).

### Problem
What is the size of the largest $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ such that every three points from $A$ determine an isosceles triangle? That is, for any three points $x,y,z$ from $A$, at least two of the distances $\lvert x-y\rvert,\lvert y-z\rvert,\lvert x-z\rvert$ are equal.

### Context
When $d=2$ the answer is $6$ (due to Kelly [ErKe47] - an alternative proof is given by Kovács [Ko24c]). When $d=3$ the answer is $8$ (due to Croft [Cr62]). The best upper bound known in general is due to Blokhuis [Bl84] who showed that\[\lvert A\rvert \leq \binom{d+2}{2}.\]Alweiss has observed a lower bound of $\binom{d+1}{2}$ follows from considering the subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ formed of all vectors $e_i+e_j$ where $e_i,e_j$ are distinct coordinate vectors. This set can be viewed as a subset of some $\mathbb{R}^d$, and is easily checked to have the required property.

Weisenberg observed in the comments that an additional point can be added to Alweiss' construction, giving a lower bound of $\binom{d+1}{2}+1$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: When $d=2$ the answer is $6$ (due to Kelly [ErKe47] - an alternative proof is given by Kovács [Ko24c]). When $d=3$ the answer is $8$ (due to Croft [Cr62]). The best upper bound known in general is due to Blokhuis [Bl84] who showed that\lvert A\rvert \leq \binom{d+2}{2}.Alweiss has observed a lower bound of $\binom{d+1}{2}$ follows from considering the subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ formed of all vectors $e_i+e_j$ where $e_i,e_j$ are distinct coordinate vectors. This set can be viewed as a subset of some $\mathbb{R}^d$, and is easily checked to have the required property.
Weisenberg observed in the comments that an additional point can be added to Alweiss' construction, giving a lower bound of $\binom{d+1}{2}+1$.
The fact that the truth for $d=3$ is $8$ suggests that neither of these bounds is the truth.
See also [[1088]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1088) for a generalisation.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
It's possible to improve Alweiss' construction by one; this can be done by adding the point whose coordinates are all $\frac{2}{n+1}$. This is on the same hyperplane, and it's obvious that every triangle with this point is isosceles. This yields a lower bound of $\binom{n+1}{2} + 1$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #507 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/507).

### Problem
Let $\alpha(n)$ be such that every set of $n$ points in the unit disk contains three points which determine a triangle of area at most $\alpha(n)$. Estimate $\alpha(n)$.

### Context
[Heilbronn's triangle problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilbronn_triangle_problem). It is trivial that $\alpha(n) \ll 1/n$. Erdős observed that $\alpha(n)\gg 1/n^2$. The current best bounds are\[\frac{\log n}{n^2}\ll \alpha(n) \ll \frac{1}{n^{7/6+o(1)}}.\]The lower bound is due to Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi [KPS82]. The upper bound is due to Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov [CPZ24] (improving on their earlier work [CPZ23] which itself improves an exponent of $8/7$ due to Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi [KPS81]).

This problem is Problem 77 on [Green's open problems list](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #508 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/508).

### Problem
What is the chromatic number of the plane? That is, what is the smallest number of colours required to colour $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that no two points of the same colour are distance $1$ apart?

### Context
The [Hadwiger-Nelson problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger%E2%80%93Nelson_problem). Let $\chi$ be the chromatic number of the plane. An equilateral triangle trivially shows that $\chi\geq 3$. There are several small graphs that show $\chi\geq 4$ (in particular the Moser spindle and Golomb graph). The best bounds currently known are\[5 \leq \chi \leq 7.\]The lower bound is due to de Grey [dG18]. The upper bound can be seen by colouring the plane by tesselating by hexagons with diameter slightly less than $1$.

Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga, and Zsámboki have proved that the fractional chromatic number of the plane is at least $4$. Croft [Cr67] has proved it is at most $4.359\cdots$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
In [Er75f,p.107], Erdős writes:

"Denote by $F(n)$ the smallest integer for which one can color the points of $n$-dimensional space by $F(n)$ colors so that two points of the same color never have distance $1$.
NELSON conjectured $F(2) = 4$. W. and L. MOSER proved $F(2)\ge 4$ and it is known that $F(2)\le 6$."

So, almost certainly this last equation $F(2)\le 6$ is an error and should have said $\le 7$.

... But what if it wasn't an error?

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #509 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/509).

### Problem
Let $f(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ be a monic non-constant polynomial. Can the set\[\{ z\in \mathbb{C} : \lvert f(z)\rvert \leq 1\}\]be covered by a set of circles the sum of whose radii is $\leq 2$?

### Context
Cartan proved this is true with $2$ replaced by $2e$, which was improved to $2.59$ by Pommerenke [Po61]. Pommerenke [Po59] proved that $2$ is achievable if the set is connected (see [[1046]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1046)).

The generalisation of this to higher dimensions was asked by Erdős as Problem 4.23 in [Ha74].

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #510 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/510).

### Problem
If $A\subset \mathbb{Z}$ is a finite set of size $N$ then is there some absolute constant $c>0$ and $\theta$ such that\[\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta) < -cN^{1/2}?\]

### Context
Chowla's cosine problem. Ruzsa [Ru04] (improving on an earlier result of Bourgain [Bo86]), proved an upper bound of\[-\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N})).\]Polynomial bounds were proved independently by Bedert [Be25c] and Jin, Milojević, Tomon, and Zhang [JMTZ25]. The best bound follows from the method of Bedert [Be25c], which proved the existence of some $c>0$ such that, for all $A$ of size $N$,\[\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta) < -cN^{1/7}.\]The example $A=B-B$, where $B$ is a Sidon set, shows that $N^{1/2}$ would be the best possible here.

This problem is Problem 81 on [Green's open problems list](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf).

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #513 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/513).

### Problem
Let $f=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n$ be a transcendental entire function. What is the greatest possible value of\[\liminf_{r\to \infty} \frac{\max_n\lvert a_nr^n\rvert}{\max_{\lvert z\rvert=r}\lvert f(z)\rvert}?\]

### Context
It is trivial that this value is in $[1/2,1)$. Kövári (unpublished) observed that it must be $>1/2$. Clunie and Hayman [ClHa64] showed that it is $\leq 2/\pi-c$ for some absolute constant $c>0$. Some other results on this quantity were established by Gray and Shah [GrSh63].

See also [[227]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/227).

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let$$
B:=\sup_f \ \liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{\max_n |a_n|\,r^n}{\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|}.
$$1. In addition to the upper bound $B<2/\pi$, [ClHa64] also proved the lower bound $B>4/7$.

2. This problem is also listed in [HaLi18] (see [arxiv link](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.07200), [springer link](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-25165-9)), where it is recorded that the best known bounds are$$
0.57143\approx \frac{4}{7} < B < \frac{2}{\pi}\approx 0.63662.
$$3. My friend He and I have just posted a paper ([arXiv:2602.12217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12217)) in which we generalize the function construction from [ClHa64] and obtain a stronger explicit lower bound$$B>0.58507.$$This work made exploratory use of ChatGPT-5.2 Pro, with all mathematical arguments subsequently checked by the human authors.

Reference.
[HaLi18] W. K. Hayman, E. F. Lingham, Research Problems in Function Theory: Fiftieth Anniversary Edition, Problem Books in Mathematics, Springer, Cham, 2019.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
I have run GPT in a near-autonomous process to try to improve the constant. Here is [the writeup](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wZnzui_eeBE32HnkrnSB7YhfcTOiYolp/view).

We did not really succeed. To summarize, the bound $B > 0.5850724$ in He-Tang is very slightly improved to $B > 0.5850788$ (both numbers rounded down to nearest). More ambitious improvements were attempted but they did not succeed.

I was debating with myself whether this should count as an improvement. But seeing the AlphaEvolve's precedents in [36] (also recorded [here](https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/1b.html)) and [1097] which are of similar scales, I believe it should count.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #517 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/517).

### Problem
Let $f(z)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_kz^{n_k}$ be an entire function (with $a_k\neq 0$ for all $k\geq 1$). Is it true that if $n_k/k\to \infty$ then $f(z)$ assumes every value infinitely often?
