problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #520 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/520).

### Problem
Let $f$ be a Rademacher multiplicative function: a random $\{-1,0,1\}$-valued multiplicative function, where for each prime $p$ we independently choose $f(p)\in \{-1,1\}$ uniformly at random, and for square-free integers $n$ we extend $f(p_1\cdots p_r)=f(p_1)\cdots f(p_r)$ (and $f(n)=0$ if $n$ is not squarefree). Does there exist some constant $c>0$ such that, almost surely,\[\limsup_{N\to \infty}\frac{\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)}{\sqrt{N\log\log N}}=c?\]

### Context
Note that if we drop the multiplicative assumption, and simply assign $f(m)=\pm 1$ at random, then this statement is true (with $c=\sqrt{2}$), the [law of the iterated logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_iterated_logarithm).

Wintner [Wi44] proved that, almost surely,\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2+o(1)},\]and Erdős improved the right-hand side to $N^{1/2}(\log N)^{O(1)}$. Lau, Tenenbaum, and Wu [LTW13] have shown that, almost surely,\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{2+o(1)}.\]Caich [Ca24b] has improved this to\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{3/4+o(1)}.\]Harper [Ha13] has shown that the sum is almost surely not $O(N^{1/2}/(\log\log N)^{5/2+o(1)})$, and conjectured that in fact Erdős' conjecture is false, and almost surely\[\sum_{m\leq N}f(m) \ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{1/4+o(1)}.\]

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #521 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/521).

### Problem
Let $(\epsilon_k)_{k\geq 0}$ be independently uniformly chosen at random from $\{-1,1\}$. If $R_n$ counts the number of real roots of $f_n(z)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n}\epsilon_k z^k$ then is it true that, almost surely,\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{R_n}{\log n}=\frac{2}{\pi}?\]

### Context
Erdős and Offord [EO56] showed that the number of real roots of a random degree $n$ polynomial with $\pm 1$ coefficients is $(\frac{2}{\pi}+o(1))\log n$.

It is ambiguous in [Er61] whether Erdős intended the coefficients to be uniformly chosen from $\{-1,1\}$ or $\{0,1\}$. In the latter case, the constant $\frac{2}{\pi}$ should be $\frac{1}{\pi}$ (see the discussion in the comments).

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Thomas Bloom
sourceComments.contentMd:
After looking again carefully at the problem in the original source, I think I have misunderstood the original question quite badly - in fact Erdős was most likely intending to ask whether, if $\epsilon_k\in \{-1,1\}$ is an infinite sequence chosen uniformly at random, and $R_n(f)$ counts the number of real roots of $\sum_{0\leq k\leq n}\epsilon_kz^k$, then\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{R_n(f)}{\frac{2}{\pi}\log n}=1.\]In other words, a more delicate version of the Erdős and Offord [EO56] result cited above.

I apologise for the inaccuracy - but this wrongly transcribed problem seems to have generated a lot of interesting discussion! I'm therefore minded to keep the problem as it's written here, but add the caveat that this is in fact *not* a problem of Erdős strictly speaking (at least, until someone can find a source asking about this one).

If I'm understanding the literature correctly, this corrected Erdős problem is the same as the question of Pritsker raised in the 2019 AIM workshop (perhaps unaware of Erdős' original question).

Furthermore, this corrected problem is still open, although the paper of Do mentioned in the comments above is partial progress.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I've also looked at page 251 of [Er61] and I think your original formulation of the problem is basically faithful to the text (now that you have corrected $\pi/2$ to $2/\pi$), as $\epsilon_k$ is defined to be "the binary expansion of $t$" and thus {0,1}-valued rather than {-1,1}-valued.  (There is a mention of {-1,1}-valued Radamacher functions earlier in section V, but this is in reference to a different set of problems; similarly the Erdos-Kac result also assumes {-1,1}-valued coefficients, but that is (confusingly) a different use of the $\epsilon_k$ notation.)  But it is possible that Erdos himself did not formulate the problem in the way he really intended, given that all the other models discussed in this section were mean zero.  But in the absence of any further repetition of the problem in other papers I guess we have to use the literal reading of the problem.

In any case, the mean zero version of the problem is likely to be a better model problem to start with, as one can reuse more of the existing literature.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Yes, tricky - my evidence was the $\{-1,1\}$ formulation required only one typo/mistake (writing binary expansion of $t\in [0,1]$ rather than centred binary expansion of $t\in [-1/2,1/2)$ say), while the $\{0,1\}$ formulation is breaks both the contextual rule that $\epsilon_k\in \{-1,1\}$ for the other problems in that section, and also the constant $\frac{2}{\pi}$ is wrong.

So I'm leaning towards Erdős intending $\{-1,1\}$ as the explanation that implies fewer mistakes on his part.

But it's definitely ambiguous, and both are natural problems, so I've opted for the rephrasing in the current problem statement and description, simply mentioning both as possible interpretations.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
Regarding the coefficients in $\{-1,1\}$ (the mean zero setting), there is one detail that might still be missing. Namely, (my dear bro) [Yen proved](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06353) in the paper that msawhney mentioned:\[ \frac{N_n([-1,1])}{\log n} \to \frac{1}{\pi} \ a.s., \]where $N_n(A)$ counts the number of roots in $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. What’s still missing is\[ \frac{N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty))}{\log n} \to \frac{1}{\pi} \ a.s. \]If $N_n(\mathbb{R})=(2/\pi+o(1))\log n$ was merely to be shown "with large probability" (in the sense of terminology used, say, with random graphs), which is the ancient result, and not "almost surely", then the distribution of roots for a fixed $n$ would be symmetric under the reflection $z\to1/z$, so the other convergence claim would follow automatically. However, this reflection reverses the coefficients, so (for a fixed time segment $1,\ldots,n$) it reverses time, and the joint distribution of the full latter infinite sequence of random variables is no longer related to the former one. You can notice that Yen talks about this in Section 7. In fact, v1 of the paper on the arXiv made precisely that logical mistake, incorrectly claiming the a.s. convergence of $N_n(\mathbb{R})/\log n$ and later retracting it.

I did very poor experimentation: a sample trajectory of $N_n([-1,1])/\log n$ typically [looks like this](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory1.gif), while a sample trajectory of $N_n((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty))/\log n$ typically [looks like this](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory2.gif). The latter seems to oscillate more, raising doubt that they might not converge a.s., but $n\leq500$ are too small numbers to conclude anything meaningful.

Regarding the coefficients in $\{0,1\}$ (the nonzero mean setting), I noticed that Yen mentions a preprint titled "Real roots of non-centered random polynomials" on [his webpage](https://profile.virginia.edu/yqd3p). I cannot find it online, but here are some [related slides](https://app.icerm.brown.edu/assets/539/9763/9763_5485_Nguyen_080420251600_Slides.pdf).  From my understanding, the strong law (i.e., the a.s. convergence) is still an open problem mentioned on slide 28.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
This looks like an important distinction [and Yen Do has privately communicated similar points to me in recent discussions].  Heuristically, for each $1 \leq j \leq \log_2 n$, there should be $O(1)$ zeroes of $f=f_n$ in the region $[-1+2^{-j-1}, -1+2^{-j}]$, and $O(1)$ zeroes in the region $[-1-2^{-j}, -1-2^{-j-1}]$.  In the former case it's the coefficients $\epsilon_i$ for $i \ll 2^j$ that should largely control the zero count, but in the latter case it is the $\epsilon_i$ for $n-i \ll 2^j$.  So the former is heuristically quite stable in $n$ (say for $n \in [n_0, 2n_0]$) but the latter can be quite unstable, and in particular the situation for $f_n$ and $f_{n'}$ should behave in some uncorrelated fashion for $n'-n \gg 2^j$.  Assuming that each $f_n$ has some positive probability of not having a zero in $[-1-2^{-j}, -1-2^{-j-1}]$, this should cause the zero count here to be quite unstable, almost certainly fluctuating by $O(1)$ for $n \in [n_0,2n_0]$ if say one is in the regime $n_0^{0.1} \leq 2^j \leq n_0^{0.9}$.  Heuristically, this would then predict the global zero count to then fluctuate by more than $O(1)$.  But it may be quite challenging to make this intuition precise - there could be some "global conspiracy" that makes all these fluctuations magically cancel each other even if locally they behave like a nice process such as a Gaussian process.  In particular the variance of the global count could experience some ridiculous cancellation that makes it smaller than the variance of the local zero counts.  I don't see how to prevent this sort of getting extremely accurate control of the process (with error terms better than $o(1/n)$ on various pair correlation functions).  Even the mean zero gaussian coefficient case, which is presumably the simplest model, looks a bit tough here.

EDIT: maybe a switching approach?  Generate two correlated samples $\epsilon_j, \epsilon'_j$ of the coefficients, which are largely the same but differ at some carefully chosen, well spaced locations, so that they have largely independent impacts on the zero statistics.  If one can show a lower bound on the variance of the difference of the global zero count for the $\epsilon_j$ polynomial and the global zero count for the $\epsilon_{j'}$ polynomial after taking a supremum over some suitable sequence of $n$, then one might be able to disprove the claimed strong law thanks to the (contrapositive of the) triangle inequality.  The hope here is that by carefully titrating the amount of switching, one might be able to cancel out most of the weird and hard to understand global correlation structure and work with something more like the sum of random variables with very low covariances between them, which is something we have a chance of getting variance lower bounds on. It might also be useful to design the joint distribution of the $\epsilon_j$ and $\epsilon'_j$ so that certain partial sums or moments agree, in order to damp out long range correlations.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd:
This is really a remarkably delicate question (and honestly really unexpected to me)! For the approach suggested in the previous reply; it would seem that the probability that the number of real roots deviates from the expected amount by $\epsilon \log n$ scales as $n^{-\epsilon'}$ with $\epsilon'$ to $0$ as $\epsilon$ to $0$. Here is maybe a hopelessly naive strategy that might be useful? (It is just based on this heuristic of which coefficients control the zeros in which buckets.)

Let us group indices at a dyadic scale $[n, 2n]$. Define an index to be ''great'' if it has $\epsilon \log n$ ''extra'' zeros below $-1-n^{-1/4}$. By the heuristic suggested above the events that a pair of indices are great should essentially completely decorrelate once the pair of indices under consideration differ by more than $n^{3/4}$ (say). (I am assuming here is possible to control the number of zeros relatively deep into the tail; not sure how possible this is.)

This second moment argument would then give many indices where there are too many zeros towards the endpoint. The next claim would be even conditional on these zeros (which are mostly determined by the last few coefficients) then typically the inner interval has the expected number of zero. Then using a first moment argument we don't have too many indices which are great but have the expected number of zeros. This gives with high probability that at least one index in the range does not satisfy the required number of real roots. (Then taking massively separated dyadic intervals would conclude the result.) This last part is rather sketchy (and possibly impossible to justify).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Here is some more detail on the switching strategy.  Pick a large $n$, then let $n < n_1 < \dots < n_m < 2n$ be $m \sim n^{0.7}$ "checkpoints" separated by $\sim n^{0.3}$.  We introduce intervals $I_j = [n_j - n^{0.2}, n_j - n^{0.1}]$ to the left of each checkpoint $n_j$.  If the almost sure conjecture is true, then for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ we will have
$$ {\bf P}( \sup_{1 \leq j \leq m} |N_{n_j}({\bf R}) - \frac{1}{\pi} \log n| \leq \varepsilon \log n ) = 1 - o(1).$$
Now let us condition all the $\epsilon_k$ outside of $\bigcup_{j=1}^m I_j$ to be fixed, so that only the coefficients inside $I_1,\dots,I_m$ remain random.  Let $\epsilon'_k$ be a resampling of $\epsilon_k$ subject to this fixing, so the signs of $\epsilon'_k$ agree with $\epsilon_k$ outside of the $I_1,\dots,I_m$ but are completely resampled within these intervals.  Actually we should not do a completely independent resampling; we should fix means,
$$ \sum_{k \in I_j} \epsilon'_k = \sum_{k \in I_j} \epsilon_k$$
and actually I think we should fix a few more moments,
$$ \sum_{k \in I_j} k^a \epsilon'_k = \sum_{k \in I_j} k^a \epsilon_k \quad (1)$$
for $a=0,\dots,1000$.  I believe that this should be doable with some local limit theorems - it only is costing a small amount of "entropy" - but let me ignore this issue for this sketch.

If we let $N'_{n_j}$ be the zero counting function associated to this new coefficients then by the triangle inequality we have
$$ {\bf P}( \sup_{1 \leq j \leq m} |N_{n_j}({\bf R}) - N'_{n_j}({\bf R})| \leq 2\varepsilon \log n ) = 1 - o(1).$$
The point is that the way we have constructed things, the zeroes of $f_{n_j}$ and $f'_{n_j}$ are nearly identical except at $[-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}]$: any further away from $-1$ and the only coefficients that matter are those that are between $n_j$ and $I_{j}$, and any closer to $-1$ then the moment conditions (1) and some Taylor expansion should also make the polynomials agree nearly completely.  So one should morally have
$$ {\bf P}( \sup_{1 \leq j \leq m} |N_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}]) - N'_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}])| \leq 3\varepsilon \log n ) = 1 - o(1).$$
Let's write this as
$$ {\bf P}( \bigwedge_{j=1}^m E_j ) = 1-o(1)$$
where $E_j$ is the event that $|N_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}]) - N'_{n_j}([-1-n^{-0.21}, -1-n^{-0.09}])| \leq 3\varepsilon \log n$.  Morally, this event depends on the signs of $\epsilon_k, \epsilon'_k$ on $I_j$, but is almost completely independent of the signs at the other $I_{j'}$, because of they are so far away (at least $n^{0.3}$ away).  So, after some minor adjustments, one should be able to replace $E_j$ by completely independent events.  So now this means that
$$ {\bf P}( E_j ) = 1-o(1/m) = 1 - o(n^{-0.7})$$
for at least one of the $j$.  But hopefully some lower bound variance calculation can rule this out since $0.7$ is large compared to the exponent $0.21$ that is controlling the scale here.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
Reply to “I believe that this should be doable with some local limit theorems – it only is costing a small amount of entropy”

Yes — this step can be made precise using a multivariate lattice local limit theorem, and the entropy cost can be quantified explicitly.

Let $I_j$ be one of your resampling blocks, of length $\ell_j \asymp n^{0.2}$. Let $
\eta_k = 2\epsilon_k - 1 \in \{-1,1\}.
$ Fix $A \ge 0$ (e.g. $A=1000$) and set $d := A+1$. For $v_k = (k^0,\dots,k^A)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^d$ write $$
S_j(\epsilon) := \sum_{k\in I_j} \epsilon_k v_k,
\qquad S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta) := \sum_{k\in I_j} \eta_k v_k.
$$ If $S_j(\epsilon) = T$ for some target $T \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, this is equivalent to $$
S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta)  = 2T - \sum_{k\in I} v_k =: t'.
$$ The map $\epsilon \mapsto \eta = 2\epsilon - 1$ is a bijection $\{0,1\}^I \to \{\pm1\}^I$ which sends the $\{0,1\}$ moment constraint $S_j(\epsilon) = T$ to the $\{\pm1\}$ moment constraint $S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta) = t'$. In particular, the feasible sets $$
\Omega_T^{(0/1)} := \{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^I : S_j(\epsilon) = T\},
\qquad \Omega_{t'}^{(\pm)} := \{\eta\in\{\pm1\}^I : S_j^{(\pm)}(\eta) = t'\}
$$ satisfy $$
|\Omega_T^{(0/1)}| = |\Omega_{t'}^{(\pm)}|,
$$ so counting solutions (or entropy) in the $\{0,1\}$ model is exactly the same as in the $\{\pm1\}$ model, up to an explicit shift of the target vector.

The moment–matching constraint on $I_j$ is $$
\sum_{k\in I_j} k^a \eta_k = \sum_{k\in I_j} k^a \epsilon_k
\quad (a=0,\dots,A),
$$ i.e. $S_j(\eta) = t'_j := S_j(\epsilon)$. The feasible set $$
\Omega_j := \{ \eta \in \{\pm1\}^{I_j} : S_j(\eta) = t'_j \}
$$ has cardinality $$
|\Omega_j| = 2^{\ell_j} \cdot \mathbb{P}(S_j = t'_j),
$$ where the probability is for $\eta_k$ i.i.d. uniform $\pm 1$.

Now apply the $d$-dimensional lattice LLT for bounded independent vectors with nondegenerate covariance $$
\Sigma_j := \sum_{k\in I_j} v_k v_k^\top.
$$ Uniformly for $t'_j$ in the central region, $$
\mathbb{P}(S_j = t'_j)
= (2\pi)^{-d/2} (\det\Sigma_j)^{-1/2} e^{ -\frac12 t'_j{}^\top \Sigma_j^{-1} t'_j }
+ o\big((\det\Sigma_j)^{-1/2}\big).
$$ A Cauchy–Binet + Vandermonde computation gives $\det\Sigma_j \asymp_d \ell_j^{\,d^2}$, so $$
\mathbb{P}(S_j = t'_j) \asymp_d \ell_j^{-d^2/2}.
$$ Thus $$
|\Omega_j| \asymp_d 2^{\ell_j} \, \ell_j^{-d^2/2}.
$$ Since the conditional distribution on $\Omega_j$ is uniform, its Shannon entropy is $$
H(\Omega_j) = \log_2 |\Omega_j|
= \ell_j - \frac{d^2}{2} \log_2 \ell_j + O_d(1).
$$ Compared to the $\ell_j$ bits of an unconstrained block, the entropy loss is $\frac{d^2}{2} \log_2 \ell_j = O(\log n)$ per block. Over $m \asymp n^{0.7}$ blocks, the total loss is $O(n^{0.7} \log n) = o(n^{0.9})$, which is indeed “a small amount of entropy” in the sense of your switching argument.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
$\pi/2$ should be $2/\pi$ in the statement of the problem.

Even in the mean zero version, I think the current concentration bounds only give a $n^{-c}$ type bound for the tail probability (see for instance the recent paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.15446), which is not enough for almost sure convergence unless one can somehow relate the zeroes of adjacent polynomials to each other. It seems that the exponent $c$ here is not expected to exceed $1$, so the almost sure claim may in fact be false.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd:
The $2/\pi$ should actually be a $1/\pi$ due to the nonzero mean (note that one does not have roots on the positive real axis). However the stronger version suggested above is also very likely to follow from the techniques in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.06353v2. The key estimate is of the form suggested in the previous comment; see Lemma 2.4.

Also the statement here is slightly unclear in whether one wants probabilistically almost surely or almost surely; the version in the original paper definitely suggest the almost surely statement. (E.g. there is a sequence of $n$'s)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
(Deleted previous response which was based on a misreading of Lemma 2.4.)

Ah, so there is a maximal function tail estimate as well; that (plus Borel-Cantelli) would indeed resolve the question positively (with the corrected constant of $1/\pi$), provided that one can adapt the arguments to the nonzero mean setting, which seems plausible.

Not sure what you mean by "probabilistically almost surely" or "almost surely".  Are you referring to the distinction between almost sure convergence and convergence in probability (strong law of large numbers vs. weak law)?

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd: Yes this what I meant for the final comment (I should have written asymptotically almost surely which is equivalent to the distinction you said).

sourceComments.author: msawhney
sourceComments.contentMd: This should certainly be known (at least implicitly). In https://arxiv.org/pdf/1507.04994v3 Theorem 1.8, one gets a very strong bound in expectation of the number of real roots. (This doesn't immediately solved the problem as a variance estimate seems difficult to locate. In the case where the coefficients are mean zero this should be known.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #522 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/522).

### Problem
Let $f(z)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n} \epsilon_k z^k$ be a random polynomial, where $\epsilon_k\in \{-1,1\}$ independently uniformly at random for $0\leq k\leq n$.

Is it true that, if $R_n$ is the number of roots of $f(z)$ in $\{ z\in \mathbb{C} : \lvert z\rvert \leq 1\}$, then\[\frac{R_n}{n/2}\to 1\]almost surely?

### Context
Random polynomials with independently identically distributed coefficients are sometimes called Kac polynomials - this problem considers the case of Rademacher coefficients, i.e. independent uniform $\pm 1$ values. Erdős and Offord [EO56] showed that the number of real roots of a random degree $n$ polynomial with $\pm 1$ coefficients is $(\frac{2}{\pi}+o(1))\log n$.

There is some ambiguity whether Erdős intended the coefficients to be in $\{-1,1\}$ or $\{0,1\}$ - see the comments section.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here are several rather obvious remarks, partly in analogy with problem 521, and produced before thinking about the problem. :-)

1) I don't think that this problem should be marked as solved, unless another reference is found. Namely, [Erdős was precise about what he meant](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-22.pdf) (p.252), and he meant "a strong law", i.e., almost sure convergence of a sequence of random variables:\[ \frac{R'_n}{n/2} \to 1 \ a.s., \]where $R'_n$ counts the number of roots of $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\epsilon_k z^k$ in $|z|\prec 1$ (even though the closed disk $|z|\leq 1$ doesn't make a big difference).
[Yakir's paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.06234) proves\[ \frac{R'_n}{n/2} \to 1 \ \text{in probability}, \]which is also commonly phrased (in the spirit of your formulation) as\[ R'_n = \Big(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\Big) n \quad\text{with large probability} \]and it is a weaker claim, except for the concrete error of order $O(n^{9/10})$.

2) On the other hand, it is not clear if Erdős meant the coefficients to be $-1,1$ valued coin tosses (i.e., the Rademacher variables) as he emphasizes in the beginning of Section 2) on the same page, or rather the $0,1$ valued coin tosses (i.e., the Bernoulli variables). Strictly speaking he wrote the latter (just as in problem 521), since he constructed $\epsilon_k$ as the $k$-th digit of $t$ taken from the sample space $[0,1)$, by writing $t=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_k(t)}{2^k}$. However, he might have had some identification on mind, or wanted to write $t=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon_k(t)+1}{2^{k+1}}$ instead. I am more inclined to think that he meant $-1,1$.

3) In both cases the a.s. claim seems experimentally quite plausible. An easy simulation shows that in the $-1,1$ case a typical trajectory of $R'_n/(n/2)$ looks [like this](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory3.gif), while in the $0,1$ case it typically looks [like this](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/images/trajectory4.gif). In both cases it seems that convergence should in fact hold almost surely as well.

4) For the source of the problem Yakir actually cites Hayman's book from 1967. [Erdős did in fact ask](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-22.pdf) (p.252) about the weaker claim as well, as you can see in the sentence beginning with "Here I cannot even prove that...".

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #524 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/524).

### Problem
For any $t\in (0,1)$ let $t=\sum_{k=1}^\infty \epsilon_k(t)2^{-k}$ (where $\epsilon_k(t)\in \{0,1\}$). What is the correct order of magnitude (for almost all $t\in(0,1)$) for\[M_n(t)=\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\left\lvert \sum_{k\leq n}(-1)^{\epsilon_k(t)}x^k\right\rvert?\]

### Context
A problem of Salem and Zygmund [SaZy54]. Chung showed that, for almost all $t$, there exist infinitely many $n$ such that\[M_n(t) \ll \left(\frac{n}{\log\log n}\right)^{1/2}.\]Erdős (unpublished) showed that for almost all $t$ and every $\epsilon>0$ we have $\lim_{n\to \infty}M_n(t)/n^{1/2-\epsilon}=\infty$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
Following Mehtaab Sawhney remarks, I was able with GPT 5.2 (with a small input from Gemini/Grok) to complete the argument. Basically giving various estimates with $\limsup$ being straightforward and $\liminf$ being more tricky. [You can find the full write-up of the arguments here](https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos524.pdf). $\limsup$ and $\liminf$ parts are indepentent. Last section is the summary of results (also below), and 6.6. considers M.S. restatement in the comments below.

For Lebesgue-a.e. $t\in(0,1)$ the signs $a_k(t)=(-1)^{\epsilon_k(t)}$ are i.i.d. Rademacher, and\[
M_n(t)=\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\Big|\sum_{k=1}^n a_k(t)x^k\Big|
\]admits a sharp almost-sure upper-envelope law:\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{M_n(t)}{\sqrt{2n\log\log n}}=1.
\]The proof is a reduction by Abel summation (Salem-Zygmund style) to maxima of two simple random walks, followed by the classical LIL (Kolmogorov-Hartman-Wintner/Chung).  The same comparison yields subgaussian tails at the $\sqrt n$ scale for each fixed $n$.

For the lower envelope, the random-walk reduction is one-sided and gives only\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\Big(\tfrac{\log\log n}{n}\Big)^{1/2}M_n(t)\le \frac{\pi}{\sqrt8},
\]with no matching reverse bound.  A more sensitive viewpoint uses the endpoint parametrization $x=\pm e^{-u/n}$, under which $M_n/\sqrt n$ becomes the supremum of two Laplace-type processes $Z_n^\pm(u)$.

Using a two-dimensional strong invariance principle (KMT/Zaitsev-type), $(Z_n^+,Z_n^-)$ can be coupled to two independent copies of $Y(u)=\int_0^1 e^{-us}\,dB(s)$; the small-deviation asymptotics of Gao-Li-Wellner, $\log\mathbb P(\sup_{u\ge0}|Y(u)|\le\epsilon)\asymp-|\log\epsilon|^3$, then give a Borel-Cantelli dichotomy on sparse subsequences showing that the minimal values occur on the scale\[
M_n(t)=\sqrt n\,\exp\!\big(-\Theta((\log\log n)^{1/3})\big)\quad\text{infinitely often},
\]with threshold constants determined (up to two-sided bounds) by the small-ball constants for $Y$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Thanks - LLM-generated proofs like this are prone to containing subtle mistakes, especially when invoking tools from the literature, so I will view this as still unresolved until either an expert can take a look and confirm this, or a formalised proof is available.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd: Of course! Looking for an expert opinion as well. Nevertheless there are basically 3 independent parts: limsup, liminf and tails. On the other hand, I'm running it through Aristotle AI for a potential formalization but I doubt these kind of analytics results are currently likely to be formalized.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd:
(1) This proof is correct (and is what I suggested in the sketch below). The lim sup argument is actually immediate (?) given the LLL so the lower bound is the only tricky part. The sketch suggested is implemented correctly with KMT.
(2) Actually since I posted (and hence I marked working on the problem) Brayden Letwin, an undergraduate at University of Alberta, reached out and pointed out this KMT argument to me and has worked out this sketch several weeks ago. We together can actually prove a much stronger result (e.g. we can improve the key Gao-Li-Wellner to determine the constant in front of of $\log(1/\varepsilon)^3$ which eventually translates to an constant in front of the $\Theta$ obtained in the above result). I will attempt to finish the writeup as soon as possible.
(3) While the result mentioned in (2) is arguably quite a satisfactory resolution, one could argue (especially reading the paper of Salem--Zygmund) that one should aim for an LLL type result which determines this minimum to within a $1+o(1)$. While we won't publish this argument, it turns out if one can obtain a sufficiently strong error term in the Gao-Li-Wellner this would be possible. However this looks like a formidable problem in the theory of Gaussian processes.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd: Thank you for the reply. In other words, the problem is solved, either by my note above (flashing out your line of thought) or by your stronger result that is coming, right?

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd: Neither of these results pins down he answer as precisely as Salem--Zygmund might have wanted. (Our result will determine the optimal function to $\exp(o(\log\log n)^{2/3})$ but one may ask for an extremely tight control which is likely true.

sourceComments.author: msawhney
sourceComments.contentMd:
It took me a while to understand what exactly this problem is attempting to ask. Note that for a fixed scale $n$ that the maximum will be around size $\sqrt{n}$. To see the lower bound, one can just examine the endpoint $x = 1$. For the upper bound one can use an argument of Salem--Zygmund that\[\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varepsilon_k x^{k} = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(x^{k} - x^{k+1})\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\varepsilon_j\Big) + x^n\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\varepsilon_j\Big).\]Now for $x\in [0,1]$, these coefficients are nonnegative and together sum to $1$ so\[\max_{x\in [0,1]}\Big|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varepsilon_k x^{k}\Big|\le \max_{k\le n}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{k}\varepsilon_j\Big|.\]Via standard bounds for the maximum of a random walk, we have that the probability this is $\ge \lambda n^{1/2}$ scales as $e^{-\Omega(\lambda^2)}$. An essentially identical analysis applies for $x\in [-1,0]$ modulo replacing $\varepsilon_j$ by $(-1)^{j}\varepsilon_j$.

My current guess for what Erdos is asking for is a function $f(n)$ such that for almost all $t$ we have that $M_n(t)\ge f(n)$ for all but finitely many $n$ but $M_n(t)\ge C f(n)$ for infinitely many $n$. For this problem, note that\[\mathbb{P}\Big[\max_{k\le n}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{k}\varepsilon_j\Big|\le \varepsilon n^{1/2}\Big]\asymp \exp(-\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)).\]Noting that for scales which are sufficiently far away (e.g. $n$ vs $n(\log n)^2$ say) these two events are essentially independent. Now as there are $(\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ such distinct scales up to $n$, setting $\varepsilon \approx 1/\sqrt{\log\log n}$ we essentially recover Chung's result.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd: This problem it turns out is very likely to follow from arguments present in the literature already; the true scale of this minimum seems to be between $n^{1/2}\exp(-c(\log\log n)^{1/3})$ and $n^{1/2}\exp(-c'(\log\log n)^{1/3})$. (Determining the exact constant $c$ is likely more technical.) The crucial point is to reparameterize $x = e^{-t/n}$ (thinking of $t$ fixed as $n\to \infty$) and we are seeing to bound\[\sum_{k=1}^{n}\varepsilon_k e^{-tk/n}\]for $t\ge 0$. This is essentially equivalent to looking at $Y(t) =\Big| \int_{0}^{1}e^{-tx}dB(x)\Big|$ and looking at the maximum for $t\ge 0$. We want to understand the probability that this maximum is small; this scaling is worked out in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.0200. (This reference was located with help from ChatGPT 5.2 Pro.) The remaining technical work is passing between the Gaussian limit and this problem.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
I just read [SZ54, p. 299] carefully, and I believe the current formulation of this problem on the website is incorrect; as stated (with coefficients $\epsilon_k(t)\in\{0,1\}$ and $x\in[0,1]$) it becomes essentially trivial. (indeed, the polynomial has nonnegative coefficients, so it is increasing on $[0,1]$, and thus \(M_n(t)=\max_{0\le x\le 1}\sum_{k\le n}\epsilon_k(t)x^k=\sum_{k\le n}\epsilon_k(t)\), reducing the question to the law of large numbers for the dyadic digits).

According to [SZ54], the intended coefficients should be random signs, i.e. Rademacher functions $\varphi_k(t)\in\{\pm1\}$ rather than binary digits $\epsilon_k(t)\in\{0,1\}$. In terms of the dyadic expansion $t=\sum_{k\ge1}\epsilon_k(t)2^{-k}$, one can set for instance\[
\varphi_k(t)=1-2\epsilon_k(t)\in\{\pm1\}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\varphi_k(t)=(-1)^{\epsilon_k(t)}.
\]Moreover, the maximization should be over $x\in[-1,1]$, not just $x\in[0,1]$. In other words, the Salem--Zygmund version is\[
M_n(t)=\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\left|\sum_{k\le n}\varphi_k(t)\,x^k\right|.
\]

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Thanks, I agree (the $[0,1]$ in place of $[-1,1]$ is my typo not Erdős' - the conflation of the $\{0,1\}$ vs $\{-1,1\}$ model is an unfortunate ambiguity that has come up in other problems from [Er61]).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #528 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/528).

### Problem
Let $f(n,k)$ count the number of [self-avoiding walks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-avoiding_walk) of $n$ steps (beginning at the origin) in $\mathbb{Z}^k$ (i.e. those walks which do not intersect themselves). Determine\[C_k=\lim_{n\to\infty}f(n,k)^{1/n}.\]

### Context
The constant $C_k$ is sometimes known as the connective constant. Hammersley and Morton [HM54] showed that this limit exists, and it is trivial that $k\leq C_k\leq 2k-1$.

Kesten [Ke63] proved that $C_k=2k-1-1/2k+O(1/k^2)$, and more precise asymptotics are given by Clisby, Liang, and Slade [CLS07].

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #529 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/529).

### Problem
Let $d_k(n)$ be the expected distance from the origin after taking $n$ random steps from the origin in $\mathbb{Z}^k$ (conditional on no self intersections) - that is, a [self-avoiding walk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-avoiding_walk). Is it true that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{d_2(n)}{n^{1/2}}= \infty?\]Is it true that\[d_k(n)\ll n^{1/2}\]for $k\geq 3$?

### Context

For $k=2$ Duminil-Copin and Hammond [DuHa13] have proved that $d_2(n)=o(n)$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #530 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/530).

### Problem
Let $\ell(N)$ be maximal such that in any finite set $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ of size $N$ there exists a Sidon subset $S$ of size $\ell(N)$ (i.e. the only solutions to $a+b=c+d$ in $S$ are the trivial ones). Determine the order of $\ell(N)$.

In particular, is it true that $\ell(N)\sim N^{1/2}$?

### Context
Originally asked by Riddell [Ri69]. Erdős noted the bounds\[N^{1/3} \ll \ell(N) \leq (1+o(1))N^{1/2}\](the upper bound following from the case $A=\{1,\ldots,N\}$). The lower bound was improved to $N^{1/2}\ll \ell(N)$ by Komlós, Sulyok, and Szemerédi [KSS75]. The correct constant is unknown, but it is likely that the upper bound is true, so that $\ell(N)\sim N^{1/2}$.

In [AlEr85] Alon and Erdős make the stronger conjecture that perhaps $A$ can always be written as the union of at most $(1+o(1))N^{1/2}$ many Sidon sets. (This is easily verified for $A=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ using standard constructions of Sidon sets.)

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #531 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/531).

### Problem
Let $F(k)$ be the minimal $N$ such that if we two-colour $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ there is a set $A$ of size $k$ such that all subset sums $\sum_{a\in S}a$ (for $\emptyset\neq S\subseteq A$) are monochromatic. Estimate $F(k)$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #535 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/535).

### Problem
Let $r\geq 3$, and let $f_r(N)$ denote the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that no subset of size $r$ has the same pairwise greatest common divisor between all elements. Estimate $f_r(N)$.

### Context
Erdős [Er64] proved that\[f_r(N) \leq N^{\frac{3}{4}+o(1)},\]and Abbott and Hanson [AbHa70] improved this exponent to $1/2$. Erdős [Er64] proved the lower bound\[f_3(N) > N^{\frac{c}{\log\log N}}\]for some constant $c>0$, and conjectured this should also be an upper bound.

Erdős writes this is 'intimately connected' with the sunflower problem [[20]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/20). Indeed, the conjectured upper bound would follow from the following stronger version of the sunflower problem: estimate the size of the largest set of integers $A$ such that $\omega(n)=k$ for all $n\in A$ and there does not exist $a_1,\ldots,a_r\in A$ and an integer $d$ such that $(a_i,a_j)=d$ for all $i\neq j$ and $(a_i/d,d)=1$ for all $i$. The conjectured upper bound for $f_r(N)$ would follow if the size of such an $A$ must be at most $c_r^k$. The original sunflower proof of Erdős and Rado gives the upper bound $c_r^kk!$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Cong
sourceComments.contentMd:
I tried to formalize the “stronger sunflower problem” phrasing here: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/2199

But as stated, this seems false without an extra restriction: for $k=1$ consider $A_m={2,4,8,\dots,2^m}.$
Then $\omega(n)=1$ for all $n\in A_m$, and for any $r\ge 3$ there is no $r$-subset with constant pairwise gcd (pairwise gcds vary with the minimal exponent), so it satisfies the “no constant pairwise gcd with coprime quotients” condition. Yet $|A_m|=m$ is arbitrarily large, contradicting any bound $|A|\le c_r^k$ (or even $c_r^k k!$ since $k=1$).

In Erdős’s 1964 paper, the set-system/sunflower step is applied to squarefree parts / prime-factor sets (he explicitly introduces squarefree numbers and decomposes $a_i=A_iB_i$ with $B_i$ squarefree). That suggests the intended sunflower-style statement meant to restrict to squarefree integers (or radicals) rather than just $\omega(n)=k$?

sourceComments.contentMd: I think the [method in my recent paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11610) disproving #121 may be able to show the claim if the density of $A$ is sufficiently close to $1$.  Basically one can look for triangles of the form $a = n_0 n_{12} n_{13}$, $b = n_0 n_{12} n_{23}$, $c = n_0 n_{13} n_{23}$, where $n_0, n_{12}, n_{13}, n_{23}$ are coprime and squarefree, and have a suitable prime factorization to make $a,b,c$ have a "typical" anatomy (perhaps one can take $n_0$ to be a largish prime and $n_{12}, n_{13}, n_{23}$ to be about the same size).  Then one should be able to win from the probabilistic method.

replies.author: DesmondWeisenberg
replies.contentMd:
The remaining two page numbers are [Er70,p.124][Er73,p.124].

The claim that if $A$ has no lcm triangles then $|A| \leq cN$ for some $c < 1$ for all large $N$ can actually be proven by purely elementary means. We do so as follows: observe that as $m$ ranges over the integers from 1 to $\lfloor\frac{N}{15}\rfloor$ with $\text{gcd}(m, 30) = 1$, the sets $\{6m, 10m, 15m\}$ are disjoint lcm triangles contained in $\{1, \dots, N\}$. (The condition $\text{gcd}(m, 30) = 1$ isn't actually necessary to make these sets lcm triangles, but it is necessary for disjointness.) The amount of such $m$ is asymptotically $\frac{1}{15} \cdot \frac{\phi(30)}{30} \cdot N$, and $\phi(30) = 8$, so this is $\frac{4}{225}N$. If $A$ is lcm triangle-free, then at least one element must be removed for every such $m$, so we have $|A| \leq (\frac{221}{225} + o(1))N$.

This proves the desired claim, but I have no doubt that it can be improved significantly. For example, I imagine we could include $m$ such that $\text{gcd}(m, 30) > 1$ as well as apply the same analysis to other lcm triangles $\{a, b, c\}$ with $\text{gcd}(a, b, c) = 1$ at the same time (as opposed to just $\{6, 10, 15\}$). The inclusion-exclusion principle might be all we need to do both of these things.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
For the record, both times Erdős asked this question, he specified that $a,b,c$ are distinct - that may be worth clarifying here. It's obvious that allowing $a = b = c$ leaves us stuck with the empty set, so that's trivial, but allowing two of them to be equal is equivalent to requiring that $A$ be a primitive set, which is an interesting variant, but not what he asks.
For convenience, call a set of three distinct numbers $\{a,b,c\}$ an *lcm triangle* if $[a,b] = [b,c] = [a,c]$. Then this problem asks how large a subset of $\{1,...,N\}$ can be if it contains no lcm triangles.

Fix a positive integer $k$ and let $S_k$ be the set of all numbers of the form $p_1 \cdots p_k$, where each $p_i$ is prime and $\pi(p_i) \equiv i \pmod{k}$ for all $i$ (but the primes are not necessarily in increasing order). It's not hard to verify that $S_k$ contains no lcm triangles. Furthermore, it's not hard to verify that $S_k$ has positive relative lower density within the set of all $k$-almost primes, and it's known that the amount of $k$-almost primes up to $N$ is $\sim_k \frac{N (\log \log N)^{k-1}}{(k - 1)! \log N}$. As such, for each $N$, we can choose the value of $k$ that maximizes the size of $S_k \cap \{1,...,N\}$. By doing so, we see that there is always an lcm triangle-free set $A \subseteq \{1,...,N\}$ such that
\begin{equation*}
|A| \gg_t \frac{N (\log \log N)^t}{\log N}.
\end{equation*}
With a bit of work, I'm sure one could make this lower bound a little more explicit.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #538 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/538).

### Problem
Let $r\geq 2$ and suppose that $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is such that, for any $m$, there are at most $r$ solutions to $m=pa$ where $p$ is prime and $a\in A$. Give the best possible upper bound for\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}.\]

### Context
Erdős observed that\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{p\leq N}\frac{1}{p}\leq r\sum_{m\leq N^2}\frac{1}{m}\ll r\log N,\]and hence\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n} \ll r\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\]See also [[536]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/536) and [[537]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/537).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #539 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/539).

### Problem
Let $h(n)$ be such that, for any set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of size $n$, the set\[\left\{ \frac{a}{(a,b)}: a,b\in A\right\}\]has size at least $h(n)$. Estimate $h(n)$.

### Context
Erdős and Szemerédi proved that\[n^{1/2} \ll h(n) \ll n^{1-c}\]for some constant $c>0$. The upper bound has been improved to $h(n)\ll n^{2/3}$ by Freiman and Lev. A proof of these bounds can be found in a paper of Granville and Roesler [GrRo99].

Granville and Roesler also reformulate this problem as one in combinatorial geometry: given $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$ of size $n$ what is the minimum size possible of\[\{ \delta(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) : \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in A\}\]where $\delta(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ has $i$th coordinate $\max(0,a_i-b_i)$. Using this formulation that obtain improved lower bounds in fixed small dimension $d$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
The problem has been studied in the meantime and the best known bounds are\[ n^{1/2} \ll h(n) \ll n^{2/3}. \]Both are easy and are elaborated in [this paper by Granville and Roesler](https://www.erdosproblems.com/ https:/www.tandfonline.com/doi/epdf/10.1080/00029890.1999.12005050) from 1999. The lower bound is, as stated, probably an observation of Erdős and Szemerédi, while for the upper bound the authors credit Freiman and Lev.
Granville and Roesler nicely reformulate the problem as a problem in combinatorial geometry, which is also the viewpoint of [Holzman, Lev, and Pinchasi](https://holzman.technion.ac.il/files/2012/09/project.pdf). The two papers also showed (in number theoretic language) that:
If $A$ consists of numbers with prime divisors $2,3$, then $h_2(n)\gg n^{2/3}$.
If $A$ consists of numbers with prime divisors $2,3,5$, then $h_3(n)\gg n^{3/5}$.
If $A$ consists of numbers with prime divisors $2,3,5,7$, then $h_4(n)\gg n^{6/11-\epsilon}$.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #545 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/545).

### Problem
Let $G$ be a graph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices. Is the Ramsey number $R(G)$ maximised when $G$ is 'as complete as possible'? That is, if $m=\binom{n}{2}+t$ edges with $0\leq t<n$ then is\[R(G)\leq R(H),\]where $H$ is the graph formed by connecting a new vertex to $t$ of the vertices of $K_n$?

### Context
A question of Erdős and Graham. The weaker question of whether\[R(G) \leq 2^{O(m^{1/2})}\]is the subject of [[546]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/546). (This is true, and was proved by Sudakov [Su11].)

LouisD in the comments has noted this fails for small $m$ (in particular for $2\leq m\leq 5$ and $7\leq m\leq 9$).

sourceComments.author: Thomas Bloom
sourceComments.contentMd:
A [1989 paper of Burr](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jgt.3190070108) lists the Ramsey numbers for all graphs with $\leq 6$ edges and no isolated points in a very useful table.

Perusing that table shows that indeed $R(G)\leq 18$ for all such graphs $G$, and so the answer to this question is yes for $m=6$.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
If not mistaken, for large sizes, the best known bounds on balanced complete bipartite graphs and complete graphs are too weak to deduce the second is larger than the first.
It was conjectured that $R(K_{n,n})$ is of the order $2^n$, while the best lower bound for $R(K_t)$ is still like $2^{t/2}$.
[https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.12926: one is maybe not far off to improve $\sqrt 2$ by an epsilon]

It may be a nice (but hard) challenge to prove this by pure comparison.

As Addenwalla said, $R(P_3)<R(2K_2)$, so the statement fails for the snallest $m$, m=2, where one can compare (m=1 has nothing to do). So the statement is indeed about the behaviour for large sizes...

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd: Judging by how this doesn't obviously fail for $m=6$ and $m=10$, it might be easier to prove the statement when $t=0$. That is, when $H$ is a complete graph.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
That is in principle true, but for large values, I think it won't make it that much easier.
The Ramsey number for $K_n$ and for the Colex graph $\mathcal C( m)$ where $m=\binom n2+1$ should indeed be the same for large $n$, as in general $R(n,n)>R(n,n-1)+n$ is expected from the exponential behaviour.
Intuitively, once one is forced to have a large red $K_n$, there is somewhere else a vertex with many neighbours in that colour as well.

If one thinks about hard constructions:
for small values, there is a space constraint and the matching $mK_2$ is the one with largest order and thus natural candidate. But this is linear behaviour.

For large values, one could think about "rare" structures like the complement of sparse structured constructions, or multipartite graphs like $K_{t,t}, K_{t,t,t}$.
If the latter would be worse, the exponential behaviour may have a different base.
On the other hand, for the wheel $W_5=K_{2,2,1}$, which has size $8$, $R(W_5)=15<R(K_4) \le R(K_5^{--}).$
Also $26\le R(K_{2,2,2})$ seems to be smaller than $R(K_5)\le 46$.

The potential structured counterexamples I thought about, likely won't beat the clique/ Colex graphs in the limit, but even the explicit comparison may be hard.

sourceComments.author: LouisD
sourceComments.contentMd:
Hopefully one last comment for now.

I see that the problem was updated to indicate that it fails for small $m$.  Just to clarify, I claim that it fails for $m\in \{3,4,5,7,8,9\}$ (in particular, I think it is true for $m=6$) and in all of these cases, the reason is $R(mK_2)=3m-1$.  From the Radziszowski survey I learned that $R(K_4-e)=10$ and $R(K_5-e)=22$ which is where the $m=4,5,8,9$ cases come from.

sourceComments.author: LouisD
sourceComments.contentMd:
In my previous comment, I indicated that I couldn't find the statement of this problem in [Er84b].  I still don't see the exact statement, but I now see the following sentence (at the top of page 11) "Probably r(G) is maximal if G is as complete as possible."  I guess this must be the intended reference.  On the other hand, he makes no reference to Graham, so I continued my search.

In https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ExtremeCliques.html, the reference "Some partition theorems in finite graphs" by Erdős and Graham (1973) is given; however, in that paper I was only able to find the statement of the first part (on page 526), not the second part about G having $\binom{n}{2}+t$ edges.

I noticed that in https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ExtremeCliques.html, there is an extra condition which says $n\ge 4$.  Presumably, this is because $R(3K_2)=8>6=R(K_3)$
(where $mK_2$ is a matching with $m$ edges).*  On the other hand, note that $R(6K_2)=17<18=R(K_4)$.

Finally I get to my point.  I claim that the conjecture is also false for $n=4$ and $t=1$.  Let $K_4^{+1}$ be the graph on $5$ vertices and $7$ edges obtained from $K_4$ by adding a new vertex adjacent to one vertex in the $K_4$.  I claim that $R(7K_2)=20>18=R(K_4^{+1})$.  We already have $18=R(K_4)\leq R(K_4^{+1})$ and to see that $R(K_4^{+1})\leq 18$, the argument is essentially the same as proving that $R(K_4)\leq 18$.  Without loss of generality, we can assume that there exists a vertex $x$ and a set $A$ with $|A|=9$ such that every edge from $x$ to $A$ is red.  If there is a red triangle in $A$, we are done, so suppose not.  If there is a vertex $u\in A$ with 6 blue neighbors in $A$, we are also done (since we will get a blue triangle in the blue neighborhood of $u$).  Since it isn't possible for every vertex in $A$ to have blue degree $5$ to $A$, we have a vertex $v\in A$ with red degree at least 4 in $A$ and we can again see that it must be exactly 4 (otherwise we would get a blue $K_5$).  Let $B$ be the set of 4 blue neighbors of $v$ in $A$.  Every edge in $B$ is blue, and thus every edge from $B$ to $A\setminus B$ is red.  So finally, we must have that every edge in $A\setminus B$ is blue in which case we have a blue $K_5$ and we are done.

So the conjecture certainly needs to be updated to add the condition that it holds provided the number of edges is large enough.  How large is large enough?  Can anyone find a counterexample with 8 edges?  We have $R(8K_2)=23$ and I wouldn't be surprised if $R(K_4^{+2})\le 22$.  However, I am out of time at the moment to attempt to prove this by hand as I did above for $K_4^{+1}$.  Conceivably, this could be checked computationally?

*In general, Cockyane and Lorimer "The Ramsey number for stripes" (1975) proved that for all positive integers $m$ and $r$, the $r$-color Ramsey number of $mK_2$ is $(r+1)m+(r-1)$.  For $r=2$, this says $R(mK_2)=3m-1$ and in this case, the upper bound can be seen by a simple inductive argument (either we have a red edge incident to a blue edge and we can remove those three vertices and apply induction, or else every edge has the same color).  The lower bound comes from taking disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ with $m-1$ and $2m-1$ vertices respectively, coloring all edges incident with $A$ red and all other edges blue.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Thanks! I realise now that the second question is also implicit in the phrasing "as complete as possible".

This is a nice example.

Surely some work has been done on this in the past 40 years? It's a natural question. I'll try a deeper search later unless anyone can beat me to it.

EDIT: I found nothing yet, but note that Sudakov [Su11] says of this problem in his introduction " This conjecture is very difficult and so far there has been no progress on this problem."

replies.author: LouisD
replies.contentMd:
I just checked the Radziszowski "Small Ramsey Numbers" survey and found that surprisingly, $R(K_5-e)=22$.

So this means there is a counterexample on both 8 and 9 edges.  We have $R(9K_2)=26>22=R(K_5-e)=R(K_4^{+3})$ and $R(8K_2)=23>22=R(K_5-e)\ge R(K_4^{+2})$.  Since $R(10K_2)=29<43\leq R(K_5)$, perhaps it is possible that the conjecture holds provided the number of edges is at least 10?

I still don't know the exact value of $R(K_4^{+2})$ and it seems too specialized to appear in the Radziszowski survey.  So this would still be interesting to know.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #548 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/548).

### Problem
Let $n\geq k+1$. Every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\frac{k-1}{2}n+1$ edges contains every tree on $k+1$ vertices.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Sós, who also conjectured that every graph with at least\[\max\left( \binom{2k-1}{2}+1, (k-1)n-(k-1)^2+\binom{k-1}{2}+1\right)\]many edges contains every forest with $k$ edges. (Erdős and Gallai [ErGa59] proved that this is the threshold which guarantees containing $k$ independent edges.)

In [Er78] Erdős says this is trivial for a star, and he and Gallai had proved it for a path.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.contentMd:
(i) P. E. Haxell in [[Ha01]](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/1097-0118%28200103%2936%3A3%3C121%3A%3AAID-JGT1000%3E3.0.CO%3B2-U) has proved the conjecture for graphs that do not contain $K_{2,s}$, where $s= \lfloor{\frac{k}{18}}\rfloor$.

(ii) S. Balasubramanian and E. Dobson in [[BaDo07]](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jgt.20261) has improved upon [Ha01] to include graphs that do not contain $K_{2,s}$, where $s< \frac{k}{12}+1$.

(iii) The result of [WLL00] (discussed in the problem description) has been improved by Dobson in [[Do02]](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/combinatorics-probability-and-computing/article/abs/constructing-trees-in-graphs-whose-complement-has-no-k2s/D2579E2AAAA9CF2DFD22AC7B1F60BA8D) to include graphs whose complements do not contain $K_{2,4}$.

(iv) A. F. Sidorenko in [[Si89]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02124681) proved the conjecture for every tree with a vertex having atleast $\lceil {\frac{k}{2}}\rceil - 1$ leaf-neighbours.

(v) This result has been improved by N. Eaton and G. Tiner in [EaTi10] to include every tree with a vertex having at least $\lceil {\frac{k}{2}}\rceil - 2$ leaf-neighbours. They have also showed that this conjecture holds for values of $k$ at most $8$.

(vi) G. Tiner and Z. Tomlin in [[TiTo22]](https://www.ajmonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/On-the-Erdos-Sos-Conjecture.pdf) has proved that the conjecture holds for $k=9$.

(vii) B. Zhou in [[Zh84]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0252960218306635) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k$.

(viii) P. Slater, S. Teo and H. Yap in [[STY85]](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jgt.3190090203) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+1$.

(ix) M. Wozniak in [[Wo96]](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-0118%28199602%2921%3A2%3C229%3A%3AAID-JGT13%3E3.0.CO%3B2-E) has proved the conjecture for trees of diameter at most $4$ having at most one vertex with degree exceeding $2$. This paper proves the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+2$.

(x) G. Tiner in [[Ti10]](https://combinatorialpress.com/article/ars/Volume%20095/volume-95-paper-13.pdf) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+3$.

(xi) L. Yuan and X. Zhang in [[YuZh17]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5430) has proved the conjecture in the case when graph $G$ has a number of vertices $k+4$.

(xii) A spider is a tree with at most one vertex of degree more than $2$. G. Fan, Y. Hong and Q. Liu in [[FHL18]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06567) has proved that the conjecture holds for all spiders.

(xiii) Balasubramaniam in his PhD thesis [[Ba]](https://scholarsjunction.msstate.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=4367&context=td) has proved the conjecture for graphs containing no $K_{2,s}$ where, $s ≥ 2$ and $k > 12(s − 1)$.

[EaTi10]: N. Eaton, G. Tiner, On the Erdős-Sós Conjecture and Graphs with large minimum degree, Ars Combin. 95 (2010) 373–382.

Plus it seems that a solution was announced for this conjecture by Ajtai, Komlós, Simonovits, and Szemerédi, but it's whereabouts are unknown...

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #552 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/552).

### Problem
Determine the Ramsey number\[R(C_4,S_n),\]where $S_n=K_{1,n}$ is the star on $n+1$ vertices.

In particular, is it true that, for any $c>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[R(C_4,S_n)\leq n+\sqrt{n}-c?\]

### Context
A problem of Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [BEFRS89]. Erdős often asked about $R(C_4,S_n)$ in the equivalent formulation of asking for a bound on the minimum degree of a graph which would guarantee the existence of a $C_4$ (see [[85]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/85)).

It is known that\[ n+\sqrt{n}-6n^{11/40} \leq R(C_4,S_n)\leq n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+1.\]The lower bound is due to [BEFRS89], the upper bound is due to Parsons [Pa75]. The lower bound of [BEFRS89] is related to gaps between primes, and assuming e.g. Cramer's conjecture on gaps between primes their lower bound would be $n+\sqrt{n}-n^{o(1)}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

The lower bound of [BEFRS89] is related to gaps between primes, and assuming e.g. Cramer's conjecture on gaps between primes their lower bound would be $n+\sqrt{n}-n^{o(1)}$.

Erdős offered \$100 for a proof or disproof of the second question in [BEFRS89]. In [Er96] Erdős asks (an equivalent formulation of) whether $R(C_4,S_n)\geq n+\sqrt{n}-O(1)$, but says this is probably 'too optimistic'.

They also ask, if $f(n)=R(C_4,S_n)$, whether $f(n+1)=f(n)$ infinitely often, and is the density of such $n$ $0$? Also, is it true that $f(n+1)\leq f(n)+2$ for all $n$? A similar question about an equivalent function is the subject of [[85]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/85).

Parsons [Pa75] proved thatR(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceilwhenever $n=q^2+1$ for a prime power $q$ andR(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+1whenever $n=q^2$ for a prime power $q$ (in particular both equalities occur infinitely often).

This has been extended in various works, all in the cases $n=q^2\pm t$ for some $0\leq t\leq q$ and prime power $q$. We refer to the work of Parsons [Pa75], Wu, Sun, Zhang, and Radziszowski [WSZR15], and Zhang, Chen, and Cheng ([ZCC17] and [ZCC17b]) for a precise description. In every known caseR(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+\{0,1\},and Zhang, Chen, and Cheng [ZCC17] speculate whether this is in fact true for all $n\geq 2$ (whence the answer to the question above would be no).
This problem is #19 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #554 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/554).

### Problem
Let $R_k(G)$ denote the minimal $m$ such that if the edges of $K_m$ are $k$-coloured then there is a monochromatic copy of $G$. Show that\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{R_k(C_{2n+1})}{R_k(K_3)}=0\]for any $n\geq 2$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Graham. The problem is open even for $n=2$.

Schur [Sc16] proved\[C^k \ll R_k(K_3) \ll k!\]for some constant $C>0$. Erdős conjectured (see [[183]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/183)) that $R_k(K_3) \leq C^k$ for some contant $C>0$.

sourceComments.author: LouisD
sourceComments.contentMd:
I believe this should say $R(T;k)\leq kn+O(1)$.  For instance it is known for sufficiently large $n$ that $R(P_n; 3)=2n-1$ if $n$ is odd and $R(P_n;3)=2n-2$ if $n$ is even (Gy\'arf\'as, Ruszink\'o, S\'ark\"ozy, Szemer\'edi "Three-color Ramsey numbers for paths" 2007).

On the other hand, for stars on $n$ vertices, we clearly have $R(K_{1,n-1};k)\geq kn-O(k)$ (and the exact result can be found in "On Ramsey numbers for stars" by Burr and Roberts (1973)).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: LouisD
replies.contentMd:
Just to preemptively challenge my own comment, I suppose $R(T;k)=kn+O(1)$ means that there exists a constant $C$ (possibly depending on $k$) such that $R(T;k)\leq kn+C$.  However, I can imagine somebody reading $R(T;k)=kn+O(1)$ and thinking it means that there exists constants $c$ and $C$ (possibly depending on $k$) such that $kn-c\leq R(T;k)\leq kn+C$.

For what it's worth Erdős and Graham (in their 1973 paper) write this conjecture as $R(T;k)< kn+O(1)$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #560 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/560).

### Problem
Let $\hat{R}(G)$ denote the size Ramsey number, the minimal number of edges $m$ such that there is a graph $H$ with $m$ edges such that in any $2$-colouring of the edges of $H$ there is a monochromatic copy of $G$.

Determine\[\hat{R}(K_{n,n}),\]where $K_{n,n}$ is the complete bipartite graph with $n$ vertices in each component.

### Context
We know that\[\frac{1}{60}n^22^n<\hat{R}(K_{n,n})< \frac{3}{2}n^32^n.\]The lower bound (which holds for $n\geq 6$) was proved by Erdős and Rousseau [ErRo93]. The upper bound was proved by Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [EFRS78b] and Nešetřil and Rödl [NeRo78].

Conlon, Fox, and Wigderson [CFW23] have proved that, for any $s\leq t$,\[\hat{R}(K_{s,t})\gg s^{2-\frac{s}{t}}t2^s,\]and prove that when $t\gg s\log s$ we have $\hat{R}(K_{s,t})\asymp s^2t2^s$. They conjecture that this should hold for all $s\leq t$, and so in particular we should have $\hat{R}(K_{n,n})\asymp n^32^n$.

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #561 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/561).

### Problem
Let $\hat{R}(G)$ denote the size Ramsey number, the minimal number of edges $m$ such that there is a graph $H$ with $m$ edges such that in any $2$-colouring of the edges of $H$ there is a monochromatic copy of $G$.

Let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be the union of stars. More precisely, let $F_1=\cup_{i\leq s} K_{1,n_i}$ and $F_2=\cup_{j\leq t} K_{1,m_j}$ with $n_1\geq \cdots \geq n_s\geq 1$ and $m_1\geq \cdots \geq m_t\geq 1$. Prove that\[\hat{R}(F_1,F_2) = \sum_{2\leq k\leq s+t}l_k\]where\[l_k=\max\{n_i+m_j-1 : i+j=k\}.\]

### Context
Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [BEFRS78] proved this when all the $n_i$ are identical and all the $m_i$ are identical.

Győri and Schelp [GySc02] proved this when $\binom{l_k}{2}> \sum_{k\leq i\leq s+t}l_i$ for all $2\leq k\leq s+t$. More special cases, including all cases when $s=1$, or $s=2$ and $n_1=n_2$, or all $n_i$ and $m_j$ are odd, or all $n_i$ are an identical odd number and $m_1$ is odd, were proved by Davoodi, Javadi, Kamranian, and Raeisi [DJKR25].

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #563 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/563).

### Problem
Let $F(n,\alpha)$ denote the smallest $m$ such that there exists a $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ so that every $X\subseteq [n]$ with $\lvert X\rvert\geq m$ contains more than $\alpha \binom{\lvert X\rvert}{2}$ many edges of each colour.

Prove that, for every $0\leq \alpha< 1/2$,\[F(n,\alpha)\sim c_\alpha\log n\]for some constant $c_\alpha$ depending only on $\alpha$.

### Context
It is easy to show via the probabilistic method that, for every $0\leq \alpha<1/2$,\[F(n,\alpha)\asymp_\alpha \log n.\]Note that when $\alpha=0$ this is just asking for a $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ which contains no monochromatic clique of size $m$, and hence we recover the classical Ramsey numbers.

### Problem
Let $R_3(n)$ be the minimal $m$ such that if the edges of the $3$-uniform hypergraph on $m$ vertices are $2$-coloured then there is a monochromatic copy of the complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices.

### Problem
Let $G$ be such that any subgraph on $k$ vertices has at most $2k-3$ edges. Is it true that, if $H$ has $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, then\[R(G,H)\ll m?\]

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #567 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/567).

### Problem
Let $G$ be either $Q_3$ or $K_{3,3}$ or $H_5$ (the last formed by adding two vertex-disjoint chords to $C_5$). Is it true that, if $H$ has $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, then\[R(G,H)\ll m?\]

### Context
In other words, is $G$ Ramsey size linear? A special case of [[566]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/566). In [Er95] Erdős specifically asks about the case $G=K_{3,3}$.

The graph $H_5$ can also be described as $K_4^*$, obtained from $K_4$ by subdividing one edge. ($K_4$ itself is not Ramsey size linear, since $R(4,n)\gg n^{3-o(1)}$, see [[166]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/166).) Bradać, Gishboliner, and Sudakov [BGS23] have shown that every subdivision of $K_4$ on at least $6$ vertices is Ramsey size linear, and also that $R(H_5,H) \ll m$ whenever $H$ is a bipartite graph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #572 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/572).

### Problem
Show that for $k\geq 3$\[\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\gg n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}.\]

### Context
It is easy to see that $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k+1})=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor$ for any $k\geq 1$ (and $n>2k+1$) (since no bipartite graph contains an odd cycle). Erdős and Klein [Er38] proved $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_4)\asymp n^{3/2}$.

Erdős [Er64c] and Bondy and Simonovits [BoSi74] showed that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\ll kn^{1+\frac{1}{k}}.\]Benson [Be66] has proved this conjecture for $k=3$ and $k=5$. Lazebnik, Ustimenko, and Woldar [LUW95] have shown that, for arbitrary $k\geq 3$,\[\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\gg n^{1+\frac{2}{3k-3+\nu}},\]where $\nu=0$ if $k$ is odd and $\nu=1$ if $k$ is even. See [LUW99] for further history and references.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #573 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/573).

### Problem
Is it true that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;\{C_3,C_4\})\sim (n/2)^{3/2}?\]

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Simonovits, who proved that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;\{C_4,C_5\})=(n/2)^{3/2}+O(n).\]Kövári, Sós, and Turán [KST54] proved that the extremal number of edges for containing either $C_4$ or an odd cycle of any length is $\sim (n/2)^{3/2}$. ### Problem
Let $Q_k$ be the $k$-dimensional hypercube graph (so that $Q_k$ has $2^k$ vertices and $k2^{k-1}$ edges). Determine the behaviour of\[\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_k).\]

### Context
Erdős and Simonovits [ErSi70] proved that\[(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))n^{3/2}\leq \mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3) \ll n^{8/5}.\](In [ErSi70] they mention that Erdős had originally conjectured that $ \mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)\gg n^{5/3}$.) problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #583 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/583).

### Problem
Every connected graph on $n$ vertices can be partitioned into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint paths.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Gallai. If we drop the edge-disjoint condition then this conjecture was proved by Fan [Fa02].

There are many partial results towards this conjecture. We list some highlights below; $G$ is an arbitrary connected graph on $n$ vertices.- Lovász [Lo68] proved that $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edge-disjoint paths and cycles, and hence into at most $n-1$ paths. This also implies the original conjecture if $G$ has at most one vertex of even degree.
- Chung [Ch78] proved that $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint trees.
- Pyber [Py96] proved that $G$ can be covered by at most $n/2+O(n^{3/4})$ paths.
- Pyber [Py96] also proved the original conjecture if the subgraph induced by vertices of even degree is a forest.
- Bonamy and Perrett [BoPe19] proved the conjecture if $G$ has maximum degree $\leq 5$.
- Blanché, Bonamy, and Bonichon [BBB21] proved this conjecture if $G$ is planar.
- Anto and Basavaraju [AnBa23] proved the conjecture if $G$ is $2$-degenerate (every subgraph has a vertex of degree $\leq 2$).
- Chu, Fan, and Zhou [CFZ26] proved the conjecture if the subgraph induced by vertices of even degree is $K_m$ for some $m\leq 15$ and $n$ is odd.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: A problem of Erdős and Gallai. If we drop the edge-disjoint condition then this conjecture was proved by Fan [Fa02].

There are many partial results towards this conjecture. We list some highlights below; $G$ is an arbitrary connected graph on $n$ vertices.- Lovász [Lo68] proved that $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edge-disjoint paths and cycles, and hence into at most $n-1$ paths. This also implies the original conjecture if $G$ has at most one vertex of even degree. - Chung [Ch78] proved that $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint trees. - Pyber [Py96] proved that $G$ can be covered by at most $n/2+O(n^{3/4})$ paths. - Pyber [Py96] also proved the original conjecture if the subgraph induced by vertices of even degree is a forest. - Bonamy and Perrett [BoPe19] proved the conjecture if $G$ has maximum degree $\leq 5$. - Blanché, Bonamy, and Bonichon [BBB21] proved this conjecture if $G$ is planar. - Anto and Basavaraju [AnBa23] proved the conjecture if $G$ is $2$-degenerate (every subgraph has a vertex of degree $\leq 2$). - Chu, Fan, and Zhou [CFZ26] proved the conjecture if the subgraph induced by vertices of even degree is $K_m$ for some $m\leq 15$ and $n$ is odd.
Hajos [Lo68] has conjectured that if $G$ has all degrees even then $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edge-disjoint cycles.

sourceComments.contentMd:
A few remarks:

1) As far as I can tell, the best result without any further restrictions on $G$ comes from [this](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X99001673) paper by Dean and Kouider, where they show that $\left \lfloor \frac{2}{3}n \right \rfloor$ edge-disjoint paths suffice. This result even holds for disconnected graphs, in which case it is actually optimal. For those of us (including myself) thinking that this bound seems worse than the one by Pyber: note that Pyber's result does not require the paths to be edge-disjoint.

2) I found various sources claiming that Yan obtained the same upper bound of $\left \lfloor \frac{2}{3}n \right \rfloor$ in their PhD thesis titled *On path decompositions of graphs*, but I couldn't find it online.

3) I couldn't find this conjecture in [[ErGa59]](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1959-10.pdf), although it does of course contain related results. In fact, [ErGa59] of course predates [[Lo68]](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Laszlo-Lovasz/publication/268652766_On_covering_of_graphs/links/5e1465b7299bf10bc3967731/On-covering-of-graphs.pdf), while the aforementioned Dean-Kouider paper writes *The written history of these ideas begins with the paper by Lovász.*

4) The other page number is [[Er71, p. 101]](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1971-25.pdf).

5) Hajos is missing a diacritic.

L. Pyber in [[Py85]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02579444) has proved this conjecture for graphs whose even-degree vertices induce a forest.

M. Bonamy and T. J. Perrett in [[BoPe19]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X19300081) have proved this conjecture for graphs with maximum degree at most 5.

A. Blanche, M. Bonamy and N. Bonichon in [[BBB21]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08870) have proved this conjecture for planar graphs.

Y. Chu, G. Fan and Q. Liu in [[CFL21]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X20303988) have proved this conjecture for graphs with maximum degree at most 6 in which the vertices of maximum degree form an independent set (with some exceptions).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #584 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/584).

### Problem
Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices and $\delta n^{2}$ edges. Are there subgraphs $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ such that- $H_1$ has $\gg \delta^3n^2$ edges and every two edges in $H_1$ are contained in a cycle of length at most $6$, and furthermore if two edges share a vertex they are on a cycle of length $4$, and
- $H_2$ has $\gg \delta^2n^2$ edges and every two edges in $H_2$ are contained in a cycle of length at most $8$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Duke, and Rödl. Duke and Erdős [DuEr82] proved the first if $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $\delta$. The real challenge is to prove this when $\delta=n^{-c}$ for some $c>0$. Duke, Erdős, and Rödl [DER84] proved the first statement with a $\delta^5$ in place of a $\delta^3$.

Fox and Sudakov [FoSu08b] have proved the second statement when $\delta >n^{-1/5}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #585 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/585).

### Problem
What is the maximum number of edges that a graph on $n$ vertices can have if it does not contain two edge-disjoint cycles with the same vertex set?

### Context
Pyber, Rödl, and Szemerédi [PRS95] constructed such a graph with $\gg n\log\log n$ edges.

Chakraborti, Janzer, Methuku, and Montgomery [CJMM24] have shown that such a graph can have at most $n(\log n)^{O(1)}$ many edges. Indeed, they prove that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for any $k\geq 2$ there is a $c_k$ such that if a graph has $n$ vertices and at least $c_kn(\log n)^{C}$ many edges then it contains $k$ pairwise edge-disjoint cycles with the same vertex set.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #588 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/588).

### Problem
Let $f_k(n)$ be minimal such that if $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ have no $k+1$ points on a line then there must be at most $f_k(n)$ many lines containing at least $k$ points. Is it true that\[f_k(n)=o(n^2)\]for $k\geq 4$?

### Context
A generalisation of [[101]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/101) (which asks about $k=4$).

The restriction to $k\geq 4$ is necessary since Sylvester has shown that $f_3(n)= n^2/6+O(n)$. (See also Burr, Grünbaum, and Sloane [BGS74] and Füredi and Palásti [FuPa84] for constructions which show that $f_3(n)\geq(1/6+o(1))n^2$.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #589 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/589).

### Problem
Let $g(n)$ be maximal such that in any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no four points on a line there exists a subset on $g(n)$ points with no three points on a line. Estimate $g(n)$.

### Context
The trivial greedy algorithm gives $g(n)\gg n^{1/2}$. A similar question can be asked for a set with no $k$ points on a line, searching for a subset with no $l$ points on a line, for any $3\leq l<k$.

Erdős thought that $g(n) \gg n$, but in fact $g(n)=o(n)$, which follows from the density Hales-Jewett theorem proved by Furstenberg and Katznelson [FuKa91] (see [[185]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/185)).

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #592 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/592).

### Problem
Determine which countable ordinals $\beta$ have the property that, if $\alpha=\omega^{^\beta}$, then in any red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_\alpha$ there is either a red $K_\alpha$ or a blue $K_3$.

### Context
Such $\alpha$ (in other words, those such that $\alpha \to (\alpha,3)^2$) are called partition ordinals.- Specker [Sp57] proved this holds for $\beta=2$ and not for $3\leq \beta <\omega$.
- Chang [Ch72] proved this holds for $\beta=\omega$.
- Galvin and Larson [GaLa74] have shown that if $\beta\geq 3$ has this property then $\beta$ must be 'additively indecomposable', so that in particular $\beta=\omega^\gamma$ for some countable ordinal $\gamma$. Galvin and Larson conjecture that every $\beta\geq 3$ of this form has this property.
- Schipperus [Sc10] have proved this is holds if $\beta=\omega^\gamma$ in which $\gamma$ is a countable ordinal which is the sum of one or two indecomposable ordinals, and this fails to hold if $\gamma$ is the sum of four or more indecomposable ordinals.

The remaining open case appears to be when $\gamma$ is the sum of three indecomposable ordinals.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #596 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/596).

### Problem
For which graphs $G_1,G_2$ is it true that- for every $n\geq 1$ there is a graph $H$ without a $G_1$ but if the edges of $H$ are $n$-coloured then there is a monochromatic copy of $G_2$, and yet
- for every graph $H$ without a $G_1$ there is an $\aleph_0$-colouring of the edges of $H$ without a monochromatic $G_2$.

### Context

Whether this is true for $G_1=K_4$ and $G_2=K_3$ is the content of [[595]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/595).

Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.
