replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
In a highly experimental use, I have tried with [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/694e76f3-db0c-8010-b756-df434d9632d0) to assess the direction of the preprint (without judging the author one way or the other). I realize this more of an art than science...

First, we discussed the general background, such as the "almost all" result and known sieve heuristics. The main obstacle is identified: transitioning from "rare" to "impossible".

The paper's strategy is identified as studying the events $E_p(n) := \{ n \mod p^2 < p \}$ with vector of indicators $X_p(n) := 1_{E_p(n)}$. We want to compare the true joint law $P$ of $(X_p)_{p \leq X}$ to the product law $Q = \prod P_p$. The quantity to control is Kullback-Leibler divergence $D(P \parallel Q)$. The author then posited the Uniformity Hypothesis (UH) and strong Uniformity Hypothesis (sUH) which are bounds on $D(P \parallel Q)$. In particular, sUH is of importance that it should imply the finiteness of the exceptional set $E$ (Claim 1). Moreover, the author claims that either the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture or generalized Riemann Hypothesis imply sUH (Claim 2).

We then see that Claims 1 and 2 are the two main pieces to assess.

After thinking for over 15 minutes, ChatGPT assessed the two claims as follows.

$\textbf{Claim 1}$. The main claim here is Theorem 6.9, whose proof is only 4 lines (!) and invokes Borel-Cantelli. ChatGPT assessed the direction of the proof as:

"- Even a very strong average bound like $\Pr_{n\le x}(n\in E)\ll 1/(\log x)^{1+\varepsilon}$ would not by itself imply the deterministic set $E$ is finite; it would only say it’s sparse on average. The paper’s proof sketch invokes Borel–Cantelli in a way that (as written) seems to apply to a random sequence of sampled integers, not to the actual set of all exceptions.
- More fundamentally: with “independence-like” behavior, the heuristic size of the exceptional set is typically $\sim x/\log x$ (because $\prod_{p\le X}(1-1/p)\sim e^{-\gamma}/\log X$). Independence pushes you toward infinitely many exceptions, not finiteness. The paper is trying to conclude the opposite from an “almost-independence” hypothesis, which is already a big red flag relative to the mechanism it sets up."

Moreover, the proof of Theorem 6.9 claims bounds $\ll 1/(\log X)^{1+\varepsilon}$. ChatGPT sketched arguments that the actual machinery should give $\ll 1/(\log X)^{1-\varepsilon}$; even under "perfect independence" that'd only get you $\ll 1/\log X$.

Conclusion: the claimed exponent appears too strong from existing machinery, and, even if we do get this exponent, it's only an average bound and that doesn't bridge to finiteness. Moreover, the "almost-independence" heuristic seems to be going in the wrong direction.

$\textbf{Claim 2}$. The implication from EH/GRH to sUH.

ChatGPT argued this is problematic for a "simpler reason": the $N(x;q,b)$ is defined as the count of integers in a residue class. Since these counts and their second moments are already elementary, we do not need EH/GRH to control them. In fact, EH/GRH is about primes in arithmetic progressions and likely irrelevant here. In ChatGPT's words:

"“EH/GRH ⇒ strong second-moment control for primes in progressions” is true in the right context, and “second-moment control ⇒ small KL divergence” is a real information-theoretic theme (they even state a χ²/KL control via an energy functional).
But the paper’s specific EH/GRH ⇒ sUH claim doesn’t line up with the objects it defined (integer residue counts), and the modulus/scale issues are not resolved."

Conclusion: there could be some right conceptual ideas, but the connections to EH/GRH are likely irrelevant.

$\textbf{Overall}$. It seems to me that both claims are difficult to fix. EH/GRH is not likely to get to Uniformity because they don't seem to apply to this setting; on the other hand, Uniformity also doesn't seem to get to finiteness due to the kind of argument used.

As always, I write from my best understanding and do not claim accuracy in the chat's statements.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
Dear Colleagues,

I am seeking collaboration on the classical Erdős problem (Er79), particularly from an analytic number theory or sieve-theoretic perspective.

Recently, I submitted a manuscript entitled *“A Conditional Negative Resolution of Erdős’s Problem via the Entropy–Sieve Method”* to **Expositiones Mathematicae**.wich it is already was commented above by Prof Tao and  Prof Alfaiz, After review, the paper was rejected, with referees indicating that the results are still premature and require further development. The main concerns were the need for a clearer and earlier definition of the proposed *entropy sieve*, a substantial improvement in exposition, and stronger arguments beyond heuristic or probabilistic reasoning. An inconsistency was also noted in the abstract regarding the interpretation of a “negative answer” versus the finiteness of exceptional integers.

Despite these criticisms, the feedback suggests that the general direction may be promising if strengthened and clarified, especially under strong hypotheses such as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis or related uniformity assumptions. The referees also suggested that the method could become more convincing if concrete applications and rigorous implementations of the entropy–sieve framework are developed.

I am therefore looking for collaborators interested in refining the entropy–sieve approach, clarifying the logical structure of the argument, and exploring rigorous conditional or unconditional results related to Erdős-type additive problems involving prime squares. Any expertise in analytic methods, sieve theory, or related probabilistic techniques would be very welcome.

I would be glad to discuss these ideas further with interested researchers.

Kind regards,
**R. Zeraoulia**

Expositiones Mathematicae

Editor and Reviewer comments:  

The research results reported are too premature for publication. More work is needed to substantiate the conclusions in your manuscript.

The authors consider a new type of sieving argument, the so-called 'entropy sieve' and uses this to attack an old conjecture of Erdos. The conjecture is that every sufficient large $n$ should be expressible as n=ap^{2} + b for some a\geq 1, some prime p, and some remainder b satisfying 0\leq b <p.

We know that almost all such $n$ can be so written. The authors claim that the generalised Riemann hypothesis implies 'a negative answer' to Erdos's question. However, there is an inconsistency in the abstract: it is claimed that the negative answer is due to the fact that only finitely many $n$ cannot be represented in the desired way. This would in fact prove the statement.

Leaving aside this inconsistency, the article is very difficult to read and would benefit from a thorough re-writing. In particular, the 'entropy-sieve' should be defined much earlier than Section 7. Moreover, it is hard to see what the entropy sieve does beyond making probabilistic/heuristic conjectures. Given that the authors list some future applications and developments of the entropy sieve, I suggest that they implement these now, make the exposition much clearer, and submit to a number-theoretic specific journal (perhaps Journal of Number Theory).

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
Greeting! I would like to share a recent attempt on [[79]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/79) (quadratic prime representations).

In my preprint I introduce an **Entropy--Sieve Method**, which combines sieve theory with information-theoretic tools (relative entropy/KL divergence and a quadratic energy functional). The key reduction shows that finiteness of the exceptional set may follow if one can establish the uniformity estimate\[
E_2(P) \;=\; \frac{1+o(1)}{M},
\qquad M=\prod_{p\le Y} p^2,
\]for the quadratic energy of the residue distribution. A change-of-measure argument via KL divergence then transforms this into a sharp tail bound for the sieve sum.

What is important here is that this framework isolates precisely the analytic input needed: if the above uniformity holds, then the \emph{exceptional set} $E$ (integers with no quadratic prime representation) is finite. In other words, only finitely many large integers could fail Erdős's representation. This directly addresses the central question of [[79]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/79). Our numerical experiments further confirm that many large numbers remain outside the representable set, showing that unconditional tools do not yet shrink $E$ to finite --- highlighting both the sharpness of our reduction and the difficulty of the problem.

Thus, our contribution is twofold: (i) it provides a conditional path to prove finiteness of $E$ under standard distributional conjectures (EH or GRH), and (ii) it clarifies why unconditional finiteness is still out of reach, since in practice large integers without representation persist far beyond current analytic barriers.

\textbf{Preprint:}
[ResearchGate link](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/395665344_ENTROPY-SIEVE_METHODS_AND_ENERGY_FUNCTIONALS_IN_THE_ERDOS_PROBLEM_ER79_ON_QUADRATIC_PRIME_REPRESENTATIONS),
DOI: [10.13140/RG.2.2.14599.05283](https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.14599.05283).

I would be especially grateful for feedback on two delicate analytic points:

1. The explicit derivation and control of the divisor-weights $w(q,M)$ in the variance decomposition.
2. The uniform lower bound $Q_r \gg 1/M$ required when passing from $\chi^2$ divergence to KL divergence.

Any references or suggestions regarding these aspects, or about related treatments of primes modulo $p^2$, would be very welcome.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Related to the setting of Selfridge and Wagstaff where the condition of primes isn't there;
If one considers
$\prod_{2 \le x \le \sqrt n} (1-1/x) =1/\sqrt(n)$,
then under some intuitive independence of chances, similar as above, one expects roughly $2n^{1/2}$ numbers up to $n$ that are not of the desired form.

Since one may expect some positive correlation (if it is small modulo $16^2$, it is with chances $1/4$ small $32^2$),
$2n^{1/2}$ is even a lower bound.

I think it is these type of estimates one wants to make rigourous,
or at least a lower bound on the number of solutions not of that form,
and not a particular construction.

For $c_n$; $c_n>3/2$ does not make sense allowing $p=2$, so there should be a more subtle question there, where the bound on $b$ is e.g. a $p^{1+o(1)}$ bound.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: Indeed, there is no doubt that the answer is negative. Good candidates for numbers that cannot be expressed as such are 3, 35, 899, and in general any number that is one less than than the square of a primorial. Any ideas as to how to prove this rigorously?

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
For $p$ small, and $n$ arbitrary, the chances that $n \pmod {p^2} $<$p$ (representant in $[0,p^2[$) is $\frac 1p.$

Thus for large $n$ arbitrary, the chance could be guessed to be (assuming some independence of the chances)
$$\prod_{p \le \sqrt n} (1-1/p) \sim 2\exp(-\gamma)/ \log n.$$
The sieve methods verify one side of this intuition in rough sense.

For a fixed value of $n$, chances are small.
But ranging over intervals, many solutions can be expected.

In particular, hte proposed numbers are not that much better than others (only slightly better).
All you know is that for $(p_k\#)^2-1$, there is such form involving a prime $p_i$ with $i\le k$ (but many larger primes remain)

So just as confirmation that the primorials do not work that often;
$n=(11\#)^2-1=5336099$ satisfies $n \equiv 3\pmod{289}$
, $n=(17\#)^2-1 \equiv 7159 \pmod{16651^2}$ and
$n=(19\#)^2-1=94083986096099 \equiv 2133 \pmod{3469^2}.$
The next ones fail modulo $31^2, 211^2, 353^2$ and
$197^2$ resp., and so do many larger ones.

### Problem
Let $M(n,k)=[n+1,\ldots,n+k]$ be the least common multiple of $\{n+1,\ldots,n+k\}$.

Is it true that for all $m\geq n+k$\[M(n,k) \neq M(m,k)?\]

sourceComments.contentMd:
I believe the stronger version is false. For every $n$, let $p_1p_2\cdots p_{m-1}$ be the largest primorial less than $n$, and let $k=n-p_1p_2\cdots p_{m-1}<p_1p_2\cdots p_m$. Then, $\omega(n-k)=m-1$, and $\log k<\vartheta(p_m)<m\left(\log m+\log\log m-1+o(1)\right)$, where $\vartheta$ is the Chebyshev function, so $\frac{\log k}{\log\log k}<\frac{\vartheta(p_m)}{\log\vartheta(p_m)}<\frac{m\left(\log m+\log\log m-1+o(1)\right)}{\log m+\log\log m+(1+o(1))\frac{\log\log m}{\log m}}<m-C$ for any constant $C$ for large $m$.

replies.contentMd:
Aristotle has [formalized](https://gist.github.com/llllvvuu/29912cd94579163bda36b094b4cb4c8b) the implication from this asymptotic expansion.

EDIT: I noticed that the way Aristotle used the asymptotic seemed weakenable to the asymptotic already proved in PNT+, so I swapped it out and re-ran Aristotle on the one lemma that used it, and it still went through.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Nice!  I was sure that one needed both $\vartheta(x) = x + o(x / \log x)$ and $p_n = n \log n + n \log\log n - n + o(n)$, both of which require a medium strength version of PNT, but indeed just knowing $p_n = (1+o(1)) n \log n$ (weak PNT) is enough because this gives $\log p_n = \log n + \log\log n + o(1)$ which is enough to give $\vartheta(p_n) = n \log n + n \log\log n - n + o(n)$ (which is what is needed here) even without the two stronger asymptotics for $\vartheta$ and $p_n$.  So I can honestly say I learned something from Aristotle; a minor thing to be sure, but still useful. (This formalization was previously recorded in Section 6 of the wiki, but I have moved it to Section 3 because of this.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #680 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/680).

### Problem
Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there exists some $k$ such that\[p(n+k)>k^2+1,\]where $p(m)$ denotes the least prime factor of $m$?

Can one prove this is false if we replace $k^2+1$ by $e^{(1+\epsilon)\sqrt{k}}+C_\epsilon$, for all $\epsilon>0$, where $C_\epsilon>0$ is some constant?

### Context
This follows from 'plausible assumptions on the distribution of primes' (as does the question with $k^2$ replaced by $k^d$ for any $d$); the challenge is to prove this unconditionally.

Erdős observed that Cramer's conjecture\[\limsup_{k\to \infty} \frac{p_{k+1}-p_k}{(\log k)^2}=1\]implies that for all $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$ there exists some $k$ such that\[p(n+k)>e^{(1-\epsilon)\sqrt{k}}.\]There is now evidence, however, that Cramer's conjecture is false; a more refined heuristic by Granville [Gr95] suggests this $\limsup$ is $2e^{-\gamma}\approx 1.119\cdots$, and so perhaps the $1+\epsilon$ in the second question should be replaced by $2e^{-\gamma}+\epsilon$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
This should be accessible with sieve methods (Maynard/Chen-style). I did some back and forth with GPT-5.2 and here's where's the difficulty lies. First of all note that if $n+1$ is composite then one may take $k=1$, since $p(n+1)\geq 2>1=k^2$. Thus the only potentially difficult values are $n=p-1$ with $p$ prime. Any admissible witness must satisfy $k^4<n+k$, hence $k\leq n^{1/4}+O(1)$, and it is natural to search on a dyadic block $K<k\leq 2K$ with $K=n^\alpha$ and $\alpha<1/4$, so that $k^2\leq 4K^2$.

Fix $\alpha\in(0,1/4)$, put $K=n^\alpha$ and $y=4K^2$, and consider the short interval $I=(n+K,n+2K]$. A sufficient condition is the existence of a composite $m\in I$ with $p(m)>y$ (then $m=n+k$ for some $k\in(K,2K]$ and $p(m)>y\geq k^2$). The sieve heuristic for $y$-rough numbers predicts $\#\{m\in I:p(m)>y\}\approx K\,\omega(u)/\log y$ with $u=\log n/\log y$ and Buchstab function $\omega$, while $\#\{m\in I:m\ \textrm{prime}\}\approx K/\log n$; since $u\omega(u)>1$ for $u>2$ (equivalently $\alpha<1/4$), the heuristic main term already suggests that $I$ should contain composite $y$-rough values. However, existing pointwise sieve methods do not currently yield such a uniform lower bound in a single length-$K$ interval when $y\asymp K^2$, because the lower linear sieve requires sieve level $R>y^2$ whereas one only has trivial remainder control for divisibility in a fixed short interval.

Unconditionally, an averaging-over-$p$ substitute appears accessible: one may sieve the primes $p\in[X,2X]$ with $K=X^\alpha$ and $y=4K^2$ using Rosser--Iwaniec linear sieve weights and the Bombieri--Vinogradov theorem (level $1/2$) to obtain a positive lower bound for the mean of $R(p)=\#\{K<k\leq 2K:(p-1+k,P(y))=1\}$ provided $s=(\log R)/(\log y)>2$. Taking $R=X^{1/4-\varepsilon}$ and $y=X^{2\alpha}$ gives $s\approx 1/(8\alpha)$, so $s>2$ holds for any fixed $\alpha<1/16$, and a standard second-moment argument (with singular series averaging as in Gallagher) then yields $R(p)\gg K/\log X$ for all but $o(\pi(X))$ primes $p\in[X,2X]$. Since primes in $(p+K,p+2K]$ contribute only $\asymp K/\log X$, one obtains for almost all such primes $p$ a shift $k\in(K,2K]$ with $p-1+k$ composite and $p(p-1+k)>k^2$. References for the sieve ingredients include J. Friedlander and H. Iwaniec, Opera de Cribro (2010), and D. R. Heath-Brown, Lectures on sieves (2002); improving the exponent toward $\alpha=1/4$ would require new distribution input beyond Bombieri--Vinogradov.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #683 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/683).

### Problem
Is it true that for every $1\leq k\leq n$ the largest prime divisor of $\binom{n}{k}$, say $P(\binom{n}{k})$, satisfies\[P\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)\geq \min(n-k+1, k^{1+c})\]for some constant $c>0$?

### Context
A theorem of Sylvester and Schur (see [Er34]) states that $P(\binom{n}{k})>k$ if $k\leq n/2$. Erdős [Er55d] proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that, whenever $k\leq n/2$,\[P\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)\gg k\log k.\]Erdős [Er79d] writes it 'seems certain' that this holds for every $c>0$, with only a finite number of exceptions (depending on $c$). Standard heuristics on prime gaps suggest that the largest prime divisor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is, for $k\leq n/2$, in fact\[>e^{c\sqrt{k}}\]for some constant $c>0$.

This is essentially equivalent to [[961]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/961).

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
It seems easy to construct a counterexample to the main problem.
Take $n=2^t$ and $k=n-1$ $(t\geq2)$. Then $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{2^t}{1}=2^t$, so $P\!\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)=2$.
Moreover $\min(n-k+1,\;k^{1+c})=\min(2,(2^t-1)^{1+c})=2$.
Hence $P\!\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)=2\not>2$,
so $(n,k)=(2^t,2^t-1)$ is a counterexample for every $c>0$.

It seems as an infinite series of counterexamples to the main problem? Or I've missed/misunderstood something.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Given the Sylvester-Schur theorem and the symmetry $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}$, it seems likely here that Erdos intended to write $\geq \min(n-k+1, \dots)$ here instead of $> \min(n-k,\dots)$ (or alternatively, to drop the "+1").

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
As Tao points out, this is just a typo - really the annoying $n-k+1$ term is just to handle $n/2<k\leq n$ in a non-trivial way. One should really view these problems as restricted to $k\leq n/2$.

As mentioned, this is just the same as [[961]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/961) (which is stated without binomial coefficients). Including both was an oversight on my part, but it feels like it would mess up too much to remove this one now.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #684 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/684).

### Problem
For $0\leq k\leq n$ write\[\binom{n}{k} = uv\]where the only primes dividing $u$ are in $[2,k]$ and the only primes dividing $v$ are in $(k,n]$.

Let $f(n)$ be the smallest $k$ such that $u>n^2$. Give bounds for $f(n)$.

### Context
A classical theorem of Mahler states that for any $\epsilon>0$ and integers $k$ and $l$ then, writing\[(n+1)\cdots (n+k) = ab\]where the only primes dividing $a$ are $\leq l$ and the only primes dividing $b$ are $>l$, we have $a < n^{1+\epsilon}$ for all sufficiently large (depending on $\epsilon,k,l$) $n$.

Mahler's theorem implies $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, but is ineffective, and so gives no bounds on the growth of $f(n)$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
Since many people are now using AI to explore problems on this site, I tried this problem using ChatGPT-5.2 Thinking and obtained a nontrivial upper bound:\[f(n)\le \Bigl\lceil n^{\frac{12}{17}+\varepsilon}\Bigr\rceil \qquad (\forall\,\varepsilon>0,\ n\ge n_0(\varepsilon)).\]A full write-up is in [this note](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-684-note/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_684.pdf).

Verification.
I audited the final lemma--proof write-up in multiple fresh and independent sessions of ChatGPT-5.2 Thinking. All audits agreed that the proof is logically correct, up to minor presentational clarifications.
EDIT: I have also carefully reviewed the proof myself and found no issues with it.

How the result was obtained.
The entire derivation was produced by the AI model, without human intervention in the mathematical reasoning or idea generation. I repeatedly asked ChatGPT-5.2 Thinking for stronger unconditional upper bounds for $f(n)$: it started from a basic bound $f(n)\le n/2$ and was iteratively strengthened, eventually yielding the polynomial improvement above. Moreover, I have only now realized that in order to reach the bound \(f(n)\le n^{12/17+o(1)},\) I did in fact perform some human intervention that required a fair amount of luck. Here is a brief summary of what happened.

In [Problem 684_v1](https://chatgpt.com/share/696f30fd-c98c-8009-a91b-181d82bf497e), the model obtained the bound $f(n)=o(n)$. In [Problem 684_v3](https://chatgpt.com/share/696f314c-b328-8009-97a9-51857a76a6cd), after it produced the upper bound \(f(n) \le n\exp(-c_1(\log n)^{3/5}(\log\log n)^{-1/5}),\) I asked whether one could obtain an even stronger bound. It then ''thought'' for a long time but ended up outputting nothing. However, I carefully read through its internal reasoning and noticed what looked like a promising line of thought that could lead to \(f(n)\le n^{12/17+\varepsilon}.\) I therefore copied and pasted that portion into a file [684_v5.txt](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-684-note/blob/main/684_v5.txt), uploaded it in [Problem 684_v2](https://chatgpt.com/share/696f3127-ffe8-8009-8f3c-bbe7e6133491), and told the model: "The txt file I am sending you contains a brainstorming attempt by another LLM on this problem. Please see whether that brainstorm can lead to meaningful progress on the upper bound for $f(n)$." After that, it produced an initial proof of \(f(n)\le n^{12/17+\varepsilon}.\)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Yes, this looks sensible. To summarise here for convenience, the observation is that\[\log v(n,k)=\sum_{k<p\leq n}\log p\sum_{j\geq 1}1_{n\pmod{p^j}<k},\]and assuming the indicator function here to be binomial with probability $k/p^j$ gives the heuristic\[\log v(n,k)=k\sum_{k<p\leq n}\frac{\log p}{p-1}=k\log(n/k)+o(k).\]Since $\log\binom{n}{k}=k\log(n/k)+k+O(\log k)$ by Stirling, this means we expect $u>n^2$, i.e. $\log\binom{n}{k}-\log v>2\log n$, at $k\sim 2\log n$.

This certainly makes sense as an 'average' observation, but I do worry that the worst case behaviour (which is the problem here) might behave a little different - one can imagine some conspiracy between $n$ and 'medium-range' primes which forces $v$ to be measurably larger than this suggests. There is also a suspicious spike in the numerical data you give at $n\approx 10^5$, much higher than the predicted $2\log n$.

It might be that $f(n)\sim 2\log n$ for almost all $n$, but perhaps for infinitely many $n$ we have $f(n)\gg (\log n)^2$, say.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Further computation supports $f(n)$ is possibly $\Theta(\log n)$. I have updated [the note](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1uFbL9utjqQORMs06hL2pJBxX9UPowJHD/view?usp=sharing), which has a new plot.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Some more updates. Numerics suggests perhaps $\liminf f(n)/\log n \approx 1$ and $\limsup f(n)/\log n \approx 8$. So I was curious what these values are.

[ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/697224f4-d4e8-8010-8c09-a7060492ab90) gives some heuristic based on random walk that the $\limsup$ might be the solution of $c_* D(2/c_* || 1/2) = 1$, which is $c_* \approx 7.88$. But it also said that such model gives $\liminf \ge 2$, so the model cannot explain the $\liminf$.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
Since we have reduced the problem to the $N$ being square case, it turns out there is some interesting literature concerning $n=0$, i.e. binomial coefficients that are squares.

Lucas' [square-pyramid problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_problem) shows that $\binom{50}{3} = 140^2$ is the only nontrivial solution when $k=3$ ($n=0$, square $N$).

Erdos [proved](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/778233/is-there-any-perfect-squares-that-are-also-binomial-coefficients) that $\binom{m}{k} = n^\ell$ has no solution when $\ell \ge 2$ and $4 \le k \le m-4$. This rules out $k \ge 4$ as well.

Hence, $N = 140^2$ is the *only* square with a representation with $k \ge 3$ and $n=0$.

sourceComments.author: MalekZ
sourceComments.contentMd:
Following up with a small amount of computational data for Problem 686.

For 'k=3', writing 'X = m+2' and 'Y = n+2' gives

'X^3 - X = N(Y^3 - Y).'

Using SageMath's 'EllipticCurve_from_cubic' with the rational point '(1:1:1)', I obtained the following Weierstrass models:

| 'N' | Cremona label | rank | torsion |
|---|---|---|---|
| '4' | '135a1' | '1' | trivial |
| '9' | '19440s1' | '2' | trivial |
| '16' | '9180a1' | '2' | trivial |
| '25' | '140400dd1' | '2' | trivial |
| '49' | '105840cu1' | '2' | trivial |
| '64' | '16380d1' | '2' | 'Z/2Z' |
| '81' | conductor '797040' | '3' | trivial |

All seven curves have positive rank. On the original cubic, a direct search for 'Y in [-50,500]' gives:

- 'N=9': admissible point '(X,Y) = (27,13)', i.e. '(m,n) = (25,11)'.
- 'N=16': admissible point '(X,Y) = (15,6)', i.e. '(m,n) = (13,4)'.
- 'N=4': the nontrivial point '(X,Y) = (3,2)', but it is not admissible.
- 'N in {25,49,64,81}': only the 9 trivial points '{-1,0,1}^2'.

Important caveat: the birational map to the Weierstrass model does not preserve integrality in general. For example, the known 'N=16' solution '(X,Y) = (15,6)' maps to a non-integral Weierstrass point. So integral points on the Weierstrass model do not by themselves prove non-representability on the original cubic.

For 'k=5' and 'N=4', let

'F(t) = (t+1)(t+2)(t+3)(t+4)(t+5).'

Then 'F(x) = 4F(y)' has no rational points at infinity, since this would require a rational root of 'u^5 - 4', which is irreducible over 'Q'. A brute-force search for '|x|, |y| <= 10000' finds only the 25 trivial zero-product points '{-5,-4,-3,-2,-1}^2', and no admissible solutions.

A congruence obstruction also cannot prove non-representability here. For every modulus 'M', the congruence

'F(m) ≡ 4F(n) (mod M)'

has admissible solutions with 'm >= n+5': for 'M >= 5', take 'n = M-1' and 'm = 3M-5', so 'F(n) ≡ F(m) ≡ 0 (mod M)' and 'm-n = 2M-4 >= 6'; for 'M <= 4', the pair '(n,m) = (0,5)' already works.

For 'N=4', this leaves the following status:

| 'k' | status | method |
|---|---|---|
| '2' | not representable | Tao |
| '3' | no admissible solution found for 'Y <= 500' | direct search on 'X^3-X = 4(Y^3-Y)'; '135a1' has rank '1' |
| '4' | not representable | natso26 |
| '5' | no admissible solution found for '|x|,|y| <= 10000' | direct search; no congruence obstruction exists |
| '6' | not representable | Vjeko |

AI disclosure: the computations were run in SageMath/CoCalc. The computational claims above were checked by me.

|---|---|---|
| 4 | '135a1', rank '1' | only nontrivial point found was '(X,Y)=(3,2)', not admissible |
| 9 | '19440s1', rank '2' | admissible point '(27,13)' giving 'm=25, n=11' |
| 16 | '9180a1', rank '2' | admissible point '(15,6)' giving 'm=13, n=4' |
| 25 | '140400dd1', rank '2' | no admissible point found in my search |
| 49 | '105840cu1', rank '2' | no admissible point found in my search |
| 64 | '16380d1', rank '2' | no admissible point found in my search |
| 81 | rank '3' on a Weierstrass model | no admissible point found in my search |

The important caveat is that my first proof strategy here was wrong: the birational map from the cubic 'X^3-X=N(Y^3-Y)' to a Weierstrass model does not preserve integrality in general. For example, for 'N=16', the admissible cubic point '(15,6)' maps to a non-integral point on the Weierstrass model. So 'integral_points()' on the Weierstrass model is not enough to prove that the original cubic has no admissible integer points.

What I can say safely is:

1. These 'k=3' curves all have positive rank, so the obstruction is not “no rational points.”
2. A brute-force search on the original cubic found the expected admissible points for 'N=9,16'.
3. The same search found no admissible points for 'N=4,25,49,64,81' up to my search bounds ('Y <= 500', and separately 'n <= 50,000').

So this is only computational evidence, not a proof, for the stuck values at 'k=3'.

If anyone knows a clean way to compute integral points directly on the cubic model 'X^3-X=N(Y^3-Y)' for these specific 'N' (for example via MAGMA on the cubic itself, or via a systematic reduction to Thue equations), I would be interested.

Disclosure: I used computer algebra / database lookup for the elliptic-curve identifications and brute-force search on the original cubic. The failed “integral points on the Weierstrass model imply integral points on the cubic” argument was caught before posting.

sourceComments.author: MalekZ
sourceComments.contentMd:
Building on natso26's results on exact $k$th-power multipliers and Vjeko Kovač's
computational data, I'd like to note two observations.

**1. An infinite family of representable perfect squares.**

For every $n \geq 0$, the perfect square $N = 4(2n+3)^2$ is representable with $k = 2$.
Set $m = (2n+3)^2 - 2$. Then:

$$\frac{(m+1)(m+2)}{(n+1)(n+2)} = \frac{((2n+3)^2 - 1) \cdot (2n+3)^2}{(n+1)(n+2)} = \frac{4(n+1)(n+2) \cdot (2n+3)^2}{(n+1)(n+2)} = 4(2n+3)^2.$$

The key step is the factorization $(2n+3)^2 - 1 = 4(n+1)(n+2)$, which creates exact
cancellation. The non-overlap condition $m \geq n + 2$ holds for all $n \geq 0$.

This gives $N = 36, 100, 196, 324, 484, 676, 900, 1156, \ldots$ — all perfect squares,
all representable. Additional representable perfect squares arise from Pell equation
families (e.g., $N = 1225 = 35^2$ via $49 \cdot 50 / (1 \cdot 2)$, and $N = 9801 = 99^2$
via $242 \cdot 243 / (2 \cdot 3)$).

In particular, the obstruction for $\{4, 25, 49, 64, 81\}$ cannot be simply "perfect
powers are not representable."

**2. Computational extension: perfect powers up to 10,000.**

I ran a systematic search over all perfect powers $N \leq 10{,}000$ with $k \leq 80$
and $n \leq 1000$. Results:

- **Representable** (39 values): $8, 9, 16, 27, 32, 36, 100, 125, 196, 216, 243, 324, 343, 484, 676, 900, 1000, 1156, 1225, 1331, 1444, 1764, 2048, 2116, 2197, 2500, 2916, 3364, 3844, 4356, 4900, 5476, 6084, 6724, 7396, 8100, 8836, 9604, 9801$

- **Not representable within search bounds** (85 values): $4, 25, 49, 64, 81, 121, 128, 144, 169, 225, 256, 289, 361, 400, 441, 512, 529, 576, 625, 729, \ldots$

All representable perfect powers found representations with $k = 2$ (some also with
$k = 3$). No perfect power that failed at $k = 2$ was rescued by a larger $k$ within
the search bounds.

Among perfect squares specifically: the representable square roots include
$3, 4, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, 35, \ldots$ while non-representable square roots
include $2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15, \ldots$. The $4(2n+3)^2$ family accounts for
the regular spacing (roots $\equiv 2 \pmod{4}$ starting from 6), while the Pell families
contribute sporadic additional values (35, 99, $\ldots$).

**Open question:** Is there a clean characterization of which perfect powers are
representable? The data suggests the answer depends on solvability of specific
generalized Pell equations for $k = 2$, but I don't see a simple closed-form criterion.

---

**Some speculative directions (not verified, flagging for discussion):**

- The Khanduja-Bhatia irreducibility criterion suggests that
  $f_k(x) - N \cdot f_k(y)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$
  whenever $N$ is not a perfect $d$th power for any $d \mid k$
  with $d \geq 2$. If correct, this would mean the curve
  $C_{k,N}: f_k(x) = N \cdot f_k(y)$ is irreducible for
  non-perfect-power $N$, and genus bounds (Faltings for $k \geq 4$,
  Siegel for $k = 3$) give per-$k$ finiteness. Does this observation
  survive scrutiny?

- The computational data shows no perfect power that failed at
  $k = 2$ was rescued by any larger $k \leq 80$. Is there a
  structural reason why $k = 2$ should be the "best chance" for
  perfect powers, or could larger $k$ eventually succeed?

- By Kummer's theorem, the problem can be rephrased in terms of
  carry-count differences in base-$p$ arithmetic. Is there a
  characterization of which valuation profiles $(v_p(N))_p$ are
  achievable as such differences across all $(k, m, n)$?

---

*Disclosure: This work used a multi-model AI pipeline (Claude for analysis and
orchestration, GPT-5.4 for mathematical reasoning). The algebraic identity was
discovered by pattern recognition in computational output, then verified by hand.
All mathematical content has been checked by me.
Thanks in advance.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
Building on Tao's and vilc's results based on Chan's and Bennett's papers, GPT-5.4 Thinking has extended the $k=3$ results as follows. Here is [the writeup](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YmV9oWARnUW2pGY7tP_BWuhSOreiquCS/view).

- For square $N\le 100$ and $k=3$: $N = 9, 16$ are representable, while $N = 4, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100$ are NOT representable.

- For general $N\le 20$ and $k=3$: $N = 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20$ are representable, while $N = 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 15, 17$ are NOT representable.

- Also, $N = 27$ and $k=3$ is NOT representable. (Cubic $N$ are easier to prove.)

Among these $N = 25, 100$ are especially difficult from the computational perspective.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Current status: We now know that $N = 4, 25, 49, 64, 81$ cannot be represented when $k \le 4$.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
Speaking of special cases, $N=64$ cannot be represented using $k=6$. Namely, expanding into a series and estimating errors explicitly, we get\[ \big((m+1)\cdots(m+6)\big)^{1/6} = m + \frac{7}{2} + f(m), \quad |f(m)|\leq\frac{2}{m}, \]\[ \big(64(n+1)\cdots(n+6)\big)^{1/6} = 2n + 7 + g(n), \quad |g(n)|\leq\frac{3}{n}. \]Therefore, if these two are equal, then $f(m)-g(n)+\frac{1}{2}\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since the equation also forces $2n-6\leq m\leq 2n+12$, we see that it is sufficient to check the cases, say, $0\leq m,n\leq100$, which is easily done.

A very similar idea was used in vilc's post. As mentioned there, in principle it takes a finite amount of computation to rule out any particular pair $(N,k)$, where $N$ is a perfect $k$-th power. Thus, numbers like $N=u^{v!}$ have very slim chances of being representable, but some effective variants of Siegel's theorem would likely be needed to rule out the cases $k>v$.

replies.author: vilc
replies.contentMd:
More generally, here is an explicit bound on $n$ when $N = a^k$. For $n \geq 1$ and $k \geq 2$:
$$n + \dfrac{k-1}{2} - \dfrac{k^2 - 1}{24n} < (n(n+1) \ldots (n+k-1))^{1/k} < n + \dfrac{k-1}{2} - \dfrac{k^2 - 1}{24n} + \dfrac{(k^2-1)(k-1)}{48n^2}$$
Applying these to $n$ and $m$, one can show the following disjunction:
- If $n\leq \dfrac{2k}{3}$ and one of $a, k$ is odd, then $m = an + \dfrac{(a-1)(k-1)}{2}$ may be a solution.
- Else, if one of $a, k$ is odd then $n < \dfrac{a(k^2 - 1)}{24}$
- Else $n < \dfrac{a(k^2 - 1)}{12}$
(the bound $n\leq \tfrac{2k}{3}$ in the first case could be marginally improved to $n\leq ck$ for some $c$ dependant on $a$ but greater than $\tfrac{1}{2}$)
We can get a lower bound on $n$ using some elementary arithmetic.
Assume that $a\geq 2$ is such that $N=a^k$ is representable for $k$. If $p$ is prime and $p^l \mid a$ then $p^{lk} \leq C_k a^2$, where $C_k = max(k, \tfrac{(k^2 + 9k - 4)}{12})$ [EDIT : fixed typo, thanks natso26].
Proof :
One has $v_p(n(n+1) \ldots (n+k-1)) \geq v_p(k!)$ for any $n \geq 1$. Moreover, if $p^j$ is the largest power of $p$ which divides one of $m, m+1, \ldots, m+k-1$, then $v_p(m(m+1) \ldots (m+k-1)) \leq j + v_p((k-1)!)$. This implies that :
$$v_p(N) = v_p(m(m+1) \ldots (m+k-1)) - v_p(n(n+1) \ldots (n+k-1)) \leq j - v_p(k) \leq j$$
Since $p^l$ divides $a$, we get $lk \leq j$, so $p^{lk} \leq m + k - 1$. Based on the above disjunction, one has (since $a \geq 2$):
- either $m+k-1 \leq ak + \dfrac{(a+1)(k-1)}{2} < 2ak \leq k a^2$
- or $m + k - 1 < a(n+k) + k - 1 \leq a\left(\dfrac{a(k^2 - 1)}{12} + k\right) + k - 1 \leq \dfrac{a^2(k^2 + 9k - 4)}{12}$
This completes the proof.
When $a = p^l$ is a prime power and $k \geq 3$, one has $a \leq C_k^{\tfrac{1}{k-2}}$. But it is easily verified that if $k \geq 5$, $C_k^{\tfrac{1}{k-2}} < 2$ ( $<3$ for $k = 4$, $<4$ for $k=3$). Therefore, since the remaining cases for small $k$ were already covered, if $a$ is a prime power, then $a^k$ is not representable with $k$ (this can be generalised easily to cases where $\omega(a)$ is small enough compared to $k$).

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Small typo: $C_k = \max(k, \frac{k^2+9k-4}{12})$ (without the $a^2$).

Thanks Vjeko and vilc for great results! In particular, we now know that it is possible to avoid $k$-representation for any $k$ in a finite set by using $N = p^{v!}$, $p$ prime and $v$ large.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Another typo: the first displayed equation should have $-\frac{k^2-1}{24n}$ instead of $-\frac{k^2-1}{2n}$ (two places).

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
GPT-5.4 Thinking has expanded vilc's argument into [this note](https://drive.google.com/file/d/16S_vIEg8iBykfopaxtw5_qfZFS-gaVfA/view).

Technically it was concurrent work that started before vilc's post, but later they merged. The note's calculations are slightly stronger. Moreover, we state an explicit generalization for $k > 2\omega(a)$ as follows:

Fix $r \ge 1$ and a finite set $S$ such that $k > 2r$ for every $k \in S$. Then for all sufficiently large $a$ with $\omega(a) \le r$, we have that $N = a^{\text{lcm}(S)}$ is not $k$-representable for any $k \in S$.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
In fact, a similar trick can often rule out a perfect square $N$ (which are all numbers we care about) and an even $k$. Let me only sketch that $N=4$ is not representable using $k=6$.
Now we expand\[ 8\big((m+1)\cdots(m+6)\big)^{1/2} = 8m^3 + 84m^2 + 259m + \frac{441}{2} + O\Big(\frac{1}{m}\Big), \]\[ 8\big(4(n+1)\cdots(n+6)\big)^{1/2} = 16n^3 + 168n^2 + 518n + 441 + O\Big(\frac{1}{n}\Big). \]In all but finitely many cases of $(m,n)$ we arrive at a contradiction with $O(1/m)-O(1/n)+1/2\in\mathbb{Z}$.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
The $k=2$ case is now settled by GPT-5.4 Thinking with near-autonomous process in [this note](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cxyR_5oIs9o9tV8XlgfURJhE0sNUJnRf/view). The solution uses Pell theory.

Combined with the previously known non-square $N$ case, the classification of representable $N$ for $k=2$ is as follows.

1. $N$ is non-square.
2. $N=a^2$, where $a = A_r(y)$ for some odd integer $y \ge 3$ and integer $r \ge 2$, and $A_r(y)$ is defined by $(y + \sqrt{y^2-1})^r = X_r(y) + A_r(y) \sqrt{y^2-1}$.

The first few polynomials $A_r(y)$ are: $A_2(y) = 2y$, $A_3(y) = 4y^2-1$, $A_4(y) = 4y(2y^2-1)$, coinciding with known parametrizations.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
I also note that $k=4$ cannot give any more representable $N$: if $(m,n)$ is a solution for $N$ and $k=4$, then $((m^2+5m)/2+1, (n^2+5n)/2+1)$ is a solution for $N$ and $k=2$.

However, finding all representable $N$ for $k=4$ appears tricky. On the plus side, Vjeko has linked a [paper by Cohn](https://msp.org/pjm/1971/37-2/p05.xhtml) which shows that $N=2$ is not representable for $k=4$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The [paper of Chan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01306) Vjeko found by literature seach shows that for any fixed $N$ and $k=3$ there are only finitely many solutions.  Here is the proof sketch, using the current notation. Writing $m+1 = Dv$ and $n+1 = Du$ where $D$ is the greatest common divisor of $m+1,n+1$, the equation can be rewritten as
$$ D^2 (v^3 - N u^3) = v - Nu.$$
Since $v-Nu$ already divides $v^3 - N^3 u^3$, the gcd of $v-Nu$ and $v^3-Nu^3$ must divide $N^3-N$ and hence $v^3 - N u^3$ also divides $N^3 - N$.  If $N$ is a perfect cube we are already done by the gaps between cubes.  Otherwise, we get a Diophantine approximation $v/u = N^{1/3} + O(u^{-3})$ which, when combined with the Thue-Siegel-Roth theorem, gives an ineffective bound on $u,v$.  Using instead a Baker type theorem one can get effective bounds (of exponential type in $N$).

For higher $k$, one could hopefully apply Siegel's theorem on integer points to show (ineffective) finiteness; one just needs to show that the curve $(y+1) \dots (y+k) = N (x+1) \dots (x+k)$ contains no genus zero curves, which should be some elementary algebraic geometry.

EDIT: it seems plausible that by adapting the proof of Theorem 1 of Chan's paper one can rule out $k=3$ solutions to specific $N$ such as  $N=4,25,49,64,81$.  To do this one has to do some numerical computations with the [results of Bennett](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~bennett/paper8.pdf) on explicit lower bounds on rational approximants to expressions such as $N^{1/3}$; the case $N=2$ is worked out explicitly in Bennett (and hence in Chan) but one has to update all the numbers to handle for instance $N=4$.  This might be a suitable task for some AI workflow. EDIT: [this earlier paper of Bennett](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/effective-measures-of-irrationality-for-certain-algebraic-numbers/9514B1BC73EBF0C72B9B470D62C448A9) may also be usable, although the later paper seems to slightly sharpen the results of this earlier paper as far as numerical constants are concerned.

replies.author: vilc
replies.contentMd:
This was done in [a paper by Beukers, Shorey and Tijdeman](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110285581.11/html) from 2001 (which I could not access) on a generalisation of Erdös's problem, according to [this other paper by Rakaczki](https://www.impan.pl/shop/publication/transaction/download/product/83210?download.pdf) [direct download link] on an even broader generalisation (Rakaczki's paper was briefly mentionned in Chan's paper). For problem 686, Theorem B in Rakaczki's paper implies that there are only a finite number of solutions for fixed $N$ and $k>2$.

EDIT:
I proved that none of $4$, $49$, $64$ have a representation for $k = 3$. First, based on my attempts here are some general remarks on applying Bennett's estimates with Chan's method :
- if two irrationnals generate the same field, an explicit estimate for one yields an estimate for the other. This fact is actually often used by Bennett (see the values of $a,N$ in the tables)
- in practice, one can get much better estimates (with an arbitrarily large constant) when $q$ is above some adequate threshold by using more computations to study the continued fraction. A larger constant dramatically improves the final bound. The main limiting factor for our purposes is therefore to obtain an exponent $<3$.
- in Bennett's formulas for $\kappa(a,n)$ the notation $ord_p(n)$ is a divisibility order, not a multiplicative order (this confused me for some time)

Chan shows that $\left|N - \dfrac{v^3}{u^3}\right| \leq \dfrac{N^{3}}{u^3}$ and $\left|\sqrt[3]{N} - \dfrac{v}{u}\right| \leq \dfrac{N^{\tfrac{7}{3}}}{u^3}$. For sufficiently large $u$, the first one is better by a factor of nearly $3$, but I will only need the second one for what follows. A bound on $x$ follows from a bound on $u$ since $D^2 \leq Nu - v \leq Nu$.
When $N$ is a cube (as for $N=64$), $\left|\sqrt[3]{N} - \dfrac{v}{u}\right| \geq \dfrac{1}{u}$ since equality does not hold. Therefore $u \leq N^{\tfrac{7}{6}}$ and $x \leq N^{\tfrac{9}{4}}$. For $64$, we need to check for $x$ up to $12000$, which I did.
$N = 4$ is an example where adapting the bound for $\sqrt[3]{2}$ works without trouble. Since $\sqrt[3]{4} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2}}$, Bennett's estimate yields for all $p,q$ $$\left|\sqrt[3]{4} - \dfrac{p}{q}\right| \geq \dfrac{\sqrt[3]{4}\times 2^{1-2.45}}{8} q^{-2.45} > 0.072 q^{-2.45}$$ This gives in turn $x \leq 2 \times 10^7$, and no further improvement was needed since I had already searched up to $2\times 10^9$.
For $N = 49$ I used Bennett's values of $a=15$ and $N = 7 \times 23^3$ [notation conflict, not the same $N$ as ours] for $\sqrt[3]{7}$, to benefit from the later paper's improved exponents (which turned out to be nearly irrelevant). By studying the continued fraction with Pari/GP, I found that if $q \geq 11004$, then $\left|\sqrt[3]{49} - \dfrac{p}{q}\right| > 223\times q^{-2.69}$. The $223$ could be improved easily for larger $q$, but this already yields $x < 4\times 10^8$, which again I could check in a reasonnable amount of time. Compare with bounds on the order of $x\leq 10^{20}$ if a general bound such as $0.1 q^{-2.69}$ had been used.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
Stijn Cambie and I were both able to represent all numbers $N\leq100$ except for\[ 4, 25, 49, 64, 81. \]For example\[ 32=\frac{(1919+1)(1919+2)}{(338+1)(338+2)}. \]Thus the smallest "problematic" number seems to be $N=4$.
In practice, numbers $N$ that are not perfect squares can be easily represented with only $k=2$ factors using the theory of generalized Pell's equation. I did not try to make this observation completely general.

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: The case of $N$ being a perfect square is particularly interesting because It can shed some light on problem [[930]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/930).

replies.author: Miklos
replies.contentMd: That's a great observation! AlphaProof formalized the non-square case using k=2 and Pell's equation here: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/2398/

replies.author: vilc
replies.contentMd:
I don't know if the formal proof is based on the same idea, but there is a deterministic algorithm for finding a representation with $k=2$ when $N$ is not a square.
Find a solution $(z, w)$ of $z^2 - Nw^2 = 1$, which is always possible by standard methods when $N$ is not a square. If $z-w$ and $z-Nw$ are both odd (always true for odd $N$, and will be true for the "squared" solution $(z^2+Nw^2, 2zw)$ if $N$ is even), then by elementary calculations $n=\dfrac{|z-w|-1}{2}$ and $m=\dfrac{|z-Nw|-1}{2}$ verify $Nn(n+1)=m(m+1)$. If $n$ and $m$ are too close, a larger initial solution $(z',w')$ will work. This also shows that there is an infinite number of solutions.
As a demonstration of the method, a representation, probably the smallest, of $N=614$ with $k=2$ is $(n = 167117648945, m = 4141012131555)$ (Pell equation solved with [Dario Alpern's online calculator](https://www.alpertron.com.ar/QUAD.HTM)).

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
I asked Gemini Deep Research to find references on the problem (the main formulation), Gemini Deep Think to actually represent as many integers $2\leq N\leq100$ as possible, and then also ChatGPT to find some references on the problem.

In about 10 mins Gemini Deep Research [made the following report](https://gemini.google.com/share/8a65afa26217) on the problem. It made a big deal reformulating the quotient as the quotient of binomial coefficients, but it did not make much use of that. It also mentioned the Sylvester-Schur theorem that, among any $k$ consecutive integers $>k$, at least one has a prime divisor $>k$. Then it mentioned the Erdős-Selfridge theorem that the product of two or more consecutive positive integers is never a perfect power. All this was just to argue that the representations are not easy to achieve in general, but no concrete implications were shown. In fact, it incorrectly conjectured that perfect powers $N\geq2$ cannot be represented, which is clearly wrong (see the above comment), take for instance $N=9$ or $N=32$. It also realized that the particular case '$k=2$ and $N$ is not a perfect square' is equivalent to solving a generalized Pell equation, but it did not succeed in characterizing when it is actually solvable.

Gemini Deep Think ran for about 30 mins and [it was able to represent](https://gemini.google.com/share/877b793ff0ab) all $2\leq N\leq100$ except for $4, 25, 49, 64, 81$. These are exactly the same exceptions mentioned in the previous post, where I reported what Stijn and I found experimentally! (Previously, I had simply performed straightforward brute-force search in Mathematica.) Then it claimed to have proven that these 5 numbers cannot be represented using $k=2$ factors.

I could only run ChatGPT for a very short period of time. It did not find any references that would say something actually useful for the main formulation of the problem, but it [found a paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.01306) on the case $k=3$, and in its references there is [a paper](https://msp.org/pjm/1971/37-2/p05.xhtml) on a very special case of the case $k=4$.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd: Inspired by your data and extensive numerical experiments, I now conjecture that $N = p^2$ (where $p \geq 5$ is prime) constitutes a sequence of integers that cannot be represented! I haven't found a counterexample so far!

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
One can establish the $k=2$ case of this conjecture as $p^2 = \frac{m(m+1)}{n(n+1)}$ implies not only the obvious factorization identity $m(m+1) = p^2 n(n+1)$ - implying that one of $m,m+1$ must be divisible by $p^2$ - but also the additional identity $(2pn+p+2m+1) (2pn+p-2m-1) = (p-1)(p+1)$ - implying that $1 \leq 2pn+p-2m-1 < p$.  (The Pell equation here has a discriminant a perfect square, so we can factor in the rational integers rather than a quadratic extension.)  Combining the two facts we see that $2pn+p-2m-1$ must be either $1$ or $p-1$.  The latter case gives $m=0$ which is absurd, the former gives $2m+1 = (p^2 - 2)/2$ which is also absurd for parity reasons.

(Disclosure: I first [asked Claude on this](https://claude.ai/share/a1d7d6b1-9a0f-4d8e-9aa8-11f717600af4), and it got the argument started, but became very handwavy at the end.)

EDIT 1: It seems these sorts of arguments should also produce representations for almost all non-prime squares, but I did not work out the details (it's mostly trying to locate divisors of the square that obey suitable parity constraints).

EDIT 2: Heuristically, the higher $k$ equations should be much less likely to provide solutions (one is now trying to find integer points on a positive genus curve instead of a zero genus curve, which one expects to be unlikely thanks to [Siegel's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%27s_theorem_on_integral_points).  Actually making this intuition rigorous looks very difficult though.  (The $k=3$ case involves an elliptic curve and might possibly be tractable though.)

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
I think the following works: assume $m(m+1) = p^2n(n+1)$ and write $m = pn + l$ with $l > 0$. We then get $$m(m+1) = (pn + l)(pn + l + 1) = p^2n^2 + (2l+1)pn + l(l+1) \equiv l(l+1) \equiv 0 \pmod{p},$$so that $l \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ or $l \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$. In particular $l \ge p-1$ from which we see that $m(m+1)$ is too large.

Edit: ah, I see that you already solved it too.

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: Waclaw Sierpinski posed as an exercise to prove that squares of odd prime powers cannot be expressed when $k=2$.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
It's straightforward to extend this to $p^{2t}$ for any prime $p$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$. Assume $m(m+1)=p^{2t}n(n+1)=p^tn(p^tn+p^t)$.
If $m\leq p^tn$ then $$m(m+1)\leq p^tn(p^tn+1)<p^tn(p^tn+p^t).$$ If $m\geq p^tn+p^t-1$ then $$m(m+1)\geq (p^tn+p^t-1)(p^tn+p^t)>p^tn(p^tn+p^t).$$ Clearly $p^tn<m<p^tn+p^t-1$, but then $m(m+1)$ is not divisible by $p^t$.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
As all non-square $n$ can be represented with $k=2$, the only $n$ where $k=2$ representability remains open is $n=t^2$ for composite $t$. The following was found using Claude Sonnet 4.6. I start from $m$ and $n$ instead of $m+1$ and $n+1$.

Consider $t^2n(n+1)=m(m+1)$. Then let $a=2n+1$ and $b=2m+1$. Substituting in we get $t^2 \frac{a^2-1}{4}=\frac{b^2-1}{4}$ and so $t^2(a^2-1)=b^2-1$. Therefore $(ta)^2-b^2=t^2-1$ and so $(ta-b)(ta+b)=t^2-1$. Set $u=ta-b$ and $v=ta+b$. Then we have a solution if and only if there exist integers $u\neq t-1$ and $v\neq t+1$ such that $uv=t^2-1$, and both $\frac{v-u}{2}$ and $\frac{v+u}{2t}$ are odd.

If $t\equiv 2\bmod 4$ then $m=\frac{t^2}{4}-1$ and $n=\frac{t-2}{4}$ suffice.

EDIT: Claude notes that $t$ can represented if and only if there exists $n$ such that $4n(n+1)t^2+1$ is a square.

Claude also makes the claim that when $r$ is odd, $t=r(r+2)$ is representable for $k=2$ if and only if $r\equiv 1\bmod 4$. The if direction is shown in the comment below by Quanyu Tang.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
You are right. Let us consider \( N = t^2 \). Let $u\ge 3$ be an odd integer. In fact, we can also find two more families of \( t \) for which solutions exist when \( k = 2 \):
1. \( t = 4u^2 - 1 \). In this case, take \( n = \frac{u-3}{2}\), \(m = \frac{u(4u^2-3)-3}{2} \).
2. \( t = 4u(2u^2 - 1) \). In this case, take \( n = \frac{u-3}{2}\), \(m = 4u^4 - 4u^2 - 1 \).

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
I have GPT with near-autonomous process work on the $k=2$ problem for a little bit. Here is [the writeup](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lq4Ji091okPnOETY7MIFb7ykINhsMAFB/view).

At the time of work, only the non-square $N$ and $N = (p^t)^2$ cases were on the forum. GPT reproduces the $N = t^2$, $t \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ case, and it proves a divisibility result which can give more examples of representable square $N$.

replies.author: vilc
replies.contentMd:
I don't know how useful this is, but here is an argument which shows that when $k = 2$ and $N = a^2$, $n$ has to be small (< $\tfrac{a}{8}$ except for the family of parametric solutions from the above post). In particular, there is only a finite number of solutions for fixed $a$, and there is an algorithm which is (quasi-)linear in $a$ for deciding wether $a^2$ is representable with $k=2$.
Let $a \geq 2$ and fix $n \geq \tfrac{a}{8}$. Assume that $m$ gives a solution to $a^2n(n+1) = m(m+1)$ . We can locate $m$ to within one unit using the following inequalities, true for all $x > 0$ :
$$1 + \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{x^2}{8} < \sqrt{1+x} < 1 + \dfrac{x}{2}$$
Setting $x= \tfrac{1}{n}$, we get $$n+ \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{8n} < \sqrt{n(n+1)} = n\sqrt{1 +\dfrac{1}{n}} < n + \dfrac{1}{2}$$
Hence
$$m < \sqrt{m(m+1)} < a\left(n + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$$
and $$m+1 > \sqrt{m(m+1)} > a\left(n + \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{8n}\right)$$
So $$an + \dfrac{a}{2} - 1 - \dfrac{a}{8n} < m < an + \dfrac{a}{2}$$
Now, if $a$ is even then $an + \tfrac{a}{2}$ is an integer. Since $\tfrac{a}{8n} \leq 1$ and the inequalities are strict, we get $m = an + \tfrac{a}{2} - 1$. Injecting this in the original equation gives $n = \tfrac{a - 2}{4}$ and $m = \tfrac{a^2}{4} - 1$. These are integers exactly when $a\equiv 2 \pmod{4}$. If $a$ is odd, we must have $m = an + \tfrac{a-1}{2}$ since $m$ is an integer, thus $m(m+1) = a^2n^2+a^2n+\tfrac{a^2-1}{4} > a^2n(n+1)$, so there is no such solution.
A similar methor should work anytime $N$ is a $k$-th power.
I also did some computations for $k = 2$. For $N$ up to $613$, I can confirm that only the squares of odd numbers and multiples of four are not representable with $k=2$. The largest solutions include (notation is $N : (n,m)$, with $Nn(n+1)= m(m+1)$):
349 : (80283570, 1499820869)
464 : (91600145, 1973127519)
524 : (107654364, 2464321040)
Beyond $m=2^{32}$ my program gets integer overflows so I had to stop there. The first few unknowns are :
614 ; 634 ; 662
I investigated the case of the squares more deeply and found some more parametric solutions by looking at the patterns in the program's results (both verified with Xcas) :
$$(a=(4n+1)(4n+3), n, m=n(4n+3)^2)$$
$$(a=4(2n+1)(8n^2+8n+1), n, m=16n(n+1)(2n+1)^2)$$
[Edit: I didn't see Tang's answer. These look like the same families, up to notation.]
The following sequence of odd squares with solutions could have a similar parametrisation, or they could even belong to a two-parameters family.
1413721 : (1, 1682)
94109401 : (2, 23762)
1431033241 : (3, 131043)
10817040025 : (4, 465124)
Two solutions which do not appear to belong to a family, the only ones I think for $a$ up to $1,000,000$ or so (I got some overflow issues around there so I am not entirely sure) :
1631432881 : (1, 57120)
277613072100 : (3, 1825200)
In all these solutions $n$ is quite small. Must $n$ be $O(\sqrt{a})$ except for the $n= \tfrac{a - 2}{4}$ case ?

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #687 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/687).

### Problem
Let $Y(x)$ be the maximal $y$ such that there exists a choice of congruence classes $a_p$ for all primes $p\leq x$ such that every integer in $[1,y]$ is congruent to at least one of the $a_p\pmod{p}$.

Give good estimates for $Y(x)$. In particular, can one prove that $Y(x)=o(x^2)$ or even $Y(x)\ll x^{1+o(1)}$?

### Context
This function (associated with Jacobsthal) is closely related to the problem of gaps between primes (see [[4]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/4)). The best known upper bound is due to Iwaniec [Iw78],\[Y(x) \ll x^2.\]The best lower bound is due to Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao [FGKMT18],\[Y(x) \gg x\frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x},\]improving on a previous bound of Rankin [Ra38].

Maier and Pomerance have conjectured that $Y(x)\ll x(\log x)^{2+o(1)}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
I believe that this problem in [[Er80,p.106]](https://old.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1980-03.pdf#page=18) refers to the same problem:
"1. Let $f (x)$ be the smallest integer so that there is a set of residues\[a_p \pmod{p}, p < f(x)\qquad\text{(1)}\]so that every integer $n < x$ satisfies one of the congruence (1). In particular must $f(x)$ be significantly larger than $x^{\frac12}$? Also it would be very useful to estimate $F(x)$ if we only require that the number of integers $n \le x$ not satisfying any of the congruences (1) is $o(x/\log x)$ (where $p < F(x)$). Is $F(x)$ significantly smaller than $f (x)$? These problems can of course be extended if more than one residue is omitted.
It is not clear who first formulated this problem---probably many of us did it independently. I offer $\max(1000\text{ dollars}, \frac12 \text{ my total savings})$ for clearing up of this problem. It is clear that many important problems could be attacked if we would know a little more."

Besides the additional reference, I wish to highlight the prize offered for the problem.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
In [[1139]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1139) I've added a missing argument that would probably also solve this problem. This is a shortened version on the core from my discussions with GPT-5.2:

If one could carry out the 2-fold covering construction in its “strong form” --- namely, for each sufficiently large $n$ choose residue classes $a_p \pmod p$ for \emph{every} prime $2\le p\le n$ so that each $j\in[1,n]$ lies in at least two of these classes --- then taking $N$ by CRT with $N\equiv -a_p\pmod p$ for all $p\le n$ would force every $N+j$ ($1\le j\le n$) to be divisible by at least two distinct primes $\le n$. Since the CRT modulus $\prod_{p\le n}p$ is astronomically large, we have $N\gg n^2$, so $N+j$ cannot equal a product of just those two primes; it must have an additional factor, hence $\Omega(N+j)\ge 3$ for all $j\le n$. In other words, this 2-fold congruence cover would directly produce length-$n$ intervals with no primes or semiprimes, giving a very strong form of the “$P_2$-free gaps” phenomenon.

Conversely, the strategy we discussed for large gaps between consecutive $\Omega\le2$ numbers is essentially an attempt to build such a 2-fold cover, but it allows two relaxations: (i) it may use only a carefully chosen subset of primes up to $n$ (to keep $\log N=\sum\log p$ small enough to make $n/\log N$ large), and (ii) it may leave a tiny exceptional set of “stragglers” handled separately. If one succeeds even with these relaxations, one gets $\limsup (u_{k+1}-u_k)/\log k=\infty$. If one succeeds in the stronger “use all primes $p\le n$ and cover everything twice” form, then it also answers your finite question outright (and in fact implies a stronger interval construction than what is needed for the $\limsup$).
