sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here are a few more details on the numerology that suggests that a construction is possible.  Let $z$ be a sufficiently large constant, and let $A$ be a parameter growing slowly with $z$, e.g., $A = \exp( (\log\log\log z)^2 )$ should work.  Assume $n$ extremely large depending on $z$.

We hold the primes $n/2 < p \leq n$ in reserve to clean up any stragglers; if we can sieve $\{1,\dots,n\}$ down to less than $n / 4 \log n$ such stragglers then we win.  Accordingly, any set of cardinality $o(n/\log n)$ we view as negligible.

We first sieve out $0 \pmod{p}$ for all $p \leq n/z$.  Up to negligible sets, this leads the primes $n/z < p_1 \leq n$ (which are completely untouched), as well as semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ where $p_1 < z$ and $n/z <p_2 \leq n/p_1$ and $p_1 < z$ (which were touched once).  (There are also a few elements of the form $p_1^j p_2$ but these are unlikely to cause trouble).  There are about $n/\log n$ primes in the first category and $n \log\log z / \log n$ in the second category.

To eliminate most of the primes in the first category, as well as semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ in the second category with $p_1 > z^{1/A}$ (of which there are about $n \log A / \log n$), we use the primes $p \geq n/z^{1/A}$.  A congruence class mod such a prime hits about $n/p$ elements in $\{1,\dots,n\}$, of which about $n/(p \log (n/p))$ are usable for this purpose (one has to sieve out multiples of any primes less than $n/p$).  We have $\sum_{n/z^{1/A} \leq p \leq z} n/(p \log (n/p)) \sim n \log\log(z^{1/A}) / \log n$ which is somewhat larger than the number $n \log A/\log n$ of targets, so a random sieve here should work well using the linear equations in primes technology (one has to design the random construction so that all primes and semiprimes have a decent chance of being hit, but this should be standard albeit tedious calculations).

To touch the semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ with $p_1 \leq z^{1/A}$ we use the primes $n/z \leq p \leq n/z^{10/A}$.  A congruence associated to such a prime $p$ can touch about $n/(p p_1 \log(n/p))$ semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ attached to $p_1$; there are about $n / p_1 \log n$ such primes, and the sum of the $n/(p p_1 \log(n/p))$ is about $n \log A / p_1 \log n$, so we (barely) win here (random constructions should then cut down the number of survivors by a factor of $A$ or so, which brings us to within range of being cleaned up by the reserve primes). Again one needs linear equations in primes technology to show that most targets get a reasonable chance of being touched at least once.

I *think* something similar can work for larger $r$ than $r=2$, although one has to split into more cases than the two outlined above.

If anyone is interested in developing these ideas into a full proof, I'd be happy to talk further.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Mehtaab has pointed out that even for $r=3$ one cannot hope to get a similar argument going with $z$ bounded independently of $n$, since sieving up to $n/z$ now produces about $n \log\log n / \log n$ surviving semiprimes $p_1 p_2$ with $z < p_1, p_2 < n/z$ and each prime $p>n/z$ can only hope to knock out $O(n/(p \log(n/p)))$ of them, which sums to $n \log\log z / \log n$ which is too small.

One could try increasing $z$ significantly to get around this obstacle, but once $z$ gets above $\log n$ or so it becomes extremely unrealistic to hope that one can find residue classes that consistently hit a near-maximum fraction of targets.  So I am now leaning towards the $r \geq 3$ version of this claim actually being false.  (From standard sieves one can show that no matter what congruences one picks, sieving up to $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ will leave $\gg n (\log\log n)^{r-1} / \log n$ survivors, which looks challenging to eradicate with the remaining congruences, requiring an unreasonably high level of efficiency for quite long arithmetic progressions.)

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd:
This is a really minor remark in the direction of formalizing the obstruction which Terry points out.

We first sieve all the primes $\le n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$; this leaves $\gg n(\log\log n)^{r-1}/\log n$ survivors. We now consider the efficiency of primes between $n/\exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$ and $n$. Note that for a fixed prime $p$ we have $n/p$ targets. Furthermore these $n/p$ targets should satisfy at most $r-2$ of the residue class conditions less than $n/p$; the set of integers which satisfy $r-1$ targets below $n/p$ are an atypical subset of those which survive until $\le n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$. The total contribution therefore from primes between $n/\exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$ and $n$ is $\ll \sum_{n/\exp((\log n)^{o(1)})\le p \le n}(n/p)\log\log(n/p)^{r-2}/\log(n/p) = o(n/\log n \cdot (\log\log n)^{r-1})$ if I computed correctly. (We are essentially sieving an AP of length $z$ by primes less than $z$ so we get an accurate upper bound.)

The question of course now is the primes between $n^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ and $n/\exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$; the upper bounds above seems really inaccurate as $n/p$ is much much bigger than $\log n$ so a random model would suggest out upper bound is far from sharp.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I tried to see whether any of these arguments can provide *upper* bounds on how large $r$ can be for a given $n$.  Just from the fact that $\sum_{p \leq n} n/p \sim n \log\log n$ and the pigeonhole principle it is clear that $r$ cannot exceed $(1+o(1))\log\log n$.  But, to my surprise, I cannot improve upon this trivial bound at all!  As far as I can tell, it is actually completely consistent with sieve theory - albeit extremely unlikely - that one can cover every number from $1$ to $n$ about $\log\log n$ times using one residue class for each prime up to $n$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
A very trivial remark: I didn't check if this was stated explicitly by Erdos, but presumably the intention was to assume that $n$ is sufficiently large, since the claim is obviously false for, e.g., $n=2$.

Also, for what it is worth, [ChatGPT did not find](https://chatgpt.com/share/69023f7c-3dc8-800e-b78b-225af491483c) any additional literature on this problem. [Gemini Deep Research](https://gemini.google.com/share/7358ed9f2ef2) was much wordier (and made much hay out of inexplicably not being able to locate Erdos problem #688), but ultimately did not also find any new references on this specific problem.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
This problem appears on page 79 of the source [Er79d,p.79] [available online here](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1979-23.pdf).  The full containing paragraph is:

"Recently, I considered the following modification of the above problem . Denote by $\varepsilon_n$ the smallest number so that there is a residue $b_p$ for every prime $p$ with $n^{\varepsilon_n} < p \leqq n$, and every positive integer $x \leqq n$ satisfies at least one of the congruences $x \equiv b_p \pmod{p}$.  Is it true that $\varepsilon_n \to 0$ as $n\to\infty$? I can prove that $\varepsilon_n > c \log \log \log n/\log \log n$. Are there residues $c_p$ for every prime $p$ with $2 \leqq p \leqq n$ so that every positive integer $x \leqq n$ satisfies at least $2$ (or at least $r$) of the congruences $x \equiv c_p \pmod{p}$?"

(The first problem stated is [[688]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/688), which also corrects the word "smallest" to "maximal".)

In particular, there is no qualification at all on $n$.  I would interpret the implied question as asking at least "(for each $r$,) is it possible for some $n$?" as well as "is it possible for all sufficiently large $n$?" but others may differ in their interpretations.

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: Agreed. "Is It possible for all sufficiently large $n$ in terms of $r$" is my interpretation, indeed.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: Sieving out $0 \pmod{p}$ for all $p \leq n/z$ for a medium sized $z$ will leave about $O(n \log\log z/\log n)$ survivors, with $\sim n/\log n$ congruences left to allocate, which could optimistically cover $\sum_{n/z \leq p \leq n} \frac{n}{p} \sim n \log z / \log n$ of the survivors, which would be more than sufficient once $z$ is moderately large.  There is a decent chance that modern "large gaps between primes" technology, such as in [this paper of Maynard](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.5110), [this paper of Ford-Green-Konyagin-T.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.4505), or [Ford-Green-Konyagin-Maynard-T.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.5029) might then close off the problem, but I'll leave this for others to work out.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd:
My suspicion is the above commenter (?) reached this point in their analysis as they obviously are rather more knowledgeable here...

 It seemed worth explaining why following to the nose the older argument of Rankin was insufficient; we follow notes of Ford (https://ford126.web.illinois.edu/lectnotes_2025.pdf; Section 2.2). The change to compute is what happens following the first part of the analysis here; we set $y=x$ as this is the case of interest. There are now instead $\approx x(\log z)/(\log x \log\log x)$ integers which remain after the initial sieving stage. The contribution from integers which are not hit at all after the first stage is still only $\lesssim x/(\log x)$ and these are easily mopped up via the second and third part of the analysis (the second part using random sieving removes almost all such integers and then we can pick of the small remainder one by one by using half to the large primes). The issue is after the first stage there are many integers of the form $pq$ with $p$ a prime between $x/z$ and $x/2$ and $q$ an integers which is coprime to all primes less than $2\log x$. The random sieving now reduces one to a subset of size $x/(\log x)$ essentially exactly; using $1$ prime at a time now becomes too expensive (and this to my understanding is where the previous generation large gaps technology was blocked). The more recent techniques in the aforementioned papers should allows one to hit 1000 primes at a time on average which would complete the proof.

It is curious that the question is so delicate (and seems to magically detect the long gaps question).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Yes, that was basically the back of the envelope calculations I was using.  In some ways the problem here has a simpler numerology than the long gaps one, and one can see the potential for a win here a bit more easily as follows.  I tend to visualize these covering congruence problems as that of knocking down a progression of toy ducks at a carnival shooting gallery: each prime $p \leq n$ represents a "spraying bullet" in one's gun that can hit all the ducks that lie in one congruence class mod $p$.  In this particular "game", each duck requires two "hits" to get knocked down, and the objective is to shoot in such a way that all ducks get knocked down.  (I apologize for the violent nature of this metaphor; if someone can propose a more neutral one, I'll be happy to switch over to it.)

Suppose one "shoots" at the congruence classes $0 \pmod{p}$ for all $p \leq n/2$.  Then almost all the ducks are already hit twice by these congruences; the only remaining ducks (that received only zero or one hits) are primes, or powers of primes - so about $n / \log n$ ducks in all.  On the other hand, we have about $n/2\log n$ congruences left in reserve (coming from primes $n/2 < p \leq n$) to position judiciously.  Each congruence can be used to hit any specific duck once, so this can knock out about $n/4\log n$ of the remaining $n/\log n$ ducks: not enough to win, but tantalizingly close.  If, as you say, one could use each of the large primes $p$ to hit many ducks simultaneously, we would have a good chance of actually winning.

Unfortunately, each prime $p > n/2$ can only hit at most two ducks in $\{1,\dots,n\}$, and in fact probably only one in practice since almost all of the remaining ducks are odd.  So this doesn't directly work, which is why I suggested the modified strategy in which one shoots out $0 \pmod{p}$ for $p \leq n/z$, leaving about $n \log\log z / \log n$ ducks remaining, but now one has as remaining ammunition some primes as small as $n/z$, each of which could potentially hit up to $z$ targets at once.  If one could indeed hit the maximum number $n/p$ of ducks with each such shot then we would be in very good shape as indicated above since $n \log z / \log n$ can be made significantly larger than $n \log\log z/\log n$.  Unfortunately one cannot quite do this well because many of the ducks are not divisible by small primes, in particular a prime $p \sim n/z$ can only hit about $O(z/\log z)$ $z$-rough targets by standard sieve theory.  If one went with this bound then the total number of hits one can hope to make is $\sum_{n/z \leq p \leq z} \frac{n}{p \log(n/p)} \sim n \log\log z /\log n$ so one is now in a similar situation to before (off by a factor of 2 rather than 4, but still not enough).  But on the other hand, only $n/\log n$ or so of the $n \log\log z/\log n$ remaining ducks are actually $z$-rough.  I did some back of the envelope estimates of the number of "ducks" at different levels of roughness, and what each remaining "bullet" can hope to "hit" in each category, and I think there is actually enough "ammunition" to hit every duck twice.

In the modern long gaps literature, there are three basic tools to try to hit a lot of primes with progressions as efficiently as possible: the Maynard sieve; the linear equations in primes theory of Green, Ziegler, and myself; and the hypergraph covering lemmas of Pippenger-Spencer (and later authors).  Here I think the Maynard sieve will not be sufficient as it only picks up about $\log z$ primes in a length $z$ progression.  This leaves the linear equations in primes theory, which as you know has significantly worse quantitative dependence on $z$ (even with your recent advances), but for this problem I think we can take $z$ to be a large absolute constant and $n$ extremely large (if we only care about the asymptotic version of the problem) and so the error terms in the linear equations in primes results should not be too important.  (As a first approximation we can try to establish the result conditionally on the prime tuples conjecture; the linear equations in primes theory roughly speaking asserts that this conjecture holds for almost all shift parameters, which should be sufficient.)  The hypergraph covering tools (using the "Rodl nibble") offer some efficiencies in making sure that different "bullets" shoot mostly disjoint sets, but there is enough room in the numerology that I think a simpler probabilistic construction will probably suffice, but one can certainly keep this tool in one's pocket in case the analysis gets too delicate.

Anyway, would be happy to discuss this further on this forum or elsewhere, in case there is interest in carrying this argument to the finish line.  (In principle one might be able to bash this out with heavy AI assistance, but I think I'd actually prefer a human collaboration (perhaps in a Polymath style) for this one.)

p.s. I am not so surprised that this problem of Erdos is related to the long gaps problem (#4), given how #4 was already closely tied to the sister problem #687 to this one.

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: Perhaps this one mentioned by Tom Crawford might come in handy: the integers of the interval can seen as aligned lily pads, and the congruences can be seen as frogs that jump on this line, each with a distance of jump of $p$ lily pads. As these frogs jump back and forth, we want each lily pad to be stepped on at least twice by the frogs.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
OK, that works for me.  I'll keep the previous message unedited with the "ducks" metaphor, but will use the "frogs" metaphor instead for subsequent comments.  (An amusing coincidence of notation with Dyson's famous "birds and frogs" metaphor, though.)

One small comment: of the $n\log\log z / \log n$ lily pads remaining above the pond surface, actually most of them (all but $O(n/\log n)$) will already have been stepped on by one frog already, and only need one more frog to sink; so in fact just having the $p$-frog for $n/z < p \leq n$ step on about $n/p(\log n/p)$ of the remaining pads would come very close (within a factor of $1-o(1)$) of sinking all the pads (rather than a factor of $2$ as I previously thought), assuming optimistically that each frog hops on an essentially disjoint set of pads.  So only a little bit of improvement over this type of strategy may be needed to close the argument.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd:
This is a really minor comment explaining why random sieving seems not to help. The one very minor advantage potentially of using the initial primes as a random sieving step is that there seem to be less issues of $z$-smoothness to think about. (I will also ignore the use of a $W$ trick; it will be required for $W\ll z$ when working through the problem.)

Fix $z \le \log n$ for now and consider setting for all primes between $[z,n/z]$ the residue class to be $0 \pmod p$. There are two categories of number left.
(1) Numbers which have not been touched at all. These are only the $z$ smooth numbers and primes larger than $n/z$; the second term is dominant. This gives $n/\log n$ integers which will be handled at the end.
(2) There are numbers which are only touched exactly once. These integers are precisely of the form $p q$ where $p$ is a prime in $[z,n/z]$ and $q$ is $z$-smooth. The dominant term (from my computations) is when $p$ is near maximal so there are $\approx n\log(z)/\log(n)$ integers remaining. (In fact if one runs through the numerics one can really only pay attention to $pq$ with $p$ prime and $q\le z^{A}$ with $A\to \infty$ arbitrarily slowly at the end.)

We now run the random sieve using primes less than $z$. We will try and be "efficient" in the end with primes of the form between $n/z$ and $n/2$; the primes between $n/2$ and $n$ will be used to handle stragglers.

This leaves us with $O(n/(\log n \log z))$ integers in the first category and therefore reserving a vanishing small portion of primes in the final category we can handle these integers. For the final category, we have a $\lesssim n/\log n$ integers which survive this sieving so we are back at the "constant" factor off regime in the above post.

We now consider using primes between $n/z$ and $n/(2z)$; due to the random sieving we only need to control the integers coming from (2). Initially for each such prime a given shift would have given us $z$ chances to hit the integers; however the random sieving gives us a "random penalty" factor of $\log z$ and so we really need to detect more than $\log z$ primes among the $z$ so the small--gaps technology is unsuitable (this is exactly what Terry says above).

For the linear equations in primes technology, it is basically sufficient to try and use primes between $n/z$ and $n/(2z)$ to handle the $pq$ products in (2) with $p\in [n/z^{A},n/z]$. This amounts to solving $p_1 = (\epsilon z) q + t$, $p_2 = (\epsilon z + 1) q + t$,... $p_{\ell} = zq + t$ with $t$ an integer, $q$ is a prime between $n/z$ and $n/(2z)$ and $p_i$ has a prime factor between $n/z^A$ and $n/z$. The set $p_i$ formed by taking products can be proven to be Gowers uniform (up to major arc issues which would be corrected by a $W$-trick) and so the result should follow. (It is also rather difficult to make this quantitative; this requires uniformity in the $k$-aspect of various $U^{k}$-Gowers norms which have not been worked out in any detail.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I think there are a few more contributions to (1), one coming from prime powers (but this is negligible), and another coming from numbers with a prime factor in $[n/z,n]$ but not itself prime.  This doesn't change the numerology too much though, one still has about $O(n \log z / \log n)$ remaining targets before the random sieving step, the bulk of which come from those numbers with a prime factor in $[n/z^A, n/z^{1/A}]$.

But it seems that we just barely lose with this strategy even with the most optimistic assumptions.  Each $p \in [n/2z, n/z]$ can at best touch $O(z)$ of these targets, or $O(z/\log z)$ after the random sieving step (from the upper bound sieve one cannot get around this $\log z$ loss except possibly for a constant factor).  Similarly for larger $p$.  Summing over $p$ we can only touch $O(n \log z / \log n )$ targets before random sieving, or $O(n / \log n)$ ones after random sieving, so we lose by a constant factor (which grows in $A$, so probably is greater by one).

[EDIT: actually the additional terms in (1) that involve a prime factor between $n/z$ and $n/z^{1/A}$ could be more problematic, as they need to be touched twice in order to win, and so the random sieve I think leaves behind $n \log\log z / \log n$ remaining targets rather than $n / \log n$ if I computed correctly.]

My calculations seem to suggest that the non-random sieve (in which one touches $0 \pmod{p}$ for all $p \leq n/z$) still has a chance; somehow the fact that the majority of the remaining targets actually lie in one of the sieved out classes $0 \pmod{p}$, $p \leq z$ seems to work slightly on one's favor, as it allows for more of the congruence class mod $p$ for $n/z < p < n/2$ to be usable for touching slightly more targets (according to my calculations, a congruence class mod $p \sim n/z$ could potentially touch $z \log\log z / \log z$ remaining targets, which is slightly above the break-even point of $z / \log z$).

As long as we take $z$ to be a large constant, I don't think the dependence on $k$ in the $U^k$ inverse theory etc. will be of relevance for $n$ large enough.  The $W$-trick obstructions to uniformity are annoying, though: it seems that the irregularities at small primes are a crucial part of this story and need to be analyzed carefully.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #690 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/690).

### Problem
Let $d_k(p)$ be the density of those integers whose $k$th smallest prime factor is $p$ (i.e. if $p_1<p_2<\cdots$ are the primes dividing $n$ then $p_k=p$).

For fixed $k\geq 1$ is $d_k(p)$ unimodular in $p$? That is, it first increases in $p$ until its maximum then decreases.

### Context
Erdős believes that this is not possible, but could not disprove it. He could show that $p_k$ is about $e^{e^k}$ for almost all $n$, but the maximal value of $d_k(p)$ is assumed for much smaller values of $p$, at\[p=e^{(1+o(1))k}.\]A similar question can be asked if we consider the density of integers whose $k$th smallest divisor is $d$. Erdős could show that this function is not unimodular.

Cambie [Ca25] has shown that $d_k(p)$ is unimodular for $1\leq k\leq 3$ and is not unimodular for $4\leq k\leq 20$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The question could be interpreted in multiple ways.
If one wants to disprove it for every $k$, then one needs to be able to quantify the irregularities of prime gaps in a sense.
(if primes would form an arithmetic progression, it would be true for all $k$)

Others agree/ believe the question may not be solved for all $k$?

Also, the numerical evidence should indicate that unimodularity is indeed just too much to ask (as Erdos thus believed himself).
So if the challenging part does not lead to (quantified) fundamental underlying statements in number theory, one might consider the problem as solved.
Wondering about the opinions of others.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Stijn, do you know of a precise statement about the irregularities of prime gaps that would be strong enough to disprove unimodularity for all large $k$ (or even infinitely many $k$)? I assume not, if I'm interpreting your comment correctly. I suppose this would be an interesting 'meta-problem', to formulate such a reasonable statement - even if it is completely hopeless to prove, at least to tie this problem into the 'mainstream' of prime number theory.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #691 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/691).

### Problem
Given $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ let $M_A=\{ n \geq 1 : a\mid n\textrm{ for some }a\in A\}$ be the set of multiples of $A$. Find a necessary and sufficient condition on $A$ for $M_A$ to have density $1$.

### Context
A sequence $A$ for which $M_A$ has density $1$ is called a Behrend sequence.

If $A$ is a set of prime numbers (or, more generally, a set of pairwise coprime integers without $1$) then a necessary and sufficient condition is that $\sum_{p\in A}\frac{1}{p}=\infty$.

### Deliverable

researchNotes: A sequence $A$ for which $M_A$ has density $1$ is called a Behrend sequence.
If $A$ is a set of prime numbers (or, more generally, a set of pairwise coprime integers without $1$) then a necessary and sufficient condition is that $\sum_{p\in A}\frac{1}{p}=\infty$.

The general situation is more complicated. For example suppose $A$ is the union of $(n_k,(1+\eta_k)n_k)\cap \mathbb{Z}$ where $1\leq n_1<n_2<\cdots$ is a lacunary sequence. (This construction is sometimes called a block sequence.) If $\sum \eta_k<\infty$ then the density of $M_A$ exists and is $<1$. If $\eta_k=1/k$, so $\sum \eta_k=\infty$, then the density exists and is $<1$.

Erdős writes it 'seems certain' that there is some threshold $\alpha\in (0,1)$ such that, if $\eta_k=k^{-\beta}$, then the density of $M_A$ is $1$ if $\beta <\alpha$ and the density is $<1$ if $\beta >\alpha$.

Tenenbaum notes in [Te96] that this is certainly not true as written since if the $n_j$ grow sufficiently quickly then this sequence is never Behrend, for any choice of $\eta_k$. He then writes 'we understand from subsequent discussions with Erdős that he had actually in mind a two-sided condition on' $n_{j+1}/n_j$.

Tenenbaum [Te96] proves this conjecture: if there are constants $1<C_1<C_2$ such that $C_1<n_{i+1}/n_i<C_2$ for all $i$ and $\eta_k=k^{-\beta}$ then $A$ is Behrend if $\beta<\log 2$ and not Behrend if $\beta>\log 2$.

(This construction is sometimes called a block sequence.) If $\sum \eta_k<\infty$ then the density of $M_A$ exists and is $<1$. If $\eta_k=1/k$, so $\sum \eta_k=\infty$, then the density exists and is $<1$.

Erdős writes it 'seems certain' that there is some threshold $\alpha\in (0,1)$ such that, if $\eta_k=k^{-\beta}$, then the density of $M_A$ is $1$ if $\beta <\alpha$ and the density is $<1$ if $\beta >\alpha$.

Tenenbaum notes in [Te96] that this is certainly not true as written since if the $n_j$ grow sufficiently quickly then this sequence is never Behrend, for any choice of $\eta_k$. He then writes 'we understand from subsequent discussions with Erdős that he had actually in mind a two-sided condition on' $n_{j+1}/n_j$.

Tenenbaum [Te96] proves this conjecture: if there are constants $1<C_1<C_2$ such that $C_1<n_{i+1}/n_i<C_2$ for all $i$ and $\eta_k=k^{-\beta}$ then $A$ is Behrend if $\beta<\log 2$ and not Behrend if $\beta>\log 2$.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Hereby experimental proof for the maximum (that also heuristically resolves the question asymptotically)Let $x= p_r\#=p_1 p_2 \ldots p_r.$
Take the first prime $q \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(x)}.$
Experiments showed $q-1=b \phi(x)$, where $b \le p_r$ (for $r \le 200$). If someone can prove this is always the case, the question is essentially resolved. (thinking about the state of the art related to Linnik's theorem, this may be very hard)

In the above situation, $\phi(bx)=b \phi(x)=\phi(q).$
Now $\frac{q}{bx} \sim \frac{ \phi(x)}{x}.$
When $bx< p_{r+1}\#$, this is the best one can hope for.

For certain $p_{r+1}\#$<$x$<$ p_{r+2}\#,$ the max may still be expected to be roughly $\frac{p_r\#}{ \phi(p_r\#)}.$

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #695 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/695).

### Problem
Let $p_1<p_2<\cdots$ be a sequence of primes such that $p_{i+1}\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$. Is it true that\[\lim_k p_k^{1/k}=\infty?\]Does there exist such a sequence with\[p_k \leq \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)})?\]

### Context
Such a sequence is sometimes called a prime chain.

If we take the obvious 'greedy' chain with $2=p_1$ and $p_{i+1}$ is the smallest prime $\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$ then [Linnik's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linnik%27s_theorem) implies that this sequence grows like\[p_k \leq e^{e^{O(k)}}.\]It is conjectured that, for any prime $p$, there is a prime $p'\leq p(\log p)^{O(1)}$ which is congruent to $1\pmod{p}$, which would imply this sequence grows like\[p_k\leq \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)}).\]An extensive study of the growth of finite prime chains was carried out by Ford, Konyagin, and Luca [FKL10].

Investigate open Erdos Problem #696 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/696).

### Problem
Let $h(n)$ be the largest $\ell$ such that there is a sequence of primes $p_1<\cdots < p_\ell$ all dividing $n$ with $p_{i+1}\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$. Let $H(n)$ be the largest $u$ such that there is a sequence of integers $d_1<\cdots < d_u$ all dividing $n$ with $d_{i+1}\equiv 1\pmod{d_i}$.

Estimate $h(n)$ and $H(n)$. Is it true that $H(n)/h(n)\to \infty$ for almost all $n$?

### Context

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
For the claim that $h(n)$ goes to infinity for almost all $n$, one can use the fact (also mentioned in that very same 1979 paper) that almost all $n$ are divisible by a prime $p \in P$ for some set of primes $P$ if, and only if, the sum $\sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p}$ diverges. More precisely, let $c \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\epsilon > 0$ both be arbitrary but fixed. Let $C$ be such that for every set of primes $P$ with $\sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} > C$ we have that the density of $n$ with a prime divisor $p \in P$ is larger than $1 - \frac{\epsilon}{c}$.

In step $1$ we let $P_1$ be any set of primes with $\sum_{p \in P_1} \frac{1}{p} > C$. Now, for $1 \le k < c$, in step $k+1$ we choose, for every prime $p \in P_k$, a set of primes $Q_p$ (disjoint from all primes chosen so far) with $q \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for all $q \in Q_p$, and $\sum_{q \in Q_p} \frac{1}{q} > C$. That this is possible follows from the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions. We then set $P_{k+1} = \bigcup_{p \in P_k} Q_p$.

The density of $n$ with a prime divisor $p_1 \in P_1$ is larger than $1 - \frac{\epsilon}{c}$. And for every $1 \le k < c$, the density of $n$ with a prime divisor $p_{k+1} \in Q_{p_k}$ is also larger than $1 - \frac{\epsilon}{c}$. By the union bound the density of $n$ with primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_c$ dividing $n$ with $p_{k+1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p_k}$ is larger than $1 - \epsilon$. Since both $\epsilon > 0$ and $c \in \mathbb{N}$ were arbitrary, this proves the claim that $h(n)$ goes to infinity for almost all $n$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #699 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/699).

### Problem
Is it true that for every $1\leq i<j\leq n/2$ there exists some prime $p\geq i$ such that\[p\mid \textrm{gcd}\left(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j}\right)?\]

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Szekeres. A theorem of Sylvester and Schur says that for any $1\leq i\leq n/2$ there exists some prime $p>i$ which divides $\binom{n}{i}$.

Erdős and Szekeres further conjectured that $p\geq i$ can be improved to $p>i$ except in a few special cases. In particular this fails when $i=2$ and $n$ being some particular powers of $2$. They also found some counterexamples when $i=3$, but only one counterexample when $i\geq 4$:\[\textrm{gcd}\left(\binom{28}{5},\binom{28}{14}\right)=2^3\cdot 3^3\cdot 5.\]This is mentioned in problem B31 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Cong
sourceComments.contentMd:
I ran a Rust implementation to test the official statement (“for every 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2 there is a prime p ≥ i dividing both binomials”) up to n = 10^7; no counterexamples found. Targeted extensions: all n = 2^k for k ≤ 27 (n ≈ 1.34×10^8) and all n = 3^m + 1 for m ≤ 17 (n ≈ 1.29×10^8).

In these ranges the official statement holds. The stronger claim “some prime p > i divides both” fails only at the pairs below; in each case the shared prime ≥ i is exactly p = i.

n         (i,j)        gcd of binomials
10        (3,5)        2^2 · 3
16        (2,6)        2^3
28        (3,14)       2^2 · 3^2
28        (5,14)       2^3 · 3^3 · 5
244       (3,122)      2^2 · 3^4
512       (2,147)      2^8
2048      (2,713)      2^10
2188      (3,1094)     2^2 · 3^6
1594324   (3,797162)   2^2 · 3^12

Observed structure:
- i = 2: occurs at powers of two (seen at 2^4, 2^9, 2^11); gcd is a pure power of 2.
- i = 3: occurs at n = 3^m + 1 with j = n/2 for m = 2, 3, 5, 7, 13; none beyond that up to m = 17.
- For i ≥ 4, only (n, i, j) = (28, 5, 14) in all searched ranges.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #700 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/700).

### Problem
Let\[f(n)=\min_{1<k\leq n/2}\textrm{gcd}\left(n,\binom{n}{k}\right).\]- Characterise those composite $n$ such that $f(n)=n/P(n)$, where $P(n)$ is the largest prime dividing $n$.
- Are there infinitely many composite $n$ such that $f(n)>n^{1/2}$?
- Is it true that, for every composite $n$,\[f(n) \ll_A \frac{n}{(\log n)^A}\]for every $A>0$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Szekeres. It is easy to see that $f(n)\leq n/P(n)$ for composite $n$, since if $j=p^k$ where $p^k\mid n$ and $p^{k+1}\nmid n$ then $\textrm{gcd}\left(n,\binom{n}{j}\right)=n/p^k$. This implies\[f(n) \leq (1+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}.\]It is known that $f(n)=n/P(n)$ when $n$ is the product of two primes. Another example is $n=30$.

For the second problem, it is easy to see that for any $n$ we have $f(n)\geq p(n)$, where $p(n)$ is the smallest prime dividing $n$, and hence there are infinitely many $n$ (those $=p^2)$ such that $f(n)\geq n^{1/2}$.

This impliesf(n) \leq (1+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}.It is known that $f(n)=n/P(n)$ when $n$ is the product of two primes. Another example is $n=30$.

For the second problem, it is easy to see that for any $n$ we have $f(n)\geq p(n)$, where $p(n)$ is the smallest prime dividing $n$, and hence there are infinitely many $n$ (those $=p^2)$ such that $f(n)\geq n^{1/2}$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
I used Gemini and ChatGPT's deep research tools to conduct a literature review on this problem.

After 6 minutes, [Gemini did not locate any additional references](https://gemini.google.com/share/aa45da6ee223) beyond the Erdos-Szekeres paper; the tool recapitulated the observations already in the paper (including those already mentioned in the commentary), computed some initial values of $f(n)$ and noted some other work involving divisibility of binomial coefficients (such as a body of work concerning the factors of the central binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$), as well as mentioning basic relevant tools such as Kummer's theorem, but nothing particularly relevant was found.

After 18 minutes, [ChatGPT located](https://chatgpt.com/share/68f27b0c-ece8-800e-b984-096915f1a9bd) this very web page, and also asserted that this problem appears in Section B33 of Guy's "Unsolved problems in number theory"; I could not directly confirm this reference, but have seen it elsewhere on the web and the section title of B33, "Largest divisor of a binomial coefficient", is certainly promising.  Some work on $\mathrm{gcd}(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j})$ is noted, such as [this paper of Bergman](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.0607), as well as the aforementioned work on central binomial coefficients, but other than that, no closely related literature was found.

EDIT: I was able to gain access to enough of Guy's book to view Section B33 (and related sections such as B31).  It does contain several open problems by Erdos and others regarding divisibility of binomial coefficients, but does not seem to reference this question directly.  So I would mark this as a hallucination by ChatGPT.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The third problem is likely very hard.
Even proving that $\gg n^{1-\epsilon}$ for small $\epsilon$ can occur, seems hard.So one wonders if $n/f(n)$ is the product of only a small fractions of its prime divisors (assuming they are not too different).

Since already checking concrete divisibilities of binomial coefficients, e.g. [[#376]](https://www.erdosproblems.com//376), seem widely open,
telling that in general $\binom{n}{k}$ is a multiple of a big divisor of $n$ for all $k$, cannot be expected to be easy.

In particular, one can wonder if $f(n)=n/P(n)$ might happen for $n$ being the product of many primes that are not too far apart.

For the product of $5$ primes (each bounded by $29$),
there are only a few values $n$ satisfying $f(n)=n/P(n)$. They are:
$$2310,4830,21318,34510,73370,86710,206074.$$

For the product of $6$ (or $7$) primes bounded by $37$ (or $47$ for $7$), there was only one value $n$ satisfying $f(n)=n/P(n)$ for each; $71677177=11 * 13 * 19 * 23 * 31 * 37$ and $34207446=2 * 3 * 7 * 13 * 31 * 43 * 47$.

The above examples indicate even more that the characterisation in the first subquestion seems hopeless. Someone who thinks it is not?

Anyone optimistic that something can be done on the third subquestion?

The second subquestion may be the one where it is possible to have a rigourous proof. A different construction may do the work. But maybe this rigourous proof would not add much to the insight the conditional proofs already gave.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The second subquestion should definitely be answered with yes.
Nevertheless, it was frustrating to not have a clear infinite family.
The following two families should do the job.*there are likely infinitely many primes of the form $q=2^k+3$ where $k \equiv 4 \pmod {20}$ (see [[oeis/A057732]](https://oeis.org/A057732))

For such a $q$ (larger than $19$, the latter being valid as well), let $n=q(q+1)$, these satisfy $f(n)=q+1.$
Notice that $q+1 \mid \binom{n}{q}$ is the only binomial which is not a multiple of $q$.
Now $2q \mid \binom{n}{r(q+1)}$ if $\frac{q-1}{2}\ge r$>$3$ and $5q \mid \binom{n}{r(q+1)}$ if $1\le r \le 3$.

*(construction by Kadi Siigur)

Let $p,q$ be two primes satisfying $2^l$ < $p$ < $q$ < $2^{l+1}$ for which $pq \equiv 1 \pmod{2^l}$ (thus $l\ge 4$).
There should be infinitely many such pairs of primes heuristically (similar to the fact that there should be infinitely many twin primes) and computations give many solutions as such.
Now $n=2pq$ has the property that $f(n)=2p$.
This is since $2q \mid \binom{2pq}{pq},$ $2q \mid \binom{2pq}{2pr}$ (for $r \in [1,q]$) and $2p \mid \binom{2pq}{2rq}$ (for $r \in [1,p]$).

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The first subquestion is likely undoable.
For $n=pqr$ the product of 3 different primes satisfying $p \le q \le r \le pq$ e.g., sometimes it is and sometimes it is not (both happen with decent proportions)
For the products of $4$ primes in the range [2,29],
19 of them satisfy $f(n)=n/P(n)$;
e.g. the values belonging to

$$[ 4466,
 14674,
 10166,
 14858,
 1785,
 4485,
 7293,
 16445,
 51359,
 147407]$$

and three of them, [1610, 8151, 10659], satisfy $\sqrt n $<$ f(n)$<$n/P(n).$
The remaining 188 options satisfy $f(n)$<$\sqrt n.$

Also when $n=q(q+1)$ for a prime $q$, sometimes it works and sometimes it is not.
E.g. for $q=1151$, it turns out that $\binom{q(q+1)}{6(q+1)}=q$<$n/q$,
while for $q=2063$ $f(q*(q+1))=q+1.$
Already for these specific constructions, it seems one has to state it as the values $q$ such that for every $1\le r \le \frac{q-1}{2}$, some digit of $r(q+1)$ written in base $p$ for some prime divisor $p$ of $q+1$ is larger than the corresponding digit in the p-ary notation of $q(q+1).$
[reduced verification can be noticed, but this seems not a like valid characterisation]

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #701 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/701).

### Problem
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of sets closed under taking subsets (i.e. if $B\subseteq A\in\mathcal{F}$ then $B\in \mathcal{F}$). There exists some element $x$ such that whenever $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq \mathcal{F}$ is an intersecting subfamily we have\[\lvert \mathcal{F}'\rvert \leq \lvert \{ A\in \mathcal{F} : x\in A\}\rvert.\]

### Context
A problem of Chvátal [Ch74], who proved it replacing the closed under subsets condition with the (stronger) condition that, assuming all sets in $\mathcal{F}$ are subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, whenever $A\in \mathcal{F}$ and there is an injection $f:B\to A$ such that $x\leq f(x)$ for all $x\in B$, then $B\in \mathcal{F}$.

Sterboul [St74] proved this when, letting $\mathcal{G}$ be the maximal sets (under inclusion) in $\mathcal{F}$, all sets in $\mathcal{G}$ have the same size, $\lvert A\cap B\rvert\leq 1$ for all $A\neq B\in \mathcal{G}$, and at least two sets in $\mathcal{G}$ have non-empty intersection.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #704 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/704).

### Problem
Let $G_n$ be the unit distance graph in $\mathbb{R}^n$, with two vertices joined by an edge if and only if the distance between them is $1$.

Estimate the chromatic number $\chi(G_n)$. Does it grow exponentially in $n$? Does\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\chi(G_n)^{1/n}\]exist?

### Context
A generalisation of the [Hadwiger-Nelson problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger%E2%80%93Nelson_problem) (which addresses $n=2$). Frankl and Wilson [FrWi81] proved exponential growth:\[\chi(G_n) \geq (1+o(1))1.2^n.\]The trivial colouring (by tiling with cubes) gives\[\chi(G_n) \leq (2+\sqrt{n})^n.\]Larman and Rogers [LaRo72] improved this to\[\chi(G_n) \leq (3+o(1))^n,\]and conjecture the truth may be $(2^{3/2}+o(1))^n$. Prosanov [Pr20] has given an alternative proof of this upper bound.

See also [[508]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/508), [[705]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/705), and [[706]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/706).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

### Problem
Let $L(r)$ be such that if $G$ is a graph formed by taking a finite set of points $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and some set $A\subset (0,\infty)$ of size $r$, where the vertex set is $P$ and there is an edge between two points if and only if their distance is a member of $A$, then $\chi(G)\leq L(r)$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #708 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/708).

### Problem
Let $g(n)$ be minimal such that for any $A\subseteq [2,\infty)\cap \mathbb{N}$ with $\lvert A\rvert =n$ and any set $I$ of $\max(A)$ consecutive integers there exists some $B\subseteq I$ with $\lvert B\rvert=g(n)$ such that\[\prod_{a\in A} a \mid \prod_{b\in B}b.\]Is it true that\[g(n) \leq (2+o(1))n?\]Or perhaps even $g(n)\leq 2n$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Surányi [ErSu59], who proved that $g(n) \geq (2-o(1))n$, and that $g(3)=4$. Their lower bound construction takes $A$ as the set of $p_ip_j$ for $i\neq j$, where $p_1<\cdots <p_\ell$ is some set of primes such that $2p_1^2>p_\ell^2$.

Gallai was the first to consider problems of this type, and observed that $g(2)=2$ and $g(3)\geq 4$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #709 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/709).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be minimal such that, for any $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\subseteq [2,\infty)\cap\mathbb{N}$ of size $n$, in any interval $I$ of $f(n)\max(A)$ consecutive integers there exist distinct $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in I$ such that $a_i\mid x_i$.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
I do not know how to solve the problem completely, but there is a simple improvement $
f(n)\gg {\log n\over \log\log n}
$.

Let $F(n,m)$ denote the least integer $L$ such that the interval $(m,m+L]$ contains distinct multiples of $1,2,\dots,n$.

For the set $A=\{2,\dots,n\}$, the defining property of $f(n)$ implies $F(n,m)\le f(n)n$ for every $m$. On the other hand, van Doorn proved that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists $m=m(n)$ such that $
F(n,m)\gg n{\log n\over \log\log n}.$ Combining the two inequalities gives the claim.

It is natural to guess that the truth is much closer to the lower bound than to the upper bound.

Disclosure statement :Based on @Prof Tao comment,I have used Chatgpt thinking 5.4 for help and for the above combination

[ErPo80] P. Erdős and C. Pomerance, Matching the natural numbers up to $n$ with distinct multiples in another interval, *Indag. Math.* 42 (1980), 147–151.

[vD26] W. van Doorn, On the length of an interval that contains distinct multiples of the first $n$ positive integers, arXiv:2601.16972, 2026.

replies.contentMd:
The main points of the above remark can be summarized as follows:
the lower bound of Erdős-Surányi proof (which gives $c = 1 - \frac{1 + \log \log 2}{\log 2} \approx 0.086$) can be improved to $f(n) \gg \frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ by restricting to the special case $A = \{2, 3, \ldots, n+1\}$ and using [van Doorn's bound](https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/aa7/aa7.pdf) on [#711](https://www.erdosproblems.com/711).  If one instead uses the results of [ErPo80], one already obtains the intermediate lower bound $f(n) \gg \sqrt{\log n/\log\log n}$.   (These observations were obtained from conversation with Wouter and GPT.)

sourceComments.author: Steven_Tolbert
sourceComments.contentMd:
Attempted a solve with opus 4.6 + a lot of compute. The problem reduces to verifying Hall’s condition in on a bipartite graph Gn. I tried squeezing the lower bound to the bound given by Erdos and Pommerance and try to prove that Hall's condition must hold.

The multiplicative combinatorics question at the heart of it:

Given integers $k \in (B, N]$ and targets $h \in (2^n, n + L]$, with edges $k \mid h$, why does the divisibility structure always produce enough expansion? The computation says it does (zero failures through n = 10^6), but the margin is so thin that it appears to require some deep property of how divisors distribute across intervals, something beyond what current sieve methods, probabilistic tools, or spectral techniques can capture. Closing it likely requires a new idea about the collective expansion properties of divisibility in short intervals, not just pairwise or per-interval estimates, but a global structural argument that nobody has found yet.

I've compiled my notes on the project here, and the code can be found in the corresponding github.

https://zenodo.org/records/18749475

I wish the next person who attempts this luck!

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd: You mention using Opus 4.6, but this is not mentioned in the 40 page document. Am I correct in thinking that the paper was written with the help of Opus 4.6?

replies.contentMd: That would be a yes haha, I have updated the document to make that more clear.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
I have [GPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/69a0434b-b494-8010-b198-6a20f7ddb631) do some preliminary checking and there seem to be several major issues, some with no obvious fixes. See the final message for details.

This is not to discourage the attempt. It's welcome; but I think feedback of this kind is important to maintain usefulness of AI in the community. Also, if I flag issues incorrectly, feedback on me is also welcome!

replies.author: Steven_Tolbert
replies.contentMd:
Before we engage in the game of my AI said to your AI! Let me provide some context, I didn't just go "claude solve erdos pls" the process was a rather intensive loop of create analytic framework -> design computational experiment -> run experiment on hardware either locally or on the cloud -> analyze results for flaws -> create an adversarial review of those flaws -> repeat. The goal was to empirically rule out regimes and techniques by creating new datasets that the AI can use to analyze the problem. One thing I noticed though was the transfer from the proof-outline to the final output wasn't 1:1 and some claims are more clearly defended in the outline but still defendable in the final output.

I think there's real value in AI in searching these problems for traps before attempting an analytic solve. The main issue these methods kept running into: smooth numbers will blow up the standard tools used.

And for the game of my AI vs yours (edit: if it wasn't clear Claude is responding from here):

GPT raised 8 issues with the paper. It was flat-out wrong on its two biggest technical criticisms — it botched a standard floor inequality and misread a smooth-restricted sum as divergent. Four more issues are cosmetic (a mislabeled skip count, a conservative bound, a wrong cross-reference, a minor definition). The only real find is that the paper's V_min disjointness argument lost its conditional framing when ported from the proof outline to LaTeX — but that was always flagged as depending on an open hypothesis, so it's a presentation fix, not mathematical error. The paper is sound; GPT mostly just made noise.

What the outline actually proves unconditionally:
  - Top half doubling (trivial)
  - Case A: Hall's condition for subsets S with max element > n/s
  - Lemma 3: Small-s regime (s ≤ some threshold)
  - Regime 1: s ≤ δ/2

  These are all sound and match what appears in the paper. The architecture is solid.

  Computational evidence tables

  The outline includes verification tables showing the Cauchy-Schwarz ratio improves with n — the worst-case margin grows from ~13% at small n to ~115% at larger n. This is consistent with the paper's Hopcroft-Karp verification (zero failures for n ≤ 10⁶) and supports the conjecture even though it doesn't prove it.

replies.contentMd:
This is not a game, and I appreciate your work. I never claim that you expend low effort; on the contrary, such work is appreciated. But we must keep to high quality of the work, whether AI is used or not.

I will not further engage in this conversation unless you present your argument in a less adversarial form, e.g. without statements such as "flat-out wrong" and "just made noise".

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: Remarkably, it seems that this problem (morally, at least) implies the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions!  Proof sketch: if the Kakeya conjecture failed, then by the tensor power trick we conclude that for sufficiently high dimension $d$, there exists Kakeya sets of dimension less than $d-1$. Discretizing (and taking some liberties with the analogy between arithmetic progressions and tubes), we get about $N^{d-1}$ arithmetic progressions of spacing $\sim N$ that occupy less than $N^{d-1}$ elements, so it is not possible to assign each such progression a distinct element.  Morally, one can then invoke the Chinese remainder theorem to conclude.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Interesting! The 1000 rupees prize seems rather undervalued then...

Does the 3/2 exponent of Erdos and Pomerance translate to anything for Kakeya using this argument?

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
It corresponds to 3D Kakeya sets having dimension at least 2, which can be established by elementary incidence geometry (mostly using the fact that two lines intersect in at most one point).

This suggests that the sums-differences approach of Bourgain (I also worked on this with Nets Katz) to Kakeya in high dimensions may make progress on this 3/2 exponent.  [This article of Green and Ruzsa](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02108) may be a starting point for anyone wanting to pursue this.  (Incidentally, Conjecture 5 from that paper relates to a problem of Erdos and Selfridge - is it already on this site?)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #713 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/713).

### Problem
Is it true that, for every bipartite graph $G$, there exists some $\alpha\in [1,2)$ and $c>0$ such that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^\alpha?\]Must $\alpha$ be rational?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Simonovits. Erdős sometimes asked this in the weaker version with just\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\asymp n^{\alpha}.\]Erdős [Er67d] had initially conjectured that, for any bipartite graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^{\alpha}$ for some constant $c>0$ and $\alpha$ of the shape $1+\frac{1}{k}$ or $2-\frac{1}{k}$ for some integer $k\geq 2$. This was disproved by Erdős and Simonovits [ErSi70].

The analogous statement is not true for hypergraphs, as shown by Frankl and Füredi [FrFu87], who proved that if $G$ is the $5$-uniform hypergraph on $8$ vertices with edges $\{12346,12457,12358\}$ then $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)=o(n^5)$ but $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\neq O(n^c)$ for any $c<5$.

A simplified proof was given by Füredi and Gerbner [FuGe21], who extended it to a counterexample for all $k\geq 5$. It remains open whether it is true for $k=3$ and $k=4$ (though Füredi and Gerbner conjecture it is not).
See also [[571]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/571).

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
For $r=3$, if $m=|E(G)|$ and $\nu(G)$ is the maximum number of \emph{edge-disjoint}
copies of $K_4^3$ in $G$, then the optimal decomposition into edge-disjoint
$K_4^3$'s plus single edges uses exactly $m-3\nu(G)$ parts.

I exhaustively checked all $2^{\binom{6}{3}}=2^{20}$ $3$-graphs on $n=6$ vertices:
$\mathrm{ex}_3(6;K_4^3)=14$, and for every $G$ on $6$ vertices one has
$m-3\nu(G)\le 14$ (so no counterexample exists for $(r,n)=(3,6)$). Code available
on request.

Also $(r,n)=(7,8)$ is immediate: on $8$ vertices there are exactly $8$ $7$-edges,
so $\mathrm{ex}_7(8;K_8^7)=7$, and any $7$-graph on $8$ vertices decomposes into
$\le 7$ single edges if $m\le 7$, or into one $K_8^7$ if $m=8$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #723 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/723).

### Problem
If there is a [finite projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane#Finite_projective_planes) of order $n$ then must $n$ be a prime power?

A finite projective plane of order $n$ is a collection of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n^2+n+1\}$ of size $n+1$ such that every pair of elements is contained in exactly one set.

### Context
These always exist if $n$ is a prime power. This conjecture has been proved for $n\leq 11$, but it is open whether there exists a projective plane of order $12$.

Bruck and Ryser [BrRy49] have [proved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruck%E2%80%93Ryser%E2%80%93Chowla_theorem) that if $n\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ or $n\equiv 2\pmod{4}$ then $n$ must be the sum of two squares. For example, this rules out $n=6$ or $n=14$. The case $n=10$ was ruled out by computer search [La97].

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: jleng01
sourceComments.contentMd: Well if you're willing to deal with brackets rather than a strange mod condition, one can rewrite $1_{n \in (p/2, p) (p)}$ as $\lfloor 2n/p \rfloor - 2\lfloor n/p \rfloor$. Not quite sure how this helps so far. I've been trying without success with introducing the Heisenberg group somehow.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Most likely they were motivated by binomial coefficients, since the number of times $p$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ is equal to $1_{n \in (p/2,p) \hbox{ mod } p}$ plus some additional terms, by Kummer's theorem.

sourceComments.author: msawhney
sourceComments.contentMd: A natural way to attempt to attack such a problem is to bound the exponential sum $\sum e(n/p)/p$. Via the method of bilinear sums, one is let to considering $\sum e(n/ab)$ and establishing cancellation when $a,b\sim \exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$. This appears to be out of reach of standard methods (in particular say Chapter 8 in Iwaniec--Kowalski). However by restricting to primes which are between $\exp((\log n)^{.99})$ and $n$ (say) one could plausibly prove a bound of $\gtrsim \log\log n$ and $(1-\Omega(1))\log\log n$.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: A back of the envelope calculation suggests that Proposition 1.12 of [this paper of Matomaki, Radziwill, Shao, Teravainen, and myself](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03335) should be able to handle the range $p \geq \exp(\log^{2/3+\varepsilon} n)$, which should give upper and lower bounds of $\gtrsim \frac{1}{6} \log \log n$ and $\lesssim \frac{5}{6} \log\log n$ if I did the calculations correctly.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd: Attacking this problem via such exponential sums does seem to require better handling issues which seem plausibly related to the zero free region of zeta. If one wants just an "average in n" version (e.g. such a stated holds for 100% of n) the problem does become substantially easier.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #727 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/727).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 2$. Does\[(n+k)!^2 \mid (2n)!\]for infinitely many $n$?

### Context
A conjecture of Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75]. It is open even for $k=2$.

Balakran [Ba29] proved this holds for $k=1$ - that is, $(n+1)^2\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for infinitely many $n$. It is a classical fact that $(n+1)\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for all $n$ (see [Catalan numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_number)).

sourceComments.contentMd: I've investigated a little whether the method in [728] can help here as well. It seems that it does allow you to handle up to moderately large primes, specifically if $n+1,\dots,n+k$ are $\exp(c \sqrt{\log n})$-smooth for some $c > 0$ it may work. Unfortunately, current techniques can only give consecutive integers that are roughly $n^\varepsilon$-smooth. Heuristically, one does expect the "$\exp(c \sqrt{\log n})$-smooth" to be true, but this seems far beyond current techniques. So probably [728] isn't helping all that much.

In particular, these may lead to the suspicion that the answer is "yes" for every $k \ge 2.$

For $k=2$, there were $913$ such values of $n$ bounded by $10^5.$

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Indeed there is a simple heuristic argument (see the comment by Will Sawin on my answer [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/492767/gap-in-binomial-coefficients#494967)) that says that for any fixed $k$ there is a positive proportion of such $n$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: The $k=2$ case is tantalizingly close to being within reach of current technology (in particular, the two-point logarithmically averaged Elliott and Chowla technology), which can provide a large number of $n$ with $n+1,n+2$ both somewhat smooth, which increases the odds of $(n+1)^2(n+2)^2$ dividing $\binom{2n}{n}$.  Unfortunately the error terms in the current estimates are still somewhat weak (particularly in view of the relatively sparse nature of smooth numbers), and may not be enough to close this problem without additional effort.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #739 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/739).

### Problem
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal and $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$. Is it true that, for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{n}< \mathfrak{m}$, there exists a subgraph of $G$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{n}$?

### Context
A question of Galvin [Ga73], who proved that this is true with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_0$. Galvin also proved that the stronger version of this statement, in which the subgraph is induced, implies $2^{\mathfrak{k}}<2^{\mathfrak{n}}$ for all cardinals $\mathfrak{k}<\mathfrak{n}$.

Komjáth [Ko88b] proved it is consistent that\[2^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_1}=2^{\aleph_2}=\aleph_3\]and that there exist graphs which fail this property (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$).

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
Komjáth, P. Consistency results on infinite graphs. Israel J. Math. 61, 285–294 (1988). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02772573

The first sentence of the abstract is the following:
"Consistently there exist $\aleph_2$-chromatic graphs with no $\aleph_1$-chromatic subgraphs."

The subgraphs here are not just the induced ones (as that previous result in mentioned in the introduction).  The consistency is with $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_3$.  I guess the problem is likely still open in the purest sense.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: We *could* add new categories to the problem status: "Not disprovable", "Not provable", and "Undecidable"; seems like this result would then place the problem in the "not provable" category (assuming set theory is consistent, of course).  Though this seems like overkill for a single problem... if it turns out that there is a second problem whose answers or partial results depend on additional set theoretic axioms then I might introduce these categories.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
There is at least one other candidate in the new [[1067]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1067), whose answer is independent of ZFC. Other examples are [[474]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/474) and [[736]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/736). (It has been speculated that the answer to [[508]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/508) might also be independent of ZFC.)

The trouble is that there is no single tag appropriate for all of these - 'Independent' works for some, 'Not disprovable' for others.

I'm sure there will be many more candidates as well - Erdős' problems on set theory and infinite graphs are probably the largest unexplored source of problems that I haven't really gone into yet.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: OK, that's enough data points to introduce the new categories of "not provable", "not disprovable", and "independent".  I've updated the database accordingly.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #743 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/743).

### Problem
Let $T_2,\ldots,T_n$ be a collection of trees such that $T_k$ has $k$ vertices. Can we always write $K_n$ as the edge disjoint union of the $T_k$?

### Context
A conjecture of Gyárfás, known as the tree packing conjecture.

Gyárfás and Lehel [GyLe78] proved that this holds if all but at most $2$ of the trees are stars, or if all the trees are stars or paths. Fishburn [Fi83] proved this for $n\leq 9$. Bollobás [Bo83] proved that the smallest $\lfloor n/\sqrt{2}\rfloor$ many trees can always be packed greedily into $K_n$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: A conjecture of Gyárfás, known as the tree packing conjecture.

Gyárfás and Lehel [GyLe78] proved that this holds if all but at most $2$ of the trees are stars, or if all the trees are stars or paths. Fishburn [Fi83] proved this for $n\leq 9$. Bollobás [Bo83] proved that the smallest $\lfloor n/\sqrt{2}\rfloor$ many trees can always be packed greedily into $K_n$.

Joos, Kim, Kühn, and Osthus [JKKO19] proved that this conjecture holds when the trees have bounded maximum degree. Allen, Böttcher, Clemens, Hladky, Piguet, and Taraz [ABCHPT21] proved that this conjecture holds when all the trees have maximum degree $\leq c\frac{n}{\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$.
Janzer and Montgomery [JaMo24] have proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that the largest $cn$ trees can be packed into $K_n$.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
Claimed proof (preprint):
Parikshit Chalise, Antwan Clark, and Edinah K. Gnang posted “A Proof of the Tree Packing Conjecture” (arXiv:2410.13840; v2 dated 23 Oct 2024), which claims to prove Gyárfás’ Tree Packing Conjecture for all $n$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13840

High-level outline (as stated by the authors):
The paper introduces a reformulation of tree packing into $K_n$ via “augmented functional trees” and reduces the existence of an edge-disjoint packing of $(T_2,\dots,T_n)$ into $K_n$ to a “complete labeling” problem.
They define a “tree packing polynomial certificate” $P_g(X,y)=V(X)E_g(X,y)$ and (Proposition 3.4) relate existence of a complete labeling to a non-vanishing condition for a canonical representative of $P_g$.
A key step is the “Composition Lemma” (Lemma 3.10), asserting that the relevant non-vanishing property is preserved under a local composition operation; iterating this is used to reduce general instances to a star-based instance, yielding Theorem 1.9 and the main claimed result.

Status note:
This is a preprint; I have not found a refereed journal version or a widely circulated independent verification. There is community discussion about related “composition lemma” approaches here:
https://mathoverflow.net/questions/482509/claimed-proofs-of-graph-labelling-conjectures

Suggestion for this page:
It may be useful to add arXiv:2410.13840 as a reference (possibly marked “claimed proof / pending verification”), and update the open/solved status if/when a vetted confirmation appears.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #750 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/750).

### Problem
Let $f(m)$ be some function such that $f(m)\to \infty$ as $m\to \infty$. Does there exist a graph $G$ of infinite chromatic number such that every subgraph on $m$ vertices contains an independent set of size at least $\frac{m}{2}-f(m)$?

### Context
In [Er69b] Erdős conjectures this for $f(m)=\epsilon m$ for any fixed $\epsilon>0$. This follows from a result of Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi [EHS82], as described by msellke in the comments.

In [ErHa67b] Erdős and Hajnal prove this for $f(m)\geq cm$ for all $c>1/4$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: msellke
sourceComments.contentMd:
The correct reference for the $f(m)=\epsilon m$ result seems to be Theorem 1 in (P. Erdős, A. Hajnal and E. Szemerédi, "On almost bipartite large chromatic graphs", Ann. Discrete Math. 12 (1982), 117–123). The stated theorem says you can find a bipartite induced subgraph with at least $(1-\epsilon) n$ vertices. Taking the larger half of the bipartition then confirms the conjecture/claim by [Er69b]/[Er94b].

(The reference was located by GPT-5, who also noticed the small deduction above by itself in the process, to my knowledge.)

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #757 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/757).

### Problem
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a set of size $n$ such that every subset $B\subseteq A$ with $\lvert B\rvert =4$ has $\lvert B-B\rvert\geq 11$. Find the best constant $c>0$ such that $A$ must always contain a Sidon set of size $\geq cn$.

### Context
For comparison, note that if $B$ were a Sidon set then $\lvert B-B\rvert=13$, so this condition is saying that at most one difference is 'missing' from $B-B$. Equivalently, one can view $A$ as a set such that every four points determine at least five distinct distances, and ask for a subset with all distances distinct.

Without loss of generality, one can assume $A\subset \mathbb{N}$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #761 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/761).

### Problem
The cochromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\zeta(G)$, is the minimum number of colours needed to colour the vertices of $G$ such that each colour class induces either a complete graph or empty graph. The dichromatic number of $G$, denoted by $\delta(G)$, is the minimum number $k$ of colours required such that, in any orientation of the edges of $G$, there is a $k$-colouring of the vertices of $G$ such that there are no monochromatic oriented cycles.

Must a graph with large chromatic number have large dichromatic number? Must a graph with large cochromatic number contain a graph with large dichromatic number?

### Context
The first question is due to Erdős and Neumann-Lara. The second question is due to Erdős and Gimbel. A positive answer to the second question implies a positive answer to the first via the bound mentioned in [[760]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/760).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #769 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/769).

### Problem
Let $c(n)$ be minimal such that if $k\geq c(n)$ then the $n$-dimensional unit cube can be decomposed into $k$ homothetic $n$-dimensional cubes. Give good bounds for $c(n)$ - in particular, is it true that $c(n) \gg n^n$?

### Context
A problem first investigated by Hadwiger, who proved the lower bound\[c(n) \geq 2^n+2^{n-1}.\]It is easy to see that $c(2)=6$. Meier conjectured $c(3)=48$. Burgess and Erdős [Er74b] proved\[c(n) \ll n^{n+1}.\]Erdős wrote 'I am certain that if $n+1$ is a prime then $c(n)>n^n$.'

Hudelson [Hu98] proved that if $(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ then $c(n) < 6^n$, and in general $c(n) \ll (2n)^{n-1}$. Connor and Marmorino [CoMa18] proved that\[c(n) \geq 2^{n+1}-1\]for all $n\geq 3$,\[c(n) \leq 1.8n^{n+1}\]if $n+1$ is prime, and\[c(n) \leq e^2n^n\]otherwise.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #770 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/770).

### Problem
Let $h(n)$ be minimal such that $2^n-1,3^n-1,\ldots,h(n)^n-1$ are mutually coprime.

Does, for every prime $p$, the density $\delta_p$ of integers with $h(n)=p$ exist? Does $\liminf h(n)=\infty$? Is it true that if $p$ is the greatest prime such that $p-1\mid n$ and $p>n^\epsilon$ then $h(n)=p$?

### Context
It is easy to see that $h(n)=n+1$ if and only if $n+1$ is prime, and that $h(n)$ is unbounded for odd $n$.

It is probably true that $h(n)=3$ for infinitely many $n$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The following has been checked (a sanity check on the intuition below with data): among the smallest $20000$ primes $p$, there are $1278$ for which $\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1)>1.$
So for $18722$ of them, we have $h(p)=3.$

Heuristically, the larger $p$ the larger the probability that $h(p)=1.$
This is since $\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1)>1$ implies there is a prime $q=kp+1$ dividing both. There are fewer values of (even) $k$ for which these are prime (behaves like one over $\log(k)+\log(p)$...), and so fewer chances that both $2$ and $3$ are $k^{th}$ powers modulo $kp+1$.

Actually, the density of primes for which $h(p)=3$ should be one.
(the probability of failing can be estimated above by $\frac{1}{\log p} \left( 1- \frac{\pi^2}{24}\right)$ for every $p$)

Anyone who thinks this can be made rigourous?

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Small observation on second problem:
we will need to prove that either there are infinitely many primes $n$ such that $h(n)=3$, or all prime powers of a fixed prime satisfy $h(p^k)=3$.
(if $h(n)=3$, then every prime divisor $d$ of $n$ satisfies $h(d)=3$ and thus only finitely many prime powers with value $3$ implies also finitely many values in general have value $3$)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
General thoughts on the last problem:
for fixed $\epsilon>0$, $n$ large and $p<n^\epsilon$ the largest prime such that $p-1 \mid n$.
Assume that $2^n-1,3^n-1 \ldots, p^n-1$ are all multiples of a prime $r>p$.

Now $2,3,\ldots, p$ are all $k^{th}$ powers modulo $r$, where $k=\frac{r-1}{\gcd(r-1,n)}>2$.

If $r \le 2n$, this should be impossible since one expects only $\Theta(\log(n))<n^{\epsilon}$ many consecutive $k^{th}$ powers modulo $r$.
(see also the discussion and links at [[stackexchange]](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4513213/is-there-any-way-to-predict-the-largest-number-of-consecutive-quadratic-or-cubic))

If $r>2n$, then $\log_k(r) \le \log_k(kn+1)<\log_2(n+1)+1$ and the same estimate implies we do not expect this to happen.

(observation: We can exclude $k$ large, in terms of $\epsilon$, by considering the number of $n^{\epsilon}$ smooth numbers up to $n$.)

$\textbf{note about small values}$
for $n=4044, h(n)=17>13$ (largest prime such that $p-1 \mid 4044$)
Here $\log_{4044}{13}>0.3$ is reasonable big.
(but so we have to think as $n$ to be sufficiently large for every $\epsilon$)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Some thoughts on non-conditional proofs:
$\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1) \not=1$ is possible when $2^p-1$ is not a prime, e.g. when $p=11.$
One may expect on the other hand that the chance that the gcd is not $1$ is somewhat small. A prime factor $kp+1$, where $k$ is even, can only occur if both $2$ and $3$ are perfect $k^{th}$ powers. ($\sum_{ 2 \mid k} 1/k^2 <1$).

Proving it for prime powers also looked an option.
E.g., if $n=5^k$, then $\gcd(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ whenever $k\le 10.$

Nevertheless, this fails for $k \ge 42$, since in that case $72*5^{42}+1$ is a divisor of both $2^n-1$ and $3^n-1$.

So there is likely no argument why it should work for all prime powers of another prime, e.g. $n=3^k$ for all k.

Showing that a certain pattern/ infinite subset among the many solutions exists, see [[oeis/A263647]](https://oeis.org/A263647) for the first $10000$ values, may be hard or even impossible.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
For the second question: so it is conjectured that $h(n)=3$ infinitely often.
Conditional on the assumption that there are infinitely many Mersenne primes, which seems to be widely believed meanwhile (see e.g. [[wiki:Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersenne_conjectures#Lenstra.E2.80.93Pomerance.E2.80.93Wagstaff_conjecture) and links for some conjecture on the counting function), this can be confirmed.

Let $q=2^p-1$ be a Mersenne prime.
Here $q=kp+1$ for some integer $k$.
We have that $q \mid 3^p-1$ if $3$ is a $k^{th}$ power modulo $q.$
But the $k^{th}$ powers modulo $q$ are exactly $1,2,2^2,2^3, \ldots,2^{p-1}$.
So $3$ is not among them.
We conclude that $\gcd(2^p-1,3^p-1)=1.$

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Guess it is important to connect this problem to [[\#820]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/820).

In particular there is the connection to the OEIS there, and a link to the conjecture that says $h(n)=3$ occurs infinitely often, see [[Ailon-Rudnick]](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/~rudnick/papers/aa113-1-03.pdf).

For the last question; guess this has to be interpreted for any $\epsilon>0$, since I expect that it is true for $\epsilon>1/3$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #774 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/774).

### Problem
We call $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ dissociated if $\sum_{n\in X}n\neq \sum_{m\in Y}m$ for all finite $X,Y\subset A$ with $X\neq Y$.

Let $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set. We call $A$ proportionately dissociated if every finite $B\subset A$ contains a dissociated set of size $\gg \lvert B\rvert$.

Is every proportionately dissociated set the union of a finite number of dissociated sets?

### Context
This question appears in a paper of Alon and Erdős [AlEr85], although the general topic was first considered by Pisier [Pi83], who observed that the converse holds, and proved that being proportionately dissociated is equivalent to being a 'Sidon set' in the harmonic analysis sense; that is, whenever $f:A\to \mathbb{C}$ there exists some $\theta\in [0,1]$ such that\[\| f\|_1 \ll \left\lvert\sum_{n\in A} f(n)e(n\theta)\right\rvert,\]where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$.

Alon and Erdős write that it 'seems unlikely that [this] is also sufficient'. They also point out the same question can be asked replacing dissociated with Sidon (in the additive combinatorial sense) (see [[328]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/328)). This latter question was resolved in the negative by Nešetřil, Rödl, and Sales [NRS24].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #776 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/776).

### Problem
Let $r\geq 2$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ be such that $A_i\not\subseteq A_j$ for all $i\neq j$ and for any $t$ if there exists some $i$ with $\lvert A_i\rvert=t$ then there must exist at least $r$ sets of that size.

How large must $n$ be (as a function of $r$) to ensure that there is such a family which achieves $n-3$ distinct sizes of sets?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Trotter. For $r=1$ and $n>3$ the maximum possible is $n-2$. For $r>1$ and $n$ sufficiently large $n-3$ is achievable, but $n-2$ is never achievable.
