problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #840 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/840).

### Problem
Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest quasi-Sidon subset $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where we say that $A$ is quasi-Sidon if\[\lvert A+A\rvert=(1+o(1))\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}.\]How does $f(N)$ grow?

### Context
Considered by Erdős and Freud [ErFr91], who proved\[\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2} \leq f(N) \leq \left(2+o(1)\right)N^{1/2}.\](Although both bounds were already given by Erdős in [Er81h].) Note that $2/\sqrt{3}=1.15\cdots$. The lower bound is taking a genuine Sidon set $B\subset [1,N/3]$ of size $\sim N^{1/2}/\sqrt{3}$ and taking the union with $\{N-b : b\in B\}$. The upper bound was improved by Pikhurko [Pi06] to\[f(N) \leq \left(\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{(\pi+2)^2}\right)^{-1/2}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2}\](the constant here is $=1.863\cdots$).

The analogous question with $A-A$ in place of $A+A$ is simpler, and there the maximal size is $\sim N^{1/2}$, as [proved by Cilleruelo](https://matematicas.uam.es/~franciscojavier.cilleruelo/Papers/quasi-Sidon%20-%20greedy%20-%20solo%20A-A.pdf).

sourceComments.contentMd:
On February 21, a DeepMind prover agent found a Lean proof falsifying this conjecture. The proof was discovered fully autonomously; the only problem-specific human input was the formal problem statement [link 1], drawn from Formal Conjectures [link 2]. The full Lean proof (compilable with Lean 4.22) is available here [link 3].

link 2: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures
link 3: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/2404258180688283e5141021c75464dc2acfb798/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/846.lean

replies.author: GTsoukalas
replies.contentMd:
Here is a summary of the proof, written by Adam Zsolt Wagner:

1. Label the vertices of the infinite complete graph with numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots$. These $x_i$ will be chosen to be a sequence that grows very quickly, to avoid accidental clashes in the following embedding.
2. We define the point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as follows. For every edge $(x_i, x_j)$ of this infinite complete graph, we include the point $(x_i + x_j, x_i^2 + x_i \cdot x_j + x_j^2)$.
3. This embedding has the property that three edges form a triangle if and only if the corresponding points are collinear.
4. The resulting point set satisfies the condition of the problem with $\epsilon = 1/2$. Indeed, given $n$ points, they correspond to a graph with n edges. Every graph with n edges has a bipartite subgraph with at least $n/2$ edges. Such a subgraph is triangle-free, so it corresponds to at least $n/2$ points with no three on a line.
5. A subset of our points with no three on a line corresponds to a triangle-free subgraph of the infinite complete graph. By infinite Ramsey, whenever the edges of the infinite complete graph are finitely colored, one of the color classes contains a triangle. So we cannot cover our point set with finitely many sets with no three on a line.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #849 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/849).

### Problem
Is it true that, for every integer $t\geq 1$, there is some integer $a$ such that\[\binom{n}{k}=a\](with $1\leq k\leq n/2$) has exactly $t$ solutions?

### Context
Erdős [Er96b] credits this to himself and Gordon 'many years ago', but it is more commonly known as [Singmaster's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singmaster%27s_conjecture). For $t=3$ one could take $a=120$, and for $t=4$ one could take $a=3003$. There are no known examples for $t\geq 5$.

Both Erdős and Singmaster believed the answer to this question is no, and in fact that there exists an absolute upper bound on the number of solutions.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #850 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/850).

### Problem
Can there exist two distinct integers $x$ and $y$ such that $x,y$ have the same prime factors, $x+1,y+1$ have the same prime factors, and $x+2,y+2$ also have the same prime factors?

### Context
This is sometimes known as the Erdős-Woods conjecture.

For just $x,y$ and $x+1,y+1$ one can take\[x=2(2^r-1)\]and\[y = x(x+2).\]Erdős also asked whether there are any other examples. Makowski [Ma68] observed that $x=75$ and $y=1215$ is another example, since\[75 = 3\cdot 5^2 \textrm{ and }1215 = 3^5\cdot 5\]while\[76 = 2^2\cdot 19\textrm{ and }1216 = 2^6\cdot 19.\](This example was also found independently by Matthew Bolan, and by Dubickas, who posed it as part of the 2024 team selection test in Lithuania.) No other examples are known. This sequence is listed as [A343101](https://oeis.org/A343101) at the OEIS.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
This looks like a viable strategy to me.  One can prove Romanoff's theorem by computing first and second moments of the representation function $r(n) = \sum_{2^k+p=n} 1$; sieve theory only gets an upper bound for the second moment that is off by a constant, so one only gets positive density in this fashion.  The GPT proof works with the representation function $R(n) = \sum_{2^k+m=n} 1$ where $m$ is constrained to not be divisible by any prime between $z$ and $x^{1/t}$ for some large constants $z,t$ (which implies that $m$ has $O_{z,t}(1)$ prime divisors for $n \leq x$).  Sieve theory is capable of estimating first and second moments here to high accuracy (if $t$ is large), and there are no irregularities coming from small primes (because $z$ is large), so this will in principle give the desired $1-\varepsilon$ type density just from the fundamental lemma of sieve theory.  (The average number of solutions here is $\asymp t \log z$, so well above $1$ and so Chebyshev's inequality has a good shot at getting the density close to $1$ if one can also hold the variance to $O(t \log z)$ as one would expect from Poisson heuristics.)

The proof should be streamlined and aligned with existing literature, preferably by a human expert, but this looks doable.  Lean formalization might barely be possible with the existing sieve theory and other analytic number theory tools present in Mathlib and PNT+ but would be a non-trivial challenge. (I don't believe the fundamental lemma of sieve theory is in either repository yet, for instance.)

EDIT: There is surprisingly little work on this problem, given that Romanoff's theorem is very well known (78 citations on MathSciNet).  The closest recent reference I could find is [this 2024 paper by Zhao](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO202405260120370.page), which focuses on [counterexamples in an arithmetic progression](https://koreascience.or.kr/article/JAKO202405260120370.page) for any fixed $r$ using the covering congruence method, but this problem of Erdos seems to have been completely overlooked in the literature.  AI Deep research tools were surprisingly useless here: [Claude](https://claude.ai/share/d9c6af06-fe26-43ad-9ed4-b6ef056719a4) and [ChatGPT Deep Research](https://chatgpt.com/share/6984f8b0-a16c-800e-94fa-655511d4c959) both confused this problem with #205.  [Gemini DeepResearch](https://gemini.google.com/share/4f2585d7f088) did give an accurate summary of related results, though lacking some of the most recent results I found with more traditional literature search.

SECOND EDIT: I can now confirm that the proof is correct.  After applying the fundamental lemma of sieve theory to estimate the first and second moments of $R$, the task boils down to showing that a singular series $\prod_{z \leq p \leq x^{1/t}: p | 2^k - 2^l} (1 + O(1/p))$ is close to $1$ on average after averaging over $k \neq l$.  The condition $p | 2^k - 2^l$ can be rewritten as the condition that $k-l$ is a multiple of $\mathrm{ord}_2(p)$.  Because of the very slow divergence of $\sum_p 1/p$, the only dangerous cases are those where $\mathrm{ord}_2(p)$ is of logarithmic size, but this occurs for very few primes $p$, because any Mersenne number $2^a-1$ can have at most $O(a)$ prime factors.  (This is quantified in Lemma 7 of the AI-generated proof.)

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd:
Rather amusingly Ben Green and I have had a version of this argument for a while. One can in fact take $k(\epsilon) = O(\log(1/\epsilon)/\log\log(1/\epsilon))$. This requires instead of using a second moment argument a high moment argument. This basically seems to be limit of a sieve theoretic approach directly though.

The more natural question after thinking about this is whether $k$ can be taken independent of $\epsilon$. This seems to an extremely difficult question closely related to covering congruences. (One can reduce this to a purely local problem however instead of a sieve theory task. The crucial thing is to allow various numbers under consideration to have an additional prime factor between $(\log n)$ and $(\log n)^{\omega(1)}$ say.

In particular based on naive probabilistic considerations one might expect that $k(\epsilon) =2$; however covering congruences plus Bang's theorem (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zsigmondy%27s_theorem) explain this is false. This is explained in the work of Erdos and therefore proving that one can take $k(\epsilon)$ bounded requires at least Hough's celebrated result.

replies.author: msawhney
replies.contentMd: The initial bound off the singular series is essentially in a paper of Matthews (Counting points modulo p for some finitely generated subgroups of algebraic groups).

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
It seems [A078515](https://oeis.org/A078515) is the inverse of this function $h(x)$, and 27 terms are available.

I think looking at small terms can be highly misleading in asymptotic number theory, but from the data so far, it ["looks exponential"](https://chatgpt.com/share/694a1309-86f4-8000-b36e-1d88e6071234).  (Link goes to a ChatGPT session with a basic plot.)  In terms of the original problem, I think this would mean $h(x) = \theta(\log n)$.

I have not even done the basic analysis of what a random model of the primes would suggest.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #854 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/854).

### Problem
Let $n_k$ denote the $k$th primorial, i.e. the product of the first $k$ primes.

If $1=a_1<a_2<\cdots a_{\phi(n_k)}=n_k-1$ is the sequence of integers coprime to $n_k$, then estimate the smallest even integer not of the form $a_{i+1}-a_i$. Are there\[\gg \max_i (a_{i+1}-a_i)\]many even integers of the form $a_{j+1}-a_j$?

### Context
This was asked by Erdős in Oberwolfach (most likely in 1986). Clearly all differences $a_{i+1}-a_i$ are even. Erdős first thought that (for large enough $k$) all even $t\leq \max(a_{i+1}-a_i)$ can be written as $t=a_{j+1}-a_j$ for some $j$, but in [Ob1] writes 'perhaps this is false', and reports some computations of Lacampagne and Selfridge that this fails for $n_k=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13$ which 'show some doubt on [his] conjecture', and says it could fail for all or infinitely many $k$.

In [Ob1] he also asks about the set of $j$ for which $a_{j+1}-a_j=\max(a_{i+1}-a_i)$, and in particular asks for estimates on the number of such $j$ and the minimal value of such a $j$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
$\textbf{Remark on different variant (not initial question)}$

If we would consider all differences of the form $a_i-a_j$, the answer becomes very different.
*if not excluding odd integers, the answer is 1 (this is also the case for the initial problem)
*if we are restricting to even integers, it is $(1-o(1))n_k$

If we denote $f(k)$ for the smallest positive even integer not of the form $a_i-a_j$,
then the right but harder question would be to estimate how large $n_k-f(k)$ is.
I could easily prove that this is $o(n_k)$ (e.g. bounded by $4n_{k-1}$), and with some work even that it is much smaller for large $k$.
Nevertheless, the right answer here should be $n_k-f(k)=(2+o(1))p_k$.

The lower bound for that is trivial.
Note that the sequence starts with $a_1=1, a_2=p_{k+1}, a_3=p_{k+2} \ldots$ (till $p_k^2$ appears at some point)
and $a_{\phi{(n_k)}+1-i}=n-a_i$.
Let $r$ be an odd composite prime smaller than $2p_{k+1}$, then $n_k-(r-1)$ cannot be written as $a_i-a_j$, since $a_{\phi{(n_k)}-1}-a_2$<$n_k-(r+1)$ and $a_{\phi{(n_k)}}-a_i=a_{\phi{(n_k)}+1-i}-a_1$ cannot be $r-1$, since $r$ is not a prime (and it is smaller than $p_k^2$).

The upper bound is not trivial (understatement)
Assumption (stronger form Goldbach's conjecture):
For an integer $q$>$0$, every even integer larger than some $2q+o(q)$ can be written as the sum of two primes larger than $q$.
It even may well be that the $o(q)$ is polylog(q).

Now take an even number (bounded by $n_k$) larger larger than $(2+o(1))p_{k}$,
this can be written as the sum $p_r+p_s$ with $r,s$>$k$ by the above assumption.
Now $p_r$ and $n_k-p_s$ are both relative prime with $n_k$ and thus of the form $a_i,a_j$.
Now $a_j-a_i=n_k-(p_r+p_s).$

From this we conclude.

For completeness, hereby also the easy proof (which can be sharpened, but not up to the right form)
By induction, for $k \ge 2$, and even $m$, does $m$ or $n_k-m$ appear as $a_i-a_j$. (base step $k=2,3$ trivial to check)

Now going to $n_{k+1}$, take an even number $m$<$n_{k+1}-4n_k$.
Let $m=r n_k + s.$
Then $s$ or $n_k-s$ appeared before as a difference.
If it is $n_k-s$, then write $n_k+a_i-a_j=s$.

Now $((r+v)n_k+a_j,vn_k+a_i)$ or $((r+v+1)n_k+a_i,vn_k+a_j)$ is a solution for some $v \in \{0,1,2\}$ since for each linear combination, only one $v$ can lead to a multiple of $p_{k+1}.$
So each such $m$ can be written as the difference of two numbers relative prime with $n_{k+1}$ smaller than $n_{k+1}.$

Summary
smallest even number not of the form $a_i-a_j$ is proven to be at most $n_k-4n_{k-1}=(1-o(1))n_k$
and conjectured to be $n_k-(2+o(1))p_k$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #855 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/855).

### Problem
If $\pi(x)$ counts the number of primes in $[1,x]$ then is it true that (for large $x$ and $y$)\[\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)?\]

### Context
Commonly known as the [second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_conjecture). In [Er85c] Erdős describes it as 'an old conjecture of mine which was probably already stated by Hardy and Littlewood'.

This is probably false, since Hensley and Richards [HeRi73] have shown that this is false assuming the [Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_conjecture). Indeed, assuming this conjecture, they prove that for every large $y$ there are infinitely many $x$ such that\[\pi(x+y)>\pi(x)+\pi(y)+(\log 2-o(1))\frac{y}{(\log y)^2},\]where the $o(1)$ term tends to $0$ as $y\to \infty$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Commonly known as the second Hardy-Littlewood conjecture. In [Er85c] Erdős describes it as 'an old conjecture of mine which was probably already stated by Hardy and Littlewood'.

This is probably false, since Hensley and Richards [HeRi73] have shown that this is false assuming the Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture. Indeed, assuming this conjecture, they prove that for every large $y$ there are infinitely many $x$ such that\pi(x+y)>\pi(x)+\pi(y)+(\log 2-o(1))\frac{y}{(\log y)^2},where the $o(1)$ term tends to $0$ as $y\to \infty$.

Erdős [Er85c] reports Straus as remarking that the 'correct way' of stating this conjecture would have been\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+2\pi(y/2).Clark and Jarvis [ClJa01] have shown this is also incompatible with the prime tuples conjecture.

In [Er85c] Erdős conjectures the weaker result (which in particular follows from the conjecture of Straus) that\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)+O\left(\frac{y}{(\log y)^2}\right),which the Hensley and Richards result shows (conditionally) would be best possible. Richards conjectured that this is false.

Erdős and Richards further conjectured that the original inequality is true almost always - that is, the set of $x$ such that $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ for all $y<x$ has density $1$. They could only prove that this set has positive lower density.
They also conjectured that for every $x$ the inequality $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ is true provided $y \gg (\log x)^C$ for some large constant $C>0$.

Hardy and Littlewood proved\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+O(\pi(y)).The best known in this direction is a result of Montgomery and Vaughan [MoVa73], which shows\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+2\frac{y}{\log y}.This is discussed in problem A9 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #856 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/856).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 3$ and $f_k(N)$ be the maximum value of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$, where $A$ ranges over all subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ which contain no subset of size $k$ with the same pairwise least common multiple.

Estimate $f_k(N)$.

### Context
Erdős [Er70] notes that\[f_k(N) \ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}.\]Indeed, let $A$ be such a set. This in particular implies that, for every $t$, there are $<k$ solutions to $t=ap$ with $a\in A$ and $p$ prime, whence\[\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{p<N}\frac{1}{p}< k \sum_{t<N^2}\frac{1}{t} \ll \log N,\]and the bound follows since $\sum_{p<N}\frac{1}{p}\gg \log\log N$.

Improved bounds have been given by Tang and Zhang [TaZh25b], who proved bounds of the shape\[(\log N)^{b_k-o(1)}\leq f_k(N)\leq (\log N)^{c_k+o(1)}\]for some constants $0<b_k\leq c_k\leq 1$, and in particular\[(\log N)^{0.438}\leq f_3(N)\leq (\log N)^{0.889},\]say, for all large $N$. The exponents here are related to progress in the sunflower conjecture [[857]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/857), to which this problem is closely related. For example, the exponents $c_k$ are $<1$ (and so the upper bound above is non-trivial) if and only if [[857]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/857) holds for $k$-sunflowers.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
In joint work with Shengtong, we wrote a paper on this problem ([arXiv:2512.20055](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.20055)) and make precise its connection to [[857]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/857).
Summary: Define the Erdős-Szemerédi $k$-sunflower-free capacity by \(\mu_k^{\mathrm S}:=\limsup_{n\to\infty} F_k(n)^{1/n}\), where $F_k(n)$ denotes the maximum size of a $k$-sunflower-free family of subsets of $[n]$. [[857]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/857) (the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture) asserts that $\mu_k^{\mathrm S}<2$ for every $k\ge 3$. Our main results are:
(1) Equivalence. For each fixed $k\ge 3$,  \( \mu_k^{\mathrm S}=2\) iff \( f_k(N)=(\log N)^{1-o(1)}.\)

(2) Lower bounds. $f_k(N)\ge (\log N)^{b_k-o(1)}$, where $b_k:=\max\{c_k, \log\mu_k^{\mathrm S}\}$ and $c_k:=\frac{k-2}{e((k-2)!)^{1/(k-2)}}.$

(3) Upper bound. $f_k(N)\ll (\log N)^{\mu_k^{\mathrm S}-1+o(1)}.$

As an illustration, when $k=3$ one has $\mu_3^{\mathrm S}\ge 1.551$ (a construction of Deuber--Erdős--Gunderson--Kostochka--Meyer) and $\mu_3^{\mathrm S}\le 3/2^{2/3}$ (Naslund--Sawin), hence\[
(\log N)^{\log(1.551)-o(1)} \ \le\ f_3(N)\ \ll\ (\log N)^{\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}-1+o(1)}.
\]Numerically, $\log(1.551)\approx 0.4389$ and $\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}-1\approx 0.8899$.

sourceComments.author: KoishiChan
sourceComments.contentMd:
It is actually possible to improve this bound: for each $\ell$, note that for each $n$ the number of solutions to
$$n = a p_1 \cdots p_{\ell}$$
where $p_i$ are distinct primes and $a \in A$ is $O(k \log(\ell k))^{\ell}$. This is because, if we associate the set $\{p_1, \cdots, p_{\ell}\}$ with such a solution, then the set system cannot contain a $k$-sunflower. The best bound on the sunflower lemma yields this result.

Thus, we have
$$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a}\sum_{n \leq N:  \omega(n) = \Omega(n) = \ell} \frac{1}{n} \ll O(k \log(\ell k))^{\ell} \log N.$$
I think when $\ell = o(\log\log N)$ we have
$$\sum_{n \leq N:  \omega(n) = \Omega(n) = \ell} \frac{1}{n} \geq \frac{1}{\ell!} \Omega(\log\log N)^{\ell}.$$
Hence the best choice of $\ell$ should be something like
$$\ell = \epsilon_k \frac{\log\log N}{\log\log\log N}$$
which yields
$$\sum_{a \in A} \frac{1}{a} \leq \log N \cdot \exp\left(-\epsilon_k \frac{\log\log N}{\log\log\log N}\right)$$
where $\epsilon_k > 0$ is some constant depending on $k$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Looks good to me, thanks. The conjectured bounds on the sunflower problem (see [[20]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/20)) would improve this upper bound to $(\log N)^{1-c_k}$ for some $c_k>0$.

What about lower bounds? For example, for $k=3$ the set of primes is an easy example, so $f_3(N)\gg \log\log N$. I feel like a better lower bound like $\gg (\log N)^c$ should be achievable via an inductive approach, where we have $a=pn$ with $p$ a large prime and $n$ an element of a smaller good set via induction.

sourceComments.author: sproutseeds
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have been working on a fully formal Lean 4 development of the weak sunflower numbers M(n,3).

Exact values certified so far:

M(1,3)=2 through M(4,3)=8 are certified in Lean using native_decide, with both lower and upper bounds formalized.

M(5,3)=12 and M(6,3)=19 are certified via a SAT+LRAT bridge. The SAT encodings are generated from Lean, and the resulting LRAT certificates are verified independently.

M(7,3)=29 is certified via SAT+LRAT. At target size 30, four independent SAT solvers (CaDiCaL, Glucose4, MapleSAT, Lingeling) all return UNSAT, and verified LRAT certificates are included in the repository. The lower bound (existence at 29) is also formalized.

All proofs in the Lean development are sorry-free. Every result is verified locally by the Lean kernel using lake build, independent of any external service.

The SAT+LRAT certificates for M(5,3), M(6,3), and M(7,3) are fully reproducible and can be re-checked using any independent LRAT verifier without involvement from any language model.

Beyond exact values, the development includes:

A formally proved Local Turán-type inequality.

A formal statement of the Balance conjecture with low/high frequency case structure developed.

Pair-weight counting machinery for structured extremal arguments.

A reusable Lean-to-SAT pipeline with verified LRAT checking for combinatorial certification.

The development was carried out collaboratively with language models (primarily OpenAI Codex via Codex CLI and Anthropic Claude via Claude CLI) generating candidate proof attempts. However, all acceptance criteria were enforced locally: every theorem was only committed if the Lean kernel verified it without sorry. The Lean kernel is the ground truth; models generated candidates, and invalid attempts were rejected and rolled back.

Early in the project I made a single exploratory call to Aristotle to inspect how it would structure a Lean formalization; those example files remain in the repository. All substantive development was subsequently performed using Codex and Claude.

The SAT+LRAT results and Lean proofs are independent of any language model once generated; they are mechanically checkable artifacts.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #858 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/858).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be such that there is no solution to $at=b$ with $a,b\in A$ and the smallest prime factor of $t$ is $>a$. Estimate the maximum of\[\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}.\]

### Context
Alexander [Al66] and Erdős, Sárközi, and Szemerédi [ESS68] proved that this maximum is $o(1)$ (as $N\to \infty$). This condition on $A$ is a weaker form of the usual primitive condition. If $A$ is primitive then Behrend [Be35] proved\[\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{1}{\sqrt{\log\log N}}.\]An example of such a set $A$ is the set of all integers in $[N^{1/2},N]$ divisible by some prime $>N^{1/2}$.

See also [[143]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/143).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #863 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/863).

### Problem
Let $r\geq 2$ and let $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a set of maximal size such that there are at most $r$ solutions to $n=a+b$ with $a\leq b$ for any $n$. (That is, $A$ is a $B_2[r]$ set.)

Similarly, let $B\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a set of maximal size such that there are at most $r$ solutions to $n=a-b$ for any $n$.

If $\lvert A\rvert\sim c_rN^{1/2}$ as $N\to \infty$ and $\lvert B\rvert \sim c_r'N^{1/2}$ as $N\to \infty$ then is it true that $c_r\neq c_r'$ for $r\geq 2$? Is it true that $c_r'<c_r$?

### Context
According to Erdős, first formulated in conversation with Berend, and later independently reformulated with Freud.

It is true that $c_1=c_1'$, and the classical bound on the size of Sidon sets (see [[30]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/30)) implies $c_1=c_1'=1$.

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #864 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/864).

### Problem
Let $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots N\}$ be a set such that there exists at most one $n$ with more than one solution to $n=a+b$ (with $a\leq b\in A$). Estimate the maximal possible size of $\lvert A\rvert$ - in particular, is it true that\[\lvert A\rvert \leq (1+o(1))\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}N^{1/2}?\]

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Freud, who prove that\[\lvert A\rvert \geq (1+o(1))\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}N^{1/2}.\]This is shown by taking a genuine Sidon set $B\subset [1,N/3]$ of size $\sim N^{1/2}/\sqrt{3}$ and taking the union with $\{N-b : b\in B\}$.

For the analogous question with $n=a-b$ they prove that $\lvert A\rvert\sim N^{1/2}$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #865 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/865).

### Problem
There exists a constant $C>0$ such that, for all large $N$, if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has size at least $\frac{5}{8}N+C$ then there are distinct $a,b,c\in A$ such that $a+b,a+c,b+c\in A$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Sós (also earlier considered by Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi [CES75], but Erdős had forgotten this). Taking all integers in $[N/8,N/4]$ and $[N/2,N]$ shows that $\frac{5}{8}$ would be best possible here.

It is a classical folklore fact that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,2N\}$ has size $\geq N+2$ then there are distinct $a,b\in A$ such that $a+b\in A$, which establishes the $k=2$ case.

researchNotes: A problem of Erdős and Sós (also earlier considered by Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi [CES75], but Erdős had forgotten this). Taking all integers in $[N/8,N/4]$ and $[N/2,N]$ shows that $\frac{5}{8}$ would be best possible here.
It is a classical folklore fact that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,2N\}$ has size $\geq N+2$ then there are distinct $a,b\in A$ such that $a+b\in A$, which establishes the $k=2$ case.

In general, one can define $f_k(N)$ to be minimal such that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ has size at least $f_k(N)$ then there are $k$ distinct $a_i\in A$ such that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums are elements of $A$. Erdős and Sós conjectured thatf_k(N)\sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sum_{1\leq r\leq k-2}\frac{1}{4^r}\right) N,and a similar example shows that this would be best possible.
Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi [CES75] have proved that, for all $k\geq 3$, there exists $\epsilon_k>0$ such that (for large enough $N$)f_k(N)\leq \left(\frac{2}{3}-\epsilon_k\right)N.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
If it is true for large N, it will be for all N (possibly with a slightly larger constant C).

Maybe interestingly, for $N=8i+6$, where $i \le 6$, the maximum is $5i+5$, except for $N=14$ when the maximum is $11.$
The latter attained e.g. by the set $\{1,2,4\} \cup [N/2, N]$.

For $N=8i$ and $3\le i \le 7$, the construction $[N/8,N/4]\cup[N/2,N]$ is actually the only extremal construction (not containing a subset of the form $\{a,b,c,a+b,b+c,a+c\}$) attaining size $5/8N+2$.

So this suggests that likely the answer to the question is yes (and $C$ can be even taken rather small).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #866 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/866).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 3$ and $g_k(N)$ be minimal such that if $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,2N\}$ has $\lvert A\rvert \geq N+g_k(N)$ then there exist integers $b_1,\ldots,b_k$ such that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums are in $A$ (but the $b_i$ themselves need not be in $A$).

Estimate $g_k(N)$.

### Context
A problem of Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi. It is clear that, for the set of odd numbers in $\{1,\ldots,2N\}$, no such $b_i$ exist, whence $g_k(N)\geq 0$ always.  Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi proved that $g_3(N)=2$ and $g_4(N) \ll 1$. van Doorn has [shown](https://github.com/Woett/Mathematical-shorts/blob/main/The%20cardinality%20of%20a%20set%20containing%20the%20pairwise%20sums%20of%20four%20integers.pdf) that $g_4(N)\leq 2032$.

Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi also proved that\[g_5(N)\asymp \log N\]and\[g_6(N)\asymp N^{1/2}.\]In general they proved that\[g_k(N) \ll_k N^{1-2^{-k}}\]and for every $\epsilon>0$ if $k$ is sufficiently large then\[g_k(N) > N^{1-\epsilon}.\]As an example, taking $A$ to be the set of all odd integers and the powers of $2$ shows that $g_5(N)\gg \log N$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
It is clear that the $b_i$ need to be distinct, and maybe one can add this requirement to the problem statement for completeness' sake. What is less clear however, is whether the $b_i$ need to be positive.

In all theorem statements in [[CES75]](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1975-39.pdf), they refer to the elements in $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ as *positive* integers, while the $b_i$ are just referred to as integers. This terminology is also used in [[Er92c, p.41]](https://hal.science/hal-01108666/document), suggesting that the $b_i$ are not required to be positive (although one can note that at most one can be non-positive, otherwise we have a negative sum).

With this in mind, define $h_k(N)$ as the smallest integer such that for all subsets $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ with $|A| \ge N + h_k(N)$ there exist distinct *positive* integers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k$ such that all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums are in $A$. With $g_k(N)$ defined as in the problem statement (i.e. without the positivity requirement), in general we then have $h_{k-1}(N) \le g_k(N) \le h_k(N)$.

Annoyingly, $g_k(N)$ and $h_k(N)$ are not the same function, and the lower bounds that Choi, Erdős and Szemerédi claim for $k = 3$ and $k = 5$ do not actually work for $g_k(N)$. In particular, the example (mentioned at the end of the remarks) of taking $A \subset \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ to be the union $$\{1, 3, \ldots, 2N-1\} \cup \{2, 4, \ldots, 2^{\lfloor \log_2 2N \rfloor} \}$$for a set for which supposedly no $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_5$ exist is incorrect as stated; with $b_1 = -1$, $b_2 = 2$, $b_3 = 3$, $b_4 = 5$, $b_5 = 6$, one can check that all pairwise sums do belong to $A$ whenever $N \ge 6$. The example does work to show the lower bound $h_5(N) \gg \log N$, and perhaps (?) it can be fixed to make it work for $g_5(N)$ as well. At the moment I have no non-trivial lower bound for $g_5(N)$, however.

For $k = 3$ on the other hand, the truth is that $g_k(N)$ is equal to $1$ for all $N \ge 3$. Which is in contrast to the equality $h_3(N) = 2$ that Choi, Erdős and Szemerédi actually (unwittingly?) prove for all $N \ge 4$.

To see why $g_3(N) \le 1$ (and therefore $g_3(N) = 1$) holds for all $N \ge 3$, let $A \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, 2N\}$ be any set with $|A| \ge N + 1$, and assume $N \ge 3$. Then $A$ contains $\{m, m+1\}$ for some odd $m \in \{1, 3, \ldots, 2N-1\}$ by the pigeonhole principle. If $A \setminus \{m \}$ only contains even integers, then $\{2, 4, 6\} \subseteq \{2, 4, \ldots, 2N\} \subset A$ and we can choose $b_1 = 0$, $b_2 = 2$, $b_3 = 4$. On the other hand, if $A$ contains an odd integer $2j+1 \neq m$, then we can choose $b_1 = j$, $b_2 = j+1$, $b_3 = m-j$, which are quickly checked to be distinct by the assumption $2j+1 \neq m$ and the fact that $m$ is odd. By the way, for $N  = 2$ one can note that the example $A = \{2, 3, 4\}$ shows $g_3(2) = 2$.

I'll hopefully have more to say in the not too distant future, but I first wanted to clear up the above subtlety.

If I find any improvements (or mistakes that change my currently claimed bound), or if I decide to put it on the arXiv, I'll be sure to update this comment.

### Problem
If $A_1,A_2$ are disjoint additive bases of order $2$ (i.e. $A_i+A_i$ contains all large integers) then must $A=A_1\cup A_2$ contain a minimal additive basis of order $2$ (one such that deleting any element creates infinitely many $n\not\in A+A$)?

### Context
A question of Erdős and Nathanson [ErNa88].

Härtter [Ha56] and Nathanson [Na74] proved that there exist additive bases which do not contain any minimal additive bases.

Let $k\geq 3$ and $A$ be an additive basis of order $k$. Does there exist a constant $c=c(k)>0$ such that if $r(n)\geq c\log n$ for all large $n$ then $A$ must contain a minimal basis of order $k$? Härtter [Ha56] and Nathanson [Na74] proved that there exist additive bases which do not contain any minimal additive bases.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #872 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/872).

### Problem
Consider the two-player game in which players alternately choose integers from $\{2,3,\ldots,n\}$ to be included in some set $A$ (the same set for both players) such that no $a\mid b$ for $a\neq b\in A$.

The game ends when no legal move is possible. One player wants the game to last as long as possible, the other wants the game to end quickly. How long can the game be guaranteed to last for?

At least $\epsilon n$ moves? (For $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ sufficiently large.) At least $(1-\epsilon)\frac{n}{2}$ moves?

### Context
A number theoretic variant of a combinatorial game of Hajnal, in which players alternately add edges to a graph while keeping it triangle-free. This game must trivially end in at most $n^2/4$ moves, and Füredi and Seress [FuSe91] proved that it can be guaranteed to last for $\gg n\log n$ moves. Biró, Horn, and Wildstrom [BPW16] proved that it must end in at most $(\frac{26}{121}+o(1))n^2$ moves.

This type of game is known as a saturation game.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

replies.author: Xiao_Hu
replies.contentMd:
One can slightly improve the GPT bound ϵ > 1/24 to ϵ > 1/15, by modifying C to include all odd numbers in between (n/5, n/3]. Now the possible multiples of s in C in the upper half interval [n/2, n] are 2s, 3s and 4s. By oddness one cannot have 2s=3s', 2s=4s' or 3s=4s' with s, s' in C. Thus these multiples are distinct and lemma 4.1 extends to this scenario. Everything else remains the same and you get ϵ > 1/15.

Edit: Further improvement to ϵ can be made by choosing C to be the set of all odd numbers in (n/7, n/3] that are not multiples of 5. Then you'll have ϵ>(1/3-1/7)*1/2*4/5=8/105

sourceComments.author: Thomas Bloom
sourceComments.contentMd:
With the help of ChatGPT I generated some code to work out the game length for each $N$ assuming both players are playing optimally, and the 'Long' player goes first. This sequence goes (from $N=2$ up to $N=40$).

1,2,2,3,3,4,4,5,5,5,5,6,6,7,7,7,7,8,8,9,9,10,10,
11,11,11,11,11,12,13,13,14,14,14,14,15,15,16,16,16,16

The corresponding sequence of $f(n)-\pi(n)$, if $f(n)$ is the length of the game, is $0$ for $2\leq N\leq 8$, $1$ for $9\leq N\leq 20$, $2$ for $21\leq N\leq 27$, $3$ for $28\leq N\leq 34$, and $4$ for $35\leq N\leq 40$.

As an instructive example, when $N=9$ (the first time this game goes on longer than the number of primes) one optimal (for both players) game goes
6 - 4 - 5 - 7 - 9

As another example, when $N=21$,
6 - 4 - 9 - 5 - 14 - 11 - 13 - 17 - 19 - 21
Or when $N=35$,
30-4-14-9-22-13-17-19-21-23-25-29-31-33-35

This (very limited) amount of computational evidence does seem to suggest that $f(n)-\pi(n)\to \infty$ at least.

It's a curious game - one might naively think that the Long player should focus on choosing large primes and the Short player should focus on choosing small primes, and indeed there is a 'prime bias' in the transcripts above (to be expected, e.g. certainly all primes in $(N/2,N]$ must appear at some point) but it seems like both players are better off choosing numbers with many factors for the first couple of turns at least.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
It seems like the long player should start with choosing the largest primorial (say $p_k$#) less than $N$, as this stops the short player from choosing any of the primes up to $p_k$. The short player then plays $2^2$. The long player then plays $p_n$#$/p_k$# for the largest $n$ such that this is less than $N$, and the short player plays $3^2$. Essentially the long player plays the product of the most consecutive primes that haven't appeared in prior turns that they can and the short player plays the smallest number that can be played. When the long player cannot do that any more, they take $\min\{2p\}$ for primes $p<N/2$ such that $2p$ can be played. I would imagine that when $N$ is large enough, the long player would perhaps move on to choosing the smallest possible $3p$ etc. Ultimately there remains a set of terms that must be chosen, such as the primes in $[N/2,N]$ or $pq>N/2$ when $2p$ and $2q$ have already been chosen.

The aim for the long player is to 'defend' as many small primes as possible, and the way to cover as many as possible at once is to choose the product of as many as you can. The aim for the short player is roughly to choose the smallest terms possible as these have the most multiples less than $N$, though there may be a preference towards small primes or squares of primes when possible.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd: Given that the player who wants the game to end quickly can just choose the primes, the game can always be ended in $\frac{n}{\log(n)}$ or $\frac{2n}{\log(n)}$ moves (depending how moves are counted).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
I don't think this is true - the other player might choose numbers with lots of prime divisors, so that after a certain point the other player has no primes left that are valid choices to play - but there still might be lots of other non-primes that are valid, so the game continues, and they have to abandon their primes-only strategy.

For example, when $N=9$, if the first player wants to end it quickly and the second wants to prolong it, and the first player tries to use only primes, then the game might go:
7 - 8 - 5 - 6 - 9
(This example still doesn't last long, but note that the first player still had the valid choice of 9 available even though all the primes were used up.)

It would be interesting to actually give an explicit strategy of the prolonger that shows they can also force it to last at least $100\frac{n}{\log n}$ (say) moves - given that Erdős was asking if the threshold was linear, presumably he believed this to be possible.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
This raises an interesting related question, which I hope can shed some light on the game: how small can a maximal primitive subset of $\{2,...,n\}$ be? The set of primes shows that it can be $\pi(n)$. Is this the smallest possible for all $n \geq 2$? If so, then the game must always last at least $\pi(n)$ moves no matter what the players do.
I'm not sure if Erdős ever asked this question. He and Cameron asked in [CaEr90] how many primitive subsets there are of $\{2,...,n\}$, and this was solved by Angelo [here](https://math.colgate.edu/~integers/s25/s25.pdf). (I don't think that problem appears on this website yet.) See, e.g., McNew's paper [here](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejc.2020.103237) for results on counting maximal primitive subsets of $\{2,...,n\}$, though more of the literature seems to focus on counting maximum-*size* primitive sets. However, I'm not sure if the question of how small a maximal primitive subset can be has ever appeared in the literature. There's a related paper [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.3007), but a quick skim didn't reveal any results that are applicable to this problem specifically.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Every maximal primitive subset must contain all primes in $(n/2,n]$, so $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$ is a lower bound.

replies.author: DesmondWeisenberg
replies.contentMd: Nice observation! That shows that if $A \subseteq \{2,...,N\}$ is a maximal primitive set, then $|A| \geq (\frac{1}{2} + o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$. In fact, it's actually not a lot harder to show that $|A| \geq (1 + o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$. This is because every prime number at least $\sqrt{n}$ must have a multiple in $A$, and no two of these primes can have a multiple in common. This shows that $|A|$ is at least the number of primes in $[\sqrt{n}, n]$, which is asymptotically $\frac{n}{\log n}$.

### Problem
Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and let $F(A,X,k)$ count the number of $i$ such that\[[a_i,a_{i+1},\ldots,a_{i+k-1}] < X,\]where the left-hand side is the least common multiple. Is it true that, for every $\epsilon >0$, there exists some $k$ such that\[F(A,X,k)<X^\epsilon?\]

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Szemerédi, who proved that for every $A$\[F(A,X,3) \ll X^{1/3}\log X,\]and there is an $A$ such that\[F(A,X,3) \gg X^{1/3}\log X\]for infinitely many $X$. There may be a sequence for which this holds for every $X$.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #875 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/875).

### Problem
Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set such that the sets\[S_r = \{ a_1+\cdots +a_r : a_1<\cdots<a_r\in A\}\]are disjoint for distinct $r\geq 1$. How fast can such a sequence grow? How small can $a_{n+1}-a_n$ be? In particular, for which $c$ is it possible that $a_{n+1}-a_n\leq n^{c}$?

### Context
A problem of Deshouillers and Erdős (an infinite version of [[874]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/874)). Such sets are sometimes called admissible. Erdős writes 'it [is not] completely trivial to find such a sequence for which $a_{n+1}/a_n\to 1$'. It is not clear from this whether Deshouillers and Erdős knew of such a sequence.

sourceComments.author: Aron Bhalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
GPT-5.2 Thinking identifies the following additional references:

1. Erdős–Nicolas–Sárközy, Sommes de sous-ensembles (J. Th'eor. Nombres Bordeaux 3 (1991), 55--72)

Here, they construct an infinite admissible set with $A(x):=\#\{a\in A:a\le x \} \gg x^{5-2\sqrt6}$ (Thm. 2). In particular this implies polynomial growth $a_n\ll n^{1/(5-2\sqrt6)}$, hence $\liminf_{n\to\infty} a_{n+1}/a_n=1$. So admissible sets of polynomial growth are known in the literature (at least since 1991).

2. Deshouillers--Freiman, On an additive problem of Erdős and Straus, 2 (Astérisque 258 (1999))

Here, they prove the sharp finite extremal bound: for $N$ large, any admissible $A\subset[1,N]$ satisfies $|A|\le 2\sqrt N + O(1)$ (indeed $\le 2\sqrt{N+\tfrac14}-1$). Consequently any infinite admissible $A=\{a_n\}$ has $A(x)\le (2+o(1))\sqrt x$ and $a_n\ge (1+o(1))n^2/4$; so an eventual gap bound $a_{n+1}-a_n\le n^c$ forces $c\ge 1$ (although it is also possible that no such $c$ exists for some choices of $A$).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #876 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/876).

### Problem
Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite sum-free set - that is, there are no solutions to\[a=b_1+\cdots+b_r\]with $b_1<\cdots<b_r<a\in A$. How small can $a_{n+1}-a_n$ be? Is it possible that $a_{n+1}-a_n<n$?

### Context
Erdős [Er98] writes that Graham 'recently proved' that there is such a sequence for which $a_{n+1}-a_n<n^{1+o(1)}$, and that Melfi proved a somewhat weaker result.

Erdős [Er62c] proved that a sum-free set has density zero. Deshouillers, Erdős, and Melfi [DEM99] constructed a sum-free set that grows like $a_n\sim n^{3+o(1)}$.

### Deliverable

problems.title: Erdos Problem #878: If $n=\prod_{1\leq i\leq t} p_i^{k_i}$ is the factorisation of $n$ into distinct primes then...
problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #878 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/878).

### Problem
If $n=\prod_{1\leq i\leq t} p_i^{k_i}$ is the factorisation of $n$ into distinct primes then let\[f(n)=\sum p_i^{\ell_i},\]where $\ell_i$ is chosen such that $n\in [p_i^{\ell_i},p_i^{\ell_i+1})$. Furthermore, let\[F(n)=\max \sum_{i=1}^t a_i\]where the maximum is taken over all $a_1,\ldots,a_t\leq n$ such that $(a_i,a_j)=1$ for $i\neq j$ and all prime factors of each $a_i$ are prime factors of $n$.

Is it true that, for almost all $n$,\[f(n)=o(n\log\log n)\]and\[F(n) \gg n\log\log n?\]Is it true that\[\max_{n\leq x}f(n)\sim \frac{x\log x}{\log\log x}?\]Is it true that (for all $x$, or perhaps just for all large $x$)\[\max_{n\leq x}f(n)=\max_{n\leq x}F(n)?\]Find an asymptotic formula for the number of $n<x$ such that $f(n)=F(n)$. Find an asymptotic formula for\[H(x)=\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}.\]Is it true that\[H(x) \ll x\log\log\log\log x?\]

### Context
Erdős [Er84e] proved that\[\max_{n\leq x}f(n)\sim \frac{x\log x}{\log\log x}\]for a sequence of $x\to \infty$.

It is trivial that $f(n)\leq F(n)$ for all $n$. It may be true that, for almost all $n$,\[F(n)\sim \frac{1}{2}n\log\log n.\]Erdős notes that $f(n)/n$ 'almost behaves as a conventional additive function', but unusually $f(n)/n$ does not have a mean value - indeed,\[\limsup \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}=\infty\]but\[\liminf \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}<\infty.\]Erdős [Er84e] proved that\[x\log\log\log\log x\ll H(x) \ll x\log\log\log x.\]See also [[879]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/879).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #879 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/879).

### Problem
Call a set $S\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ admissible if $(a,b)=1$ for all $a\neq b\in S$. Let\[G(n) = \max_{S\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}} \sum_{a\in S}a\]and\[H(n)=\sum_{p<n}p+ n\pi(n^{1/2}).\]Is it true that\[G(n) >H(n)-n^{1+o(1)}?\]Is it true that, for every $k\geq 2$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then the admissible set which maximises $G(n)$ contains at least one integer with at least $k$ prime factors?

### Context
Erdős and Van Lint proved that\[H(n)-n^{3/2-o(1)}<G(n)<H(n)\]and\[\frac{H(n)-G(n)}{n}\to \infty.\]They proved that $G(n)>H(n)-n^{1+o(1)}$ assuming 'plausible (but hopeless) assumptions about the distribution of primes'. They also prove the second claim when $k=2$.

See also [[878]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/878).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #883 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/883).

### Problem
For $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ let $G(A)$ be the graph with vertex set $A$, where two integers are joined by an edge if they are coprime.

Is it true that if\[\lvert A\rvert >\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{n}{3}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{n}{6}\rfloor\]then $G(A)$ contains all odd cycles of length $\leq \frac{n}{3}+1$?

Is it true that, for every $\ell\geq 1$, if $n$ is sufficiently large and\[\lvert A\rvert >\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{n}{3}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{n}{6}\rfloor\]then $G(A)$ must contain a complete $(1,\ell,\ell)$ triparite graph on $2\ell+1$ vertices?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Sárkőzy [ErSa97], who prove that if\[\lvert A\rvert >\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor+\lfloor\tfrac{n}{3}\rfloor-\lfloor\tfrac{n}{6}\rfloor\]then $G(A)$ contains all odd cycles of length $\leq cn$ for some constant $c>0$.

This threshold is the best possible, since one could take $A$ to be the set of $m\leq n$ which are divisible by either $2$ or $3$, in which case $G(A)$ contains no triangles.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
Quoting from the paper, Erdős wrote this a few days before he died:

"We hope to return to this problem in the near future (if there is a future for me), but Sárközy will surely return to these problems”.

Sárközy therefore wrote:

"Sadly, due to Paul’s death, we have not been able to continue the work jointly. It is a tremendous honor for me to fulfill Paul’s moving prediction with this paper.”

sourceComments.author: DanielLarsen
sourceComments.contentMd: [Here](https://github.com/Larsen-Daniel/Erdos-884/blob/main/884.pdf) is an unconditional disproof. Tao gave a construction which showed this asymptotic doesn't hold in general if you omit the 1. The basic strategy here is to repeat that construction over many scales so that the left-hand side becomes arbitrarily large, making the 1 unimportant. To do that, you need to ensure that the per–scale left-hand side decays extremely slowly (somewhat surprisingly this is possible even though you seemingly cannot make it diverge unconditionally) and (less seriously) you need to make sure the cross–scale contributions are negligible.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: I can disprove this conjecture assuming the prime tuples conjecture (details [here](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/erdos-884.pdf)).  The basic idea is to take an $n$ of the form $n = (t-h_1) \dots (t-h_K)$ where $h_1,\dots,h_K$ is an admissible tuple of diameter $\asymp K^2$ (with consecutive elements $\gg K$-separated) and $t$ is a large natural number chosen to make all the $t-h_1,\dots,t-h_K$ prime (this is where the prime tuples conjecture is used).  The numerology *almost* lets one remove the prime tuples hypothesis, but I was unable to do so; perhaps someone else would like to try their luck.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: This is nice and elegant even as a conditional result.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd: Nice! Wouldn't surprise me if the dependency on the prime tupjes conjecture can be removed with some effort. By the way, small typo at the end: 'However, some portions of non-constant case.'

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Thanks... the sentence should read "However, some portions of the non-constant case cause difficulty".  The basic problem is that I couldn't prevent two polynomials from having unexpectedly close values for various integer $t$, even though heuristically this should not happen very often.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
It is very likely that the inequality does not hold for any finite constant. Here is a list of the numbers $n$ for which LHS/RHS attains record values (together with a list of those values):
\begin{align*}
2 &\quad  0.5\\
4 &\quad  0.733333\\
6 &\quad  0.985\\
12 &\quad  1.33079\\
24 &\quad  1.52022\\
36 &\quad  1.56233\\
48 &\quad  1.63123\\
60 &\quad  1.8228\\
120 &\quad  2.08166\\
180 &\quad  2.08355\\
240 &\quad  2.17849\\
360 &\quad  2.35522\\
720 &\quad  2.46943\\
1080 &\quad  2.49631\\
1440 &\quad  2.54697\\
1680 &\quad  2.62517\\
2520 &\quad  2.75932\\
5040 &\quad  2.93135\\
10080 &\quad  3.05244\\
15120 &\quad  3.05365\\
20160 &\quad  3.06831\\
25200 &\quad  3.1364\\
30240 &\quad  3.1965\\
50400 &\quad  3.20699\\
55440 &\quad  3.3257\\
110880 &\quad  3.43151\\
166320 &\quad  3.47018\\
221760 &\quad  3.47634\\
332640 &\quad  3.59847
\end{align*}
One might suspect that the numbers on the right converge to infinity (even though very slowly).
These $n$ are reminiscent of the highly composite numbers, but they are not exactly the same sequence.
It seems that the "worst" examples are the numbers $n$ with densely packed small divisors (ideally all small positive integers $1,2,3,4,5,\ldots$) and somewhat spreadout large divisors.
Thus counterexample could also in theory be made of the factorials
\begin{align*}
2! &\quad  0.5\\
3! &\quad  0.985\\
4! &\quad  1.52022\\
5! &\quad  2.08166\\
6! &\quad  2.46943\\
7! &\quad  2.93135\\
8! &\quad  3.08558\\
9! &\quad  3.23805\\
10! &\quad  3.44367\\
11! &\quad  3.80363\\
12! &\quad  3.88206\\
13! &\quad  4.176 \\
14! &\quad  4.30012
\end{align*}
etc.
Another attractive sequence would be primorials (independently also suggested by several people that I know), or any other products of densely packed primes. However, it is still not clear how to make this heuristics precise, since it is already tricky to prohibit large divisors come too close to each other.

sourceComments.author: RobertGerbicz
sourceComments.contentMd:
Not a big issue but on page $358$ in EoRo97, asked the number of divisors in the $(\sqrt{n},\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{n}^{1-\varepsilon})$ interval.
An easy result on a wide range of $\varepsilon$: on $(\sqrt{n},\sqrt{n}+\sqrt[6]{n})$ interval we can not have three or more divisors.
Easily, if $d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}$ are divisors on this interval, then using inclusion exclusion principle the
$[1]:\quad \frac{d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}gcd(d_{1},d_{2},d_{3})}{gcd(d_{1},d_{2})gcd(d_{2},d_{3})gcd(d_{3},d_{1})}$ also divides $n$
Here $gcd(d_{1},d_{2}),gcd(d_{2},d_{3}),gcd(d_{3},d_{1})<\sqrt[6]{n}$, since for example $gcd(d_{1},d_{2})$ divides the $|d_{2}-d_{1}|<\sqrt[6]{n}$.
So using [1] and the above (strict) upper bounds, since the left side divides $n$ we get:
$n^{\frac{3}{2}-3\cdot\frac{1}{6}}<n$, it is a contradiction.

ps. after this asked chatgpt, and said that Imre Z. Ruzsa proved this in 2005 ( and behind journal paywalls ). Don't know what was his approach.

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
Might there be a constant $c$ missing in the statement "Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97] proved that there are infinitely many $n$ such that there are four divisors of $n$ in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/4})$."? From quickly looking at page 356 on https://eudml.org/doc/206983 it seems like it should be $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+cn^{1/4})$?

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
A recent formulation and discussion (including the case of intervals starting at $n^{1/2}$) appears as Conjecture~1 in Letendre's preprint https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.12146. Letendre establishes upper bounds for\[
D_n(X,Y):=\#\{d\mid n:\ X\le d\le X+Y\}
\]in several parameter ranges and explains constraints on how a hypothetical uniform bound $k_\epsilon$ could depend on $\epsilon$ (in particular, it cannot stay small as $\epsilon\to 0$).

In particular, specializing Letendre's bounds to $\theta=\tfrac12$ yields a uniform estimate above the $n^{1/4}$ scale: for any $\delta\in(0,\tfrac14)$,\[
D_n\!\bigl(n^{1/2},\,n^{1/4-\delta}\bigr)\ \ll\ \frac1\delta
\]uniformly in $n$. Hence, if the interval length is $n^{1/2-\epsilon}$ with $\epsilon>\tfrac14$ (so $1/2-\epsilon=1/4-\delta$ where $\delta=\epsilon-\tfrac14>0$), one obtains\[
\#\{d\mid n:\ \sqrt n<d\le \sqrt n+n^{1/2-\epsilon}\}\ =\ O\!\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon-\tfrac14}\right),
\]i.e. the conjectured $O_\epsilon(1)$ bound is known for every $\epsilon>\tfrac14$. For $\epsilon\le\tfrac14$ the existence of a uniform bound remains open in general; at the endpoint $\epsilon=\tfrac14$, Erdős and Rosenfeld constructed infinitely many $n$ with four divisors in $(\sqrt n,\sqrt n+n^{1/4})$, showing any universal bound there (if true) must be at least $4$.

### Problem
Is there an absolute constant $K$ such that, for every $C>0$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then $n$ has at most $K$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$.

A question of Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97], who proved that there are infinitely many $n$ with $4$ divisors in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/4})$, and ask whether $4$ is best possible here.

This should be correct under Bomberi-Lang, though unconditionally it appears very hard.

sourceComments.author: Masty13
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think a heuristic approach for the asymptotic exponent can be as following:

The computational data (as shared in my previous comment here) suggests \(f_{sf}(n) \sim n/(\log n)^{\alpha}\) with \(\alpha \approx 0.35\).

A heuristic derivation to explain this value can be reducing the problem to finding a maximum independent set in a 4-uniform hypergraph  \(H_n\), where edges correspond to solutions of \(abcd=\square\). The count of such solutions is related to the concentration of divisors, characterized by Ford's constant \(\delta \approx 0.08607\) [Ford, 2008]. Heuristically, the four-variable interaction \(abcd=\square\) suggests a cumulative density loss of \(4\delta \approx 0.3443\).

A matching lower bound might be achieved by optimizing over slices of integers with \(\sim \lambda \log \log n\) prime factors (using Sathe-Selberg), the upper bound would follow from the Hypergraph Container Lemma if certain pseudo-randomness conditions (co-degree hypotheses) hold for \(H_n\).

This "non-formal" approach might provide a reasonable origin for the observed decay and a clear target for future work: to prove that \(f(n) \asymp n/(\log n)^{4\delta + o(1)}\).

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here is a proof of Sarkozy's result $|A|=o(n)$.  The main input is Turan-Kubilius inequality (anatomy of integers) to separate the role of smooth and rough numbers, and the multiplication table bound that only $o(n^2)$ numbers are the product of two numbers of size $O(n)$.  ([Much better bounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tenenbaum%E2%80%93Ford_constant) are known than this, but weaker estimate (which follows for instance from the Hardy-Ramanujan law) suffices for Sarkozy's $|A|=o(n)$ bound.) The basic point is that the small number of values of the multiplication table creates a large number of unwanted collisions.

Let $0 < \delta < 1$, and introduce parameters
$$ 1 < \frac{1}{\delta} \ll C \ll z \ll n$$
with each parameter in this sequence assumed sufficiently large compared to the previous parameters, e.g., $z$ is sufficiently large depending on $\frac{1}{\delta}$ and $C$.

Suppose for contradiction that we have a set $A \subset \{1,\dots,n\}$ of density $\geq \delta$ with the stated property.  Any element $a$ of $A$ can then be factored as $a = a_{\leq z} a_{>z}$ where $a_{\leq z}$ is the $z$-smooth part (product of primes up to $z$) and $a_{>z}$ is the $z$-rough part (product of primes larger than $z$).

By Turan-Kubilius, for $z$ large enough, we have $C \leq a_{\leq z} \ll_z 1$ for all but at most $\delta n /2$ of the natural numbers up to $n$, hence for $\gg \delta n$ of the $a \in A$.   By pigeonholing, we can then find a dyadic scale $C < L \ll_z 1$ such that out of all the numbers of the form $a_{\leq z} a_{>z}$ with $a_{\leq z} \sim L$ $z$-smooth and $a_{>z} \lesssim n/L$ $z$-rough, $\gg \delta$ of these products will lie in $A$.

If we let $S$ be the set of $z$-smooth numbers of size $\sim L$ and $R$ the set of $z$-rough numbers of size $\lesssim n/L$, the set $A$ is now occupying $\gg \delta |S| |R|$ of the products of $S$ and $R$.  Note that $S$ and $R$ are large compared with $1/\delta$, and $R$ is in fact quite large: $|R| \gg_{L,z} n$.  By Cauchy-Schwarz, we now have $\gg \delta^2 |S| |R|^2$ pairs $a_{\leq z} a_{>z}, a_{\leq z} a'_{>z}$ that both lie in $A$.  By another Cauchy-Schwarz and the multiplication table bound, there are $\gg \delta^4 |S|^2 |R|^4 / |R \cdot R|$ quadruples
$$a_{\leq z} a_{>z}, a_{\leq z} a'_{>z}, b_{\leq z} b_{>z}, b_{\leq z} b'_{>z}$$
 such that
$$ a_{\leq z} \neq b_{\leq z}$$
and
$$ a_{>z} a'_{>z} = b_{>z} b'_{>z}.$$
These four elements of $A$ multiply to a square, so the product of two of them must equal the other two.  Some case analysis then reveals that this forces $a_{>z}, a'_{>z}$ to be a permutation of $b_{>z}, b'_{>z}$, thus the four elements here basically form a "rectangle" in $S \times R$, so there are only $O(|S|^2 |R|^2)$ possible such quadruples.  This gives
$$ \delta^4 |S|^2 |R|^4 / |R \cdot R| \ll |S|^2 |R|^2$$
which leads to a contradiction since $|R| \gg_{L,z} n$ and $|R \cdot R| = o(n^2)$ by the multiplication table bound.

sourceComments.author: Masty13
sourceComments.contentMd:
This is my contribution to the study of Erdős Problem 888. I used Gemini 3 pro and Claude Opus 4.5 with multiple iterations. I didn't perform an extensive literature review so it's possible some proof strategies or methods were discussed somewhere before. Your feedback and verification would be much appreciated.

 [You can access the PDF version from here](https://github.com/MaskoMys/Erdos-Problems-/blob/main/Erdos_888.pdf)

SUMMARY:
1. Kernel Constraint (Theorem 1): Any admissible set contains at most one element from each square-free equivalence class, giving \( f(n) \le Q(n) \).

2. Fixing Mechanism (Theorem 3): Non-square-free representatives can resolve obstructions, proving that the kernel map does not preserve admissibility.
- Counterexample : The set\[A = \{3, 5, 126, 210\}\]is admissible, but its kernel $K = \{3, 5, 14, 210\}$, is not admissible.

3. Hypergraph Algorithm (Section 3): An \( O(n^2) \) algorithm computes \( f_{sf}(n) \) exactly.

4. Asymptotic Bounds (Theorem 4): We establish \( \pi(n) \le f_{sf}(n) \le f(n) \le Q(n) \).

5. Computational Results (Section 6): Exact values of \( f_{sf}(n) \) for\[ n \leq 5000 \]supporting $f(n) = o(n)$.

6. Curve Fitting: The data is well-modeled by\[
    f(n) \approx \frac{n}{(\log n)^\alpha}, \quad \alpha \approx 0.35.
    \]Edit: The PDF document was modified to reflect the latest updates.

sourceComments.author: arturgoulao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Generate the proposed solution using GPT 5.2 Thinking, Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Pro, share here for verification.

[Document](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gx9Ankr1qQOoFTR7Xj4u6Nc8SWkgEPe6/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=103837779541880341884&rtpof=true&sd=true)

Summary:
We want the largest \(A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\) such that for all \(a\le b\le c\le d\in A\), if \(abcd\) is a square then \(ad=bc\) (allowing repeats).

Step 1 (kernel reduction). Write \(x=\kappa(x)t^2\) with \(\kappa(x)\) squarefree.
If \(A\) contains two distinct numbers with the same \(\kappa\), then \((x,x,x,y)\) gives a square product but forces \(xy=x^2\), impossible. Hence at most one element per kernel. Moreover, if \(A\) is good then the kernel-set \(K=\{\kappa(x):x\in A\}\) is also good, so it suffices to work with squarefree sets.

Step 2 (candidate). Let \(L(n)\) be all squarefree numbers \(\le n\) with at most two prime factors (primes and squarefree semiprimes), and include \(1\) only when \(n\le 14\). This set is good: with supports of size \(\le2\), any square-trigger quadruple must have the "rectangle'' parity pattern, which forces \(ad=bc\).

Step 3 (compression / maximality). Suppose \(K\) is a maximum good squarefree set but misses some "light'' element (first a prime, then a semiprime). Add the missing light element. If the new set becomes bad, one can classify the obstruction: adding a prime \(p\) creates a violation iff there exist \(b,c\in K\) with \(p\nmid b,c\) and \(d=p\cdot bc/\gcd(b,c)^2\in K\); the quadruple \((p,b,c,d)\) is then forced and violates \(pd=bc\). So we delete the witness \(d\) and keep \(p\). This preserves size and strictly decreases the total number of prime factors \(\sum_{x\in K}\omega(x)\). Iterating forces all primes (and then all semiprimes) into the set, eliminating all \(\omega\ge3\) elements.

Step 4 (the \(1\) cutoff). If \(1\in K\) and \(pq,pr,qr\in K\), then \(1\cdot pq\cdot pr\cdot qr\) is a square but \(1\cdot qr\ne (pq)(pr)\). The first such triangle is \(\{6,10,15\}\), so \(1\) is compatible only for \(n\le14\).

Conclusion. The maximum size is\[
M(n)=\pi(n)+\#\{pq\le n:\ p<q\text{ primes}\}+\mathbf{1}_{n\le14},
\]achieved by taking all primes and all squarefree semiprimes (and also \(1\) only when \(n\le14\)).

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Lemma 2, reducing to the case where $A$ consists of only squarefree numbers, is false for 2 fatal reasons.

1. If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are squarefree and $\alpha \delta / (\beta \gamma)$ is square, this doesn't imply it must equal $1$.

2. Even if somehow we fix that issue, the ordering $a \le b \le c \le d$ is not preserved when you remove the square parts from $a,b,c,d$.

(Joint with [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/696e5614-d148-8010-a59f-72c8dd2defb0).)

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Since $\{a,b,c,d\}$ do not have to be different elements, one can observe the following:
Lemma 1: there are no two different elements $a_1, a_2 \in A$ such that $a_1a_2$ is a perfect square
proof: otherwise $a_1a_2^3$ is a perfect square without equal decomposition (so $A$ has not property P)

Sadly enough, the following statement is not that easy to prove, if true,
"We may assume that all elements in $A$ are square-free."

Possibly one could check what happens with $A_k$, the subset of $A$ with the elements having exactly $k$ different prime divisors.
While $A_1$ and $A_2$ can clearly be as large as possible (taking into account Lemma 1), for $A_k$ with $k \ge 3$ this is not the case anymore.
So if, e.g., $A_2$ would be larger than all others (the size of $A_k$ sufficiently rapid decreasing e.g.), the conclusions might follow up to some smaller terms.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
It might already be hard to conjecture what a largest set $A$ for $n$ large might be.

Let $A$ be the set containing all primes and all product of two different primes (bounded by $n$).
Checking the possible forms of $abcd$ which are a perfect square, we easily deduce that this set $A$ satisfies the constraint (denoted property P as above).
If $p^4 \mid A$, then all elements contain a factor $p$ and it becomes trivial.
So remaining to check: $(pqrs)^4,(pqr)^2,(pq)^2$ and all of them are easy to check.

For large $n$, $A$ is not a maximal set (for $n \le 14$ neither, as then one can add $1$ as well).
One can e.g. add some products of disjoint sets of $7$ different primes (bounded by $n$ again). Since no such product will be a divisor of any square product of $4$ elements, the extended set still has the property P.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have an interesting lemma that may or may not be useful. Say a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has *Property P* if for all $a \leq b \leq c \leq d \in A$ with $abcd$ square, we have $ad = bc$. Then this problem is asking how large a subset of $\{1,...,n\}$ can be if it has Property P. Say $A$ has *Property Q* if for all $a \leq b \leq c \leq d \in A$ with $abcd$ square, we have $a = b$ and $c = d$. Then every set with Property Q also has Property P. (The converse isn't true, though; a counterexample is $\{2,3,4,6\}$.)
A nice fact is that if $U$ and $V$ have Property Q and $\gcd(u,v) = 1$ for all $u \in U, v \in V$, then the product set $UV$ has Property P. This is not too hard to verify.

Unfortunately, the two stronger statements that you might have wondered about when reading this are false. The set $UV$ need not have Property Q; for example, $U = \{1,2\}$ and $V = \{1,3\}$ have Property Q but $UV = \{1,2,3,6\}$ does not have Property Q. Also, if we weaken the hypotheses so that $U$ only needs to have Property P, then $UV$ need not have Property P; for example, $U = \{2,3,4,6\}$ has Property P and $V = \{1,5\}$ has Property Q, but $UV$ contains $\{2,6,15,20\}$ and so it does not have Property P.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #889 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/889).

### Problem
For $k\geq 0$ and $n\geq 1$ let $v(n,k)$ count the prime factors of $n+k$ which do not divide $n+i$ for $0\leq i<k$. Equivalently, $v(n,k)$ counts the number of prime factors of $n+k$ which are $>k$.

Is it true that\[v_0(n)=\max_{k\geq 0}v(n,k)\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$?

### Context
A question of Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe67], who could only show that $v_0(n)\geq 2$ for $n\geq 17$. More generally, they conjecture that\[v_l(n)=\max_{k\geq l}v(n,k)\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$, for every fixed $l$, but could not even prove that $v_1(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$.

This is problem B27 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.contentMd:
The general version of the conjecture with $l > 0$ follows easily from the case $l = 0$, using the inequality $v(n+1,k) \leq v(n,k+1)+1$.

This reduction was noticed with the help of [Aristotle](https://aristotle.harmonic.fun).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #890 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/890).

### Problem
If $\omega(n)$ counts the number of distinct prime factors of $n$, then is it true that, for every $k\geq 1$,\[\liminf_{n\to \infty}\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega(n+i)\leq k+\pi(k)?\]Is it true that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\left(\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega(n+i)\right) \frac{\log\log n}{\log n}=1?\]

### Context
A question of Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe67], who observe that\[\liminf_{n\to \infty}\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega(n+i)\geq k+\pi(k)-1\]for every $k$. This follows from Pólya's theorem that the set of $k$-smooth integers has unbounded gaps - indeed, $n(n+1)\cdots (n+k-1)$ is divisible by all primes $\leq k$ and, provided $n$ is large, all but at most one of $n,n+1,\ldots,n+k-1$ has a prime factor $>k$ by Pólya's theorem.

It is a classical fact that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\omega(n)\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}=1.\]

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Agustín Meza
sourceComments.contentMd:
The first problem Erdös and Selfridge state is not about $\omega (n)$, but a little variation which only counts the prime factors of n+k which are greater than k. Otherwise the sum $\sum_{0 \le i \le k}\omega (n) \gg \log\log(k)k$ from Turán-Kubilius inequality over the set of primes less than $\sqrt{k}$.

The case for fixed $k$ would follow from the $k$-tuples conjecture the following way: Let $N$ be sufficiently large in terms of $k$. Then linear forms $L(n;j) = N!n + j$ for $1 \le j \le k+1$ form an admissible $k$-tuple if $N$ is sufficiently large. Then, by the $k$-tuples conjecture, there exists infinitely many $n$ such that $L(n;j)$ is prime for all $1 \le j \le k+1$. This implies that $N!n + j$ is equal to a prime $p_{j}$ times $j$ infinitely often.

The sum that Erdös and Selfridge were considering would be equal to $k+ \pi(k)$ (each $N!n + j$ will contribute $1$ if $j-1$ is not prime and $2$ if it is). Note: the condition $j-1$ being prime or not comes from the fact that we've shifted the beginning of the string of consecutive integers to $N!n + 1$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: I'm not sure I understand your first comment - in this question I'm sure that Erdős and Selfridge intended to ask about $\omega$, rather than the variant you describe. (They did discuss other problems involving this variant in that paper.) Indeed, it has to be $\omega$, otherwise the lower bound construction they give doesn't work!

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I thik Agustin is correct and Erdos and Selfridge messed up slightly in their statement: every prime $p \leq k$ will in fact divide at least $\lfloor k/p\rfloor$ of the $n,\dots,n+k-1$, so their $\pi(k)$ should really be $\sum_{p \leq k} \lfloor k/p \rfloor$ (which is $\sim k \log\log k$ as Agustin points out).  Then the first part of the problem is indeed a variant of the prime tuples conjecture.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #891 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/891).

### Problem
Let $2=p_1<p_2<\cdots$ be the primes and $k\geq 2$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there must exist an integer in $[n,n+p_1\cdots p_k)$ with $>k$ many prime factors?

### Context
Schinzel deduced from Pólya's theorem [Po18] (that the sequence of $k$-smooth integers has unbounded gaps) that this is true with $p_1\cdots p_k$ replaced by $p_1\cdots p_{k-1}p_{k+1}$.

This is unknown even for $k=2$ - that is, is it true that in every interval of $6$ (sufficiently large) consecutive integers there must exist one with at least $3$ prime factors?

Weisenberg has observed that Dickson's conjecture implies the answer is no if we replace $p_1\cdots p_k$ with $p_1\cdots p_k-1$. Indeed, let $L_k$ be the lowest common multiple of all integers at most $p_1\cdots p_k$. By Dickson's conjecture there are infinitely many $n'$ such that $\frac{L_k}{m}n'+1$ is prime for all $1\leq m<p_1\cdots p_k$. It follows that, if $n=L_kn'+1$, then all integers in $[n,n+p_1\cdots p_k-1)$ have at most $k$ prime factors.

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: It follows from Catalan's conjecture that any three consecutive positive integers starting from 8 onward must contain a number with at least two distinct prime divisors. This was also an exercise posed by Waclaw Sierpinski iirc. EDIT: It could be added that we are requiring more than $k$ distinct prime factors, because otherwise It can be misunterstood that counting with multiplicity is allowed.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
While Desmond's remark would possibly leading to saying "no",
I also want to add observations leading to a plausible "yes".

Observation:
If this is not the case for some large $n$, one of the elements in the interval is of the form $p_1^{e_1} p_2^{e_2} \ldots p_k^{e_k}$.
So it is sufficient to consider the neighbourhood of these powers and check if many of them have few prime factors.
This seems unlikely.

Quantitave for $k=2$:
Let $n>4372$ (likely the necessary bound), where $r=6 \lfloor n/6 \rfloor =2^i*3^j$.
Then $r-2$ and $r+2$ are both multiples of $2$, and $r-3, r+3$ are both multiples of $3$.
If $i,j>1$, then furthermore the exponents of the small primes are one.
So the probability that is works, is bounded by a function of the form $1/ \log(x)^2.$
Also the other elements in the interval are likely not pseudoprimepowers, so the sum of chances to find one is small.

For $r=3*2^i$, one needs that $r-3$ or $r+3$ is almost prime.
So $i$ needs to be prime or a power of $2$ (the latter is expected to be excluded, as there is likely no Fermat number above $2^{32}+1$).
So take $p$ such that $2^p-1$ is a Mersenne prime.
Now $3*2^p-1=t*s$ and $3*2^p-2=2*q$ should already both have at most $2$ prime factors.
For $r=2*3^i$, one can guess along the same lines.

Nonetheless, fully making the above rigourous, may be hard.
Anyone else ideas? Cases to exclude?
**
for $k=3$, $n>8611$ may be the quantitative "large enough".

Investigate open Erdos Problem #892 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/892).

### Problem
Is there a necessary and sufficient condition for a sequence of integers $b_1<b_2<\cdots$ that ensures there exists a primitive sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ (i.e. no element divides another) with $a_n \ll b_n$ for all $n$?

In particular, is this always possible if there are no non-trivial solutions to $(b_i,b_j)=b_k$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Sárközy, and Szemerédi [ESS68]. It is known that\[\sum \frac{1}{b_n\log b_n}<\infty\]and\[\sum_{b_n<x}\frac{1}{b_n} =o\left(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}\right)\]are both necessary. (The former is due to Erdős [Er35], the latter to Erdős, Sárközy, and Szemerédi [ESS67].)

One can ask a similar question for sequences of real numbers, as in [[143]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/143).

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
With $\delta = 1 - \frac{1 + \log \log 2}{\log 2} \approx 0.086$ we have $$\frac{\big(1+o(1)\big)N^2}{\log N} \le \max_{A,B \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}} F(A, B) \ll \frac{N^2}{\log^{\delta} N (\log \log N)^{3/2}}.$$The upper bound follows from the determination of the number of elements in the multiplication table $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\} \times \{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ by Ford.

For the lower bound we can use a construction Szemerédi gives in [this](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022314X76900032) paper (the one where he solved [#490](https://www.erdosproblems.com/490)): set $A$ to be the set of primes in $\left[\frac{N}{\log N}, N\right]$ and choose $B$ to be the subset of integers in $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$ which are not divisible by any $a \in A$. Then $|A| = \frac{\big(1+o(1)\big)N}{\log N}$ by the prime number theorem, $|B| = \big(1+o(1)\big)N$, and every element $m \in AB$ has a unique representation.

For what it's worth, one can replace $\log N$ in the interval $\left[\frac{N}{\log N}, N\right]$ defining $A$, by any function $f(N)$ that goes to infinity with $N$ slower than $N^{\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon > 0$.

Erdős suggests in [Er72] that the ideas in the aforementioned paper by Szemerédi can perhaps be used to attack this problem as well.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #901 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/901).

### Problem
Let $m(n)$ be minimal such that there is an $n$-uniform hypergraph with $m(n)$ edges which is $3$-chromatic. Estimate $m(n)$.

### Context
In other words, the hypergraph does not have [Property B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_B). Property B means that there is a set $S$ which intersects all edges and yet does not contain any edge.

It is known that $m(2)=3$, $m(3)=7$, and $m(4)=23$. Erdős proved\[2^n \ll m(n) \ll n^2 2^n\](the lower bound in [Er63b] and the upper bound in [Er64e]). Erdős conjectured that $m(n)/2^n\to \infty$, which was proved by Beck [Be77], who proved $m(n)\gg (\log n)2^n$, and later [Be78] improved this to\[n^{1/3-o(1)}2^n \ll m(n).\]Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan [RaSr00] improved this to\[\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}2^n \ll m(n).\]Pluhar [Pl09] gave a very short proof that $m(n) \gg n^{1/4}2^n$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.
