Investigate open Erdos Problem #902 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/902).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be minimal such that there is a tournament (a complete directed graph) on $f(n)$ vertices such that every set of $n$ vertices is dominated by at least one other vertex. Estimate $f(n)$.

### Context
Schütte asked Erdős this in the early 1960s.

It is easy to check that $f(1)=3$ and $f(2)=7$. Erdős [Er63c] proved\[2^{n+1}-1 \leq f(n) \ll n^22^n.\]Szekeres and Szekeres [SzSz65] proved that $f(3)=19$ and\[n2^n \ll f(n).\]

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #906 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/906).

### Problem
Is there an entire non-zero function $f:\mathbb{C}\to \mathbb{C}$ such that, for any infinite sequence $n_1<n_2<\cdots$, the set\[\{ z: f^{(n_k)}(z)=0 \textrm{ for some }k\geq 1\}\]is everywhere dense?

### Context
Erdős [Er82e] writes that this was solved in the affirmative 'more than ten years ago', but gives no reference or indication who solved it. From context he seems to attribute this to Barth and Schneider [BaSc72], but this paper contains no such result.

Tang points out that the problem is trivial if we take $f$ to be a polynomial, so presumably it is intended the function $f$ is transcendental.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
I used the Gemini and ChatGPT research tools to do a literature review on this problem.

[Gemini correctly explained](https://gemini.google.com/share/a330ad9ab5b4) why the Barth-Schneider paper did not resolve the Erdos problem, but then went on to hallucinate a nonsensical solution to the Erdos problem (the error is in assuming that any subsequence of a dense sequence remains dense).  No further relevant references were found (Maclane's theorem that the derivatives of a generic holomorphic function are dense in the locally uniform topology, already mentioned in another comment, is cited, but is useless for this problem due to the above error).

ChatGPT [found this web page](https://chatgpt.com/share/68f2bab0-bc60-800e-bda3-41d16b96621d) and also noted that the Barth-Schneider paper solves a *different* problem of Erdos concerning derivatives of holomorphic functions, attributed to Problem 2.30 of [Hayman's book](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=217268).  It is possible that Erdos confused the two problems. Like Gemini, Maclane's theorem was also noted, though this time it was correctly pointed out that this result was insufficient to establish the result.  It seems that most of ChatGPT's response was drawn from this very web page, revealing no further references; this raises the issue of a circularity in which the utility of such tools for this web site may become diminished if this site becomes authoritative enough to become a major primary source for such tools.

Nevertheless, I would agree with the emerging consensus that there is currently no solution to this problem in the literature.

sourceComments.author: cjbartsch
sourceComments.contentMd:
I claim no transcendental $f$ that is entire can satisfy the hypothesis of Problem 2 above.

Let $f$ be an entire function. Suppose that for every nonempty open set $U \subset \mathbb{C}$, there exists an integer $N(U) > 0$ such that, for all $n \geq N(U)$, the derivative $f^{(n)}$ possesses a zero in $U$. Then $f$ is a polynomial.

Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that $f$ satisfies the hypothesis but is transcendental. Then its Taylor expansion at the origin is given by\[ f(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k z^k, \qquad c_k = \frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}, \]and infinitely many coefficients $c_k$ are nonzero; that is, for all $N \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists an $n \ge N$ such that $c_n \neq 0$. Since $f$ is entire, the series converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact subset of $\mathbb{C}$.
Differentiating term by term yields\[
        f^{(n)}(z) = \sum_{k=n}^\infty k(k-1)\cdots(k-n+1) c_k z^{k-n}
    = n!c_n + \sum_{k>n} n! \binom{k}{n} c_k z^{k-n}
    \]Because [the radius of convergence of each derivative of $f$ equals that of $f$](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Radius_of_Convergence_of_Derivative_of_Complex_Power_Series), the series above converges uniformly on any closed disc $\overline{B(0,R)}$; let $U = B(0,R)$ be the open disc. For sufficiently large $n$,\[ g(z) = \sum_{k>n} n! {k \choose n} c_k z^{k-n} \]satisfies\[ |g(z)| < |n! c_n| \quad \text{for all } |z| < R. \]Hence, by [Rouché’s theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouch%C3%A9%27s_theorem), $f^{(n)}(z) = n! c_n + g_n(z)$ and the constant function $n!c_n$ have the same number of zeros in $U$—namely—none, a contradiction.

Therefore, all but finitely many coefficients $c_n$ are zero, and $f$ is a polynomial.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
There seems to be a gap in the proof posted above.
The step claiming that for sufficiently large \(n\),\[
|g(z)| < |n!c_n| \quad \text{for all } |z|<R
\]does not follow from uniform convergence and is generally false.
A concrete counterexample is \(f(z)=e^{z^2}\). We have\[
f(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{2j}}{j!},\qquad
c_{2j}=\frac1{j!},\quad c_{2j+1}=0.
\]For even orders \(n=2k\),\[
f^{(n)}(z)=n!c_n+\sum_{m\ge1} n!\binom{n+m}{n}c_{n+m}z^{\,m}.
\]The coefficient ratio of the \(z^2\)-term to the constant term equals\[
\frac{n!\binom{n+2}{n}c_{n+2}}{n!c_n}
=\frac{(2k+2)(2k+1)}{2(k+1)}=2k+1.
\]Hence for any fixed radius \(R>0\),\[
\frac{|\,\text{$z^2$ term}\,|}{|\,\text{constant term}\,|}
=(2k+1)R^2\to\infty\quad(k\to\infty).
\]Therefore\[
\sup_{|z|=R}|g(z)|
\ge (2k+1)R^2|n!c_n|>|n!c_n|
\]for all sufficiently large even \(n=2k\). Thus the inequality \(|g(z)|<|n!c_n|\) fails, and the Rouché comparison used in that argument cannot be justified.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
The webpage states: ''Erdős [Er82e] writes that this was solved in the affirmative 'more than ten years ago', but gives no reference or indication who solved it. From context he seems to attribute this to Barth and Schneider [BaSc72], but this paper contains no such result.''  I agree with this assessment.  Below I make a short clarification.

First, one easily checks that Problem #906 is equivalent to the following formulation:

**Problem 2**. Does there exist a transcendental entire function $f(z)$ such that for every nonempty open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}$ there is an integer $N(U)>0$ with the property that, for all $n\ge N(U)$, the $n$-th derivative $f^{(n)}$ has a zero in $U$?

After a careful reading of Barth and Schneider [BaSc72], I found that the methods in [BaSc72] only yield the following weaker positive result for *Problem 2*. I state it here as Proposition 1:

**Proposition 1**. There exists a nonzero transcendental entire function $f(z)$ such that for every nonempty open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}$ there are infinitely many integers $n$ for which $f^{(n)}$ has a zero in $U$.

Proof of Proposition 1. Let $S_k:=\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{Z}+\frac{i}{k}\mathbb{Z}$ denote the square lattice of mesh $1/k$. By [BaSc72, Theorem 1], there exist a sequence of positive integers $(n_k)$ and an entire function $f$ such that\[
f^{(n_k)}(z)=0 \quad\text{for every } z\in S_k,\qquad k=1,2,\dots.
\]Given any nonempty open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}$, there exists $K(U)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $U\cap S_k\neq\emptyset$ for all $k\ge K(U)$ (since the lattices $S_k$ become dense as $k\to\infty$). Hence, for every $k\ge K(U)$ the function $f^{(n_k)}$ has a zero in $U$. This produces infinitely many integers $n$ with the required property, proving the proposition.

In particular, [BaSc72] yields the weaker density conclusion that the union $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{z:\,f^{(n)}(z)=0\}$ is dense in $\mathbb C$, but it does not establish the stronger uniform property required in Problem #906.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
In addition to the weaker positive result from Barth--Schneider [BaSc72] (cf. Proposition 1 above), I found two further relevant results in the paper of Boas--Reddy [[BoRe73]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022247X73901534):
R.~P. Boas Jr. and A.~R. Reddy, Zeros of successive derivatives of entire functions, Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications 42(1973), 466--473.

By Theorem 1 in [[BoRe73]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022247X73901534), we know that for entire functions of at most order $2$ and finite type, there is no function $f$ satisfying the property in Problem 2 above.

By Theorem 2 in [[BoRe73]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022247X73901534), if $p>2$, then there exists an entire function of order $p$ and a constant $A>0$ such that every disk of radius $A$, anywhere in the plane, contains a zero of every derivative $f^{(i)}$.

These two theorems show that Problem 2 cannot be solved for functions of small order. Once the order exceeds $2$, one can indeed find entire functions with particular zero-distribution properties, but this still does not resolve Problem 2.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
One more remark. I found a new proof of the *Proposition 1* above. Let \(H(\mathbb{C})\) be the space of all entire functions on $\mathbb{C}$ with the compact open topology. By a result of MacLane (see Theorem 6 in [[Ma52]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02786968) or Theorem 2 in [[ArMa02]](https://www.math.kent.edu/~aron/aron-markose-10-29-02.pdf)), there exists an entire function \(f\) such that the set \(\{f^{(n)}: n\in\mathbb{N}\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb{C})\). From this one obtains the density of the union of zero sets of the derivatives via a short Rouché-argument, as follows.

Fix any point \(z_0\in\mathbb{C}\) and radius \(r>0\), and set the closed disk \(K=\overline{D(z_0,r)}\). Let \(g(z)=z-z_0\). Note that \(|g(z)|=r\) on \(\partial D(z_0,r)\). Since \(\{f^{(n)}\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb{C})\), there exists \(N\) with\[
  \sup_{z\in K}\,|f^{(N)}(z)-g(z)|<r.
\]Restricting to \(\partial D(z_0,r)\) gives \(|f^{(N)}(z)-g(z)|<|g(z)|\). By Rouché’s theorem, \(f^{(N)}\) and \(g\) have the same number of zeros in \(D(z_0,r)\). Since \(g\) has exactly one zero at \(z_0\), the function \(f^{(N)}\) has a zero in \(D(z_0,r)\). Because \(z_0\) and \(r\) were arbitrary, we conclude that\[
  \bigcup_{n\ge 1}\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\ f^{(n)}(z)=0\}
\]is dense in \(\mathbb{C}\). This completes the proof of Proposition 1.

The above discussion naturally leads to:

**Problem 3**. Does there exist \(f\in H(\mathbb{C})\) such that for every infinite subset \(S\subset\mathbb{N}\) the set \(\{D^{n}f : n\in S\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb{C})\)?

If Problem 3 were true, it would give an affirmative solution to Problem #906. However, *Problem 3* is in fact false. Here is a short proof.

Proof that Problem 3 is false. Let \(U,V\subset H(\mathbb C)\) be two disjoint nonempty open sets. Assume there exists \(f\in H(\mathbb C)\) such that for every infinite \(S\subset\mathbb N\) the set \(\{D^{n}f:n\in S\}\) is dense in \(H(\mathbb C)\). For any nonempty open \(W\subset H(\mathbb C)\) define\[
N_W:=\{\,n\in\mathbb N:\ D^{n}f\in W\,\}.
\]Then necessarily \(S\cap N_W\neq\varnothing\). Indeed, if \(N_W\) were not cofinite, taking \(S=\mathbb N\setminus N_W\) (which is infinite) would force \(\{D^{n}f:n\in S\}\subset H(\mathbb C)\setminus W\), contradicting its density. Hence both \(N_U\) and \(N_V\) are cofinite, so \(N_U\cap N_V\neq\varnothing\). Pick \(n\in N_U\cap N_V\), then \(D^{n}f\in U\cap V=\varnothing\), a contradiction. Therefore no such \(f\) exists.

References.
[Ma52] MacLane, Gerald R. "Sequences of derivatives and normal families." Journal d’Analyse Mathématique 2.1 (1952): 72-87.
[ArMa02] ARON, RICHARD, and DINESH MARKOSE. "ON UNIVERSAL FUNCTIONS OCTOBER 29, 2002."

In view of the above, a negative resolution of Problem #906 appears plausible, yet this observation is merely suggestive and falls well short of a proof.

### Problem
If\[n! = \prod_i p_i^{k_i}\]is the factorisation into distinct primes then let $h(n)$ count the number of distinct exponents $k_i$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
One can predict the value of $c$ using the Cramer random model for the primes.  Firstly some reductions.  Legendre's formula states that
$$k_i = \lfloor n/p_i \rfloor + \lfloor n/p_i^2 \rfloor + \dots.$$
Both the main term $\lfloor n/p_i \rfloor$ and the tail $\lfloor n/p_i^2 \rfloor + \dots$ are non-increasing in $i$; but the latter only changes value $O(n^{1/3})$ times (consider the cases $p_i \leq n^{1/3}$ and $p_i \geq n^{1/3}$ separately).  Thus, deleting this term only modifies $h$ by a lower order error, and the problem is equivalent to that of counting the number of distinct values of $\lfloor n/p_i \rfloor$.

For any $\varepsilon$, the primes less than $\varepsilon \sqrt{n \log n}$ are only $O(\varepsilon (n/\log n)^{1/2})$ in number, and for the primes $p_i$ larger than $\varepsilon^{-1} \sqrt{n \log n}$ the value of $\lfloor n/p_i\rfloor$ is $O(\varepsilon (n/\log n)^{1/2})$.  So up to lower order error we can restrict attention to the primes $p_i \asymp \sqrt{n \log n}$, for which $k_i \asymp (n/\log n)^{1/2}$.

A given $k \asymp (n/\log n)^{1/2}$ will be of the form $\lfloor n/p_i \rfloor$ iff there is a prime in the interval $(n/(k+1),n/k]$.  If $k = t (n/\log n)^{1/2}$, this is an interval of length approximately $t^{-2} \log n$ of numbers of size $\asymp \sqrt{n \log n}$ - so the prime density here is approximately $2/\log n$.  The Cramer random model then predicts a prime to be present with probability approximately $1-e^{-2t^{-2}}$.  So this leads to the prediction

$$ c = \int_0^\infty 1 - e^{-2t^{-2}}\ dt = \sqrt{2\pi} = 2.50663\dots$$

(the value here was provided by an LLM and verified by Wolfram alpha; it can be derived from the usual gaussian integral identities by a routine substitution and the Feynman trick of replacing $2$ by a parameter that one then differentiates in.)  A quick AI request to plot the ratio between $h(n)$ and $\sqrt{2\pi} (n/\log n)^{1/2}$ [seems to back up this prediction](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/output-2/).

Proving this claim unconditionally, even on average in $n$, would likely require information about the distribution of prime gaps that currently is only available under strong hypotheses such as the prime tuples conjecture.

EDIT: By plugging in the AI-provided values of $h$ into the OEIS, I discovered that the function $h(n)$ is [OEIS A071626](https://oeis.org/A071626).  As observed in the paper linked there, the deletion of the tail in fact does not affect $h$ at all (basically because the tail only jumps when the main term does).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
Write \(v_p(m)\) for the exponent of a prime \(p\) in \(m\). Since \(\gcd(n,n+1)=1\), the prime factorisation of \(n(n+1)\) is just the disjoint union of the factorisations of \(n\) and of \(n+1\), so the condition is equivalent to:\[
\{\,v_p(n):p\mid n\,\}\ \cup\ \{\,v_p(n+1):p\mid n+1\,\}
\quad\text{has no repeats.}
\]A first (very strong) necessary consequence is that exponent \(1\) can occur at most once. So:

- \(n\) cannot have two distinct primes to the first power (else you’d already repeat "1" inside \(n\));
- \(n+1\) cannot have two distinct primes to the first power;
- and you cannot have a prime to the first power in both \(n\) and \(n+1\).

In particular, at least one of \(n\) or \(n+1\) must be powerful/squareful (every prime divisor occurs with exponent \(\ge 2\)): if \(n\) uses exponent \(1\) anywhere, then \(n+1\) must avoid exponent \(1\) entirely, hence \(n+1\) is powerful; if \(n\) uses no exponent \(1\), then \(n\) itself is powerful.

That already puts the problem in "prime values of structured sequences" territory, and with current techniques this is far beyond what we can prove in general. In fact, even very special subfamilies are open - for example, proving infinitely many solutions with exponent set \(\{1,2,3\}\) via\[
n=8p^2-1,\qquad n+1=2^3p^2
\]amounts to proving infinitely many primes \(p\) with \(8p^2-1\) prime, which is a special case of standard prime-producing conjectures (Bateman-Horn / Schinzel).

So conditionally: Under Schinzel’s Hypothesis H (or Bateman-Horn), the suggested family works, and much more is predicted. For any distinct integers \(a,b\ge 2\), Hypothesis H predicts infinitely many primes \(p\) with \(p\) and \(2^a p^b-1\) prime; then\[
n=2^a p^b-1,\quad n+1=2^a p^b
\]gives exponents \(\{1,a,b\}\) all distinct. The above example is \((a,b)=(3,2)\).

For what it’s worth, small examples exist in abundance (e.g. \(n=63\) gives \(n(n+1)=2^6\cdot 3^2\cdot 7^1\), exponents \(\{1,2,6\}\)), but turning that into an infinite proof seems to require exactly this kind of conjectural input, so the problem looks hard.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Also true if the conjecture about infinitely many Mersenne primes is true.
So yes, many conjectures would do the job.

The abundancy of small examples is less convincing as an argument.
For large values of $n$ and $n+1$, the prime factorisation typically has many (order $\log \log n$) different prime factors with multiplicity 1.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Minor correction: Schinzel H needs irreducible polynomials, so "any distinct integers $a,b \ge 2$" needs to be weakened to also $\gcd(a,b) = 1$. Credit to ChatGPT for the observation.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #917 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/917).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 4$ and $f_k(n)$ be the largest number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices which has chromatic number $k$ and is critical (i.e. deleting any edge reduces the chromatic number).

Is it true that\[f_k(n) \gg_k n^2?\]Is it true that\[f_6(n)\sim n^2/4?\]More generally, is it true that, for $k\geq 6$,\[f_k(n) \sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}\right)n^2?\]

### Context
Erdős [Er93] wrote 'I learned of this definition from Dirac in 1949 and immediately asked whether $f_k(n)=o(n^2)$. To my great surprise Dirac constructed a $6$ critical graph on $n$ vertices with more than $\frac{n^2}{4}$ edges.' In fact Dirac [Di52] proved\[f_6(4n+2) \geq 4n^2+8n+3,\]as witnessed by taking two disjoint copies of $C_{2n+1}$ and adding all edges between them.

Erdős [Er69b] observed that Dirac's construction generalises to show that, if $3\mid k$, there are infinitely many values of $n$ (those of the shape $mk/3$ where $m$ is odd) such that\[f_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k/3}\right)n^2 + n.\]Toft [To70] proved that $f_k(n)\gg_k n^2$ for $k\geq 4$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: Erdős [Er93] wrote 'I learned of this definition from Dirac in 1949 and immediately asked whether $f_k(n)=o(n^2)$. To my great surprise Dirac constructed a $6$ critical graph on $n$ vertices with more than $\frac{n^2}{4}$ edges.' In fact Dirac [Di52] provedf_6(4n+2) \geq 4n^2+8n+3,as witnessed by taking two disjoint copies of $C_{2n+1}$ and adding all edges between them.

Erdős [Er69b] observed that Dirac's construction generalises to show that, if $3\mid k$, there are infinitely many values of $n$ (those of the shape $mk/3$ where $m$ is odd) such thatf_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k/3}\right)n^2 + n.Toft [To70] proved that $f_k(n)\gg_k n^2$ for $k\geq 4$.

Constructions of Stiebitz [St87] show that, for $k\geq 6$, there exist infinitely many values of $n$ such thatf_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor+\delta_k}\right)n^2where $\delta_k=0$ if $k\equiv 0\pmod{3}$, $\delta_k=1/7$ if $k\equiv 1\pmod{3}$, and $\delta_k\equiv 24/69$ if $k\equiv 2\pmod{3}$, which disproves Erdős' conjectured asympotic for $k\not\equiv 0\pmod{3}$.

Stiebitz also proved the general upper boundf_k(n) < \mathrm{ex}(n;K_{k-1})\sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k-2}\right)n^2for large $n$. Luo, Ma, and Yang [LMY23] have improved this upper bound tof_k(n) \leq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k-2}-\frac{1}{36(k-1)^2}+o(1)\right)n^2See also [[944]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/944) and [[1032]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1032).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #918 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/918).

### Problem
Is there a graph with $\aleph_2$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_1$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?

Is there a graph with $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_\omega$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?

### Context
A question of Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa68b], who proved that for every finite $k$ there is a graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ where each subgraph on less than $\aleph_k$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$.

In [Er69b] it is asked with chromatic number $=\aleph_0$, but in the comments louisd observes this is (assuming subgraph and not induced subgraph was intended) trivially impossible, and hence presumably the problem was intended as written here (which is how it is posed in [ErHa68b]).

sourceComments.author: Salvatore Mercuri
sourceComments.contentMd:
Should that be $\leq\aleph_0$ at the end of both questions? Note that in [his 1969 paper](https://old.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1969-13.pdf#page=2) Erdős uses the same wording as on this page, but the original source, Problem 2 of [the 1968 paper](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1968-04.pdf#page=5) there is a $\leq$ appearing.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: It's unclear - as you say, the two sources differ, and I'm not close enough to this area to say which is the more sensible question. I'll add a note pointing out the ambiguity, and hopefully an expert can weigh in at some point.

replies.author: LouisD
replies.contentMd:
If he really means "subgraph" as opposed to "induced subgraph," then it must be $\le \aleph_0$ because otherwise you could just take any set of $\aleph_1$ many vertices with no edges as a subgraph with chromatic number 1.  So I would guess that $\le \aleph_0$ is the correct interpretation.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Salvatore Mercuri
replies.contentMd: Even if “induced subgraph” is intended then a similar argument for a negative answer was discovered by AlphaProof as follows. Assume $(V, E)$ is such a graph. If $V’\subseteq V$ is any subset of vertices of size $\aleph_1$, then it has a coloring $c$ on $\aleph_0$ colors. By a pigeonhole principle argument, there’s a fiber $V_y =  \{v \in V’ | c(v) = y\}$ of $c$ size $\aleph_1$. The induced subgraph $G[V_y]$ then has chromatic number $1$, but by assumption it has chromatic number $\aleph_0$. So indeed I think it must be $\leq\aleph_0$ in the statement.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #919 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/919).

### Problem
Is there a graph $G$ with vertex set $\omega_2^2$ and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph whose vertices have a lesser type has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$?

What if instead we ask for $G$ to have chromatic number $\aleph_1$?

### Context
This question was inspired by a theorem of Babai, that if $G$ is a graph on a well-ordered set with chromatic number $\geq \aleph_0$ there is a subgraph on vertices with order-type $\omega$ with chromatic number $\aleph_0$.

Erdős and Hajnal showed this does not generalise to higher cardinals - they (see [Er69b]) constructed a set on $\omega_1^2$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every strictly smaller subgraph has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$ as follows: the vertices of $G$ are the pairs $(x_\alpha,y_\beta)$ for $1\leq \alpha,\beta <\omega_1$, ordered lexicographically. We connect $(x_{\alpha_1},y_{\beta_1})$ and $(x_{\alpha_2},y_{\beta_2})$ if and only if $\alpha_1<\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1<\beta_2$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #920 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/920).

### Problem
Let $f_k(n)$ be the maximum possible chromatic number of a graph with $n$ vertices which contains no $K_k$.

Is it true that, for $k\geq 4$,\[f_k(n) \gg \frac{n^{1-\frac{1}{k-1}}}{(\log n)^{c_k}}\]for some constant $c_k>0$?

### Context
Graver and Yackel [GrYa68] proved that\[f_k(n) \ll \left(n\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}\right)^{1-\frac{1}{k-1}}.\]It is known that $f_3(n)\asymp (n/\log n)^{1/2}$ (see [[1104]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104)).

The lower bound $R(4,m) \gg m^3/(\log m)^4$ of Mattheus and Verstraete [MaVe23] (see [[166]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/166)) implies\[f_4(n) \gg \frac{n^{2/3}}{(\log n)^{4/3}}.\]A positive answer to this question would follow from [[986]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/986). The known bounds for that problem imply\[f_k(n) \gg \frac{n^{1-\frac{2}{k+1}}}{(\log n)^{c_k}}.\]See [[1104]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104) (and also [[1013]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1013)) for the case $k=3$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #928 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/928).

### Problem
Let $\alpha,\beta\in (0,1)$ and let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime divisor of $n$. Does the density of integers $n$ such that $P(n)<n^{\alpha}$ and $P(n+1)<(n+1)^\beta$ exist?

### Context
Dickman [Di30] showed the density of smooth $n$, with largest prime factor $<n^\alpha$, is $\rho(1/\alpha)$ where $\rho$ is the [Dickman function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function).

Erdős also asked whether infinitely many such $n$ even exist, but Meza has observed that this follows immediately from Schinzel's result [Sc67b] that for infinitely many $n$ the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$ is at most $n^{O(1/\log\log n)}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Erdős asked whether the events $P(n)<n^\alpha$ and $P(n+1)<(n+1)^\beta$ are independent, in the sense that the density of $n$ satisfying both conditions is equal to $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
No doubt this question already appears in the literature somewhere (do let me know if it does), but I suspect one could propose a more general mutual independence conjecture: let $0 \leq k_1 < \cdots < k_t$ be integers, and let $\alpha_1, \cdots, \alpha_t \in (0, 1)$. Must the density of $n$ satisfying $P(n + k_i) < (n + k_i)^{\alpha_i}$ for all $i$ exist and be equal to the product of all $\rho(1/\alpha_i)$?

If this is true, it would resolve [[369]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/369), and with a bit of analysis, I suspect it could also be used to resolve [[372]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/372).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #929 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/929).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 2$ be large and let $S(k)$ be the minimal $x$ such that there is a positive density set of $n$ where\[n+1,n+2,\ldots,n+k\]are all divisible by primes $\leq x$.

Estimate $S(k)$ - in particular, is it true that $S(k)\geq k^{1-o(1)}$?

### Context
It follows from Rosser's sieve that $S(k)> k^{1/2-o(1)}$.

It is trivial that $S(k)\leq k+1$ since, for example, one can take $n\equiv 1\pmod{(k+1)!}$. The best bound on large gaps between primes due to Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao [FGKMT18] (see [[4]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/4)) implies\[S(k) \ll k \frac{\log\log\log k}{\log\log k\log\log\log\log k}.\]

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #930 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/930).

### Problem
Is it true that, for every $r$, there is a $k$ such that if $I_1,\ldots,I_r$ are disjoint intervals of consecutive integers, all of length at least $k$, then\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq r}\prod_{m\in I_i}m\]is not a perfect power?

### Context
Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe75] proved that the product of consecutive integers is never a power (establishing the case $r=1$). The condition that the intervals be large in terms of $r$ is necessary for $r=2$ - see the constructions in [[363]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/363).

See also [[363]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/363) for the case of squares.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #931 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/931).

### Problem
Let $k_1\geq k_2\geq 3$. Are there only finitely many $n_2\geq n_1+k_1$ such that\[\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(n_1+i)\textrm{ and }\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(n_2+j)\]have the same prime factors?

### Context
Tijdeman gave the example\[19,20,21,22\textrm{ and }54,55,56,57.\]Erdős [Er76d] was unsure of this conjecture, and thought perhaps if the two products have the same prime factors then $n_2>2(n_1+k_1)$. It is not clear but it is possible that he meant to ask this question also permitting finitely many counterexamples. Indeed, without this caveat it is false - AlphaProof has found the counterexample\[10! = 2^8\cdot 3^4\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\]and\[14\cdot 15\cdot 16 = 2^5\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7,\]so that $n_1=0$, $k_1=10$, $n_2=13$, and $k_2=3$.

See also [[388]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/388).

sourceComments.author: MalekZ
sourceComments.contentMd:
I've been studying Problem 931 for the case $(k_1, k_2) = (4, 3)$ and have two results plus computational evidence.

**Result 1 (Local finiteness):** For fixed $n_1$, only finitely many $n_2$ are valid. Proof: Set $S = \text{Supp}(\prod(n_1+i))$. If $\text{Supp}(B) = S$, then each term of the second block is $S$-smooth. By Størmer's theorem, finitely many consecutive $S$-smooth integers exist. Since $k_2 \geq 2$, the pair $(n_2+1, n_2+2)$ are consecutive $S$-smooth integers, giving finitely many $n_2$. (Note: $k_2 \geq 2$ suffices, not $k_2 \geq 3$.)

**Result 2 (Gap-fixed finiteness):** For fixed gap $d = n_2 - n_1$, only finitely many pairs exist. Key lemma: for any prime $p > k_1$ in the common support, $p \mid \prod(d+t)$ for $t \in {1-k_1, \ldots, k_2-1}$. This confines all large primes to a short "$d$-window," giving a fixed finite prime set $S_d$ for each $d$. Størmer again gives finiteness.

**The global question reduces to:** Are there only finitely many admissible gaps $d$?

**Computational search:** Exhaustive for $n_1 \leq 10^6$, $n_2 \leq 1.1 \times 10^7$. Found exactly 26 valid pairs, all with $n_1 \leq 636$ and $n_2 \leq 10{,}932$. Complete solution table and CSV available.

**What Level 3 needs:** Four approaches were attempted (prime counting, smoothness via reverse inclusion, weighted divisibility, $|S(n_1)|$ growth rate comparison). All stalled. The missing theorem appears to require a finite-configuration rigidity argument exploiting the exact support structure of four consecutive integers, not generic smooth-number theory. A full write-up is available.

This work was conducted with AI assistance (Claude for orchestration, GPT-5.4 for strategy/computation).

replies.contentMd:
*This was my second or third proof so apologies in advance.*
Problem 931 — Full Note Case $(k_1, k_2) = (4, 3)$ Overview
We study Problem 931 for the specific case $(k_1, k_2) = (4, 3)$: are there infinitely many pairs $(n_1, n_2)$ such that $\prod_{i=0}^{3}(n_1 + i)$ and $\prod_{j=0}^{2}(n_2 + j)$ have the same prime support (i.e., the same set of prime divisors)?

We present two finiteness results, computational evidence, and a reduction of the global question.

**Update (March 14, 2026):** As Prof. Tao noted, Result 1 (local finiteness) likely follows from the work of Beukers, Shorey, and Tijdeman (1999) on products of consecutive integers. The connection to Problem 686 methods (Bennett's irrationality measure for $\sqrt[3]{2}$) may also be relevant. We include our elementary proofs below for completeness, pending a full comparison with the Beukers-Shorey-Tijdeman results.

Result 1: Local Finiteness (Fixed $n_1$)
**Theorem.** For fixed $n_1$, only finitely many $n_2$ are valid.

**Proof.** Set $S = \text{Supp}(\prod_{i=0}^{3}(n_1 + i))$, the prime support of the block of 4 consecutive integers starting at $n_1$. If $(n_1, n_2)$ is a valid pair, then $\text{Supp}(\prod_{j=0}^{2}(n_2 + j)) = S$.

This means each term of the second block $n_2, n_2+1, n_2+2$ is $S$-smooth (all prime factors in $S$). Since $S$ is a fixed finite set, each $n_2 + j$ is an $S$-smooth integer. By Størmer's theorem, there are only finitely many pairs of consecutive $S$-smooth integers. Since $k_2 \geq 2$, the pair $(n_2 + 1, n_2 + 2)$ consists of consecutive $S$-smooth integers, so only finitely many $n_2$ exist. $\square$

**Note:** The condition $k_2 \geq 2$ suffices; we do not need $k_2 \geq 3$.

Result 2: Gap-Fixed Finiteness
**Theorem.** For fixed gap $d = n_2 - n_1$, only finitely many pairs exist.

**Proof.** Fix $d = n_2 - n_1$. For any prime $p > k_1$ in the common support $S$, the prime $p$ must divide at least one element of each block. In the first block ${n_1, n_1+1, n_1+2, n_1+3}$, $p$ divides exactly one element (since $p > 4$, consecutive terms can share a prime factor only if $p \leq k_1$). Similarly for the second block.

The key lemma: $p$ divides $\prod_{t=0}^{k_1-1}(d + t)$ for every such prime $p$. To see this: if $p \mid n_1 + i$ (for some $0 \leq i \leq 3$) and $p \mid n_2 + j = n_1 + d + j$ (for some $0 \leq j \leq 2$), then $p \mid (d + j - i)$. Since $-3 \leq j - i \leq 2$, we have $p \mid (d + t)$ for some $t \in {-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2} \subset {1 - k_1, \ldots, k_2 - 1}$.

This confines all large primes $p$ (those $> k_1$) to the fixed set $S_d := \text{Supp}(\prod_{t=1-k_1}^{k_2-1}(d+t))$. The "$d$-window" $S_d$ is a finite set depending only on $d$.

Now the common support $S$ must satisfy: $S \subseteq {\text{primes} \leq k_1} \cup S_d$. This is a fixed finite set. Both blocks consist of consecutive $S$-smooth integers (with $S$ finite and fixed). By Størmer's theorem, there are finitely many such blocks. $\square$

The Global Reduction
**The global question reduces to:** Are there only finitely many admissible gaps $d$?

An admissible gap is a value $d = n_2 - n_1$ for which at least one valid pair exists. If we could show only finitely many gaps are admissible, finiteness of the full problem would follow from Result 2 (finitely many pairs per gap).

We attempted four approaches to prove finiteness of admissible gaps:- **Prime counting:** Comparing $\pi$-type bounds on support sizes. Stalled because the support of $k$ consecutive integers near $n$ has size $\sim k \log n / \log \log n$, and the ratio between 4-blocks and 3-blocks doesn't separate cleanly.
- **Smoothness via reverse inclusion:** Trying to show that for large $d$, the $S_d$ window forces implausibly smooth numbers. Stalled because smooth-number density (Dickman $\rho$) only gives subpolynomial decay.
- **Weighted divisibility / $|S(n_1)|$ growth rate:** Comparing the growth of support sizes. Stalled because both grow as $O(\log n / \log \log n)$ with comparable constants.
- **Finite-configuration rigidity:** The most promising direction. The missing theorem appears to require exploiting the exact structure of supports of 3–4 consecutive integers, not just generic smooth-number estimates.

 Computational Search
Exhaustive search for $n_1 \leq 10^6$ and $n_2 \leq 1.1 \times 10^7$:

**Found exactly 26 valid pairs**, all satisfying $n_1 \leq 636$ and $n_2 \leq 10{,}932$.

**Observation:** The largest $n_1$ in any valid pair is 636, and the largest $n_2$ is 10,932. The data strongly suggests global finiteness, but we cannot prove it with current methods.

What Level 3 (Full Resolution) Needs
The missing theorem appears to require a finite-configuration rigidity argument exploiting the exact support structure of four consecutive integers, not generic smooth-number theory. The four approaches described above all stalled because they treat the blocks too generically — they don't use the fact that consecutive integers have very constrained prime factorization patterns.

References - F. Beukers, T.N. Shorey, and R. Tijdeman, "Irreducibility of polynomials and arithmetic progressions with equal products of terms," 1999. (Noted by T. Tao as relevant to Result 1.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #932 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/932).

### Problem
Let $p_k$ denote the $k$th prime. For infinitely many $r$ there are at least two integers $p_r<n<p_{r+1}$ all of whose prime factors are $<p_{r+1}-p_r$.

### Context
Erdős thought this was true but that there are very few such $r$. He could show that the density of $r$ such that at least one such $n$ exist is $0$.

This problem has been [formalised in Lean](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/932.lean) as part of the [Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project](https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/).

sourceComments.author: Dogmachine
sourceComments.contentMd: Would the heuristics also make one expect existence of $k$ $(p_{r+1}-p_{r})$-smooth numbers inside the interval for every $k$?

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I'm not sure I understand the question.  If only one smooth number is required, one can just take the prime gap around powers of 2 and get a 2-smooth number between $p_r$ and $p_{r+1}$ for infinitely many $r$.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd: Yes, but I don't think there's as simple a construction to show that there exist at least 2 number in such intervals infinitely many times.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Ah, I now see that the intended question was "$k$ many $(p_{r+1}-p_r)$-smooth numbers" rather than "$(k \times (p_{r+1}-p_r))$-smooth numbers, which seemed like a minor modification of old-bielefelder's question.  Heuristically, one now needs a density of about $x^{-1/k+o(1)}$ of smooth numbers to make this pattern occur, which corresponds to $\log^{k+o(1)} x$-smoothness, but gaps as large as $\log^{k+o(1)} x$ are not expected to occur for large $x$ for $k>2$.  So I would tentatively expect that one should not expect infinitely many $k$-tuples of such smooth numbers within a single prime gap for any $k>2$

sourceComments.author: old-bielefelder
sourceComments.contentMd:
How much easier would be the following question:

Let p_k  denote the k-th prime. Do there exist infinitely
many r such that there are at least two integers m and n
with p_r < m < n < p_(r+1) all of whose prime factors
are < 2 * (p_(r+1) − p_r)?

So, how much does the factor 2 (or some other constant
factor > 1) help to enable or simplify things?

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I think one would need to accept smoothness on the scale of $(p_{r+1}-p_r)^{1+c}$ rather than $C (p_{r+1}-p_r)$ for some $c>0$ in order for the heuristics to become noticeably more favorable.  This is still well out of reach of current technology though.  I think the state of the art on consecutive smooth numbers of size $x$, for instance, is to be able to produce pairs of numbers that are $y$-smooth for $y$ of size about $x^{\log\log\log x / \log \log x}$, which is far larger than the $\log^A x$ type size we would need here (this is from Theorem 1.7 of [my recent paper with Joni](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01739)).

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: This looks really delicate.  It is basically asking to produce a pair of nearby $y$-smooth numbers, both living in a prime gap of length $y$.  Cramer's conjecture predicts that the longest prime gap is of size about $\log^2 x$, and de Bruijn type asymptotics say that the density of $\log^2 x$-smooth number is about $x^{-1/2+o(1)}$, which is only barely enough to expect a near-collision on probabilistic grounds.  So the problem seems exactly on the border between being heuristically true or heuristically false, and resolving it would require going beyond Cramer's conjecture which is considered hopeless by current methods (cf. problem #4).

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
It seems like conditionally on uniform $3$-adic expansion of residue classes (expected behavior), this is true. Here's GPT-5.2 argument:

Fix an odd integer $a$ with $(a,3)=1$ and assume $a \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. Put $u=-1/(2a)\in 1+3\mathbb{Z}_3$. For each integer $\delta\ge 1$ there is a unique residue class $t \bmod 3^{\delta-1}$ such that $4^t \equiv u \pmod{3^\delta}$; let $t_\delta\in\{0,1,\dots,3^{\delta-1}-1\}$ be its least representative. Equivalently, if $T=\log_3(u)/\log_3(4)\in\mathbb{Z}_3$ (so that $4^T=u$ inside $1+3\mathbb{Z}_3$), then $t_\delta \equiv T \pmod{3^{\delta-1}}$. Now set $\alpha_\delta=2t_\delta+1$ and $n_\delta=a2^{\alpha_\delta}$; then $4^{t_\delta}\equiv u \pmod{3^\delta}$ implies $a2^{\alpha_\delta}+1\equiv 0 \pmod{3^\delta}$, hence $3^\delta$ divides $n_\delta+1$, while $3$ does not divide $n_\delta$ and $2$ does not divide $n_\delta+1$.

Write the base-$3$ expansion $T=\sum_{j\ge 0} d_j 3^j$ with digits $d_j\in\{0,1,2\}$, so $t_\delta=\sum_{j=0}^{\delta-2} d_j 3^j$ is the $(\delta-1)$-digit truncation. Assume (THIS IS CONDITIONAL) that the digits $d_j$ behave like independent uniform random variables on $\{0,1,2\}$. For each $\delta$ let $L(\delta)=\lfloor \log_3 \delta \rfloor$ and let $E_\delta$ be the event that the top $L(\delta)$ digits of this truncation are zero, namely $d_{\delta-2}=d_{\delta-3}=\cdots=d_{\delta-1-L(\delta)}=0$. Then $\mathbb{P}(E_\delta)=3^{-L(\delta)}$, and since $3^{L(\delta)}\le \delta<3^{L(\delta)+1}$ we have $1/\delta \le \mathbb{P}(E_\delta)<3/\delta$. Choose a subsequence $\delta_1<\delta_2<\cdots$ by $\delta_1=3$ and $\delta_{j+1}=\delta_j+2L(\delta_j)+4$; then the digit blocks defining $E_{\delta_j}$ are disjoint, so the events $E_{\delta_j}$ are independent, and also $\delta_j \le C j \log j$ for some constant $C>0$, hence $\sum_j \mathbb{P}(E_{\delta_j})$ diverges by comparison with $\sum_j 1/(j\log j)$. By the second Borel-Cantelli lemma, infinitely many $E_{\delta_j}$ occur, and on each occurrence we have $t_{\delta_j}<3^{\delta_j-1-L(\delta_j)}\le 3^{\delta_j}/\delta_j$.

For $n_\delta=a2^{2t_\delta+1}$ we have a factorization $n_\delta(n_\delta+1)=2^k 3^l m$ with $(m,6)=1$ where $k=v_2(n_\delta)=2t_\delta+1$ and $l=v_3(n_\delta+1)\ge \delta$. Therefore
$$\frac{2^k 3^l}{n_\delta \log n_\delta}=\frac{2^{2t_\delta+1}3^l}{a2^{2t_\delta+1}\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})}=\frac{3^l}{a\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})}\ge \frac{3^\delta}{a\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})}.$$
For $t_\delta\ge 1$ we have $\log(a2^{2t_\delta+1})=\log a+(2t_\delta+1)\log 2\le (\log a+3\log 2)t_\delta$, hence
$$\frac{2^k 3^l}{n_\delta \log n_\delta}\ge \frac{3^\delta}{a(\log a+3\log 2)t_\delta}.$$
Along the infinitely many indices $\delta=\delta_j$ for which $t_{\delta_j}\le 3^{\delta_j}/\delta_j$, this gives
$$\frac{2^k 3^l}{n_{\delta_j}\log n_{\delta_j}} \ge \frac{3^\delta}{a(\log a+3\log 2)(3^{\delta-1}/\delta)}=\frac{\delta}{a(\log a+3\log 2)}.$$

Since the right-hand side tends to infinity with $\delta$, the values of $(2^k3^l)/(n\log n)$ along the subsequence $n=n_{\delta_j}$ are unbounded, and in particular $\limsup_{n\to\infty}(2^k3^l)/(n\log n)=\infty$. The only conditional input is the digit hypothesis on $T=\log_3(-1/(2a))/\log_3(4)$: it is enough that the base-$3$ digits of $T$ have the Borel-Cantelli property that blocks of $L(\delta)=\lfloor\log_3\delta\rfloor$ consecutive zeros at the top of the truncation occur infinitely often (independence is a convenient sufficient condition).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Yes, this is a heuristic argument.  Here is a simplified version (taking $a=7$ for concreteness):

In the 3-adics ${\bf Z}_3$, let $t  = \frac{\log (1-3 \times 5/14)}{\log(1+3)} \in {\bf Z}_3$ be the unique solution to the equation $(1 + 3)^t = 1 - \frac{3 \times 5}{14}$ in ${\bf Z}_3$, or equivalently $14 \times (1+3)^t+1=0$.  This is well-defined due to the convergence of the power series for the logarithm $\log(1+3x)$ in the 3-adics, and it is a routine matter to compute the first few (ternary) digits of this 3-adic number.  A [quick ChatGPT query](https://chatgpt.com/share/6995f252-8480-800e-9e2d-4fa0fd08fb3f) for instance gives

$$ t = \dots 2102120122012_3$$
Now make the plausible heuristic assumption that this number contains arbitrarily long blocks of 0s in its ternary expansion.  Thus, for any $L$, there exists some $l$ such that the $l-L,\dots,l-1$ ternary digits of $t$ vanish, so that $t = 3^l q + r$ for some $q \in {\bf Z}_3$ and $0 \leq r < 3^{l-L}$.  If one sets $k := 2r+1$ and $n := 7 \times 2^k$, then
$$n+1 = 14 \times (1+3)^r+1 = 14 \times (1+3)^t + 1 = 0 \pmod{3^l}.$$
So $n(n+1)=2^k 3^l m$ for some $m$ coprime to $6$, and
$$ \frac{2^k 3^l}{n \log n} \asymp \frac{2^k 3^l}{2^k r} \gg 3^L$$
and so this quantity goes to infinity conditionally on the hypothesis of arbitrarily long blocks of zeroes.

But this type of hypothesis is comparable to infamous questions about whether standard irrational numbers such as $e$, $\pi$, or $\sqrt{2}$ are normal in various bases, and seems well out of reach of current methods.  (There is a slim chance that one could get some mileage out of also varying $a$ and using Diophantine approximation tools, but this looks delicate at best - the gains in $L$ one might make by this method could be more than offset by the losses in the $a$ factor (which is suppressed in the above analysis as we took $a=7$).)

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
It looks like you are only checking the cases where $\{n, n+1\}$ contains either a power of two or a power of three. But this is not required; it is possible that $\{n, n+1\} = \{2^x a, 3^y b\}$ with $a,b$ both larger than $1$.

EDIT: I found a counterexample to your main claim that the ratio is uniformly bounded by $\frac{3}{\log 2}$. The integer $n = 1487503359$ is divisible by $3^{14}$, while $n+1$ is divisible by $2^{15}$, giving $\frac{2^x 3^y}{n \log n} \approx 4.99 > \frac{3}{\log{2}}$

### Problem
Let $h_t(d)$ be minimal such that every graph $G$ with $h_t(d)$ edges and maximal degree $\leq d$ contains two edges whose shortest path between them has length $\geq t$.

Estimate $h_t(d)$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Nešetřil. Erdős [Er88] wrote 'This problem seems to be interesting only if there is a nice expression for $h_t(d)$.'

It is easy to see that $h_t(d)\leq 2d^t$ always and $h_1(d)=d+1$.

researchNotes: A problem of Erdős and Nešetřil. Erdős [Er88] wrote 'This problem seems to be interesting only if there is a nice expression for $h_t(d)$.'
It is easy to see that $h_t(d)\leq 2d^t$ always and $h_1(d)=d+1$.

Erdős and Nešetřil and Bermond, Bond, Paoli, and Peyrat [BBPP83] independently conjectured that $h_2(d) \leq \tfrac{5}{4}d^2+1$, with equality for even $d$ (see [[149]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/149)). This was proved by Chung, Gyárfás, Tuza, and Trotter [CGTT90].

Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang [CCJK22] conjectured thath_3(d) \leq d^3-d^2+d+2,with equality if and only if $d=p^k+1$ for some prime power $p^k$, and proved that $h_3(3)=23$. They also conjecture that, for all $t\geq 3$, $h_t(d)\geq (1-o(1))d^t$ for infinitely many $d$ and $h_t(d)\leq (1+o(1))d^t$ for all $d$ (where the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $d\to \infty$).
The same authors prove that, if $t$ is large, then there are infinitely many $d$ such that $h_t(d) \geq 0.629^td^t$, and that for all $t\geq 1$ we haveh_t(d) \leq \tfrac{3}{2}d^t+1.

Erdős and Nešetřil and Bermond, Bond, Paoli, and Peyrat [BBPP83] independently conjectured that $h_2(d) \leq \tfrac{5}{4}d^2+1$, with equality for even $d$ (see [[149]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/149)). This was proved by Chung, Gyárfás, Tuza, and Trotter [CGTT90].

Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang [CCJK22] conjectured that\[h_3(d) \leq d^3-d^2+d+2,\]with equality if and only if $d=p^k+1$ for some prime power $p^k$, and proved that $h_3(3)=23$. They also conjecture that, for all $t\geq 3$, $h_t(d)\geq (1-o(1))d^t$ for infinitely many $d$ and $h_t(d)\leq (1+o(1))d^t$ for all $d$ (where the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $d\to \infty$).
The same authors prove that, if $t$ is large, then there are infinitely many $d$ such that $h_t(d) \geq 0.629^td^t$, and that for all $t\geq 1$ we have\[h_t(d) \leq \tfrac{3}{2}d^t+1.\]

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd: Isn't $K_3$ a counterexample to the claim that $h_1(2)=3$?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: It seems to be, yes. I got $h_1(d)=d+1$ from [[CCJK22]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.118982) - this is true for $d\geq 3$, but fails for $d=2$ because of $K_3$ as you say (although this is the only graph which causes a problem).

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
It is indeed assumed $d$ is large/ at least 3, since the d=2 case is a trivial case,
since the only connected graphs with $\Delta \le 2$ are paths and cycles, and thence $h_t(2)=2t+2.$

For $d \ge 3$, let G have at least $d+1$ edges, then all other $d$ edges are incident to $uv$ and thus $u$ or $v$.
They cannot all be adjacent to a fixed one.
Now any edge incident with $u$ has to be incident with any edge incident to $v$, thus all of them are of the form $uz, vz$ for the same vertex $z$, which cannot happen.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #935 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/935).

### Problem
For any integer $n=\prod p^{k_p}$ let $Q_2(n)$ be the powerful part of $n$, so that\[Q_2(n) = \prod_{\substack{p\\ k_p\geq 2}}p^{k_p}.\]Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$ and $\ell\geq 1$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then\[Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))<n^{2+\epsilon}?\]If $\ell\geq 2$ then is\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^2}\]infinite?

If $\ell\geq 2$ then is\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^{\ell+1}}=0?\]

### Context
Erdős [Er76d] writes that if this is true then it 'seems very difficult to prove'.

A result of Mahler implies, for every $\ell\geq 1$,\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))}{n^2}\geq 1.\]All these questions can be asked replacing $Q_2$ by $Q_r$ for $r>2$, only keeping those prime powers with exponent $\geq r$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
This question is essentially the same as [#367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367) (although I do note that we look at the powerful part of the product here, as opposed to the product of the powerful parts. But that changes at most a constant). In particular, the construction by Aletheia is also the one found in the comments on #367 (even though they only show unboundedness of the ratio, as opposed to the extra log-term we got here). It is certainly possible that Aletheia came up with it independently, but reading the Aletheia paper they do write that this was done early December 2025, roughly two weeks after the comments on #367.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Thanks. Both could be possible, since we do not know system internals of Aletheia. I do think that the explanation of adaptation from #367 is plausible. On the other hand, the paper's own description "This solution is certainly well-known to experts" (because it is short and simple) is not substantiated.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I think it is more the use of the solutions to Pell's equation, which is a standard trick in this area (see the commentary to #364, #365, #366, #672, as well as Wouter's solution to #367).

replies.author: Kevin Barreto
replies.contentMd: FYI, yes. I added that line directly on the suggestion of Thomas Bloom. The Pell's equation approach is the standard idea here.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
I do think it is important to include the fact that #935 and #367 turned out to contain the same problems, with Aletheia's result already having been obtained in the comment section here. But I guess you agree, since quoting from the paper:

*it is certainly possible that we missed earlier solutions to these problems by human mathematicians. Therefore, our initial classification into categories is, at best, an upper bound on novelty. It is subject to revision after further investigation by the public.*

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Yes, I think it was just missed (apparently by everyone, including me and AI) the obvious connection between [[367]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367) and [[935]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/935). Of course, this connection is obvious once you have them both in mind, but they were added some time apart. I also see now that [[367]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367) does not contain the key words 'powerful' or 'squarefull', so presumably when adding this problem (perhaps over a year since [[367]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367)) I searched for such key words, saw no similar problems, so added this thinking it was unique. Since then the database is better connected, and I'm wiser to such errors, so hopefully this will be the last such (near) duplicate discovered.

replies.author: fengt
replies.contentMd:
Can you advise on whether we should revise our paper to update the classification of Erdos-935 accordingly? If I understand correctly, the solution to both questions involves the same construction, while the questions are not exactly the same (and are asked on different occasions by Erdos), but essentially equivalent. I guess we already call this solution a "graduate student exercise" which is "well-known to experts". (Also, please feel free to e-mail me to advise further adjustments if necessary; I don't plan on following each problem page.)

EDIT: we can confirm that the problem page for Erdos-367 was not accessed in the thinking logs for the solution to Erdos-935. Also, the date of the comments on Erdos-367 is after the knowledge cutoff for training.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
Based on your edit I think we can safely conclude that Aletheia came up with it independently, which is rather exciting. I am however slightly surprised then that Aletheia did not think of the exact same idea when considering [#367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367), but okay.

In any case, I would now argue that it's more appropriately placed in Section 4 of your paper, rather than Section 3. Although I do understand if you would ideally like to keep Section 4 for independent discoveries that fully settle an Erdős problem as written here. That being said, what counts as a 'full' or 'partial' solution can be rather arbitrary. It may hinge on the exact way Thomas decides to write down the problem (of which there is a often more than one sensible approach), and whether several related questions get their own problem page or not.

replies.author: fengt
replies.contentMd: On #367: the attempt was self-filtered out in the initial 700 -> 212 stage, so humans never saw the output. I dug it up from the logs: Aletheia found the Erdos problem page and acknowledged not solving the problem completely. For #935, Aletheia incorrectly asserted solving the whole problem, which is why the solution to part (2) reached human eyes.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: Might there be more interesting partial progress on other problems in the other responses?

replies.author: fengt
replies.contentMd:
Yes, that is probably the case. In fact, someone on our team pointed out that the solution candidate to Erdos-281 was arguably close to correct. Given the pace of improvements to the base model and agent, though, it would be more efficient for a team of our size to keep rerunning the open problems rather than examining old outputs. Personally I would only be inclined to revisit the Erdos problems after improving the model's capability substantially. To find more problems that can be solved with the current capability, I think it would be better to just give our tools to the public.

The Erdos problems were actually not a consideration when building Aletheia; we ran them later when it became clear that they would become a common discussion point. It turned out to be useful for us to get a large-scale picture of the model's capabilities, but I think our team is happy to leave the results as a case study instead of trying to optimize the number of Erdos problems solved. We each have our own pet research problems that we want to get back to :)

P.S. Tonight's arXiv update will move our Erdos-935 result to the "Independent Rediscovery" section, crediting Woett appropriately.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #936 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/936).

### Problem
Are\[2^n\pm 1\]and\[n!\pm 1\]powerful (i.e. if $p\mid m$ then $p^2\mid m$) for only finitely many $n$?

### Context
Cushing and Pascoe [CuPa16] have shown the answer to the second question is yes assuming the abc conjecture - in fact, for any fixed $k\geq 0$, there are only finitely many $n$ and powerful $x$ such that $\lvert x-n!\rvert \leq k$.

CrowdMath [Cr20] has shown that the answer to the first question is yes, again assuming the abc conjecture.

replies.contentMd: The meaning of "possible" given at https://github.com/teorth/erdosproblems/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md is "there may be a theoretically computable sequence associated to the problem that is in the OEIS and not already listed on the table; but it needs enough values actually computed that one can cross-check with that database."

replies.contentMd: Yes - in general the 'possible' tag is left to indicate that there seem to be more OEIS sequences that could be added here - which is certainly the case here.

sourceComments.author: seewoo5
sourceComments.contentMd: Similar to Brocard's problem [[398]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/398), Cushing and Pascoe proved that there are finitely many powerful numbers "close to factorials", i.e. for given $k$, $|x - n!| \le k$ has finitely many integer solutions $(x, n)$ where $x$ is powerful ([arxiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01192)), assuming ABC conjecture. Similarly, [this arxiv paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07321) shows that, for given coprime integers $k, r$ there are finitely many powerful numbers of the form $k^n + r$, again assuming ABC conjecture (Theorem 2.3). So the answer is positive conditionally. Note that both references are found by GPT-5.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #939 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/939).

### Problem
Let $r\geq 2$. An $r$-powerful number $n$ is one such that if $p\mid n$ then $p^r\mid n$.

If $r\geq 4$ then can the sum of $r-2$ coprime $r$-powerful numbers ever be itself $r$-powerful? Are there at most finitely many such solutions?

Are there infinitely many triples of coprime $3$-powerful numbers $a,b,c$ such that $a+b=c$?

### Context
The answer to the third question is yes: Nitaj [Ni95] has proved that there are infinitely many triples of coprime $3$-powerful numbers $a,b,c$ such that $a+b=c$, such as\[2^3\cdot 3^5\cdot 73^3+271^3 = 919^3.\]In Nitaj's construction at least two of $a,b,c$ are perfect cubes. Cohn [Co98] constructed infinitely many such triples, none of which are perfect cubes. An alternative construction was given by Walsh [Wa24].

Euler had conjectured that the sum of $k-1$ many $k$th powers is never a $k$th power, but this is false for $k=5$, as Lander and Parkin [LaPa67] found\[27^5+84^5+110^5+133^5=144^5.\]Cambie has found several examples of the sum of $r-2$ coprime $r$-powerful numbers being itself $r$-powerful. For example when $r=5$\[3^761^5=2^83^{10}5^7+2^{12}23^6+11^513^5.\]Cambie has also found solutions when $r=7$ or $r=8$ (the latter even with the sum of $5$ $8$-powerful numbers being $8$-powerful).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
At firt sight, no.

More exactly:
If Ramaekers's variant would have been true, the answer would have been yes.
Since then $a_1+ \ldots +a_{s}=x$ for coprime $r$-powerful numbers $a_i, 1 \le i \le s\le r-2$ and $x$ implies that
$\lvert x \rvert \le \lvert x \rvert^{(1+o(1))(s+1)/r}$, and thus $x$ is bounded.

But by HKS25, we know that one is false, and the bounds are too weak to conclude.
(or one needs additional things, like while the $a_i$ are coprime, they have pairwise large gcd's, for which I do not see any particular reason)

For reference on the state of the art on the n conjecture, I had a look at
[[HKS25]](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/improved-lower-bounds-for-strong-nconjectures/881532D8B69924BBFA5C76A32A52063A).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #940 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/940).

### Problem
Let $r\geq 3$.  A number $n$ is $r$-powerful if for every prime $p$ which divides $n$ we have $p^r\mid n$.

Are there infinitely many integers which are not the sum of at most $r$ many $r$-powerful numbers? Does the set of integers which are the sum of at most $r$ $r$-powerful numbers have density $0$?

### Context

For $r=3$ it is not even known if those integers which are the sum of at most three cubes has density $0$.

In the Oberwolfach problem book this is recorded in 1986 as a problem of Erdős and Ivić.

sourceComments.contentMd: Why is density $0$ 'easy' for $r = 2$? I know that Erdős claims this in the referenced paper, but for us mere mortals?

replies.author: Dogmachine
replies.contentMd: I believe it is more like classic than easy, in the sense that you probably could mimic the proof of Edmund Landau that set of numbers that are sums of two squares have density zero to prove the corresponding result here.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: I've been thinking, but I don't see anything easy. Even adapting Landau's proof is not obvious - what are the prime obstructions here? And given the negative solution to [[1081]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1081) it can't be as simple as primes congruent to 3 mod 4.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Presumably the references listed in [#1081](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1081) answer this question?

replies.contentMd: Blomer and Granville [BlGr06] does.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Yes sorry, should have clarified - this is certainly known, and I believe was first proved by Baker and Brüdern [BaBr94]. Their proof was an application of the large sieve.

I meant that I'm not sure what the 'easy' proof of just zero density was that Erdős had in mind. Maybe it was something like this.

(I'll update the remarks to represent this.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
OK, here is an "easy" proof.  A powerful number is a product of a square and a cube, so one is asking to count $n \leq x$ of the form $n = c^3 a^2 + d^3 b^2$ for some $a,b,c,d$.  This forces $a = O(x^{1/2}/c^{3/2})$ and $b = O(x^{1/2}/d^{3/2})$, so for any fixed $c,d$ the number of such $n$ is $O(x / c^{3/2} d^{3/2})$.  This converges in $c,d$, so to get zero density one can restrict attention to the bounded case $c,d=O(1)$ (dominated convergence).  But then one is essentially in the sum of two squares case (in a suitable number field).

Disclosure: I also tried asking ChatGPT Pro about this, but [it confidently gave a hopelessly wrong answer](https://chatgpt.com/share/68fb8a83-63d4-800e-80ad-cd260073bc2a) (key error: assuming one could upper bound a ratio by upper bounding the denominator).  These tools still focus too much on getting arguments that *look* right, and lack the sense of "smell" that their argument is going awry.

Let $h(n)$ count the number of powerful (if $p\mid m$ then $p^2\mid m$) integers in $[n^2,(n+1)^2)$. Estimate $h(n)$. In particular is there some constant $c>0$ such that\[h(n) < (\log n)^{c+o(1)}\]and, for infinitely many $n$,\[h(n) >(\log n)^{c-o(1)}?\]

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
ChatGPT's Deep Research tool gave me the following reference, where they prove much more than the unboundedness of $h(n)$:

Jean-Marie De Koninck and Florian Luca, *Sur la proximité des nombres puissants*, Acta Arithmetica, Volume 114, Issue 2, 149-157, 2004.

Their Theorem 1 states that $h(n)$ is infinitely often larger than $\frac{9}{20} \left(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n} \right)^{1/3}$, which is more or less a lower bound in the form that Erdős expected. Their proof makes use of Diophantine approximation results as well, so it seems that these techniques are important for this problem. De Koninck and Luca furthermore give the specific density of $n$ (roughly $0.275$) for which $h(n)$ is equal to $1$ (i.e. those $n$ for which the only powerful integer in the interval $[n^2, (n+1)^2)$ is $n^2$).

Another (less relevant) reference that I found with ChatGPT is

Tsz Ho Chan, *A note on powerful numbers in short intervals*, Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society, Volume 108, issue 1, 99-106, 2023.

This paper gives a uniform upper bound of $\ll \frac{y}{\log y}$ on the number of powerful integers in any interval of length $y$, with a further $\log^c y$ improvement in the denominator if one assumes the abc conjecture. However, by the nature of its uniformity such results can never establish an upper bound of the form required here.

All other results on powerful integers in short intervals that I managed to find (both with and without AI) concern intervals $(x, x + x^{c})$ with $c > \frac{1}{2}$, which are therefore not directly relevant to the question at hand.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
The following proof that $h(n)$ is unbounded was found with the help of Gemini (but written down by me in my own words, so any mistakes are mine).

Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ be arbitrary, let $2 = p_1 < p_2 < \ldots < p_k$ be the first $k$ primes, and define $\beta_i = p_i \sqrt{p_i}$ for $1 \le i \le k$. We then define $\theta_i = \frac{\beta_k}{\beta_i}$ and $\alpha_i = 0$ for $1 \le i \le k-1$, while we let $\theta_k = \beta_k$ and $\alpha_k = \frac{1}{2}$. Finally, set $\epsilon = \frac{1}{4\beta_k}$.

It follows from a theorem by Besicovitch (see [here](https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/jlms/s1-15.1.3)) that $1, \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_k$ are rationally independent so that we may apply Kronecker's approximation theorem. We therefore deduce that there exist integers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k$ and $q$ such that $$\left|q \theta_i - x_i - \alpha_i \right| < \epsilon \hspace{10pt} (1)$$holds for all $1 \le i \le k$.

Using $(1)$ for $i = k$ we obtain $$x_k + \frac{1}{4} < q \beta_k < x_k + \frac{3}{4},$$while using $(1)$ for some $i$ with $1 \le i \le k-1$ and multiplying by $\beta_i$ we obtain $$q \beta_k - \frac{1}{4} <  x_i \beta_i < q \beta_k + \frac{1}{4}.$$In particular, by writing $n = x_k$ we have $$q \beta_k \in (n, n + 1)$$ and $$x_i \beta_i \in (n, n + 1)$$ for all $1 \le i \le k-1$. Squaring all of these values and we deduce $$(q \beta_k)^2 = q^2 p_k^3 \in (n^2, (n+1)^2)$$ and $$(x_i \beta_i)^2 = x_i^2 p_i^3 \in (n^2, (n+1)^2).$$In other words, there are at least $k$ powerful integers between $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$, so that $h(n)$ is indeed unbounded as $k$ was arbitrary.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

I did an intensive back-and-forth with GPT-5.4 Pro on this problem and [here is the write-up with](https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos943.pdf):

a) an unconditional partial result

 $ r(n):=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:\ a+b=n\} \ll_\epsilon n^{2/5+\epsilon}$

b) the strongest exact reformulations we currently have for a coprime model, and isolate where the square-sieve approach really breaks.

c) summarization of the 2025–2026 literature surrounding squarefull values, modular square roots, quadratic large sieves, and related averaging problems, and explain precisely which theorem is still missing. There is an on-going research work, so noting this will probably help finish the full problem in the near future (either by humans or new LLMs).

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
There's an interesting geometric approach to the problem and a pretty extensive literature focused on that if you search for Campana points, Manin-type conjectures. Start with the identity \(r(n)=(1_A*1_A)(n)=\#\{(a,b)\in A^2:a+b=n\}\).  View \((a,b)\) as an integral point on the affine plane \(\mathbb A^2\subset \mathbb P^2\) via \((a,b)\leftrightarrow [x:y:z]=[a:b:1]\), and impose the linear condition \(a+b=n\) as the moving line\[
L_n:\ x+y=nz\subset \mathbb P^2.
\]Now encode “powerful” as an orbifold integrality condition (Campana condition) along the coordinate divisors \(D_x=\{x=0\}\), \(D_y=\{y=0\}\) by taking the boundary\[
\Delta=\Big(1-\frac12\Big)(D_x+D_y).
\]Then a rational point \([x:y:1]\) is a \(\Delta\)-Campana \(\mathbb Z\)-point precisely when for every prime \(p\), the valuation \(v_p(x)\) (resp. \(v_p(y)\)) is either \(0\) or \(\ge 2\), i.e. \(x\) and \(y\) are powerful.  The pair \((\mathbb P^2,\Delta)\) is klt and log Fano because \(-\!\big(K_{\mathbb P^2}+\Delta\big)\) is ample.  In this language, the question is a uniform fiber problem: bound the number of Campana \(\mathbb Z\)-points on the members \(L_n\), i.e.\[
r(n)=\#\big(L_n(\mathbb Q)\cap (\mathbb P^2,\Delta)(\mathbb Z)\big)\stackrel{?}{\ll_\varepsilon} n^\varepsilon \quad(\forall \varepsilon>0).
\][The paper arXiv:2104.14946](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.14946) analyzes closely related phenomena for Campana points on \(\mathbb P^1\) with boundary \(D=\tfrac12[0]+\tfrac12[1]+\tfrac12[\infty]\), which (on an integral model) forces squareful/squarefull-type divisibility conditions on the homogeneous coordinates and certain linear combinations; in particular it highlights that, even in very low-dimensional log Fano orbifolds, the expected Manin-type leading constant can be destabilized by Campana thin subsets and “accumulating” contributions coming from covers or special subfamilies.  A key takeaway is that “log Fano + Campana-Manin” by itself does not automatically give uniform control on individual fibers of a fibration (or pencil of curves): thin sets can be engineered so that removing them changes leading constants dramatically, and there may be no canonical geometrically-defined thin set whose removal yields the “correct” constant.  For our \(r(n)\), this is a warning that any approach that counts Campana points globally on \((\mathbb P^2,\Delta)\) and then hopes to deduce pointwise bounds on intersections with \(L_n\) must also control how exceptional thin sets intersect the pencil \(\{L_n\}\) uniformly in \(n\).

Beyond 2104.14946, a precise route to \(r(n)=n^{o(1)}\) is to strengthen the log-Fano/Campana counting philosophy from global asymptotics to uniform fiberwise non-concentration.  One clean conjectural package is: (i) a Campana–Manin asymptotic for \((\mathbb P^2,\Delta)\) after removing a thin exceptional set \(T\), and simultaneously (ii) a uniform bound \(\#(T\cap L_n)\ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon\) for all \(n\), so that thin exceptional points cannot “pile up” on a single line \(L_n\).  This is naturally tied to Hilbert-property/weak-approximation expectations for Campana points (which aim to prevent the Campana set itself from being thin and to constrain thin images), combined with an effective uniformity principle for the pencil (morally: the Campana points equidistribute across the base \(\mathbb P^1\) at subpolynomial scale).  If one could prove (or assume) such a fiberwise thin-set control statement for this specific log Fano orbifold, then the desired bound \(r(n)\ll_\varepsilon n^\varepsilon\) would follow immediately from the geometric reformulation.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Here $1_A\ast 1_A(n)$ denotes the additive convolution, not multiplicative, so it is counting the number of $a,b\in A$ such that $a+b=n$. (In particular $1_A\ast 1_A(p)=0$ for all prime $p$ is false.) Even if it were true, it does not disprove $1_A\ast 1_A(n)=n^{o(1)}$, since that is (in a slight abuse of notation) short for saying, for all $\epsilon>0$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then\[1_A\ast 1_A(n)\leq n^\epsilon.\]

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #944 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/944).

### Problem
A critical vertex, edge, or set of edges, is one whose deletion lowers the chromatic number.

Let $k\geq 4$ and $r\geq 1$. Must there exist a graph $G$ with chromatic number $k$ such that every vertex is critical, yet every critical set of edges has size $>r$?

### Context
A graph $G$ with chromatic number $k$ in which every vertex is critical is called $k$-vertex-critical.

This was conjectured by Dirac in 1970 for $k\geq 4$ and $r=1$. Dirac's conjecture was proved, for $k=5$, by Brown [Br92]. Lattanzio [La02] proved there exist such graphs for all $k$ such that $k-1$ is not prime. Independently, Jensen [Je02] gave an alternative construction for all $k\geq 5$. The case $k=4$ and $r=1$ remains open.

### Deliverable

Martinsson and Steiner [MaSt25] proved this is true for every $r\geq 1$ if $k$ is sufficiently large, depending on $r$. Skottova and Steiner [SkSt25] have improved this, proving that such graphs exist for all $k\geq 5$ and $r\geq 1$. The only remaining open case is $k=4$ (even the case $k=4$ and $r=1$ remains open).

Erdős also asked a stronger quantitative form of this question: let $f_k(n)$ denote the largest $r\geq 1$ such that there exists a $k$-vertex-critical graph on $n$ vertices such that no set of at most $r$ edges is critical. He then asks whether $f_k(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Skottova and Steiner [SkSt25] have proved this for $k\geq 5$, establishing the boundsn^{1/3}\ll_k f_k(n) \ll_k \frac{n}{(\log n)^C}for all $k\geq 5$, where $C>0$ is an absolute constant.
This is Problem 91 in the graph problems collection. See also [[917]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/917) and [[1032]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1032).

Martinsson and Steiner [MaSt25] proved this is true for every $r\geq 1$ if $k$ is sufficiently large, depending on $r$. Skottova and Steiner [SkSt25] have improved this, proving that such graphs exist for all $k\geq 5$ and $r\geq 1$. The only remaining open case is $k=4$ (even the case $k=4$ and $r=1$ remains open).

Erdős also asked a stronger quantitative form of this question: let $f_k(n)$ denote the largest $r\geq 1$ such that there exists a $k$-vertex-critical graph on $n$ vertices such that no set of at most $r$ edges is critical. He then asks whether $f_k(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Skottova and Steiner [SkSt25] have proved this for $k\geq 5$, establishing the bounds\[n^{1/3}\ll_k f_k(n) \ll_k \frac{n}{(\log n)^C}\]for all $k\geq 5$, where $C>0$ is an absolute constant.

This is [Problem 91](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/NoncriticalEdges.html) in the graph problems collection. See also [[917]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/917) and [[1032]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1032).

sourceComments.contentMd: pedantically, I believe the $k$-dependence is $(1/k)n^{1/3}\ll f_k(n)\ll_k \frac{n}{(\log n)^c}$, where $c>0$ does not have to depend on $k$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #945 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/945).

### Problem
Let $F(x)$ be the maximal $k$ such that there exist $n+1,\ldots,n+k\leq x$ with $\tau(n+1),\ldots,\tau(n+k)$ all distinct (where $\tau(m)$ counts the divisors of $m$). Estimate $F(x)$. In particular, is it true that\[F(x) \leq (\log x)^{O(1)}?\]In other words, is there a constant $C>0$ such that, for all large $x$, every interval $[x,x+(\log x)^C]$ contains two integers with the same number of divisors?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Mirsky [ErMi52], who proved that\[\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}\ll F(x) \ll \exp\left(O\left(\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}\right)\right).\]Erdős [Er85e] claimed that the lower bound could be improved via their method 'with some more work' to $(\log x)^{1-o(1)}$. Beker [has improved](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1dPzHQw08tetxr-OwIlWddELunW0DXvxJ/view) the upper bound to\[F(x) \ll \exp\left(O\left((\log x)^{1/3+o(1)}\right)\right).\]Cambie has observed that [Cramér's conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cram%C3%A9r%27s_conjecture) implies that $F(x) \ll (\log x)^2$, and furthermore if every interval in $[x,2x]$ of length $\gg \log x$ contains a squarefree number (see [[208]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/208)) then every interval of length $\gg (\log x)^2$ contains two numbers with the same number of divisors, whence\[F(x) \ll (\log x)^2.\]See [[1004]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1004) for the analogous problem with the Euler totient function.

This problem is discussed in problem B18 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

replies.author: Woett
replies.contentMd:
This is very nice Adrian! A few comments that may or may not be fruitful:

0) Where you write $\le (\log x)^{1/3}$ in the middle of page $2$, I think this should actually be equality.
1) For the number of possibilities for $f(n)$ you take $v_p(n) \le \log_2(n)$, presumably for simplicity. You are certainly aware of this, but here we could use the fact that $p > |I|/6$ so that $v_p(n) \le \log_{|I|/6}(n) \le (\log x)^{2/3}$. In the end this only changes the implicit constant in the exponent, but it seemed worth mentioning.
2) For the number of possibilities for $g(n)$ you similarly note that $n$ has at most $\log_2(n)$ prime factors. Perhaps using some version of Erdős-Kac in short intervals, an analogue of Lemma $2.1$ still holds where $S$ only contains integers with approximately $\log \log n$ prime factors. Again, this only marginally impacts the final bound (if it even works). But again, I still wanted to point it out ;)

replies.author: abeker
replies.contentMd:
Thanks Wouter for your comments!

Regarding 0), you are absolutely right, this is in fact an equality. As for 1), I'm aware of this, but as you said, it doesn't impact the final shape of the bound. Also, it did occur to me that 2) might lead to an improvement, but I'm not sure whether something along these lines is feasible. In particular, it again seems to be difficult to control the behaviour of the large prime factors.
