problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #948 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/948).

### Problem
Is there a function $f(n)$ and a $k$ such that in any $k$-colouring of the integers there exists a sequence $a_1<\cdots$ such that $a_n<f(n)$ for infinitely many $n$ and the set\[\left\{ \sum_{i\in S}a_i : \textrm{finite }S\right\}\]does not contain all colours?

### Context
Erdős initially asked whether this is possible with the set being monochromatic, but Galvin showed that this is not always possible, considering the two colouring where, writing $n=2^km$ with $m$ odd, we colour $n$ red if $m\geq F(k)$ and blue if $m<F(k)$ (for some sufficiently quickly growing $F$).

This is open even in the case of $\aleph_0$-many colours.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: LouisD
sourceComments.contentMd: This problem is also mentioned as Problem 4.2 in "Some Ramsey-type theorems" by Erdos and Galvin (1991).  (However, the version for $\aleph_0$ - many colors is not mentioned as it is in the earlier problem paper.)  The main reason I mention this is that the Galvin example is explicitly described in Theorem 4.1 and this might help clear up some of the discussion in the comments.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Since Galvin excluded the cases of a $2$-colouring, I will explain that construction.

Assume such a sequence exists which is monochromatic.
$\textbf{red}$
There is a large $n$, such that $n>k_0 2^{k_0}$ with $F(k_0)>2^{k_0}f(n)$,
and all sumsets formed with $a_1, a_2 , \ldots, a_n$ (which are bounded by $f(n)$) are red.
By definition of the colouring, and the above choice, the pigeon hole principle says that there is a valuation $k< k_0$ such that at least $2^{k_0}$ values $a_i$ ($i \le n$) have $2$-adic valuation $k$.
Then (again by the pigeon hole principle) there are some (and we need no more than $2^{k_0}$ of them) of the $a_i$ who sum to a multiple of $2^{k+k_0}$.
Now $\sum a_i <2^{k_0} f(n)<F(k_0)<F( v_2( \sum a_i) ),$
and thus it was coloured blue, leading to a contradiction with being monochromatic.

$\textbf{blue}$
Since $k=v_2(a_1)$ is fixed, it is bounded.
Now for $n>2^{k+1}F(k)$, either there are half of $a_1$ up to $a_n$ with $2$-adic valuation bounded by $k$, or half of them above $k$.
In both cases, we can take a subset of them (with at least $(n-1)/2$ elements) whose sum $\sum a_i$ has $2$-adic valuation bounded by $k$.
But that sum is coloured red, leading to a contradiction.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
(post to save time on failed attempt)
Two natural extensions of Galvin do not work already for $3$ colours;
*having multiple function $F_1,F_2$ (suff. quick growing) such that the size of the odd part (as function of $v_2$) determines the colour.
[one can ensure that the odd part is either small or big, but never medium]
*partitioning red (or blue) numbers depending on parity of $v_2$ into two colours
[by taking numbers with different $v_2$, one is free to avoid one of the two colours]

replies.contentMd: also the counterexample seems over complicated to me. can't we simply color all $m>f(1)$ red, and $m\le f(1)$ blue? and for the multicolor version, why can't we have $m\le f(1)$ color one, $m\in (f(1),\sum_{i=1}^{f(1)} f(i)]$ color 2, and so on, so that all sufficiently large $n$ hit every color?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
I'm not sure what you mean by not supposed to depend on $n$ - in [Er77c] Erdős certainly writes $a_1<\cdots <a_n$, so I interpreted that as choosing $n$ elements from $[1,f(n)]$. (He earlier discusses another question of his which fixes a single infinite sequence $a_i$ independent of $n$, for which Galvin's construction was originally introduced, but this problem is slightly different).

Regarding your colouring, we could take $A$ to be any subset of $[f(1),f(n)]$, so all subset sums are red, which works provided $f(n)-f(1)\geq n$ (but I assume you're talking about a different problem here, taking your first comment into account).

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd: if the sequence can depend on $n$, then this should just be true by Folkman's Theorem (subset sums are partition regular).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Doh, of course. So on a third reading you're right, the sequence shouldn't depend on $n$ (my brain had inserted a $<$ where one didn't exist somehow).

So I think the revised problem is 'Is there an $f(n)$ and integer $k$ such that in any $k$-colouring there is a sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ such that $a_n<f(n)$ for infinitely many $n$ and the set $\sum_{i\in S}a_i$ (as $S$ ranges over all finite sets) does not contain all colours?'

So your simple example still doesn't work (we only need $a_n<f(n)$ infinitely often).

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Erdos wrote there are two potential versions to extend the initial question. In the first interpretation, he also adds a weaker statement for $\aleph_0$ with almost disjoint sets, but if the interpretation is as above, the latter should be a stronger variant, isn't it?

It may be those are indeed just directions of what would be a potential good question, without Erdos knowing yet what would be.

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd: I think Galvin's construction is mistated. you want to infinitely flip flop between red and blue.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Note that it flips infinitely often, since the colouring depends on the $2$-adic valuation of the number.
I have given the explanation why the colouring works below.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
We want $f: \mathbb Z^+ \to \mathbb Z^+$ and $k \ge 3$ such that there is an infinite sequence with $a_n<f(n)$ infinitely often.
For fixed $f$, this implies that Folkman's theorem does not work due to the additional restriction already for length $n$, and the infinite sequence is not implied either.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #949 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/949).

### Problem
Let $S\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a set containing no solutions to $a+b=c$. Must there be a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$ of cardinality continuum such that $A+A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$?

### Context
Erdős suggests that if the answer is no one could consider the variant where we assume that $S$ is Sidon (i.e. all $a+b$ with $a,b\in S$ are distinct, aside from the trivial coincidences).

In the comments Dillies gives a positive proof of this, found by AlphaProof: in other words, if $S\subset \mathbb{R}$ is a Sidon set then there exists $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$ of cardinality continuum such that $A+A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
I can prove the problem when $S$ has Baire property (a bit orthogonal to $S$ being Sidon), and also remark that Yael Dillies argument give a proof for $|S|< \mathfrak{c}$ without assuming $S$ being Sidon. So if there's a counter example in general to it, it would be very pathological (non Sidon, non measurable, non BP).

So let's assume $S$ has BP. We split into cases.

Case 1: $\mathbb R\setminus S$ contains a neighborhood of $0$.
Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\cap S=\varnothing$.
Let $A=(0,\varepsilon/2)$. Then $A\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S$ and\[
A+A=(0,\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S,
\]so we are done.

Case 2: $\mathbb R\setminus S$ contains no neighborhood of $0$.
Then $0\in\overline S$.

Claim: $S$ is meagre.
Suppose for a contradiction that $S$ is not meagre. Since $S$ has the Baire property,
there exists a nonempty open interval $I=(a,b)$ such that $C:=S\cap I$ is comeagre in $I$.
Let $\ell:=b-a>0$. As $0\in\overline S$, choose $s\in S$ with $0<|s|<\ell$.
Then the overlap\[
J:=I\cap(I-s)
\]is a nonempty open interval. Since $C$ is comeagre in $I$, the set $C\cap J$ is comeagre in $J$.
Also $C-s$ is comeagre in $I-s$, hence $(C-s)\cap J$ is comeagre in $J$.
Therefore\[
D:=(C\cap J)\cap\bigl((C-s)\cap J\bigr)
\]is comeagre in $J$, in particular $D\neq\varnothing$. Pick $x\in D$. Then $x\in C\subseteq S$,
and $x\in C-s$ implies $x+s\in C\subseteq S$. Together with $s\in S$ we get
$x+s\in S\cap(S+S)$, contradicting that $S$ is sum-free. Hence $S$ is meagre.

Now define the set of ''bad pairs'' $R\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ by\[
R \;:=\; (S\times\mathbb R)\ \cup\ (\mathbb R\times S)\ \cup\ \{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:\ x+y\in S\}.
\]Since $S$ is meagre in $\mathbb R$, both $S\times\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R\times S$
are meagre in $\mathbb R^2$.
For the third set, write $S=\bigcup_{n} N_n$ where each $N_n$ is nowhere dense.
Let $\phi:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $\phi(x,y)=x+y$. The map $\phi$ is continuous and open,
so for each $n$ the preimage $\phi^{-1}(N_n)$ is nowhere dense in $\mathbb R^2$:
indeed, if $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is nonempty open, then $\phi(U)$ is nonempty open in $\mathbb R$,
so $\phi(U)\not\subseteq \overline{N_n}$, hence $U\not\subseteq \overline{\phi^{-1}(N_n)}$.
Thus $\phi^{-1}(S)=\bigcup_n \phi^{-1}(N_n)$ is meagre.
Consequently $R$ is meagre in $\mathbb R^2$.

By Mycielski's theorem, there exists a perfect set $P\subseteq\mathbb R$ such that\[
(P\times P)\cap R=\varnothing.
\]Then for all $x,y\in P$ we have $x\notin S$, $y\notin S$, and $x+y\notin S$.
Hence $P\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S$ and $P+P\subseteq\mathbb R\setminus S$.
Taking $A:=P$ completes the proof.

sourceComments.author: YaelDillies
sourceComments.contentMd:
For the question from the additional material:
“Erdős suggests that if the answer is no, one could consider the variant where we assume that $S$ is Sidon.”
AlphaProof found the following solution:

We case on whether $S$ has cardinality the continuum or strictly less.
If $S$ has cardinality strictly less than the continuum, then we pick by Zorn some maximal $A$ such that both $A$ and $A + A$ are disjoint from $S$. Now, to see $A$ has size the continuum, note that
$$A \cup \bigcup_{a \in A} (S - a) \cup S \cup S/2 = \mathbb R$$
by maximality of $A$. By assumption, $|S^c \cap (S /  2)^c| = |\mathbb R|$. If $|A| < |\mathbb R|$, we would therefore have
$$|\mathbb R| = |S^c \cap (S /  2)^c| ≤ |A \cup \bigcup_{a \in A} (S - a)| ≤ |A| + |A| |S| <|\mathbb R|,$$
contradiction.
If $S$ has cardinality the continuum, then we pick some $a\ne 0$ in $S$ and set $A := (S \setminus \{a\} - a / 2) \setminus S$. Since $S$ is Sidon and $a\ne 0$,
$$(S - a / 2) \cap S \supseteq (S \setminus \{a\} - a / 2) \cap S$$
has at most one element. In particular, $|A| = |S \setminus \{a\} - a / 2| = |S| = |\mathbb R|$ as wanted.
Since $S$ is Sidon,
$$A + A \subseteq S \setminus \{a\} + S \setminus \{a\} - a$$
is disjoint from $S$, as wanted.

[Here](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/1509) is the Lean proof discovered by AlphaProof as well as a cleaned up version.

The problem here is not reformulated correctly from [the original paper](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1977-27.pdf) (p. 57). In this notation one asks for a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\setminus S$ of cardinality continuum such that $A+A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\setminus S$.
For Desmond's example one can just take $A=\cup_{n=1}^{\infty}[3n,3n+1/2)$.
Do you have a counterexample for this formulation as well?

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: DesmondWeisenberg
replies.contentMd: Ah, thanks for pointing that out. Unfortunately, no, I don't have a counterexample to the corrected formulation.

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd:
your choice of $A$ is somewhat overkill. taking $A:= [0,1/2)$ would already suffice.

this sounds like a very strong criterion... what's a non-trivial example of set $S$ where $A+A\cap S\neq \emptyset$ for all $A\subset \mathbb{R}\setminus S$? can we construct such an $S$ which at least has a subsequence $s_1,s_2,\dots$ so that:
i) $s_i\to 0$;
ii) $S-S\cap \{s_1,s_2,\dots\}= \emptyset$.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: Zach, the way you formulated the question, it is not possible to find such a set $S$. Namely, the condition $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus S\implies 2x\in S$ (i.e., $A=\{x\}$) forces $0\in S$, but then $S-S\supseteq S$. How nontrivial you ask $A$ to be?

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd:
oops, I meant to quantify over $A\subset \mathbb{R}\setminus S$ which have the cardinality of the continuum. (without this condition, we could even take $A$ to be empty, which spoils everything for stupid vacuous reasons).

the point of my condition is that $S$ must be sum-free, but it must contain points $s_i$ arbitrarily close to the origin (otherwise taking $A$ to be a ball of tiny radius around zero would have $A+A$ disjoint from $S$). so here I'm just asking for $S$ to "look sum-free" on a sequence whose limit is the origin, rather than on its entire set.

sourceComments.author: DesmondWeisenberg
sourceComments.contentMd:
The answer is no. Let $S$ be the set of all intervals of the form $[3n+1, 3n + 2)$, with $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $S$ is sum-free. Furthermore, if $a \in \mathbb{R}\backslash S$ and $a$ is not a multiple of $3$, then $a$ has a multiple in $S$. As such, the only subsets of $\mathbb{R}\backslash S$ that are closed under addition are the sub-semigroups of $3\mathbb{Z}$, so $\mathbb{R}\backslash S$ certainly has no uncountable subsets that are closed under addition.
The website mentions the variant where we instead require that $S$ is Sidon. That's probably a lot harder, and my construction is very much not Sidon.

EDIT: Vjeko pointed out that the problem should actually ask about $A$ such that $A + A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$, not $A + A \subseteq A$. So my construction actually doesn't resolve the corrected problem.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #950 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/950).

### Problem
Let\[f(n) = \sum_{p<n}\frac{1}{n-p}.\]Is it true that\[\liminf f(n)=1\]and\[\limsup f(n)=\infty?\]Is it true that $f(n)=o(\log\log n)$ for all $n$?

### Context
This function was considered by de Bruijn, Erdős, and Turán, who showed that\[\sum_{n<x}f(n)\sim \sum_{n<x}f(n)^2\sim x.\]The existence of some $c>0$ such that there are $\gg n^c/\log n$ many primes in $[n,n+n^c]$ implies that $\liminf f(n)>0$.

Erdős writes that a 'weaker conjecture which is perhaps not quite inaccessible' is that, for every $\epsilon>0$, if $x$ is sufficiently large there exists $y<x$ such that\[\pi(x)< \pi(y)+\epsilon \pi(x-y).\](Compare this to [[855]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/855).) He notes that if\[\pi(x)< \pi(y)+O\left(\frac{x-y}{\log x}\right)\]for all $y<x-(\log x)^C$ for some constant $C>0$ then $f(n)\ll \log\log\log n$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
I'm having trouble reconstructing the de Bruijn-Erdos-Turan claim $\sum_{n < x} f(n)^2 \sim x$ (which is not detailed in the reference given).  Upper bound sieves can give a bound of the shape $\sum_{n < x} f(n)^2 \ll x$, but to get the asymptotic seems to require an understanding of the error term in the prime number theorem in almost all intervals of the form $[x, x+x^\theta]$ for $\theta$ close to zero, and at our current level of understanding this is only available on the density hypothesis (and hence on the Lindelof or Riemann hypothesis).

In another direction, it seems likely that one can at least show that the lim sup will be infinite assuming the Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture, by working with suitable dense clusters of primes.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Related to the trivial remark that it is sufficient to understand $f(p)$ and $f(p+1)$, in the sense that $f(p_n+1)\ge f(p_n+2) \ge \ldots \ge  f(p_{n+1})$ holds strict, I guess also
 $$\sum_{p\le x} f(p+1)^2 \sim 4 \pi(x).$$

The latter nevertheless does also not give any indication that the limsup should be infinity.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #951 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/951).

### Problem
Let $1<a_1<\cdots$ be a sequence of real numbers such that\[\left\lvert \prod_i a_i^{k_i}-\prod_j a_j^{\ell_j}\right\rvert \geq 1\]for every distinct pair of non-negative finitely supported integer tuples $k_i,\ell_j\geq 0$. Is it true that\[\#\{ a_i \leq x\} \leq \pi(x)?\]

### Context
Erdős says this question was asked 'during [his] lecture at Queens College [by] one member of the audience (perhaps S. Shapiro)'. Such a sequence of $a_i$ is sometimes called a set of Beurling prime numbers (and the sequence of products called the associated generalised integers).

Beurling conjectured that if the number of reals in $[1,x]$ of the form $\prod a_i^{k_i}$ is $x+o(\log x)$ then the $a_i$ must be the sequence of primes.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
[This note](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1SIATgVENtE5696MERLjesEmKgNWh5wFK/view?usp=sharing) by me+ChatGPT shows, for each $3 \le n \le 7$, existence of $n$ generators less than $p_n$, the $n$th prime, for a free multiplicative semigroup whose elements differ by at least $1$.

This is basically an operationalized version of Tao's probabilistic sketch in the comments.

By the Barreto-Price extension step, this shows that the inequality in the problem can fail for $x = 5-\varepsilon, 7-\varepsilon, 11-\varepsilon, 13-\varepsilon, 17-\varepsilon$ for small $\varepsilon > 0$. We think it can fail for arbitarily large $x$ but do not know how to prove.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
I+ChatGPT have obtained in [this note](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1gykR98vV0FiWwUl_S9SLy33vb9loN8-P/view?usp=sharing) that
$$ a_1 = 101/42 \approx 2.40, \quad a_2 = 367/103 \approx 3.56, \quad a_3 = 113/24 \approx 4.71 $$
generate a free multiplicative semigroup whose elements differ by at least $1$.

The approach here uses tools from computational Diophantine approximation, by Matveev + LLL reduction by de Weger.

By using the extension step in Barreto-Leeham, we can extend to an infinite sequence. Since $a_3 < p_3 = 5$, the primes are not everywhere minimal, which is the same version of the problem disproved by Barreto-Leeham. The eventually minimal version appears more difficult and cannot be directly tackled by this method.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
It occurs to me that a probabilistic construction, together with some brute force numerics, should also work here.  Numerical trial and error should be able to generate intervals of values for candidate $a_i$ (e.g., to follow Nat's example, one could try $a_1 \in [2.40,2.41]$, $a_2 \in [3.56, 3.57]$, $a_3 \in [4.71, 4.72]$ which can be shown by interval arithmetic to avoid near-collisions $|\prod_i a_i^{k_i} - \prod_j a_j^{\ell_j}| < 1$ for all $k_i, \ell_j$ below a certain threshold, say $\sum_i k_i \log a_i \leq 50$ (I am taking a total guess with this threshold), regardless of where in the interval $a_1,a_2,a_3$ are (note that this also forces $\sum_j \ell_j \log a_j$ to be bounded by $50$ up to some negligible error).  To handle the remaining cases when $\sum_i k_i \log a_i > 50$, one can try the probabilistic method, choosing $a_1,a_2,a_3$ randomly; the probability of a collision for any given $k_1,k_2,k_3,\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$ should drop off exponentially in these parameters (in particular gaining a factor like $e^{-50}$ at some point) and so hopefully one can keep the total failure probability below 1, at which point one wins.  On the one hand this is not as constructive an example as the other ones, but the numerical verification may be easier and so one might be able to explore what happens at other values of $x$ than $4.71$ or $10$.

EDIT: Ooh, I can set AlphaEvolve to work on this!  I'll try it now.

SECOND EDIT (20 mins later): For the $x=7-\varepsilon = p_4-\varepsilon$ problem, AE has already produced the candidate

$$a_1 = 2.6728591026637005, a_2 = 3.733826126571687, a_3 = 4.841402115246144, a_4 := 5.999121968603969$$
which verifies the $1$-separation condition for all $\prod_{i=1}^4 a_i^{k_i} \leq e^{64.25}$ (this is about 230,000 numbers, or about $e^{12.34}$, so well below the threshold for the birthday paradox to trigger).  I imagine almost any reasonable probabilistic analysis would show that some perturbation of this would show that one can break the inequality $\# \{ a_i \leq x\} \leq \pi(x)$ for $x=7-\varepsilon$ (or even $x=6$).  It seems that counterexamples are in fact numerically plentiful.

THIRD EDIT: It may get significantly harder to produce counterexamples as $x$ increases by such probabilistic methods.  Already the birthday paradox suggests that it will be hard to randomly produce $\ggg \sqrt{x}$ values of $a_i$ in $[1,x]$ whose pairwise products $a_i a_j$ are all $1$-separated, let alone $>\pi(x)$ many such values.  Possibly a hybrid approach where one first finds a (log-)algebraic construction with good separation properties for small products, followed by a probabilistic perturbation to guarantee good separation for large products as well, may work.

FOURTH EDIT: Perhaps the theory of Sidon sets (and B_h[g] sets, etc.) can be used to provide good constructions?

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: This seems perhaps most computationally promising among the 3 approaches. I’ll try to see if we can get $n$ generators below $p_n$ for a few small $n$ by this and will report back.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Obtained $n$ generators below $p_n$ for each $3 \le n \le 7$! The case $n=7$ is becoming tricky to certify, so I choose to (arbitrarily) stop here.

Noteworthy: there are more details to work through than initially expected. Luckily, with the new GPT-based workflow, tried out for the first time here, we brought it to the finish line in 44 turns and more than 8 hours from GPT's side. If I were to work alone, it would've taken much longer (likely already abandoned).

Will write it up soon.

sourceComments.author: Kevin Barreto
sourceComments.contentMd:
After about 20 back-and-forth prompts of asking different GPT-5.2 Pro instances to come up with, and then double-check the argument the prior instance gave autonomously, Leeham managed to get GPT-5.2 Pro to disprove this essentially fully autonomously (his only involvement being to ask the previous instance to write a LaTeX prompt for an AI to fix the proof and passing that to the next instance, until nothing wrong was identified by the model). All credit goes to him for this one. It should be classified as a section 1(a) result assuming things are correct.

He asked that I have a look, and I personally think its construction is genuinely creative! Up to issues of floating point precision, it seems right and novel to me; I could not locate any prior resolution in the literature. We are waiting for Aristotle to come back with a formalisation, but in the meantime, I would appreciate others having a look [here](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1CRBMOMCTdAuuVp8Wqace1AQ_dpK9BeTV/view).

replies.author: natso26

Intuitively, it does speak to a real fundamental barrier in research: ideas take time to build, so it is inherently difficult for a single (say 90-minute) session to settle a big problem. replies.author: Kevin Barreto
replies.contentMd: Yes, I think this speaks to a difference in methodology: one-shot attempts are unlikely to succeed currently, leading to large databases of LLM attempts on all the Erdos problems being essentially full of entirely incorrect attempts. replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Hmm, this looks like a nice idea, but if I'm reading it right it just disproves it for $x=10$? So this construction of an infinite sequence could still have the number of $a_i\leq x$ being $\leq \pi(x)$ for all large $x$? Is there a possibility it can be tweaked to get some measurable failure of this inequality for infinitely many $x$?

(This may come under the category of number theoretic questions that fail for small examples for law of small numbers reasons, but the spirit of the question is really about the asymptotic behaviour.)

To be clear, this is a nice clever construction, and something non-trivial is going on here! It would be good to push further on the theory side I think to develop this idea into a more robust construction.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: I+[ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/697947b7-7ba0-8010-9798-1bb6519ae0df) have assessed and are reasonably confident that the note is correct as written.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Nice result.  The numerical computations in particular need to be verified, but there does not seem to be any theoretical reason why this would not work, though as Thomas points out the proof technique relies heavily on being able to produce a counterexample in the bounded $x$ regime (in fact $x=10$ in this argument) rather than the asymptotic regime $x \ggg 1$.  This changes the game considerably, and the AI proof observes that one can now convert the problem to one in Diophantine approximation.

The first observation is that once one is committed to producing a counterexample at a single value of $x$, the choices of $a_i$ larger than $x$ are pretty much irrelevant; they can be constructed by a standard greedy algorithm.  So now one is looking at a multiplicative semigroup generated by a bounded number of generators $\{ a_i \leq x \}$, which is expected to become exponentially sparse at infinity (cf. [Størmer's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C3%B8rmer%27s_theorem) or [Baker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem)).  But as the AI observes, one does not need the fanciest transcendence theorems such as Baker's theorem involving logs of algebraic numbers, because the $a_i$ are not required to be algebraic; instead, by taking the $a_i$ to be exponentials of algebraic numbers, one now just needs good lower bounds on Diophantine approximation by algebraic numbers, for which the most classical of bounds - [Liouville's bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantine_approximation#Approximation_of_algebraic_numbers,_Liouville's_result) - is already powerful, giving lower bounds that are polynomial in the height (after extending to higher-dimensional approximation in a standard fashion), whereas to get unit separation one needs lower bounds that are at worst exponentially decaying in the height.  This is a lot of room, and already guarantees unit separation for all sufficiently large products, reducing things to a finite check.  (This already shows by the way that merely assuming asymptotic unit separation would not be enough to get the required bound; if the problem had any hope of a positive answer, one would need unit separation at all scales, not just the large ones.)

A human at this point would perhaps balk at the significant numerical experimentation one would now have to do to find a set of generators for which the required finite number of separation conditions actually hold; but apparently an AI (prompted sufficiently many times) has much less reluctance to attempt some sort of search (possibly brute force or trial-and-error in nature).  What is not currently clear is how much "room" there is here - would any reasonable set of generator choices in a reasonable algebraic number field have had a good chance to succeed?  Perhaps further numerical exploration will clarify this.

As this question is not directly from Erdos, but from someone in the audience at a talk he gave (see [[p. 68, Er77c](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1977-27.pdf)]) it is harder than usual to divine intent for this question, and in particular whether $x$ was intended to range over all natural numbers or only sufficiently large ones.  Both formulations of the question are interesting, but for different reasons: the latter is more in the spirit of "Beurling prime number theory", but the former has the flavor of a rigidity theorem (in the spirit of Hamburger's rigidity theorem for the zeta function).  Another variant which could be interesting if one requires the $a_j$ to be algebraic, which rules out the AI construction and would require one to use the more transcendental Diophantine approximation theorems if one wanted to mimic the same strategy. (But perhaps one could still win by performing an infinitesimal perturbation of the transcendental example.)

Given the social media circus from past 1(a) candidates, I think we can afford to take a more measured approach with evaluating this particular submission, so that we have time for literature review, Lean formalization, and numerical exploration.  I will move it to the "pending assessment" category for now.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Ok, agreed. I may be too hasty putting it as "partial result" from assuming asymptotic intent. Clearly there are a few interesting variants!

I+ChatGPT is working independently and seems to obtain $3$ *rational* ($\mathbb{Q}$) generators, by a slightly different method. I'm writing it up now. This may help answer the question regarding algebraic $a_i$. (Note: it doesn't directly answer it yet, because the extension argument in the note is measure-theoretic, and doesn't seem to go though when we try to get a rational $a_i$ because the set of rational numbers has measure zero.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Now that the situation has stabilized and we have more of a consensus as to the intent of the problem and status of the solution, I have listed the various results here under Sections 1(a), 1(b), and 1(d) of the wiki as partial results.

I think the policy of placing results that have a significant probability of going viral on social media under pending assessment (Section 3) for a few days is one I will try to adopt more systematically going forward.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
From what I've seen of similar papers and results concerning Beurling primes and 'generalised integers', I believe that the asymptotic question was intended (and generally when thinking of these problems a general real sequence of $a_i$ is considered, rather than algebraic numbers or integers, although of course these are subproblems).

I've had a bit of a look at papers, and surprisingly can't find anything on this problem - there are a few problems which say that if the number of 'generalised integers' in $[1,x]$ are $\sim Ax$ then what kind of asymptotic on the number of 'generalised primes' $a_i\leq x$ can be obtained, but nothing (that I've found) about what happens if you just assume that the generalised integers are $1$-separated, as in this problem.

It might be that even the strict inequality for all large $x$ is stronger than what Erdős (or rather the question asker, perhaps Shapiro) intended, and maybe even something like $\#\{a_i\leq x\} \leq (1+o(1))\pi(x)$ is the real spirit of the question.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd: Very nice! I like the process and looking forward to confirmation of the construction. I was actually trying to prove it with GPT-5.2 and didn't get far (no wonder), but managed to prove it in the case when all $a_i$ are integers. This is pretty trivial but worth mentioning. Non-integer case looked difficult.

sourceComments.contentMd: For $s>1$, one has $\sum_{k_1,k_2,\dots} \frac{1}{(\prod_i a_i^{k_i})^s} \leq \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^s}$, hence $\prod_i (1-\frac{1}{a_i^s})^{-1} \leq \zeta(s)$, so on taking logarithms $\sum_i \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{1}{j a_i^{js}} \leq \log \zeta(s)$.  This may be enough to get a Mertens type bound, but the prime number theorem type bound seems out of reach by this method.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Wikipedia says "Computational searches have shown that the origin is separated from infinity by a moat of width 6" and links to this reference: Tsuchimura, Nobuyuki (2005), "[Computational results for Gaussian moat problem](https://www.keisu.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp/data/2004/METR04-13.pdf)", IEICE Transactions on Fundamentals of Electronics, Communications and Computer Sciences, 88 (5): 1267–1273, Bibcode:2005IEITF..88.1267T, doi:10.1093/ietfec/e88-a.5.1267.

I really enjoyed the article.  In the end, the author includes some simple but nice plots.  Their computational results are very consistent with a random model of Gaussian primes, for which the answer is "no, such a bounded infinite sequence does not exist".

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
There is an $M$ and a sequence of Gaussian primes $\{\gamma_j\}_{1^\infty}$, such that $|\gamma_1| < M$, $|\gamma_j - \gamma_{j-1}| < M$ and $\lim |\gamma_j| = \infty$.

J. H. Jordan and J. R. Rabung has showed that if the conjecture is true, then $M \geq 4$, in [A Conjecture of Paul Erdős Concerning Gaussian Primes(1970)](https://www.ams.org/journals/mcom/1970-24-109/S0025-5718-1970-0256976-8/).

Thanks To Vjeko for pointing the mistakes out!

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
As far as I can see, Jordan and Rabung did not establish the conjecture (I mean the Gaussian moat problem), but rather
''report that if the conjecture is true then $M\geq4$''.
They also performed a computer search that led them to believe that the conjecture *might* be true.
Last time I checked the literature, it seemed that the claim was still open.

replies.author: Alfaiz
replies.contentMd:
This fact was stated in a paper of Tuza as "An analogous version of Gaussian moat problem by Erdos was solved by Jordan and Rabung". So, I just had a cursory look on the paper itself.

Thanks for clarifying.

P.S. This conjecture is new and therefore needs to be included in the site.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd: I might not have been reading your post carefully either, because now I see that you mention some alternative conjecture, and that it does not make sense. The condition $|\gamma_j|<M$ is in a contradiction with $\lim|\gamma_j|=\infty$. So this was just a typo somewhere! What Jordan and Ranburg actually write is $|\gamma_1|<M$, in which case this is the original "Gaussian moat problem". There was no alternative version of the conjecture at all.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #953 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/953).

### Problem
Let $A\subset \{ x\in \mathbb{R}^2 : \lvert x\rvert <r\}$ be a measurable set with no integer distances, that is, such that $\lvert a-b\rvert \not\in \mathbb{Z}$ for any distinct $a,b\in A$. How large can the measure of $A$ be?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Sárközi. Erdős [Er77c] writes that 'Sárközi has the sharpest results, but nothing has been published yet'.

The trivial upper bound is $O(r)$. Koizumi and Kovac have observed in the comments that Sárközy's lower bound in [[466]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/466) can be adapted to give a lower bound of $\gg_\epsilon r^{1/2-\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$.

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
The problem could be attributed to Erdős, Graham, and Sárközi. I could not find any subsequent publications on the problem. When Erdős said
"Sárközi has the sharpest results, but nothing has been published yet"
this might mean that he had the sharpest results among the three of them, but nothing was sufficiently nontrivial or definite to warrant publication. :-)
It is trivial to see that the order of growth is $O(r)$: just consider intersections of $A$ with translates of the horizontal integer lattice.
In the other direction, one can use Sárközy's result on Problem [[466]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/466) (taking the set $A$ to be a union of congruent disks) and obtain something like $\Omega(r^{0.26})$.
I suspect that the true order of magnitude could be around $r^{1/2}$, but I was not able to modify Konyagin's beautiful solution of Problem [[465]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/465) to work here as well.

replies.author: J_Koizumi_144
replies.contentMd:
Using Sárközy’s result, one obtains a stronger bound $\Omega(X^{1/2-\varepsilon})$. More precisely, Sárközy’s theorem asserts that for any sufficiently small $\delta>0$ and all $X > X_0(\delta)$, one has
$$N(X,\delta) > X^{1/2-\delta^{1/7}},
$$where $N(X,\delta)$ is the function defined in [465]. Taking $\delta=\varepsilon^7$, it suffices to place disks of radius $\delta/3$ centered at each point of Sárközy’s point set.

As for the upper bound, if one works out the implied constant in Konyagin’s proof of the estimate $N(X,\delta)\ll_{\delta} X^{1/2}$ for [465], one obtains something like
$$N(X,\delta) \delta^{5/2}\ll X^{1/2}.
$$To apply this to the present problem, one would need to improve the left-hand side to $N(X,\delta) \delta^{2}$. However, I suspect that a better construction should exist.

replies.author: Vjeko_Kovac
replies.contentMd:
You are right about the lower bound. That way for every small $\varepsilon>0$ you get\[ f(r) \geq \Big(\frac{\varepsilon^7}{3}\Big)^2 \pi r^{1/2-\varepsilon} . \]I don't remember why I wrote $f(r)\geq r^{0.26}$. I guess I was using some other bound from his paper. So the readily available lower bound in fact is $f(r)=\Omega(r^{1/2-\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

For the upper bound I only see that Konyagin's proof applies to unions of disks and not general sets $A$. He cleverly constructs linear combinations of Bessel functions that get wild only *near* integers, which is why they don't immediately say something about a set that only forbids precisely integer distances. I tried to reuse the same Bessel construction from his proof, even with different weights, but I remember that I couldn't get any nontrivial bound from it. It still smells a lot like similar distance-avoiding problems (like Furstenberg-Katznelson-Weiss), but a different Bessel construction should be needed to get a nontrivial bound, perhaps anything that is $o(r)$ and I am skeptical about the possibility of getting $O(r^{1/2})$.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #954 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/954).

### Problem
Let $0=a_0<a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of integers defined by $a_0=0$ and $a_1=1$, and $a_{k+1}$ is the smallest integer $n$ for which the number of solutions to $a_i+a_j \leq n$ (with $0\leq i\leq j\leq k$ and $j\geq 1$) is $<n$.

Is the number of solutions to $a_i+a_j \leq x$ equal to $x+O(x^{1/4+o(1)})$?

### Context
This sequence was constructed by Rosen. Note that the number of solutions to $a_i+a_j\leq x$ is always at least $x$ by construction, but Erdős and Rosen could not even prove whether it is at most $(1+o(1))x$.

The sequence begins\[0,1,3,5,9,13,17,24,31,38,45,\ldots.\]

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think $a_0 = 0$ should be added to the formulation, otherwise, we're quickly getting "no":

Let $F(x):=\#\{(i,j): i\le j,\ a_i+a_j\le x\}$. For each $k$, set
$f_k(n):=\#\{(i,j): 1\le i\le j\le k,\ a_i+a_j\le n\}$.

By definition, $a_{k+1}$ is the smallest $n$ with $f_k(n)<n-k$. Hence:

For $n=a_{k+1}-1$ we do not have $f_k(n)<n-k$, so
$f_k(a_{k+1}-1)\ge (a_{k+1}-1)-k = a_{k+1}-k-1$.

But at $n=a_{k+1}$ we do have $f_k(a_{k+1})<a_{k+1}-k$, so (since $f_k$ is integer-valued)
$f_k(a_{k+1})\le a_{k+1}-k-1$.

Therefore $f_k(a_{k+1})=a_{k+1}-k-1$.

Now observe that at $x=a_{k+1}$, no pair involving $a_{k+1}$ can contribute, because
$a_1+a_{k+1}=1+a_{k+1}>a_{k+1}$. So $F(a_{k+1})=f_k(a_{k+1})$, and thus
$F(a_{k+1})=a_{k+1}-k-1$.

Equivalently, $F(a_m)=a_m-m$ for $m\ge 2$.

In particular, the error $|F(a_m)-a_m|=m$ occurs infinitely often (for every $m$). Also,
$a_m-m = F(a_m)\le \#\{(i,j):1\le i\le j\le m-1\}=\frac{(m-1)m}{2}$,
so $a_m\ll m^2$, i.e. $m\gg \sqrt{a_m}$. Hence
$|F(a_m)-a_m| = m \gg \sqrt{a_m}$,
so $F(x)=x+O(x^{1/4+o(1)})$ is impossible.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Aha, good catch, thanks. It is odd since Erdős explicitly considers the alternative definition in which $a_0=0$ and the condition is that the number of solutions of $a_i+a_j\leq x$ with $0\leq i\leq j\leq k$ (and $j>0$) is $<x$.

I guess that Rosen described it to Erdős in the latter form, and Erdős noted that these two constructions produce the same sequence, but did not notice that the count of $a_i+a_j\leq x$ in the conclusion is also changed when switching between the two.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #955 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/955).

### Problem
Let\[s(n)=\sigma(n)-n=\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}}d\]be the sum of proper divisors function.

If $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ has density $0$ then $s^{-1}(A)$ must also have density $0$.

### Context
A conjecture of Erdős, Granville, Pomerance, and Spiro [EGPS90]. It is possible for $s(A)$ to have positive density even if $A$ has zero density (for example taking $A$ to be the product of two distinct primes). Erdős [Er73b] proved that there are sets $A$ of positive density such that $s^{-1}(A)$ is empty.

Pollack [Po14b] has shown that this is true if $A$ is the set of primes. Troupe [Tr15] has shown that this is true if $A$ is the set of integers with unusually many prime factors. Troupe [Tr20] has also shown this is true if $A$ is the set of integers which are the sum of two squares.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #956 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/956).

### Problem
If $C,D\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ then the distance between $C$ and $D$ is defined by\[\delta(C,D)=\inf_{\substack{c\in C\\ d\in D}}\| c-d\|.\]Let $h(n)$ be the maximal number of unit distances between disjoint convex translates. That is, the maximal $m$ such that there is a compact convex set $C\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and a set $X$ of size $n$ such that all $(C+x)_{x\in X}$ are disjoint and there are $m$ pairs $x_1,x_2\in X$ such that\[\delta(C+x_1,C+x_2)=1.\]Determine $h(n)$ - in particular, prove that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $h(n)>n^{1+c}$ for all large $n$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Pach [ErPa90], who proved that $h(n) \ll n^{4/3}$. They also consider the related function where we consider $n$ disjoint convex sets (not necessarily translates), for which they give an upper bound of $\ll n^{7/5}$.

It is trivial that $h(n)\geq f(n)$, where $f(n)$ is the maximal number of unit distances determined by $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (see [[90]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/90)).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #959 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/959).

### Problem
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of size $n$ and let $\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}$ be the set of distinct distances determined by $A$. Let $f(d)$ be the number of times the distance $d$ is determined, and suppose the $d_i$ are ordered such that\[f(d_1)\geq f(d_2)\geq \cdots \geq f(d_k).\]Estimate\[\max (f(d_1)-f(d_2)),\]where the maximum is taken over all $A$ of size $n$.

### Context
More generally, one can ask about\[\max (f(d_r)-f(d_{r+1})).\]Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu [CDL25], have shown that\[\max (f(d_1)-f(d_2))\gg n\log n.\]More generally, for any $1\leq k\leq \log n$, there exists a set $A$ of $n$ points such that\[f(d_r)-f(d_{r+1})\gg \frac{n\log n}{r}.\]They conjecture that $n\log n$ can be improved to $n^{1+c/\log\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #960 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/960).

### Problem
Let $r,k\geq 2$ be fixed. Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no $k$ points on a line. Determine the threshold $f_{r,k}(n)$ such that if there are at least $f_{r,k}(n)$ many ordinary lines (lines containing exactly two points) then there is a set $A'\subseteq A$ of $r$ points such that all $\binom{r}{2}$ many lines determined by $A'$ are ordinary.

Is it true that $f_{r,k}(n)=o(n^2)$, or perhaps even $\ll n$?

### Context
Turán's theorem implies\[f_{r,k}(n) \leq \left(1-\frac{1}{r-1}\right)\frac{n^2}{2}+1.\]See also [[209]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/209).

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #961 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/961).

### Problem
Let $f(k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that every set of $n$ consecutive integers $>k$ contains an integer divisible by a prime $>k$. Estimate $f(k)$.

### Context
In other words, how large can a consecutive set of $k$-smooth integers be? Sylvester and Schur (see [Er34]) proved $f(k)\leq k$ and Erdős [Er55d] proved\[f(k)<3\frac{k}{\log k}.\]Jutila [Ju74] and Ramachandra, and Shorey [RaSh73] proved\[f(k) \ll \frac{\log\log\log k}{\log \log k}\frac{k}{\log k}.\]It is likely that $f(k) \ll (\log k)^{O(1)}$.

This is essentially equivalent to [[683]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/683).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #962 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/962).

### Problem
Let $k(n)$ be the maximal $k$ such that there exists $m\leq n$ such that each of the integers\[m+1,\ldots,m+k\]are divisible by at least one prime $>k$. Estimate $k(n)$.

### Context
Erdős [Er65] wrote it is 'not hard to prove' that\[k(n)\gg_\epsilon \exp((\log n)^{1/2-\epsilon})\]and it 'seems likely' that $k(n)=o(n^\epsilon)$, but had no non-trivial upper bound for $k(n)$.

It is not clear what he meant by a non-trivial bound for this problem, but Tao in the comments has given a simple argument proving $k(n) \leq (1+o(1))n^{1/2}$.

sourceComments.author: KoishiChan
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think I can show that

Main Claim: Let $A$ be a set of size $n$. Then $A$ contains a disassociated subset of size $(1 - o(1))\log_2 n$.

A standard reduction shows that we may assume $A$ is a subset of the integers. We further assume that elements of $A$ are positive integers.

Throughout assume $n$ is large. Let $d_d(A)$ be the size of the largest disassociated subset of $A$, and let
$$f(n) = \min_{|A| = n, A \subset \mathbb{Z}_+} d_d(A).$$
We are going to establish a recursive bound of the form
$$f(n) \geq \frac{1}{12} \log_2 n + f\left(\frac{n^{11/12}}{\log^4 n}\right).$$
Our strategy is as follows. Fix a prime number $p \in [n^{1/12} / 2, n^{1/12}]$. Suppose for a moment that the elements of $A$ are equi-distributed modulo $p$. Let $A_p$ be the subset of $A$ with elements divisible by $p$, and let $a_i$ be an element of $A$ with residue $i$ modulo $A$. If we let $\Gamma = \{1, 2, \cdots, 2^{\lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} - 1}\}$ be a disassociated set modulo $p$ of order $\lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor}$, and $D'$ be a disassociated subset of $A_p$, then the set
$$D = D' \sqcup \{a_i: i\in \Gamma\}$$
must be disassociated. Therefore, we have
$$d_d(A) \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + d_d(A_p) \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + f\left(\frac{n}{p}\right)$$
precisely what we want.

In general, we do not have this "equi-distributed modulo $p$" condition. However, we will ensure this condition by using an old trick of Erdős: take a sufficiently large prime $q$ greater than all elements of $A$, pick $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$ uniformly at random, and replace $A$ with $A' = (r \cdot A) \mod{q}$. Our hope is that when cast back to the integers, $A'$ will be uniformly distributed modulo $p$, and we can proceed with the previous argument. The remaining proof is devoted to justifying this hope.

First, note that if a set of positive integers is disassociated modulo $q$, and $q$ is greater than all elements in the set, then the set is disassociated over $\mathbb{Z}$.

Let $A \subset \mathbb{Z}_+$ be such that $d_d(A) = f(n)$. Let $k = d_d(A) + 1$, and WLOG assume $k \leq \log_2 n$ (for otherwise $f(n) \geq \log_2 n - 1$ as desired). Let $q$ be as above. For each $i \in [0, p - 1]$, we define the following subset of $(\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$
$$B_{p, i} = \{px + i: x \in \{1, 2, \cdots, \lfloor{\frac{q - 1}{pk}\rfloor}\}\}.$$
We want to find an $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$ such that most $rA \cap B_{p, i}$ are large. This follows from the key lemma below.

Lemma: Let $q$ be a prime, and $L$ be a parameter. Let $A \subset (\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$ be a set of size at least $L^{10}$, and let $B$ be an arithmetic progression in $(\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$ of size at least $\frac{q}{L}$. Then, for a uniformly random $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$, we have
$$\mathbb{P}\left(|r \cdot A \cap B| \leq \frac{|A||B|}{2(q - 1)}\right) \ll \frac{1}{L^3}.$$

Proof:    We use the second moment bound. We want to compute
$$\mathbb{E}_{r} |r \cdot A \cap B|^2.$$
Using Fourier analysis, we have
$$|r \cdot A \cap B| = \frac{1}{q - 1}\sum_{a \in A, b \in B} \sum_{\chi} \chi(ra b^{-1})$$
where $\chi$ goes over all Dirichlet characters of $(\mathbb{Z} / q \mathbb{Z})^*$. Hence, we have
$$|r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2}\sum_{a, a' \in A, b, b' \in B} \sum_{\chi, \chi'} \chi(ra b^{-1}) \chi'(ra' b'^{-1}).$$
Summing over $r$, all contributions from $\chi' \neq \bar{\chi}$ vanish, giving
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2}\sum_{a, a' \in A, b, b' \in B} \sum_{\chi} \chi(a b^{-1}) \bar{\chi}(a' b'^{-1}).$$
Thus we obtain
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2} \sum_{\chi} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2.$$
Isolating the trivial character, we obtain
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{|A|^2 |B|^2}{(q - 1)^2} + \frac{1}{(q - 1)^2}\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2.$$
We now use the fact that $B$ is an AP. If we consider the quantity
$$M(\chi) = \sup_{r} |\sum_{i = 1}^r \chi(i)|$$
then we have
$$|\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)| \leq 2 M(\chi).$$
A theorem of Montgomery and Vaughen, "MEAN VALUES OF CHARACTER SUMS" (1979), states that
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} M(\chi)^4 \ll q^3.$$
So we have
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2 \leq \left(\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^4\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^4\right)^{1/2}$$
where
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^4 \ll q^3$$
and
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^4 \leq |A|^2  \sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0}|\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 \leq q|A|^3.$$
So we conclude that
$$\sum_{\chi \neq \chi_0} |\sum_{a \in A} \chi(a)|^2 |\sum_{b \in B} \chi(b)|^2 \ll q^{2} |A|^{3/2}.$$
Substituting back, we have
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B|^2 = \frac{|A|^2 |B|^2}{(q - 1)^2} + O\left(|A|^{3/2}\right).$$
As we also have
$$\mathbb{E}_r |r \cdot A \cap B| = \frac{|A| |B|}{(q - 1)}$$
we obtain by Chebyshev's inequality that
$$\mathbb{P}\left(|r \cdot A \cap B| \leq \frac{|A||B|}{2(q - 1)}\right) \ll \frac{(q - 1)^2}{|A|^{1/2}|B|^2}.$$
Substituting $|A| \geq L^{10}, |B| = \frac{q}{L}$, we obtain
$$\mathbb{P}\left(|r \cdot A \cap B| \leq \frac{|A||B|}{2(q - 1)}\right) \ll \frac{1}{L^3}$$
as desired. QED.

Use this lemma on $B = B_{p, i}$, $A = A$, and $L = pk + 1$, and make a union bound over $i$. We conclude that there exists $r \in (\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z})^*$ such that
$$|r \cdot A \cap B_{p, i}| \geq \frac{|A||B_{p, i}|}{2(q - 1)} \geq \frac{|A|}{2(pk + 1)}$$
for all $i$.

Finally, let $A_{p, i}'$ denote the lift of $r \cdot A \cap B_{p, i}$ back to the integers. Recall our definition of $\Gamma$ as a large disassociated set of size $\mathbb{Z} / p\mathbb{Z}$. Take any $a_i \in A_{p, i}'$ for $i \in \Gamma$, and let $D'$ be a disassociated subset of $A_{p, 0}'$ of maximum size. Now we show that
$$k = d_d(A) + 1 \geq |D'| + |\Gamma| + 1.$$
Suppose the contrary.

1) Analyzing mod $p$, we see that $D' \cup \{a_i: i \in \Gamma\}$ is disassociated over $\mathbb{Z}$. Let $D''$ be any subset of $D' \cup \{a_i: i \in \Gamma\}$ with size $k$.

2) As each element of $D''$ lies in $\sqcup_i B_{p, i}$, each element of $D''$ lies in $\left[1, \frac{q}{k}\right]$. As $|D''| = k$, we see that $D''$ is disassociated in $\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z}$.

3) Thus, $r^{-1}D'' \subset A$ is disassociated in $\mathbb{Z} / q\mathbb{Z}$, hence disassociated when lifted back to $A \subset \mathbb{Z}$. So $A$ contains a disassociated subset of size $k > d_d(A)$, contradiction!

Therefore, we conclude that
$$d_d(A) \geq |\Gamma| + |D'| \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + f\left(|A'_{p, 0}|\right) \geq \lfloor{\log_2 p\rfloor} + f\left(\frac{|A|}{2(pk + 1)}\right).$$
As $p \in [n^{1/12} / 2, n^{1/12}]$ and $k \leq \log_2 n$ by assumption, we obtain that for sufficiently large $n$, we have.
$$f(n) \geq \min\left(\log_2 n - 1, \frac{1}{12} \log_2 n - O(1) + f\left(\frac{n^{11/12}}{4 \log_2 n}\right)\right).$$
Iterating, we obtain $f(n) \geq (1 - o(1)) \log_2 n$, as desired.

replies.contentMd: Nice!  For the purpose of optimizing the bounds, it may be worth removing the hypothesis that $p$ is prime (which may not even be used at all in the argument).  In particular, making it close to a power of 2 may be more efficient.  The hypothesis that $q$ is prime is used a little bit more strongly, but is less impactful on the bounds (one could maybe relax it to $q$ being an almost prime, though the calculations become a little fiddly as a consequence).

\]Am I missing something here?

sourceComments.author: utahisnotastate
sourceComments.contentMd:
\textbf{Solution to Erdős Problem 963/ AI Gemino Pro 3.5 used}

\textbf{Answer:} Yes, the estimate $f(n) \ge \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ holds.

\textbf{Reasoning:}
Let $f(n)$ denote the maximal size $k$ such that any set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ of size $n$ contains a dissociated subset of size $k$.
A subset $B$ is dissociated if all subset sums $\sum_{b \in S} b$ (for $S \subseteq B$) are distinct. This is analogous to linear independence over the field $\mathbb{F}_2$ but in the context of integer addition.

To estimate $f(n)$, we consider the "worst-case" scenario, which minimizes the size of the largest dissociated subset. This occurs when the set $A$ has a high degree of additive structure (redundancy).
Consider the set of the first $n$ integers:\[ A = \{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\} \]In this set, we can construct a dissociated subset $B$ by selecting powers of 2:\[ B = \{2^0, 2^1, 2^2, \dots, 2^m\} \]such that $2^m \le n$. The sums of subsets of $B$ correspond to the binary representations of integers up to $\sum B$, which are unique by the properties of the binary numeral system.
The largest power of 2 less than or equal to $n$ is $2^{\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor}$.
Thus, the size of this subset is $|B| = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$.

Since the set $\{1, \dots, n\}$ represents the structure with maximal additive dependencies (minimizing potential dissociated subsets), and even here we find a subset of size $\approx \log_2 n$, it follows that for any arbitrary set $A$ of size $n$, we can find a dissociated subset of at least size $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.

\textbf{Conclusion:}\[ f(n) \ge \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor \]The lower bound is established.

replies.contentMd:

Investigate open Erdos Problem #968 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/968).

### Problem
Let $u_n=p_n/n$, where $p_n$ is the $n$th prime. Does the set of $n$ such that $u_n<u_{n+1}$ have positive density?

### Context
Erdős and Prachar [ErPr61] proved that\[\sum_{p_n<x} \lvert u_{n+1}-u_n\rvert \asymp (\log x)^2,\]and that the set of $n$ such that $u_n>u_{n+1}$ has positive density.

Erdős also asks whether\[u_n<u_{n+1}<u_{n+2}\]or\[u_n>u_{n+1}>u_{n+2}\]have infinitely many solutions.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The answer to the problem is positive assuming both the Riemann hypothesis and a weak form of the pair correlation conjecture, specifically estimate (5) of [this paper of Heath-Brown](http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/aa/aa41/aa4118.pdf).  By Corollary 1 of that paper, we have for any $A$ that
$$ \sum_{p_n \leq x: p_{n+1}-p_n \geq A \log x} (p_{n+1}-p_n) \ll \frac{1}{A} x \quad (1)$$
for any $A > 0$.  From telescoping series we have
$$ \sum_{p_n \leq x} (p_{n+1}-p_n) = (1+o(1)) x$$
hence by the prime number theorem
$$ \sum_{p_n \leq x: p_{n+1}-p_n \leq \log x} (\log x - (p_{n+1}-p_n)) =
\sum_{p_n \leq x: p_{n+1}-p_n > \log x} ((p_{n+1}-p_n) - \log x) + o(x).$$
From known results about small gaps between primes (such as the GPY result mentioned in my previous comment) the left-hand side is $\gg x$, hence the right hand side is also.  Combining this with (1) we conclude that there exist $0 < \varepsilon < A$ such that $(1+\varepsilon) \log x \leq p_{n+1}-p_n \leq A \log x$ for $\gg x/\log x$ values of $p_n$.  For such values we have $u_n < u_{n+1}$, giving the claim.

It is also straightforward to deduce the claim from a sufficiently uniform version of the prime tuples conjecture (which, by a well known [calculation of Gallagher](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematika/article/on-the-distribution-of-primes-in-short-intervals/DCE557AC8750333E68426FCEEC11858C), implies that the normalized prime gaps $(p_{n+1}-p_n) / \log p_n$ are asymptotically exponentially distributed).

This seems close to the limit of current technology, so further progress may need to await some breakthrough on the pair correlation conjecture or the prime tuples conjecture.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
[Completely rewrote this answer, which previously was based on a sign error.]

The claim $u_n < u_{n+1}$ rearranges to $p_{n+1}-p_n > \frac{p_n}{n}$ so by the prime number theorem this is essentially asking for a large prime gap $p_{n+1}-p_n \gtrsim \log n$.  In the other direction, one can recover Erdos's previous result from the more recent result of [results of Goldston, Pintz, and Yildirim](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.5886) that for a positive density of $n$, one has $p_{n+1}-p_n \leq \eta \log n$ for any fixed $\eta> 0$.

I imagine that with the modern Maynard sieve one can similarly conclude that $u_n > u_{n+1} > u_{n+2}$ for a set of positive density by exhibiting many clusters of three nearby primes, but I haven't checked this carefully (and it may already be in the literature).

The enemy preventing one from proving $u_n < u_{n+1}$ for a set of positive density is if almost all prime gaps in say $[x,2x]$ are less than $\log x$, and a small number (zero density) of prime gaps are much larger than $\log x$.  Possibly one could use some of the large prime gap theory or the Maier matrix method to produce a positive density of clusters of moderately large prime gaps to finish off the problem though?

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #969 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/969).

### Problem
Let $Q(x)$ count the number of squarefree integers in $[1,x]$. Determine the order of magnitude in the error term in the asymptotic\[Q(x)=\frac{6}{\pi^2}x+E(x).\]

### Context
It is elementary to prove $E(x)\ll x^{1/2}$, and the prime number theorem implies $o(x^{1/2})$. The best known unconditional upper bound is of the shape $x^{1/2-o(1)}$, due to Walfisz [Wa63]. Evelyn and Linfoot [EvLi31] proved that\[E(x) \gg x^{1/4},\]and this is likely the true order of magnitude. The Riemann Hypothesis would follow from $E(x)\ll x^{1/4}$.

The true order of magnitude is unknown even assuming the Riemann Hypothesis. Conditional on this assumption, the best known upper bound is\[E(x)\ll x^{\frac{11}{35}+o(1)},\]due to Liu [Li16].

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #970 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/970).

### Problem
Let $h(k)$ be Jacobsthal's function, defined to as the minimal $m$ such that, if $n$ has at most $k$ prime factors, then in any set of $m$ consecutive integers there exists an integer coprime to $n$. Determine the order of magnitude of $h(k)$. In particular, is it true that\[h(k) \ll k^2?\]

### Context
That $h(k)\ll k^2$ is a conjecture of Jacobsthal. Iwaniec [Iw78] proved\[h(k) \ll (k\log k)^2.\]The best lower bound known is\[h(k) \gg \frac{(\log k)(\log\log\log k)}{(\log\log k)^2}k,\]due to Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao [FGKMT18].

This is a more general form of the function considered in [[687]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/687).

sourceComments.contentMd: I asked [Claude](https://claude.ai/chat/ed008660-32ee-4871-aa20-25ed77a39056) for a literature review.  For the larger quantity $\max_a p(a,d)$ (where one only seeks $p(a,d)$ to be large for a single $a$ rather than a positive fraction of $a$), the problem is analogous to #4: [Pomerance in 1980](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022314X80900566) got a lower bound of $(e^\gamma-o(1)) \phi(d) \log d$, and [Li-Shakan-Pratt](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.02543) has the improved lower bound $\gg \phi(k) \log k \log\log k \log\log\log\log k / \log\log\log k$, in parallel with #4, and conjectured that the true order of growth here is around $\phi(k) \log^2 k$.  For the stated problem where one needs a positive density of $k$, Claude did not locate any literature, but reproduced (at least at a heuristic level) the Poisson statistic calculation that suggests the answer is positive assuming the prime tuples conjecture.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
This is true conditionally on Hardy-Littlewoods ("Conditional Poisson law at the Linnik scale"):
Let $c>0$ be fixed, let $d\to\infty$, and set\[
x:=(1+c)\phi(d)\log d,\qquad
N_a:=\pi(x;d,a)=\#\{p\le x:\ p\equiv a\!\!\pmod d\}\quad((a,d)=1).
\]Assume the following uniform prime $r$-tuple asymptotic for every fixed $r\ge1$: for all distinct integers $0\le k_1,\dots,k_r\le \lfloor x/d\rfloor$, writing $h_i:=(k_i-k_1)d$,\[
\#\{n\in [1,d]:\ n,\ n+h_2,\dots,n+h_r\ \text{are prime}\}
=\Bigl(\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)+o(1)\Bigr)\frac{d}{(\log x)^r},
\]uniformly in $d$ (here $\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)$ is the usual singular series), and in addition the average singular series over such tuples has the expected value\[
\frac{1}{K^r}\!\!\sum_{\substack{0\le k_1,\dots,k_r\le K\\ \text{distinct}}}\!\!\mathfrak S(\mathbf h)
=\Bigl(\frac{d}{\phi(d)}\Bigr)^{r-1}(1+o(1)),\qquad K:=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\Bigr\rfloor.
\]Then expanding factorial moments and averaging over $a\in(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z)^\times$ gives\[
\mathbb E[(N_a)_r]\ :=\ \frac{1}{\phi(d)}\sum_{(a,d)=1} N_a(N_a-1)\cdots(N_a-r+1)
\ \sim\ \Bigl(\frac{x}{\phi(d)\log x}\Bigr)^r\ =:\ \lambda^r.
\]Hence (method of moments) $N_a$ is asymptotically $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ as $a$ varies, with\[
\lambda=\frac{x}{\phi(d)\log x}\sim 1+c.
\]In particular,\[
\#\{a\bmod d:\ (a,d)=1,\ N_a=0\}=(e^{-\lambda}+o(1))\phi(d)\sim e^{-(1+c)}\phi(d),
\]equivalently for a positive proportion of reduced residue classes one has
$p(a,d)>(1+c)\phi(d)\log d$.
as wanted

sourceComments.author: zach hunter
sourceComments.contentMd:
write $q(a,d)$ to be the least $q>0$ so that $qd+a$ is prime. then we have that $p(a,d)=q(a,d)d+a$, unless $p(a,d)=a$.

now heuristically we expect the values of $q(a,d)$ to distributed like samples from a geometric random variable with success probability $\frac{d}{\phi(d)}\cdot \frac{1}{\log(d)}$. this has mean $\mu = \frac{1}{d}\phi(d)\log(d)$ whence it seems $p(a,d)$ should have expectation $\approx d\mu =\phi(d)\log(d)$.

and we'd expect this conjecture to be true due to how geometric random variables fluctuate. you'd in fact expect that for each $C$, that $\Omega_C(\phi(d))$ values of $a$ have $p(a,d)>C\phi(d)\log(d)$, if I'm not mistaken.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #972 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/972).

### Problem
Let $\alpha>1$ be irrational. Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $\lfloor p\alpha\rfloor$ is also prime?

### Context
Vinogradov [Vi48] proved that the sequence $\{p\alpha\}$ is uniformly distributed for every irrational $\alpha$, and hence there are infinitely many primes $p$ of the shape $p=\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for every irrational $\alpha>1$. Indeed, this occurs if and only if\[\frac{p}{\alpha}\leq n<\frac{p+1}{\alpha},\]which is true if and only if $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}>1-\alpha^{-1}$, which happens infinitely often by the uniform distribution of $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}$.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The result should be true for every $\alpha \in \mathbb R^+ \setminus \mathbb N$.
For $\alpha = 1/2$, it is e.g. equivalent with the existence of infinitely many Sophie Germain primes, for which one guess there are $2C(1+o(1)) \frac{x}{\ln^2 x}$ many up to $x$.
Here $C$ is Hardy–Littlewood's twin prime constant (somewhat confirming the connection).

In general, one indeed expects for fixed valid $\alpha$ ($\alpha \in \mathbb N$ are excluded for obvious reasons, where $\alpha=1$ is trivially a special case) the number of valid primes indeed to be of the order $\frac{x}{\ln^2 x}$.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: This looks comparable in difficulty to the twin prime conjecture.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #973 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/973).

### Problem
Does there exist a constant $C>1$ such that, for every $n\geq 2$, there exists a sequence $z_i\in \mathbb{C}$ with $z_1=1$ and $\lvert z_i\rvert \geq 1$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$ with\[\max_{2\leq k\leq n+1}\left\lvert \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}z_i^k\right\rvert < C^{-n}?\]

### Context
This is Problem 7.3 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.

Erdős proved (as described on p.35 of [Tu84b]) that such a sequence does exist with $\lvert z_i\rvert\leq 1$. Indeed, Erdős' construction gives a value of $C\approx 1.32$.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
As an additional remark, if we consider the conditions of Problem #973, one can also derive the following partial result.

From Theorem 6.1 (the First Main Theorem) of [Tu84], if $\min_i|z_i|=1$ (hence $|z_i|\ge1$) and $g(\nu)=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i z_i^\nu$, then for any $m\ge0$\[
\max_{\nu=m+1,\dots,m+n} |g(\nu)| \;\ge\;
\left(\frac{n}{2e(m+n)}\right)^{\!n}\,\left|\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\right|.
\]Taking $b_i\equiv1$ and $m=1$ (so $\nu=2,\dots,n+1$) yields\[
\max_{2\le k\le n+1}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^k\right|
\;\ge\; n\left(\frac{n}{2e(n+1)}\right)^{\!n}.
\]Therefore, if an exponential upper bound $C^{-n}$ exists in the $|z_i|\ge1$ setting of Problem #973, one must have $C\le 2e+o(1)$.

Reference.
[Tu84] P. Turán, On a New Method of Analysis and Its Applications, John Wiley & Sons, 1984.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
The page mentions ''Erdős proved (but I cannot find the reference) that such a sequence does exist with $|z_i|\le1$.''

I believe I have found the missing reference. The result appears as Theorem 4.1 on page 35 of [Tu84]. In that theorem Turán attributes the result to Erdős, proving that for\[
S_2=\{2,3,\dots,n,n+1\}, \qquad
M_2=\min_{\{z_j\}}\max_{\nu\in S_2}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n z_j^{\nu}\right|,
\]under the normalization $\max_j|z_j|=1$, one has\[
M_2\le 2(n+1)^2 e^{-\vartheta_0 n} < 1.32^{-n} \qquad (n>n_0),
\]where $\vartheta_0\approx0.2784$ satisfies $x e^{x+1}=1$.

EDIT: Furthermore, in [Er92] Erdős refines the result and provides a more detailed asymptotic estimation for \(M_2\), showing that for sufficiently large \(n\),\[
n^{-0.7823} e^{-2\vartheta_0 n} \leq M_2 \leq n^{4.5} e^{-2\vartheta_0 n}.
\]For \(n > n_0\), we also have the following bounds for \(M_2\):\[
\frac{1}{1.746^n} < M_2 < \frac{1}{1.745^n}.\]References.
[Tu84] Paul Turán, On a New Method of Analysis and Its Applications, published posthumously with the assistance of Gábor Halász and János Pintz, John Wiley & Sons, New York, 1984 (Pure and Applied Mathematics series).
[Er92] L. Erdős, "On Some Problems of P. Turán Concerning Power Sums of Complex Numbers," Acta Mathematica Hungarica, 59.1 (1992): 11-24.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
Interestingly, as observed in Erdos's paper, the answer is completely different if one replaces the range $2 \leq k \leq n+1$ by $1 \leq k \leq n$.  Here one has the example of the $(n+1)^{th}$ roots of unity (if $n+1$ is prime) to show that the max can be 1, but it was shown [by Atkinson](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02066680) that it must be $\gg 1$ (and possibly even $\geq 1/2$)!  Turan conjectures a lower bound of $1-o(1)$ as $n \to \infty$.

It is not clear whether there is a similar construction showing that $1$ can be attained (or beaten) in the $2 \leq k \leq n+1$ case.

EDIT: Here is a summary of Atkinson's argument.  Suppose for contradiction that the power sums $s_k = \sum_{1 \leq i \leq n} z_i^k$ are all small for $1 \leq k \leq n$.  The function $g(\theta) = -\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{s_k e(k\theta)}{k}$ is the Fourier expansion of $\sum_{1 \leq i \leq n} \log(1-z_i e(\theta))$ up to degree $n$, hence the Fourier expansion of $e^{g(\theta)}$ agrees with $\prod_{1 \leq i \leq n} (1-z_i e(\theta))$ up to degree $n$.  If we set $z_1=1$, we conclude that at $\theta=0$, $e^{g(0)}$ is equal to the tail of its Fourier expansion after degree $n$; thus $e^{g(0)}$ is formally equal to the inner product of $e^{g(\theta)}$ and $\sum_{m=n+1}^\infty e(m\theta)$, or on integrating by parts of $e^{g(\theta)} g'(\theta)$ and $-\sum_{m=n+1}^\infty e(m\theta)/2\pi i -m$.  Thus the inner product of $e^{g(\theta)-g(0)} g'(\theta)$ and $-\sum_{m=n+1}^\infty e(m\theta)/2\pi i m$ is equal to $1$.  But using Plancherel's theorem to control the derivative of $g'$, one can show by standard estimates that this inner product is small if the $s_k$ are all small, giving the result.

More informally: $e^{g(\theta)-g(0)}$ has significant presence at high frequencies, which is why $g'$ cannot have all of its Fourier coefficients small.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #975 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/975).

### Problem
Let $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible non-constant polynomial such that $f(n)\geq 1$ for all large $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Does there exist a constant $c=c(f)>0$ such that\[\sum_{n\leq X} \tau(f(n))\sim cX\log X,\]where $\tau$ is the divisor function?

### Context
Van der Corput [Va39] proved that\[\sum_{n\leq X} \tau(f(n))\gg_f X\log X.\]Erdős [Er52b] proved using elementary methods that\[\sum_{n\leq X} \tau(f(n))\ll_f X\log X.\]Such an asymptotic formula is known whenever $f$ is an irreducible quadratic, as proved by Hooley [Ho63]. The form of $c$ depends on $f$ in a complicated fashion (see the work of McKee [Mc95], [Mc97], and [Mc99] for expressions for various types of quadratic $f$). For example,\[\sum_{n\leq x}\tau(n^2+1)=\frac{3}{\pi}x\log x+O(x).\]Tao has a [blog post](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2011/07/23/erdos-divisor-bound/) on this topic.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #976 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/976).

### Problem
Let $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial of degree $d\geq 2$. Let $F_f(n)$ be maximal such that there exists $1\leq m\leq n$ with $f(m)$ is divisible by a prime $\geq F_f(n)$. Equivalently, $F_f(n)$ is the greatest prime divisor of\[\prod_{1\leq m\leq n}f(m).\]Estimate $F_f(n)$. In particular, is it true that $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$ for some constant $c>0$? Or even $\gg n^d$?

### Context
Nagell [Na22] and Ricci [Ri34] proved that\[F_f(n) \gg n\log n,\]which Erdős [Er52c] improved to\[F_f(n) \gg n(\log n)^{\log\log\log n}.\]In [Er65b] he claimed a proof of\[F_f(n) \gg n\exp((\log n)^c)\]for some constant $c>0$, but said he had never published the proof, which was 'fairly complicated'. This seems to have been flawed, since Erdős and Schinzel [ErSc90] later published a weaker bound. A proof of the stronger bound above was finally provided by Tenenbaum [Te90].

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
I did some literature search and in full generality (arbitrary irreducible $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ of degree $\ge 2$), the strongest unconditional lower bounds known for\[
F_f(n)=P^+\Bigl(\prod_{m\le n} f(m)\Bigr)
\]are superlinear but subpower: they grow like $n^{1+o(1)}$, e.g.\[
F_f(n)\ \ge\ n\exp\exp\bigl(c(\log\log n)^{1/3}\bigr)
\](and related refinements). These come from global "Chebyshev/Erdos-Schinzel" methods controlling how often primes can divide polynomial values, but they do not reach any fixed power $n^{1+c}$.

Fixed-power bounds $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$ are known for certain special low-degree polynomials, because one can prove that in each dyadic interval $(X,2X]$ a positive proportion of values $f(m)$ have a prime factor $\ge X^{1+c}$; this immediately implies $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$. This has been proved for example for the cubic $n^3+2$ (Irving) and for certain quartics with cyclic/dihedral Galois group (Dartyge-Maynard), via deep sieve arguments plus strong "Type I/II" distribution estimates for $f(n)$ in residue classes.

For quadratics such as $n^2+1$, there are powerful results showing $P^+(n^2+1)\ge n^{1+c}$ infinitely often (with explicit $c$), but not (currently) the kind of dyadic positive-proportion statement that would force $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$ uniformly for all large $n$. Broadly, pushing $n^{1+c}$ for general $f$ seems to require much stronger distribution/trace-function/automorphic input than is available in the "generic" case, while special algebraic structure can make the needed analytic estimates accessible.

References:
Erdős-Schinzel (lower bounds for $P^+(\prod_{m\le x} f(m))$ of size $x^{1+o(1)}$):
https://www2.math.ethz.ch/EMIS/classics/Erdos/cit/71511050.htm

Irving (positive proportion of $n\in(X,2X]$ with a prime factor $>X^{1+c}$ for $n^3+2$):
https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.0024

Dartyge-Maynard (positive proportion / large prime factors for certain quartics; cyclic/dihedral Galois group):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.03381

Deshouillers-Iwaniec (large prime factors of $n^2+1$ infinitely often; classic AIF paper):
https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/aif.891.pdf

Merikoski (improved exponent for large prime factors of $n^2+1$, infinitely often):
https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.08816

Arango-Pineros-Keliher (Mertens-type theorems for Chebotarev sets; density-weighted prime sums):
https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14747

Lagarias-Odlyzko (effective Chebotarev density theorem; analytic input for Chebotarev prime-counting):
https://aareyanmanzoor.github.io/assets/articles/lagarias-odlyzko.pdf

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #978 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/978).

### Problem
Let $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial of degree $k>2$ (and suppose that $k\neq 2^l$ for any $l\geq 1$) such that the leading coefficient of $f$ is positive.

Does the set of integers $n\geq 1$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-1)$-power-free have positive density?

If $k>3$ then are there infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-2)$-power-free?

In particular, does\[n^4+2\]represent infinitely many squarefree numbers?

### Context
Erdős [Er53] proved there are infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-1)$-power-free, except when $k=2^l$ and $2^{k-1}\mid f(n)$ for all $n$. This latter exception is possible, for example if\[f(x)=k!\left(\binom{x}{k}+1\right).\]Hooley [Ho67] settled the first question, in fact providing a precise asymptotic for the number of such $n\leq x$.

Heath-Brown [He06] proved the answer to the second question is yes when $k\geq 10$, and Browning [Br11] extended this to $k\geq 9$ (in fact establishing an asymptotic formula for the number of such $n$).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
The DeepMind prover agent has formally verified that the answer to the second part of the question is 'False' by constructing an explicit counterexample polynomial (assuming our [formalisation](https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos978.erdos_978.parts.ii)) of the question is correct).

The polynomial $f(X) = X^6 + 33X^5 + 21X^4 + 63X^3 + 18X^2 + 24X + 48$ satisfies all the hypotheses (irreducible, degree $> 3$, degree not a power of $2$, positive leading coefficient, no fixed $p^5$ divisor) yet $f(n)$ is never $4$-powerfree. Irreducibility follows from Eisenstein's criterion at $p = 3$, since $3$ divides all non-leading coefficients but $3^2 = 9 \nmid 48$, the constant coefficient. The key observation is that $f(X) \equiv X(X-1)(X-2)(X-3)(X-4)(X-5) \pmod{16}$, and the product of $6$ consecutive integers is always divisible by $6! = 720$, which is divisible by $16 = 2^4$. So $2^4 \mid f(n)$ for all $n$, meaning $f(n)$ is never $4$-powerfree - contradicting the conclusion that infinitely many values should be. The full formal proof in Lean 4 is available [here](https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/47d9e68df4323b995bb9875b6d5199a4f7026bfb/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/978.lean#L62)).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
On looking at the literature, in most papers on the subject (e.g. [Heath-Brown](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1103.2028) or [Browning](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00013-011-0224-7)) when asking for $f(n)$ to take on infinitely many $r$th power-free values they assume the natural condition that, for all primes $p$, there exists at least one integer such that $p^r\nmid f(n)$.

For example in [Br11] Browning writes 'It is conjectured that this is the only obstruction to $f$ taking on infinitely many $r$-free values'.

Although Erdős does not state this explicitly in [Er65b] or [Er81h] he was certainly aware of this obstruction, and he probably had it in mind - when he wrote about this problem he generally had specific polynomials like $n^4+2$ in mind.

I think the existence of irreducible polynomials of degree $6$ that fail this necessary criterion, as in your example, is well-known to people in the field.

replies.contentMd:
So might it make sense to modify the problem statement here and add a condition like: "Suppose further that for every prime $p$, there exists some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $p^{k-2} \nmid f(n)$"
for the part of the question
"If $k > 3$ then are there infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-2)$-power-free?"?

Are there other implicit assumptions here?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Indeed (this has been changed). I'm not aware of any additional assumptions (and the Heath-Brown and Browning papers don't seem to mention any). As with many other problems in number theory, the question is asked 'modulo the obvious obstructions', and we often update what an 'obvious obstruction' is with the benefit of hindsight!
