In [Er53], Erdos defined $l$-th power free to be "not divisible by any integral $l$-th power greater than 1" and also assumed that "the highest coefficient in $f(x)$ is positive". This definition of power free suggests that Erdos considered $f n$ as natural numbers/nonnegative integers (at least for large enough $n$), which suggests that the assumption that the highest coefficient in $f(x)$ needs to be positive is necessary. If we don't assume this, infinitely many values of $f(n)$ may be negative and then it does not make sense to talk about set with positive density. May we include this assumption in the problem statement?

I also suggests changing "Does the set of integers ..." to "Does the set of natural numbers ..."

replies.contentMd:
See [[Er53]](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1953-02.pdf).

There are polynomials, the presented example is $k! \binom xk+k!$ ($k$ needs to be even or it is reducible), that are a multiple of $2^{k-1}$ when $k=2^{\ell}$.
So a condition had to be imposed for the general case to ensure there are infinitely many examples which are $(k-1)$ power-free.
Nevertheless, one could say the density is zero otherwise. So no additional condition was necessary for the subquestion.

For the final question: this is an example where the expression may be square-free. (so there is no obvious reason ruling out that it can infinitely often square-free, as was the case with $x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)+24$)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd: Anyone an idea how the $k=3$ case may have been settled?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Erdős [Er65b] wrote precisely 'I can also prove [the case $k=3$] (unpublished), and the proof of this seems to need some special properties of primes.'

Which doesn't give a lot of clues. It is of course possible that Erdős' proof also had a flaw, which he later discovered.

One idea is to adapt Mahler's disproof of Hypothesis K for $k=3$ (see [this exposition for example](http://thomasbloom.org/notes/hypothesisk.html)). This relies on the fact that, if $n=m^{12}$, then\[ n = (9t^4)^3 + (m^4-9mt^3)^3 + (9m^3t-9t^4)^3.\]In particular, choosing $t\ll m$ sufficiently small gives $\gg m=n^{1/12}$ many ways to write $n$ as the sum of three positive cubes.

So one approach would be to give a similar parametric family of solutions (for some $n$ of a special form) and then use sieve theory to show that the forms are simultaneously prime infinitely often. This looks hard, since we know very little about how to find primes among the values of polynomials of degree $>2$, but perhaps one can take advantage of a large number of variables and averaging to make this work.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
It might well be that the answer is yes at the end.
(average behaviour and extremal behaviour can be expected to be very different)

Below some heuristic thinking (not made precise, since proving it in the context will be still hard)

Notice there are at least $(\pi(\sqrt[k]{N/k}))^k =\tilde \Omega_k (N)$ and at most  $(\pi(\sqrt[k]{N}))^k =\tilde O_k (N)$ many combinations of primes whose sum of k^th powers is bounded by $N.$

Now, if this is somewhat random distributed (it is not uniform random, but should be good for heuristic estimate since one can check $[N/2,N]$..),
then one can think about the Birthday paradox for $m$ collisions.
See e.g. [[oeis/A225852]](https://oeis.org/A225852) and
[[oeis/A225871]](https://oeis.org/A225871).
Rough estimates, tell that for every bound on $m$, the critical region should be at some power of $N$ with exponent less than $1$ (similar to [[stackexchange]](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/25876/probability-of-3-people-in-a-room-of-30-having-the-same-birthday)).
Since $\tilde\Theta_k(N)$ is linear up to polylog, one expects indeed there are values which appear at least $m$ times...

This is true for the set of all integers when $k=3$, which is surprising for the same heuristic reasons Stijn mentions.

replies.contentMd: I'm sorry to say, but I don't think your argument can be correct. It is generally assumed that eg $a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5$ has no non-trivial solutions in positive integers, let alone in primes. See for example problem [#324](https://www.erdosproblems.com/324).

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
There is written "One would expect this result to be true for density reasons".
Actually, when thinking about the problem, I had exactly the opposite thought.
Up to $N^k$, there are less than $\pi(N)^k<<N^k$ many options for the $k$-tuple of primes. So on average, a number in $[0,N^k]$ is almost never hit, i.e., $\mathbb E[ p_k(n)] \to 0$ ($n$ taken at random in large interval).
[Let alone, when one considers the sum of only two $k$-powers, then for $k>4$ one may expect no different solutions, as commented by Wouter]

researchNotes: The regular polygon shows that $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is the best possible here.

This would be implied if there was a vertex such that no three vertices of the polygon are equally distant to it, which was originally also conjectured by Erdős [Er46b], but this is false (see [[97]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/97)).

Let $f(n)$ be the maximal number of such distances that are guaranteed. Moser [Mo52] proved thatf(n) \geq \left\lceil\frac{n}{3}\right\rceil.This was improved by Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi94] tof(n) \geq \left\lfloor \frac{n}{3}+1\right\rfloor,thenf(n) \geq \left\lceil \frac{13n-6}{36}\right\rceilby Dumitrescu [Du06b], and most recentlyf(n) \geq \left(\frac{13}{36}+\frac{1}{22701}\right)n-O(1)by Nivasch, Pach, Pinchasi, and Zerbib [NPPZ13].

In [Er46b] Erdős makes the even stronger conjecture that on every convex curve there exists a point $p$ such that every circle with centre $p$ intersects the curve in at most $2$ points. Bárány and Roldán-Pensado [BaRo13] noted that the boundary of any acute triangle is a counterexample.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #983 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/983).

### Problem
Let $n\geq 2$ and $\pi(n)<k\leq n$. Let $f(k,n)$ be the smallest integer $r$ such that in any $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ of size $\lvert A\rvert=k$ there exist primes $p_1,\ldots,p_r$ such that $>r$ many $a\in A$ are only divisible by primes from $\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}$.

Is it true that\[2\pi(n^{1/2})-f(\pi(n)+1,n)\to \infty\]as $n\to \infty$?

In general, estimate $f(k,n)$, particularly when $\pi(n)+1<k=o(n)$.

### Context
It is trivial that $f(k,n)\leq \pi(n)$. Erdős and Straus [Er70b] proved that\[f(\pi(n)+1,n)=2\pi(n^{1/2})+o_A\left(\frac{n^{1/2}}{(\log n)^A}\right)\]for any $A>0$ and, for any constant $1>c>0$,\[f(cn,n)=\log\log n+(c_1+o(1))\sqrt{2\log\log n},\]where\[c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{c_1}e^{-x^2/2}\mathrm{d}x.\]

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: CalebDeLeeuw
sourceComments.contentMd:
Thank you Woett for the detailed clarification on the "strictly more than $r$" vs "at least $r$" distinction. That's an important correction to the problem statement.

I'd like to raise a related question about the quantifier structure of $f(k,n)$ that came up during computational investigation (discussion at github.com/teorth/erdosproblems#216).

The current problem statement reads:

$f(k,n)$ be the smallest integer $r$ such that in any $A \subseteq {1,\ldots,n}$ of size $|A|=k$ there exist primes $p_1,\ldots,p_r$ such that [more than] $r$ many $a \in A$ are only divisible by primes from ${p_1,\ldots,p_r}$.

This "for any $A$, there exist primes" formulation suggests an adversarial/worst-case problem: the set $A$ is chosen first (adversarially), then we find covering primes.

Question: Is this the correct quantifier order from [Er70b]?

In the GitHub discussion, it was suggested that Erdős-Straus may have defined $f(k,n)$ with reversed quantifiers:

"there exist primes $p_1,\ldots,p_r$ such that at least $k$ integers $m \leq n$ have all prime divisors contained in ${p_1,\ldots,p_r}$"

Under this alternative interpretation, primes are chosen first to maximize coverage, making small primes $\leq \sqrt{n}$ optimal (each generates many smooth composites), naturally yielding $f \approx 2\pi(\sqrt{n})$.

Under the adversarial interpretation currently stated, computational testing suggests $f$ is much smaller. For example, with $k = \pi(n)+1$:

Any set $A$ of squarefree composites has "triangle" structure: three primes $p,q,r$ cover the semiprimes $pq, pr, qr$ (if present), giving efficient coverage
Testing up to $n = 10{,}000$ consistently yields small values that don't approach $2\pi(\sqrt{n})$
Could someone with access to [Er70b] ("Some applications of graph theory to number theory", 1969) confirm the exact quantifier structure in the original definition?

Woett's lower bound construction (using $A_0$ with paired products plus primes) is illuminating, but I want to ensure I'm understanding the correct problem before analyzing it further.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
The reference is [[Er70b, p. 138](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1970-20.pdf)].  I think the quantifier order is as stated (the primes depend on the set $A$), this can be seen from context by looking at the various proofs of partial results in [Er70b].  The numerical discrepancy you detected is most likely due to the other correction that Woett pointed out.

By the way, any use of AI tools to generate comments here needs to be disclosed as per forum rules.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let $2 = p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_t$ be those primes smaller than or equal to $(2 - \epsilon)\sqrt{n}$. Erdős and Straus then construct a set $A_0$ of size $t$, where $A_0$ consists of certain pairs of products $p_ip_j < n$ such that every $p_i$ (with $i \le t$) occurs in exactly two products. Finishing up, they let $A$ (with $k = |A| = \pi(n)+1$) be the union $$A := A_0 \cup \{2p_{t+1}, 3p_{t+1}\} \cup \bigcup_{i = t+2}^{\pi(n)} p_i.$$For this set $A$ one can then check that $r = t+1$, as $\{p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_{t+1}\}$ is the smallest set of primes such that there are more than $r$ elements $a \in A$ whose prime decompositions only contain $p_1, \ldots, p_{r}$. Hence, we get the lower bound $f(\pi(n)+1, n) > t =\pi((2-\epsilon)\sqrt{n})$.

Now note that, for fixed $n$, $f(k, n)$ is a non-increasing function of $k$. Since Erdős and Straus also showed $f(\pi(n)+1,n) \le 2\pi(\sqrt{n}) + 1$, this gives $f(k, n) \le 2\pi(\sqrt{n}) + 1$ for all $k > \pi(n)$. On the other hand, we could have slightly tweaked the lower bound construction we just saw as follows:

Let $A_0$ still consist of $t$ pairs of products $p_ip_j < n$ as explained in [[Er70b]](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1970-20.pdf), but as opposed to using the primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_t$, we use $p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_{t+1}$ instead. We then set $$A := A_0 \cup \bigcup_{i=2}^{\pi(\frac{1}{2}n)} \{2p_i\} \cup \bigcup_{i = t+2}^{\pi(n)} p_i.$$In this case we still get $r = t+1$, while $k = \pi(n) + \pi(\frac{1}{2}n) - 2$. Combining upper and lower bound and using the prime number theorem we deduce $f(k,n) = (4 + o(1))\frac{n^{1/2}}{\log n}$ for all $k$ with $\pi(n) < k < (\frac{3}{2} + o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$. One can probably increase the range of $k$ for which this estimate holds by tweaking $A$ further.

Based on the proven value of $f(cn, n)$, presumably some kind of phase-shift occurs somewhere, if we let $k$ increase from $\frac{cn}{\log n}$ to $cn$.

Finally, $f(k,n)$ might still be interesting for the range $(1-o(1))n < k < n$. To give two quick examples, if $k > n - \pi(\sqrt{n})$, then we are guaranteed to have $\{p, p^2\} \subset A$ (so that $f(k,n) = 1$), and if $k > n - \pi(\frac{1}{4}n)$ we are guaranteed to have $\{p, 2p, 4p\} \subset A$ (so that $f(k,n) \le 2$). One can wonder what the slowest growest function $g(n)$ is such that $k < n - g(n)$ implies $f(k,n) \rightarrow \infty$. By the value of $f(cn, n)$ we know $g(n) = o(n)$, while generalizing the second example we just gave leads (I think) to $g(n) > (1 - o(1))\pi(n)$.

sourceComments.author: Aron Bhalla
sourceComments.contentMd:
GPT-5.4 Thinking finds the following relevant progress:

1. Let $G(p)$ denote the least prime primitive root modulo a prime $p$. Nongkynrih (Acta Arith. 72 (1995), 45–53) studied the distribution of prime primitive roots and proved that for almost all primes $p$ one has an asymptotic formula for the number of prime primitive roots $\le H$ is $N(H,p) \sim \frac{\varphi(p-1)}{p-1}\pi(H)$ provided $H$ is sufficiently large (polylogarithmic in $p$). Since $\varphi(p-1)/(p-1) \gg 1/\log\log p$, taking $H=(\log p)^A$ with $A$ large enough implies that $G(p) \le (\log p)^A$ for almost all primes $p$. In particular, for a set of primes of natural density $1$ there exists a prime primitive root $q \le (\log p)^A < p$. Thus the conjectured property holds for almost all primes $p$.

2. Related work of Martin (“The least prime primitive root and the shifted sieve”, 1997) shows that similar bounds for $G(p)$ follow from shifted sieve methods and that, assuming GRH, one obtains bounds implying $G(p) \ll (\log p)^C$ for all sufficiently large primes $p$. Under GRH this would therefore imply the statement of the problem for all sufficiently large $p$.

3. Computationally, extensive searches for the least prime primitive root $G(p)$ (e.g. Oliveira e Silva’s tables up to at least $10^{14}$) have not produced any counterexample to the statement that $G(p) < p$.

Therefore, the problem appears to remain open in full generality, but it is known that $G(p) \le (\log p)^A$ for almost all primes $p$ (unconditionally), and that $G(p) \ll (\log p)^C$ for all sufficiently large primes $p$ under GRH. Both results imply that the conjecture holds for all sufficiently large primes in the corresponding sense.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd: Of course, $p > 2$ is required. Moreover, the (plausibly too) naive heuristic says this should be true (up to at most finitely many counterexamples): there are $\varphi(p-1) \ge \frac{cp}{\log \log p}$ many primitive roots modulo $p$, and $\frac{(1+o(1))p}{\log p}$ many primes below $p$. The probability that random sets with these growth rates don't intersect goes to 0 quite quickly.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #986 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/986).

### Problem
For any fixed $k\geq 3$,\[R(k,n) \gg \frac{n^{k-1}}{(\log n)^c}\]for some constant $c=c(k)>0$.

### Context
Spencer [Sp77] proved this for $k=3$ and Mattheus and Verstraete [MaVe23] proved this for $k=4$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #987 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/987).

### Problem
Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots \in (0,1)$ be an infinite sequence and let\[A_k=\limsup_{n\to \infty}\left\lvert \sum_{j\leq n} e(kx_j)\right\rvert,\]where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$.

Is it true that\[\limsup_{k\to \infty} A_k=\infty?\]Is it possible for $A_k=o(k)$?

### Context
This is Problem 7.21 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.

Erdős [Er64b] remarks it is 'easy to see' that\[\limsup_{k\to \infty}\left(\sup_n\left\lvert \sum_{j\leq n} e(kx_j)\right\rvert\right)=\infty.\]Erdős [Er65b] later found a 'very easy' proof that $A_k\gg \log k$ for infinitely many $k$. Clunie [Cl67] proved that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often, and that there exist sequences with $A_k\leq k$ for all $k$. Tao has independently found a proof that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often (see the comment section).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

The question of whether $A_k=o(k)$ is possible (repeated in [Er65b] and [Ha74]) seems to still be open.

Erdős [Er64b] remarks it is 'easy to see' that\[\limsup_{k\to \infty}\left(\sup_n\left\lvert \sum_{j\leq n} e(kx_j)\right\rvert\right)=\infty.\]Erdős [Er65b] later found a 'very easy' proof that $A_k\gg \log k$ for infinitely many $k$. Clunie [Cl67] proved that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often, and that there exist sequences with $A_k\leq k$ for all $k$. Tao has independently found a proof that $A_k\gg k^{1/2}$ infinitely often (see the comment section).

Liu [Li69] showed that, for any $\epsilon>0$, $A_k\gg k^{1-\epsilon}$ infinitely often, under the additional assumption that there are only a finite number of distinct points. Clunie observed in the Mathscinet review of [Li69], however, that under this assumption in fact $A_k=\infty$ infinitely often.
The question of whether $A_k=o(k)$ is possible (repeated in [Er65b] and [Ha74]) seems to still be open.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
In the followup paper of Erdos the repaired question is posed as to whether $\limsup_{n \to \infty} |\sum_{j \leq n} e(k x_j)| \gg k$ for infinitely many $k$.  I actually suspect that the answer is negative, and that one can construct a sequence $x_j$ with $|\sum_{j \leq n} e(k x_j)| \ll k^{1/2+o(1)}$ for all $k \geq 1$ and $n \geq 1$.  Heuristically, the construction should be to choose the $x_j$ randomly subject to the conditions $\sum_{2^i m < j \leq 2^i (m+1)} e(k x_j) = 0$ for all $i \geq 0$, $m \geq 0$, and $k \leq 2^{i-\varepsilon}$.  Naive degree of freedom counts suggest that the $x_j$ should still behave fairly randomly even after imposing all these constraints, enough to get the near-square root cancellation required here.  But proving this rigorously may require some effort.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
After some digging, I see that Erdos himself [actually solved this problem](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1965-18.pdf) shortly afterwards, saying that he "overlooked the fact that it is very easy to show" a logarithmic type lower bound for the inner supremum for a susbequence of $k$.  There is followup work improving the bounds [by Clunie](https://doi.org/10.1112/jlms/s1-42.1.133) obtaining a square root lower bound.  Conjecturally, there should be linear growth (which would be optimal); this was shown up to an epsilon loss [by Liu](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2036452) assuming the sequence is finitely valued (though as observed by Clunie in the [MathSciNet review](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=245795), in this case the inner supremum is in fact infinite for infinitely many $k$).  I could not find any followup work after the 1969 paper of Liu.

EDIT: I seem to recover the same square root bound as Clunie, and it seems that the proof techniques are similar.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The answer is yes.  Proof: assume not, then there exists $k_0, C$, and $x_1,x_2,\dots$ such that
$$ \limsup_{n \to \infty} |\sum_{j \leq n} e(kx_j)| \leq C$$
for all $k \geq k_0$.  In particular, for any $K \geq k_0$, there exists $N_K$ such that
$$ |\sum_{j \leq n} e(kx_j)| \leq C+1$$
whenever $k_0 \leq k \leq K$ and $n \geq N_K$.  In particular, by the triangle inequality we have
$$ |\sum_{N_K < j \leq N_K + n} e(kx_j)| \leq 2(C+1)$$
whenever $k_0 \leq k \leq K$ and $n \geq 0$, which we can relabel as
$$ |\sum_{j \leq n} e(kx_{N_K+j})| \leq 2(C+1). \quad (1)$$
The key point here is that $n$ is no longer required to be sufficiently large depending on $K$.

By weak compactness (Arzela-Ascoli), we can pass to a subsequence of $K$ where the $x_{N_K+j}$ converge pointwise mod 1 to some limit $y_j \in [0,1)$.  We now have
$$ |\sum_{j \leq n} e(ky_j)| \leq 2(C+1)$$
for all $k \geq k_0$ and $n \geq 0$.  Squaring and averaging in $K$, we see that
$$ \limsup_{K \to \infty} \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K |\sum_{j \leq n} e(ky_j)|^2 \leq 4(C+1)^2$$
for any $n \geq 0$.  Expanding out the square, the left-hand side can be computed explicitly to be
$$ | \{ 1 \leq i,j \leq n: y_i = y_j \} |.$$
But this is clearly at least $n$; taking $n$ larger than $4(C+1)^2$, we obtain the desired contradiction.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Great, thanks Terry! I'll update the site tomorrow.

As usual with these older more obscure problems (that were not later repeated), they may well have been solved a long time ago in some obscure paper, but I couldn't find anything for this problem.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
An alternate, more quantitative, proof avoiding the weak compactness step.  For fixed $n,K$, argue as before to get to (1).  Now use the identity
$$ \sum_{k,k' \leq K} |\sum_{j \leq n} e((k-k') x_{N_K+j})|^2 = \sum_{j,j' \leq n} |\sum_{k \leq K} e(k (x_{N_k+j}-x_{N_k+j'}))|^2.$$
By considering the diagonal $j=j'$, we see that the RHS is at least $nK^2$.  On the other hand, from (1) (for $|k-k'| \geq k_0$) and the trivial triangle inequality bound (for $|k-k'| < k_0$) the left-hand side is at most $4(C+1)^2 K^2 + n^2 K (2k_0-1)$.  So we have
$$ nK^2 \leq 4(C+1)^2 K^2 + n^2 K (2k_0-1)$$
for all $n,K$.  Taking $n > 4(C+1)^2$ and then $K$ sufficiently large depending on $C,n,k_0$ we obtain a contradiction.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: It was relatively straightforward to [formalize this latter proof in Lean](https://github.com/teorth/analysis/blob/main/analysis/Analysis/Misc/erdos_987.lean).

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd: My guess is that Erdos's 'easy' argument is that by the simultaneous Dirichlet approximation theorem, one can for fixed $n$ find arbitrarily large $k$ so that all of the $kx_1,\dots,kx_n$ are simultaneously close to an integer, so that $|\sum_{j \leq n} e(kx_j)|$ is arbitrarily close to $n$.  However, the original question is concerned with the opposite regime where $n$ is extremely large compared to $k$, rather than vice versa, and seems to be a rather different problem.

Some references from [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/68f6c348-d8a0-800e-b3f9-2f716b7e0db3) and [Gemini](https://gemini.google.com/share/eace5889bab9):

* Subsequent proofs of the Erdos-Turan inequality: [Ganelius](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/arkiv-for-matematik/volume-3/issue-1/Sequences-of-analytic-functions-and-their-zeros/10.1007/BF02589280.full) (1954), [Amoroso-Mignotte](https://www.numdam.org/item/AIF_1996__46_5_1275_0.pdf) (1996), [Soundararajan](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.06506) (2018),  [Shu-Wang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.11006) (2021), culminating in the optimal constant being computed.
* Some equidistribution results on "fewnomials" in the direction of this conjecture, e.g., an application of the rule of signs in [this MathOverflow post](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/219888/angular-distribution-of-zero-sets-of-sparse-polynomials), or [this paper of Steinerberger](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.09079) from 2019.

However, the stated problem appears to still be open.  (Gemini was of the opinion that it was false, while ChatGPT had the opposite opinion that partial results suggested it to be true.  Neither AI made a particularly convincing case in my opinion.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #993 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/993).

### Problem
The independent set sequence of any tree or forest is unimodal.

In other words, if $i_k(G)$ counts the number of independent sets of vertices of size $k$ in a graph $G$, and $T$ is any tree or forest, then for some $m\geq 0$
$$i_{0}(T)\leq i_{1}(T)\leq\cdots\leq i_{m}(T)\geq i_{m+1}(T)\geq i_{m+2}(T)\geq\cdots.$$

### Context
A question of Alavi, Malde, Schwenk, and Erdős [AMSE87], who showed that this is false for general graphs $G$ (in fact every possible pattern of inequalities is achieved by some graph).

The sequence which counts the number of independent sets of edges of a given size was proved to be unimodal (for any graph) by Schwenk [Sc81]. In [AMSE87] they also ask whether every possible unimodal pattern of inequalities is achieved by some graph.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: BrettRey
sourceComments.contentMd:
A follow-up to the Jan. 7, 2026 comment: I have public code/result artifacts for the n <= 29 verification here: https://github.com/BrettRey/erdos-problem-993

In particular, the completed exhaustive runs record:
  - n = 28: 2,023,443,032 trees, 0 unimodality failures
  - n = 29: 5,469,566,585 trees, 0 unimodality failures

I also completed a log-concavity / near-miss audit at n = 28:
  - 19 log-concavity failures, all at k = 14
  - 0 non-unimodal trees
  - top near-miss ratio 0.8565665724120973 at k = 13

I have not yet completed the analogous LC / near-miss audit at n = 29.

On the structural side, I also have a manuscript in preparation developing a subdivision-contraction identity
  I(T_e; x) = I(T; x) + x I(T/e; x),
together with a reduction via Hub Exclusion + Transfer to the d_leaf <= 1 regime and a mean bound mu(T) < n/3 in that regime. I am not claiming a full solution at this stage; one closure route remains conditional on a separate mode-mean inequality, which I have verified computationally through n <= 23.

Disclosure: AI assistance was used for computational exploration, code development, and proof-strategy exploration, but the numerical claims above come from executed computations recorded in the linked repository.

sourceComments.author: JakeMallen
sourceComments.contentMd: I verified computationally that the independent set sequence is unimodal for every tree with $n \leq 29$ vertices,  extending Radcliffe's $n \leq 25$ verification cited in [Basit and Galvin [arXiv:2006.12562]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.12562). Basit and Galvin also show that asymptotically almost surely ~49.5% of the sequence is increasing and ~38.8% of the sequence is decreasing, which may be worth adding to the problem's description.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #996 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/996).

### Problem
Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be a lacunary sequence of integers, and let $f\in L^2([0,1])$. Let $f_n$ be the $n$th partial sum of the Fourier series of $f(x)$. Is there an absolute constant $C>0$ such that, if\[\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log\log\log n)^{C}}\]then\[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=\int_0^1 f(x)\mathrm{d}x\]for almost every $\alpha$?

### Context
Raikov proved the conclusion always holds (for every $f\in L^2([0,1])$, with no assumption on $\| f-f_n\|_2$) if $n_k=a^k$ for some integer $a\geq 2$. Erdős [Er64b] also asked whether this is true for $n_k=\lfloor a^k\rfloor$ for some $a>1$.

Kac, Salem, and Zygmund [KSZ48] proved that the conclusion holds if\[\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log n)^{c}}\]for some constant $c>1$. Erdős [Er49d] proved that the conclusion holds if\[\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log\log n)^{c}}\]for some constant $c>1$. Matsuyama [Ma66] improved this to $c>1/2$.

### Problem
Call $x_1,x_2,\ldots \in (0,1)$ well-distributed if, for every $\epsilon>0$, if $k$ is sufficiently large then, for all $n>0$ and intervals $I\subseteq [0,1]$,\[\lvert \# \{ n<m\leq n+k : x_m\in I\} - \lvert I\rvert k\rvert < \epsilon k.\]Is it true that, for every $\alpha$, the sequence $\{ \alpha p_n\}$ is not well-distributed, if $p_n$ is the sequence of primes?

### Context
The notion of a well-distributed sequence was introduced by Hlawka and Petersen [Hl55].

Erdős proved that, if $n_k$ is a lacunary sequence, then the sequence $\{ \alpha n_k\}$ is not well-distributed for almost all $\alpha$.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1002 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1002).

### Problem
For any $0<\alpha<1$, let\[f(\alpha,n)=\frac{1}{\log n}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}(\tfrac{1}{2}-\{ \alpha k\}).\]Does $f(\alpha,n)$ have an asymptotic distribution function?

In other words, is there a non-decreasing function $g$ such that $g(-\infty)=0$, $g(\infty)=1$,
and\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\lvert \{ \alpha\in (0,1): f(\alpha,n)\leq c\}\rvert=g(c)?\]

### Context
Kesten [Ke60] proved that if\[f(\alpha,\beta,n)=\frac{1}{\log n}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}(\tfrac{1}{2}-\{\beta+\alpha k\})\]then $f(\alpha,\beta,n)$ has asymptotic distribution function\[g(c)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\rho c}\frac{1}{1+t^2}\mathrm{d}t,\]where $\rho>0$ is an explicit constant.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
The literature here is somewhat confusing because the results are very sensitive to what is being averaged here: one can work with "temporal" averaging (averaging in $n$), "spatial" averaging (averaging in $\beta$), "quenched" averaging (fixed $\alpha$), and "annealed" averaging (averaging in $\alpha$).  In particular, Erdos's question involves only the annealed notion of average.  The most recent paper I could find (with the help of [Gemini](https://gemini.google.com/share/00677f953e73) and [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/6907fad4-3180-800e-ba64-f11f8afb5608), whose outputs were somewhat unreliable due to the subtleties mentioned above) was [a 2024 paper of Fruhworth-Hauke](https://ahl.centre-mersenne.org/item/10.5802/ahl.200.pdf), which seem to indicate that the Erdos problem remains open as stated, although with additional averaging the claim is true (e.g., if one also averages in $n$ the claim was obtained [by Dolgopyat and Sarig](https://math.umd.edu/~dolgop/QARot13.pdf)).

The problem here seems remarkably delicate, and probably the first step to anyone interested in trying to solve this problem is to carefully go through the literature (of which the above two papers are only a small sample).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Some notes on the problem (all familiar to experts on this problem, I assume, but it was somewhat novel to me).  I was initially rather confused as to the logarithmic Cauchy behavior here, since square root cancellation heuristics would naively $f(\alpha,n)$ should oscillate like $\sqrt{n}$ times a Gaussian instead of $\log n$ times a Cauchy distribution.  But it turns out the series is extremely subrandom, and the behavior of $f(\alpha,n)$ is closely tied with how $n$ interacts with the successive approximants $p_j/q_j$ of $\alpha$ in the continued fraction expansion, as per the [Denjoy-Koksma inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denjoy%E2%80%93Koksma_inequality).  Suppose for instance that $q_j \leq n < q_{j+1}$ with $j$ even, then by standard continued fraction theory we have $q_{j+1} = a_{j+1} q_j + q_{j-1}$ with $a_{j+1}$ the $j+1^{th}$ term in the continued fraction expansion (which would be expected to be distributed according to the [Gauss-Kuzmin law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Kuzmin_distribution), which is a discrete Cauchy distribution, and $\alpha = \frac{p_j}{q_j} + \delta$ for some $0 < \delta < \frac{p_{j+1}}{q_{j+1}}-\frac{p_j}{q_j} = \frac{1}{q_j q_{j+1}}$).  One can then write $n = c_{j+1} q_j + n'$ for some $0 \leq c_{j+1} \leq a_{j+1}$ and $n' < q_j$ (if $c_{j+1}=a_{j+1}$ one can improve the upper bound on $N'$ to $N' < q_{j-1}$); the sequence of $c_{j+1}$ represent a sort of "base $(q_j)_{j=1}^\infty$ expansion" of $n$ (e.g., if $\alpha$ is the golden ratio then this is essentially [Fibonacci coding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibonacci_coding)).  A key point here is that if $k \leq n$ then $\alpha k$ has the same integer part as $p_j k / q_j$.  As such one can write
$$ f(\alpha,n) \log n = \sum_{k \leq n} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \} + p_j k / q_j - \alpha k) = \sum_{k \leq n} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) - \frac{\delta n(n+1)}{2}$$
and similarly
$$ f(\alpha,n') \log n' = \sum_{k \leq n'} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) - \frac{\delta n'(n'+1)}{2}.$$
The function $\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}$ is $q_j$-periodic and sums to $-\frac{1}{2}$ on each period, so
$$ \sum_{k \leq n} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) = \sum_{k \leq n'} (\frac{1}{2} - \{p_j k / q_j \}) - \frac{c_{k+1}}{2}.$$
Hence we obtain a recursion
$$ f(\alpha,n) \log n = f(\alpha,n') \log n' + X_j$$
where
$$ X_j = \frac{\delta}{2} (n(n+1)-n'(n'+1)) - \frac{c_{j+1}}{2} = \frac{c_{j+1}}{2} (\delta q_j (n+n'+1) - 1) $$
(I may have gotten some signs wrong here).  There is a similar formula (with some signs changed) when $j$ is odd instead of even.  Each $X_j$ can be calculated to be of size $O(a_{j+1})$ and is primarily determined by the "digit" $c_{j+1}$ in the expansion of $n$ (as well as the continued fraction coefficient $a_{j+1}$).  There are $\asymp \log n$ relevant values of $j$ here, with the $a_{j+1}$ behaving like iid copies of the heavy-tailed Gauss-Kuzmin distribution, and so the sum generically should be dominated by $O(1)$ terms where $a_{j+1} \asymp \log n$, each of which contributes a term of size $O(\log n)$ (but there is a rare "major arc" event in which one of the terms is much larger, which seems to defeat most moment-based strategies for this problem).  This is where the $\log n$ normalization comes from, and the Cauchy distribution presumably reflects some basin of attraction property that I did not work out carefully (it reminds me of how the Cauchy distribution shows up in the analysis of the Saint Petersburg paradox).

To solve this problem, therefore, one needs to understand the behavior of the digits $c_{j+1}$ in the expansion of a large but fixed number $n$, with respect to the base $(q_j)_{j=1}^\infty$ generated by a random continued fraction, and with a particular focus on those rare digits where $a_{j+1}$ is as large as $\log n$.  It seems that the most significant digits (where $q_j$ is not much smaller than $n$) can be relatively well understood, but there is some weird mixing process going on with the operation $n \mapsto n'$ of taking successive remainders with respect to the $b_{j+1}$ that I don't understand past the first few steps (it reminds me a little bit of the Collatz iteration, actually, which is unnerving for the purposes of actually proving anything rigorous).

sourceComments.author: Steve Fan
Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
There's a good amount of literature on $\phi(n)=\phi(n+k)$, where $k$ is a fixed positive integer.
See, for instance, [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12155) by K. Ford.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
As noted as far back as Schinzel, the problem is a lot easier (though still non-trivial) if one replaces the shift by 1 by larger shifts.  For instance, if $p$ and $2p-1$ are both prime then we have $\phi(n+2)=\phi(n)$ for $n = 2(2p-1)$, so $n+2 = 4p$.  See [this paper by Ford](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.12155") for further explorations of this idea.

Unfortunately, for the unit shift problem here, no such ansatz involving products of a small number of primes can work.  If $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$ for a large $n$ then $\frac{\phi(n)}{n} = \prod_{p|n} \frac{p-1}{p}$ has to be very close, but not equal to, $\frac{\phi(n+1)}{n+1} = \prod_{p|n+1} \frac{p-1}{p}$.  On the other hand, one of the $n,n+1$ has to be even, so one of these products involves $\frac{1}{2}$ and the other does not.  As these products are all distinct (mostly due to the denominators being distinct primes), this forces larger and larger numbers of factors to show up for at least one of these products as $n$ increases.

sourceComments.author: Steve Fan
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think the result of Erdős, Pomerance, and Sárközy mentioned here was actually proved as Theorem 2 in P. Erdős, C. Pomerance, A. Sárközy, On locally repeated values of certain arithmetic functions, II., Acta Math. Hungar. 49 (1--2) (1987), 251--259.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Theorem 2 in [[EPS87]](https://math.dartmouth.edu/~carlp/PDF/58.pdf) seems indeed correct, but there is even not a constant there.

Related to this, they explicitly state "We cannot prove, however, that there are even infinitely many solutions for either equation.".

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1005 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1005).

### Problem
Let $\frac{a_1}{b_1},\frac{a_2}{b_2},\ldots$ be the [Farey fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farey_sequence) of order $n\geq 4$. Let $f(n)$ be the largest integer such that if $1\leq k<l\leq k+f(n)$ then $\frac{a_k}{b_k}$ and $\frac{a_l}{b_l}$ are similarly ordered - in other words,\[(a_k-a_l)(b_k-b_l)\geq 0.\]Estimate $f(n)$ - in particular, is there a constant $c>0$ such that $f(n)=(c+o(1))n$ for all large $n$?

### Context
The function $f(n)$ was first considered by Mayer [Ma42], who proved $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Erdős [Er43] proved $f(n)\gg n$.

van Doorn [vD25b] has proved that\[\left(\frac{1}{12}-o(1)\right)n\leq f(n) \leq \frac{1}{4}n+O(1),\]and conjectures that the upper bound is optimal.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1011 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1011).

### Problem
Let $f_r(n)$ be minimal such that every graph on $n$ vertices with $\geq f_r(n)$ edges and chromatic number $\geq r$ contains a triangle. Determine $f_r(n)$.

### Context
Turán's theorem implies $f_2(n)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$. Erdős and Gallai [Er62d] proved $f_3(n)=\lfloor \frac{1}{4}(n-1)^2\rfloor+2$.

Simonovits showed in his PhD thesis (see the discussion on p. 358 of [Si74]) that\[f_r(n)=\frac{n^2}{4}-\frac{g(r)}{2}{n}+O(1),\]where $g(r)$ is the largest $m$ such that, for any triangle-free graph with chromatic number $\geq r$, at least $m$ vertices of $G$ need to be removed to obtain a bipartite graph. Simonovits [Si74] notes\[\frac{\log r}{\log\log r}r^2 \ll g(r) \ll (\log r)^2r^2.\]Hunter in the comments has noted that other results imply $g(r)\asymp r^2\log r$ - in fact\[(1/2-o(1))r^2\log r\leq g(r)\leq (2+o(1))r^2\log r.\]The lower bound follows from work of Davies and Illingworth [DaIl22] (see [[1104]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104)). The upper bound follows from work of Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender [HHKP25] on $R(3,k)$.

I think the upper bound for $g(r)$ can be improved. observe that $g(r)\le \min\{R(3,k)-2k: R(3,k)/k>r-1\}$. consequently, $g(r)\le (1+o(1))r^2\log(r)$.

Tom, the upper bound for $g$ follows from the nice construction from a couple days ago.

Argh sorry, too many bounds flying around! I'm away from my laptop now but will update soon.

Although doesn't that mean the upper bound is actually more like $2r^2\log r$?

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd: no, because their construction has $n$ vertices and no independent set of size $h_\epsilon(n):=(1+\epsilon)\sqrt{n\log n}$ for all $n>n_0(\epsilon)$ (see Theorem 1.3 of [https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19718](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19718)). and we have that $\frac{r^2\log(r)}{h_\epsilon(r^2\log(r))}= (1+\Theta(\epsilon))r$, I believe. but I could be flipping something incorrectly too.

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd:
for the other direction, observe that $g(r)\ge \min\{n: \text{ there exists an $n$-vertex triangle-free graph with chromatic number } r-2\}$. then Raphael Steiner shared this paper [https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/21M1437573](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/21M1437573) to me, which implies that $g(r)\ge (1/4-o(1))r^2 \log r$ (this improves upon a more standard application of Shearer's by a factor of two).

hopefully I did not messup converting constants.

replies.contentMd:
The result in the linked paper of Davies and Illingworth gives $r-2\leq (2+o(1)) \sqrt{n/ \log n}$ for every triangle-free graph with $n$ vertices and chromatic number $r-2$.
I believe it even implies $g(r)=n\geq (1/2-o(1)) r^2 \log r$.

Also: I get that $\frac{r^2 \log (r)}{h_\epsilon(r^2 \log(r))}$ is of the order $(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\Theta(\epsilon)) r$ rather than $(1+\Theta(\epsilon))r$, so maybe TFBlooms remark still stands that the upper bound argument actually leads to $g(r)\leq (2+o(1))(\log r) r^2$?

Probably I'm messing up constants too.. Will check it again in the morning.

Additional chromatic conditions" (Discrete Math. 7 (1974), 349–376), Simonovits states the answer is $n^2/4 -g_3(t)n/2 + O(1)$ for an explicit function $g_3(t)$. problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1013 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1013).

### Problem
Let $h_3(k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that there exists a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices with chromatic number $k$. Find an asymptotic for $h_3(k)$, and also prove\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{h_3(k+1)}{h_3(k)}=1.\]

### Context
The function $h_3(k)$ is dual to the function $f(n)$ considered in [[1104]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104), in that $h_3(k)= n$ if and only if $n$ is minimal such that $f(n)=k$.

Graver and Yackel [GrYa68] proved\[h_3(k)\gg \frac{\log k}{\log\log k}k^2.\]The bounds for $f(n)$ from [[1104]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104) imply\[\left(\frac{1}{2}-o(1)\right)k^2\log k\leq h_3(k) \leq (1+o(1))k^2\log k.\]See also [[920]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/920) for a generalisation to $K_r$-free graphs.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: zach hunter
sourceComments.contentMd:
note that if $R(3,n/k)>n$, then $n\le h_3(k)$. thus we should get an optimal construction from the best know bounds for #165.

meanwhile, the other bound should not be due to Shearer, since that (I believe) is just about independent sets. instead, you want to quote a result for chromatic number, which I believe is originally due to Johansson.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
I think this is the other way around - if $R(3,n/k)>n$ then there is a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices with independence number $\leq n/k$, and so chromatic number $\geq k$, and hence (deleting vertices if necessary to get chromatic number $=k$) $h_3(k) \leq n$.

Johansson's bound for the chromatic number of triangle-free graphs (if I've found the right result) says that $\chi(G) \ll \frac{n}{\log n}$, which implies the lower bound $h_3(k)\gg (\log k)k$, which is weaker than the Graver-Yackel bound given here.

EDIT: In fact this is the dual function to [[1104]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104).

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: I agree with Bloom.

replies.author: Wouter CvB
replies.contentMd: For the record: as in problem 1104, the application of Johansson's theorem is more subtle. It says that $\chi(G)\ll  \frac{\Delta}{ \log \Delta}$ where $\Delta$ is the maximum degree of a triangle-free graph $G$. This implies $\chi(G)\ll \sqrt {\frac{n}{\log n}}$, hence $h_3(k) \gg k^2 \log k$. The proof in a nutshell:  If $\Delta \leq \sqrt{n \log n}$ then it's immediate. Otherwise select a vertex $v$ with maximum degree and apply induction to $G-N[v]$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Aha of course, I misread Johansson's result. Incidentally, I can't find a copy of their paper anywhere online, do you know if there's a copy available somewhere?

replies.author: Wouter CvB
replies.contentMd:
Johansson's result was in a technical report ["Asymptotic choice number for triangle free graphs"](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=2059623545831993455&hl=en&oi=scholarr) from 1996, which he famously never published.
There doesn't seem to exist a stable link to the report online, and I have never seen it. However, if I remember well, the write-up in chapters 12 and 13 of the book ["Graph colouring and the probabilistic method"](https://web.xidian.edu.cn/zhangxin/files/20150823_173652.pdf)(2002) by Michael Molloy and Bruce Reed follows Johansson's proof.
It used a rather technical (semi-random) method. Since 2017 there have been shorter proofs and improvements, using e.g. entropy compression, or Lovász Local Lemma, and even just the first moment method.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
There is indeed a little mistake in wording here.
The correct version should be

Denote by $h_3(k)$ the smallest integer for which there is a graph of
$h_3(k)$ vertices which contains no triangle and has chromatic number $k$.

(note it is not because there is an example on $h_3(k)$ vertices satisfying it, all graphs with higher order have the same property.)

The related OEIS sequence is [[A292528]](https://oeis.org/A292528/list). Computing $h_3(k)$ is tough

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Thanks for checking Stijn, a crucial couple of words that makes all the difference. Corrected now.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd: There are triangle free graphs with arbitrarily large chromatic number, so the question as written doesn't seem to make sense.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: I don't see why? This question is about the relationship between the number of vertices and chromatic number in triangle-free graphs. The fact you mention is just showing $h_3(k)\to \infty$.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd: The question implies that for a fixed k, all graphs on sufficiently many vertices with chromatic number k have a triangle. But I can take a triangle free graph with chromatic number k, and then add as many vertices as I want by joining a arbitrarily large path to one of the vertices. This doesn't change the chromatic number or create a triangle.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Hmm, yes. I'll check the source later.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd: Judging by how it is linked to [920], I'd guess it's meant to be about the largest chromatic number a triangle free graph on $n$ vertices can have.

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd: Note that the latter interpretation was impossible (or way more typos were there); the chromatic number is bounded by the order, so a lower bound above $k^2$ would not be the best

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd: The source was [[Er71(-25)]](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1971-25.pdf) and has been checked.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
This is just an attempt that might solve the case \(k=3\).

We prove that\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{R(3,n+1)}{R(3,n)}=1.
\]By the Greenwood-Gleason recurrence,\[
R(3,n+1)\le R(2,n+1)+R(3,n)=(n+1)+R(3,n),
\]since \(R(2,m)=m\). Dividing by \(R(3,n)\) yields\[
\frac{R(3,n+1)}{R(3,n)}\le 1+\frac{n+1}{R(3,n)}.
\]Monotonicity gives \(R(3,n+1)\ge R(3,n)+1\), so\[
\frac{R(3,n+1)}{R(3,n)}\ge 1+\frac{1}{R(3,n)}.
\]It is known (Ajtai–Komlós–Szemerédi 1980, Kim 1995) that
\(R(3,n)=\Theta(n^2/\log n)\). Hence there exists \(c>0\) with
\(R(3,n)\ge c\,n^2/\log n\) for large \(n\), implying\[
\frac{n+1}{R(3,n)}\le\frac{(n+1)\log n}{c\,n^2}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.
\]From the lower bound we get \(\liminf R(3,n+1)/R(3,n)\ge 1+\lim 1/R(3,n)=1\).
From the upper bound and the limit above we get \(\limsup R(3,n+1)/R(3,n)\le 1+0=1\).
Thus \(\liminf=\limsup=1\), so the limit exists and equals \(1\). ∎

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
The monotonicity of $R(3,n)$ is not known to be strict, but otherwise the argument here seems to be correct.  Such a result would already have been known to Erdos at the time of [Er71], given that [Erdos himself proved](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-06.pdf) $R(3,n) \gg n^2/\log^2 n$ back in 1961, and the [Greenwood-Gleason paper](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/BF0DEBC881488344266BCD77CBBCD86B/S0008414X00030091a.pdf/combinatorial_relations_and_chromatic_graphs.pdf) is from 1955.  Looking at [[Er71](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1971-25.pdf), p.99] it seems that Erdos was attributing the $k=3$ case of determining the exact rate of growth of $R(k,l)$ as open, not the problem of establishing that the ratio $R(k,l+1)/R(k,l)$ converges to $1$.  (And Erdos seems to have mistyped the known upper and lower bounds of $R(3,l)$ (which he calls $f(3,l)$) in his equation (2);  he writes $n^2 \log n / \log\log n \ll f(3,n) \ll n^2 \log^2 n$ but I think he meant $n^2 / \log^2 n \ll f(3,n) \ll n^2 \log\log n / \log n$.  The correct order of growth $f(3,n) \asymp n^2 / \log n$ was determined [by Kim](https://people.tamu.edu/~huafei-yan/Teaching/Math689/ramsey5.pdf) in 1995.)

p.s.  It is the policy of this site to disclose all use of AI tools.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1016 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1016).

### Problem
Let $h(n)$ be minimal such that there is a graph on $n$ vertices with $n+h(n)$ edges which contains a cycle on $k$ vertices, for all $3\leq k\leq n$. Estimate $h(n)$. In particular, is it true that\[h(n) \geq \log_2n+\log_*n-O(1),\]where $\log_*n$ is the iterated logarithmic function?

### Context
Such graphs are called pancyclic. A problem of Bondy [Bo71], who claimed a proof (without details) of\[\log_2(n-1)-1\leq h(n) \leq \log_2n+\log_*n+O(1).\]Erdős [Er71] believed the upper bound is closer to the truth, but could not even prove $h(n)-\log_2n\to \infty$.

A proof of the above lower bound is provided by Griffin [Gr13]. The first published proof of the upper bound appears to be in Chapter 4.5 of George, Khodkar, and Wallis [GKW16].

sourceComments.contentMd:
Some updated references arising from use of [Gemini](https://gemini.google.com/share/ca486d2a4276) (after 5 mins) and [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/68f2e107-c4a0-800e-9955-057d700685e6) (after 7 mins).

Bondy's paper actually claims the slightly weaker bounds $\log_2 (n-1) - 1 \leq h(n) \leq \log_2 n + \log_* n + O(1)$, contrary to what Erdos writes, but with no proof given for either inequality.  An actual proof of the lower bound was only provided in 2013 [by Bi-George-Rui](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.0274), though [this 2023 paper of Alon and Krivelevich](https://www.math.tau.ac.il/~krivelev/pancyclic-rg.pdf) suggests that a equivalent statement was [established by Shi in 1994](https://pdf.sciencedirectassets.com/271536/1-s2.0-S0012365X00X02312/1-s2.0-0012365X94900310/main.pdf) (but it is difficult for me to confirm this as the notation is somewhat different).  An [obscure 1996 paper of Jia](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=1431994) (which I was not able to directly obtain, but could see their results mentioned in [this 2014 survey of Lai and Liu](https://combinatorialpress.com/article/jcmcc/Volume%20091/vol-091-paper%204.pdf)) establishes $h(n) \leq \frac{3}{2} \log_2 n + 1$ for all $n$ and $h(n) \leq \log_2 n + \log_2 \log_2 n + O(1)$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and also makes the conjecture #1016.  The first literature proof of the upper bound $h(n) \leq \log_2 n + \log_* n + O(1)$ that seems to exist is in Chapter 4.5 of [this 2016 book of George, Khodkar, and Wallis](https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=3495006).   The consensus seems to be that Bondy's bounds, which are now proven in the literature, remain the state of the art except for very small $n$ where there is some work by [George, Marr, and Wallis](https://combinatorialpress.com/article/jcmcc/Volume%20086/vol-086-paper%207.pdf).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1017 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1017).

### Problem
Let $f(n,k)$ be such that every graph on $n$ vertices and $k$ edges can be partitioned into at most $f(n,k)$ edge-disjoint complete graphs. Estimate $f(n,k)$ for $k>n^2/4$.

### Context
The function $f(n,k)$ is sometimes called the clique partition number.

Erdős, Goodman, and Pósa [EGP66] proved that $f(n,k)\leq n^2/4$ for all $k$ (and in fact the complete graphs can be taken to be edges and triangles), which is best possible in general, as witnessed for example by a complete bipartite graph. In [Er71] Erdő asks vaguely whether this result can be 'sharpened' for $k>n^2/4$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceMetadata.statusNote: This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
researchNotes: The function $f(n,k)$ is sometimes called the clique partition number.

In [Er71] Erdő asks vaguely whether this result can be 'sharpened' for $k>n^2/4$.

Lovász [Lo68] proved that every graph on $n$ vertices and $k$ edges is the union of $\binom{n}{2}-k+t$ complete graphs, where $t$ is maximal such that $t^2-t\leq \binom{n}{2}-k$, but without the assumption that the complete graphs are edge disjoint. Lovász's result is sharp in many cases.

If $k>n^2/4$ and the graph contains no $K_4$ then this is equivalent to finding the minimum number of edge disjoint triangles. This special case was also asked about by Erdős. A complete answer was provided by Györi and Keszegh [GyKe17], who proved that every $K_4$-free graph with $n$ vertices and $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+m$ edges contins $m$ pairwise edge disjoint triangles.

See also [[184]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/184) for an analogous problem decomposing into edges and cycles, and [[583]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/583) for decomposing into paths. The clique partition problem for chordal graphs is the subject of [[81]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/81).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1020 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1020).

### Problem
Let $f(n;r,k)$ be the maximal number of edges in an $r$-uniform hypergraph which contains no set of $k$ many independent edges.

For all $r\geq 3$,\[f(n;r,k)=\max\left(\binom{rk-1}{r}, \binom{n}{r}-\binom{n-k+1}{r}\right).\]

### Context
Erdős and Gallai [ErGa59] proved this is true when $r=2$ (when $r=2$ this also follows from the [Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Ko%E2%80%93Rado_theorem)).

The conjectured form of $f(n;r,k)$ is the best possible, as witnessed by two examples: all $r$-edges on a set of $rk-1$ many vertices, and all edges on a set of $n$ vertices which contain at least one element of a fixed set of $k-1$ vertices.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceMetadata.statusNote: Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample.
researchNotes: Erdős and Gallai [ErGa59] proved this is true when $r=2$ (when $r=2$ this also follows from the Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem).

The conjectured form of $f(n;r,k)$ is the best possible, as witnessed by two examples: all $r$-edges on a set of $rk-1$ many vertices, and all edges on a set of $n$ vertices which contain at least one element of a fixed set of $k-1$ vertices.
Frankl [Fr87] proved $f(n;r,k) \leq (k-1)\binom{n-1}{r-1}$.

This is sometimes known as the Erdős matching conjecture. Note that the second term in the maximum dominates when $n\geq (r+1)k$. There are many partial results towards this, establishing the conjecture in different ranges. These can be separated into two regimes. For small $n$:- The conjecture is trivially true if $n<kr$. - Kleitman [Kl68] when $n=kr$. - Frankl [Fr17] whenkr \leq n\leq k\left(r+\frac{1}{2r^{2r+1}}\right). - Kolupaev and Kupavskii [KoKu23] when $r\geq 5$, $k>101r^3$, andkr \leq n < k\left(r+\frac{1}{100r}\right).

For large $n$:- Erdős [Er65d] when $n>kc_r$ (where $c_r$ depends on $r$ in some unspecified fashion). - Frankl and Füredi [Fr87] when $n>100 k^2r$. - Bollobás, Daykin, and Erdős [BDE76] when $n\geq 2kr^3$. - Frankl, Rödl, and Ruciński [FRR12] when $r=3$ and $n\geq 4k$. - Huang, Loh, and Sudakov [HLS12] when $n\geq 3kr^2$. - Frankl, Luczak, and Mieczkowska [FLM12] when $n> 2k\frac{r^2}{\log r}$. - Luczak and Mieczkowska [LuMi14] when $r=3$ (for all $k$).

The mistake happens in Lemma 4 (which is referred to in the updated arxiv version when dealing with page 11, II, bad -> good), case 2,

If $F \in \mathcal F^{i_t}$, it is not that for all $1 \le k \le r$ we have $\mathcal C_{i_kj_k}(F)=F$.

A simple counterexample for the whole thing (the algorithm in section 3) can be obtained with $n=6, k=2, s=3$ and $\mathcal F= \{12,13,14,15,16,23,24,34\},$ where $A=34$ and $B=25$ or $26$.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1029 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1029).

### Problem
If $R(k)$ is the Ramsey number for $K_k$, the minimal $n$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $K_k$, then\[\frac{R(k)}{k2^{k/2}}\to \infty.\]

### Context
In [Er93] Erdős offers \$100 for a proof of this and \$1000 for a disproof, but says 'this last offer is to some extent phoney: I am sure that [this] is true (but I have been wrong before).'

Erdős  and Szekeres [ErSz35] proved\[k2^{k/2} \ll R(k) \leq \binom{2k-1}{k-1}.\]One of the first applications of the probabilistic method pioneered by Erdős gives\[R(k) \geq (1+o(1))\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}e}k2^{k/2},\]which Spencer [Sp75] improved by a factor of $2$ to\[R(k) \geq (1+o(1))\frac{\sqrt{2}}{e}k2^{k/2}.\]See also [[77]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/77) for a more general problem concerning $\lim R(k)^{1/k}$, and discussion of upper bounds for $R(k)$.

### Deliverable

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1030 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1030).

### Problem
Let $R(k,l)$ be the usual Ramsey number: the smallest $n$ such that if the edges of $K_n$ are coloured red and blue then there exists either a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_l$.

Prove the existence of some $c>0$ such that\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{R(k+1,k)}{R(k,k)}> 1+c.\]

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Sós, who could not even prove whether $R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)>k^c$ for any $c>1$.

It is trivial that $R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)\geq k-2$. Burr, Erdős, Faudree, and Schelp [BEFS89] proved\[R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)\geq 2k-5.\]See also [[544]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/544) for a similar question concerning $R(3,k)$, and [[1014]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1014) for the general off-diagonal case.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: zach hunter
sourceComments.contentMd: personally I find #181 more relevant (compared to #576). naive DRC says that $\approx 2^n(1-c)^{-n}$ vertices should at least suffice. and for fixed $c>0$, the arguments of Tikhomirov can show there is $c'\in (0,c)$ so that $2^n (1-c')^{-n}$ vertices suffice for large $n$.

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd:
I'll note that the "blow-up case" should be clear here (at least if you want $m=(1+o(1))2^n$ vertices).

let $H_0$ be any $m_0$ graph with minimum degree $>m_0/2$. by Dirac's theorem, $H_0$ should contain a Hamilton cycle, $C=v_1,\dots,v_{m_0}$.

now, consider consider the homomorphism $\phi$ which sends the $i$-th layer of the hypercube to $v_{i\pmod{m_0}}$. this is clearly a homomorphism, and the pre-image of any vertex has size $\sim 2^n/m_0$ (since the binomial coefficeints do not vary significantly).

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd: actually, maybe by an appropriately quantified blow-up lemma, we can actually get a $(1+o(1))2^n$ bound in general?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: What do you mean by a blow-up lemma in this case?

replies.author: zach hunter
replies.contentMd:
"the blow-up lemma" is a very deep result about doing spanning or nearly spanning embeddings of bounded degree $H$ into graphs $G$, based off of the regularity partition of $G$ (essentially if various parameters are right, we can embed $H$ as long as it has homomorphism into a certain auxiliary graph based on the partition).

usually the bounds of various dependencies are fairly poor. but since we are embedding something bipartite (and just using pathwidth, rather than a more complicated), I could fathom it being possible for the bounds to work out (at least if we are willing to just aim for a nearly spanning embedding).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Aha, you meant [THAT blow-up lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blow-up_lemma), just with actually good dependencies. Thanks!

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1038 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1038).

### Problem
Determine the infimum and supremum of\[\lvert \{ x\in \mathbb{R} : \lvert f(x)\rvert < 1\}\rvert\]as $f\in \mathbb{R}[x]$ ranges over all non-constant monic polynomials, all of whose roots are real and in the interval $[-1,1]$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that the measure of the set in question is always at most $2\sqrt{2}$ under the assumption that all the roots are in $\{-1,1\}$, and conjecture this is the best possible upper bound.

They also note that the infimum of the set in question is less than $2$, as witnessed by $f(x)=(x+1)(x-1)^m$ for $m\geq 3$. They further note that if the roots are restricted to $[-2,2]$ then the infimum is zero, as witnessed by a small perturbation of the Chebyshev polynomials.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
GPT-5.4 Thinking has written up and completed some material in this thread for the $\inf$ problem in these [progress notes](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1u2zqzI06c6plsL9hZUPVHTLIAyUTFzsO/view).

Summary of material:

- Tao's notes prove some results for a minimizer $\mu$ with a convenient assumption of minimal variance. It turns out this assumption can be removed. So for a minimizer $\mu$, it must be a point mass in each interval of $E_\mu := \{ U_\mu > 0 \}$. Moreover, up to reflection and translation, $\mu(\{-1\}) \ge 1/2$ and $\text{supp }\mu \subseteq \{-1\} \cup [0, 1]$.

- Under some regularity assumptions on $\mu$, first variation is worked out. Let
$$ \lambda_\partial := \sum_{a \in \text{bd }E_\mu} \frac{1}{|U'_\mu(a)|} \delta_a, \quad Z_0 := \{ U_\mu = 0 \} \setminus \text{bd }E_\mu. $$
Then there is $c \ge 0$ and measure $\xi$ supported on $Z_0$, not both zero, such that
$$ \lambda := c \lambda_\partial + \xi $$
satisfies: 1) $U_\lambda \ge 0$ in $[-1, 1] \setminus \{ U_\mu = 0 \}$ and Lebesgue-a.e.; 2) $U_\lambda = 0$ $\mu$-a.e.

- We do calculations related to the ansatz we're doing in the thread, recovering the description of the conjectured minimizer. We also record an alternative transport viewpoint using pushforward measure that potentially does similar things.

sourceComments.author: DustinMixon
sourceComments.contentMd:
I am curious: what is the latest status for this conjecture?

That is, what are the best known bounds, what is expected to be true, and what is still missing?

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: The current commentary accurately records what we actually know for sure: the sup is known to be exactly $2\sqrt{2}$, and the inf is between 1.519 and 1.835; [these notes](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/erdos-1038-2.pdf) basically contain these results.  The upper bound is likely to be sharp, but we do not yet have a proof.  One needs to construct a dual measure for each candidate set $E$ of measure at most $1.835$, namely a probability measure $\nu$ supported outside $E$ for which $U_\nu$ is non-negative on $[-1,1]$.  We can do this when $E$ is an interval, and it seems from numerics and theory that we can also do it when $E$ is the union of a large interval and a small interval (which was the most likely candidate for a counterexample to the conjecture to be located), but we don't have a clear way forward to construct this dual measure for general $E$.  (But in the case where $E$ is the union of finitely many intervals, it seems the candidate measure should have a Cauchy-Stieltjes transform that looks something like a square root of a rational function with singularities at the endpoints of the intervals.)

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: As a warmup, GPT-5.4 Thinking did some [check](https://chatgpt.com/share/69b5c2fc-f05c-8010-895a-9e1023675532) on this note. Good news is there is no substantive error found. There are some minor things to fix, but we don't have to fix them now.

replies.author: MalekZ
replies.contentMd: Professor Tao mentioned that the candidate dual measure $\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$ should have a Cauchy–Stieltjes transform resembling a square root of a rational function with singularities at the interval endpoints. Has anyone attempted to make this ansatz explicit for the two-interval case (one large interval and one small interval near $1 - \varepsilon$)? The numerical evidence from the LP and AlphaEvolve work seems to consistently produce measures with that shape; a few atoms plus a continuous part with square-root behavior. It seems like writing down a closed-form family parametrised by $\varepsilon$ and verifying $U_{\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}} \geq 0$ analytically might be more tractable than pushing the numerics further. Is the obstacle here that the atom locations don't have clean closed forms, or is there a deeper issue?

I'm working on writing up the first variation result outlined in this thread.

Interestingly, GPT-5.4 Thinking has already found a gap. I used an "arbitrary" test measure $\nu$ to conclude $U_\lambda \ge 0$ from $\int U_\lambda \,d\nu \ge 0$. But there was a Hahn-Banach modification which constrains $\nu$ to not really be arbitrary!

Good news is this appears to be fixable with more arguments and hypotheses.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
Against all (or at least some) odds, I have constructed a dual measure $\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$ for $\varepsilon = 0.002$. We have $\min U_{\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}} \approx 1.5 \cdot 10^{-4}$ at $t \approx 0.989$. That the minimum is positive has been validated on at least an order of $10^5$ points (actually more and with a few other methods). In general, it is difficult to validate such things because the optimization generally overfits to the sampling, and "denser" sampling can reveal that the solution is actually invalid. (This is a general property optimization methods, which many people misinterpret in the case of AI as the AI being "tricky" or something like that.) However, in this case we seem to have enough margin (on the order of $10^{-4}$), and enough things check out that I think we can be reasonably confident this is valid. This seems notable because AlphaEvolve was not able to achieve this task after running for over 24 hours. The algorithm is the "standard" cutting plane method for solving LP. However, it underwent several rounds of practical improvements, some coming from human suggestions. This highlights an interesting phenomenon that humans still possess some kind of "intangible" cognitive abilities that allow one to succeed in tasks that current LLMs may get stuck, even though the human does not clearly possess any extra knowledge in particular. On the other hand, without LLMs, I can say with confidence that this task is way out of reach for me, after seeing what is required in the final code. In any case, the final code is a huge mess, and will need some improvements before I try to tackle lower $\varepsilon$ such as $0.001$. The runtime for $\varepsilon = 0.002$ is 20-25 minutes and could go up with lower $\varepsilon$. [Description of $\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$](https://pastebin.com/gUbqNi59); [Plot of $\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$](https://i.postimg.cc/RZghwS4q/eps_0002_lambda.png); [Plot of $U_{\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}}$](https://i.postimg.cc/C5pxwdH6/eps_0002_U_lambda.png); [Plot of $U_{\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}}$ (zoom)](https://i.postimg.cc/9XyfJtCv/eps_0002_U_lambda_zoom.png); [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/695aa530-e7e4-8010-9869-4aa1aa606a2b); [Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1lG-iEE3btkMbeHANE7KiZngHpBbNpK5p?usp=sharing
).

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Thanks for this!

I'm suspecting that the optimal $\lambda = \lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$ takes an explicit form, relating to a function of the form
$$ f(z) = \frac{z+A_\varepsilon}{(z-(x_L+\varepsilon)) (z-x_R) (z-1)} \sqrt{ (z-a) (z-1+\varepsilon)} $$
for some parameter $A_\varepsilon$ (I'm guessing it is a little bit larger than 1.2, but not sure on this - $-A_\varepsilon$ should be where $U_{\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}}$ attains a local minimum) and a suitable choice of square root.  The measure $\lambda$ should be like the imaginary part of this function, divided by $\pi$, so should take the form
$$ \lambda = \mathrm{Res}(f;x_L+\varepsilon) \delta_{x_L+\varepsilon} + \mathrm{Res}(f; x_R) \delta_{x_R} + g(x) 1_{[a,1-\varepsilon]}(x)\ dx$$
(possibly up to sign error) with $g(x) = \frac{x+A_\varepsilon}{\pi (x-(x_L+\varepsilon)) (x-x_R) (x-1)} \sqrt{(x-a) (x-1+\varepsilon)}$, and its Hilbert transform $H\lambda$ should look like the real part, thus (up to some possible sign error and/or factor of $\pi$)
$$ H\lambda = \frac{x+A_\varepsilon}{(x-(x_L+\varepsilon))(x-x_R) (x-1)} \sqrt{|x-a| |x-1-\varepsilon|} 1_{x \notin [a, 1-\varepsilon]}.$$
As usual, one should try to set $A_\varepsilon$ so that $U_\lambda$ vanishes on $[a,1-\varepsilon]$.  I think things are set up so that the derivative $-H\lambda$ of $U_\lambda$ is positive just to the right of $1-\varepsilon$ and negative just to the left of $a$, so that we get a good shot at positivity of $U_\lambda$.

Note in this ansatz that the densty $g$ of $\lambda$ does not become singular at the right-endpoint $1-\varepsilon$ of the interval $[a,1-\varepsilon]$, in contrast to the $\varepsilon=1$ case where there is a square root blowup at $1$.  Instead we have a square root vanishing at $1-\varepsilon$ but also a simple pole at $1$ which in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$ should recover the behavior of $\lambda^{(0)}$.

At this point I'm not confident in my ability to avoid sign errors, but given that ChatGPT was able to previously work out a viable $\lambda$ in the $\varepsilon=0$ case, it might be able to confirm this ansatz for positive $\varepsilon$ as well.  Previously my ansatz was losing a factor of $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ when evaluating $U_\lambda$ near $1$, but here I think one is instead gaining a factor of this form, so one is potentially in better shape (though I don't understand what $U_\lambda$ is doing near the opposite endpoint -1, which is the other place where positivity could be in doubt.)

Some progress on this.

In short: I'm not sure if such a measure $\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$ exists for all $\varepsilon > 0$ whose support avoids $(x_L+\varepsilon,x_R) \cup (1-\varepsilon,1)$ with the property that $U_\lambda \ge 0$ on $[-1,1]$.

First, in order to perform these computations we need the conjectured minimizer to higher precision. We worked this out to be:
$$ \begin{align*}
& a \in [0.804461, 0.804463], A \in [0.8245215, 0.8245220], \\
& x_L \in [-1.8081076, -1.8081072], x_R \in [0.0263228, 0.0263233].
\end{align*} $$
This should be useful for other purposes as well (such as running AlphaEvolve for smaller $\varepsilon$). In practice we take the midpoint i.e. $x_L = -1.8081074$, $x_R = 0.02632305$.

$\textbf{First try}$. We put $\text{supp }\lambda$ on the endpoints $\{x_L+\varepsilon,x_R,1-\varepsilon,1\}$ exactly ($4$ atoms). Then it reduces to a linear programming (LP) problem, and we use the cutting-plane method.

This turns out to work for large $\varepsilon$ but not smaller $\varepsilon$. Specifically, it works for $\varepsilon \in \{0.1,0.05\}$ but doesn't work for $\varepsilon \in \{0.02,0.01,0.005,\dots\}$.

$\textbf{Second try}$. We add another atom in the interval $(x_R, 1-\varepsilon)$ to $\text{supp }\lambda$. For each position of this atom, we run an LP algorithm. A coarse sweep works for $\varepsilon = 0.02$ but not $\varepsilon = 0.01$. Then, we do local refinement to target the best region, which works for $\varepsilon = 0.01$ but not for $\varepsilon = 0.005$.

$\textbf{Third try}$. We add $2$ atoms. But now optimization becomes tricky. We employ the [Nelder-Mead method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelder%E2%80%93Mead_method) to optimize, but it still doesn't work for $\varepsilon = 0.005$.

$\textbf{Fourth try}$. We use support augmentation: we start with $4$ original atoms, find the "weakest" position where $U_\lambda$ is minimized, and put an atom there. Then we iterate until $U_\lambda \ge 0$ on $[-1,1]$.

For $\varepsilon = 0.005$, a solution was found with $10$ atoms.

For $\varepsilon = 0.002$, the algorithm unfortunately stagnates at $26$ atoms and was not able to find a solution.

$\textbf{Conclusion}$. I believe I have numerical evidence that such a measure $\lambda^{(\varepsilon)}$ exists for large $\varepsilon$, specifically $\varepsilon \ge 0.005$. But I am not sure whether it exists for all $\varepsilon > 0$; perhaps the strategy so far is not smart enough in some way. In particular, AlphaEvolve might be smarter!

Details can be found in this [ChatGPT chat](https://chatgpt.com/share/69550ae5-6d00-8010-9b9f-94d264a56526).

Very nice natso26! I wonder whether it suffices to obtain $U_\lambda > 0$ only on $\{-1\} \cup [0,1]$, since Tao showed that one may assume the support of a minimizing measure $\mu$ is contained in this set. If so, there may be room to take $\varepsilon$ smaller.

In fact, using this observation, I was able to obtain a small improvement to the $\inf$ lower bound using two atoms, showing that it is at least $1.614$ and that we may assume $(-1.53,0] \subseteq \{ U_\mu > 0 \}$. I am quite confident that this can be further improved by considering three or four atoms.

First, we performed a search for useful measures $\nu = \delta_a + B\,\delta_b$, with $a \le 0 \le b$ and $B > 0$, such that $U_\nu(x) > 0$ for all $x \in [-1,1]$. I asked ChatGPT to generate code for a simple brute-force search and then modified it slightly for efficiency, it is available [here](https://notebooksharing.space/view/da97d7138ff952887f9265bad00186e0548e7653fae89e73f3482fa7745a4a26#displayOptions=). This produced the admissible region for $(a,b)$ shown [here](https://postimg.cc/T5DZD06s). The minimum possible value of $a$ is $-1.518$ at $b = 0.395$, in agreement with J_Koizumi_144’s approach to the $\inf$ lower bound.

Next, we searched for measures $\nu$ of the same form, but requiring only that $U_\nu(x) > 0$ for $x \in \{-1\} \cup [0,1]$. This yields a larger admissible region, shown [here](https://postimg.cc/H8yfyzgK). The minimum possible value of $a$ is now $-1.614$, attained at $b = 0.60$. For each $a \in [-1.614,0]$, there is a corresponding interval $(b_{\min}(a), b_{\max}(a))$ of admissible values of $b$. Now assume that the supremum of $[-1.614,-\sqrt{2}] \setminus \{ U_\mu > 0 \}$ exists and equals $a_0$. Then, by the duality principle, we have $(a_0,0) \sqcup (b_{\min}(a_0), b_{\max}(a_0)) \subseteq \{ U_\mu > 0 \}$, and hence $-a_0 + b_{\max}(a_0) - b_{\min}(a_0) \leq \lvert \{ U_\mu > 0 \} \rvert$. [Plotting](https://postimg.cc/8J32c32S) $-a + b_{\max}(a) - b_{\min}(a)$, we find that it is at least $1.835$ for $a \in [-1.53,-\sqrt{2}]$, and that it decreases to $1.614$ as $a$ decreases further. This establishes the claimed bounds.

replies.contentMd:
Ok, I think the logic is correct. Anyone else is welcome to check.

Logic: Let $\mu$ be a minimizer. By Tao's results, $\mu$ is supported on $\{-1\} \cup [0,1]$. Assume for contradiction that $|\{U_\mu > 0\}| < 1.614$. Then the largest interval $(a_0, 0] \subset \{U_\mu > 0\}$ must have $a_0 < 1.614$.

By the admissible plot, for such $a_0$ there is a corresponding interval $(b_\min(a_0), b_\max(a_0))$ such that $\nu = \nu_{a_0,b} := \delta_{a_0} + B(b) \delta_b$ for $b \in (b_\min(a_0), b_\max(a_0))$ satisfies $U_\nu > 0$ on $\{-1\} \cup [0,1]$.

By duality, $\int U_\nu \,d\mu = \int U_\mu \,d\nu$. LHS is $> 0$ due to support assumptions. RHS is $U_\mu(a_0)+B(b)U_\mu(b)$. $U_\mu(a_0) = 0$ because $a_0$ is a boundary point. Thus, $U_\mu(b) > 0$.

We conclude $(a_0, 0] \cup (b_\min(a_0), b_\max(a_0)) \subset \{U_\mu > 0\}$. When we plot the length of $(a_0, 0] \cup (b_\min(a_0), b_\max(a_0))$ as a function of $a_0$, it comes out at least $1.614$, a contradiction.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Following J Koizumi's approach which builds on jspier's approach, I've proved $\inf \ge 1.7205$ with empirical numerical verification (gives enough confidence in practice but for a proof one needs to do further rigorous computations, which can be done later).

This is pretty close to the conjectured inf of $\approx 1.835$, suggesting maybe this approach can get even closer?

The idea is to optimize $3$ atoms. For $d=2.6476$ and $M=1.7205$, for each $a \in [-M,-\sqrt 2]$, there exist $k(a)$ and $m(a)$ such that the measure
$$ \lambda_a = \delta_a + k(a) \delta_{-\sqrt 2 - a} + m(a) \delta_{a + d} $$
satisfies $U_{\lambda_a} > 0$ on $\{-1\} \cup [0,1]$.

As with J Koizumi's logic, one of $a, -\sqrt 2 - a, a + d$ must be in $\{U_\mu > 0\}$ for a minimizer $\mu$. Since we know $(-\sqrt 2, 0] \subset \{U_\mu > 0\}$, $|\{U_\mu > 0\}|$ is at least $\sqrt 2 + (M - \sqrt 2) = M$.

replies.author: jspier
replies.contentMd:
Nice work, natso26! I had already given up on the three atom approach, and I am surprised that you managed to push it further. This motivated me to look at the four atom case. However, before doing so I'm going to show that we may assume $[-1.708,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$ for a minimizing measure $\mu$.

For $a \in [-1.708,-\sqrt{2}]$ and $b \in [0,1.836+a]$, consider
$$
\nu_{a,b} = \delta_a + (1.395-b)\delta_b + C\,\delta_{1.071-b},
$$
where $C>0$ is chosen so that $U_{\nu_{a,b}}(-1)=0.0001$. As can be seen [here](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/jhxbwiyy3p), we have $U_{\nu_{a,b}} > 0$ on $\{-1\} \cup [0,1]$.

We now claim that $[-1.708,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$. Assume otherwise, then the infimum of $\{U_\mu>0\}$ is $a_0 \in [-1.708,0]$, with $U_\mu(a_0)=0$. Since $U_{\nu_{a_0,b}}>0$ on $\{-1\}\cup[0,1]$ for every $b \in [0,1.836+a_0]$, by the duality principle, either $b$ or $1.071-b$ belongs to $\{U_\mu>0\}$. Note that both $b$ and $1.071-b$ are positive and are never equal to each other. It follows that $\{U_\mu>0\} \cap (0,+\infty)$ has measure at least $1.836+a_0$. Since we also have $(a_0,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$, we conclude that $|\{U_\mu>0\}| \geq 1.836$, and therefore $\mu$ cannot be a minimizing measure.

Now we turn to the four atom approach. We are going to show that $\inf \geq 1.8$. For $a \in [-1.8,-\sqrt{2}]$, consider
$$\lambda_a=\delta_a + 1.08\,\delta_{a+1.8} + 0.2107\,\delta_{a+2.66996}+ 0.1326\,\delta_{a+2.79}.$$
As can be checked [here](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/n7eq5iopin), we have $U_{\lambda_a} > 0$ on $[-1,1]$. Therefore, for $a \in [-1.8,-1.708)$, at least one of $a$, $a+1.8$, $a+2.66996$, $a+2.79$ belongs to $\{U_\mu>0\}$. Note that for $a$ in this range these four numbers are distinct, and none of them lies in $[-1.708,0]$. It follows that $|\{U_\mu>0\} \setminus [-1.708,0]| \geq 1.8 - 1.708$. Since we already know that $[-1.708,0] \subseteq \{U_\mu>0\}$, we conclude that $\inf \geq 1.8$.

Finally, I would like to mention that I did not optimize these parameters, and there is likely room for further improvement. The measures above were obtained using the program that I shared [earlier](https://notebooksharing.space/view/da97d7138ff952887f9265bad00186e0548e7653fae89e73f3482fa7745a4a26#displayOptions), together with some experimentation in Desmos.
