sourceComments.author: Yongxi Lin
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think there is some confusion about this problem.

Problem 1 of [EHP58] is asking about the infimum/supremum of $|\{x\in\mathbb{R}: |f(x)|<1\}|$ over all monic polynomials $f$ with all its (real) roots contained in $[-1,1]$. There's no dependence on the degree of a polynomial, and I was kind of confused by the current statement on the website when I was trying to formalize this in Lean.

Problem 2 of the same source is asking about the infimum of $|\{x\in\mathbb{C}: |f(x)|<1\}|$ over all monic polynomials $f$ of degree $n$ with all its roots contained in the closed unit disk of the complex plane (note that there's a dependence on the degree of a polynomial here). This is an entirely different problem as it is asking about the two dimensional measure, and Pommerenke's result is about the two dimensional measure.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have explored this notion of "dual measure" $\lambda$ associated with a candidate minimizing measure $\mu$, with [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/share/694bfb79-7470-8010-8e68-14114649a5c3).

First, recall that we claim that a measure $\lambda := \lambda(\mu)$ can be constructed possessing the properties:
1) $U_\lambda \geq 0$ on $[-1,1]$.
2) $U_\lambda = 0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.
3) $\text{supp }\lambda \subset \{U = 0\}$. More precisely,
$$ \lambda = \sum_{a \in \text{bd}(\{U > 0\})} \frac{1}{|U_\mu'(a)|} \delta_a + \xi, \quad \text{supp }\xi \subset \{U = 0\} \setminus \text{bd}(\{U > 0\}). $$

$\textbf{Two Diracs}$. The case of $\mu_p = (1-p)\delta_{-1} + p\delta_1$.

In this case, Tao has computed $p \approx 0.1459$ is minimizing within this family. However, numerically, the constructed $\lambda$ according to the formula above does not satisfy the three properties.

More precisely, it is indeed true that $U_\lambda(-1) \approx 0$, $U_\lambda(1) \approx 0$ as required. But it is not true that $U_\lambda \geq 0$ on $[-1,1]$; it dips to $\approx -0.23$ somewhere near $1$. Quick numerical check confirms this is not rounding error but is truly negative, but I did not attempt to confirm any digit. See images [Plot for $U_\mu$](https://i.postimg.cc/nLSmdYCR/U_mu_p_01459.png), [Plot for $U_\lambda$](https://i.postimg.cc/nLSmdYCG/U_lambda_p_01459.png).

This means that, by first variation, this $\mu_p$ for $p \approx 0.1459$ is not a local minimizer.

$\textbf{Corollary}$. Any linear combination of two Diracs is not a local minimizer.

$\textbf{Proof}$. If the two Diracs are not at $-1,1$, we can pull them apart. Let's look at the interval of $\{U > 0\}$ containing $-1$. Suppose this interval is fixed and we move $1$ rightward. This decreases the potential $U_\mu$ at the endpoints; therefore the endpoints must move closer to $-1$, decreasing its length. By symmetry, the interval containing $1$ also decreases its length. Hence this is not a local minimizer.

Now suppose the two Diracs are at $-1,1$. By Tao's calculations, the only possibility for a local minimizer is at $p \approx 0.1459$. But we have argued above this is not a local minimizer, either. So two Diracs are not local minimizers. $\blacksquare$

$\textbf{Conjectured global minimizer}$. This is
$$ \mu = A\delta_{-1} + f(x) 1_{[a,1]}(x) \,dx, \quad f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\cdot \frac{x + (1 - A\sqrt{2(1+a)})}{(x+1) \sqrt{(1-x)(x-a)}}, $$
$a \approx 0.805$, $A \approx 0.825$.

The dual measure $\lambda$ has an explicit form
$$ \lambda = \zeta_L\delta_{x_L} + \zeta_R\delta_{x_R} + g(x) 1_{[a,1]} \, dx. $$
Here $x_L \approx -1.808$, $x_R \approx 0.026$ are the two boundary points of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$. We have $\zeta_L = 1/|U_\mu'(x_L)| \approx 0.922$, $\zeta_R = 1/|U_\mu'(x_R)| \approx 1.653$. And
$$ g(x) = \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{(1-x)(x-a)}} \left( c_0 + \frac{\zeta_L R(x_L)}{x-x_L} + + \frac{\zeta_R R(x_R)}{x-x_R} \right), $$
where $R(z) = \sqrt{(z-a)(z-1)}$ is taken on the branch with $R(z) \sim z$ as $z \to \infty$; for real $x<a$ this is $R(x) = -\sqrt{(x-a)(x-1)}$. Finally, $c_0 \approx 2.805$ is chosen so that $U_\lambda(x) = 0$ for $x \in [a,1]$. Note that no attempts were made to confirm the numerical digits.

This $\lambda$ satisfies all three properties, as numerically verified by code. See also the [Plot for $U_\mu$ and $U_\lambda$](https://i.postimg.cc/W4YZ96hX/conj_minimizer_U_mu_U_lambda_overlay.png).

Regarding Tao's comment about Schwarz-Christoffel mapping, ChatGPT explains that "...the square-root endpoints $a,1$ behave like SC “prevertices” with exponent $-1/2$..."; the full explanation is in the chat but I do not claim accuracy.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Thanks for doing the (ChatGPT-assisted) analysis!  By the way, I think the $U_\lambda$ plot in the two Diracs case is just a repeat of the $U_\mu$ plot with different axes (a ChatGPT hallucination perhaps?).

The dual function $\lambda = \zeta_L \delta_{x_L} + \zeta_R \delta_{X_R} + g(x) 1_{[a,1]}\ dx$ could be the key to actually showing that the conjectural extremizer $\mu$ is the actual infimum.  Suppose we have some competing extremizer $\tilde \mu = \mu + \eta$ to $\mu$, which we can take to have a similar structure of a large mass at $-1$ and some remaining mass somewhere in $(0,1]$, so $U_{\tilde \mu} = U_\mu + U_\eta$ (with $\eta$ a signed measure of total variation at most $2$) similarly is positive on a large interval containing $(-1,0)$ but also additionally is positive on $\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta > 0 \}$.

Morally speaking, the effect of $U_\eta$ on the large interval is to increase its length by
$$ \approx \int U_\eta\ d(\zeta_L \delta_{x_L} + \zeta_R \delta_{x_R})$$
although this is just the linearized (first variation) approximation and there is a correction term I don't understand yet (though the convexity properties of $U_\mu$ suggest that the correction term may mostly have a favorable sign).  Ignoring this correction for now, we can write this increase as
$$ \int U_\eta\ d\lambda - \int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx = \int U_\lambda(x)\ d\eta - \int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx.$$
So, morally speaking, to establish the global infimum, one needs an inequality of the form
$$ \int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx \leq |\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta(x) > 0\}| + \int U_\lambda(x)\ d\eta$$

(One could also add in the contribution in the region between $[a,1]$ and the large interval where $U_\mu + U_\eta$ becomes positive, but this looks tricky to exploit.)

The term $U_\lambda(x)\ d\eta$ is non-negative (and would vanish if the modification $\eta$ is restricted to $\{-1\} \cup [a,1]$), so the main issue is to see to what extent
$\int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx$ is controlled by $|\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta(x) > 0\}|$.  If $U_\eta$ and $g$ were both bounded (by sufficiently small constants) then there would be a clear route to getting this control.  Unfortunately $g$ has a mild singularity at the endpoints of $[a,1]$, and $U_\eta$ also can have logarithmic singularities.  However, $U_\eta$ is of bounded mean oscillation (BMO), and thus obeys distributional inequalities such as the John-Nirenberg inequality that can be used in some applications as a substitute for boundedness.

It may be that one has to do some brute force numerics to cover the space of all possible $\eta$ by some finite number of balls in weak topologies and verify the required inequality to sufficient accuracy on each ball, although first one needs to control the error in the linearized analysis.

I am on vacation right now, but in a few days I might set up some further AlphaEvolve experiments to see if there is a chance to prove inequalities such as $\int_a^1 U_\eta(x) g(x)\ dx \leq |\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta(x) > 0\}|$ which the above analysis suggests would go a long way to establishing the global infimum property.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I don't think one can proceed purely through variations here, because the quantity $|\{ U_{\tilde \mu} > 0\}|$ does not vary in a differentiable (or even continuous) fashion with respect to $\tilde \mu$.  In particular, if one were to consider a path of measures $\mu + t\eta$ with $0 \leq t \leq 1$, the quantity $|\{ U_{\mu+t\eta} > 0\}|$ would immediately experience a jump discontinuity by $\{ x \in [a,1]: U_\eta(x) > 0\}$ as soon as $t$ became positive, though it may possibly decline afterwards as $t$ continues onwards to $1$.  So one has to somehow compare the $t=0$ and $t=1$ cases directly rather than try to show that some derivative has a favorable sign along the path.

On the other hand, I think we may at least be able to solve the model problem in which we assume in advance that $\{ U_{\tilde \mu} > 0\}$ is an interval.  Specifically, the existence of the dual measure $\lambda$ to the putative minimizer $\mu$ already shows that any competitor set $\{ U_{\tilde \mu} > 0\}$ cannot be a proper subinterval of the interval $\{ U_\mu > 0 \}$, for if this were the case then $\int U_{\tilde \mu}\ d\lambda$ woud be negative, which makes $\int U_\lambda\ d\tilde \mu$ negative, which is absurd since $U_\lambda$ is non-negative on $[0,1]$.  If one can find other dual weights $\lambda$ corresponding to various shifts $(-1.808+\delta,0.026+\delta)$ of the interval $(-1.808, 0.026) = \{ U_\mu > 0 \}$ (i.e. measures supported outside of these intervals with $U_\lambda \geq 0$ on $[-1,1]$), then one could rule out $\{ U_{\tilde \mu}>0\}$ being equal to any interval that is strictly shorter than $(-1.808, 0.026).

replies.contentMd:
As a follow up, I have tried to answer the question: is there a non-global local minimum that we can study?

Turns out I still can't find any! This updates my intuition to: perhaps local minima are rare in this setup, which means first variation (by cleverly chosen duality) has a chance of disproving minimality of large classes of things. This validates Tao's latest strategy...

sourceComments.contentMd:
I have succeeded in doing a variational analysis for general measures. Some parts may be "handwaved".

By the [coarea formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coarea_formula) in geometric measure theory,
$$ |\{U > 0\}| = \int 1_{U > 0} \, dx = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} \frac{1}{|U'(x)|} \, dx \, dt. $$
The inner integral is just the counting measure. Now I want to replace $U$ with $U + \varepsilon V$ and take $d/d\varepsilon$ at $\varepsilon = 0$. The result is, at $\varepsilon = 0$,
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} \frac{1}{|(U + \varepsilon V)'(x(\varepsilon))|} \, dx \, dt = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} -\frac{\text{sgn } U'(x)}{U'(x)^2} \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}(U + \varepsilon V)'(x(\varepsilon)) \, dx \, dt. $$
To compute the remaining quantity, I want the derivative of $U'(x) + \varepsilon V'(x)$ where $x = x(\varepsilon)$ varies as $U(x) + \varepsilon V(x) = t$. This works out to be $-U''V/U' + V'$. So
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int_{t > 0} \int_{U = t} -\frac{\text{sgn } U'}{U'^2} \left( -\frac{U''V}{U'} + V' \right) \, dx \, dt. $$

Now apply coarea formula in reverse:
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int -1_{U > 0} \frac{1}{U'} \left( -\frac{U''V}{U'} + V' \right) \, dx = \int -1_{U > 0} \left(\frac{V}{U'}\right)' \, dx. $$
This is
$$ \frac{d}{d\varepsilon} |\{U + \varepsilon V > 0\}| = \int_{\text{bd}(\{ U > 0 \})} \frac{V}{|U'|} \, dx \geq 0 $$
if $U = U_{\mu}$, $V = U_{\nu}$, $\mu$ is a minimizer and $\nu$ is arbitrary.

Now we want to apply duality. Define
$$ \lambda = \sum_{\text{bd}(\{ U_\mu > 0 \})} \frac{1}{|U_\mu'(a)|} \delta_a. $$
Then the first variation is
$$ \int U_\nu \, d \lambda = \int U_\lambda \, d \nu \geq 0. $$
Since $\nu$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $U_\lambda \geq 0$. But $\lambda$ is supported on $\{ U_\mu = 0 \}$, so
$$ \int U_\lambda \, d \mu = \int U_\mu \, d \lambda = 0. $$
Therefore $U_\lambda = 0$ $\mu$-a.e.!

I realize that this may not solve everything (in particular, what if $U_\mu$ isn't differentiable?), but this looks "clean" enough that it seems it should be useful somehow.

replies.contentMd:
One consequence of this:

Away from $\text{supp }\lambda$, $U_\lambda$ is strictly convex. So in each open interval of $[-1,1] \setminus \text{supp }\lambda$, $U_\lambda = 0$ at at most one point. Since $U_\lambda = 0$ $\mu$-a.e., $\text{supp }\mu$ has at most one point in each open interval of $[-1,1] \setminus \text{supp }\lambda$. So $\mu$ must be a combination of Diracs and something supported on $\{U_\lambda = 0\}$.

A Dirac gives $+\infty$ potential near it, so it's in an interval of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$. Conversely you've shown each interval of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$ has exactly one Dirac.

For points that are isolated in $\{U_\mu = 0\}$, $\mu$ can't have support on them because if so these must be Diracs, but Diracs must be in intervals of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$.

Therefore: $\mu$ must have the following structure. It's a combination of Diracs, which map one-to-one with open intervals of $\{U_\mu > 0\}$ containing each one; plus something supported in the region $\{U_\mu = 0\}$ excluding its isolated points. (In short: Diracs plus "flat regions" which make $U_\mu = 0$.)

If this is correct, it gives some structure to work with. However: as with isoperimetric-type problems, once we've reached this stage the configuration is probably resistant to naive variations already. (In proof of [Double Bubble conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bubble_theorem), they quickly established constraints like a minimizer must be a surface of revolution; but this still retains many nonstandard configurations that are difficult to rule out.) So this is roughly the limits of what this kind of argument should be able to do with this amount of effort.

But there could be other clever ways to finish it off from here, with or without using variations.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
For the sup problem, it seems that the following general duality lemma can be useful:

**Duality lemma (sup version)**  If $\nu$ is a (sufficiently nice) positive measure with $U_\nu(t) > 0$ for all $t \in [-1,1]$, then the set $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0\}$ cannot contain the support of $\nu$.

**Proof:** This is immediate from the Fubini identity $\int U_\nu(t)\ d\mu(t) = \int U_\mu(x)\ d\nu(x)$. $\Box$

Some examples:  - setting $\nu$ to be a Dirac mass $\delta_x$ at some $x \notin [-2,2]$ shows that $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0\}$ cannot contain any point outside of $[-2,2]$.
- Setting $\nu$ to be a two point combination of $\delta_{-M}$ and $\delta_m$ and optimizing shows that $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0\}$ cannot contain both $-M$ and $m$ for $1 \leq m,M \leq 2$ satisfying the condition $\log(M-1) \log(m-1) < \log(M+1) \log(m+1)$.  This can be used to recover the previous analysis ruling out the case $\sqrt{2} \leq M < 1.7624$ and $M+m \geq 2 \sqrt{2}$.

[Here is a plot](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/remaining.png) (produced by Gemini) of the remaining $M + m > 2 \sqrt{2}$ cases not yet ruled out (namely the two small cusp regions on the top left and bottom right of the plot).  The two bounding curves are very close to each other (and tangent at $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$) but do not have any actual intersection outside of the two visible cusps.

I feel like other well chosen choices of $\nu$ could yield more information.

There is also an inf version (slightly easier to state and prove with non-strict inequality):

**Duality lemma (inf version)**  If $\nu$ is a (sufficiently nice) positive measure with $U_\nu(t) \leq 0$ for all $t \in [-1,1]$, then the set $\{ x: U_\mu(x) \leq 0\}$ must intersect the support of $\nu$.

Some examples of $\nu$ that obey this latter condition, implicitly used in previous arguments:- $\nu = \frac{1}{2} \delta_a + \frac{1}{2} \delta_{-a}$ for $0 \leq a \leq 1$.
- $\nu = \frac{1}{2} \delta_{-1+c} + \frac{1}{2} \delta_{1+c}$ for $0 \leq c \leq \sqrt{2}-1$.
- $\nu = \frac{1}{3} \delta_{\alpha-c} + \frac{2}{3} \delta_{\beta-c}$ for $\alpha=2^{4/3}$, $\beta =2^{-2/3}$, and $1 \leq c \leq \alpha-1$.

Perhaps there are other useful choices of $\nu$?

Suppose that $M \geq 1.7987$.  Let $
u$ be the measure
$$ 
u = \delta_{-M} + A 1_{[-M+a, -M+2\sqrt{2}]}\ dx$$
with $A = 0.723$ and $a = 2.2687$ which is a mixture of discrete and continuous measures (these parameter choices were found by AlphaEvolve).  Direct calculation shows that $U_
u(x) \geq 0$ for $x \geq -M + 2.7987$, and hence for $x \geq -1$.  ([Here is a graph](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/log-potential.png), generated by Gemini at the endpoint case $M = 1.7987$; the other cases are translates of this case.) Combined with the duality lemma, this already shows that $\{ U_\mu < 0 \}$ cannot contain $[-M, -M + 2 \sqrt{2}]$, which is the toy version of the problem.

More generally, suppose for contradiction that $M \geq 1.7987$ and that $\{ U_\mu < 0\}$ has measure greater than $2\sqrt{2}$ and infimum $-M$.  We consider the modified function
$$ 	ilde 
u = \delta_{-M} + A 1_E$$
where $E$ is a set of the form $E = \{ U_\mu \leq 0 \} \cap [-M+a, T]$ with $T$ chosen so that $E$ has the same measure $2\sqrt{2}-a$ as the interval $[-M+a, -M+2\sqrt{2}]$; think of $E$ as this interval but with some of the mass moved to the right.  By construction, $	ilde 
u$ is supported on $\{ U_\mu \leq 0\}$.  From the Hardy-Littlewood rearrangement theorem, we have $U_{	ilde 
u}(x) \geq U_
u(x)$ for all $x$ to the left of the midpoint $p = -M + a/2 + \sqrt{2}$ of $[-M+a, -M+2\sqrt{2}]$.  To the right of this midpoint, the rearrangement inequality gives the weaker inequality $U_{	ilde 
u}(x) \geq U_
u(p)$.  In either case, we conclude that $U_{	ilde 
u}(x) > 0$ for $x \geq -1$, and this and the duality lemma is enough to give a contradiction (maybe doing an epsilon perturbation to change non-strict inequalities into strict inequalities if desired).

Ah, I realize now why your numbers are different from mine; there is an additional difficulty that shows up in the general case of a measure $\sqrt{2}$ set in $[-M,+\infty)$ compared to that of the model case $[-M,-M+2\sqrt{2}]$.  It has to do with the question of lower bounding $U_{1_E}(x)$ when $E$ is some measure $L$ set contained in $[-M+a, +\infty]$ (in our application we take $L = 2\sqrt{2}-a$).  The model case of $E$ is $[-M+a,-M+a+L]$, and we would like to have the lower bound $U_{1_E}(x) \geq U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+a+L]}}(x)$ as this would imply that the interval $[-M+a,-M+a+L]$ is the worst case.  But the [Hardy-Littlewood rearrangement inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Littlewood_inequality) only guarantees this as long as $x$ is to the left of the midpoint $-M+a+\frac{L}{2}$.  To the right of this interval, we only get the weaker lower bound $U_{1_E}(x) \geq U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+a+L]}}(-M+a+\frac{L}{2})$.  So to handle the general case with $\nu = \delta_{-M} + A 1_E + C \delta_m$, it is not enough to obtain the lower bound
$$ U_{\delta_{-M}}(x) + A U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+2\sqrt{2}]}}(x) + C U_{\delta_{-M+2\sqrt{2}}}(x) \geq 0$$
for $x \in [-1,1]$; one has to obtain the slightly stronger bound
$$ U_{\delta_{-M}}(x) + A U_{1_{[-M+a,-M+2\sqrt{2}]}}(\min(x,-M+\frac{a}{2}+\sqrt{2})) + C U_{\delta_{-M+2\sqrt{2}}}(x) \geq 0.$$

It's quite possible that one can do better with more complex $\nu$, but the rearrangement analysis becomes trickier.

EDIT: I think i understand the rearrangement ste better and one should be able to bypass the aboce technicalities and effectively pretend that the sublevel set is a single interval (ie it suffices to understand the toy problem and use arbitrary trst measures). replies.author: jspier
replies.contentMd:
Thank you for your comments and correction, natso26! The original argument was inspired by your suggestion of moving the $C\,U_{\delta_{-M+2\sqrt{2}}}$ term. Unfortunately, as you pointed out in Q3, the argument is problematic and is in fact incorrect.

Nevertheless, it is still possible to make the rearrangement inequality work directly on the full range $[-M+2.4,\,-M+2\sqrt{2}]$ (at least when $\mu$ is discrete), as follows.

Define $v_{a,b} = A \, 1_{(a,b)} + B\,\delta_b$, where $A, B>0$, $a<b$, and $b>1$. Then $U'_{v_{a,b}}(x)= A(\log|x-a|-\log|x-b|) + B/(x-b)<0$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$ (EDIT: this holds for $A=0.723$, $B=0.1$, $0.6 \leq a < b$, and $b>1$, and is verified numerically in this range). Thus, for any $\Delta>0$, $U_{v_{a,b}}(x) \leq U_{v_{a+\Delta,\,b+\Delta}}(x)$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$ (EDIT: with the same choices of $A$, $B$, $a$ and $b$). As a consequence, given $a<c<b$ and $\Delta>0$, we have $U_{v_{a,b}}(x)
\leq A\,U_{1_{(a,c)}}(x) + U_{v_{c+\Delta,\,b+\Delta}}(x)$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$.

Now fix $1.771 \le M \le 1.7987$, and consider $\nu = \delta_{-M} + \nu_{-M+2.4,\,-M+2\sqrt{2}}$, with  $A=0.723$ and $B=0.1$. Then, $U_\nu(x) \ge 0$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$. By repeatedly applying the $\nu_{a,b}$ inequality above (EDIT: this is possible since $0.6\leq -M+2.4\leq 1<-M+2\sqrt{2}$), we can construct a measure $\tilde{\nu}$ whose support is contained in $\{U_\mu \le 0\}$ and which satisfies $0 \le U_\nu(x) \le U_{\tilde{\nu}}(x)$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$. The conclusion then follows from the duality lemma.

sourceComments.contentMd:
I’m thinking about how all the three AE optimizers (2 sups, 1 inf) all have the same structure: a big mass at $1$/$-1$, and a bunch of masses that “keep” the potential close to $0$. For the inf case, these produce small intervals; in the sup case they don’t. But this seems to be an artifact of the approximation using masses - the continuous measure will probably just produce a flat horizontal segment there?

This makes me think about this. Assume that a minimizer/maximizer exists as a measure (hope it does?). Then any admissible variation must not decrease/increase. Now that’s hard to think about so I’m going back to discrete masses… That means either
1. It’s an interior point with zero derivative
2. It’s a boundary point - mass at $1$/$-1$, and masses with weight $0$
3. It’s a nonsmooth point - that’s exactly where the potential is zero! (The combined length is nonsmooth because an interval is coming in and out of existence.)

Somehow the AE optimizers all have case 2 and 3 but not case 1. So maybe there’s something wrong with interior point with zero derivative in this setup?

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Let the masses be $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with weights $w_1,\dots,w_n$. We consider
$$ U(a, X) = \sum_j w_j \log |a - x_j|. $$
$X$ is the parameters $(x, w)$.

Suppose we're at an optimizer which is a "smooth interior point" (not well defined at this point). Consider $a$ which is an endpoint of an interval, i.e. $U(a, X) = 0$. If I move $X$ while maintaining this constraint, we have
$$ da = -[1/(\partial U/\partial a)] (\partial U/\partial X)dX. $$
Then
$$ d(\text{interval_lengths}) = \sum_a \text{sgn}(\partial U/\partial a) da = \sum_a -[1/|\partial U/\partial a|] (\partial U/\partial X)dX = 0. $$

Now we can't assume much, only that there is an $i$ such that $x_i \neq 1, -1$ and that $\partial U/\partial a \neq 0$. Then we can move $x_i$ and $w_i$ freely in a local region (only two coords). Unfortunately that equation doesn't seem to give a contradiction as such.

However I was able to salvage the following argument. Note
$$ \frac{\partial U}{\partial w_i}(a, X) = \log |a - x_i|. $$
Then
$$ \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_i} = - \sum_a \frac{\log |a - x_i|}{|\partial U/\partial a|}. $$
Now suppose there is an invisible $x_{i,L}$ and $x_{i,R}$ near $x_i$ with weight $0$. If this configuration is a maximizer, we must have
$$ \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_{i,L}} \leq 0, \quad \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_i} = 0, \quad \frac{d(\text{interval_lengths})}{dw_{i,R}} \leq 0. $$
But $x \mapsto -\log |x|$ is strictly convex. So you can't actually have those three things simultaneously satisfied.

Conclusion: for a maximizer (this doesn't work for minimizer), you can't move the parameters that way.

For the case that some $a$ has $\partial U/\partial a = 0$: this is actually even easier because an interval is coming into existence and the length is increasing like $O(\sqrt \varepsilon)$ which dominates $O(\varepsilon)$ from other $a$'s.

This seems to roughly prove that a maximizer must consist of atoms at $1,-1$ plus "potential-zero regions" only. But I see that the interpretation of "potential-zero region" for discrete masses is not exactly well defined in terms of what I wrote above. So I think this doesn't cleanly "prove" it yet, due to the discrete and continuous cases not being exactly analogous? But perhaps this is fixable?

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Update: this variational method is standard in many problems (e.g. the proof of Double Bubble conjecture), where you take a minimizer/maximizer and finds out its structure by perturbation.

However, in the form written above, it doesn’t work in the general setting of measures yet. A rough analog to the above in the general setting would be to add a small Dirac mass and see that combined interval length must not increase for a maximizer. This encounters a particular difficulty if $\partial U/\partial a = \infty$ for some interval endpoint $a$. Actually the AE optimizers have exactly this case, so this is not just a technicality but a real feature to consider.

Given that other approaches are more successful at the moment, I’m not pursuing this further right now (but I have only tried a little bit so there’s probably a lot of room to explore here!). But I write this down to note about what has been thought about, etc.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
On taking logarithms and normalizing by the degree, one sees that the question is equivalent to finding the infimum or supremum of $| \{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0 \}|$, where $\mu$ ranges over probability measures in $[-1,1]$, and $U_\mu(x) = \int \log |x-y|\ d\mu(y)$ is the logarithmic potential.  (A regularization and approximation argument allows one to restrict to those $\mu$ that are discrete with rational probability masses, and then they are the empirical zero distribution of some high-degree polynomial.)

AlphaEvolve gave this example of a probability measure (expressed as a pairs of points together with the mass associated to that point) that showed that the infimum can be as low as 1.84:  [(-0.84, 0.01607282659569635), (-0.87, 0.018668276991332278), (-0.96, 0.015722736638053406), (-1.0, 0.02786639212010361), (-0.94, 0.016135713032333365), (-0.91, 0.018142805612153572), (1.0, 0.8305116235730803), (-0.8, 0.026585242076298716), (-0.99, 0.013889666827470722), (-0.98, 0.016404716533477668)].  (Caveat: I used a crude discretization method to estimate the size of the level set, so I do not claim more than two decimal points of precision here.)  Readers are invited to "beat the AI" on this!  EDIT: [here is an image](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/min.png) of what the log potential of this candidate minimizer looks like.

On the other hand, the following simple argument shows that the infimum must be at least 1.  For any $0 < a < 1$, the polynomial $(a-x)(-a-x)$ has absolute value strictly less than $1$ on $[-1,1]$, hence $|f(a) f(-a)| < 1$ for all monic polynomials $f$ with roots in $[-1,1]$ (or equivalently $U_\mu(a) + U_\mu(-a) < 0$ for all probability measures $\mu$ on $[-1,1]$).  We conclude that at least one of $a,-a$ lie in $\{ x: |f(x)| < 1 \}$ (or $\{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0 \}$), giving the lower bound of $1$. Probably one can do better than this (for instance, by somehow taking advantage of the points outside of $[-1,1]$).

On the supremum side, AlphaEvolve seems convinced that $2 \sqrt{2}$ (corresponding to the uniform distribution on $\{-1,+1\}$) is optimal.  Even adding a penalty to getting too close to this distribution fails to budge AE from this unless the penalty is quite large.  Not a proof, but perhaps some support for the conjecture.  EDIT: AE numerics suggest that there may be a possibility of a computer assisted proof, possibly along the following lines: (a) establish the result by a rigorous perturbative analysis when the measure $\mu$ is sufficiently close to being supported on $\{-1,+1\}$, e.g., by requiring that $\int x^2\ d\mu(x)$ is sufficiently close to 1.  (b) In all other cases, discretize the space of probability measures somehow (in something like the vague topology or the Levy metric, for which the space to discretize is compact) and show numerically that some robust version of the statistic $| \{ x: U_\mu(x) < 0 \}|$ is bounded away from $2 \sqrt{2}$.  If the gap with $2 \sqrt{2}$ is large compared to the discretization scale, one may then be able to cover all cases.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Some further details on the strategy.  Let $-M$ and $m$ denote the inf and sup of $\{x: U_\mu < 0 \}$.  By symmetry we may assume $M \geq m$.  If $M + m \leq 2\sqrt{2}$ then we are done, so we may assume $M + m > 2 \sqrt{2}$, so $M > \sqrt{2}$.  The function $U_\mu$ is increasing on $(1,\infty)$, decreasing on $(-\infty,-1)$, and positive outside of $[-2,2]$, so we may assume that $\sqrt{2} < M < 2$, that $U_\mu(-M)=0$, and $U_\mu(-M + 2 \sqrt{2}) \leq 0$. (EDIT: technically, one needs $-M+2\sqrt{2} > 1$, or $M < 1.828$, to make this deduction, but this condition is satisfied in the analysis below, so this isn't a problem.)

Numerically it seems that for $M$ in the range $\sqrt{2} < M \leq 1.7624$, that there exists some positive real $\alpha$ such that the concave function $\log |x+M| + \alpha \log |x-(-M+2\sqrt{2})|$ is positive at $x = \pm 1$, hence positive on all of $[-1,1]$.  Integrating against $\mu$ we get $U_\mu(-M) + \alpha U_\mu(-M + 2 \sqrt{2}) > 0$, a contradiction.

This leaves the range $1.7624 < M \leq 2$.  Here one has to work harder and try to force some positivity of $U_\mu$ inside of $[-1,1]$.  However one is now quite far away from the conjectural extremizer (for which $M = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$) and there should be room to play all sorts of additional tricks.

This does suggest a toy problem to work on: for $1.7624 \leq M \leq 2$, can one rule out the possibility that $U_\mu(x) \leq 0$ for all $x \in [-M, -M+2\sqrt{2}]$?  AE suggests this should be possible, and hopefully whatever method handles this toy case can exclude all the remaining potential counterexamples as well.  It would already imply the partial result that any connected interval in the set $\{ U_\mu \leq 0\}$ has length at most $2\sqrt{2}$.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
If we look at $-1 + \delta$ and $1 + \delta$, then roots in between have product of distances to these values $\leq 1$. Outside of $[-1 + \delta, 1 + \delta]$, the product is maximized at root $= -1$. So if we want $|f(-1 + \delta)f(1 + \delta)| \leq 1$ the strictest constraint is $\delta (\delta + 2) = 1$. Or $\delta = \sqrt 2 - 1$. So one of $-1 + \delta$ and $1 + \delta$ must be chosen (this utilizes values outside of $[-1, 1]$ as you suggested). Similarly we do the same thing near $1$ instead of $-1$. And in the middle $[-1 + \delta, 1 - \delta]$ we use the original $-a,a$ strategy. This gives combined length at least $\delta + \delta + (1 - \delta) = \sqrt 2$. So the inf is $\geq \sqrt 2$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: J_Koizumi_144
replies.contentMd:
It seems that the statement you pointed out, namely that the infimum is at least $\sqrt{2}$, is already proved as Theorem 1 in [EHP58]. More precisely, it is shown that if the mean of the roots of $f(x)$ is nonnegative, then the set $\{x:|f(x)|<1\}$ contains an interval of length at least $\sqrt{2}$ that contains $(0,1)$. However, I think that by extending your (and TerenceTao’s) argument to cubic polynomials as follows, one can even prove that the infimum is at least $2^{4/3}-1 = 1.519842\cdots$.

(EDIT: We first assume by symmetry that the mean of the roots of $f(x)$ is nonnegative.) Let $\alpha=2^{4/3}=2.519\cdots$ and $\beta=2^{-2/3}=0.629\cdots$. Consider the function $g(x)=(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)^2$. It satisfies $-1<g(x)<0$ for almost every $x\in[0,\alpha]$. Hence, for each $x\in[-1,1]$, we have $|g(x+\delta)|<1$ for almost every $\delta\in[1,\alpha-1]$. Since\[
g(x+\delta)=(\alpha-\delta-x)(\beta-\delta-x),\quad (\text{EDIT: this should be }(\alpha-\delta-x)(\beta-\delta-x)^2)
\]it follows that for almost every $\delta\in[1,\alpha-1]$ we have $|f(\alpha-\delta)f(\beta-\delta)|<1$ (EDIT: this should be $|f(\alpha-\delta)f(\beta-\delta)^2|<1$). This means that more than half of the set $[1,\alpha-1]\cup[\beta-\alpha+1,\beta-1]$ is contained in $\{x: |f(x)|<1\}$. Combining this with the above-mentioned theorem (or TerenceTao's argument) gives the desired claim.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Nice! Two corrections: in order to use Theorem 1 of EHP58 one should first use symmetry to reduce to the case of non-negative mean; and secondly I think you need to square the factor $\beta-\delta-x$ and $f(\beta-\delta)$ in your argument.  (I think my original argument's can't supply a measure of $1$ in the remaining region $[\beta-1,1]$, which in any event would require some additional hypothesis on the polynomial, as the example $x+1$ shows.)

The full proof of Theorem 1 of EHP58 is lengthy, but the portion needed here, namely that the zero set contains [0,1] if the mean of the zeroes is non-negative (and contains [-1,0] instead of the mean is non-positive) is a simple application of Jensen's inequality.  In the language of log potentials: if the barycenter $\overline{t} := \int t\ d\mu(t)$ is non-negative, then for any $x \in [0,1]$ we have from Jensen
$$ U_\mu(x) = \int \log |x-t|\ d\mu(t) \leq \log \int |x-t|\ d\mu(t) \leq \log \left(\int |x-t|\ d\mu(t) + x \overline{t}\right)$$ $$= \log \int |x-t| + x t\ d\mu \leq \log \int 1\ d\mu = 0$$
as required.

EDIT: In a similar vein, Theorem 2 of EHP58 shows that the sup is at most 3.  So we currently have $2^{4/3}-1 = 1.519\dots \leq \inf \leq 1.852\dots$ and $2\sqrt{2} = 2.828\dots \leq \sup \leq 3$.

replies.author: J_Koizumi_144
replies.contentMd: Thank you for the corrections. If we set $I=[1,\alpha-1]\cup [\beta-\alpha+1,\beta-1]$, then $I\cap(-I)=\emptyset$, and by symmetry, half of $-I$ is also contained in $\{x:|f(x)|<1\}$. The remaining region lies in $[-1,1]$ and is symmetric, so I think your argument applies there. I also feel that one might be able to improve this a bit further by combining this kind of argument with the reduction step used in the proof of [EHP58, Theorem 1].

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: One particular step of the proof of [EHP58, Theorem 1] that might be useful for the inf problem: once one has located an interval $J$ on which $|f(x)| \leq 1$, one can replace all the zeroes in $J$ by their arithmetic mean, since by Jensen's inequality (or the AM-GM inequality) this only serves to decrease $|f(x)|$ to the left or right of $J$, and thus cannot increase the measure of the set $\{ |f(x)| \leq 1\}$.  Hence without loss of generality we may assume that every interval in the set contains only one zero (possibly with high multiplicity).  This is consistent with the AE examples, where we typically have a large interval containing a single mass at $\pm 1$.  The [EHP58, Theorem 1] analysis also tells us that this single mass should have measure at least $1/2$, and I think wlog one can use a translation to place it at an endpoint $\pm 1$.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
You’re right! Should’ve studied the original paper more closely…

Yes, the inf lower bound has improved to $1.519…$. (We apply the argument symmetrically like my argument to get $0.52 + 0.52 + (1-0.52)$.)

sourceComments.contentMd:
Gemini Deep Research [concluded that](https://gemini.google.com/share/ad91215c22a2) this problem was a "cold case" and had no significant followup literature, despite the extensive work done on other problems raised in [EHP58].  However, it also pointed out a correction to the above: [EHP58] only proved the $2 \sqrt{2}$ upper bound under the additional assumption that all the roots lie on the endpoints $\{-1,+1\}$ of the interval, and leave open the question of obtaining this bound in the general case where the roots are also allowed to lie in the interior $(-1,1)$ as a conjecture.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1039 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1039).

### Problem
Let $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n(z-z_i)\in \mathbb{C}[z]$ with $\lvert z_i\rvert \leq 1$ for all $i$. Let $\rho(f)$ be the radius of the largest disc which is contained in $\{z: \lvert f(z)\rvert< 1\}$.

Determine the behaviour of $\rho(f)$. In particular, is it always true that $\rho(f)\gg 1/n$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian, who note that $f(z)=z^n-1$ has $\rho(f) \leq \frac{\pi/2}{n}$.

Pommerenke [Po61] proved that\[\rho(f) \geq \frac{1}{2en^2}.\]Krishnapur, Lundberg, and Ramachandran [KLR25] proved\[\rho(f) \gg \frac{1}{n\sqrt{\log n}}.\]

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: Houi
sourceComments.contentMd:
Using Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic), I obtained a partial result on the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian conjecture ($\rho_n \ge c/n$ for monic degree-$n$ polynomials with roots in the closed unit disc).
Main result. Call $P$ non-degenerate if every critical value has modulus $\ge 1$. Equivalently, $P$ has no branch points over $\mathbb{D}$ , so every inverse branch $\psi_j$ with $\psi_j(0) = z_j$ extends univalently across all of $\mathbb{D}$,  with $\psi_j(\mathbb{D}) \subset \Lambda_P(1)$.

**Theorem.** If $P$ is non-degenerate with roots in the closed unit disc, then $\operatorname{inrad}(\Lambda_P(1)) \ge \frac{1}{4n}$.
*Proof sketch.* The Koebe quarter theorem gives $\Lambda_P(1) \supset B\left(z_j, \frac{1}{4|P'(z_j)|}\right)$ for each root. The Fekete energy of $n$ points in the closed disc is maximized by $n$-th roots of unity, giving $$\sum_j \log |P'(z_j)| \le n \log n,$$so by pigeonhole $$\min_j |P'(z_j)| \le n.$$Combining: $\operatorname{inrad} \ge \frac{1}{4n}$. The conjectured extremizer $z^n − 1$ is non-degenerate with $|P'(\omega_k)| = n$ for each root.

**Reduction.** The full EHP conjecture reduces to: the inradius minimizer is non-degenerate. For degenerate components containing $k$ roots,
the Riemann map $\varphi : \mathbb{D} \rightarrow \mathcal{C}$ gives a degree-$k$ Blaschke product $B = P \circ \varphi$, and the inradius bound becomes $\operatorname{inrad}(C) ≥ \frac{|B'(0)|}{4|P'(z^*)|}$. For all $k \ge 2$, the hyperbolic Blaschke invariants degenerate as the component approaches a pinch point — for $k = 2$, $$|B''(wc)|(1−|wc|^2)^2 = 2(1−|B(wc)|²) \rightarrow 0$$as the critical value approaches the boundary; for $k \ge 3$, the family $B_a(w) = w^2 \cdot \frac{w−a}{1−\overline{a}w}$ with $a \rightarrow 0$ shows the same degeneration at all critical points simultaneously. This creates a uniform structural obstruction for the conformal approach in the entire degenerate case.

**Numerical evidence.** Over several hundred random configurations with $n = 10$ (roots on $\mathbb{T}$,  in $\mathbb{D}$,  clustered,  adversarial),  the minimum of $n \cdot \operatorname{inrad}$ was always attained by roots of unity. Degenerate configurations consistently had larger inradii, typically $n \cdot \rho \ge 4$.
The approach is entirely conformal — no area or perimeter estimates — and is independent of KLR (2025). A literature search (via deep research) found no prior work establishing these results or using these methods.
Paper: https://github.com/huy209vn/INRADIUS-OF-POLYNOMIAL-LEMNISCATES-THE-NON-DEGENERATE-CASE-AND-BEYOND
Lean formalization is in progress.

replies.author: Houi
replies.contentMd:
Thanks old-bielefelder, both catches were correct.

Fixed Lemma 5.1: the old simple connectivity argument broke because a bounded complementary component can contain other lemniscate components with roots, so log|P| isn't harmonic there. Replaced with the subharmonicity argument — if γ ⊂ U bounds a domain D_γ, then |P| < 1 on γ and |P| is subharmonic, so maximum principle gives |P| < 1 on D_γ, done.

Fixed the k ≥ 3 example: B_a(w) = w²(w−a)/(1−aw) has a double zero at 0, violating the squarefree hypothesis. Replaced with B_a(w) = w · (w−a)/(1−aw) · (w−2a)/(1−2aw), three simple zeros, verified the critical-point invariants still degenerate as O(a) → 0.

Neither fix touches the main theorem or the Lean formalization.

On Lean: good news is that Claude and Aristotle managed to cover the whole paper now. no sorry's.

Four classical axioms (Koebe 1/4, Hadamard's inequality, monodromy/univalent branches, minimizer existence) plus two axioms combining classical complex analysis not yet in Mathlib (lemniscate component structure, conformal factorization — both need the Riemann mapping theorem, which is on Mathlib's open wishlist as issue #6091).

The main theorem, the reduction, the z^n − 1 verification, the Fekete bound (proved from Hadamard + Vandermonde), dual Fekete (from Gauss-Lucas, which is in Mathlib), P'' identity, Lemma 5.2 chain rule, Corollary 5.3, k=2 Blaschke identity, and conformal factorization bound are all machine-checked from those axioms.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1040 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1040).

### Problem
Let $F\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be a closed infinite set, and let $\mu(F)$ be the infimum of\[\lvert \{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}\rvert,\]as $f$ ranges over all polynomials of the shape $\prod (z-z_i)$ with $z_i\in F$.

Is $\mu(F)$ determined by the transfinite diameter of $F$? In particular, is $\mu(F)=0$ whenever the transfinite diameter of $F$ is $\geq 1$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who show that the answer is yes if $F$ is a line segment or disc, and that if the transfinite diameter is $<1$ then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}$ always contains a disc of radius $\gg_F 1$.

Erdős and Netanyahu [ErNe73] proved that if $F$ is also bounded and connected, with transfinite diameter $0<c<1$, then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}$ always contains a disc of radius $\gg_c 1$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: kram86
sourceComments.contentMd:
There are partial results for the case when the capacity (=transfinite diameter) is strictly larger than $1$.
Let $K\subset\mathbb{C}$ be compact with logarithimic capacity $c(K) > 1$. Suppose in addition at least one of the following conditions hold:

(a) there exist positive constants $C, \epsilon$ such that the equilibrium measure $\nu$ of $K$ satisfies $\nu(B(z, r)\leq C r^{\epsilon}$ for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$ and all $r> 0$.

(b) K is a connected set.

Then, $\mu(K) = 0$.

For the proof of this result when $(a)$ holds, see Corollary $1.6$ and its proof, in the paper titled "INRADIUS OF RANDOM LEMNISCATES",  by Krishnapur, Lundberg, and Ramachandran, Journal of Approximation theory, ($299$), ($2024$), paper no. $106018$.

The proof when $(b)$ holds follows from the proof of part $(b)$ of Theorem $2.2$ in the paper titled "NUMBER OF COMPONENTS OF POLYNOMIAL LEMNISCATES: A PROBLEM OF ERDOS, HERZOG, AND PIRANIAN" by Ghosh and Ramachandran, Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications $540$, ($2024$),  Paper no. $128571$. The result regarding area is not explicitly stated there but the proof easily gives that for all large $n,$ the minimal area for degree $n$ polynomials of the given shape is bounded above by $\exp(-\alpha n)$ for some $\alpha = \alpha(K) > 0$.

Just to add some context to the condition $(a)$ above: If the set $K$ is a union of finitely many disjoint $C^2$ smooth domains (along with their boundaries), then it is known that the equilibrium measure satisfies $(a)$ with $\epsilon = 1$. There are also some Cantor sets $K$ whose equilibrium measure satisfies condition $(a)$, see the paper titled "CANTOR SETS WITH ABSOLUTELY CONTINUOUS HARMONIC MEASURE" by Guy David,  Cole Jeznach, and Antoine Julia, in Journal de l'Ecole polytechnique, Mathematiques, $(2023)$, pg $1277 - 1298$.

Summarising, the second condition $(b)$ only imposes a mild topological requirement of connectedness, without any other additional regularity on K, while the first condition $(a)$ can deal with certain disconnected sets, including some fractals. Taken together, these results seem to cover the question for "most" compact sets of capacity larger than $1$. It would be interesting to see (I am not aware of it)  if there is a necessary and sufficient condition for $(a)$ to hold. This seems to be a non-trivial question in geometric measure theory/PDE.

sourceMetadata.statement: Let $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n(z-z_i)\in \mathbb{C}[z]$ with $\lvert z_i\rvert < 1$ for all $i$. Must there always exist a path of length less than $2$ in\{z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}which connects two of the roots of $f$?
sourceMetadata.statementMd:
Let $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n(z-z_i)\in \mathbb{C}[z]$ with $\lvert z_i\rvert < 1$ for all $i$.

Must there always exist a path of length less than $2$ in\[\{z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}\]which connects two of the roots of $f$?
sourceMetadata.statusNote: Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample.
researchNotes: A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that this set always has a connected component containing at least two of the roots.
researchNotesMd: A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that this set always has a connected component containing at least two of the roots.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I'm willing to rate the argument as being plausibly correct.  With regards to having publication-level quality of exposition and literature review, the manuscript still needs a lot of work however, on a number of fronts.  Much of this is tied to the tendency of current-level AI writing to dwell far too much on routine results (often without citing relevant literature), or technical details, and not enough time emphasizing the high level structure.

In this case, the high-level structure is that there are four key results that resolve the Erdos problem, each of which is independently interesting:

1. The EHP component lemma (at least one component $U$ with two or more zeroes).

2.  An integral bound $\int_U |f'(z)/f(z)|\ dA \leq 2\pi m$, where $m$ is the number of zeroes (Proposition 4).

3.  A lemma asserting that on any given region $U$, there is a tree connecting the $m$ zeroes of $U$ (formed by following the Morse gradient flow on $\log |f|$, basically) of total length at most $\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_U |f'(z)/f(z)|\ dA$, at least assuming some technical non-degeneracy hypotheses on $f$. (Proposition 12)

4.  A simple combinatorial lemma that asserts that any tree contains a path of length at most twice the total length of the tree, divided by the number of vertices of the tree.  (Lemma 17)

There is also a technical

0.  One can perturb $f$ to obey the non-degeneracy conditions required for the third ingredient to work. (Lemma 14)

Combining all these ingredients, the Erdos problem follows.  But the AI-generated exposition spends a lot of time on the least interesting parts of this process (e.g., Step 0), and many steps could be proven much more quickly.  For instance Lemma 3 is obvious because the level sets of $p$ are algebraic sets of dimension less than 2, and thus immediately of measure zero (e.g., by the Crofton formula).  Several pages of argument are used to establish the formula $\int_{\varepsilon < u < t} |\nabla u|^2\ dA = 2\pi m(t-\varepsilon)$ on page 5, but this is just the area formula noting that $f$ is $m$-to-one on $U$, so (a suitable branch of) $\log f$ is also $m$-to-one mapping to a fundamental domain of $\{ \varepsilon < \mathrm{Re} z < t \}$.

I also suspect that there is a less convoluted way to arrive at Proposition 4 from this area formula and the Polya inequality than the one provided in the AI-generated text, although I have not tried too hard to locate such a simplified argument.  Similarly, the perturbative component of the argument (Step 0) seems to occupy far more space in the AI-generated document than it needs to: I think the cleanest thing to do is first resolve the Erdos problem for "generic" polynomials f (perhaps with some sort of "padding") and use some sort of Rouche theorem argument to deduce the general case from this, instead of spend so much time constructing explicit perturbations of polynomials.

Finally, it's a bit concerning that the AI-generated article cites almost none of the extensive literature on lemniscates, and I suspect that many of the arguments here have precursors or other links to the literature that need to be explored; it may be that the AI tool implicitly relied upon such literature arguments without explicitly disclosing the connection.  All of this would have to be resolved (preferably by a primarily human-generated document) before this result would be suitable for submission to a peer-reviewed journal.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Yes, some people do use that strategy of not browsing to frame the problem as if it has a known solution or should be easily doable with existing techniques.

There are also other ways to coax it, see e.g. qrdl's comment in the AI thread.

My way of doing something like this is to present it with a promising approach - so seed it with something first. This gets it started immediately without worrying about the open status. (If you don't have a promising approach you can probably ask it to generate approaches, and then follow through in the same way!)

But, from the current situation, I now see that the "not browsing" approach can also have this weakness. In framing the problem as "potentially not open", any *real* difficulty or issue it encounters is likely to be viewed as easily surmountable (since the problem IS not open). When in fact - this may be precisely where the gaps lie!

replies.author: natso26

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Regarding the use of "scepticism" framing itself. While it may seem like a good idea, I believe a neutral framing is better. The reason is that a good check also addresses high-level issues, which is quite hard to see if you zoom in locally. In the past, I've had problems where *every* local part is checked - but there's some global or high-level strategy that doesn't quite work out; these require understanding beyond simple local checks. So I'm now prioritizing big pictures somewhat, and it seems that a scepticism framing may encourage it to be more local. So while it may catch more local issues, it could miss the more global major gaps. At least that's what I think.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
After working [with Claude](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10958-013-1432-4) and doing some literature search, I have a shorter proof of Proposition 4 (Step 2).  From the area formula (noting that $f$ is an $m$-fold map from $U$ to the disk) one has
$$ \int_U |f'(z)|^2 / |f(z)|^{2-1/m}\ dA(z) = m \int_{D(0,1)} 1/|w|^{2-1/m}\ dA(w) = 2 \pi m^2$$
so by Cauchy--Schwarz it suffices to show that
$$ \int_U |f(z)|^{-1/m}\ dA(z) \leq 2\pi.$$
By the layer-cake decomposition it suffices to show that the level sets $\{ z \in U: |f(z)| \leq s \}$ have area at most $\pi s^{2/m}$ for all $0 < s \leq 1$.  By Theorem 1 of [this paper of Dubinin](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10958-013-1432-4) (a Polya type inequality), this area is at most $s^{2/m}$ times the area of $U$; and by the classical Polya inequality, $U$ has area at most $\pi$.  The claim follows.

The arguments used here and in the AI-generated article are also rather similar to those in [this paper of Crane](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0302189).

I'm going to look at Proposition 12 (Step 3) next.  I have a suspicion that one does not need quite so much working out of the topology of the situation, and should be able to proceed by more purely analytic arguments; but I have not digested it yet.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I now believe that there is a serious issue with Proposition 12, in that the topological claims made by the AI are not actually correct.  In particular, the invocation of Lemma 8 on page 21 is unjustified, and likely unjustifiable, because the boundary of the sets $S$ outside of flow-line sides will typically be contained in more than two level sets.  [Here is a ChatGPT Pro explanation of this](https://chatgpt.com/share/69c36796-0700-83e8-9e5c-f1f5d1f5dfb3).  (ChatGPT Pro does propose a fix, but I believe it does not work: by removing much longer regions from $\Omega$, one can no longer afford to glue together vertices on the boundary of the regions removed without incurring a much larger length penalty.)

I found this by trying to draw a picture of the situation and finding it did not agree with the topological claims; removing small balls around each zero and critical point does not split the domain into strips with the structure of Lemma 8, and more broadly the flow lines do not seem to organize into connected trees which is essential for the entire strategy to work.  Any new version of the paper should, at minimum, have some actual pictures (ideally plotted numerically from actual polynomials) to double-check the claims of the AI.

(I had initially been rather impressed by the AI's topological arguments, which were reaching all sorts of conclusions that I did not think were possible... but now I think it is because the AI was simply wrong.  It appears to me that avoiding errors in topological arguments are a weakness for large language models, who do not have a direct capability for visual intuition.)

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I can elaborate a bit further on why I am now pessimistic on the entire approach.  The strategy is to try to connect zeroes of $f$ together by performing gradient flow on $u = \log \frac{1}{|f|}$, which is (locally at least) the same thing as working on level curves of the harmonic conjugate $\mathrm{arg} f$, and hoping that this creates a tree of short total length that one can then cut up (along an Eulerian path) to find a path connecting two zeroes together.

The problem is that this flow simply does not create trees, which becomes obvious once one generates a visual plot.  [Here is a plot](https://gemini.google.com/share/ac2d9dab2039) of what the gradient flow lines look like for $f(z) = z^2-1$; the construction given is to basically take two arcs of the same color, which connect the two zeroes $\pm 1$ to the boundary of the region $U$ under consideration, but do not connect to each other.  There is a critical point at $0$ that can connect the zeroes together, but only two flow lines go into that point and two flow lines go out, and a random flow line construction will never find this.  (The integral $\int_U |f'/f|\ dA$, by the way, can be viewed as the average value of the total flow line length for a randomly chosen color.)

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:

It says that plot's interpretation is accurate, but that the actual strategy is not "random" in that way. I'm now not sure whether it's right or wrong. replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: I would challenge any AI tasked with making this strategy work to actually generate a picture of how this tree is plausibly going to look like.

replies.author: natso26

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: OK, that was a better attempt than I expected, but it does show that the only flow lines coming from the zeroes that are of plausible use are the ones pointing towards the critical point; the majority of flow lines emenating away from the zeroes will not be useful for this purpose.  On the other hand, the integral expression $\int_U |f'/f|\ dA$ is almost entirely dominated by contributions from these "useless" flow lines, particularly if one shrinks the disk around the critical point down from the exaggerated size shown in the AI plot in order to reduce the excess length coming from the degree three vertex of the tree inside that disk.  So if this strateegy is to work, one needs to obtain control on something other than these sorts of area integral quantities, which do not isolate the correct geometry for this problem.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: It's interesting that all the AI tools here are trying to conflate together two inconsistent decompositions to make the argument strategy work.  In order to keep all the excess length coming from stitching together the decompositions under control, one can only remove a small neighborhood around the critical point (as depicted in this AI image, and in the incorrect long version of the AI paper).  But in order to get the topological flow structure given by Lemma 8, one has to remove a much longer strip (the neighborhood of a lemniscate of Bernoulli (or more colloquially, the infinity symbol $\infty$), in the $z^2-r^2$ case), which solves the Lemma 8 problem but now creates a huge problem in trying to stitch together the pieces while keeping the length under control (this is not pictured in the AI image, most likely because the AI cannot figure out how to make this picture look at all plausible).  I don't think either approach is salvageable with anything resembling the current strategy, but somehow the fact that both versions of the approach have a different half of the argument working seems to be enough to convince the AIs that the argument is fixable.

replies.author: old-bielefelder
replies.contentMd:
Very interesting, thanks for sharing your proof.

13 years ago I was interested in such paths not between two
zeros of a polynomial f, but between one zero of f and one
zero of its derivative f'.

EDIT: I am working at transfering Shtuka's approach
to get path length $\le 1$  for the  $f -> f'$ transfer
(instead of $\le 2$ in the #1041 problem).

Here is a link to some diagrams from 2013 (the ones in the
lower part of that site are more interesting):

[Diagrams and some German text](https://althofer.de/tanz-der-nullstellen.html)

By "Tanz der Nullstellen" I mean the picture from "Musical Chairs":
n persons and n-1 chairs.

The persons are the zeros of f. The chairs are the zeros of the derivative.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
This is quite interesting.

By Riemann-Hurwitz, a component of $\Lambda_f := \{z: |f(z)| < 1\}$ with $m$ zeros of $f$ will have $m-1$ zeros of $f'$. (Note: zeros must be counted with multiplicity.)

The two proofs combined, if correct, appear to claim the following. Consider any component $U$ of $\Lambda_f$ with at least two roots of $f$. By [EHP58], such a component $U$ exists. Then:
- There is a path in $U$ joining two roots of $f$ with length $< 2$.
- There is a path in $U$ joining a root of $f$ and a root of $f'$ with length $< 1$.

However, at present, both proofs at least require revision. I would encourage the authors here to work on it.

Credit to GPT-5.4 Thinking for discussion.

replies.author: old-bielefelder
replies.contentMd:
Thanks for pointing to Riemann-Hurwitz. In my backhead I
have some hope that (always or often) chains $z_i$ -> $y_j$ -> $x_k$
with "flat" paths  and path lengths < 1 exist, where $z_i$ is a
zero of polynomial $f$, $y_j$ a zero of derivative $f'$, $x_k$ a zero of
the second derivative $f''$...

ChatGPT gave a proof for cubic polynomials, but failed to do so
for degree $\ge 4$. Gemini explained that Riemann-Hurwitz does not
give chain structures. Nevertheless It would be nice to have "flat"
paths - and I believe in "niceness" here. Perhaps someone has a
more proof-friendly definition of "flat paths".

Here is a link to some diagrams from the diploma thesis (2012) of
Konrad Kaffka (Jena University), giving examples how root ensembles
of $f, f', f'', f''' ...$ can behave.

[Kaffka Diagrams](https://althofer.de/kaffka-bilder.html)

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd: Also, FYI, if we're not interested in the lemniscate $\{z: |f(z)| < 1\}$, *every* root of $f'$ is indeed within distance $< 1$ of some root of $f$. (Here all roots of $f$ lie in unit disk). Here is a [solution](https://chatgpt.com/share/69bc1a51-e08c-8010-bd49-42980c0596fe) using convex combination by GPT-5.4 Thinking.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: Just a remark that the opposite problem of asking whether every root of $f$ is within distance $1$ of a root of $f'$ is a [famous open conjecture of Sendov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendov%27s_conjecture).

replies.author: old-bielefelder
replies.contentMd:
Sendov's Conjecture is interesting. Having in mind the "musical chair"
picture for roots and critical points of polynomial $f$ one can look at
the following variant of Sendov's:

Let be $n \ge 1$. Let $f$ be a polynomial of degree n with zeros $z_1, ..., z_n$,
all in the complex unit ball. Let $f'$ be the derivative (thus with degree $n-1$)
with roots $y_1$, ..., $y_{n-1}$. Add the auxiliary point $y_n = 0$.

** Conjecture: Then there exists a permutation $p$ of {1, 2, ..., n}
such that distance $(x_i, y_{p(i)}) \le 1$ for $i=1, ..., n$. The
condition for $i=n$ holds trivially, because $0$ is central in the
unit ball. The interesting remaining cases are $i=1, ..., n-1$. **

The conjecture is in some sense weaker than Sendov's,
because $y_n$ gives a free meal for one root of $f$. But it is
stronger than Sendov's in another sense, because all the
other roots of $f$ need different near-distance $f'$-roots as
their partners.

For $n=3$ the conjecture has a simple proof by Hall's
marriage theorem.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
This is not a bad conjecture. It proposes that you can match all $n-1$ roots of $f'$ one-to-one with some $n-1$ roots of $f$ (leaving one out) so that the distance between each pair is $< 1$.

GPT-5.4 Thinking does not recognize this as a named conjecture nor can it find it in literature. The case $n=3$ follows by Sendov's conjecture + the "opposite" version above + Hall's marriage theorem (or brute force enumeration). It's also true if all roots of $f$ are real because roots of $f'$ are between the consecutive roots of $f$. Randomizing roots does not easily give a counterexample.

In principle, Sendov's conjecture and this matching variant can be proved or disproved for any specific $n$ with finite computation. GPT-5.4 Thinking attempts a geometric proof for the case $n=4$ but does not succeed.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd: [Over](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/1342) on the Formal Conjectures project, Salvatore Mercuri notes that there is some intricacy with repeated roots.  It appears that: for roots with multiplicity, the 0-length path connecting them should count for this problem.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1045 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1045).

### Problem
Let $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in \mathbb{C}$ with $\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert\leq 2$ for all $i,j$, and\[\Delta(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=\prod_{i\neq j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert.\]What is the maximum possible value of $\Delta$? Is it maximised by taking the $z_i$ to be the vertices of a regular polygon?

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that, for any monic polynomial $f$, if $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert <1\}$ is connected and $f$ has roots $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ then $\prod_{i\neq j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert <n^n$.

The value of $\Delta$ when the $z_i$ are the vertices of a regular polygon is $n^n$ when $n$ is even and\[\cos(\pi/2n)^{-n(n-1)}n^n \sim e^{\pi^2/8}n^n\]when $n$ is odd.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Include a rigorous proof, counterexample, or a precise explanation of the remaining gap.

researchNotes: A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that, for any monic polynomial $f$, if $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert <1\}$ is connected and $f$ has roots $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ then $\prod_{i\neq j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert <n^n$.
The value of $\Delta$ when the $z_i$ are the vertices of a regular polygon is $n^n$ when $n$ is even and\cos(\pi/2n)^{-n(n-1)}n^n \sim e^{\pi^2/8}n^nwhen $n$ is odd.
Pommerenke [Po61] proved that $\Delta \leq 2^{O(n)}n^n$ for all $z_i$ with $\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert \leq 2$.

Hu and Tang (see the comments) found examples when $n=4$ and $n=6$ that show that vertices of a regular polygon do not maximise $\Delta$. Cambie (also in the comments) showed that, in general, the vertices of a regular polygon are not a maximiser for all even $n\geq 4$.

There is a lot of discussion of this problem in the comments. It is now known that, for even $n$,\liminf \frac{\max \Delta}{n^n}\geq Cfor some $C>0$. This was proved with $C\approx 1.0378$ by Sothanaphan [So25]. An alternative construction by Cambie, Dong, and Tang (see the comments by Stijn Cambie) achieves $C\approx 1.304457$ for $6\mid n$, and $C\approx 1.26853$ for all even $n$.
It remains possible that the regular polygon is a maximiser for odd $n$.

Minor remark:
the liminf may be different from the bound obtained for $6 \mid n$.
Restricting to $2 \nmid n$, we conjecture $\exp(\pi^2/8)$ is correct.
For $2 \mid n, 6 \nmid n$ the constant might be slightly different from the one for $6 \mid n$.

The best lower bounds for $C$ obtained in restricted regimes, are
for $2 ,4 \pmod 6$: $\exp\left(\frac{7}{24}\zeta(3)-\frac{\pi^4}{864}\right) \sim 1.26853$
$6 \mid n$: $\frac{3^{9/4}}{2^3}\exp \left( \frac{\pi^2-2 \sqrt 3 \pi}{8} \right) \sim 1.304457$
$2 \nmid n$: $\exp(\pi^2/8)\sim 3.43391$

A paper (5 people: Cambie, Decadt, Dong, Hu and Tang) with all progress should appear in a decent amount of time.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
I finally succeeded in proving that there is $C > 1$ such that for all sufficiently large even $n$, $\Delta \geq C n^n$ !

The proof is as follows:

Consider the "new diameter construction" in my comment at [11:17 on 10 Dec 2025]. But instead of having a single $\delta_k$, I'm having $\delta_k(t) = (1 - 4k/n) t$.

In other words, these are "velocity vectors", and I'm increasing from $t=0$ to $t=O(1/n)$.

Formally, we're looking at $z_k(t) = z_k + v_k t$, where $z_k$ here are the original vertices of the regular polygon, and $v_k$ is some velocity vector.

So we must differentiate
$$ \log |(z_i-z_j) + (v_i-v_j)t| = \text{const} + \log |1 + \rho_{ij} t|, \quad \rho_{ij} = \frac{v_i-v_j}{z_i-z_j}. $$

With help of Wolframalpha, I found that
$$ \left( \log \sqrt{(1 + ax)^2 + (bx)^2)} \right)'(0) = a. $$
However, by symmetry of the construction, the same $v_i,v_j$ will match with all four of $\pm z_i, \pm z_j$. So the sum of the first derivative is zero. We must look at the second derivative.
$$ \left( \log \sqrt{(1 + ax)^2 + (bx)^2)} \right)''(0) = b^2 - a^2. $$
This one doesn't trivially cancel. Plugging in, if $\rho = a + bi$, I simplify this to $- \text{Re} (\rho^2)$. So we must show that
$$ \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n/2} \frac{(v_i-v_j)^2}{(\pm z_i \pm z_j)^2} $$
has negative real part with magnitude at least $O(n^2)$. Why $O(n^2)$: this is the second derivative and the distance to move is $O(1/n)$, so that will cancel out out to $O(1)$.

Now I'm getting rid of the $\pm$'s:
$$ \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n/2} \frac{(v_i-v_j)^2(z_i^2 + z_j^2)}{(z_i^2 - z_j^2)^2}. $$

Now here's the magic. I have $v_j = (1 - 4j/n)z_j$. Now $z_j^2$ here are the $n/2$th roots of unity. If its angle is $\theta$, actually $4j/n = \theta/\pi$. So what I'm looking at is actually a Riemann sum of a double integral involving $\theta$! To say the sum has negative real part with $O(n^2)$ is equivalent to saying the integral has negative real part (since we have $O(n^2)$ terms).

Writing everything out correctly, I must show that
$$ \text{Re} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{((1 - \frac{x}{\pi})e^{ix/2} - (1 - \frac{y}{\pi})e^{iy/2})^2 (e^{ix} + e^{iy})}{(e^{ix} - e^{iy})^2} \, dx \, dy < 0. $$

By Wolframalpha, this integral seems to be a real number with value
$$ -0.481436 < 0. $$

This completes the proof!

Note: sadly this proof as written doesn't give explicit $C$ or the sufficiently large threshold for $n$. But it works.

It's also not something of the form I would "expect"...

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Your remark on delicateness was that it converges to $1$, while here it is to $1.3+$, so the issue is not there.

For the sums; perturbing $6$ angles by $\delta= \frac{\pi}{n}$ implies that distances between two vertices (initially at distance dist) change into
$dist+  f_1* \delta+f_2*\delta^2+...$ for $\delta \to 0,$ where $dist, f_1, f_2...$ are functions of just a few angles that can be expressed in term of their location on the polygon (relative to the perturbed vertices).
Combining these in symmetric pairs, we get a product equal to $dist^2-g1 *\delta^2+O( \delta^3)$.

This implies that the ratio behaves like $1- \frac{g_1}{dist^2} \delta^2+O(\delta^3) \sim \exp \left( - \frac{g_1}{dist^2} \delta^2+O(\delta^3) \right)$.

Now $\prod ratio \sim \exp \left( \sum  - \frac{g_1}{dist^2} \delta^2 \right).$

Here $\sum  \frac{g_1}{dist^2} \delta^2$ has to be partitioned in $3$ different sums, each converging to some integral.
This by the number of edited angles in between (which is a number between $0$ and $3$, but $0$ changes implies that the ratio was just 1 => does not have to be considered)

One of those integrals (when there is one angle in between) should be
$$\int_{0}^{ \frac \pi 6} \int_{0}^{ \frac \pi 6} \frac{2(\sin^2(x)+\sin^2(y))\sin(x)\sin(y)\cos(x+y)}{\left( \sin^2(x)+\sin^2(y)+2\sin(x)\sin(y)\cos(x+y) \right)^2} dx dy$$
$$+ \int_{0}^{ \frac \pi 6} \int_{0}^{ \frac \pi 6} \frac{8\sin^2(x)\sin^2(y)\cos(x+y)}{\left( \sin^2(x)+\sin^2(y)+2\sin(x)\sin(y)\cos(x+y) \right)^2} dx dy.$$

So the details would be just to do all the computations exactly and check how the function $\frac{g_1}{dist^2}$ look like and over which region we are integrating.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Follow up:

1) About the value of $C = \lim_{n\to\infty} \Delta/n^n$ in this construction.

Calculating back, we should expect, if $I \approx -0.481436$ is the value of that integral,
$$ C = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\Delta}{n^n} = \exp\left( -I \frac{\pi^2}{128} \right) \approx 1.0378. $$

This checks out perfectly with the numerics (which came out as $1.037...$)! Hence, this bolsters the confidence that the proof is correct.

2) How fast does it converge?

Numerically seems to be $\Delta/n^n = C(1 + O(1/n))$.

I will also prove this below, again to strengthen the confidence of the argument.

3) Is the integral singular (dividing by $0$)?

No. There is factor of $(x-y)^2$ in the denominator, which also appears in the numerator. In fact the integrand is bounded! Thus, convergence of the Riemann sum to the integral is assured.

4) There is a gap: I calculated the second derivative at $t=0$; but we need all the way to $t=O(1/n)$.

Yes. I will now patch that as follows.

First, notice
$$ \log |1 + \rho t| = \text{Re} \log(1 + \rho t) = \text{Re} \left( \rho t - \frac{\rho^2 t^2}{2} + \frac{\rho^3 t^3}{3} - \frac{\rho^4 t^4}{4} + \dots \right). $$
(This means I actually don't need those Wolframalpha's calculations; the Taylor expansion is explicit.) By symmetry, the odd powers will cancel. So the error term is the $t^4$ term. Also, I must consider nonzero $t=O(1/n)$. (Explictly: we're using the Lagrange form of the remainder in Taylor's theorem.) Hence we must estimate
$$ \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n/2} \frac{(v_i-v_j)^4}{((\pm z_i \pm z_j) + (v_i-v_j)t)^4} = \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n} \frac{\rho_{ij}^4}{(1 + \rho_{ij} t)^4}. $$
Here
$$ \rho_{ij} = \frac{v_i - v_j}{z_i-z_j}. $$
(Note on summing $n/2$ or $n$ terms: $z_{n/2+i} = -z_i$ but $v_{n/2+i} = v_i$.)

Now here's the key point: $\rho_{ij}$ is in fact bounded (independent of $n$). So
$$ \sum |\rho_{ij}^4| = O(n^2). $$
(This is like we're doing that integral, but put the absolute value in the integrand instead i.e. we're using that the integrand is absolutely integrable.)

This means that if I can get $|\rho_{ij} t| < \varepsilon$, the estimate will work:
$$ |\text{fourth derivative}| = \text{const} \left| \text{Re} \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n} \frac{\rho_{ij}^4}{(1 + \rho_{ij} t)^4} \right| \leq \text{const} \sum_{0 \leq i,j < n} \frac{|\rho_{ij}^4|}{(1 - \varepsilon)^4} = O(n^2). $$
And then the contribution in log-space of the error term will be
$$ O(n^2)t^4 = O(1/n^2). $$
(We only need $o(1)$ so this is stronger.)

But: $\rho_{ij}$ is bounded and $t=O(1/n)$, so actually $|\rho_{ij} t| < \varepsilon$ is obtained easily.

This fixes the gap and proves that the error does not derail the desired growth rate.

5) Now, let's prove $\Delta/n^n = C(1 + O(1/n))$.

We must notice there are three error terms:

1. The fourth derivative: already shown to contribute $O(1/n^2)$.

2. The Riemann sum. The error is $O(1/n)$ per term, so the integral $I$ can be off by a factor of $O(1/n)$. From the $C$'s expression in terms of $I$, it contributes error of $O(1/n)$.

3. The $t=O(1/n)$, distance to move. It is not difficult (see below) to show
$$ t = \frac{\pi^2}{4n} \left(1 + O(1/n)\right) $$
is the maximum you can go to maintain diameter of $2$. Since we're going $(\text{second derivative}) t^2/2$, this comes out to $O(1/n)$ error as well.

Together this shows $\log (\Delta/n^n) - \log C = O(1/n)$, which gives the claim.

How to estimate $t$: there are probably many ways. Here is one way. We solve
$$ |(z_i-z_j) + (v_i-v_j)t| = 2 $$
Now I pull factor of $z_i-z_j$ out, rewriting to $\rho$ and rearranging to get
$$ t = -\log |(z_i-z_j)/2|(1 + O(t))/\text{Re}(\rho). $$
By explicit calculation $\text{Re}(\rho) = 1 - (\text{angle between } z_i,z_j)/\pi$. It's most restrictive if you take that angle to be $\pi - 2\pi/n$ (almost-diameter). Also $O(t) = O(1/n)$. Now use all that and it comes out right in the end.

6) Conclusion. What was proved?

There is a construction for all even $n$ in which one has
$$ \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\Delta}{n^n} = C \approx 1.0378 > 1. $$
More specifically, for this construction, $\Delta = Cn^n (1 + O(1/n))$.

This implies that for even $n$, $\liminf_{n\to\infty} \Delta_{\max}/n^n \geq C > 1$.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
I'm in the process of writing this up as a pdf so we have a better reference to this argument.

As for Stijn/Quanyu/Yanni's $n=6k$ "circular arcs" construction, maybe this would help:

What I'm doing with that argument is that we define a fixed vector field
$$ z' = v(z) := \left(1 - \frac{2}{\pi}|\arg z|\right) \frac{z}{|z|}, \quad \arg z \in [-\pi, \pi). $$
Note this is independent of $n$; that's important to get an integrand that's independent of $n$.

Then I move the unit circle along this vector field ("flow"). In reality, it's a discrete version of this where we take the $n$th roots of unity and move them by $O(1/n)$.

But it turns out that the "continuous" version is a good enough approximation, allowing us to even calculate $C$ exactly as stated above.

It could be that the "circular arcs" construction can also be defined as flows along a fixed vector field. Then we may able to get similar results. But I'm not working on this at the moment.

In any case, this is an interesting and unexpected technique (from differential geometry) which initially seemed to have nothing to do with this "combinatorial" problem!
