sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here's a record of another of my failed attempt, for other (at least 3?) people working on this problem.

In the original [EHP58] paper, it was shown
$$ \frac{\Delta}{n^n} = \prod_{z \in \{\text{roots of f'}\}} |f(z)|. $$
Here $f$ is monic polynomial with roots $z_i$ and $f'$ is the derivative.

This is directly used in their proof that if $\bar{E} = \{z: |f(z)| \leq1\}$ is connected then $\Delta \leq n^n$. It's a really short proof so I'll reproduce it.

$\textbf{Proof}$ ([EHP58]). It suffices to show $|f(z)| \leq 1$ when $z$ is root of $f'$. We consider the lemniscates $\{z: |f(z)| = B\}$ and increase $B$ starting from $0$. A lemniscate has a multiple point iff $f'$ vanishes at that point. So if $\bar{E}$ is connected, there is no multiple point for $B > 1$. Hence a root of $f'$ cannot satisfy $|f(z)| > 1$. $\blacksquare$

So the attempt is to find a polynomial $f$ that is close to $z^n - 1$ but has easy explicit coefficients. Then that formula should allow for easy computation.

However, I have been trying polynomials such as $z^n \pm \varepsilon z^m - 1$ and $z^n \pm \varepsilon (z^{n-1} + \dots + z) - 1$. All of these that I tried are worse than the original $z^n - 1$ (the regular polygon). Note when computing we must scale like so: $\Delta / (n^n \text{diam}^{n(n-1)})$.

This presents a conundrum: the polynomial description (via coefficients) is easy to compute, but I can't perturb it to get a good one. In contrast, the geometric description (via roots) has explicit constructions that are good, but I can't compute with them. It seems I can't do "explicit construction" and "easy to compute" together currently! It's also known that there is no simple way to translate between the two descriptions: even though there is continuous dependence, the problem can be ill-conditioned see e.g. Wilkinson's polynomial.

The thought process still continues...

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
I have been making progress towards proving $\Delta \geq Cn^n$ for large $n$ even and some fixed $C>1$. This has proven to be more challenging than expected. In particular, I have discovered some Fourier-type(?) phenomenon that may illustrate where the difficulty lies:

$\textbf{A new "diameter" construction}$. First, following my heuristic (which will later shown to be flawed) that we should get $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)}$, I devised the following arrangement for even $n$ that is hopefully easier to get a closed form.
$$ \delta_k = c \left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{4k}{n^2}\right), z_k = \left(1 + \delta_k \right) e^{\frac{2\pi i k}{n}}, z_{k+n/2} = -\left(1 - \delta_k \right) e^{\frac{2\pi i k}{n}}, \quad k=0,1,\dots,\frac{n}{2}-1. $$
Here $c = c_{\max}(n)$ is the maximum quantity that maintains the diameter of $2$. It is found numerically that $c_{\max}(n) \to \pi^2/4$ for $n$ large (probably not hard to prove).

The idea here is that I'm moving diameters radially by $\delta_k$. I want $O(1/n)$ perturbation, but to maintain max distance of $2$ the consecutive $\delta_k$ can only differ by $O(1/n^2)$. Finally, $c/n$ has to become $-c/n$ on the other side to maintain consistency - this forces that we must decrease by $4c/n^2$ each time if we want linear interpolation of $\delta_k$.

So far so good. Also, numerical evidence suggests $\Delta/n^n \to 1.037...$ for large even $n$. That's promising. I still can't prove that, though.

$\textbf{Trouble with delicateness}$. However, here lies the trouble. I naively thought that any $\delta_k$ that is $O(1/n)$ and decreases by $O(1/n^2)$ should work, so I now observe that we can take
$$ \delta_k = \frac{c}{n} \cos \left(\frac{2\pi k}{n}\right), $$
which satisfies those conditions and also interpolates from $c/n$ to $-c/n$. The advantage is that if we let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$, then
$$ z_k = \left(1 + \frac{c}{n} \left(\frac{\omega^k + \omega^{-k}}{2}\right) \right) \omega^k $$
is polynomial in $\omega^k$. This simplifies calculations. We also have numerically $c_{\max}(n) \to \pi/2$. Nevertheless, it is found $\Delta/n^n \to 1$ (very rapidly in fact), destroying any hoped-for gain.

This shows that the manner in which the radii interpolate matters in delicate details...

$\textbf{Refined intuition?}$. At first, I thought that we can perhaps make "local" estimates and combine them piece by piece; my $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)} \geq C$ heuristic reflects that. But the new construction and the "bad" variant show that the "global" arrangement of the whole configuration matters in ways that may be difficult to understand.

In particular, this seems reminiscent of the phenomenon that convergence of sums can depend very much on how we choose to "space" points. I'm reminded of the Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature, which is a numerical integration method where we make a change of variable $x = \cos \theta$, and how that becomes more accurate and stable than Newton-Cotes simply by spacing points differently.

Note this perspective is not so alien because we're actually looking at a quadrature of
$$ \int_{z(s),z(t) \in \text{ curve}} \log |z(s) - z(t)| \, ds dt, $$
where both the curve and sampling points change with each $n$. (I don't think viewing it this way helps with the calculations, though.)

So: any proof/approach that ignores the global spacing won't work - that's at least useful to know.

$\textbf{Conclusion (for now)}$. There are now at least two candidates for $\Delta \geq Cn^n$ for $n$ even.

1. Stijn's construction for $n=6k$ based on $6$ circular arcs in my description above. We now see that the "circular" part probably matters; I didn't think it matters before.

2. The diameter construction in this comment where we interpolate radii "smoothly". We also know that the exact interpolation matters.

Still, no proof :( !

Credit: ChatGPT for these numerical investigations.

sourceComments.author: natso26
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here are some counterexamples with improved asymptotics. First we look at Stijn's "yanking a diameter" construction for even $n$:

$\textbf{Claim}$. Let $n$ be even. From a regular $n$-gon, take any diameter and translate that radially as far as possible so as to still retain the same diameter of the set. Then $\Delta/n^n = 1 + O(1/n^2)$.

So, contrary to TFBloom's expectation, the improvement to regular polygons is extremely modest.

$\textbf{Proof}$. Let $1,\omega,\dots,\omega^{n-1}$ be the roots of unity. We're looking at
$$ f(z) := \prod_{k \neq 0, n/2} |z - \omega^k| = \frac{|z^n - 1|}{|z^2-1|}. $$
Now
$$ f(1+\varepsilon)f(1-\varepsilon) = \frac{n^2}{4} + \frac{n^2(n^2-6n+8)}{48} \varepsilon^2 + O(\varepsilon^4) $$
(via Wolframalpha). So if we're yanking out by $\varepsilon$, the improvement is $1 + O(n^2\varepsilon^2)$. Direct calculation shows we can take at most $\varepsilon = O(1/n^2)$. That gives the claim. $\blacksquare$

Of course, the question is: can this be improved? It turns out the answer is "yes" - why not yank out all diameters at the same time? If we do that, we can optimistically expect improvement of
$$ (1 + O(1/n^2))^{O(n)} = 1 + O(1/n). $$
Here's one way that seems "good". We alternate between pushing and pulling consecutive diameters. To make this consistent we must have $n = 4k+2$ (not just $n$ even). This turns out to be "Reuleaux polygon plus arc midpoints". Incidentally, this is also Quanyu's construction for $n=6$ - so it's one of the strongest candidates for that case.

$\textbf{Claim}$. Let $n = 4k+2$. Consider a Reuleaux $(2k+1)$-gon with arc midpoints. Then $\Delta/n^n = 1 + O(1/n)$.

$\textbf{Proof}$. Let $z_1,\dots,z_{2k+1}$ be the polygon vertices on the unit circle and $w_1,\dots,w_{2k+1}$ the arc midpoints. Let the diameter be $2(1 - \varepsilon)$. We have $\varepsilon = O(1/n^2)$. Note $|w_i| = 1 - 2\varepsilon$. Then
$$ \begin{align}
\Delta_{z_i \text{ only}} &= (2k+1)^{2k+1} \\
\Delta_{w_i \text{ only}} &= (1-2\varepsilon)^{2k(2k+1)} (2k+1)^{2k+1} \\
\Delta_{z_i \text{ to } w_j} &= \prod |w_i^{2k+1} - 1|^2 = ((1-2\varepsilon)^{2k+1}+1)^{4k+2}
\end{align} $$
(Note $w_i^{2k+1} = - |w_i|^{2k+1}$.) Hence the ratio is
$$ \frac{\text{prod of those three}}{(1 - \varepsilon)^{(4k+1)(4k+2)} (4k+2)^{4k+2}} = 1 + 4k^2(2k+1) \varepsilon^2 + O(\varepsilon^3) $$
(again by Wolframalpha). For $\varepsilon = O(1/n^2)$, we get $1 + O(1/n)$. $\blacksquare$

It could be that this asymptotics is optimal. Otherwise, the heuristic above suggests we need constructions that differ substantially from "yanking diameters"; so far all constructions (even the kite for $n=4$) are of this form.

natso26
replies.contentMd: Cool! What is the most recent progress? Even if the Reuleaux configuration isn’t maximizing, there are still related questions about them: 1) is it optimal in the asymptotics (which could be good enough for a “solution” to the problem if the exact value is messy)?, 2) are we still moving diameters slightly as I seem to suggest, or are we looking at different ways entirely?

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
1) Seems it is not, and it indeed gets messy.
For $6 \mid n$, thus $n=6k$ for some integer $k$, we have the following construction that should prove that there is no $(1+o(1))n^n$ upper bound. (it is not the optimal construction for $n \ge 12$)
Take a regular $n$-gon with diameter $2/cos(\pi/2n)$, $A_1 A_2 \ldots A_{6k}$
(so all angles are $\pi- 2\pi/n$ initially, it attains the maximum perimeter, and since $n$ is even the diameter is too large at this point, but it is the analogue of the odd $n$-gon)

Now increasing the angles in $A_k,A_{3k}$ and $A_{5k}$ by $\pi/n$
while decreasing the angles in $A_{2k},A_{4k}$ and $A_{6k}$ by $\pi/n$.

But so it is still a challenge at this point to formally prove it is $>C n^n$ for some fixed $C>1$.

2) No. (The moving diameters idea is now one out of three arguments that shows that the regular $n$-gon is not extremal for $2 \mid n$)

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
As a follow-up, I have translated the construction in part 1) of Stijn’s comment (07:48 on 07 Dec 2025) into Mathematica code. Based on extensive numerical experiments, it seems that the limit of $\Delta/n^n$ is greater than 1.3 (although it is still possible that there are issues with my implementation or with numerical precision). For example, when $n=600000$, the code gives $\Delta/n^n > 1.304$.

The Mathematica code is available on my GitHub page (see [here](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/counterexamples-problem-1045/blob/main/stijn_n_equals_6k_construction.nb)) for reference. However, it appears quite difficult to compute the limit directly from the description implemented in the Mathematica code, and a new perspective may be needed to handle the case $6|n$.

replies.author: natso26
replies.contentMd:
Thanks both Stijn and Quanyu. I've been investigating this Stijn's $n=6k$ construction following Quanyu's code. I haven't been able to show that $\Delta$ should be large, though. But I have empirically confirmed $\Delta / n^n \approx 1.30$ for $n$ large.

For future reference, since the parameterization is a bit messy and difficult to do calculations, I (also credit: ChatGPT) derived the following parametrization which is hopefully cleaner:

$\textbf{Description.}$ This configuration consists of $6$ congruent circular arcs and has a $D_3$ symmetry. In the coordinates where the center of the symmetry is $0$ and the reflection is conjugation, a canonical fundamental domain, consisting of $\arg z \in [0, \pi/3]$, is precisely one such circular arc given by:
$$ \tan \frac{\pi}{2n} \left(i-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + \sec \frac{\pi}{2n} \exp \left(i \left(2j-\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{\pi}{n}\right), \quad j = 0,1,\dots,\frac{n}{6}. $$
Some notes: there are only $3$ circles - the opposite arcs belong to the same circle. There are two kinds of orbits.
1. The "edge" points corresponding to $j=0$ and $j=n/6$ are special. Their orbits have size $3$ (corresponding to $C_3$ action) and each is a (differently sized) equilateral triangle.
2. The remaining $n/6-1$ points have orbits of size $6$.
The orbits of the edge points are also precisely the $6$ intersections of the $3$ circles. $\blacksquare$

This can give us preliminary insight into why we should expect $\Delta \geq Cn^n$. In my Reuleaux-based config, the modulus of each $z$ is $1 + O(1/n^2)$. This makes each diameter contribute roughly $1 + O(1/n^2)$, resulting in $(1 + O(1/n^2))^{O(n)} = 1 + O(1/n)$. But this new config is a union of circles with centers displaced by $O(1/n)$ and radius $1 + O(1/n^2)$ - so the modulus is actually $1 + O(1/n)$! Of course there are cancellations, but we might think heuristically as follows.

Utilizing $C_3$ symmetry ($120$ deg rotation), we might expect each equilateral triangle here to contribute $1 + O(1/n)$, analogous to the "diameter", due to roots-of-unity style grouping/cancellation. (Note: I don't have proof.) Then we have $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)} \geq C$.

But since we don't have closed-form expressions in this case, I don't know how to show this if it is true. Nevertheless, it may be possible to construct other configs that amount to $(1 + O(1/n))^{O(n)}$ that could be easier to handle.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The question should be phrased a little different, see [[EHP58]](https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1958-05.pdf).

They ask about the maximum, and in particular ask if the vertices of a regular polygon is a maximizer;

For a fixed $n$, what is the maximum value of $\Delta(z_i)= \prod_{1 \le i <j \le n} |z_j-z_i|^2$ when all $z_i \in \mathbb C$ and $|z_j-z_i| \le 2$ for every $1 \le i,j \le n.$
Is the maximum achieved if the $z$, are the vertices of a regular $n$-gon
whose greatest diagonal has length $2$?

replies.contentMd:
The n=5 case is the easiest one.
(Edit: thought Quanyu had mentioned before n=4,5 was verified, but it was 4,6 which is numerically verified)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Hereby some related literature, since the problem has been considered in some other settings (these may be considered more natural). Here one usually considers diameter $1$, equivalent with $|z_i-z_j| \le 1$ (thus just a rescaling of Erdos' condition)

For maximum area, width, perimeter and sum of diagonals, it turns out that for particular values of $n$, the best polygon is also an approximation or behaves complex (so one only has a numeric approximation)

$\underline{General\ background}$

The diameter graph of a polygon with diameter $1$, has vertex set equal ot the vertices of the polygon, and edges equal ot the pairs of vertices at distance $1.$

It is known that a diameter graph $G$ satisfies $|V(G)| \ge |E(G)|.$

$\textbf{Area}$
[[ Foster, Szabo '07]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0097316507000428)
[[Audet, Hansen,Svrtan '21]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10898-020-00908-w ) (even $n$ starting from $6$ are already hard)

$\textbf{Perimeter}$
[[Datta95 ]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/A:1004997002327) (classical work that shows the maximum perimeter is known if $n$ has an odd divisor)
[[ Bingane21]](https://optimization-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/8430.pdf ) (on both perimeter and width)
[[Audet, Hansen, Messine ]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0097316506000537 ) (even for $n=8$, max perimeter is hard)

$\textbf{Sum of all diagonals}$
[[Audet, Guillou, Hansen, Messine, Perron '10]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10898-010-9572-2) (the sum of diagonals for odd $n>5$ is not maximised by a regular $n$-gon)

***
*This is an update, indicating the problem cannot be expected to be easy.*
The thought process with multiple people still continues...

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The additional question can be answered in the negative for every even $n \ge 4$.

For this, consider a regular $n$-gon, with $A=(-1,0)$ and $B=(1,0)$ as two oppositive vertices.

Now if one replaces these two points with $A'=(-1+ \epsilon)$ and $B'=(1+ \epsilon)$ for $\epsilon>0$ (sufficiently small such that the diameter of the construction is still $2$), we can check that the discriminant of the construction $\Delta$ increases.

To see this; a simple computation shows that for every $1\ge x>0$, the vertices $C=(1-x, \sqrt{2x-x^2})$ and $D=(-(1-x), \sqrt{2x-x^2})$ satisfy
$d(A,C)d(A,D)d(B,C)d(B,D)<d(A',C)d(A',D)d(B',C)d(B',D)$.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
Great! I still have not found any counterexample when $n$ is odd. Perhaps the next step is to try to prove that in the odd case the regular $n$-gon indeed maximizes $\Delta$. Besides, it may also be interesting to determine the extremal configurations for even $n$ where the maximum is attained.

PS. I feel that this problem is quite similar to [[974]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/974). At that time, we first found counterexamples for even $n$, and then proved all the odd-$n$ cases. I have carefully searched the literature and have not found this problem resolved; I hope it is not, as with [[974]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/974), already settled by earlier work.

replies.author: Quanyu Tang
replies.contentMd:
For the case \(n=4\), Stijn and I also conjecture that the kite-shaped configuration I found is indeed the extremal one, although at the moment we do not yet have a proof.
For the case \(n=6\), I guess that the extremal configuration is the following:\[
z_1=(-1,0),\quad z_2=(1,0),\quad z_3=(0,\sqrt{3}),\quad z_4=(0,-(2-\sqrt{3})),\quad z_5=(\sqrt{3}-1,1),\quad z_6=(-(\sqrt{3}-1),1).
\]These six points lie evenly on a Reuleaux triangle.

EDIT: We have already been able to prove the case where \(n=4\).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Very nice! I suppose this configuration still satisfies $\Delta_n \ll n^n$, so that Pommerenke's bound of $\ll 2^{O(n)}n^{n}$ can probably be improved. It would be interesting if there was a construction where $\Delta_n/n^n\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$. Perhaps your construction already has this property if you can find many candidates $C$ and $D$ where the relevant part of the discriminant to $A'$ and $B'$ grows?

I have looked carefully but couldn't find anything else in the literature - of course there may be papers which don't cite Erdős or Pommerenke's paper, and are lacking obvious key words, in which case it's difficult for a search to uncover them.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
Tao Hu and I found counterexamples for this Problem.

In particular, when $n=4$ the following four points form a counterexample:\[
z_1=(0,0),\quad z_2=(\sqrt{3},1),\quad z_3=(\sqrt{3},-1),\quad z_4=(2,0).
\]All pairwise distances are $\le 2$, and we compute\[
\Delta(z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4)\approx 294.08 \;>\; 256=\Delta(\text{square}),
\]so the regular quadrilateral is not maximal.

We also constructed a counterexample for $n=6$. However, we did not find any counterexample for $n=5$, which suggests that the problem might still hold for odd $n$. Details can be found on my GitHub page [here](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/counterexamples-problem-1045/blob/main/Counterexamples_for_Erdos_Problem_1045.pdf).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Interesting, thanks Quanyu. This is probably one of those problems where there might be errant examples for small $n$, but things settle down eventually.

It would be great if you could find an infinite sequence of counterexamples.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
It seems that there is a small typo in the statement for odd $n$. If the $z_i$ are vertices of a regular $n$-gon, then\[
\Delta = \cos(\pi/2n)^{-n(n-1)}n^{n}  \sim e^{\pi^2/8}n^n,
\]not $\cos(\pi/2n)^{-\frac{n}{n-1}}$.

### Problem
A unitary divisor of $n$ is $d\mid n$ such that $(d,n/d)=1$. A number $n\geq 1$ is a [unitary perfect number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_perfect_number) if it is the sum of its unitary divisors (aside from $n$ itself).

### Context

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1053 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1053).

### Problem
Call a number $k$-perfect if $\sigma(n)=kn$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum of the divisors of $n$. Must $k=o(\log\log n)$?

### Context

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1054 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1054).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be the minimal integer $m$ such that $n$ is the sum of the $k$ smallest divisors of $m$ for some $k\geq 1$.

Is it true that $f(n)=o(n)$? Or is this true only for almost all $n$, and $\limsup f(n)/n=\infty$?

sourceComments.author: Vjeko_Kovac
sourceComments.contentMd:
This was disproved (quite strongly) by Terry Tao in the comments on [[468]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/468), where he showed that the upper density of all $\{n\in\mathbb{N} : f(n)\leq \delta n\}$ is $\ll \delta^2$ (in a slightly different but equivalent formulation).

Namely, denoting by $\sigma_k(n)$ the sum of divisors of $n$ excluding the $k$ largest ones, Terry proved that\[ \sum_{k\geq 0} \sum_{n\leq x} \sigma_k(n) \ll x^2. \]Therefore, for any $x,C>0$ we get
\begin{align*}
& \# \{N\geq Cx : f(N)\leq x\} \\
& \leq \# \{(n,k) : n\leq x, k\geq0, \sigma_k(n)\geq Cx\} \\
& = \sum_k \# \{ n\leq x : \sigma_k(n)\geq Cx\} \\
& \ll \frac{1}{Cx} \sum_{k\geq0} \sum_{n\leq x} \sigma_k(n) \ll \frac{x}{C}.
\end{align*}
For any $\delta,t>0$ we choose $C=1/(2\delta)$, $x=\delta t$ to obtain\[ \# \{ N\in [t/2, t] : f(N)\leq \delta N \} \ll \delta^2 t . \]Now split an arbitrary interval $[1,X]$ dyadically, i.e., apply the obtained inequality to $t=X/2^j$, $j=0,1,2,\ldots$ and sum in $j$ to finally get\[ \# \{ N\leq X : f(N)\leq \delta N \} \ll \delta^2 X . \]

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.contentMd: I agree. Thing is, the function f itself has not been shown to be well-defined, which makes this problem open anyway.

sourceComments.contentMd: This is essentially a duplicate of the last question of [[468]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/468), meaning that the function $f$ defined here is obtained by merely shifting indices by 1 (since here we count 1 as a divisor). I gave some comments and experimental observations on the behavior of $f$ in the last paragraph under [[468]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/468). Either this problem is redundant, or the last question from [[468]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/468) should be moved here, or (if nothing else) the two problems should link to each other.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1055 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1055).

### Problem
A prime $p$ is in class $1$ if the only prime divisors of $p+1$ are $2$ or $3$. In general, a prime $p$ is in class $r$ if every prime factor of $p+1$ is in some class $\leq r-1$, with equality for at least one prime factor.

Are there infinitely many primes in each class? If $p_r$ is the least prime in class $r$, then how does $p_r^{1/r}$ behave?

### Context
A classification due to Erdős and Selfridge. It is easy to prove that the number of primes $\leq n$ in class $r$ is at most $n^{o(1)}$.

The sequence $p_r$ begins $2,13,37,73,1021$ ([A005113](https://oeis.org/A005113) in the OEIS). Erdős thought $p_r^{1/r}\to \infty$, while Selfridge thought it quite likely to be bounded.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1056 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1056).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 2$. Does there exist a prime $p$ and consecutive intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_k$ such that\[\prod_{n\in I_i}n \equiv 1\pmod{p}\]for all $1\leq i\leq k$?

### Context
This is problem A15 in Guy's collection [Gu04], where he reports that in a letter in 1979 Erdős observed that\[3\cdot 4\equiv 5\cdot 6\cdot 7\equiv 1\pmod{11},\]establishing the case $k=2$. Makowski [Ma83] found, for $k=3$,\[2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 5\equiv 6\cdot 7\cdot 8\cdot 9\cdot 10\cdot 11\equiv 12\cdot 13\cdot 14\cdot 15\equiv 1\pmod{17}.\]Noll and Simmons asked, more generally, whether there are solutions to $q_1!\equiv\cdots \equiv q_k!\pmod{p}$ for arbitrarily large $k$ (with $q_1<\cdots<q_k$).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1057 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1057).

### Problem
Let $C(x)$ count the number of [Carmichael numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_number) in the interval $[1,x]$. Is it true that $C(x)=x^{1-o(1)}$?

### Context
Erdős [Er56c] proved\[C(x) < x \exp\left(-c \frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right)\]for some constant $c>0$. Pomerance [Po89] gave a heuristic suggesting that this is the true order of growth, and in fact\[C(x)= x \exp\left(-(1+o(1))\frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right).\]Alford, Granville, and Pomerance [AGP94] proved that $C(x)\to \infty$, and in fact $C(x)>x^{2/7}$ for large $x$. The lower bound\[C(x)> x^{0.33336704}\]was proved by Harman [Ha08]. This exponent was improved to $0.3389$ by Lichtman [Li22].

Korselt observed that $n$ being a Carmichael number is equivalent to $n$ being squarefree and $p-1\mid n-1$ for all primes $p\mid n$.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1063 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1063).

### Problem
Let $k\geq 2$ and define $n_k\geq 2k$ to be the least value of $n$ such that $n-i$ divides $\binom{n}{k}$ for all but one $0\leq i<k$. Estimate $n_k$.

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Selfridge posed in [ErSe83]. Erdős and Selfridge noted (and a proof can be found in [Mo85]) that if $n\geq 2k$ then there must exist at least one $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ does not divide $\binom{n}{k}$.

We have $n_2=4$, $n_3=6$, $n_4=9$, and $n_5=12$. Monier [Mo85] observed that $n_k\leq k!$ for $k\geq 3$, since $\binom{k!}{k}$ is divisible by $k!-i$ for $1\leq i<k$. Cambie observes in the comments that this can be improved to\[n_k\leq k[2,3,\ldots,k-1]\leq e^{(1+o(1))k},\]where $[\cdots]$ is the least common multiple.

### Deliverable

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Small observation related to the one by Monier:
$n_k\le  k \cdot lcm( \{2,3,\ldots,k-1\})$ by the same reason for $k \ge 3$.

This implies an exponential upper bound $\exp((1+o(1))n).$

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
The behaviour could be exponential.
Hereby it is not sure if it is of the form $c^{(1+o(1))n}$ for some constant $c$, or there is an exponential lower- and upper-bound of the latter form, but $1/k \log n_k$ does not converge.
The minimum and maximum of $n_k^{1/k}$ for $k \le 37$ were attained in $k=10$ and $k=31$ with $(n_k)^{1/k} \sim 2.178$ and $(n_k)^{1/k} \sim 1.337$ respectively.

As a test, I checked the distribution of the number of $0 \le i <k$ for which $n-i$ is not a divisor of $\binom n k$, for $2k \le n \le n_k$.
For $k=23$ this gave e.g.
$[0,
 1,
 4,
 26,
 131,
 299,
 432,
 453,
 428,
 254,
 165,
 121,
 87,
 56,
 57,
 45,
 20,
 14,
 2]$

(no more than $18$ numbers i were bad here, but letting $n$ above $n_k$, one can reach higher numbers as well)

(The distribution seems not to be approximated by a binomial distribution)

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
By the Bateman–Horn conjecture, the answer should be yes for every fixed combination of $k>0$ and $\ell.$
In particular, the number of Sophie-Germaine primes is expected to be infinite.

In the other direction, $q=271129$ is an example for which no $2^n\cdot q+1$ is prime.
See [[SierpinskiNumbers]](https://t5k.org/glossary/page.php?sort=SierpinskiNumber).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1066 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1066).

### Problem
Let $G$ be a graph given by $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where any two distinct points are at least distance $1$ apart, and we draw an edge between two points if they are distance $1$ apart.

Let $g(n)$ be maximal such that any such graph always has an independent set on at least $g(n)$ vertices. Estimate $g(n)$, or perhaps $\lim \frac{g(n)}{n}$.

### Context
Such graphs are always planar. Erdős initially thought that $g(n)=n/3$, but Chung and Graham, and independently Pach, gave a construction that shows $g(n)\leq \frac{6}{19}n$. Pach and Toth [PaTo96] improved this to $g(n)\leq \frac{5}{16}n$.

Pollack [Po85] noted that the [Four colour theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/four_color_theorem) implies $g(n)\geq n/4$, since the graph is planar. Pollack reports that Pach observed that this in for unit distance graphs the four colour theorem can be proved by a simple induction.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: ebarschkis
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think it would be worth noting that the answer to this problem depends heavily on the definition of connectivity. If interpreted as edge-connectivity, this problem is solved. Thomassen ([2016 paper](https://backend.orbit.dtu.dk/ws/files/124108162/Erdos_Hajnal_final.pdf)) proved that every graph with uncountable chromatic number contains a subgraph of infinite edge-connectivity.

However, the problem remains open for vertex-connectivity. I suggest updating the problem statement to explicitly specify "infinitely vertex-connected" to avoid ambiguity.

Another important detail is that it is known that such a graph does not need to contain an uncountable infinitely vertex-connected subgraph ([arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05984v1)).

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Yes the vertex-connected interpretation was intended, I have edited to make this clearer.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1070 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1070).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that, given any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, there exist $f(n)$ points such that no two are distance $1$ apart. Estimate $f(n)$. In particular, is it true that $f(n)\geq n/4$?

### Context
In other words, estimate the minimal independence number of a unit distance graph with $n$ vertices. If $\omega$ is the independence number and $\chi$ is the chromatic number then $\omega \chi\geq n$, and hence $f(n)\geq n/\chi$, where $\chi$ is the answer to the Hadwiger-Nelson problem [[508]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/508).

The [Moser spindle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moser_spindle) shows $f(n)\leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n$. Larman and Rogers [LaRo72] noted that if $m_1$ is the supremum of the upper densities of measurable subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ which have no unit distance pairs then\[f(n)\geq m_1n.\]Croft [Cr67] gave the best-known lower bound of $m_1\geq 0.22936$ and hence\[0.22936n \leq f(n) \leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n.\]Ambrus, Csiszárik, Matolcsi, Varga, and Zsámboki [ACMVZ23] have proved that $m_1\leq 0.247$, and hence this approach cannot achieve $f(n)\geq n/4$. See [[232]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/232) for more on $m_1$.

### Deliverable

sourceMetadata.statement: Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that, given any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, there exist $f(n)$ points such that no two are distance $1$ apart. Estimate $f(n)$. In particular, is it true that $f(n)\geq n/4$?
sourceMetadata.statementMd: Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that, given any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, there exist $f(n)$ points such that no two are distance $1$ apart. Estimate $f(n)$. In particular, is it true that $f(n)\geq n/4$?
sourceMetadata.statusNote: This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
researchNotes: In other words, estimate the minimal independence number of a unit distance graph with $n$ vertices. If $\omega$ is the independence number and $\chi$ is the chromatic number then $\omega \chi\geq n$, and hence $f(n)\geq n/\chi$, where $\chi$ is the answer to the Hadwiger-Nelson problem [[508]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/508).

The Moser spindle shows $f(n)\leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n$. Larman and Rogers [LaRo72] noted that if $m_1$ is the supremum of the upper densities of measurable subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ which have no unit distance pairs thenf(n)\geq m_1n.Croft [Cr67] gave the best-known lower bound of $m_1\geq 0.22936$ and hence0.22936n \leq f(n) \leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n.Ambrus, Csiszárik, Matolcsi, Varga, and Zsámboki [ACMVZ23] have proved that $m_1\leq 0.247$, and hence this approach cannot achieve $f(n)\geq n/4$. See [[232]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/232) for more on $m_1$.

Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga, and Zsámboki [MRVZ23] have improved the upper bound tof(n) \leq \left(\frac{1}{4}+o(1)\right)n.They conjecture that $m_1=0.22936\cdots$ (the lower bound of Croft mentioned above) and $f(n)=(1/4+o(1))n$.
If we also insist that no two points are distance $<1$ apart then this is problem becomes [[1066]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1066).

sourceComments.author: danielvarga
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let me note that our not-yet-peer-reviewed paper [FCN4] makes progress on this question by presenting unit distance graphs with independence ratio arbitrarily close to 1/4. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first improvement of the trivial 2n/7 upper bound, to n/4+o(n). It is reasonable to conjecture that either Croft's 0.22936 or our 1/4 is sharp, [FCN4] Conjecture 1 states the latter.

[FCN4] Máté Matolcsi, Imre Z. Ruzsa, Dániel Varga, Pál Zsámboki
 - The fractional chromatic number of the plane is at least 4, arXiv:2311.10069

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
The problem above was solved by G.~Csizmadia in his paper
\emph{On the independence number of minimum distance graphs},
Discrete Comput. Geom. \textbf{20}, 179--187 (1998).
\url{https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009381}. In this work, Csizmadia studies the
unit-distance graph defined on a finite planar point set whose minimum
pairwise distance is~1, and asks for the size of the largest independent
set, that is, a subset containing no two points at distance exactly~1.

Csizmadia improved an earlier result of Pollack by proving that every
such set of \(n\) points contains an independent subset of size at least\[
   \frac{9}{35}\,n \approx 0.2571\,n.
\]In particular,\[
   f(n) \ge \frac{9}{35}\,n > \frac{1}{4}\,n,
\]so the conjectured lower bound \(f(n) \ge n/4\) is true (and even
slightly improved). The paper also provides an \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm
which constructs such a large independent subset for any given
configuration of \(n\) points.

\bigskip
\noindent
References

[Cs98] G. Csizmadia, \emph{On the independence number of minimum distance graphs}, Discrete Comput. Geom. \textbf{20}, 179--187 (1998). \url{https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009381}.

[ACMVZ23] G. Ambrus, A. Csiszárik, M. Matolcsi, D. Varga, and P. Zsámboki, \emph{The density of planar sets avoiding unit distances}, arXiv:2207.14179 (2023).

[Cr67] H. T. Croft, \emph{Incidence incidents}, Eureka (1967), 22--26.

[LaRo72] D. G. Larman and C. A. Rogers, \emph{The realization of distances within sets in Euclidean space}, Mathematika (1972), 1--24.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1074 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1074).

### Problem
Let $S$ be the set of all $m\geq 1$ such that there exists a prime $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m!+1\equiv 0\pmod{p}$. Does\[\lim \frac{\lvert S\cap [1,x]\rvert}{x}\]exist? What is it?

Similarly, if $P$ is the set of all primes $p$ such that there exists an $m$ with $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ such that $m!+1\equiv 0\pmod{p}$, then does\[\lim \frac{\lvert P\cap [1,x]\rvert}{\pi(x)}\]exist? What is it?

### Context
Questions raised by Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao, who called the set $S$ 'EHS numbers' and the set $P$ 'Pillai primes', and proved that both $S$ and $P$ are infinite. Pillai [Pi30] raised the question of whether there exist any primes in $P$. This was answered by Chowla, who noted that, for example,\[14!+1\equiv 18!+1\equiv 0\pmod{23}.\]The sequence $S$ begins\[8,9,13,14,15,16,17,\ldots\]and is [A064164](https://oeis.org/A064164) in the OEIS. The sequence $P$ begins\[23,29,59,61,67,71,\ldots\]and is [A063980](https://oeis.org/A063980) in the OEIS.

Regarding the first question, Hardy and Subbarao computed all EHS numbers up to $2^{10}$, and write '...if this trend conditions we expect [the limit] to be around $0.5$, if it  exists. The frequency with which the EHS numbers occur - most often in long sequences of consecutive integers - makes us believe that their asymptotic density exists and is unity. Erdős, though initially hesitant, later agreed with this view.'

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
I would guess that the natural density of $S$ is $1$.

Heuristic: write $N_m=m!+1$. For every prime $q\le m$, we have $m!\equiv 0 \pmod q$, hence $N_m\equiv 1 \pmod q$, so every prime divisor of $N_m$ is $>m$. The condition $m\notin S$ means that every prime divisor $p$ of $N_m$ satisfies $p\equiv 1 \pmod m$. Thus the exceptional set consists of those $m$ for which all prime factors of $m!+1$ lie in the single residue class $1 \pmod m$.

Now treat $N_m$ as having “random-looking” prime divisors, subject only to the local restrictions above. Since $\log\log(m!+1)\sim \log m$, one expects $N_m$ to have about $\log m$ distinct prime factors. For a random large prime not dividing $m$, the chance of lying in the class $1 \pmod m$ should be about $1/\varphi(m)$. So the chance that all prime factors of $N_m$ lie in that one class should be roughly
$$(1/\varphi(m))^{\log m},$$
which tends to $0$ extremely fast. This suggests that the number of exceptional $m\le x$ should be $o(x)$, and therefore
$$|S\cap [1,x]|/x \to 1.$$

So my guess for the first question is that the limit exists and equals $1$.

This also seems more plausible than a limit near $1/2$: the condition defining the complement of $S$ is much more rigid than merely asking for one prime factor in a prescribed congruence class. One is requiring that every prime factor of $m!+1$ fall into the same residue class $1 \pmod m$, and heuristically that should be very rare.

References:
Hardy and Subbarao, *On Euclid’s algorithm and the theory of infinitely many primes*, Colloq. Math. 44 (1981), 47–59.
Subbarao, *Some remarks on Euclid’s number*, in *Number Theory and its Applications* (Ankara, 1996), Lecture Notes in Pure and Appl. Math. 204, Dekker, 1999, 281–290.
Guy and Selfridge, unstarred problem on Erdős–Selfridge–Hardy numbers / Pillai primes, as listed on Erdős Problems.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1082 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1082).

### Problem
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no three on a line. Does $A$ determine at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances? In fact, must there exist a single point from which there are at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances?

I have found a construction disproving the stronger conjecture in literature here from 2002: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X01001340
The construction provided here is identical to the one used by DeepMind, so I wouldn't consider this an original solve by the agent.

I was suspect of the originality of the quite simple construction DeepMind had provided, and I also had a gut feeling I had seen this exact construction before, but I couldn't place it. I was able to find this literature source from Google AI results from searching for "8 vertex configuration local 3 distance set erdos".

sourceComments.author: GTsoukalas
sourceComments.contentMd:
On February 14, a DeepMind prover agent found a Lean proof falsifying the second part of this conjecture. Of course, the conjecture had already been resolved, so the finding is not fundamentally novel. However, an interesting characteristic of our proof is that it constructs a counterexample with 8 points, smaller than the one @eigensolver gives in the thread below. The proof was discovered fully autonomously; the only problem-specific human input was the formal problem statement [link 1], drawn from Formal Conjectures [link 2]. The full Lean proof (compilable with Lean 4.22) is available here [link 3].

replies.contentMd:
[Here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plby/lean-proofs/refs/heads/main/other/Erdos1082gdm.png) is a picture of the configuration of eight points.  In words, one description of the configuration might be: Let four of the points be vertices of a square.  Then, on each side of the square, construct an equilateral triangle.  The remaining four points are the other vertices of those triangles.  (The triangles can either all face outward or all face inward, but the resulting configuration is the same in both cases.)

Also, note that the main conjecture is still open.  Both this construction, and [the one by eigensolver](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1082#post-2279), disprove the second/"stronger" part of the conjecture.

sourceComments.author: eigensolver
sourceComments.contentMd:
Following @StijnC's idea, I seem to have found a counterexample to the second question. It consists of $42$ points:

[Image Link](https://ibb.co/Df0sR3nc)
[GeoGebra Link](https://www.geogebra.org/classic/vphxsnc9)

This counterexample is composed of two concentric regular $N$-gons ($N = 21$), denoted as $A_1A_2\dots A_N$ and $B_1B_2\dots B_N$ counterclockwisely, with inner and outer radius ratio equal to $r_0=\frac12\left(1-\sqrt{5-8\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}}\right)=0.4450418679\dots$, a root of $x^3-x^2-2x+1=0$. This set of points satisfies $|A_1A_4|=|A_1B_4|$ and $|B_1B_{10}|=|B_1 A_5|$, which degenerates distances, and for any $B_k$, the line $A_1 B_k$ does not pass through any other points. Due to symmetry, each point determines only $N−1 = 20$ distinct distances, thus constituting a counterexample to the second problem.

The method I used involved solving quadratic equations in terms of $r$, of the form $|A_1 B_i| = |A_1 A_j|$ and $|B_1 B_k| = |B_1 A_l|$, obtaining solution sets $R_1$ and $R_2$, and then selecting $r$ from their intersection such that no three points are collinear. However, due to precision errors, I might have misjudged the solutions. I would be immensely grateful if someone could help verify this.

By the way, all $(N, r)$ pairs I found are of the form:

$$(42k+21, r_0),\quad (42k+21, 1-r_0)\quad (k\in\mathbb{N})$$

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
Great :)
I checked that $(21,r_0)$ and $(21,1-r_0)$ are solutions with Maple.
(the computations are purely goniometric)

Since $42k+21$ is an odd multiple of $21$, the same result applies there,
and so one has infinitely many examples, but all of them come from the core configuration with two $21$-gons.

For $1-r_0$, one has $|A_1A_4|=|A_1B_4|$ and $|B_1B_7|=|B_1A_5|$ (the labeling in the geogebra file does not correspond with the usual numbering).

replies.author: llllvvuu
replies.contentMd: This counterexample has been [verified](https://gist.github.com/llllvvuu/5e0b51804e7676c0650856c680d03856) in Lean 4 using [Aristotle](https://aristotle.harmonic.fun/).

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
I tried to disprove the additional (stronger version of the) question,
but didn't get there:
take n odd, and two concentric regular n-gons $A_1A_2 \ldots A_n$ and $B_1B_2 \ldots B_n$ (common circumcenter $O$), with $O,A_i,B_i$ colinear for every $i$.
By choosing $n$ and $|OA_i|/|OB_i|$ right, it might be that $|A_iA_j|=|A_i B_k|$ and $|B_iB_j|=|A_i B_\ell|$ for some $i,j,k,\ell$, while no $3$ points of the construction are colinear.
If so, we would conclude.
(satisfying 1 out of 2 of the first is easy)

Update: checked for odd $n \le 250$, and no positive result.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
A note that the second question is a stronger form of [[982]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/982) (I'll add this remark).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
(Question prompted by construction with $n=21$ below.)

When you checked odd $n\le 250$, were you assuming that $A_i$ and $B_i$ had exactly the same angle?

replies.author: StijnC
replies.contentMd:
The incompleteness was that the check happened under the $|A_iA_j|=|A_iB_i|$ condition (i.e., not all possible combinations were taken)
So I am very happy eigensolver did the effort to check all combinations,
while I indeed only did a quick easy search.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1083 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1083).

### Problem
Let $d\geq 3$, and let $f_d(n)$ be the minimal $m$ such that every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ determines at least $m$ distinct distances. Estimate $f_d(n)$ - in particular, is it true that\[f_d(n)=n^{\frac{2}{d}-o(1)}?\]

### Context
A generalisation of the distinct distance problem [[89]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/89) to higher dimensions. Erdős [Er46b] proved\[n^{1/d}\ll_d f_d(n)\ll_d n^{2/d},\]the upper bound construction being given by a set of lattice points.- Clarkson, Edelsbrunner, Gubias, Sharir, and Welzl [CEGSW90] proved $f_3(n)\gg n^{1/2}$.
- Aronov, Pach, Sharir, and Tardos [APST04] proved $f_d(n)\gg n^{\frac{1}{d-90/77}-o(1)}$ for any $d\geq 3$ (for example, $f_3(n)\gg n^{0.546}$).
- Solymosi and Vu [SoVu08] proved $f_3(n) \gg n^{3/5}$ and\[ f_d(n)\gg_d n^{\frac{2}{d}-\frac{c}{d^2}}\]for all $d\geq 4$ for some constant $c>0$. (The result in their paper for $d=3$ is slightly weaker than stated here, but uses as a black box the bound for distinct distances in $2$ dimensions; we have recorded the consequence of combining their method with the work of Guth and Katz on [[89]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/89).)

The function $f_d(n)$ is essentially the inverse of the function $g_d(n)$ considered in [[1089]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1089) - with our definitions, $g_d(n)>m$ if and only if $f_d(m)<n$. The emphasis in this problem is, however, on the behaviour as $d$ is fixed and $n\to \infty$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1084 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1084).

### Problem
Let $f_d(n)$ be minimal such that in any collection of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, all of distance at least $1$ apart, there are at most $f_d(n)$ many pairs of points which are distance $1$ apart. Estimate $f_d(n)$.

### Context
This is sometimes known as the contact number problem.

It is easy to see that $f_1(n)=n-1$ and $f_2(n)<3n$ (since there can be at most $6$ points of distance $1$ from any point). Erdős [Er46b] showed\[f_2(n)<3n-cn^{1/2}\]for some constant $c>0$, which the triangular lattice shows is the best possible up to the value of $c$. In [Er75f] he speculated that the triangular lattice is exactly the best possible, and in particular\[f_2(3n^2+3n+1)=9n^2+3n.\]Harborth [Ha74b] proved this, and more generally\[f_2(n)=\lfloor 3n-\sqrt{12n-3}\rfloor\]for all $n\geq 2$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

In [Er75f] he claims the existence of $c_1,c_2>0$ such that6n-c_1n^{2/3}< f_3(n) < 6n-c_2n^{2/3}.An upper bound off_3(n) < 6n-0.926n^{2/3}for all $n\geq 2$ was proved by Bezdek and Reid [BeRe13].

sourceComments.author: Moritz Firsching
sourceComments.contentMd:
Regarding the formula $f_2(3n^2+3n+1)=9n^2+6n$: Might there be a typo in [Er75f] and it should read $f_2(3n^2+3n+1)=9n^2+3n$?
This would be https://oeis.org/A045945
and the right thing if we are looking for the number of edges in the $n$-hexagonal graph/triangular lattice.
This came up when AlphaProof found [a disproof of this](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/58666281575b792b51b05e241025bce16f10dd1a/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/1084.lean#L62) for the case $n=1$.
Could also be an unrelated misformalisation, but is there are construction where the number $9n^2 + 6n$ appears and not $9n^2 + 3n$? This is also mentioned in the next sentence in [Er75f].

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd: $f_2(3n^2+3n+1)=9n^2+3n$ is consistent with the next equation $f_2(n)=\lfloor 3n-\sqrt{12n-3}\rfloor$.

Let $f_d(n)$ be minimal such that, in any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, there exist at most $f_d(n)$ pairs of points which distance $1$ apart. Estimate $f_d(n)$.

### Context
The most difficult cases are $d=2$ and $d=3$. When $d=2$ this is the unit distance problem [[90]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/90), and the best known bounds are\[n^{1+\frac{c}{\log\log n}}< f_2(n) \ll n^{4/3}\]for some constant $c>0$, the lower bound by Erdős [Er46b] and the upper bound by Spencer, Szemerédi, and Trotter [SST84].

When $d=3$ the best known bounds are\[n^{4/3}\log\log n \ll f_3(n) \ll n^{3/2}\beta(n)\]where $\beta(n)$ is a very slowly growing function, the lower bound by Erdős [Er60b] and the upper bound by Clarkson, Edelsbrunner, Guibas, Sharir, and Welzl [CEGSW90].

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1086 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1086).

### Problem
Let $g(n)$ be minimal such that any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ contains the vertices of at most $g(n)$ many triangles with the same area. Estimate $g(n)$.

### Context
Equivalently, how many triangles of area $1$ can a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determine? Erdős and Purdy attribute this question to Oppenheim. Erdős and Purdy [ErPu71] proved\[n^2\log\log n \ll g(n) \ll n^{5/2},\]and believed the lower bound to be closer to the truth. The upper bound has been improved a number of times - by Pach and Sharir [PaSh92], Dumitrescu, Sharir, and Tóth [DST09], Apfelbaum and Sharir [ApSh10], and Apfaulbaum [Ap13]. The best known bound is\[g(n) \ll n^{20/9}\]by Raz and Sharir [RaSh17].

Erdős and Purdy also ask a similar question about the higher-dimensional generalisations - more generally, let $g_d^{r}(n)$ be minimal such that any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contains the vertices of at most $g_d^{r}(n)$ many $r$-dimensional simplices with the same volume.

### Deliverable

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1091 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1091).

### Problem
Let $G$ be a $K_4$-free graph with chromatic number $4$. Must $G$ contain an odd cycle with at least two diagonals?

More generally, is there some $f(r)\to \infty$ such that every graph with chromatic number $4$, in which every subgraph on $\leq r$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq 3$, contains an odd cycle with at least $f(r)$ diagonals?

### Context
Erdős originally asked about the existence of just one diagonal, which is true, and was proved by Larson [La79]. In fact Larson proved the following stronger conjecture of Bollobás and Erdős: if $G$ is a $K_4$-free graph containing no odd cycle with a diagonal then either $G$ is bipartite, or $G$ contains a cut vertex, or $G$ contains a vertex with degree $\leq 2$.

The pentagonal wheel shows that three diagonals are not guaranteed.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1092 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1092).

### Problem
Let $f_r(n)$ be maximal such that, if a graph $G$ has the property that every subgraph $H$ on $m$ vertices is the union of a graph with chromatic number $r$ and a graph with $\leq f_r(m)$ edges, then $G$ has chromatic number $\leq r+1$.

Is it true that $f_2(n) \gg n$? More generally, is $f_r(n)\gg_r n$?

### Context
A conjecture of Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi. This seems to be closely related to, but distinct from, [[744]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/744).

Tang notes in the comments that a construction of Rödl [Ro82] disproves the first question, so that $f_2(n)\not\gg n$.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
It seems that the result of Rödl [Rö82, Theorem 1.5] implies that $f_{2}(n)\not\gg n$, which therefore gives a negative answer to the first problem.

Specifically, Rödl gave an explicit construction $K^{*}(n,k)$ and proved in [Rö82, Theorem 1.5] that for any $\varepsilon>0$ and any positive integer $k$, when $n$ is sufficiently large,\[
\chi\!\left(K^{*}(n,k)\right)=k+2,
\quad\text{and every subgraph }H\text{ becomes bipartite after deleting }
\le \varepsilon|V(H)|\text{ edges.}
\]Now we argue by contradiction.  Assume that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$, $f_{2}(n)\ge c n$. Let $\varepsilon=c/2$ and $k \geq 2$. By [Rö82, Theorem 1.5], there exists a graph $G=K^{*}(n,k)$ (for large $n$) satisfying that every subgraph $H$ can be made bipartite by deleting at most $\varepsilon|V(H)|$ edges, while $\chi(G)=k+2\ge4$. This means that $G$ satisfies the assumption of the definition of $f_{2}$, since every subgraph $H$ is the union of a bipartite graph and a graph with at most $\varepsilon|V(H)|$ edges, and $f_{2}(m)\ge c m\ge\varepsilon m$. However, the conclusion $\chi(G)\le3$ fails (because $\chi(G)=k+2$). This contradiction shows that no such linear lower bound $c$ can exist.

[Rö82] Rödl, Vojtěch. "Nearly bipartite graphs with large chromatic number." Combinatorica 2.4 (1982): 377-383.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1093 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1093).

### Problem
For $n\geq 2k$ we define the deficiency of $\binom{n}{k}$ as follows. If $\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by a prime $p\leq k$ then the deficiency is undefined. Otherwise, the deficiency is the number of $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ is $k$-smooth, that is, divisible only by primes $\leq k$.

Are there infinitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency $1$? Are there only finitely many with deficiency $>1$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS88], that was also asked in the 1986 problem session of West Coast Number Theory (as reported [here](https://westcoastnumbertheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/wcnt-problems-1991.pdf)).

In [ELS93] they prove that if the deficiency exists and is $\geq 1$ then $n\ll 2^k\sqrt{k}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Kevin Barreto
sourceComments.contentMd:
For $\binom{n}{k}$ with defined deficiency (i.e. $\gcd\left(\binom{n}{k},\,k!\right)=1$), we shall write $\delta(n,k)$ for its associated deficiency. This is probably useless, but I can give a resolution to the second problem under two rather strong conjectures:

$\textbf{Conjecture A}$ (Strengthening of the [$xyz_{\mathrm{fin}}$-conjecture](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0911.4147) of Lagarias-Soundararajan). There exists $\kappa_0>1$ such that for all $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many primitive integer triples $X+Y=Z$ with $$\max\{p\in\mathbb{P}:p\mid XYZ\}=:S(X,Y,Z)<(\log H(X,Y,Z))^{\kappa_0-\varepsilon},$$
where $H(X,Y,Z):=\max\{|X|,\,|Y|,\,|Z|\}$.

$\textbf{Conjecture B}$ (Height forcing). Let $h_2(k)$ be the least $n\geq 2k$ such that $\binom{n}{k}$ has defined deficiency $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$. There exists $\alpha>1/\kappa_0$ such that for all sufficiently large $k$, $$h_2(k)<\infty\implies\log h_2(k)\geq ck^{\alpha}$$for some fixed $c>0$. (By PNT, we can at least show that if there is such an $\alpha>0$, then $\alpha\leq 1$).

Now, we state our result:

$\textbf{Theorem}$. Assume Conjecture A and Conjecture B. Then, there are only finitely many pairs $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 2k$ and $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$.
$\textit{Proof.}$ Suppose, for contradiction, that there are infinitely many such $(n,k)$. Fix one with $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$, then $\exists i,j\in\mathbb{N}$ with $i\neq j$ such that $x:= n-i$ and $y:=n-j$ are both $k$-smooth, lying in $(n-k,n]$. Set $\Delta:=\left|x-y\right|=\left|i-j\right|$, so $1\leq\Delta<k$. Since $\Delta<k$, all prime factors of $\Delta$ are $\leq k$, hence $\Delta$ is $k$-smooth. Now, consider the equation $y+\Delta=x$. Let $d:=\gcd(y,\Delta)$, and set $$A:=\frac{y}{d},\qquad B:=\frac{\Delta}{d},\qquad C:=\frac{x}{d},$$then $A+B=C$ is primitive. Because $x,y,\Delta$ are $k$-smooth and dividing by $d$ removes only primes $\leq k$, we have $S(A,B,C)\leq k$. Moreover, since $x\in(n-k,n]$, and $d\leq\Delta<k$, $$H(A,B,C)\geq C=\frac{x}{d}\geq\frac{n-k}{k}.$$Thus, $\log H\geq\log n-\mathcal{O}(\log k)$. Now, invoke Conjecture B: Since $\delta(n,k)\geq 2$, we have $\log n\gg k^{\alpha}$, hence $\log H\gg k^{\alpha}\iff k\ll(\log H)^{1/\alpha}$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ s.t. $\alpha(\kappa_0-\varepsilon)>1$ (which is possible as we have assumed $\alpha>1/\kappa_0$). Then, for all sufficiently large members of the infinite family, $$S(A,B,C)\leq k\ll(\log H)^{1/\alpha}<(\log H)^{\kappa_0-\varepsilon}.$$This produces infinitely many primitive triples violating Conjecture A, a contradiction. $\square$

sourceComments.author: Kevin Barreto
sourceComments.contentMd:
FWIW, I think, as in [ELS88], that we want $n\geq 2k$, otherwise the second question is trivial: For a prime $p$, $\binom{p}{p-1}=p$ has deficiency $p-2$, so there are infinitely many with deficiency $>1$.

Also, the current listing of $\binom{8113}{28},\binom{8114}{28},\binom{96022}{42}$ as having deficiency $2$ seems incorrect to me. They appear to have undefined deficiency: $\binom{8113}{28}$ and $\binom{8114}{28}$ are divisible by $2,3,11,13,17,19$, and $\binom{96022}{42}$ is divisble by $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,29,41$.
I believe the intended entries are $\binom{8413}{28}$, $\binom{8414}{28}$, and $\binom{96622}{42}$, which all appear to have deficiency $2$. Moreover, $\binom{174}{12}$ and $\binom{239}{14}$ also have deficiency $2$.
For $n\leq 10^5$, there are $58$ deficiency $1$ examples, $8$ deficiency $2$ examples, $6$ deficiency $3$ examples, and $1$ example for deficiences $4$ and $9$ each.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1094 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1094).

### Problem
For all $n\geq 2k$ the least prime factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is $\leq \max(n/k,k)$, with only finitely many exceptions.

### Context
A stronger form of [[384]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/384) that appears in a paper of Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS88]. Erdős observed that the least prime factor is always $\leq n/k$ provided $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $k$. Selfridge [Se77] further conjectured that this always happens if $n\geq k^2-1$, except $\binom{62}{6}$.

The threshold $g(k)$ below which $\binom{n}{k}$ is guaranteed to be divisible by a prime $\leq k$ is the subject of [[1095]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1095).

### Deliverable

This is related to [[1093]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1093), in that the only counterexamples to this conjecture can occur from $\binom{n}{k}$ with deficiency $\geq 1$.
There is an interesting discussion about this problem on MathOverflow.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1095 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1095).

### Problem
Let $g(k)>k+1$ be the smallest $n$ such that all prime factors of $\binom{n}{k}$ are $>k$. Estimate $g(k)$.

### Context
A question of Ecklund, Erdős, and Selfridge [EES74], who proved\[k^{1+c}<g(k)\leq \exp((1+o(1))k)\]for some constant $c>0$, and conjectured $g(k)<L_k=[1,\ldots,k]$, the least common multiple of all integers $\leq k$, for all large $k$. In [EES74] they further conjecture that\[\limsup \frac{g(k+1)}{g(k)}=\infty\]and\[\liminf \frac{g(k+1)}{g(k)}=0.\]The lower bound was improved by Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS93] and Granville and Ramaré [GrRa96]. The current record is\[g(k) \gg \exp(c(\log k)^2)\]for some $c>0$, due to Konyagin [Ko99b].

Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS93] write 'it is clear to every right-thinking person' that $g(k)\geq\exp(c\frac{k}{\log k})$ for some constant $c>0$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: shtuka
sourceComments.contentMd:
I gave this problem to 5.4 pro, while it wasn't able to fully prove $\log g( k) \asymp \frac{k}{\log k}$, it was able to [show](https://shtuka123.github.io/gk_writeup.pdf)(verified by Opus 4.6, Gemini  3.1 Pro, and myself) the following weaker form of the bound: Let $\mathcal{A}(k) := \{ n \geq 0 : p \nmid {n \choose k} \text{ for every prime } p \leq k  \} $, and let $\Delta(k)$ denote its natural density. If $S(k) := \log \Delta(k)^{-1}$, then we have $S(k) \asymp \frac{k}{\log k}$.

GPT also proposes the following strategy for proving the full asymptotic bound - I have not fully looked into this but it seems very roughly plausible, at least to me. Write $g(k) = k + Q(k) h_*(k)$, where\[ Q(k) := \prod_{p \leq k } p^{v_p(k+1)}\]Write $\tilde{\Delta}(k) = Q(k) \Delta(k)$ and\[ N(k) := \prod_{p \leq k} p^{L_p - v_p(k+1)} \]where $L_p = \lfloor{\log_p k} \rfloor + 1$. Then if one can show a bound of the form\[ h_*(k) \ll \tilde{\Delta}(k)^{-1} ( \log N(k) )^A   \]for some absolute $A$, this should imply the desired bound of $ \log g(k) \asymp \frac{k}{\log k}$.

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
Before Alex Meiburg's [comment](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1095#post-2596), this page said that [EES74] conjectured that $g(k) < \exp(k^{1+o(1)})$.  This statement then made its way into the [Formal Conjectures](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/3d6dc14ba924f82ab5200288f6c6ee1be1326a2d/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/1095.lean#L48-L55) project.  Aristotle was able to prove that statement all by itself.  Unfortunately, [the definition of $g(k)$](https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/3d6dc14ba924f82ab5200288f6c6ee1be1326a2d/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/1095.lean#L31-L37) on that page was misformalized, because it was missing the $g(k) > k+1$ condition.  This actually doesn't affect the validity of the proof, but nonetheless, I fixed that misformalization and reran Aristotle.  It was still able [to prove this result](https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/ErdosProblems/Erdos1095.md) by itself.  (It was not able to prove any of the open variants of the problem.)  [Type-check it online!](https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.24.0&url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fplby%2Flean-proofs%2Frefs%2Fheads%2Fmain%2Fsrc%2Fv4.24.0%2FErdosProblems%2FErdos1095b.lean)

This page now says that [EES74] proved $g(k) < \exp(k^{1+o(1)})$, but I think it is actually $g(k) < \exp(k(1+o(1)))$.  Note the difference in "exponentiation" versus "multiplication".  Aristotle was not able to prove this version.  (The straightforward approach here uses the Prime Number Theorem.)

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.author: Ameiburg
sourceComments.contentMd:
[EES74] proved, not conjectured, that $g(k) < \exp(k(1+o(1))$. The conjecture they give there is that $g(k) < L_k = \textrm{lcm} \{1 \dots n\}$, which should hold for all $k \ge 7$.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

sourceComments.contentMd:
Sorenson, Sorenson, and Webster in [An algorithm and estimates for the Erdős–Selfridge function (2020)](https://msp.org/obs/2020/4-1/obs-v4-n1-p23-p.pdf) define the same function $g(k)$ and introduce an approximating function $\tilde g(k)$ based on counting admissible residues.
They prove\[
  0.530684 + o(1) \le \frac{\log \tilde g(k)}{k/\log k} \le 1 + o(1),
\]so in particular\[
  \log \tilde g(k) = \Theta\left(\frac{k}{\log k}\right).
\]Under a uniform distribution heuristic of theirs, they show that\[
  \log g(k) = \log \tilde g(k) + O(\log k),
\]which implies that $g(k)$ is, with high probability, within a polynomial factor of $\tilde g(k)$. Consequently, they heuristically expect $\log g(k) = \Theta\left(k/\log k\right)$, equivalently\[
  g(k) = \exp\left(\Theta\left(\frac{k}{\log k}\right)\right),
\]a growth rate that is larger than Konyagin’s proven lower bound $g(k) \gg \exp\left(c(\log k)^2\right)$. However, this faster $\exp\left(\Theta(k/\log k)\right)$ growth for $g(k)$ is only supported by their heuristic and has not been proved unconditionally.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1096 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1096).

### Problem
Let $1<q<1+\epsilon$ and consider the set of numbers of the shape $\sum_{i\in S}q^i$ (for all finite $S$), ordered by size as $0=x_1<x_2<\cdots$.

Is it true that, provided $\epsilon>0$ is sufficiently small, $x_{k+1}-x_k \to 0$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Joó posed in the [1991 problem session](https://westcoastnumbertheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/wcnt-problems-1991.pdf) of Great Western Number Theory.

They speculate that the threshold may be $q_0$, where $q_0\approx 1.3247$ is the real root of $x^3=x+1$, and is the smallest [Pisot-Vijayaraghavan number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisot%E2%80%93Vijayaraghavan_number).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: A problem of Erdős and Joó posed in the 1991 problem session of Great Western Number Theory.
They speculate that the threshold may be $q_0$, where $q_0\approx 1.3247$ is the real root of $x^3=x+1$, and is the smallest Pisot-Vijayaraghavan number.
In [EJK90] Erdő, Joó, and Komornik prove that any Pisot-Vijayaraghavan number cannot have this property, and also prove that, for any $1<q\leq 2$, $x_{k+1}-x_k\leq 1$ for all $k$.
The sequence always begins $0,1,q$.

Bugeaud [Bu96] proved that $1<q\leq 2$ is a Pisot-Vijayaraghavan number if and only if\liminf (x_{k+1}^m-x_k^m)>0for all $m\geq 1$, where $x_k^m$ is the set of those numbers which can be written as a finite sum $\sum_{n\geq 0}c_nq^n$ for some $c_n\in \{0,\ldots,m\}$ (so that the sequence in the question is $x_k^1$). Erdős, Joó, and Schnitzer [EJS96] improved this to show that, if $1<q<(1+\sqrt{5})/2$, then $q$ is a Pisot-Vijayaraghavan number if and only if\liminf (x_{k+1}^2-x_k^2)>0.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1097 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1097).

### Problem
Let $A$ be a set of $n$ integers. How many distinct $d$ can occur as the common difference of a three-term arithmetic progression in $A$? Are there always $O(n^{3/2})$ many such $d$?

### Context
A problem Erdős posed in the [1989 problem session](https://westcoastnumbertheory.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/wcnt-problems-1989.pdf) of Great Western Number Theory.

He states that Erdős and Ruzsa gave an explicit construction which achieved $n^{1+c}$ for some $c>0$, and Erdős and Spencer gave a probabilistic proof which achieved $n^{3/2}$, and speculated this may be the best possible.

### Deliverable

researchNotes: A problem Erdős posed in the 1989 problem session of Great Western Number Theory.

He states that Erdős and Ruzsa gave an explicit construction which achieved $n^{1+c}$ for some $c>0$, and Erdős and Spencer gave a probabilistic proof which achieved $n^{3/2}$, and speculated this may be the best possible.

In the comment section, Chan has noticed that this problem is exactly equivalent to a sums-differences question of Bourgain [Bo99], introduced as an arithmetic path towards the Kakeya conjecture: find the smallest $c\in [1,2]$ such that, for any finite sets of integers $A$ and $B$ and $G\subseteq A\times B$ we have\\lvert A\overset{G}{-}B\rvert \ll \max(\lvert A\rvert,\lvert B\rvert, \lvert A\overset{G}{+}B\rvert)^c\\in G$).

This is equivalent in the sense that the greatest exponent $c$ achievable for the main problem here is equal to the smallest constant achievable for the sums-differences question. The current best bounds known are thus1.77898\cdots \leq c \leq 11/6 \approx 1.833.The upper bound is due to Katz and Tao [KaTa99]. The lower bound is due to Lemm [Le15] (with a very small improvement found by AlphaEvolve [GGTW25]).

The description says 'This is equivalent in the sense that the greatest exponent c
 achievable for the main problem here is equal to the smallest constant achievable for the sums-differences question.'

The only time $c$ in mentioned in the description with respect to this problem is when it says 'He states that Erdős and Ruzsa gave an explicit construction which achieved $n^{1+c}$ for some $c>0$.' sourceComments.author: KoishiChan
sourceComments.contentMd: Take $X = A \cup B \cup \frac{1}{2} (A +_G B)$. Then for any $(a, b) \in G$, the sequence $a, \frac{1}{2}(a + b), b$ is an AP with difference $\frac{1}{2}(b - a)$. Hence, $D(X) \geq |A -_G B|$.

replies.contentMd:
Of course, thanks! I think this neatly resolves the problem (in the sense that it's exactly equivalent to a more well-known problem at least). The lower bound has been improved, the current record is $1.77898$ (see page 41 of the [AlphaEvolve paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.02864)). (Compare to $11/6\approx 1.833$.)

sourceComments.author: KoishiChan
sourceComments.contentMd:
Ok I think this is actually equivalent to a problem first considered by Bourgain in "On the Dimension of Kakeya Sets and Related Maximal Inequalities" and Rusza in "Sums of Finite Sets": If $A, B$ are finite set of integers, and $G \subset A \times B$ satisfies
$$|A|, |B|, |A+_G B| \leq N$$
then what is the smallest $c$ such that $|A -_G B| \leq N^c$?

To see the connection, simply consider $X = A \cup B \cup \frac{1}{2}\cdot (A +_G B)$.

Bourgain proved an upper bound of $c \leq 2 - \frac{1}{13}$. The best upper bound I can find is due to Katz and Tao who proved $c \leq 2 - \frac{1}{6}$. In the same paper a lower bound of $c \geq \log(6) / \log(3) = 1.6309$ was established.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Aha, yes - embarrassed I missed this since I've been thinking about this very problem recently! I agree that the upper bounds here imply an upper bound for this problem (taking $G$ to be the set of $(a,b)\in A^2$ such that $a+b\in 2\cdot A$), which implies an upper bound of $2-1/6$ (this has not been improved over the Katz-Tao paper).

I'm not sure I see why they're equivalent though, can you explain why a lower bound for this latter problem implies the same for this page's problem?

sourceComments.author: KoishiChan
sourceComments.contentMd:
Using my previous comment, together with recent results by AlphaEvolve, Robert Gerbicz, and Fan Zheng, I can disprove the prediction in the problem statement.

The above (together with a small tensor power argument) shows that
$$\sup_A \frac{\log |D(A)|}{\log |A|} \geq \sup_U \frac{\log |U + U| + \log |U - U| - \log |U|}{\log |U + U|}.$$
Now, pp. 3 of this paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.16105 seems to give quite a nice $U$. Specifically, the $U$ in the paper satisfies (base 10)
$$\log |U - U| \geq 75899, \log |U+U| \leq 61229, \log |U| \leq 43547.$$
So we obtain
$$\frac{\log |U + U| + \log |U - U| - \log |U|}{\log |U + U|} \geq 1.528.$$
Hence, we obtain $A$ with
$$|D(A)| \geq |A|^{1.528 - o(1)}.$$
This is slightly better :).
Of course, I might just be stupid, and some very easy construction gives close to $2$ in the exponent. Who knows :))

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Nice! This is the sort of construction that Imre Ruzsa would approve of.  I'll launch an AlphaEvolve run optimizing this score rather than the one studied in the previous papers, and see if we can do significantly better than 1.528.

EDIT: AlphaEvolve instantly produced the example $U = \{0,3,7,15,16,21\}$ with $|U|=6$, $|U+U|=21$, $|U-U|=31$, giving a score of $(\log(21)+\log(31)-\log(6))/\log(21) \approx 1.5394$ (so your search of subsets of $\{0,\dots,17\}$ was only just shy of working).  I'll let it run for a few hours and see what improvements it can get.  Incidentally, this example, combined with the previous construction, should be within the capability of current autoformalization tools to convert into a Lean disproof of the second claim.

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd: After 10 hours, AlphaEvolve was only able to come up with one slightly better construction: $U = \{-1214, -729, -248, -89, 447, 206, -2209, 887, 665, -3302, -261, -195, -134, -1537\}$, with a score of $1.5523$ ($|U|=14, |U+U|=105, |U-U|=183$).  Most likely using the high-dimensional constructions in the papers of Gerbicz, Zheng, or Gyarmati-Hennecart-Ruzsa will do better, but I haven't tried this.  This seems like a good "beat the AI" challenge!

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
I think that, as you indicate, the high-dimensional construction of Hennecart, Robert, and Yudin ('On the number of sums and differences', Astérisque 1999, p. 173-178) does better, around $1.5828$.

If one checks the final page of that paper, you find a construction of a set $U$ (namely taking those non-negative integer vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^{2m}$ with total weight $\leq m$) such that\[ \lvert U+U\rvert =\lvert U\rvert^{c_1+o(1)}\]and\[ \lvert U-U\rvert =\lvert U\rvert^{c_2+o(1)}\]where\[c_1=\frac{4\log 2}{3\log 3-2\log 2}\]\[c_2 =\frac{4\log(1+\sqrt{2})}{3\log 3-2\log 2}.\]This gives a score of\[\frac{\log(64/27)+4\log(1+\sqrt{2})}{\log(16)}\approx 1.5828.\]

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Very nice! I think the limit of your construction is an exponent of $5/3$:

Let the size of A be $K\lvert U\rvert$. By Plunnecke-Ruzsa the size of your $D(A)$ is at most either $K^2\lvert A\rvert$ or $\lvert U\rvert\lvert A\rvert$. If $K$ is greater than $\lvert U\rvert^{1/2}$ use the latter, else use the former.

sourceComments.author: KoishiChan
sourceComments.contentMd:
There seems to be a mysterious connection between this problem and the sum / difference set problem.

To motivate the discussion, we first provide a explicit construction of the $\Omega(n^{3/2})$ bound. Take $X$ to be a finite set with no non-trivial solution to $x + y = z + w$, and set $A = (X - X) \cup \frac{1}{2} \cdot (X - X)$. Then $|A| = \Theta(|X - X|) = \Theta(|X|^2)$. Let $D(A)$ denote the set of common differences. Note that for any $x, y, z \in X$, the sequence $x - y, \frac{1}{2}(x - z), y - z$ forms an AP in $A$ with common difference $\frac{1}{2}(x + z - 2y)$. Hence, we have
$$|D(A)| \geq |X + X - 2\cdot X| = \Omega(|X|^3) = \Omega(|A|^{3/2}).$$
Now, how do we improve this? Well, we can use the construction above except with any $X$, and we win if
$$|X + X - 2 \cdot X| \geq |X - X|^{3/2 + \epsilon}.$$
A standard tensor power argument shows that we win if
$$|X + X - 2 \cdot X| > |X - X|^{3/2}.$$
However, I searched over subsets of $[1,...17]$ and found no counterexample.

Another strategy is to introduce more arguments. Here let me choose sets $U$ and $Y$ with elements of $Y$ spaced sufficiently far apart compared to $U$, and set
$$A = (U + Y) \cup (-U - Y) \cup \frac{1}{2}\cdot (U + U).$$
For any $u_1, u_2 \in U$ and $y \in Y$, the following is an AP in $A$:
$$u_1 + y, \frac{1}{2}(u_1 + u_2), -u_2 - y, $$
with common difference $\frac{1}{2} (u_2 - u_1) - y$. Hence, we have
$$|D(A)| \geq |U - U - 2 \cdot Y|.$$
By our choice of $Y$, we have
$$|A| = 2|U||Y| + |U + U|, |D(A)| \geq |U - U||Y|.$$
Taking $|Y|$ appropriately, we have
$$|A| = \Theta(|U + U|), |D(A)| = \Omega(|U + U||U - U||U|^{-1}).$$
Now the connection with sum / difference becomes obvious!

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1100 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1100).

### Problem
If $1=d_1<\cdots<d_{\tau(n)}=n$ are the divisors of $n$, then let $\tau_\perp(n)$ count the number of $i$ for which $(d_i,d_{i+1})=1$.

Is it true that $\tau_\perp(n)/\omega(n)\to \infty$ for almost all $n$? Is it true that\[\tau_\perp(n)< \exp((\log n)^{o(1)})\]for all $n$?

Let\[g(k) = \max_{\omega(n)=k}\tau_\perp(n),\]where $\omega(n)$ counts the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, and $n$ is restricted to squarefree integers. Determine the growth of $g(k)$.

### Context
The function $\tau_\perp(n)$ was considered by Erdős and Hall [ErHa78]. It is trivial that $\tau_\perp(n)\geq \omega(n)$ (with equality for infinitely many $n$). Erdős and Hall prove, for all $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $x$,\[\max_{n<x} \tau_\perp(n) > \exp((\log\log x)^{2-\epsilon}).\]Erdős and Simonovits (see [Er81h]) proved\[(2^{1/2}+o(1))^k < g(k) < (2-c)^k\]for some constant $c>0$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.
