sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
A few remarks, perhaps to whet some appetite.
1) Of course $\tau_\perp(n) < \tau(n)$, and since $\tau(n) < \exp\left(\frac{c \log n}{\log \log n}\right)$, this is an upper bound for $\tau_\perp(n)$ as well. As far as I know it is not even known whether $\tau_\perp(n) = \exp\left(o(\frac{\log n}{\log \log n})\right)$ holds, which feels at least plausibly doable.

2) The equality $\tau_\perp(n) = \omega(n)$ holds whenever $n = p_1p_2 \cdots p_k$ with $p_j > p_1p_2 \cdots p_{j-1}$ for all $j$ with $2 \le j \le k$. Indeed, this latter equality makes it so that all divisors $d$ of $n$ with $p_{j-1} \le d < p_j$ are divisible by $p_{j-1}$.

3) The proofs of the Erdős-Simonovits bounds on $g(k)$ do not appear in [Er81h]. Perhaps it would be worthwhile to recreate them. They do state that these bounds are based on the following claim: let $A = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}$ be a set for which all subset sums are distinct. Order the subsets $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_{2^k}$ of $A$ such that $\sum_{a \in A_i} a < \sum_{a \in A_{i+1}} a$ holds for all $1 \le i \le 2^{k}-1$. Then $g(k)$ is equal to the maximum number of $i$ (taken over all sets $A$ with distinct subset sums) such that $A_i \cap A_{i+1} = \emptyset$.

4) I can ever so slightly sharpen the proof that $\tau_\perp(n) > \exp((\log \log n)^{2-o(1)})$ holds for infinitely many $n$, in the sense that I can make the $o(1)$-term explicit.

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many $n$ for which $\tau_\perp(n) > \exp\left(\frac{(\frac{1}{2} - o(1))(\log \log n)^{2}}{\log \log \log n}\right).$

*Proof.* Let $\epsilon \in \left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right)$ be arbitrary, let $x$ be arbitrary but large, and choose $n$ to be the product of all primes in the interval $(x, 2x]$, so that $n = e^{(1+o(1))x}$ by the prime number theorem. We now consider all divisors $D_1 < D_2 < \cdots < D_r$ of $n$ with exactly $y := \left \lfloor \frac{(\frac{1}{2} - \epsilon) \log x}{\log \log x} \right \rfloor$ prime factors. Then $$x^y < D_1 < D_2 < \cdots < D_r < (2x)^y < x^{y+1}. \hspace{20pt} (1)$$From these inequalities it follows that all of those divisors $D_i$ are actually consecutive divisors of $n$. To calculate how many $D_i$ there are, we note that
\begin{align*}
r &= \binom{\pi(2x) -\pi(x)}{y} \\
&> \left(\frac{x}{2 y \log x} \right)^y \hspace{116pt} (2)\\
&> \left(x^{1-o(1)}\right)^y \\
&= \exp\left(\frac{(\frac{1}{2} - \epsilon - o(1))\log^2 x}{\log \log x}\right) \\
&= \exp\left(\frac{(\frac{1}{2} - \epsilon - o(1))(\log \log n)^2}{\log \log \log n}\right). \\
\end{align*}As $\gcd(D_i, D_{i+1}) > 1$ implies $D_{i+1} - D_i > x$, the number of such pairs of consecutive divisors which are not coprime is at most $2^y x^{y-1}$ by the second to last inequality in $(1)$. We claim that this is $o(r)$, which would finish the proof. By equation $(2)$ it suffices to show $(4y \log x)^y = o(x)$;
\begin{align*}
(4y \log x)^y &< \left(\log x)^{2}\right)^y \\
&= e^{2y \log \log x} \\
&\le e^{(1 - 2\epsilon)\log x} \\
&= o(x).
\end{align*}5) The right-most inequality in $(1)$ above already holds as long as $y < \log_2 x$, so if one can bound the number of pairs $(D_i, D_{i+1})$ which are not coprime in a better way, then plausibly the above argument could be improved to provide infinitely many $n$ with  $\tau_\perp(n) > \exp\left((\frac{1}{\log 2} - o(1))(\log \log n)^{2}\right).$

6) (added 17-03-2026) Just for funsies I asked Aristotle to formalize the proof of the above theorem, under the assumption that the product of all primes in $(x, 2x]$ is $e^{(1 + o(1))x}$. [And it did!](https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem1100.lean) You used to be able to type-check it online [here](https://live.lean-lang.org/#project=mathlib-v4.24.0&url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2FWoett%2FLean-files%2Fmain%2FErdosProblem1100.lean), but unfortunately that website no longer seems to support Lean version 4.24.0.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1101 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1101).

### Problem
If $u=\{u_1<u_2<\cdots\}$ is a sequence of integers such that $(u_i,u_j)=1$ for all $i\neq j$ and $\sum \frac{1}{u_i}<\infty$ then let $\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ be the sequence of integers which are not divisible by any of the $u_i$. For any $x$ define $t_x$ by\[u_1\cdots u_{t_x}\leq x< u_1\cdots u_{t_x}u_{t_x+1}.\]We call such a sequence $u_i$ good if, for all $\epsilon>0$, if $x$ is sufficiently large then\[\max_{a_k<x} (a_{k+1}-a_k) < (1+\epsilon)t_x \prod_{i}\left(1-\frac{1}{u_i}\right)^{-1}.\]Is there a good sequence such that $u_n< n^{O(1)}$? Is there a good sequence such that $u_n\leq e^{o(n)}$?

### Context
Erdős [Er81h] believed the answer to the first question is no and the second question is yes. He proved the existence of some good sequence (in which all the $u_i$ are primes).

An easy sieve argument proves that we always have, for any sequence $u$ with those properties,\[\max_{a_k<x} (a_{k+1}-a_k)> (1+o(1))t_x \prod_{i}\left(1-\frac{1}{u_i}\right)^{-1}.\]The strong form of [[208]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/208) is asking whether if $u_i=p_i^2$, the sequence of prime squares, is good.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
1) From what I understand from his proof of the existence of a good sequence (which, truth be told, isn't much), it seems like Erdős shows that any sequence of primes that grows like $2^{2^n}$ is good. Based on this I think showing that a good sequence exists which grows merely exponentially fast, would already be a significant improvement.
2) All problems with [Er81h] as a reference seem to have superfluous enter in the title of the paper. But apologies if I'm not sufficiently respecting Chesterton's fence here.
3) His 1966 paper 'On the difference of consecutive terms of sequences defined by divisibility properties' (see [here](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1966-14.pdf), at the top of page 177) is presumably the first reference where he alluded to this problem. There he already claimed the existence of a good sequence.

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1103 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1103).

### Problem
Let $A$ be an infinite sequence of integers such that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. How fast must $A$ grow?

### Context
Erdős notes there exists such a sequence which grows exponentially, but does not expect such a sequence of polynomial growth.

In [Er81h] he asked whether there is an infinite sequence of integers $A$ such that, for every $a\in A$ and prime $p$, if\[a\equiv t\pmod{p^2}\]then $1\leq t<p^2/2$. He noted that such a sequence has the property that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. He wrote 'I am doubtful if such a sequence exists. I formulated this problem while writing these lines and must ask the indulgence of the reader if it turns out to be trivial.'

### Deliverable

researchNotes: Erdős notes there exists such a sequence which grows exponentially, but does not expect such a sequence of polynomial growth.

In [Er81h] he asked whether there is an infinite sequence of integers $A$ such that, for every $a\in A$ and prime $p$, ifa\equiv t\pmod{p^2}then $1\leq t<p^2/2$. He noted that such a sequence has the property that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. He wrote 'I am doubtful if such a sequence exists. I formulated this problem while writing these lines and must ask the indulgence of the reader if it turns out to be trivial.'
Indeed, there are trivially at most finitely many such $a$, since there cannot be any primes $p\in (a^{1/2},(2a)^{1/2}]$, but there exist primes in $(x,\sqrt{2}x)$ for all large $x$.

If $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ is such a sequence then van Doorn and Tao [vDTa25] have shown that $a_j > 0.24j^{4/3}$ for all $j$, and further that there exists such a sequence (furthermore with squarefree terms) such thata_j < \exp(5j/\log j)for all large $j$. A superior lower bound of $a_j \gg j^{15/11-o(1)}$ had earlier been found by Konyagin [Ko04] when considering the finite case [[1109]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1109).
They also obtain further results for the generalisation from squarefree to $k$-free integers, and also replacing $A+A$ with $A\cup (A+A)\cup(A+A+A)$.
See also [[1109]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1109) for the finite analogue of this problem.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
The [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01087) Terence Tao and I just uploaded is mostly aimed at resolving [#1102](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1102), but we have some results for this problem as well. In particular, we improve upon the $0$ density result in my earlier comment and, in the other direction, we show the existence of a sequence with sub-exponential growth. More precisely, define $\mathcal{SF} \subset \mathbb{N}$ to be the set of squarefree integers, let $kA$ be the set of $k$ (not necessarily distinct) elements of $A$, and let us say that $A$ has squarefree sums if $2A \subset \mathcal{SF}$. We then have the following results:

**Theorem 1.** For any sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \} \subset \mathbb{N}$ with squarefree sums, we have $a_j > 0.24j^{4/3}$ for all $j \in \mathbb{N}$.

**Theorem 2.** There exists a sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \} \subset \mathcal{SF}$ with squarefree sums for which $a_j < \exp(5j / \log j)$ holds for all large enough $j \in \mathbb{N}$.

We furthermore observe that the proofs of Theorem 1 and 2 can be modified to obtain the following two bonus results on $k$-free sums and sums of three elements respectively:

**Theorem 3.** For any $k \ge 2$ and any sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \} \subset \mathbb{N}$ with $k$-free sums, we have $a_j \gg j^{2k/(2k-1)}$ for all $j \in \mathbb{N}$.

**Theorem 4.** There exists an absolute constant $C$ and a sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \}$ with $A \cup 2A \cup 3A \subset \mathcal{SF}$ for which $a_j < \exp(Cj^2 / \log j)$ holds for all $j \in \mathbb{N}$.

Note that Theorem 4 can not be extended to sums of four elements, as $4A$ of course contains elements divisible by $4$, if $A$ is non-empty.

EDIT: Some of our results have turned out to be obsolete by the results from Konyagin mentioned below, so Terry and I rewrote the relevant parts of our paper. The original arXiv version containing proofs of the above theorems can be found [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.01087v1).

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
Benjamin Bedert has pointed out to us that there is in fact a significant body of literature on this problem already, namely

* P. Erdős and A. Sárközy. On divisibility properties of integers of the form a + a′. Acta Math. Hungar., 50(1-
2):117–122, 1987. doi:10.1007/BF01903370.
* S. V. Konyagin. Problems of the set of square-free numbers. Izv. Ross. Akad. Nauk Ser. Mat., 68(3):63–90, 2004.
doi:10.1070/IM2004v068n03ABEH000486.
* G. N. Sárközy. On a problem of P. Erdős. Acta Math. Hungar., 60(3-4):271–282, 1992. doi:10.1007/BF00051645.
* Katalin Gyarmati. On divisibility properties of integers of the form ab + 1. Period. Math. Hungar., 43(1-2):71–79,
2001. doi:10.1023/A:1015229531017.

In particular, the results of Konyagin give the improved lower bound
$$ a_j \gg j^{15/11} \exp\left( -O\left(\frac{\log j}{\sqrt{\log\log j}} \right)\right).$$

Konyagin also constructs subsets of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with squarefree sums of cardinality $\gg \log^2 N \log\log N$.  If there was a way to paste these constructions together for various $N$, this would give an example with
$$ a_j \ll \exp( O( j^{1/2} / \log^{1/2} j ))$$
for all $j$, but we have not checked whether such a pasting is possible.

(The site has been updated to address this comment.)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Thanks! I see that Erdős and Sárközy were just looking at the finite case, which (although obviously closely related) feels like a different enough problem to me that I've separated it at [[1109]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1109).

Hopefully I've managed to capture all the relevant results and references between the two problems, please let me know if not.

(I believe there is a typo in your Konyagin lower bound, the exponent should be $15/11$.)

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
For a prime $p$, let $A_p$ be the set of residue classes $x \pmod{p^2}$ for which at least two distinct $a \in A$ exist with $a \equiv x \pmod{p^2}$. Then $|A_p| < \frac{p^2}{2}$ for all $p$ by the assumption that $A + A$ only contains squarefree integers. Taking the product $M = (p_1p_2 \cdots p_k)^2$ of distinct primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$ then gives that the number of residue classes $x \pmod{M}$ that occur more than once among the $a \in A$ is smaller than $\frac{M}{2^k}$. By the infinitude of primes we therefore obtain $A \cap \{1, 2, \ldots, x\} = o(x)$.

I understand that this is a terrible bound which is clearly improvable, but hey, you have to start somewhere!

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1104 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1104).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be the maximum possible chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices. Estimate $f(n)$.

### Context
The best bounds available are\[(1-o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2}\leq f(n) \leq (2+o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2}.\]The upper bound is due to Davies and Illingworth [DaIl22], the lower bound follows from a construction of Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender [HHKP25].

One can ask a similar question for the maximum possible chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on $m$ edges. Let this be $g(m)$. Davies and Illingworth [DaIl22] prove\[g(m) \leq (3^{5/3}+o(1))\left(\frac{m}{(\log m)^2}\right)^{1/3}.\]Kim [Ki95] gave a construction which implies $g(m) \gg (m/(\log m)^2)^{1/3}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Wouter CvB
sourceComments.contentMd:
Here's some further non-exhaustive context and speculation.

Before the work of Davies and Illingworth, in [this paper](https://doi.org/10.37236/8650) the same upper bounds were confirmed for the fractional chromatic number $\chi_f(G)$. And slightly worse bounds were given on the chromatic number $\chi(G)$, a factor $\sqrt{2}$ higher for the upper bound on $f(n)$, and a factor $2^{1/3}$ higher for the upper bound on $g(n)$.

Moreover, it was shown that $\chi_f(G) \leq (\sqrt{2}+o(1)) \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}$ and  $\chi_f(G) \leq (18^{1/3}+o(1)) \frac{m^{1/3}}{(\log m)^{2/3}}$ hold for all $\textit{regular}$ triangle-free graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. This (and other evidence) motivated a conjecture that the condition of regularity could be dropped, which was later confirmed in a very nice paper of [Martinsson and Steiner](https:// doi:10.1017/fms.2025.10112). Perhaps the same will be true for the chromatic number instead, thus improving the state of the art for Problem 1104.

The vague intuition is that the largest independent set $\alpha(G)$ seems to govern the right answer; we know that $\chi(G)\geq \frac{n}{\alpha(G)}$, but for this type of problem it appears that also something like $\max_{|G|=n}\chi(G) \lessapprox \frac{n}{\min_{|G|=n}\alpha(G)}$ holds. Plugging in Shearer's lower bound $(1/\sqrt{2}+o(1)) \sqrt{n \log n}$ on the independence number leads to the guess that $\chi(G) \leq (\sqrt{2}+o(1)) \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}$.

Following the conjectures made in the latest breakthroughs papers on $R(3,t)$, one might even guess tight bounds $\alpha(G) \geq (1+o(1)) \sqrt{n \log n}$ and $\chi(G)\leq (1+o(1)) \sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}$.

(And from there the heavy speculation continues; e.g. is the (list) chromatic number of a triangle-free graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ at most $(1/2+o(1)) \frac{\Delta}{\log \Delta} $ ? This would be tight. By the Johansson-Molloy theorem, it is currently known with $(1+o(1))$ instead, and this was used to prove some of the results mentioned above.)

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1106 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106).

### Problem
Let $p(n)$ denote the [partition function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_(number_theory)) of $n$ and let $F(n)$ count the number of distinct prime factors of\[\prod_{1\leq k\leq n}p(k).\]Does $F(n)\to \infty$ with $n$? Is $F(n)>n$ for all sufficiently large $n$?

### Context
Asked by Erdős at Oberwolfach in 1986. Schinzel noted in the Oberwolfach problem book that $F(n)\to \infty$ follows from the asymptotic formula for $p(n)$ and a result of Tijdeman [Ti73]. This is not obvious; details are given in a paper of Erdős and Ivić (see page 69 of [ErIv90]).

Schinzel and Wirsing [ScWi87] have proved $F(n) \gg \log n$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1107 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1107).

### Problem
Let $r\geq 2$. A number $n$ is $r$-powerful if for every prime $p$ which divides $n$ we have $p^r\mid n$. Is every large integer the sum of at most $r+1$ many $r$-powerful numbers?

### Context
Given in the 1986 Oberwolfach problem book as a problem of Erdős and Ivić.

This is true when $r=2$, as proved by Heath-Brown [He88] (see [[941]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/941)).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1108 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1108).

### Problem
Let\[A = \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}n! : S\subset \mathbb{N}\textrm{ finite}\right\}.\]If $k\geq 2$, then does $A$ contain only finitely many $k$th powers? Does it contain only finitely many powerful numbers?

### Context
Asked by Erdős at Oberwolfach in 1988. It is open even whether there are infinitely many squares of the form $1+n!$ (see [[398]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/398)).

This was motivated in part by a problem of Mahler which he discussed with Erdős a few days before his death in 1988: if $k\geq 5$ and\[A_k= \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}k^n : S\subset \mathbb{N}\textrm{ finite}\right\}\]then does $A_k$ contain only finitely many squares? Mahler showed that there are infinitely many squares in $A_k$ for $k\leq 4$, and found only one square for $k\geq 5$, namely\[1+7+7^2+7^3=400.\]Brindza and Erdős [BrEr91] proved that, for any $r$, if $n_1!+\cdots+n_r!$ is powerful then $n_1\ll_r 1$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
The OEIS sequences for the initial problem (some variants) are known:
A051761
A115645
A025494

The largest number here is $1183893^2$ equals the sum of $i!$ for $i \in \{1,2,3,7,8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15\}$.

Heuristically, one of course expects a finite number of elements of this form.

sourceComments.author: StijnC
sourceComments.contentMd:
Related to the problem discussed with Mahler:

$\textbf{remark on equivalent solutions}$
One should not be allowed to count equivalent ones.
E.g. every set $S$ of $4$ consecutive numbers, starting with an even number $2j$, results in a square (of $20 \cdot 7^j$).
For this reason, we may impose that we only count the sets $S$ containing $0.$

Also $1+k$ may be a square, so for additional special ones we of course need to impose $\max S>2.$
(the case $\max S=2$ does not lead to a solution)

$\textbf{Heuristical remark}$
A literature search didn't result in much.
As sketched in [[BLPPPV21]](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1225717/square-numbers-whose-only-digits-are-0-and-1), for every $k>4$, the number of squares of the desired form for the fixed $k$, can be estimated by $\frac{k}{k-4}$, and so one can expect there are finitely many for fixed $k$.
Furthermore, with the additional imposed values, also over all $k \ge 5$, the expected number of solutions is finite, since $\sum_k 1/k^2$ is finite.
I would estimate it slightly different myself, but all that is needed is some heuristics that prove finiteness.
The underlying idea of the birthday paradox also says that $k=4$ should be the threshold.

$\textbf{Small max S}$
For $\max S \le 4$, Wolfram Alpha should find all integral points.
Here $20^2=1+7+7^2+7^3$ and $611^2=1+72+72^3$ are the only examples with $k\ge 5.$

$\textbf{More examples}$
The solutions with $k\ge 5$ and values bounded by $10^{19}$ (the expected number of larger solutions is likely very small/ this list may even be complete) are

$$20^2=1+7+7^2+7^3$$
$$521^2=1+12^2+12^3+12^4+12^5$$
$$611^2=1+72+72^3$$
$$11677^2=\sum_{i \in S} 8^i \mbox{ for } S=[0,1,2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9]$$
$$972799^2= \sum_{i \in S} 5^i \mbox{ for } S=[0,2, 4, 5, 11, 12, 15, 16,17]$$
$$3051273374^2=\sum_{i \in S} 5^i \mbox{ for } S=[0,3, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27]$$
($400, 271441,373321,136352329,946337894401$ or related did not appear in OEIS)
(full list so far: $400, 271441,373321,136352329,946337894401,9310269202881343876$)

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1109 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1109).

### Problem
Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. Estimate $f(N)$. In particular, is it true that $f(N)\leq N^{o(1)}$, or even $f(N) \leq (\log N)^{O(1)}$?

### Context
First studied by Erdős and Sárközy [ErSa87], who proved\[\log N \ll f(N) \ll N^{3/4}\log N,\]and guessed the lower bound is nearer the truth. Sárközy [Sa92c] extended this to consider the case of $A+B$ and also looking for sumsets which are $k$-power-free.

Gyarmati [Gy01] gave an alternative proof of $f(N)\gg \log N$, and also gave new bounds for the case of $A+B$. Konyagin [Ko04] improved this to\[ \log\log N(\log N)^2\ll f(N) \ll N^{11/15+o(1)}.\]The infinite analogue of this problem is [[1103]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1103). (In particular upper bounds for this $f(N)$ directly imply lower bounds for the size of the $a_j$ considered there.)

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: AlexisOlson
sourceComments.contentMd:
I computed $f(N)$ for $1 \le N \le 250$.

Method: The vertices are odd squarefree integers $a \le N$ (even or non-squarefree $a$ fail since $2a$ is not squarefree), with an edge between distinct $a,b$ if $a+b$ is not squarefree. Then $f(N)$ is the maximum independent set size. I used branch-and-bound with bitsets, cross-checked against brute-force for small $N$.

$$\begin{aligned}
  1   &\le N \le 4      &:\qquad f(N) &= 1\\
  5   &\le N \le 18    &:\qquad f(N) &= 2\\
 19  &\le N \le 22    &:\qquad f(N) &= 3\\
 23  &\le N \le 36    &:\qquad f(N) &= 4\\
 37  &\le N \le 40    &:\qquad f(N) &= 5\\
 41  &\le N \le 58    &:\qquad f(N) &= 6\\
 59  &\le N \le 86    &:\qquad f(N) &= 7\\
 87  &\le N \le 100  &:\qquad f(N) &= 8\\
101 &\le N \le 104  &:\qquad f(N) &= 9\\
105 &\le N \le 112  &:\qquad f(N) &= 10\\
113 &\le N \le 130  &:\qquad f(N) &= 11\\
131 &\le N \le 150  &:\qquad f(N) &= 12\\
151 &\le N \le 158  &:\qquad f(N) &= 13\\
159 &\le N \le 166  &:\qquad f(N) &= 14\\
167 &\le N \le 194  &:\qquad f(N) &= 15\\
195 &\le N \le 202  &:\qquad f(N) &= 16\\
203 &\le N \le 238  &:\qquad f(N) &= 17\\
239 &\le N \le 250  &:\qquad f(N) &= 18
\end{aligned}$$

Example: $f(101) = 9$ is achieved by $\{5, 17, 29, 41, 53, 65, 77, 89, 101\}$, an arithmetic progression with common difference 12. All pairwise sums have the form $10 + 12k$, which is squarefree for $k \le 16$.

The sequence of transition points $(1, 5, 19, 23, 37, 41, 59, 87, 101, 105, 113, 131, 151, 159, 167, 195, 203, 239, \ldots)$ does not appear in OEIS.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1110 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1110).

### Problem
Let $p>q\geq 2$ be two coprime integers. We call $n$ representable if it is the sum of integers of the form $p^kq^l$, none of which divide each other.

If $\{p,q\}\neq \{2,3\}$ then what can be said about the density of non-representable numbers? Are there infinitely many coprime non-representable numbers?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96], who proved that there are finitely many non-representable numbers if and only if $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$.

Indeed, in [Er92b] Erdős wrote 'last year I made the following silly conjecture': every integer $n$ can be written as the sum of distinct integers of the form $2^k3^l$, none of which divide any other. He wrote 'I mistakenly thought that this was a nice and difficult conjecture but Jansen and several others found a simple proof by induction.'

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

researchNotes: A problem of Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96], who proved that there are finitely many non-representable numbers if and only if $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$.

Indeed, in [Er92b] Erdős wrote 'last year I made the following silly conjecture': every integer $n$ can be written as the sum of distinct integers of the form $2^k3^l$, none of which divide any other. He wrote 'I mistakenly thought that this was a nice and difficult conjecture but Jansen and several others found a simple proof by induction.'

This simple proof is as follows: one proves the stronger fact that such a representation always exists, and moreover if $n$ is even then all the summands can be taken to be even: if $n=2m$ we are done applying the inductive hypothesis to $m$. Otherwise if $n$ is odd then let $3^k$ be the largest power of $3$ which is $\leq n$ and apply the inductive hypothesis to $n-3^k$ (which is even).

Yu and Chen [YuCh22] prove that the set of representable numbers has density zero whenever $q>3$ or $q=3$ and $p>6$ or $q=2$ and $p>10$. They also prove that there are infinitely many coprime non-representable numbers if $q>3$ or $q=3$ and $p\neq 5$ or $q=2$ and $p\not\in \{3,5,9\}$.

Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96] also asked whether all large integers $n$ can be written as a sum of $2^k3^l$, none of which divide another, each of which is $>f(n)$ for some $f(n)\to \infty$. Let $f(n)$ be the fastest growing such $f(n)$. Yu and Chen [YuCh22] proved\frac{n}{(\log n)^{\log_23}}\ll f(n) \ll \frac{n}{\log n}.Yang and Zhao [YaZh25] improved the lower bound to $f(n)\gg n/\log n$.

The case of three powers is the subject of [[123]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/123), and see also [[845]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/845) for more on the case $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$. The problem [[246]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/246) addresses the topic without the non-divisibility condition.

sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let $f(n)$ be the largest integer such that every integer $N \ge n$ can be written as a sum of distinct $3$-smooth integers, all larger than $f(n)$, and such that no two distinct elements divide each other. Then the remarks mention somewhat recent bounds on $f(n)$ by Yu-Chen and Yang-Zhao. However, essentially optimal bounds were already obtained back in $1998$ by Blecksmith, McCallum and Selfridge.

R. Blecksmith, M. McCallum, J.L. Selfridge, *3-smooth representations of integers*. The American Mathematical Monthly, Volume 105, No. 6, 529–543, 1998.

You can find their paper [here](http://jstor.org/stable/2589404). In particular, their Theorem $2$ states that every integer larger than or equal to $$2 \sum_{2^a3^b \le m} 2^a 3^b$$can be written as a sum of distinct $3$-smooth integers, all larger than $m$, and such that no two distinct elements divide each other. On the other hand, every such way of writing the integer $$2 \sum_{2^a3^b \le m} 2^a 3^b - 1$$contains an element smaller than or equal to $m$.

If I'm not mistaken, this gives $$f(n) = \left(\frac{\log 2 \log 3}{2} + o(1) \right) \frac{n}{\log n}.$$

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1111 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1111).

### Problem
If $G$ is a finite graph and $A,B$ are disjoint sets of vertices then we call $A,B$ anticomplete if there are no edges between $A$ and $B$.

If $t,c\geq 1$ then there exists $d\geq 1$ such that if $\chi(G)\geq d$ and $\omega(G)<t$ then there are anticomplete sets $A,B$ with $\chi(A)\geq \chi(B)\geq c$.

### Context
A problem of El Zahar and Erdős [ElEr85], who show that it suffices to consider the case $t\leq c$. Let $d(t,c)$ be the minimal such $d$.

El Zahar and Erdős note that a result of Wagon [Wa80b] implies $d(t,2)\leq \binom{t}{2}+1$ (and in fact $d(t+1,2)\leq d(t,2)+t$). We also have $t(2,2)=2$ and $t(3,2)=4$ and $t(4,2)=5$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Alfaiz
sourceComments.contentMd:
From ["Bounding the Chromatic Number of Dense Digraphs by Arc Neighborhoods(2024)"](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00493-024-00098-z) by F. Klingelhoefer and A. Newman, the problem is equivalent to asking:

For all $c ≥ 0$, there exists $d ≥ 0$ such that if $T$ is a tournament with $\vec{χ}(T) ≥ d$, there are two sets $A, B ⊆ V (T)$ such that $\vec{χ}(T[A]), \vec{χ}(T[B]) ≥ c$ and all arcs between $A$ and $B$ go from vertices of $A$ to vertices of $B$.

The above is essentially a conjecture from ["Some results and problems on tournament structure(2023)"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02364) by T. Nguyen, A. Scott and P. Seymour.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1112 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1112).

### Problem
Let $1\leq d_1<d_2$ and $k\geq 3$. Does there exist an integer $r$ such that if $B=\{b_1<\cdots\}$ is a lacunary sequence of positive integers with $b_{i+1}\geq rb_i$ then there exists a sequence of positive integers $A=\{a_1<\cdots\}$ such that\[d_1\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq d_2\]for all $i\geq 1$ and $(kA)\cap B=\emptyset$, where $kA$ is the $k$-fold sumset?

### Context
Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] noted that if $B=\{b_1<b_2<\cdots\}$ with $b_1\geq 5$ and $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i$ then there is a set $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ with $2\leq a_{k+1}-a_k\leq 3$ for all $k$ such that $(A+A)\cap B=\emptyset$. Bollobás, Hegyvári, and Jin [BHJ97] showed that such an $A$ must exist if $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i-O(1)$, and that this is best possible.

Erdős and Graham go on to say 'whether such behavior can hold for $A+A+A$ (or more summands) is not known'. The above question is my best interpretation of what they intended.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceMetadata.statusNote: This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
researchNotes: Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] noted that if $B=\{b_1<b_2<\cdots\}$ with $b_1\geq 5$ and $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i$ then there is a set $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ with $2\leq a_{k+1}-a_k\leq 3$ for all $k$ such that $(A+A)\cap B=\emptyset$. Bollobás, Hegyvári, and Jin [BHJ97] showed that such an $A$ must exist if $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i-O(1)$, and that this is best possible.
Erdős and Graham go on to say 'whether such behavior can hold for $A+A+A$ (or more summands) is not known'. The above question is my best interpretation of what they intended.

Bollobás, Hegyvári, and Jin [BHJ97] provide a negative answer in that, for any sequence of integers $1\leq r_1<r_2<\cdots$, there is a $B$ as above with $b_{i+1}\geq r_ib_i$ such that $(A+A+A)\cap B\neq\emptyset$ for any $A$ with $2\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq 3$.

They define, more generally, $r_k(d_1,d_2)$ as the smallest $r$ (if it exists) such that if $b_{i+1}\geq rb_i$ then there exists $A$ with $d_1\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq d_2$ such that $(kA)\cap B=\emptyset$, where $kA$ is the $k$-fold sumset.

It follows from the above results that $r_2(2,3)=2$ and that $r_3(2,3)$ does not exist. Chen [Ch00] proved that $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ for any integers $a<b$ with $b\neq 2a$, and that $r_2(a,2a)\geq 2$ for all integers $a$. The more general question of existence of $r_k(a,b)$ for $k\geq 3$ remains open.
Some further technical non-existence results are given by Tang and Yang [TaYa21].
[Note the stated problem is a generous interpretation of a very ambiguous remark in [ErGr80], so it might be more appropriate to call this a problem 'inspired by Erdős and Graham'.]

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd: In [Ch00], he proves those results with the constraint that $a_{i+1} -a_i=\{d_1,d_2\}$ instead of $d_1<a_{i+1}-a_i<d_2$. Therefore under the notation defined on this page, $r_2(a,b)>2$ if $b>2a$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: I don't follow this - Theorem 1 of [Ch00] implies in particular that if $b_{n+1}\geq 2b_n$ then there is a sequence $A$ in which $a_{n+1}-a_n\in \{a,b\}$ and $(A+A)\cap B=\emptyset$. We then certainly have $a\leq a_{n+1}-a_n\leq b$, and hence $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$, using the definitions above.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
Yes, my issue is actually the other way around.
"Chen [Ch00] proved that $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ for any integers $a<b$ with $b\neq 2a$, and that $r_2(a,2a)\geq 2$ for all integers $a$."
Due to how $r_k(a,b)$ is phrased here, for $a_1\leq a<b\leq b_1$, $r_k(a_1,b_1)\leq r_k(a,b)$. So as $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ for $b<2a$, we must have $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ for $b=2a$ when $a>1$.

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: Ah, I see. I still don't think that $r_2(a,b)>2$ if $b>2a$ is right though - I think the simplest fix is just to say that $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ for any $a<b$ (noting that this follows from e.g. $r_2(a,b)\leq r_2(a,a+1)$ and then using [Ch00] with $b=a+1$.

replies.author: Adenwalla
replies.contentMd:
My first comment was wrong. I agree $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ if $b>2a$.

Also, Theorem 2 of [CH00] shows that $r_2(1,2)$ does not exist.

sourceComments.author: Adenwalla
sourceComments.contentMd: The question asks about $r\in \mathbb{Z}$, so is $r_k(a,b)$ defined as the smallest integer $r$ that satisfies the condition, or the smallest real $r$?

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd: I guess it makes sense to have it be smallest real $r$ in the quantitative question of $r_k(a,b)$ (although, as already noted, this is going beyond what Erdős himself ever asked about, and this definition only appears in the later work [BHJ97]).

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1113 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1113).

### Problem
A positive odd integer $m$ such that none of $2^km+1$ are prime for $k\geq 0$ is called a [Sierpinski number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierpi%C5%84ski_number). We say that a set of primes $P$ is a covering set for $m$ if every $2^km+1$ is divisible by some $p\in P$.

Are there Sierpinski numbers with no finite covering set of primes?

### Context
Sierpinski [Si60] proved that there are infinitely many Sierpinski numbers, using covering systems to construct suitable covering sets for any $m$ satisfying a certain congruence. This establishes that there is a positive density set of such $m$.

The smallest Sierpinski number is believed to be $78557$, which was found by Selfridge.

### Deliverable

researchNotes: Sierpinski [Si60] proved that there are infinitely many Sierpinski numbers, using covering systems to construct suitable covering sets for any $m$ satisfying a certain congruence. This establishes that there is a positive density set of such $m$.
The smallest Sierpinski number is believed to be $78557$, which was found by Selfridge.

Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] asked whether there are Sierpinski numbers for which a covering system is not 'responsible', for which the best interpretation seems to be the above question. This is formulated precisely in problem F13 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. Erdős and Graham thought the answer is yes (in that there are such Sierpinski numbers), since otherwise this would imply there are infinitely many Fermat primes.

There is now further evidence with a concrete example: an argument of Izotov [Iz95], given in more detail by Filaseta, Finch, and Kozek [FFK08], suggests that $m=734110615000775^4$ is a Sierpinski number without a covering set. (Izotov proved that this $m$ is indeed a Sierpinski number.)

Filaseta, Finch, and Kozek [FFK08] give a revised conjecture, suggesting that every Sierpinski number is either a perfect power or else has a finite covering set of primes. They also prove that for every $l\geq 1$ there is an $m$ such that $2^km^i+1$ is composite for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $k\geq 0$.
See also [[203]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/203), and [[276]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/276) for another problem in which the question is whether covering systems are always responsible.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1117 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1117).

### Problem
Let $f(z)$ be an entire function which is not a monomial. Let $\nu(r)$ count the number of $z$ with $\lvert z\rvert=r$ such that $\lvert f(z)\rvert=\max_{\lvert z\rvert=r}\lvert f(z)\rvert$. (This is a finite quantity if $f$ is not a monomial.)

Is it possible for\[\limsup \nu(r)=\infty?\]Is it possible for\[\liminf \nu(r)=\infty?\]

### Context
This is Problem 2.16 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.

The answer to the first question is yes, as shown by Herzog and Piranian [HePi68]. The second question is still open, although an 'approximate' affirmative answer is given by Glücksam and Pardo-Simón [GlPa24].

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1120 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1120).

### Problem
Let $f\in \mathbb{C}[z]$ be a monic polynomial of degree $n$, all of whose roots satisfy $\lvert z\rvert\leq 1$. Let\[E= \{ z : \lvert f(z)\rvert \leq 1\}.\]What is the shortest length of a path in $E$ joining $z=0$ to $\lvert z\rvert =1$?

### Context
This is Problem 4.22 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős. In [Ha74] it is reported that Clunie and Netanyahu (personal communication) showed that a path always exists which joins $z=0$ to $\lvert z\rvert=1$ in $A$.

Erdős wrote 'presumably this tends to infinity with $n$, but not too fast'.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1122 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1122).

### Problem
Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{R}$ be an additive function (i.e. $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$ whenever $(a,b)=1$). Let\[A=\{ n \geq 1: f(n+1)< f(n)\}.\]If $\lvert A\cap [1,X]\rvert =o(X)$ then must $f(n)=c\log n$ for some $c\in \mathbb{R}$?

### Context
Erdős proved that $f(n)=c\log n$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ if $A$ is empty, or if $f(n+1)-f(n)=o(1)$.

Partial progress was made by Mangerel [Ma22], who proved that this is true if\[\lvert A\cap [1,X]\rvert \ll \frac{X}{(\log X)^{2+c}}\]for some $c>0$, and if $g(p)$ does not have very large values (in a certain technical sense).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1131 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1131).

### Problem
For $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[l_k(x)=\frac{\prod_{i\neq k}(x-x_i)}{\prod_{i\neq k}(x_k-x_i)},\]which are such that $l_k(x_k)=1$ and $l_k(x_i)=0$ for $i\neq k$.

What is the minimal value of\[I(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\int_{-1}^1 \sum_k \lvert l_k(x)\rvert^2\mathrm{d}x?\]In particular, is it true that\[\min I =2-(1+o(1))\frac{1}{n}?\]

### Context
Erdős first conjectured this minimum was achieved by taking the $x_i$ to be the roots of the integral of the Legendre polynomial, since Fejer [Fe32] had earlier shown these to be minimisers of\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\sum_k \lvert l_k(x)\rvert^2.\]This was disproved by Szabados [Sz66] for every $n>3$.

Erdős, Szabados, Varma, and Vértesi [ESVV94] proved that\[2-O\left(\frac{(\log n)^2}{n}\right)\leq \min I\leq 2-\frac{2}{2n-1}\]where the upper bound is witnessed by the roots of the integral of the Legendre polynomial as above.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Final version:I previously posted here an earlier version of my work on Erdős’s $L^2$ extremal problem for Lagrange interpolation (Erdős problem~1131) (See my first comment). I would like to inform readers that I have now uploaded a revised, substantially expanded, and structurally completed version of the paper.

The revised preprint studies the asymptotic behavior, as $n \to \infty$, of
[
I_n(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\int_{-1}^1 \sum_{k=1}^n |l_k(x)|^2 , dx,
]
where $l_k$ are the Lagrange basis polynomials associated with nodes
$x_1,\dots,x_n\in[-1,1]$.

The new version is available on Zenodo at: [10.5281/zenodo.18290797](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18290797)

\medskip
The main novelty of the revised version is that it completes the conceptual
foundation of the proof. Two new sections have been added which place
Erdős’s functional within the classical theory of minimal $L^2$-norm
interpolation. In particular, the functional $I_n$ is interpreted as the squared
Hilbert--Schmidt norm of the Lagrange interpolation operator, and classical
rigidity and uniqueness results of Kilgore and de~Boor--Pinkus are invoked to
justify the variational framework (Thanks to @ Prof N Somani and @ Prof Thoams Bloom for reference attention). This resolves a structural gap present in the
earlier version and makes the argument self-contained.

The revised paper proves unconditionally that any asymptotically minimizing
sequence of nodes must equidistribute with respect to the arcsine measure on
$[-1,1]$, fixing the macroscopic structure of minimizers. It also improves the
previously known lower bound of order
$O!\bigl((\log n)^2/n\bigr)$ due to Erdős--Szabados--Varma--V'ertesi to the
optimal order $O(1/n)$.

Assuming an endpoint universality conjecture for discrete Christoffel functions,
the revised version derives the first-order asymptotic expansion
[
\inf I_n = 2 - \frac{c}{n} + o!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),
]
with an explicit constant $c>0$ expressed in terms of the Airy kernel, and proves
asymptotic optimality and rigidity of the Legendre--integral nodes.

The paper also contains extensive numerical experiments supporting the predicted
$1/n$ correction, endpoint Airy scaling, and an entropy rigidity hypothesis. The
numerics strongly suggest that the constant equals $c=2$.

For internal consistency and clarity checks, the revised manuscript was also
reviewed using ChatGPT as a technical writing assistant; all mathematical
arguments, proofs, and conclusions are entirely my own.

At this stage, I do not plan to submit the paper to a journal. I would very much
welcome feedback from experts in approximation theory, orthogonal polynomials,
and interpolation, particularly regarding the endpoint universality conjecture,
which remains the only open step toward a fully rigorous asymptotic resolution
of Erdős’s problem.

sourceComments.contentMd:
Edit. I previously posted here an earlier version of my work on Erdős’s $L^2$ extremal problem for Lagrange interpolation (Erdős problem 1131). I would like to inform readers that I have now uploaded a revised and substantially expanded version of the paper.

The revised preprint studies the asymptotic behavior, as $n \to \infty$, of\[
I_n(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\int_{-1}^1 \sum_{k=1}^n |l_k(x)|^2 \, dx,
\]where $l_k$ are the Lagrange basis polynomials.

The current revised version has now appeared on preprints.org and is available at:
[https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202601.0875](https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202601.0875)

Main updates and contributions.

(1) Equidistribution. It is proved that any asymptotically minimizing sequence of nodes must equidistribute with respect to the arcsine measure on $[-1,1]$, fixing the macroscopic structure of minimizers.

(2) Sharp lower bound. The previously known lower bound of order $O((\log n)^2/n)$ is improved to the optimal order $O(1/n)$.

(3) Conditional asymptotic expansion. Assuming an endpoint universality conjecture for discrete Christoffel functions, the revised version derives\[
\inf I_n = 2 - \frac{c}{n} + o\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),
\]with an explicit constant $c>0$, and establishes asymptotic optimality of the Legendre--integral nodes.

(4) Numerical verification. The new version contains extensive numerical experiments supporting the endpoint Airy scaling and indicating that the constant is $c=2$, together with an entropy rigidity hypothesis supported by numerical verification.

Update. The revised version of the preprint has now been assigned a new ResearchGate DOI:

DOI: [10.13140/RG.2.2.11709.93925](https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.11709.93925)

The same version is also archived on Zenodo:

DOI: [10.5281/zenodo.18210226](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18210226)

I would welcome feedback on the revised version, especially concerning the endpoint universality conjecture (Conjecture~5.1), which remains the main open step toward a fully rigorous solution of Erdős’s problem.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1132 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1132).

### Problem
For $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[l_k(x)=\frac{\prod_{i\neq k}(x-x_i)}{\prod_{i\neq k}(x_k-x_i)},\]which are such that $l_k(x_k)=1$ and $l_k(x_i)=0$ for $i\neq k$.

Let $x_1,x_2,\ldots\in [-1,1]$ be an infinite sequence, and let\[L_n(x) = \sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\lvert l_k(x)\rvert,\]where each $l_k(x)$ is defined above with respect to $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

Must there exist $x\in (-1,1)$ such that\[L_n(x) >\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1)\]for infinitely many $n$?

Is it true that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\geq \frac{2}{\pi}\]for almost all $x\in (-1,1)$?

### Context
A result of Bernstein [Be31] implies that the set of $x\in(-1,1)$ for which\[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\geq \frac{2}{\pi}\]is everywhere dense.

Erdős [Er61c] proved that, for any fixed $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$,\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\lvert l_k(x)\rvert>\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1).\]See also [[1129]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1129) for more on $L_n(x)$, and also [[1153]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1153).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.contentMd: In [this new paper of mine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.21453) I obtain a weak version of the first result: given any function $\omega(n)$ that goes to infinity as $n \to \infty$, there exists a dense set of $x \in (-1,1)$ such that $L_n(x) \geq \frac{2}{\pi} \log n - \omega(n)$ for infinitely many $n$.

sourceComments.author: JakeMallen
sourceComments.contentMd: Erdős and Vértesi in [On the almost everywhere divergence of Lagrange interpolatory polynomials for arbitrary system of nodes (1980)](https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-03.pdf) in Theorem 3.1 prove that for any node system $X$ there exists continuous $F$ such that $|L_n(F,X,x)|\to\infty$ for almost all $x\in[-1,1]$. Since $|L_n(F,X,x)| \le \|F\|_\infty L_n(x)$, this implies $\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} L_n(x)=\infty$ for almost all $x\in[-1,1]$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1133 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1133).

### Problem
Let $C>0$. There exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently large the following holds.

For any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ there exist $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in [-1,1]$ such that, if $P$ is a polynomial of degree $m<(1+\epsilon)n$ with $P(x_i)=y_i$ for at least $(1-\epsilon)n$ many $1\leq i\leq n$, then\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert >C.\]

### Context
Erdős proved that, for any $C>0$, there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently large and $m=\lfloor (1+\epsilon)n\rfloor$ then for any $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in [-1,1]$ there is a polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ such that $\lvert P(x_i)\rvert\leq 1$ for $1\leq i\leq m$ and\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert>C.\]The conjectured statement would also imply this, but Erdős in [Er67] says he could not even prove it for $m=n$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1135 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1135).

### Problem
Define $f:\mathbb{N}\to \mathbb{N}$ by $f(n)=n/2$ if $n$ is even and $f(n)=\frac{3n+1}{2}$ if $n$ is odd.

Given any integer $m\geq 1$ does there exist $k\geq 1$ such that $f^{(k)}(m)=1$?

### Context
The infamous [Collatz conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collatz_conjecture). For a detailed discussion of the history and theory surrounding this problem we refer to the overview by Lagarias [La10].

This is not a problem due to Erdős; it was first devised by Collatz before 1952. Erdős referred to this problem on several occasions as 'hopeless'. As Lagarias [La16] notes, the closest Erdős ever came to working on problems of this nature is the theorem described in the remarks to [[1134]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1134).

sourceComments.contentMd:
A historical comment.

Both Erdos and Lothar Collatz were participants in the ICM 1950 in Harvard. Erdos was invited speaker, Collatz normal participant without official talk (but in the breaks he spread "his" 3n+1 problem like a salesman).

There is a big photo online showing the whole conference group:
https://legacy-www.math.harvard.edu/history/icm1950/photos/conference2-l.jpg

On the left boarder Lothar Collatz directly right of his former boss Alwin Walther (from the wartime days at TH Darmstadt) can be seen. Here enlarged:

https://althofer.de/icm-1950-walther-collatz-2.jpg
Collatz is the egghead in the orange frame. Journalist
Annette Erbe had identified Collatz (in 2023) in that photo.

Who can identify Paul Erdos in the big (linked) photo?
Kind regards, Ingo.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
Heuristically this is not true by Cramer like conjecture.
Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$ be prime gaps and define $M(x):=\max_{n<x} d_n$ and $P(x):=\max_{n<x} d_{n-1}d_n$. In a Cramer-Poisson heuristic one treats the normalized gaps\[
X_n:=\frac{d_n}{\log p_n}
\]as approximately i.i.d. exponential random variables with mean $1$ (locally, on the scale of $\log p_n$), and also approximately independent for neighboring indices.

For $N$ i.i.d. $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ variables, the maximum satisfies $X_{(1)}=\max_{1\le n\le N}X_n=(1+o(1))\log N$ with high probability. Translating back, this predicts\[
M(x)\approx (\log p_x)\,\log x,
\]up to lower-order factors, consistent with the usual extreme-value behavior in the model.

Consider adjacent pairs $(X_n,X_{n-1})$ and set a threshold $t=a\log N$. Under independence,\[
\mathbb{E}\#\{1\le n\le N:\; X_{n-1}\ge t,\ X_n\ge t\}
\approx N\,\mathbb{P}(X\ge t)^2
= N e^{-2t}
= N^{\,1-2a}.
\]Hence for any $a<\tfrac12$ there are typically many indices with $X_{n-1},X_n\ge a\log N$, while for $a>\tfrac12$ there are typically none; this places the largest adjacent pair around $t\approx \tfrac12\log N$ in each coordinate. Consequently,\[
\max_{n\le N} X_{n-1}X_n \approx \left(\tfrac12 \log N\right)^2
\quad\text{while}\quad
\left(\max_{n\le N}X_n\right)^2 \approx (\log N)^2,
\]so the ratio $P(x)/M(x)^2$ is heuristically bounded away from $0$ (on the order of a positive constant, plausibly about $1/4$ in this simplified model), rather than tending to $0$.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1138 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1138).

### Problem
Let $x/2<y<x$ and $C>1$. If $d=\max_{p_n<x} (p_{n+1}-p_n)$, where $p_n$ denotes the $n$th prime, then is it true that\[\pi(y+Cd)-\pi(y)\sim\frac{Cd}{\log y}?\]

### Context
In other words, prove the expected asymptotic formula for the number of primes in the interval $[y,y+Cd]$. This is a curious combination of two well-studied problems: find the minimum $h=h(y)$ for which one obtains the expected asymptotic\[\pi(y+h)-\pi(y)\sim \frac{h}{\log y},\]and understand the asymptotic behaviour of $d=\max_{p_n<x}(p_{n+1}-p_n)$.

The conjectured size of $d$ is $\approx (\log x)^2$ which is far below the $h$ we can obtain such an asymptotic for, even assuming the Riemann hypothesis (which delivers an asymptotic for $h=y^{1/2+o(1)}$).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

replies.author: Przemek Chojecki
replies.contentMd:
Indeed, seems like the core is the same or very similar. This is what I got while poking GPT-5.2 for the connection and a missing argument one might need for both: A convenient finite/combinatorial reformulation of our goal is the following 2-fold covering problem: for large $n$, can one choose residue classes $a_p \pmod p$ (for primes $p$ in some set, possibly all $p\le n$) so that every $j\in[1,n]$ satisfies at least two congruences $j\equiv a_p\pmod p$? If we can do this using distinct primes, then choosing $N$ by CRT so that $N\equiv -a_p\pmod p$ for all used $p$ forces each $N+j$ to be divisible by at least two distinct primes $\le n$. Since the CRT modulus is huge (typically $N\gg n^2$ when many primes $\le n$ are used), $N+j$ cannot equal a product of only those two primes, hence $\Omega(N+j)\ge 3$ for all $1\le j\le n$. Thus a 2-fold congruence cover of $[1,n]$ yields an interval $[N+1,N+n]$ with no integers of $\Omega\le 2$, giving gaps in the sequence $u_k$ of primes/semiprimes; moreover, tracking $\log N\asymp\sum_{p\in S}\log p$ is what determines the gap factor $n/\log N$ and hence $\limsup (u_{k+1}-u_k)/\log k$.

We take $z\to\infty$ slowly, set $y:=n/z$, and run an Erdős--Rankin style multi-stage cover. Stage~0 sets $a_p=0$ for all primes $p\le y$, giving one ''touch'' for each small prime divisor. Up to negligible sets, the indices with $\le 1$ touch are (i) primes $j\in(y,n]$, of size $\sim n/\log n$, and (ii) semiprimes $j=p_1p_2$ with $p_1<z$ and $p_2>y$, of size $\sim (n/\log n)\log\log z$; semiprimes with $p_1>z^{1/A}$ contribute $\sim (n/\log n)\log A$. The numerology is that if we now use primes $p\asymp y$, then one residue class mod $p$ hits $\asymp n/p\asymp z$ indices, and among those the usable targets occur with density $\asymp 1/\log(n/p)\asymp 1/\log z$, giving $\asymp z/\log z$ useful hits per prime. This suggests that with $R\asymp \frac{y\log z}{\log n}(1+\log A)$ primes $p\asymp y$ one can add enough touches to kill most primes and most semiprimes with $p_1>z^{1/A}$, and with another comparable batch reduce the remaining ''small-$p_1$'' semiprimes by an extra factor $\approx A$.

The modulus bookkeeping is the key link to the original $\limsup$ question. Using primes $p\asymp y$ keeps $\sum\log p$ under control: combining stages yields\[
\log N \asymp \sum_{p\in S}\log p \asymp y\,\log z\,(1+\log A),
\]so the resulting gap factor is\[
\frac{n}{\log N}\asymp \frac{z}{\log z\,(1+\log A)}\to\infty
\quad\text{for choices like}\quad
A=\exp((\log\log\log z)^2).
\]Cleanup must avoid using $\asymp n/\log n$ ''reserve primes'' near $n$ (which would force $\log N\asymp n$ and destroy the gap factor); instead one cleans up with primes $\asymp y$, where each prime hits $\asymp z$ indices so $|S|$ stragglers can be handled using $\ll |S|/z$ primes at modulus cost $\ll y$.

The main bottleneck is to make the ''random sieve'' steps rigorous in this 2-fold setting. One needs a multi-covering/hypergraph-cover lemma (a 2-fold cover rather than the usual 1-fold cover for prime gaps) ensuring that for many primes $p\asymp y$ one can choose residue classes that hit about the expected number of targets (primes and the structured semiprime families attached to small $p_1$), with suitably small codegrees to drive survivor counts down by factors like $A$. This is where one expects to use distribution-in-progressions and ''linear equations in primes'' technology as in modern large prime gap work, but an explicit statement tailored to these mixed target sets appears to be the central technical gap.

ChatGPT and Tang [have shown](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-1141/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_1141.pdf) that the number of such $n$  in $[1,N]$ is at most $N^{1/2+o(1)}$.

sourceComments.author: KylePratt
sourceComments.contentMd:
I think one can say something nontrivial by using upper-bound sieves. Given a large $n$, the total number of $k$ under consideration is $\approx \frac{\phi(n)}{n}\sqrt{n}\gg \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\log \log n}$, where $\phi(n)$ denotes the Euler totient function. If the number of $k<\sqrt{n}$ with $\text{gcd}(k,n)=1$ such that $n-k^2$ is prime is less than this, then there must be some such $k$'s with $n-k^2$ not prime.

Using an upper-bound sieve, the number of $k<\sqrt{n}$ with $\text{gcd}(k,n)=1$ such that $n-k^2$ is prime is $\lessapprox \mathfrak{S}(n) \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\log n}$. Here $\mathfrak{S}(n)$ is some kind of "singular series." This upper bound is good enough as long as $\mathfrak{S}(n)$ is not too big, say $\mathfrak{S}(n) \lessapprox \frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$.

This singular series ought to be $\approx 1/L(1,\chi_n)$, where $\chi_n$ is some Dirichlet character depending on $n$ and $L(s,\chi_n)$ is the associated Dirichlet $L$-function. If one assumes the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), one can complete $\mathfrak{S}(n)$ to $\approx 1/L(1,\chi_n)$. GRH also gives $L(1,\chi_n)\gtrapprox (\log \log n)^{-1}$, which is good enough.

It seems difficult to argue unconditionally, because of Landau-Siegel zeros. However, one can use zero-density estimates to show that, for most $n$, the singular series can be completed to $1/L(1,\chi_n)$, and, furthermore, for most $n$, the $L$-value is not too small. I think one should be able to show that the set of exceptional $n$'s is very thin.

sourceComments.author: Quanyu Tang
sourceComments.contentMd:
Let $g(N)$ denote the number of integers $n\le N$ such that $n-k^{2}$ is prime for every integer $k$ with $(n,k)=1$ and $k^{2}<n$. In [[1142]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1142), I saw that Vaughan’s result [Va73] gives an upper bound estimate for the number $f(N)$ of integers $n\le N$ satisfying the condition in [[1142]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1142). Somewhat surprisingly, for the present problem [[1141]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1141), I could not find any prior work giving a corresponding upper bound for $g(N)$.

Therefore, in the spirit of Vaughan’s result [Va73] for [[1142]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1142), after several rounds of iteration with ChatGPT-5.2 Thinking, I obtained the following nontrivial bound:\[ g(N)\ll N^{1/2+o(1)}. \]The proof can be found in [this note](https://github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-1141/blob/main/On_Erd%C5%91s_Problem_1141.pdf).

As a sanity check, I asked [ChatGPT-5.2 Pro](https://chatgpt.com/share/697650aa-2cf4-800b-b114-7185b40ba2b1) to audit the argument, and it did not find any issues.

Reference.
[Va73] Vaughan, R. C., Some applications of {M}ontgomery's sieve. J. Number Theory (1973), 64--79.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1144 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1144).

### Problem
Let $f$ be a random completely multiplicative function, where for each prime $p$ we independently choose $f(p)\in \{-1,1\}$ uniformly at random. Is it true that\[\limsup_{N\to \infty}\frac{\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)}{\sqrt{N}}=\infty\]with probability $1$?

### Context
This model of a random multiplicative function is sometimes called a Rademacher function, although this is sometimes reserved for a merely multiplicative function (which is $0$ on non-squarefree integers). See [[520]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/520) for the partial sums of this alternative model.

It should also be compared to another popular model of random completely multiplicative functions, Steinhaus functions, which have $f(p)$ uniformly distributed over the unit circle.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1145 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1145).

### Problem
Let $A=\{1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ and $B=\{1\leq b_1<b_2<\cdots\}$ be sets of integers with $a_n/b_n\to 1$.

If $A+B$ contains all sufficiently large positive integers then is it true that $\limsup 1_A\ast 1_B(n)=\infty$?

### Context
A conjecture of Erdős and Sárközy. Some condition relating $A$ and $B$ is necessary since, for example, if $A$ is the set of all integers with only even binary digits and $B$ is the set of all integers with only odd binary digits than $1_A\ast 1_B(n)=1$ for all $n$.

This is a stronger form of [[28]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/28). See also [[331]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/331).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1150 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1150).

### Problem
Does there exist a constant $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$ and all polynomials $P$ of degree $n$ with coefficients $\pm 1$,\[\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert P(z)\rvert > (1+c)\sqrt{n}?\]

### Context
In other words, does there exist an 'ultraflat' polynomial with coefficients $\pm 1$. The answer is yes if the coefficients can take any values on the unit circle (see [[230]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/230)).

The lower bound\[\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert P(z)\rvert\geq \sqrt{n}\]is trivial from Parseval's theorem.

I performed a Gemini Deep Research query for related literature and it brought up this paper by el Abdalaoui [[El25]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.21499) which seems to answer this problem in the affirmative by proving that there does not exist an ultraflat polynomial with coefficients $\pm1$.

[[El25]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.21499) cites [[Od18]](https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~odlyzko/doc/ultraflat.pdf), where Odlyzko made progress on this problem via computational methods. Oddly enough, el Abdalaoui also cites problem 22 in [[Er57]](https://www.wfnmc.org/erdosunsolvedproblems.pdf) as the problem they are providing an answer to, but that problem reads like [[230]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/230). Maybe someone with more expertise can take a look at this literature and confirm or deny my understanding.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1151 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1151).

### Problem
Given $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[\mathcal{L}^nf(x) = \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}f(a_i)\ell_i(x)\]be the unique polynomial of degree $n-1$ which agrees with $f$ on $a_i$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ (that is, the Lagrange interpolation polynomial).

Let $a_i$ be the set of [Chebyshev nodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_nodes). Prove that, for any closed $A\subseteq [-1,1]$, there exists a continuous function $f$ such that $A$ is the set of limit points of $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)$.

### Context
This is as the problem is given in [Va99], but I am unclear exactly what is intended here - is this meant for fixed, arbitrary, $x\in [-1,1]$?

Erdős [Er41] proved that, if $x=\cos(\pi p/q)$ for some odd integers $p,q\geq 1$, then there is a continuous function $f$ such that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\mathcal{L}^nf(x)=\infty,\]where the limit is taken over the sequence of Chebyshev nodes as $n\to \infty$. In [Er43] he claims (without proof) that for any closed set $A$ there exists a continuous $f$ such that the limit points of $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)$ is $A$ (for specific $x$ of this shape).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1152 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1152).

### Problem
For $n\geq 1$ fix some sequence of $n$ distinct numbers $x_{1n},\ldots,x_{nn}\in [-1,1]$. Let $\epsilon=\epsilon(n)\to 0$.

Does there always exist a continuous function $f:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ such that if $p_n$ is a sequence of polynomials, with degrees $\deg p_n<(1+\epsilon(n))n$, such that $p_n(x_{kn})=f(x_{kn})$ for all $1\leq k\leq n$, then $p_n(x)\not\to f(x)$ for almost all $x\in [-1,1]$?

### Context
Erdős, Kroó, and Szabados [EKS89] proved that, if $\epsilon>0$ is fixed and does not $\to 0$, then there exist sequences $x_{ij}$ such that, for any continuous function $f$, there exists a sequence of polynomials $p_n$, with degrees $\deg p_n<(1+\epsilon)n$, such that $p_n(x_{kn})=f(x_{kn})$ for all $1\leq k\leq n$, and $p_n(x)\to f(x)$ uniformly for all $x\in [-1,1]$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1153 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1153).

### Problem
For $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ let\[l_k(x)=\frac{\prod_{i\neq k}(x-x_i)}{\prod_{i\neq k}(x_k-x_i)},\]which are such that $l_k(x_k)=1$ and $l_k(x_i)=0$ for $i\neq k$.

Let\[\lambda(x)=\sum_k \lvert l_k(x)\rvert.\]Is it true that, for any fixed $-1\leq a< b\leq 1$,\[\max_{x\in [a,b]}\lambda(x)> \left(\frac{2}{\pi}-o(1)\right)\log n?\]

### Context
Bernstein [Be31] proved this for $a=-1$ and $b=1$, and Erdős [Er61c] improved this to\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lambda(x)> \frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1).\]This is best possible, since taking the $x_i$ as the roots of the $n$th Chebyshev polynomial yields\[\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lambda(x)<\frac{2}{\pi}\log n+O(1).\]See also [[1129]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1129) and [[1132]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1132).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: TerenceTao
sourceComments.contentMd:
[ChatGPT Deepresearch](https://chatgpt.com/share/697fefd4-8d34-800e-8f04-9726cf2ceade) did not find any literature on the $[a,b]$ problem, although it had plenty of links for the $[-1,1]$ problem.

This problem looks amenable to a modern, potential-theoretic / mean field approximation approach.  Suppose we have an asymptotic counterexample in which the $x_i$ are distributed according to some probability measure $\mu = \rho(x)\ dx$ on $[-1,1]$ and that $\lambda(x) \leq (\frac{2}{\pi} - c) \log n$ on $[a,b]$, in particular $|l_k(x)| \leq \lambda(x) = o(n)$ for all $k$ and all $x$ in this interval.  This I think already forces $U(x) \geq U(x_k)+ o(1)$ (maybe in some weak sense) for all $x \in [a,b]$ and $y \in [-1,1]$, where $U(x) = \int \log \frac{1}{|x-y|}\ d\mu(y)$ is the log potential; in particular this should force $U$ to be constant and bounded away from zero on $[a,b]$.  This should in turn lead to some lower bounds on $\rho$ on this interval, perhaps in an averaged sense (if $\rho$ was too small here than $U$ should behave more like a convex function than a constant function on this interval). So the zeroes in at least some portion of $[a,b]$ should behave (weakly) like an arithmetic progression of spacing $\asymp 1/n$, and the polynomial should exhibit broadly sinusoidal behavior which should then recover the $\frac{2}{\pi} \log n$ type behavior after some perturbative analysis.  I won't have time to work on this, though, so am happy to have someone else have a go at this problem.  (Though I think this problem actually requires some human expertise in potential theory, and in the absence of such expertise, I would not recommend a purely AI-based approach for this one, as it will be much harder to detect subtle errors (one could of course try autoformalization to help verify AI output, but I think potential theory is still a bit challenging for the autoformalizers currently).)

replies.author: TerenceTao
replies.contentMd:
I revisited this problem and was able to [push it all the way to a full solution](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-1153.pdf).  On looking at the older arguments of Bernstein and Erdos, a key step was (unsurprisingly) the Bernstein inequalities for polynomials (or trigonometric polynomials) with the sharp constant.  I found a nice treatment of these inequalities [by Queffelec and Zarouf](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10801) using complex-analytic methods (Rouche's theorem and Gauss-Lucas) which was adaptable for this problem once one could find some reasonably large interval where the zeroes behaved like they were equally spaced at mesoscopic scales.  This in turn could be deduced from potential theory arguments (here I used an adaptation of Nat+GPT's estimates as a starting point).

I already passed the preprint once through GPT Pro to pick up some minor issues, but there may well be further small corrections to be made.

replies.author: Aron Bhalla
replies.contentMd:
Congratulations. I am still discussing the full solution with GPT-5.2 Thinking, but for now, it identifies the following minor errors:

* Introduction: Current: adopts the normalisation $Q(0)=0$. Suggested: change to the normalisation $Q(0)=1$” (consistent with (2.29) and the intended cosine comparison).

* p.6 (Section 2.6): “in an subinterval J” → “in a subinterval J”.

* p.6 (Section 2.6): the kernel denominator uses $(x^0 - y)^2 + \eta^2$; this looks like a notation slip and should presumably be $((x - y)^2 + \eta^2)$ (since the integration limits and surrounding discussion are in terms of $x$, not $x^0$).

* p.6 (end of Section 2.5 / start of Section 2.6): sign in explanatory sentence
    Current: “$U_\mu(x+i \eta)$ is harmonic ... as is $\alpha+\eta G(x^0)) …$”
    Suggested: “$U_\mu(x+i \eta)$ is harmonic ... as is $\alpha-\eta G(x^0)) …$”

* p.6 (Section 2.6, line immediately before (2.22)): missing factor $1/\pi$ in an intermediate line
    Current (intermediate line): “$\mu(J)=\int_J G(x),dx+\dots$”
    Suggested: “$\mu(J)=\frac1\pi\int_J G(x),dx+\dots$” (the displayed (2.22) is already correct).

* p.10 (Lemma 2.2 proof): Current: the proof writes, for “$z=y_1+O(1)$”, $\log\frac{|Q(z)|}{|Q(y_1)|}=\sum_k \log\left|\frac{z-y_k}{y_1-y_k}\right| \le \sum_k \log\big(1+\frac{O(1)}{(y_1-y_k)^2}\big)+O(1)$, and then concludes $Q(z)=O(1)$ on a neighbourhood of $y_1$ and applies Cauchy to bound $Q'(y_1)$.
Suggested: as written, the $(y_1-y_k)^2$ bound seems to rely on taking $z-y_1$ purely imaginary; it is not immediate uniformly for a full complex neighbourhood (e.g. points on the Cauchy circle with real shift give only $O(1)/|y_1-y_k|$). Easiest fix is to replace the proof using (2.34)+Rolle: any interval of length $2\log^4 n$ in the window contains at least two real zeros of $Q$, hence some $y$ in the interval has $Q'(y)=0$. This proves Lemma 2.2 (indeed with $C_0=0$).

* p.11 (just before Lemma 2.4): “Now we can count zeroes of $f$ …” → should be “zeroes of $f_\omega$ …” (since $f$ hasn’t been introduced there).

* p.13 (Lemma 2.4(a) proof): the displayed line begins with $f_\omega(\cdots)=\dots$ but it should be $f'_\omega(\cdots)=\dots$ (missing prime).

* p.14 (Lemma 2.4(c), contour-estimate paragraph): “upper side” / “lower side” labels swapped
    Suggested: swap the wording so that (2.44) corresponds to $\Im z=-\log^4 n$ (lower side) and (2.45) to $\Im z=+\log^4 n$ (upper side).

Investigate open Erdos Problem #1154 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1154).

### Problem
Does there exist, for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$, a ring or field in $\mathbb{R}$ with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$?

### Context
Erdős and Volkmann [ErVo66] proved that, for any $\alpha\in[0,1]$, there exists a group of real numbers of Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$.

Falconer [Fa84] proved that any subring with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha \in(1/2,1)$ cannot be a Borel or Suslin set. Edgar and Miller [EdMi01] proved that any real closed analytic subfield of $\mathbb{R}$ has Hausdorff dimension either $0$ or $1$. Later the same authors [EdMi03] proved that any subring of $\mathbb{R}$ which is Borel or analytic either has Hausdorff dimension $0$ or is equal to $\mathbb{R}$.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceMetadata.statement: Does there exist, for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$, a ring or field in $\mathbb{R}$ with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$?
sourceMetadata.statementMd: Does there exist, for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$, a ring or field in $\mathbb{R}$ with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$?
sourceMetadata.statusNote: Open in general, but there exist models of set theory where the result is true.
researchNotes: Erdős and Volkmann [ErVo66] proved that, for any $\alpha\in[0,1]$, there exists a group of real numbers of Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$.

Falconer [Fa84] proved that any subring with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha \in(1/2,1)$ cannot be a Borel or Suslin set. Edgar and Miller [EdMi01] proved that any real closed analytic subfield of $\mathbb{R}$ has Hausdorff dimension either $0$ or $1$. Later the same authors [EdMi03] proved that any subring of $\mathbb{R}$ which is Borel or analytic either has Hausdorff dimension $0$ or is equal to $\mathbb{R}$.
Mauldin [Ma16b] proved that subfields of $\mathbb{R}$ exist with Hausdorff dimension any $\alpha \in [0,1]$ assuming the continuum hypothesis.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1155 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1155).

### Problem
Construct a random graph on $n$ vertices in the following way: begin with the complete graph $K_n$. At each stage, choose uniformly a random triangle in the graph and delete all the edges of this triangle. Repeat until the graph is triangle-free.

Describe the typical parameters and structure of such a graph. In particular, if $f(n)$ is the number of edges remaining, then is it true that\[\mathbb{E}f(n)\asymp n^{3/2}\]and that $f(n) \ll n^{3/2}$ almost surely?

### Context
A problem of Bollobás and Erdős, described in [Va99] as 'motivated by the task of generating a random triangle-free graph'. In [Bo98] it says they asked this at the 'Quo Vadis, Graph Theory?' conference in Fairbanks, Alaska, in 1990, 'while admiring the playful bears'.

Grable [Gr97] proved that, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[\mathbb{P}(f(n)>n^{7/4+\epsilon})\to 0.\]Bohman, Frieze, and Lubetzky [BFL15] proved that $f(n)=n^{3/2+o(1)}$ almost surely - in other words, for every $\epsilon>0$,\[\mathbb{P}(n^{3/2-\epsilon}<f(n)<n^{3/2+\epsilon})\to 1.\]

### Deliverable

sourceComments.contentMd:
Bohman, Frieze, and Lubetzky prove in [Random Triangle Removal (2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.4223) that with high probability the final number of edges in random triangle removal is equal to $n^{3/2+o(1)}$, confirming an exponent of $3/2$ conjectured by Bollobás and Erdős.

According to [To Prove and Conjecture: Paul Erdős and His Mathematics (1998)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2589077?origin=crossref&seq=1) pages 231-232, Bollobás and Erdős came up with the problem "at the 'Quo Vadis, Graph Theory?' conference in Fairbanks, Alaska, in 1990, while admiring the playful bears...." I've uploaded a copy of this article [here](https://jayyhk.github.io/papers/bollobas1998.pdf) for those without institutional access.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1156 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1156).

### Problem
Let $G$ be a random graph on $n$ vertices, in which every edge is included independently with probability $1/2$.

Is there some constant $C$ such that that chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is, almost surely, concentrated on at most $C$ values?

Is it true that, if $\omega(n)\to \infty$ sufficiently slowly, then for every function $f(n)$\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))<1/2\]if $n$ is sufficiently large?

### Context
Bollobás [Bo88] proved that $\chi(G) \sim \frac{n}{2\log_2n}$ with high probability.

Shamir and Spencer [ShSp87] proved that, for any function $\omega(n)$ such that $\omega(n)/\sqrt{n}\to \infty$, there is a function $f(n)$ such that\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))\to 1\]as $n\to \infty$. This is proved with $\omega(n)\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}}\to \infty$ in Exercise 3 of Section 7.9 of Alon and Spencer [AlSp16] (a proof is also given by Scott [Sc17]).

### Deliverable
