sourceComments.author: Woett
sourceComments.contentMd:
Since the results by Heckel and Riordan seem so close to resolving this problem, I sent Annika Heckel an e-mail to ask about the limits of their methods, and she kindly responded to me. Some interesting things I learned (where whp stands for 'with high probability', i.e. with probability tending to $1$):

1) In [[HeRe23]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14014) they prove that there are infinitely many $n$ for which the smallest interval on which $\chi(G)$ is concentrated whp has length at least $\frac{c\sqrt{n} \log \log n}{\log^3 n}$, for some absolute constant $c$. They conjecture that this is the correct order of growth, up to the value of $c$.

2) It is furthermore conjectured that there are infinitely many $n$ for which $\chi(G)$ is whp concentrated on an interval of length $\frac{C n^{1/4}}{\log^{7/4} n}$, for some absolute constant $C$ .

3) Combining the first two points, the length of the concentration interval is thought to fluctuate between $n^{1/4 + o(1)}$ and $n^{1/2 + o(1)}$. See Figure $2$ and Conjectures $10, 11, 12$ in [[HeRe23]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14014) for more details.

4) The following crazy scenario has not been excluded: for almost all $n$, $\chi(G)$ is one-point concentrated whp. In particular, the second question remains open. Note that this does not contradict the first point above, as only the existence of *infinitely many* $n$ for which the concentration interval is large can be guaranteed.

5) The following equally crazy scenario has also not been excluded: for all $n$, $\chi(G)$ is two-point concentrated whp. In particular, the first question also remains open. Note that this also does not contradict the first point above, as it is theoretically possible that, even for those $n$ for which the concentration interval is large, $\chi(G)$ is concentrated on two points that are far apart. Often the question is stated with $C$ *consecutive* values, in which case we do know the answer by [[He21]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.11808).

6) Heckel has given various nice lectures on this topic which are available online. See [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YDuQOSDRu5Y) for one example.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1157 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1157).

### Problem
Let $t,k,r\geq 2$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the family of all $r$-uniform hypergraphs with $k$ vertices and $s$ edges. Determine\[\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F}).\]

### Context
This is a very difficult and general question, and many partial results are known. The paper of Brown, Erdős, and Sós [BES73] contains many of them, in particular the general lower bound, for all $k>r$ and $s>1$,\[\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F})\gg_{k,s} n^{\frac{rs-k}{s-1}}.\]A general conjecture of Brown, Erdős, and Sós is that, for all $r>t\geq 2$ and $s\geq 3$,\[\mathrm{ex}_t(n,\mathcal{F})=o(n^t)\]whenever $k\geq (r-t)s+t+1$. The case $t=2$ is the subject of [[1178]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1178).

The case $s=r=3$ and $k=6$ is the subject of [[716]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/716). The case of $r=3$ and $k=s+2$ is the subject of [[1076]](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1076).

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

### Problem
Determine whether there exists a constant $C>1$ such that the following holds.

Let $P$ be a finite [projective plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_plane). Must there exist a set of points $S$ such that $1\leq \lvert S\cap \ell\rvert \leq C$ for all lines $\ell$?

### Context
A set which meets all lines at once is called a blocking set. In [Er81] Erdős asks the stronger question of whether this is true for all pairwise balanced block designs.

Erdős, Silverman, and Stein [ESS83] proved this is true with $\lvert S\cap\ell \rvert\ll \log n$ for all lines $\ell$ (where $n$ is the order of the projective plane).

sourceComments.author: BorisAlexeev
sourceComments.contentMd:
The [Wikipedia page on $p$-groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-group) says that "there is a folklore conjecture asserting that almost all finite groups are 2-groups: the fraction of isomorphism classes of 2-groups among isomorphism classes of groups of order at most n is thought to tend to 1 as n tends to infinity".

[Random numerology: There are $14$ groups of order $16$ and also $14$ groups of order in $(8,16)$.  Similarly, there are $51$ groups of order $32$ and also $51$ groups of order in $(16,32)$.]

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
Thanks! I've just found some more background and results on this problem, which you might be interested in - added to the remarks above.

The reference to Pantelidakis was found in [BNV07], but I haven't managed to find an online copy of the original DPhil thesis to double check this. Assuming this result is reported accurately, the conjecture for all odd $n$ is reduced to a finite check, which perhaps may be in range of some clever modern computations?

EDIT: For more numerology, a list of $g(n)$ for $n\leq 2000$ can be found on the last couple pages of [this report](https://www.math.auckland.ac.nz/~obrien/research/2000.pdf) by Besche, Eick, and O'Brien.

replies.author: BorisAlexeev
replies.contentMd:
Thanks.  My numerology was in the direction of "Question 22.18 of [BNV07]", except I wanted it true for all $m$.  So one version might be that $\sum_{2^{m-1}<n<2^m} g(n) \le g(2^m)$, which is true for small $m$ (and tight for $m=4$ and $m=5$).  (This would imply the original Erdős conjecture above.)

The table you mention is easy to look at as a human.  For a computer, the OEIS has a file for $n\le 2047$ linked [here](https://oeis.org/A000001/b000001.txt).  It's also available as FiniteGroupCount[n] in Mathematica.

sourceComments.contentMd:
I would probably interpret this as distribution over all subgroups of S_n. Perhaps it is asking something along the lines of "Let $Sub(S_n)$ be the set of all subgroups of $S_n$. Choose a subgroup uniformly at random from this finite set. Then treat $|H|$ as a random variable. What are its (statistical) properties as $n$ grows?

Based off of this interpretation there are some relatively natural questions like, what is the typical siez of $|H|$ relative to $n!$, what is the distribution of $log (|H|)$, how often is $|H|$ divisible by a fixed prime $p$, what is the typical p-adic valuation $v_p(|H|)$ or what is the typical number of distinct prime divisors of $|H|$.
Just a few questions that poppde into my head.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
Thank you for the clarification and for pointing out the original conditions in the Erdős–Hajnal list.

Even with the condition \(\gamma \ge 2\), however, a size obstruction can still occur:
if some \(\kappa_\alpha > \lambda\), then the conclusion \(\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)^r_{\alpha<\gamma}\) would require a subset of \(\lambda\) of size \(\kappa_\alpha > \lambda\), which is impossible, while the hypothesis might still hold non-vacuously.

Thus, to ensure the problem is nontrivial in ZFC, it seems necessary to also require \(\kappa_\alpha \le \lambda\) for all \(\alpha < \gamma\) (or at least for those \(\alpha\) that could correspond to the color of a large homogeneous set in the stepping-up coloring).

In any case, the literal unrestricted statement — without any bound on \(\kappa_\alpha\) relative to \(\lambda\) — remains false, as my minimal counterexample shows.  The intended formulation (with \(\gamma \ge 2\), \(r < \omega\), \(\kappa_\alpha > r\), and presumably \(\kappa_\alpha \le \lambda\)) is the interesting open problem.

I appreciate your maintaining this valuable list of problems and your careful attention to these details.

sourceComments.author: Zeraoulia Rafik
sourceComments.contentMd:
I uploaded a short note pointing out that the \emph{literal} fully-quantified statement of Erdős--Hajnal--Rado Problem 1167 (as written in the book/problem list) is falsified by a simple size obstruction.

If one allows some target $\kappa_\alpha>\lambda$, then the conclusion\[
\lambda\to(\kappa_\alpha)^r_{\alpha<\gamma}
\]is impossible, while the hypothesis can still hold. In fact, taking $\gamma=1$ and $\kappa_0=\lambda^+$, the premise\[
2^\lambda\to(\kappa_0+1)^{r+1}_{<1}
\]is automatic (a coloring into $<1$ colors is vacuous; equivalently it just requires $2^\lambda\ge \kappa_0+1$), but the conclusion would require a subset of $\lambda$ of size $\lambda^+$, contradiction.

This suggests the intended nontrivial formulation should explicitly assume $\kappa_\alpha\le\lambda$ for all $\alpha<\gamma$; under this restriction the general heterogeneous implication still seems open (beyond the classical uniform stepping-up/stepping-down consequences for $r\ge3$).

Any references, known partial results, or corrections to the intended statement of \#1167 would be very welcome.

[DOI: 10.13140/RG.2.2.22305.06242](https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.22305.06242)

replies.author: Thomas Bloom
replies.contentMd:
This is also Problem 2 in the [Erdős-Hajnal problem list](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-symbolic-logic/article/abs/erdoshajnal-problem-list/9FBE6099BE9441516445D0B95F4B1208), which gives the additional conditions that $\gamma \geq 2$ (it actually says $\gamma \leq 2$, but I assume this is an obvious typo). It also has the additional conditions $r<\omega$ and $\kappa_\alpha >r$. Some known special cases are listed there (I'll update this on the site soon).

The condition $\kappa_\alpha\leq \lambda$ does not appear there, however - presumably $\gamma\geq 2$ suffices to rule out the vacuous problem you noted.

Let $q(n,k)$ denote the least prime which does not divide $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)$. Is it true that there exists some $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$,\[q(n,\log n)<(1-c)(\log n)^2?\]

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that there is a connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $f(n)$ edges such that\[R(K_3,G)= 2n-1.\]Let $F(n)$ be maximal such that every connected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $\leq F(n)$ edges has\[R(K_3,G)= 2n-1.\]Estimate $f(n)$ and $F(n)$. ### Context
A problem of Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp.

It is trivial that $f(n)\geq F(n)$, and that $R(K_3,G)\geq 2n-1$ for any connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices. By a result of Chavátal $R(K_3,T)=2n-1$ whenever $T$ is a tree on $n$ vertices, whence $F(n)\geq n-1$.

Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Roussea, and Schelp [BEFRS80] proved\[\frac{17n+1}{15}\leq F(n)\leq \left(\frac{27}{4}+o(1)\right)n(\log n)^2,\]the lower bound for all $n\geq 4$. They also proved\[(\log n)^{1/2}n^{3/2} \ll f(n) \ll n^{5/3}(\log n)^{2/3}.\]The first few values of $F(n)$ and $f(n)$ (beginning with $n=2$) are $1,2,5,7,8$ and $1,2,5,8,12$ respectively, as reported in [BEFRS80].

Similar questions can be asked with $K_3$ replaced by $K_m$ (where the $2n-1$ is replaced with $(m-1)(n-1)+1$). For the corresponding generalisations of $f$ and $F$ Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Roussea, and Schelp [BEFRS80] proved\[n^{\frac{2}{m-1}}\ll F_m(n)-n\ll n^{\frac{4}{m+1}+o(1)}\]and\[n^{1+\frac{1}{m-1}}\ll f_m(n) \ll n^{1+\frac{2}{m}+o(1)}.\]

sourceComments.author: ebarschkis
sourceComments.contentMd:
Unless I’m missing something, Stephan Brandt’s bound $f(n;3)\le Cn$ in his paper ["Expanding graphs and Ramsey numbers"](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2827547_Expanding_graphs_and_Ramsey_numbers) already answers the $F(n)/n\to \infty$ question negatively.
I was unable to find a copy of his paper online, so I reconstructed it based off a few fragments I found in university archives in LaTeX.
In his paper he proves a linear bound of the form $[
f(n;3) \le C n
]$ (for example $f(n;3)/n<84$ for sufficiently large $n$).
I think this implies $f(n)/n$ is bounded, so the question $f(n)/n\to\infty$ has a negative answer.

Here is the reconstructed [Latex code](https://github.com/ebarschkis/ErdosProblem/blob/main/Problem1182/Brandt.tex) and compiled [PDF](https://github.com/ebarschkis/ErdosProblem/blob/main/Problem1182/Brandt.pdf) of the Brandt’s paper.

EDIT: Brandt used different notation where the universal Ramsey-goodness threshold f(n;3) is the same as the parameter F(n) in BEFRS80 if I am not mistaken.

replies.author: JakeMallen
replies.contentMd: The .dvi and .ps files of Brandt's paper can be found [here](http://ftp.math.fu-berlin.de/pub/math/publ/pre/1996/index.html) for reference.

replies.contentMd: Compiling the .ps file to PDF, resulted in a lot of OCR corruptions. So having a Latex rewrite is good if someone wants to try formalizing this in Lean.

problems.description:
Investigate open Erdos Problem #1183 from [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1183).

### Problem
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that in any $2$-colouring of the subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ there is always a monochromatic family of at least $f(n)$ sets which is closed under taking unions and intersections. Estimate $f(n)$.

Let $F(n)$ be defined similarly, except that we only require the family be closed under taking unions. Estimate $F(n)$. In particular, is it true that $F(n)\geq n^{\omega(n)}$ for some $\omega(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$, and $F(n)<(1+o(1))^n$?

### Context
A problem of Erdős and Ulam.

It is trivial that $f(n)\geq \frac{n+1}{2}$, since there is a sequence of $n+1$ many nested subsets. This seems to be all that they knew; Erdős [Er78] wrote 'we have no plausible conjecture for the true order of magnitude of $f(n)$'.

### Deliverable
Submit a rigorous proof, counterexample, or clearly delimited partial progress. If the problem remains open, a high-quality literature synthesis or a sharp gap analysis is still valuable.

sourceComments.author: Przemek Chojecki
sourceComments.contentMd:
With GPT-5.4 Pro I've managed to get some [partial results that you can view here](https://www.ulam.ai/research/erdos1183.pdf). There's not much literature around the problem.

We answer affirmatively the subexponential half of the problem.

The proofs are probabilistic, but the structural inputs are quite different. For $F(n)$ the key observation is that the free rank of a union-closed family is exactly the VC-dimension of a complementary set system. For $f(n)$ we use the fact that every family closed under union and intersection is a finite distributive lattice, hence isomorphic to an ideal lattice $J(P)$ by Birkhoff's representation theorem. A large antichain in $P$ yields a Boolean cube inside $J(P)$, and after ruling out large cubes by random colouring one is left with counting bounded-width posets.
